p.seg: One's moral conduct may be consistently virtuous,
but official advancement is not consistently opportune.
Whether one is virtuous or not
depends on one's ability;
whether one encounters opportunity or not
depends on the times.
Those with superior talent and pure conduct
cannot be guaranteed honor and nobility;
those with meager ability and corrupt conduct
cannot be guaranteed lowliness and poverty.
Some with high talent and pure conduct,
failing to encounter opportunity,
retreat to lower positions;
some with meager ability and corrupt conduct,
encountering opportunity,
rise above the masses.
Each era has its own way of selecting scholars,
and scholars each have their own means of advancement.
Advancement lies in encountering opportunity,
retreat in failing to encounter it.
Those in honored and prominent positions
are not necessarily virtuous—
they have encountered opportunity;
those in lowly and humble positions
are not necessarily foolish—
they have not encountered opportunity.
Thus, when encountering opportunity,
some with corrupt conduct
may be honored in Jié's court:
when not encountering opportunity,
some upholding pure integrity
may be humbled in Yáo's court.
The reasons for encountering or not encountering opportunity
are not uniform:
sometimes the virtuous assist the wicked;
sometimes great talent follows minor talent;
sometimes both have great talent, but their paths differ in purity and corruption;
sometimes those without virtue and morality gain favor through skills;
sometimes those without skills or ability gain favor through physical charm.
Wǔ Yuán and Bó Xǐ
both served Fū Chāi,
Bó Xǐ was honored and respected,
while Wǔ Yuán was executed.
This illustrates different conduct under the same ruler.
Sometimes the conduct is the same but the rulers differ,
and there is still encountering or not encountering opportunity,
as with Yī Yǐn and Jīzǐ.
Yī Yǐn and Jīzǐ were equally talented,
yet Yī Yǐn became prime minister,
while Jīzǐ became a slave;
Yī Yǐn encountered Chéng Tāng,
while Jīzǐ encountered Shāng Zhòu.
When the virtuous serve a virtuous ruler,
and the ruler desires orderly governance,
the ministers assist with their virtuous talents,
their choices and actions coinciding,
their encounter is naturally fitting;
when the virtuous serve a wicked ruler,
and the ruler does not desire orderly governance,
the ministers assist with loyal conduct,
their principles and intentions clashing,
not encountering opportunity is naturally fitting.
Sometimes even sagely ministers,
meeting rulers who desire orderly governance,
still end up not encountering opportunity,
as with Kǒngzǐ and Mèng Kē.
Kǒngzǐ was stranded without food in Chén and Cài,
Mèng Kē was trapped in Qí and Liáng,
not because the rulers of the time rejected goodness,
but because their talents were inferior and understanding shallow,
unable to employ great talent.
Those who can驾驭 Jì Lù horses
must be like Wáng Liáng;
those who can employ ministers like Yǔ, Jì, and Gāo Yáo
must be like Yáo and Shùn.
With the hands suited for a hundred lǐ,
yet trying to control a thousand-lǐ steed,
there will inevitably be the disaster of broken crossbars and snapped yokes;
with the talent to manage mediocre officials,
yet trying to employ the wisdom of great ministers,
there will inevitably be the calamity of closed minds and blocked intentions.
Thus, profound advice is discarded,
sages and worthies are rejected,
not because of hatred for sages and worthies,
nor distaste for profound words,
but because sages and worthies aim high,
and profound words are hard to implement.
When great talent meets minor talent,
the minor talent cannot accept it,
so not encountering opportunity is natural.
Sometimes ministers with great talent
meet rulers with great talent,
yet there is still encountering or not encountering opportunity,
as with Yú Shùn, Xǔ Yóu, Tài Gōng, and Bó Yí.
Yú Shùn
and Xǔ Yóu were both sages,
living in the time of Táng,
both appearing before Yáo,
Yú Shùn inherited the imperial lineage,
while Xǔ Yóu retreated to the mountains and forests.
Tài Gōng and Bó Yí were both worthies,
emerging in the state of Zhōu,
both appearing before King Wǔ;
Tài Gōng received a fief,
while Bó Yí starved to death.
Though sages and worthies share the same Way, with aligned wills and unified purposes,
Yú Shùn and Tài Gōng acted in harmony,
while Xǔ Yóu and Bó Yí conducted themselves contrarily,
because they were born in the wrong era,
emerging at the wrong time.
Though the Way is the same,
within sameness there is difference;
though wills are aligned,
within alignment there is divergence.
Why is this?
The Way has refinement and coarseness,
and wills have purity and turbidity.
Xǔ Yóu,
a helper for sovereigns,
was born in the time of emperors;
Bó Yí,
an assistant for emperors,
emerged in the era of kings.
Both acted through virtue and morality,
both manifested benevolence and righteousness,
but when the ruler practiced virtue and morality,
if it was not pure, they would not stay;
when the ruler pursued benevolence and righteousness,
if it was not elevated, they would not cease—
this is why they did not encounter opportunity.
Yáo was murky, Shùn was turbid;
King Wǔ executed the cruel,
Tài Gōng punished the violent—
both turbid and coarse,
their actions equally aligned,
this is why they encountered opportunity.
Thus, when Shùn ruled the world,
Gāo Yáo assisted in governance,
while Běirén Wú Zé deeply hid and did not appear;
when Yǔ ruled the world,
Bó Yì assisted in governance,
while Bó Chéng Zǐgāo resigned his post to farm.
It was not that Gāo Yáo's talent surpassed Wú Zé's,
nor that Bó Yì's ability exceeded Zǐgāo's,
but Gāo Yáo and Bó Yì were advanced and employed,
while Wú Zé and Zǐgāo retreated and hid,
because advancement and employment aligned with action,
while retreat and hiding contradicted conduct.
In retreat and hiding, circumstances differed;
though personally humbled,
they had no desire for advancement;
the ruler did not need their words,
dismissed them,
and they felt no regret—
this is mutual lack of admiration.
Shāng Yǎng thrice advised Duke Xiào of Qín,
the first two proposals were not heeded,
the last one was adopted—
the first two
were discussions on imperial rule,
the last one
was a proposal for hegemony.
Holding discussions on imperial rule,
and advising a ruler seeking hegemony,
even if refined, they were rejected;
switching to proposals for hegemony,
even if coarse, they were accepted.
Why?
The refined met what Duke Xiào could not attain,
the coarse met what Duke Xiào desired to implement.
Thus, persuasion does not depend on goodness,
but on the listener approving it;
talent does not depend on worthiness,
but on the employer deeming it worthy.
The horse keeper's advice, though unprincipled,
was liked by the rustic;
Zǐgòng's advice, though righteous,
was not heeded by the rustic.
The flute player produced beautiful music,
but because the King of Yuè did not like it,
he switched to rustic tunes,
and the King of Yuè was greatly pleased.
Thus, offering goodness to a ruler who does not desire goodness,
even if good, it is not loved;
offering non-goodness to a ruler who desires non-goodness,
even if not good, it is not hated.
This is using petty skills to match,
matching leads to encounter;
not matching leads to no encounter.
When a rat has stepped into the rice,
it is discarded and not eaten.
The flavor of the discarded rice
is the same as that of the uncontaminated rice,
but because the rat is considered defiling,
it is abandoned and not consumed.
The hindrances and harms to a gentleman,
like those sterile grains and uneaten rice, are of the same nature;
they all come from external sources,
hence they are called hindrances and harms.
Cultivating one's character and rectifying one's conduct
cannot necessarily bring fortune;
trembling with caution and vigilance
cannot necessarily avoid disaster.
The arrival of fortune and disaster
depends on luck or the lack thereof.
Therefore, it is said:
"Gaining not by one's own effort,
thus it is called fortune;
coming not by my own doing,
thus it is called disaster."
What does "not by my own doing" mean?
It means from where does it arise?
It arises from the local community and the imperial court.
In the local community, there are three hindrances;
in the imperial court, there are three harms.
Hindrances are born in the local community,
harms emerge in the imperial court.
Throughout history, many talented and virtuous individuals have encountered these.
What are the three hindrances and three harms?
In general, people's conduct
cannot always carefully choose friends.
Friends of like mind are deeply affectionate,
those of different minds become distant and cold.
Distance and coldness lead to resentment,
damaging one's conduct—
this is the first hindrance.
People's talents vary in level,
not all equal.
When advancing together at the same time,
the highly talented gain honor,
the lesser ones feel shame and resentment,
damaging one's conduct—
this is the second hindrance.
In social interactions,
people cannot always be harmonious.
Harmony leads to closeness,
anger leads to estrangement.
Estrangement breeds resentment,
damaging one's conduct—
this is the third hindrance.
Positions are few, people many;
officials compete for advancement,
those advancing contend for positions.
Seeing superiors, they slander each other,
exaggerating and fabricating faults.
If the superior is ignorant and unclear,
they readily accept such words—
this is the first harm.
Officials have different preferences,
pure and corrupt hold distinct conducts.
Pure officials enhance their spotless purity,
offering subtle advice;
corrupt officials harbor resentment,
slowly seeking out their faults,
using minor slanders
to impose punishments—
this is the second harm.
If a superior favors a subordinate,
trusting their words;
and the subordinate lacks integrity,
they will promote people out of turn.
Those who oppose or disappoint them
are excessively slandered;
upright and honest officials
uphold their principles and aspirations,
thus becoming disliked,
harmed by the superior—
this is the third harm.
Before entering office,
one suffers the three hindrances;
after being employed,
one faces the three harms.
Even Kǒng Qiū or Mò Dí could not avoid them,
nor could Yán Huí or Zēng Shēn preserve themselves unharmed.
In every action,
in every endeavor,
envious people
rise like clouds following.
Thorns hook onto one's body,
swarms of wasps and scorpions
sting with venomous bitterness—
how can it be limited to just these six?
These six are evident,
yet the world fails to see them.
Those who do not examine the scholar's conduct face three hindrances,
and in officialdom, three harms.
Those who remain unscathed are called pure,
those slandered are deemed disgraced;
those promoted are considered good,
those dismissed are seen as evil.
To remain unscathed and be promoted
is fortune,
and they are praised;
to be slandered and dismissed
is misfortune,
and they are vilified.
With such a mindset,
they surely do not understand the three hindrances and three harms.
Critics neither know where hindrances and harms come from, nor that those afflicted may be virtuous and pure.
Smearing mud on a clean path,
dotting ink on silk—
who can discern the original state?
Purity gathers dust,
whiteness attracts grime;
where blue flies defile,
it is often on white silk.
Those at heights are in danger,
full shapes tend to diminish;
things that fall
often hang precariously.
Qū Yuán was pure and white,
yet village dogs barked in packs—
they bark at the unusual.
Doubting the exceptional and suspecting the outstanding
is indeed the way of the mediocre.
Great men, seated with outstanding talent,
attract the chorus of barking.
Thus,
should one strive to be like the lowly and follow the unworthy?
The unworthy and lowly
are not to be emulated.
Should one then conform to the vulgar to preserve oneself and silence slander?
Conforming to the vulgar to preserve oneself
makes one a village hypocrite.
Village hypocrites,
seemingly flawless in conduct,
have no faults to accuse,
no errors to criticize.
Yet these are whom Kǒngzǐ condemned,
and Mèng Kē faulted.
Ancient sages, supremely virtuous,
had no means to protect themselves.
Thus, those who follow their nature and endure hindrances and harms
are truly the virtuous and pure!
When slandered to the extreme,
the reality of their virtue and purity becomes visible.
Establishing traces of virtue and purity,
how can the dust of slander not arise?
Lute players wish to break Bó Yá's fingers,
charioteers desire to crush Wáng Liáng's hands.
Why?
To monopolize the name of excellence,
resenting others for surpassing them.
Thus, the beautiful woman of Wèi
had her nose cut off by Zhèng Xiù;
Cháo Wú's loyalty
led to his exile by Wú Jì.
The ugly are full of envy,
the flatterers abound in cunning.
Hence, a damp hall needs no dusting,
a low house needs no windbreak;
what the wind strikes cannot thrive,
the bank where water rushes cannot be steep.
So it is
that the ordeals in Yǒulǐ, Chén, and Cài can be understood,
and drowning in rivers comprehended.
Using exceptional talent to seek favor with the vulgar,
striving for complete merit and fame from superiors,
if one avoids the fate of Dèng Xī,
or escapes the execution of Wǔ Zǐxū,
it is fortune indeed.
No one stabs Mèng Bēn's corpse—
because his spirit is gone.
because their light is extinguished.
Displaying one's body and wisdom,
shining light and energy in the world,
aspiring high above the crowd,
standing out uniquely in society,
inevitably draws slander and envy from the conventional.
Using an upright heart to face worldly hindrances,
seeking gain but suffering loss—
this is why Kǒngzǐ worried,
and Mèng Kē lamented.
Those of great virtue attract slander,
scholars often face gossip.
Using splendid sounds to cover the troubles of tongues,
seeking to avoid the harm of danger and collapse,
is far from achievable.
The slander of Zāng Cāng
has never ceased,
the calumny of Gōng Bó Liáo
has never vanished,
anthills become mountains,
stains turn into rivers.
Thus,
the rumor of a tiger in the market,
the mistake of dropping the shuttle,
are not surprising,
then jade turning to stone,
pearls transforming into gravel,
are not strange.
Why?
It is the dim and obscure understanding of the mind that causes this.
King Wén was regarded as dirt,
while È Lái was seen as gold and jade,
not because King Zhòu hated sages and loved the wicked,
but because his mind was deluded and obscured.
If obscurity and delusion cannot be discerned,
then even if Wēizǐ left ten times,
Bǐgàn was cut open five times,
it would not be enough to grieve over.
Thus, the three supervisors slandered the sage,
and the Duke of Zhōu fled to Chǔ.
A stepmother defamed a filial son,
and Bó Qí was exiled.
Who in that Zhōu era was not deluded?
Later, "The Owl" was composed, and "The Millet Sways" arose,
those who chanted them,
felt sorrow.
Thus, without the changes of thunder and wind,
the Duke of Zhōu's ill repute would not vanish;
if frost did not fall in summer,
Zōu Yǎn's crime would not be absolved.
Virtue cannot move heaven,
sincerity cannot alter changes,
a noble person firmly believes
in examining oneself,
how can one prevent harm and trouble from befalling others?
Sages do not cultivate fame,
when harm comes, they do not avoid it,
their flaws are exposed,
their strengths concealed,
they do not clear their own grievances,
nor quell rumors,
they endure disgrace and accept slander,
not seeking purity and perfection,
thus their faults are seen but their goodness not revealed,
their conduct flawed and their deeds not prominent.
Deceitful and false people,
cultivate themselves to suit vulgar customs,
practice deceit to align with the masses,
like artisans painting lacquer on plates and bowls,
holes in the wall go unseen;
like performers juggling balls and swords,
their fingers go unnoticed.
The world does not see their flaws,
thus all praise them;
leaders do not hear of their faults,
thus promote and employ them.
In this way,
those whom the world calls virtuous and pure,
may not be without wickedness;
those called evil and corrupt,
may not be without goodness.
Some say:
"Words can invite trouble,
actions can summon shame,
this often comes from petty people."
Petty people are those who fear trouble and shame,
born with deceit,
roaming with falsity,
immersed in harm and trouble,
how can they invite or summon anything?
Thus, those born of fire are not harmed by dampness,
those dwelling in water do not drown,
fire does not suffer from heat,
water does not pain from cold,
such is their natural disposition.
To invite and summon,
is the act of a noble person,
using loyal words to invite trouble,
with noble conduct to summon shame,
in what era is it not so?
Yet, the faults of Tàishān,
a noble person cannot claim;
the goodness of a hair,
a petty person cannot possess.
In terms of defilement,
the clean gather dust and the white take on grime;
in terms of slander,
the chaste and good are envied,
the lofty and exceptional are criticized;
in terms of encountering blame,
loyal words invite trouble,
noble conduct summons shame;
in terms of impurity,
jade has flaws and pearls have defects.
Jiāo of Chénliú's elder brother,
renowned in Yǎnzhōu,
with flawless conduct and pure deeds,
not a shred of slander against him;
yet when he was to be appointed as an attendant,
Governor Jiāo Kāng dismissed and did not employ him.
Before advancement, he suffered three burdens;
after employment, he endured three harms,
even Kǒng Qiū and Mò Dí could not avoid this,
Yán Huí and Zēng Shēn could not preserve themselves.
Why?
Those with widespread pure praise,
are not truly virtuous.
From dukes and marquises downward,
jade and stone are mixed;
the conduct of worthy scholars,
good and evil are intertwined.
Those who mine jade break rocks to extract jade,
those who select scholars discard the wicked and choose the good,
thus,
those burdened with harm carry the world in their actions,
where can the accusers go?
Whenever people encounter fortune or suffer harm,
it is all due to fate.
There is fate of life and death, longevity and premature death,
and also fate of nobility and baseness, poverty and wealth.
From kings and nobles to commoners,
from sages to the foolish,
all who have heads and eyes,
all blood-containing beings,
none are without fate.
If fate dictates poverty and lowliness,
even if granted wealth and honor,
they will still encounter disasters and lose that wealth and honor;
if fate dictates wealth and honor,
even if made poor and lowly,
they will still meet fortune and goodness, leaving that poverty and lowliness behind.
Thus, those fated for nobility
will rise from lowly places on their own,
those fated for lowliness
will face danger from positions of wealth.
Thus, wealth and honor seem aided by gods,
poverty and lowliness seem plagued by ghosts.
Those fated for nobility,
though studying together, alone succeed;
though serving together, alone are promoted;
those fated for wealth,
though seeking together, alone obtain;
though acting together, alone achieve.
Poverty and lowliness are the opposite,
hard to succeed, hard to advance,
hard to obtain, hard to achieve;
they incur faults and receive punishment,
suffer illness and loss,
lose their wealth and honor,
and remain poor and lowly.
Therefore, high talent and solid conduct
do not guarantee wealth and honor;
little wisdom and thin virtue
do not confirm poverty and lowliness.
Sometimes, with high talent and solid conduct,
but evil fate,
one is cast aside and not advanced;
with little wisdom and thin virtue,
but good fate,
one rises and surpasses.
Thus, handling affairs wisely or foolishly,
having pure or turbid conduct,
depends on nature and talent;
official rank and social status,
managing wealth and poverty,
depend on fate and timing.
Fate cannot be forced,
timing cannot be compelled,
the wise attribute it to heaven,
thus they are open-hearted and tranquil,
even in poverty and lowliness.
If gaining wealth and honor were like digging ditches or cutting firewood,
by increasing effort and haste,
applying vigorous strength,
digging without cease deepens the ditch,
chopping without stop multiplies the firewood,
then those without fate
could all achieve their desires,
how could there be the troubles of poverty, lowliness, and danger?
However, sometimes the ditch is not yet dug when flooding comes,
the firewood not yet gathered when tigers appear.
Not gaining honor in office,
not acquiring wealth in management,
is like digging a ditch and meeting flood,
cutting firewood and encountering tigers.
Having talent but unable to apply it,
possessing wisdom but unable to act upon it,
or applying it yet achieving no merit,
or acting yet accomplishing nothing,
even with wisdom and talent like Confucius,
one still may lack established achievements.
When ordinary people see someone with lofty conduct,
they say:
"Since this person is so wise and virtuous,
why are they not noble?"
When they see someone with deep strategic thinking,
they say:
"Since this person is so eloquent and intelligent,
why are they not wealthy?"
Nobility and wealth are determined by fate and fortune,
not by wisdom and virtue or eloquence and intelligence.
Hence it is said:
"Wealth cannot be obtained through calculation,
nobility cannot be achieved through talent and ability."
Some have deep wisdom but no wealth,
high ability but no official position.
Those wearing silver seals and purple ribbons,
may not necessarily have the talent of Jì or Xiè;
those accumulating gold and jade,
may not necessarily possess the wisdom of Táo Zhū.
Sometimes the most foolish possess thousands in gold,
the dull-witted govern cities.
Thus officials with equal talent,
have different noble status due to fate;
those with equal knowledge in livelihood,
attain different wealth due to fortune.
Fortune determines poverty and wealth,
knowledge cannot increase or decrease it;
destiny determines nobility and baseness,
talent cannot advance or retreat it.
King Chéng's talent was inferior to the Duke of Zhōu's;
Duke Huán's wisdom was less than Guǎn Zhòng's,
yet Chéng and Huán received honored positions,
while Zhōu and Guǎn held humble ranks.
Consider that ancient rulers rarely failed to learn from ministers,
the profoundly knowledgeable rarely failed to become teachers,
yet rulers without ability remained in their positions,
while ministers with great talent served as menial laborers.
Thus nobility and baseness lie in fate,
not in wisdom or foolishness;
poverty and wealth lie in fortune,
not in dullness or intelligence.
Those who discuss affairs in the world believe the highly talented should be generals and ministers,
the less capable should be farmers and merchants.
When seeing intelligent people without high office,
they strangely criticize them saying:
"They must have flawed conduct and character."
Those of good conduct and character also strangely criticize them saying:
"They must lack talent and wisdom."
They fail to realize that although talent, wisdom and conduct may be high,
official position and wealth depend on fate.
When talented people,
undertake actions in prosperous times and fortune comes,
people say their talent and wisdom are brilliant;
when misfortune comes in decline,
they are called foolish and ignorant.
They don't understand this is due to the fate of fortune and misfortune,
the fortune of prosperity and decline.
Bái Guī and Zǐ Gòng traded goods to become wealthy,
accumulating gold and jade.
People say their methods were good and learning bright,
but this is not so. Zhǔfù Yǎn was humiliated in Qí,
rejected and unused;
he went to the court and submitted memorials,
was then employed by Hàn,
and rose to be Chancellor of Qí.
Xú Lè of Zhào also submitted a memorial,
which coincided with Yǎn's, and the emperor approved his words, appointing him as a court gentleman.
People say this was due to Yǎn's talent,
Lè's intelligence, but this is not so.
When Confucian scholars master a classic,
study it in the capital,
as brilliant as Kuāng Zhìguī,
as profound as Zhào Bàozǐdū,
initially pass the highest examinations,
and are promoted to court gentlemen or academicians,
people say this comes from their mastery of classics and high talent,
but this is not so.
Or take Fàn Jū's approach to Qín Zhāo,
where he was enfeoffed as Marquis of Yìng;
Cài Zé's persuasion of Fàn Jū,
where he was appointed as a guest minister.
People say this was due to Jū and Zé's excellence,
but this is not so,
it was all because the time for their noble fortune and wealth had come.
Confucius said:
"Life and death are governed by fate,
wealth and honor depend on Heaven."
When Duke Píng of Lǔ wished to see Mencius,
his favorite Zāng Cāng slandered Mencius and stopped it.
Mencius said:
"It is Heaven's will!"
Confucius was a sage,
Mencius a worthy,
teaching people to follow the Way,
never mistaken about right and wrong.
When they spoke of fate,
they recognized its certainty.
The Huáinánzǐ says:
"Humanity and baseness depend on timing, not conduct;
benefit and harm depend on fate, not wisdom."
Jiǎshēng said:
"Heaven cannot be anticipated,
the Way cannot be plotted with,
speed and slowness are fated,
how can one recognize their timing?"
When Emperor Gāozǔ attacked Qíng Bù,
he was hit by a stray arrow,
and became gravely ill.
Empress Lǚ brought a skilled physician,
who said:
"It can be cured."
Emperor Gāozǔ scolded him:
"I, a commoner, took the world with a three-foot sword,
was this not Heaven's mandate!
Fate lies with Heaven,
what use is even Biǎn Què?"
When Hán Xìn discussed military affairs with the emperor,
he said to Emperor Gāozǔ:
"What Your Majesty has is bestowed by Heaven,
not obtained by intelligence or strength."
Yáng Zǐyún said:
"To meet or not meet opportunity,
is a matter of fate."
Grand Historian Sīmǎ Qiān said:
"Wealth and honor do not avoid poverty and baseness,
poverty and baseness do not avoid wealth and honor."
This means following wealth and honor to poverty and baseness,
following poverty and baseness to wealth and honor.
Wealth and honor do not desire poverty and baseness,
yet poverty and baseness come of themselves;
poverty and baseness do not seek wealth and honor,
yet wealth and honor are obtained of themselves.
Spring and summer imprison and kill,
autumn and winter reign and assist,
none can control this;
the sun rises at dawn and sets at dusk,
none can seek this,
it is the natural Way of Heaven.
Dài King entered the capital from Dài to become Emperor Wén,
Zhōu Yǎfū as a lesser son became Marquis of Tiáo,
at that time the Dài King was not crown prince,
Yǎfū was not the primary heir,
they encountered the right time and opportunity,
and suddenly it came to pass.
Those fated poor may through hard work become wealthy,
but die when wealth comes;
those fated base may through talent gain nobility,
but are dismissed when nobility comes.
If one gains wealth and honor through talent and strength,
but fate and fortune cannot sustain it,
it is like a vessel's capacity,
or the hand's holding strength.
A vessel holding one shēng,
with one shēng remains level,
if given more than one shēng,
it overflows;
a hand lifting one jūn,
with one jūn remains steady,
if lifting more than one jūn,
it stumbles and falls.
Previous generations understood right and wrong,
attributing it to fate,
recognizing fate's certainty.
Those who believe in fate,
can live secluded awaiting their time,
without laboring spirit and straining body seeking it,
like pearls and jade in mountains and marshes,
not seeking high price from people,
yet people value them.
Heaven's mandate is hard to know,
people cannot patiently examine it,
even with abundant fate,
they still lack self-confidence,
thus they necessarily seek it.
If they knew themselves,
even fleeing wealth and avoiding honor,
they ultimately could not escape.
Hence it is said:
"Strength overcomes poverty,
caution overcomes misfortune."
Exert effort in work to attain wealth,
hone talent and clarify conduct to gain honor;
farmers plow vigorously to get more grain,
merchants travel far to gain deeper profits. Wasting time and neglecting tasks,
yet desiring wealth and honor,
is unattainable.
Although we speak of having fate,
we must still seek it.
If one believes in fate and does not seek it,
claiming that it will come of its own accord,
can one attain it without borrowing,
achieve without acting,
or arrive without moving?
Those destined for wealth naturally possess strong physical strength,
those destined for nobility naturally have superior intelligence and talent,
like a thousand-mile steed,
whose energy and strength are inherently vigorous,
with head, eyes, hooves, and limbs naturally well-proportioned.
There are cases where seeking does not lead to attainment,
but it does not mean that there are necessarily cases of attainment without seeking.
With diligent study, one need not seek nobility,
for nobility will come naturally;
with hard work, one need not seek wealth,
for wealth will arrive on its own.
The blessings of wealth and nobility
cannot be sought and obtained;
the misfortunes of poverty and lowliness
cannot be arbitrarily removed.
From this perspective,
those with a destined fortune and nobility
will attain it without seeking.
Those who believe in fate say:
"Knowing one's own auspiciousness,
one need not wait to seek it.
If heaven's mandate is richly auspicious,
it will come without seeking;
if heaven's mandate is heavily ominous,
seeking it is futile."
If things can arise without being sought,
then there are also people who become noble without seeking nobility.
Human nature includes those who are good without being taught,
and those who remain ungood despite teaching;
innate nature is like fate.
King Yì of Yuè fled into the mountains,
with utmost sincerity unwilling
yet hoping someone would take his place.
The Yuè people smoked him out of his cave,
and he could not avoid it,
being forcibly made ruler.
Thus, heaven's mandate is inevitable;
even if one tries to escape it,
one ultimately cannot avoid it.
Is this not an example of nobility attained without seeking?
All humans receive two kinds of fate:
one is the fate of encountered events,
the other is the fate of strength, weakness, longevity, or premature death.
Encountered events refer to
war, fire, crushing, or drowning;
strength, longevity, weakness, or premature death
refers to the thickness or thinness of one's endowed vitality.
War, fire, crushing, or drowning—encountering these depends on one's endowed fate,
not necessarily with a fixed timing.
As for strength, weakness, longevity, or premature death,
it is measured by a hundred years;
those who do not reach a hundred
are naturally deficient in vitality.
Those endowed with thick vitality have strong bodies,
and strong bodies lead to long lives;
those with thin vitality have weak bodies,
and weak bodies lead to short lives,
with more illness
and early death.
Dying at birth
or perishing before delivery
is due to weak endowment;
those with thick, strong vitality will surely live out their lifespan.
If one encounters no misfortunes
but lives in idleness and hardship,
dying from shortness of breath,
this is due to thin endowment
and exhaustion of vitality.
This, along with dying at birth
or perishing before delivery, is one fate,
all arising from insufficient endowed vitality,
unable to reach a hundred years.
Human endowed vitality
may be full and firm,
or empty, inferior, and soft.
Full and firm vitality
determines one's years of life;
empty, inferior, and soft vitality
leads to loss of one's body.
Heaven and earth produce things,
yet some things do not thrive;
parents bear children,
yet some children do not mature.
Some fruits form,
but wither and fall;
some children are born,
but die young.
If the fruit did not wither,
it would reach full maturity;
if the child did not die young,
it would live to a hundred years.
Yet fruits and children that wither and die young
have thin endowed vitality;
even if their form is complete,
their vitality is deficient and scarce,
unable to fill it.
When a child is born,
if its cry is loud, clear, and vigorous, it will live long;
if it is hoarse, choked, and weak, it will die young.
Why?
Because the fate of longevity or premature death
depends on the amount of vitality as the primary nature.
Women with spaced births have living children,
while those with frequent births have dying children,
like a calabash plant,
with many flowers but few fruits.
Why?
Spacing allows thick vitality,
making the child strong;
frequency leads to thin vitality,
making the child weak.
If a woman has previously borne a child that died,
the child she now carries is believed not to survive,
and it is called a 'huái' (doomed) child.
The idea is that since the previously born child died,
the affected child in the womb loses its nature.
When the born child dies and the carried child is ill-fated,
it is due to frequent childbirth,
with thin vitality unable to complete development;
even if the human form is achieved,
it is easily affected and harmed,
prone to early illness,
and the illness is uniquely untreatable.
A hundred-year lifespan
is the standard.
Those who do not reach a hundred,
though not standard,
still have a fate.
It is like a human height of ten feet
being the standard form,
calling a man a 'zhàngfū' (husband/tall man)
and honoring elders as 'zhàngrén' (elder).
Those not reaching ten feet
fall short of the standard,
but they still have a form.
One cannot call it not a form just because it falls short of ten feet;
similarly, one cannot call it not a fate just because it falls short of a hundred years.
It is not that heaven has long or short fates,
but that humans each receive different endowments.
From this perspective, humans receive vital fate from heaven,
whether complete or not, it is the same.
A saying goes:
"If aiming to become king fails,
one can still become a hegemon as a second best."
Hegemony is the flawed version of kingship.
Hegemony should originally lead to kingship, just as longevity should reach a hundred years.
If one cannot become king,
one retreats to hegemony;
if one cannot reach a hundred,
one declines into premature death.
Kingship and hegemony are the same endeavor,
with different names for superiority and inferiority;
longevity and premature death may share the same vitality,
but differ in length.
How do we know that not reaching a hundred is premature death,
while a hundred years is the standard lifespan?
Because the size and length of the body are of the same grade.
A hundred-year body
and a fifty-year body are no different;
the body is not different,
the blood and vitality are not distinct;
birds and beasts have different forms from humans,
so their lifespans differ from humans in number.
How can we prove that a hundred years is the human lifespan?
It exists in the world.
Confucian scholars say:
"In times of peace,
people are tall and robust, living around a hundred years,
born from harmonious vitality."
The "Yáo Diǎn" says:
"I have been on the throne for seventy years."
Seeking to abdicate, he found Shùn,
and Shùn was tested for thirty years before taking the throne.
Yáo retired in old age
and died eight years later,
Before ascending the throne,
he must have already reached adulthood.
Now, calculating, it amounts to over a hundred years.
It is also said:
"Shùn lived to thirty,
was employed for twenty,
reigned for fifty years,
and died while on an inspection tour."
Exactly a hundred years.
King Wén said to King Wǔ:
"I am a hundred,
you are ninety,
I shall give you three of mine."
King Wén passed away at ninety-seven,
King Wǔ died at ninety-three.
The Duke of Zhōu,
younger brother of King Wǔ,
the age difference between brothers did not exceed ten years.
After King Wǔ's death,
the Duke of Zhōu acted as regent for seven years,
then returned governance and retired in old age,
living to nearly a hundred years.
Shào Gōng,
elder brother of the Duke of Zhōu,
until the time of King Kāng,
still served as Grand Guardian,
living over a hundred years.
Sages embody harmonious qì,
thus their lifespans attain the proper measure.
Harmonious qì brings peace and order,
hence in eras of great peace, there are many long-lived people.
A lifespan of a hundred years
is likely the proper measure of human years,
just as things die by autumn, the proper term of their existence.
If things come before or after autumn,
it is like human death,
some exceeding a hundred years, some falling short;
before or after autumn marks the term,
exceeding or falling short defines the measure.
Some things die upon emerging from the earth,
like humans dying young at birth;
some things survive past autumn,
just as some people live beyond a hundred, even up to three hundred.
Historical records claim: Lǎozǐ lived over two hundred years,
Shào Gōng one hundred eighty.
Emperor Gāo Zōng enjoyed a reign of a hundred years,
King Mù of Zhōu also reigned for a hundred years,
and beyond their time on the throne,
both lived to over a hundred thirty or forty years.
In human conduct, some are worthy, some foolish,
and when encountering fortune or misfortune,
some are lucky, some unlucky.
Actions may be right or wrong,
and when facing reward or punishment,
some coincide favorably, some do not.
Exposed to warfare at the same time,
those hidden are not hit;
frost on the same day,
sheltered ones remain unharmed.
Being hit or harmed doesn't necessarily imply evil,
being hidden or sheltered doesn't necessarily mean good,
sheltering is fortunate,
being hit is unfortunate.
All wish to offer loyalty,
yet some are rewarded, some punished;
all intend to do good,
yet some are trusted, some doubted.
Rewarded and trusted may not be truly deserving,
punished and doubted may not be truly false,
reward and trust are coincidental,
punishment and doubt are not.
Among Confucius' disciples, over seventy in number,
Yán Huí died early.
Confucius said:
"Unfortunately, he died young."
Calling early death unfortunate
implies that long life is fortunate,
short life unfortunate.
Those who follow the way of sages and worthies,
practicing benevolence and righteousness,
should receive blessings.
Bó Niú having an illness
is also like Yán Huí's case,
both unfortunate.
Ants crawl on the ground,
people step and walk over them;
where the foot falls,
ants are crushed to death;
where the foot doesn't tread,
they survive unharmed.
Fire burns wild grass,
where carts have passed,
the fire doesn't burn;
people sometimes rejoice at this,
calling it 'lucky grass'.
Where the foot doesn't step,
where fire doesn't reach,
may not be due to goodness,
but raising a foot or lighting a fire
happens by chance.
From this perspective,
the eruption of abscesses and ulcers
is also of one nature.
Qì congeals and accumulates, blocked,
gathering into abscesses,
rupturing into ulcers and sores,
bleeding and discharging pus.
Can the site of an abscess or ulcer
be a favorable spot on the body?
It's where the flow of yíng and wèi qì
encounters obstruction. Spiders spin webs,
flying insects pass through;
some escape, some are caught.
Hunters set nets,
beasts crowd in turmoil;
some are captured, some escape.
Fishermen net fish in rivers and lakes;
some are caught, some remain.
Some commit grave crimes like treason or theft unnoticed,
others are discovered for minor offenses punishable by fines.
Disastrous qì affecting people
is also of this kind;
the unfortunate encounter it and die,
the lucky avoid it and live.
The unfortunate are those without luck.
Confucius said:
"Man is born upright;
the unscrupulous survive by luck."
Thus, those who follow the way and yet meet misfortune are the unfortunate.
Standing under a precarious wall,
crushed by its collapse;
treading on a cracked bank,
falling with its landslide.
Encountering danger without cause,
thus deemed unfortunate.
The gate of Lǔ's city wall, long decayed and about to collapse,
Confucius passed by,
hurrying quickly.
His followers said:
"It's been like this for long!"
Confucius replied:
"I dislike its long decay."
Confucius was extremely cautious;
had he encountered a collapse while passing,
it would have been called misfortune.
Therefore, Confucius said:
"The noble man may have misfortune but not luck,
the petty man may have luck but not misfortune."
He also said:
"The noble man abides in ease awaiting fate,
the petty man risks danger seeking luck." Those of the fawning and favored sort,
like Hóng and Jí Rú's ilk,
without virtue and meager in talent,
relying on looks to flatter,
undeserving of love yet receiving favor,
unfit for closeness yet gaining attachment,
contrary to reason and principle,
thus Sīmǎ Qiān composed biographies for them.
Wicked men opposing the way yet receiving grace and favor
fall into the same category;
hence, he grouped them under the title "Favorites and Flatterers".
Without virtue receiving favor,
without fault encountering disaster,
are of the same nature.
All imbued with primordial qì,
some become humans, some animals.
Among humans,
some noble, some base, some poor, some rich.
The rich may amass gold, the poor beg for food;
noble up to enfeoffment, base down to slavery.
Not that heaven bestows unevenly,
but beings receive natures of varying depth.
All practicing virtue,
yet fortunes differ;
all upholding benevolence and righteousness,
yet gains and losses vary.
Duke Wén of Jìn cultivated civil virtue,
King Yǎn of Xú practiced benevolence and righteousness;
Duke Wén was rewarded,
King Yǎn was destroyed.
A man of Lǔ avenged his father,
walked calmly without fleeing, pursuers spared him;
Niú Quē was robbed by bandits, remained calm and unafraid,
yet the bandits returned and killed him.
Cultural virtue and humaneness with righteousness are the same,
Not fleeing and not fearing are equivalent,
Yet Duke Wén and the people of Lǔ obtained blessings,
While King Yǎn and Niú Quē met with calamity—
This is because Duke Wén and the people of Lǔ were fortunate,
While King Yǎn and Niú Quē were unfortunate.
Hán Zhāohóu lay drunk and grew cold,
And the crown attendant covered him with a garment.
Upon waking, he inquired about it,
Knowing the crown attendant cared for him,
Yet, for overstepping his duties, he punished him with a crime.
In Wèi, the chariot attendant, seeing the driver’s error,
Shouted to stop the chariot from behind,
Acting with the duty to rescue from danger,
And was not punished for it.
Now, the chariot attendant’s shouting
And the crown attendant’s covering with a garment
Arose from the same intention.
Covering with a garment feared the lord would be cold,
Shouting to stop the chariot feared the ruler would be in peril—
The feelings of benevolence and kindness
Both sprang from the heart.
Yet in Hán, it was a crime,
In Wèi, it was loyalty:
The chariot attendant was coincidentally fortunate,
The crown attendant was not.
Not only in human actions,
But in things as well, this exists.
Bamboo several ren tall,
Trees so large they span an embrace,
Are cut and used by artisans,
Some fashioned into vessels and held in esteem,
Some left as unused material and discarded.
It is not that the artisans have love or hatred,
But the application of knife and axe is a matter of chance.
Steaming grain makes cooked rice,
Fermenting rice produces wine:
When the wine is ready,
Its sweetness or bitterness differs in flavor;
When the rice is cooked,
Its firmness or softness varies in texture.
It is not that the cooks or vintners intentionally differ,
But the adjustments of their hands happen to suit by chance.
Cooked rice of differing textures is kept in separate baskets,
Sweet wine is stored in different vessels;
If an insect falls into one vessel,
The wine is discarded and not drunk;
If a rat treads in one basket,
The rice is thrown away and not eaten.
Now, among all kinds of plants and herbs,
Each has its benefits,
Yet when encountered by physicians who gather them,
They become good medicine;
Or left to wither in the marshes,
They are burned by fire.
Equal in being metal,
Some become swords and halberds,
Some become blades and points.
Alike in being wood,
Some serve as beams in palaces,
Some as pillars in bridges.
All being fire,
Some melt candles,
Some burn dry grass.
Uniform in being earth,
Some form foundations of halls,
Some plaster corridors and doors.
All being water,
Some boil in cauldrons and pots,
Some wash filth and decay.
Things, whether good or bad alike,
Encounter human use—
Their unfortunate chance
Is still lamentable;
How much more so for beings endowed with vital essence?
Yú Shùn, a sage,
In life should have enjoyed complete safety and blessings,
Yet his father was obstinate, his mother harsh,
His brother Xiàng arrogant and wild;
Without fault, he was hated,
Without wrongdoing, he incurred blame—
How profoundly unfortunate!
Confucius,
Next to Shùn in stature,
Was born without an inch of land,
Traveled widely responding to summons,
Yet his traces were erased, and he faced starvation.
Both, with their sagely talents,
Were equally unfortunate by chance.
Shùn at least encountered Yáo and received the throne,
While Confucius died in Quèlǐ.
With the talent of sages,
They still met with misfortune by chance;
Among ordinary people,
Those struck by misfortune
And chance—their calamities must be numerous indeed!
The Mohist school argues
That human death is not fated;
The Confucian school contends
That human death is fated.
Those who speak of fate
Cite Zǐxià’s words:
"Life and death are fated,
Wealth and honor depend on Heaven."
Those who deny fate
Point to Lìyáng’s capital, which sank overnight into a lake;
Or Qín general Bái Qǐ burying alive the surrendered soldiers of Zhào at Chángpíng,
Where four hundred thousand perished simultaneously;
In the Spring and Autumn period,
Armies that suffered defeat
Left the dead covering the grass,
Corpses numbering tens of thousands;
In years of famine,
The starving filled the roads;
With warm epidemics and plagues,
Thousands of households were wiped out.
If fate necessarily exists,
Why are Qín and Qí alike in this?
Those who affirm fate reply:
"The world is vast,
Its people numerous;
One Lìyáng capital,
One Chángpíng pit—
Those sharing the same fate died together—
This is not strange.
Destined to drown,
They thus gathered in Lìyáng;
Destined to be crushed,
They thus accumulated in Chángpíng."
Just as when Gāozǔ first rose,
Physiognomists entering the regions of Fēng and Pèi
Found many destined to be enfeoffed as marquises—
It need not be that old and young, men and women
Were all noble and had auspicious signs,
But outstanding ones appeared occasionally,
Often in such a manner.
Yet in Lìyáng’s capital,
Men and women all perished;
In Chángpíng’s pit,
Old and young were buried alike.
Among tens of thousands,
There must have been long-lived ones not fated to die,
Who encountered an age of decline,
With wars arising everywhere,
And thus could not live out their years.
Human life has its length and brevity,
Times have their prosperity and decline;
Decline brings illness—
This is evidence of suffering disaster and meeting calamity.
Sòng, Wèi, Chén, and Zhèng suffered calamities on the same day;
Among the people of these four states, there must have been those with flourishing fortunes not due to decline,
Yet they all met with disaster—
The state’s misfortune overwhelmed them.
Thus, the fate of the state overcomes human fate,
And lifespan overcomes fortune fate.
Humans have signs of longevity or premature death,
As well as patterns of poverty, wealth, honor, and lowliness,
All visible in the body.
Hence, the length of lifespan is endowed by Heaven;
The quality of bone structure is seen in the body.
If fate dictates premature death,
Even with exceptional conduct,
One ultimately cannot live long;
If fortune dictates poverty and lowliness, even with a virtuous nature,
One ultimately cannot succeed.
Xiàng Yǔ, nearing death,
Turned and said to his followers:
"My defeat is due to fate,
Not to faults in using troops."
This statement is true.
In reality,
Xiàng Yǔ’s use of troops surpassed Gāozǔ’s,
But Gāozǔ’s rise
Was due to the Mandate of Heaven.
The fate of the state is tied to the multitude of stars;
The auspicious or inauspicious positions of the constellations
Bring fortune or calamity to the state;
As the stars shift,
People experience prosperity and decline.
That humans have good and ill fortune
Is like years having abundance or scarcity;
Fate has its decline and flourishing,
As things have their nobility and baseness.
Within a single year,
There is one noble and one base;
Within a single lifespan,
There is one decline and one flourishing.
The value or worthlessness of things
does not lie in their abundance or scarcity;
the decline or prosperity of individuals
does not depend on their wisdom or foolishness.
Zǐxià said:
"Life and death are governed by destiny,
wealth and honor depend on Heaven."
But why did he not say:
"Life and death depend on Heaven,
wealth and honor are governed by destiny"?
The reason is:
life and death have no celestial manifestations
but are primarily determined by innate nature.
Those endowed with a robust nature
possess abundant vitality and strong physique,
strength leads to long life,
and long life means no premature death.
Those with a weak nature
have scant vitality and frail constitution,
frailty results in short life,
and shortness means early death.
Hence it is said "governed by destiny",
where destiny means nature.
As for the endowment of wealth and honor,
it resembles the vital energy received at birth,
obtaining the essence of the stars.
The stars reside in Heaven,
where Heaven displays its patterns;
those receiving prosperous patterns become prosperous,
those receiving poor patterns become poor,
hence it is said "depend on Heaven".
How does this dependence manifest?
Heaven has its officials,
Heaven has its stars,
Heaven emanates vital energy
while the stars distribute essences;
the energy emitted by Heaven
contains the energies of all stars.
Humans receive this energy at birth,
nourish it through growth,
gaining nobility if destined for it,
poverty if destined otherwise.
Nobility may have varying ranks,
wealth may differ in amount,
all conferred according to the stars'尊卑 and magnitudes.
Thus Heaven has its officials,
Heaven has its stars,
Earth has its myriad people
and the essences of the Five Emperors and Three Sovereigns.
Heaven has constellations like Wángliáng and Zàofǔ,
humans also possess their counterparts;
receiving their energy
enables exceptional charioteering skill.
The Records state:
"Destiny manifests in three forms:
first is proper destiny,
second is responsive destiny,
third is circumstantial destiny."
Proper destiny
means inherent endowment naturally bringing good fortune.
With inherently virtuous nature,
one need not cultivate conduct to seek blessings - good fortune arrives spontaneously,
hence called proper destiny.
Responsive destiny
means diligence in conduct brings good fortune,
while indulgence brings calamity,
hence called responsive destiny.
Circumstantial destiny
means good deeds yield bad outcomes,
contrary to expectations,
encountering external misfortunes
that bring disaster,
hence called circumstantial destiny.
All humans receive their destiny
at conception during parental energy transmission,
when good or bad fortune is already determined.
Nature and destiny differ:
some have good nature but ill destiny,
others bad nature but good destiny.
Moral conduct reflects nature;
good or bad fortune reflects destiny.
Some doing good yet suffering misfortune
exemplify good nature with ill destiny;
some doing evil yet enjoying good fortune
exemplify bad nature with good destiny.
Nature inherently contains good and evil,
destiny inherently contains fortune and misfortune.
Those with fortunate destiny
may avoid good deeds
yet not necessarily lack blessings;
those with ill destiny
may strive morally
yet not necessarily avoid calamity.
Mèngzǐ said:
"Seek through proper means,
obtain through destiny's decree."
Good nature enables seeking,
good destiny enables obtaining.
With good nature but ill destiny,
seeking cannot yield results.
Evildoers
should face imminent disaster,
yet Dào Zhí and Zhuāng Qiāo rampaged across the land,
gathered thousands of followers,
plundered people's possessions,
dismembered human bodies,
were utterly immoral,
deserved calamity,
but died of old age.
Given this,
how can responsive destiny be verified?
Circumstantial destiny
means internal goodness
meets external misfortune.
Take Yán Yuān and Bó Niú as examples -
why did they encounter misfortune?
Yán Yuān and Bó Niú
were virtuous men
deserving responsive destiny,
with blessings following accordingly;
why then did they suffer misfortune?
Yán Yuān exhausted himself in studies,
dying from overexertion;
Bó Niú lived secluded yet contracted vile disease.
Consider Qū Yuán and Wǔ Yún -
utterly loyal assistants to their rulers,
fulfilling ministers' duties completely,
yet Chǔ exiled one
while Wǔ boiled the other's corpse.
Good deeds should bring responsive destiny's blessings,
yet they encountered circumstantial destiny's calamities -
why?
If responsive destiny exists, circumstantial destiny cannot,
and vice versa;
how then can the Confucian three-destiny theory
be firmly established?
Moreover, destiny is determined at birth,
evident in bone structure.
Now if we say destiny follows moral conduct,
this places destiny at life's end,
not its beginning;
thus wealth, honor, poverty, and humility
are all determined at initial endowment,
not attained later in life
through moral conduct.
Proper destiny means dying at hundred years,
responsive destiny means dying at fifty,
circumstantial destiny means encountering misfortune during initial energy reception,
such as exposure to malign influences during pregnancy,
or experiencing thunderstorms and anomalies,
leading to premature death in adulthood.
These constitute the three destinies.
There are also three natures:
proper,
responsive,
and circumstantial.
Proper nature
means endowment with the Five Constant Virtues;
responsive nature
means inheriting parents' nature;
circumstantial nature
means acquiring characteristics from malign influences.
Thus pregnant women eating rabbit
produce hare-lipped children.
The Monthly Ordinances state:
"In this month,
when thunder begins sounding,
those careless in behavior
will bear defective children
destined for great misfortune."
Muteness, deafness, lameness, blindness
result from prenatal energy damage,
producing deranged natures.
When Yángshé Xiàngwǒ was born,
his voice resembled wolves';
growing up with vicious nature,
he died by violent death.
While in the womb,
he acquired this nature -
similar to Dān Zhū and Shāng Jūn's cases.
Since nature and destiny originate prenatally,
the Rites prescribe fetal education methods:
during pregnancy,
sit only on properly placed mats;
eat only properly cut food;
view only correct colors;
hear only proper sounds.
When the child grows,
assign eminent teachers
to instruct in ruler-minister and father-son principles.
Worthiness or unworthiness is determined at this stage.
When receiving the vital energy,
if the mother is not cautious, harboring wild and wicked thoughts;
then when the child grows up,
they will be rebellious and unkind,
with an ugly and repulsive appearance.
Sùnǚ explained to Huángdì
the methods of the five women,
not only harming the parents' bodies,
but also corrupting the nature of both boys and girls.
Humans have destiny,
have fortune,
have encounters,
and have luck.
Destiny refers to
poverty, wealth, nobility, and baseness;
fortune refers to
prosperity, decline, rise, and fall.
If one's destiny is to be wealthy and noble,
and they encounter a flourishing fortune,
they will always be safe and free from danger;
if one's destiny is to be poor and lowly,
and they meet with a declining fortune,
then calamities will arrive,
and they will often suffer without joy.
Encounter refers to
meeting with unusual changes,
such as Chéng Tāng being imprisoned in Xiàtái,
or King Wén being confined in Yǒulǐ.
With their sage and brilliant virtue,
yet suffering the change of imprisonment and distress,
this can be called an encounter.
Although the change is very great,
if one's destiny is good and fortune flourishing,
the change will not harm them,
hence it is called an encountered misfortune.
What Yànzǐ encountered
can be considered great,
with straight blades pointing at his chest,
curved blades pressed against his neck,
treading on the land of death,
facing the points of swords and halberds,
yet he grasped death and returned alive.
His destiny was good and fortune flourishing,
so the encountered misfortune
could not harm him.
In the city of Lìyáng,
or the pit of Chángpíng,
there must have been people with good destiny and flourishing fortune,
who died overnight buried together,
because the encountered misfortune was too great,
and even good destiny and flourishing fortune could not avert it.
It is like water and fire contending with each other,
when water is strong, it overcomes fire,
when fire is strong, it overcomes water.
Luck refers to
meeting one's lord and being employed.
Even with a good destiny and flourishing fortune,
if one does not meet a lord who understands them,
they cannot achieve validation.
Fortune refers to
the good or evil one encounters by chance.
Being guilty yet escaping punishment,
is fortune;
being innocent yet detained,
is misfortune.
If detained not for long,
and pardoned to be released,
it is because one's destiny is good and fortune flourishing,
so the calamity of heavenly disaster cannot harm them.
Opportunity means
serving a ruler with mutual fit.
Serving the ruler with the Way,
the ruler approves of their words,
and thus employs them,
is opportunity;
if one's conduct conflicts with the ruler,
they retreat and are kept at a distance,
that is lack of opportunity.
If after retreating and being distant not long,
a superior official records and summons them,
it is because their destiny is good and fortune flourishing,
so the harm of lack of opportunity cannot detain them.
Therefore, encounters, luck, fortune, and opportunity,
sometimes align with destiny and fortune,
sometimes deviate from destiny and fortune.
When encounters, luck, fortune, and opportunity align,
one achieves completeness;
when encounters, luck, fortune, and opportunity do not align,
one faces failure and injury,
this is alignment with destiny and fortune.
If midway one does not achieve completion,
good turns into evil,
this is deviation from destiny and fortune.
Thus, humans in the world,
have the nature of good and bad fortune,
have calamities and blessings of prosperity and decline,
further compounded by the happenings of encounters, luck, fortune, and opportunity,
to follow through life and death and complete their good or evil conduct,
achieving the aspirations in their hearts is rare.
Humans receive primordial energy from heaven,
each endowed with a destiny of longevity or premature death,
to establish a form of tall or short stature,
just as a potter uses clay to make guǐ, lián, and wǔ vessels,
or a smelter uses copper to make pán and yú utensils.
Once the vessel's form is completed,
it cannot be made small or large;
once the human body is set,
it cannot be reduced or increased.
Using energy to form nature,
nature completes and destiny is fixed.
Body energy and physical form embrace each other,
life and death correspond to their appointed times.
The form cannot be changed,
destiny cannot be reduced or added to.
Speaking in terms of pottery and smelting,
the shortness or length of human life
can be discussed.
Some may object:
The potter uses clay to make guǐ, lián, and wǔ vessels,
once the guǐ, lián, and wǔ are formed,
they eventually break and decay,
and cannot change again.
But as for the smelter using copper to make pán and yú, pán and yú
though already formed into vessels,
can still be melted again,
pán can be made into a zūn,
but zūn cannot be made into a guǐ.
Humans receive energy from heaven,
though each is endowed with a destiny of longevity or premature death,
established with a physical form,
if they obtain good methods and divine medicine,
the form can be changed,
destiny can be increased.
The response:
When a smelter changes and remakes a vessel,
they must first smelt it with fire,
only then can it be made large, small, short, or long.
If humans hope to extend their years,
and wish to compare themselves to copper vessels,
they should have a transformation like that of furnace and charcoal,
then their form can be altered;
if the form is altered,
longevity can also be increased.
But how can humans change their form,
just as fire melts copper vessels?
The "Lǐ" says:
"When floods descend,
do not offer fish and turtles."
Why?
Because rainwater falls violently,
insects and snakes transform,
changing into fish and turtles.
These are insects that have temporarily changed from their original true form,
so ministers and sons, being cautious,
dare not offer them.
Do humans wish for their bodies to change,
hoping to be like the transformation of insects and snakes?
Now, insects and snakes that have not transformed
are better than those that have.
When insects and snakes have not transformed,
humans do not eat them;
when they transform into fish and turtles,
humans then eat them.
Being eaten means their lifespan becomes short,
which is not what they hoped for.
As years and months pass,
energy changes and transforms creatures,
toads become quails,
sparrows become clams.
Do humans wish for their bodies to change,
hoping to be like quails, clams, fish, and turtles?
Humans set traps to catch clams,
and those caught are eaten.
Even if one's body does not transform,
their lifespan may not be long,
but that is not what they hope for.
Gōngniú Āi of Lǔ lay ill,
and after seven days transformed into a tiger;
Gǔn was executed at Yǔshān,
and transformed into a yellow néng.
Do those who wish their bodies to change
hope to be like Gōngniú Āi becoming a tiger,
or Gǔn becoming a néng?
But the lifespan of tigers and néng
cannot surpass that of humans.
In the nature of heaven and earth,
humans are the most noble.
To change the human form,
into that of birds and beasts,
is not what one should hope for.
What is truly praiseworthy
is when an old man transforms into an infant,
or next, when white hair turns black again,
lost teeth regrow,
the body's energy remains robust,
and one can leap onto chariots without decline.
That is precious indeed.
Merely changing one's form
without extending lifespan
—what benefit is there?
Moreover, transformations in things follow their inherent energy,
as if responding to governance,
manifesting certain signs,
not because Heaven desires longevity
by altering their forms,
nor by obtaining divine herbs or rare medicines
to consume and transform.
Humans consistently take medicine to secure longevity,
seeking to enhance their innate nature,
benefiting their bodily years.
Occasional transformations due to circumstances
are not Heaven's proper energy,
nor the true nature humans receive.
Heaven and Earth unchanged,
sun and moon unaltered,
stars not vanishing—
this is normality.
Humans receive this proper energy,
hence their bodies do not change.
Occasionally, males transform into females,
females into males,
just as high banks become valleys,
deep valleys become hills,
responding to governance with change,
a change due to governance,
not the constant nature.
When the Hàn rose,
an old man gave Zhāng Liáng a book,
which then turned to stone,
thus the essence of the stone
became an auspicious sign for Hàn's rise,
just as the river spirit appeared as a man
holding a jade to the Qín envoy,
an omen of Qín's demise.
Silkworms eat mulberry leaves and age,
spin cocoons,
then transform into moths,
moths having two wings,
shedding the silkworm form.
Grubs turn into pupae,
pupae develop into cicadas,
cicadas grow two wings,
unlike grubs.
All living creatures that crawl or fly
often change their forms,
alter their bodies;
only humans do not change,
for they receive what is proper.
Born as infants,
growing into men,
aging into elders,
from birth to death,
never changing—
this is natural.
What is naturally unchanging
cannot be made to change again;
what changes
cannot be prevented from changing.
As for the lifespan of those that change,
it does not surpass the unchanging.
If humans wish to alter their forms,
and thereby increase their years,
that would be acceptable.
But if only the form changes without added years,
then they are like cicadas—
why would humans desire that?
The dragon as a creature
appears and disappears,
now short, now long;
the nature of the dragon
is to change in an instant,
constantly becoming extraordinary.
From this perspective,
humans are beings
endowed with unchanging forms;
their forms cannot be altered,
their years cannot be increased or decreased.
The records claim that Emperor Gāozōng had the omen of mulberry and grain,
repented his errors, and restored good governance,
enjoying blessings for a hundred years—
this is false.
It is said that Duke Jǐng of Sòng uttered three virtuous statements,
causing Mars to retreat three stations,
extending his life by twenty-one years—
this too is false.
Also, that Duke Mù of Qín had brilliant virtue,
so God bestowed nineteen years upon him—
this is also false.
They say Chìsōng and Wángqiáo loved the Way and became immortals,
transcending the world undying—
this too is false.
Suppose a person's form at birth is called A;
until old age and death, it always remains A.
If loving the Way made one an immortal,
no one has ever made A become B.
Forms cannot be changed,
years cannot be reduced or increased.
Why?
Form, energy, and nature
are from Heaven.
Form corresponds to spring,
energy to summer.
Humans rely on energy for longevity;
the form moves with the energy.
If energy and nature are uneven,
the body differs accordingly.
Oxen live half as long as horses,
horses half as long as humans;
thus, the forms of oxen and horses differ from humans'.
Endowed with the form of an ox or horse,
one naturally gets their lifespan;
since oxen and horses don't become human,
their years are shorter than humans'.
The world speaks of those like Emperor Gāozōng,
not mentioning changes in their bodies,
but only their extended years—
hence some believe it.
The blood and energy in the form
are like grain stored in a sack.
If the grain is one shi,
the sack's size fits exactly one shi.
If the grain is increased or decreased,
the sack changes accordingly.
Humans rely on energy for longevity;
energy is like the grain,
the form like the sack.
To increase or decrease longevity,
the body must also change;
how can the form remain as before?
If one argues human form differs from a sack,
and energy from grain,
then use a calabash as metaphor.
The juice of a calabash
is like human blood;
its flesh
is like human meat.
Try to have someone increase or decrease the calabash's juice
while keeping its form unchanged—
can it be done?
If humans cannot alter the calabash's juice without changing its form,
how can Heaven change human years without altering the body?
Human years cannot be increased or decreased;
so for those like Emperor Gāozōng, who added to them,
how can they claim an increase?
If they said such people
had transformed their bodies
and their years increased,
then it might be credible.
But now they speak only of added years,
not bodily change—
it is not credible.
Why?
Humans receive energy from Heaven;
once energy is complete, the form is set.
Then life and form depend on each other until death;
the form cannot change,
nor can years be added.
How to verify this?
In life, humans can walk;
in death, they fall stiff.
Death means the energy extinguishes,
the form decays and crumbles.
Humans born of received energy—their forms
cannot be changed;
how then can their years be increased?
From birth to old age,
what changes in the body
are the hair and skin.
In youth, hair is black;
in old age, it turns white;
long white, it yellows.
The change in hair
is not a change in form.
In youth, skin is fair;
in old age, it darkens;
long dark, it becomes dull,
as if stained.
With yellow hair and grimy skin,
hence the Rites state:
"Yellow-haired and soiled, may they be boundless."
Hair and skin change,
so humans age slowly and die late;
but bones and flesh do not change,
and when longevity ends, they die.
Among the five elements,
the one that can be altered
is only earth.
Kneaded into a horse,
transformed into a human,
this is called that which has not yet entered the kiln to be fired again.
If it is made into a vessel,
enters the kiln and is fired again,
it becomes solid and can no longer be changed.
Now people are considered to be molded and fired by heaven and earth,
their forms already fixed;
how can they be altered again?
Depictions of immortals' forms,
with bodies growing hair,
arms turning into wings,
walking on clouds, then their years increase,
not dying for a thousand years—
these are false depictions.
The world has false words,
and also false images.
Even if it were so,
they would be like cicadas and moths,
not true humans.
Beyond the seas in thirty-five countries,
there are hairy people and feathered people;
feathered means winged.
These hairy and feathered peoples
are products of earthly forms,
not said to have grown hair and feathers through cultivation.
Yǔ and Yì saw Xīwángmǔ,
and did not mention she had hair or feathers.
The undying people
are also in foreign lands,
but not said to have hair or feathers.
The hairy and feathered peoples
are not said to be undying;
the undying peoples
are not said to have hair or feathers.
Having hair and feathers cannot prove undying;
that immortals have wings—
how can that suffice to verify longevity?
Discussing human nature,
it certainly has good and evil.
The good
is inherently good;
the evil
can be taught, admonished, led, and encouraged,
to make it good.
All rulers and fathers,
carefully observe the nature of their ministers and sons;
if good, then nurture and encourage them,
not letting them near evil;
if near evil, then support, protect, restrain, and guard them,
making them gradually become good.
Good gradually turns to evil,
evil transforms into good,
becoming their nature and conduct.
Zhào Gōng admonished King Chéng, saying:
"Now the king first receives his mandate,
oh!
Like giving birth to a child, everything depends on its initial upbringing."
"Giving birth to a child" refers to a fifteen-year-old;
if the initial intent is toward good,
it ends in good;
if the initial intent is toward evil,
it ends in evil.
The Book of Songs says:
"That fine lad,
what can be given to him?"
The commentary states:
"It is like raw silk:
dyed with indigo, it becomes blue;
dyed with cinnabar, it becomes red."
A fifteen-year-old is like silk.
That which is gradually transformed into good or evil
is like indigo and cinnabar dyeing raw silk,
making it blue or red.
Once blue or red is set,
the true color shows no difference.
Hence, Yángzǐ wept at the fork in the road,
and Mòzǐ wept over raw silk,
grieving over departing from the root,
which cannot be changed back.
Human nature
can change from good to evil,
and from evil to good,
similar to this.
Weeds growing among hemp
stand straight without support;
white silk entering black dye
turns black without additional dyeing.
The nature of those weeds is not straight,
the substance of the silk is not black;
the hemp supports and the dye colors,
making them straight and black.
Human nature
is like weeds and silk;
it changes to good or evil depending on gradual influence.
Wáng Liáng and Zàofǔ are praised as skilled drivers,
but they cannot make bad horses good.
If they could only handle good horses,
and the bad ones could not be tamed,
then this is just the skill of a common driver or mediocre trainer—
what is remarkable for the world to praise?
Hence it is said:
"When Wáng Liáng mounts the carriage,
the horses are not worn out or inferior;
when Yáo and Shùn govern,
the people are not wild or foolish."
The commentary says:
"The people of Yáo and Shùn
could be enfeoffed house by house;
the people of Jié and Zhòu
could be executed house by house."
"These people
are why the three dynasties could follow the straight path."
The people of a sage ruler are like that,
the people of a wicked ruler are like this—
ultimately, it lies in transformation, not in nature.
Those who hear of Bóyí's character
become廉洁 even if greedy, and
cowards gain resolve;
those who hear of Liǔxià Huì's character
become sincere even if shallow, and narrow-minded become broad.
Merely hearing of their reputations,
some still change their conduct;
how much more so when personally meeting and being earnestly admonished?
The seventy disciples of Confucius's school
all served in capacities of ministers and chancellors;
clothed in sagely teachings,
their literary talents refined,
knowledge and ability tenfold—
this is the merit of instruction and the power of gradual influence.
Before entering Confucius's school,
they were ordinary and unremarkable in their villages.
The most unruly of them
was Zǐlù.
The world called Zǐlù an inconstant common man;
before entering Confucius's school,
he wore a rooster and carried a pig,
fierce and rude;
upon hearing recitation,
he would shake his rooster and brandish his pig,
raising his lips to make noise,
grating on the ears of sages and worthies—
extremely wicked.
Confucius guided and taught him,
gradually influencing and tempering him,
opening and guiding, enlightening and advancing him;
his fierceness diminished,
his arrogance bent,
until he could handle governance,
ranked among the four disciplines.
This is clear evidence of transforming nature from evil to good.
Fertile and barren,
are the inherent nature of soil.
Fertile and rich soil has good nature,
crops grow lush;
barren and poor soil has bad nature,
but with deep plowing and careful hoeing,
adding ample manure,
exerting human effort
to aid the land's strength,
its crops can resemble those of fertile soil.
The height and lowness of land
are also like this.
Using spades to dig the earth,
adding soil to raise the low,
then the low becomes level with the high.
If more spadework is added,
then the low not only levels
but becomes even higher,
and the high instead becomes low.
If human nature has good and evil,
like land having high and low,
by earnestly applying instruction,
the good will align with goodness.
Goodness, through rich transformation,
nurtured by instruction,
changes to become good,
and this goodness may then
even surpass previous goodness—
just as low land increased by spadework
becomes higher than high land.
"Cì does not accept fate, yet engages in trade."
Cì originally did not receive heaven's mandate for wealth; what accumulated
wealth and goods,
making him a rich man of the world,
was due to his mastery of trade methods.
If one obtains the method,
even without receiving the mandate,
one can still enrich oneself.
People with evil natures,
though not endowed with heavenly goodness,
can have their aspirations and conduct transformed
by the teachings of the sages.
It is said that a sharp sword is worth a thousand pieces of gold,
such as those from Tángxī, Yúcháng,
Lóngquán, and Tài'ē.
Their base material,
is ordinary iron from the mountains,
yet through the forging and tempering by skilled smiths,
they become sharp and effective.
Is it because the forging and tempering of a sharp sword involve a different substance?
It is due to the excellence of the craftsmen and the skill of the masters,
and the repeated tempering.
Take a sword from the east worth only one piece of gold,
forge and temper it thoroughly again,
apply sufficient fire,
and sharpen it evenly,
and it will be like a sword worth a thousand pieces of gold.
Now, iron and stone are natural,
yet they can be altered in their original substance by forging and tempering;
how much more so for humans, who contain the nature of the five constants?
If sages and worthies have not thoroughly tempered them,
why worry that their nature is not good?
In ancient times, skilled physicians were valued
for their ability to know the origin of severe illnesses
and to cure them with acupuncture and medicine.
If one only knows the name of the illness
and sits back observing it,
what is remarkable about that?
If a person has faults,
it is a disease of their innate nature.
Without teaching and correction,
and expecting them to change,
is it not difficult?
The way of heaven has genuineness and artifice;
the genuine naturally corresponds to heaven,
while the artificial involves human knowledge and skill,
yet it is no different from the genuine.
How can this be verified?
The "Yǔ Gòng" says:
"Qiú, lín, and lánggān."
Qiú is jade,
lín is pearl,
lánggān is a type of pearl;
these are the genuine jades and pearls
produced by the earth.
However, Daoists melt and refine the five minerals
to make jade of five colors,
which, compared to genuine jade,
shows no difference in luster.
Similarly, pearls from fish and clams,
and the "qiú lín" from the "Yǔ Gòng,"
are all genuine jades and pearls.
Yet the Marquis of Suí used drugs to make pearls,
brilliant and shining like real ones,
achieved through the teachings of Daoists
and the application of knowledge and skill.
The yangsui takes fire from the sky;
on the bingwu day in the fifth month at noon,
the five minerals are melted and refined,
cast into a vessel,
polished until it gleams,
and when held up toward the sun,
fire comes forth.
This is the true method of obtaining fire.
Now, if one arbitrarily uses a crescent hook of a sword or blade,
polishes it until bright and white,
and holds it up toward the sun,
fire can also be obtained.
The crescent hook is not a yangsui,
but it can still obtain fire
due to the polishing.
Now, for people with evil natures,
if they are of the same category as those with good natures,
they can be guided and encouraged to do good;
if they are of a different category,
they can still be like the jade cast by Daoists,
the pearls made by the Marquis of Suí, or the polished crescent hooks of swords,
taught through learning,
immersed in virtue,
and they will gradually develop the conduct of benevolence and righteousness.
Huángdì and Yándì contended to become the Son of Heaven;
Huángdì taught bears, pí, pixiu, and tigers to fight on the plains of Bǎnquán,
and after three battles achieved his aim,
with Yándì suffering defeat.
Yáo yielded the empire to Shùn,
while Gǔn, as a feudal lord,
desired to become one of the three highest ministers,
but Yáo would not listen.
Gǔn, angered, used fierce beasts,
intending to create chaos,
arraying the beasts' horns like a city wall,
raising their tails like banners,
with fierce hearts and high spirits,
resisting battle to show strength.
Now, beasts and humans have different forms,
yet they can be commanded to fight;
how much more so for people of the same kind?
Extending this argument,
"the hundred beasts dancing in unison,"
"the deep pool fish coming out to listen,"
and "the six horses raising their heads from feeding"
should no longer be doubted.
Different kinds can be made similar despite their differences,
while the same kind can be made different despite their similarity;
the cause lies not in the things themselves,
but in the people.
All creatures with blood and qi
can be differently transformed through teaching.
The people of Sānmiáo,
some worthy, some unworthy,
were equalized by Yáo and Shùn
through the application of benevolent teaching.
The people of Chǔ and Yuè,
living between Zhuāng and Yuè,
over time
became relaxed and slow,
due to the influence of customs.
Hence it is said:
"Qí is relaxed and slow,
Qín is negligent and easygoing,
Chǔ is hurried and urgent,
Yān is simple and direct."
Considering Zhuāng and Yuè,
the people of these four states,
interacting with each other,
if they live long in isolation,
their natures are bound to change.
As for those with evil natures,
their hearts are like wood and stone;
yet wood and stone can still be used by people,
