how much more so if they are not wood and stone!
In the traces of the noble person,
this can almost be seen.
There are those with the illness of madness,
singing and crying on the road,
unaware of east and west,
not seeing dry or wet,
not feeling sickness,
not knowing hunger or fullness,
their nature already damaged,
beyond help,
with no foresight,
and no fear of consequences.
Therefore, the king's laws do not abolish the officials of schools,
nor remove the officers of justice,
intending that the masses see the teachings of ritual and righteousness.
Schools encourage them beforehand,
laws and prohibitions guard them afterward,
so that even the aspirations of Dānzhū can be encouraged.
How can this be verified?
The soldiers of the three armies
are not inherently controllable,
yet brave generals lead and encourage them,
making them look upon death as going home.
Moreover, Hélú tested his soldiers by the side of Wǔhú Lake,
having blades pressed to their shoulders,
with blood flowing to the ground.
Gōujiàn also tested his soldiers in the courtyard of his palace,
and those who rushed into the fire to die
were too many to count.
Fire
and blades are not what human nature desires,
yet the two rulers motivated and led them,
making them disregard their lives.
Therefore, the methods of the army
lightly draw blood;
though Mèngbēn was brave,
he feared upon hearing the military orders.
Thus, Shūsūn Tōng established rituals and ceremonies,
and the ministers who had drawn swords contending for merit
bowed in reverence upon receiving the rites,
initially arrogant but later humble and obedient—
such is the power of sage-like teaching and virtue
to transform nature.
Do not worry about evil nature;
worry instead about not submitting to sage-like teaching,
acting willfully and thus bringing about disaster.
The seeds of beans and wheat are different from rice and millet,
yet eating them can relieve hunger.
Are petty persons and noble persons endowed with different natures?
Compare them to the five grains, all useful;
the substance is not different, but the effects vary—
it is because the endowment of qì has thickness and thinness,
hence natures have goodness and evil.
When one is impaired, they receive
the thin energy of unkindness,
while anger endows them with abundant courage.
With thin kindness, one becomes cruel and lacking in compassion;
with abundant courage, violent and devoid of righteousness.
Moreover, if harmonious energy is insufficient,
joy and anger are mistimed,
plans become frivolous and foolish.
Those who act recklessly
commit evil deliberately.
Humans receive the five constant virtues,
containing the five organs,
all present in the body.
If one's endowment is meager,
their conduct falls short of that of good people,
much like wine that may be strong or weak,
not because the brewing differs in strength or weakness,
but due to the amount of yeast used.
Thus, the strength of wine,
comes from the same yeast;
the goodness or evil in humans,
shares a single primal energy.
The energy varies in quantity,
hence nature differs in wisdom and folly.
Xīmén Bào was impatient,
so he wore a leather belt to remind himself to slow down;
Dǒng Ānyú was sluggish,
so he carried a bowstring to urge himself on.
Impatience and sluggishness,
both miss the mean of harmony,
yet with leather and string attached to their persons,
they became complete individuals.
If one can adopt the teachings of leather and string,
supplementing their deficiencies,
then the names of Bào and Ānyú
can be matched.
A poor and inferior house,
lacking walls and a roof that reaches,
people will point and criticize it.
If wealth increases,
and one builds walls for the house,
to shelter oneself,
making it a proper residence,
people will no longer fault it.
In Wèi, the land allocation was a hundred mǔ per person,
but Yè alone had two hundred,
and Xīmén Bào irrigated it with the Zhāng River,
turning it into fertile land,
yielding one zhōng per mǔ.
Human nature is like the fields of Yè,
moral teaching like the Zhāng River;
the worry is not being able to transform it,
not that human nature is hard to guide.
The roads in Luòyáng city had no water,
so water workers channeled water into the city,
making it flow day and night,
a feat of the water workers.
From this, it is said,
staying close to noble individuals,
with the way of benevolence and righteousness frequently applied to oneself,
Mèng's mother moving homes
serves as proof of this.
Water in human settlements is turbid,
while in the wild, it is clear.
Both are the same water,
sourced from the horizon,
some turbid, some clear,
due to the conditions of their location.
King Zhào Tuó of Nányuè,
originally a worthy man of Hàn,
adopted the customs of the southern barbarians,
turning his back on royal institutions,
wearing a topknot and sitting cross-legged,
as if it were his nature.
Lù Jiǎ persuaded him with Hàn's virtue,
intimidating him with imperial authority,
making him rise abruptly,
awakening to change and remorse,
submitting to the system and declaring allegiance,
and as for the topknot and cross-legged sitting,
he despised it as if it were his nature.
Before, he was one way,
after, another.
From this, it is said,
it also depends on teaching,
not solely on nature.
All humans receive noble fate from heaven,
and there must be auspicious signs on earth,
appearing on earth,
hence there is heavenly mandate.
The signs are not uniform,
sometimes through people or objects,
sometimes through omens,
sometimes through light or energy.
The tradition says
Huángdì was carried for twenty months before birth,
born with divine intelligence,
able to speak in infancy;
when grown, he led the nobles,
and they submitted to him;
he taught bears and panthers to fight,
to attack Yándì,
and Yándì was defeated.
His nature differed from others,
hence he remained in his mother's womb for ten extra months;
destined to be emperor,
he could command creatures,
and they served him.
Yáo's presence,
approaching him was like facing the sun,
gazing at him was like viewing clouds.
Floods reached the heavens,
snakes and dragons caused havoc,
Yáo sent Yǔ to control the waters,
driving away the snakes and dragons,
the waters were tamed and flowed east,
and the snakes and dragons hid away.
Having extraordinary bones,
there were bizarre signs;
possessing a divine mandate,
there was evidence of commanding things.
His fate destined him for nobility,
so from being a lord of Táng, he ascended to the throne as emperor.
Before Shùn encountered Yáo,
he was a widower in obscurity,
with Gǔsǒu and Xiàng
plotting to kill him.
Sent to repair a granary,
they set fire beneath it;
ordered to dredge a well,
they covered it with earth above.
Yet Shùn escaped the granary,
unharmed by the fire;
dug a tunnel from the well,
avoiding the earth's harm.
Yáo heard and summoned him,
testing him in office,
where he governed effectively and duties were well-managed,
with no affairs neglected or disordered.
Sent into the wilds of the great mountains,
tigers and wolves did not attack,
vipers and snakes did not bite;
encountering fierce winds and torrential rain,
he walked without confusion.
Though people wished to kill him,
they could not harm him;
in lands of venomous stings,
beasts and insects could not injure him.
Finally, he received the imperial mandate,
and ascended the Son of Heaven's throne.
Hòujì's mother,
stepped in a giant's footprint,
or some say she wore Emperor Kù's garment,
sat where Emperor Kù had rested,
and became pregnant.
Finding it strange, she abandoned him in a narrow alley,
but oxen and horses dared not tread on him;
placed him on ice,
birds covered him with their wings,
gathering to protect him.
His mother, realizing his divinity,
took him back and raised him.
When grown, he assisted Yáo,
rising to the position of Minister of War.
The king of Wūsūn was named Kūnmò,
and the Xiōngnú attacked and killed his father,
yet when Kūnmò was born,
abandoned in the wild,
crows brought meat to feed him.
The Chányú found it strange,
deemed him divine, and took him in to raise
him.
When he came of age,
he was made a general,
achieving many merits,
and the Chányú
restored his father's people to Kūnmò,
ordering him to guard the Western Regions.
Hòujì was not meant to be abandoned,
so oxen and horses did not tread on him,
and birds covered and cherished him with their wings;
Kūnmò was not meant to die,
so crows came with meat to feed him.
In the northern barbarian state of Tuó lí, a king's maid became pregnant,
and the king wanted to kill her.
The maid replied:
"There was an energy as large as an egg,
descending from the sky,
hence I became pregnant."
Later she gave birth to a child,
and abandoned him in a pigsty.
The pigs warmed him with their breath,
and he did not die.
She then moved him to a horse stable,
intending for the horses to trample him to death.
But the horses also warmed him with their breath,
and he did not die.
The king suspected he was a Son of Heaven,
so he ordered his mother to take him back and raise him as a slave,
naming him Dōngmíng,
and assigned him to herd cattle and horses.
Dōngmíng was skilled in archery,
and the king feared he would seize his kingdom,
so he wanted to kill him.
Dōngmíng fled,
heading south until he reached the Yǎnhūshuǐ River.
He struck the water with his bow,
and fish and turtles surfaced to form a bridge,
allowing Dōngmíng to cross.
The fish and turtles then dispersed,
and the pursuing troops could not cross.
He thus established his capital and became king of Fúyú,
hence the northern barbarians had the kingdom of Fúyú.
When Dōngmíng's mother was first pregnant,
she saw a vapor descending from heaven.
When he was born,
he was abandoned,
but pigs and horses warmed him with their breath, allowing him to live.
When he grew up,
the king wanted to kill him,
so he struck the water with his bow,
and fish and turtles formed a bridge.
Heaven's mandate decreed he should not die,
hence there was the rescue by pigs and horses;
his destiny was to become king of Fúyú,
thus there was the aid of the fish and turtle bridge.
When Yī Yǐn was about to be born,
his mother dreamed someone said to her:
"When the mortar emits water,
quickly flee east,
do not look back!"
The next morning,
she saw the mortar emitting water,
and immediately fled east for ten lǐ.
Looking back at her village, it was all submerged in water.
Yī Yǐn's fate decreed he should not perish,
so his mother received the dream and fled.
Extending this reasoning,
the capital of Lìyáng,
if its destiny was like that of Yī Yǐn,
must have had prior signs
manifesting in other places.
During the troubles of Duke Xiāng of Qí,
Duke Huán was then a prince,
contending with Jiǔ Zhì for the throne.
Guǎn Zhòng assisted Jiǔ Zhì,
while Bào Shū supported Duke Huán.
When Guǎn Zhòng fought with Duke Huán,
he drew his bow and shot at him,
hitting his belt hook.
Now, a person's body is seven chǐ tall,
the belt fastens around the waist,
the hook hangs from the belt,
covering an area on the body
no more than an inch wide.
It is both tiny and hard to hit,
and also smooth and slippery,
so when a sharp blade hits the hook,
it invariably deflects.
When Guǎn Zhòng shot,
he precisely hit the center of the hook,
the arrow struck and fell off,
without piercing the flesh beside it.
His destiny decreed wealth and nobility,
so there was divine assistance,
hence the proof of the deflected arrow.
King Gòng of Chǔ had five sons:
Zhāo, Wéi, Gàn,
Xī, and Qìjí.
All five were favored,
and King Gòng had no designated heir,
so he made offerings to the mountains and rivers,
asking the gods to decide.
He then buried a jade disc with Consort Bā
in the courtyard of the ancestral temple,
and ordered the five sons to enter in sequence and bow.
King Kāng stepped over it;
Wéi touched it with his elbow;
Gàn and Xī both stayed far from it;
Qìjí was young,
and was carried in,
bowing twice, he pressed directly on the cord.
Thus, after King Gòng's death,
Zhāo became King Kāng,
but lost the throne in his son's generation;
Wéi became King Líng,
and was assassinated during his reign;
Gàn became king,
for just over ten days;
Xī was not established,
and fearing execution,
both died without heirs.
Qìjí later ascended the throne,
ultimately continuing the Chǔ lineage,
as the divine sign had indicated.
The length of their reigns
corresponded to their proximity to the disc during the bowing.
The disc was buried underground,
unknown to the five sons,
yet as they followed each other bowing,
their distances varied,
and pressing the cord seemed as if the gods had instructed them.
When Tú Àngǔ of Jìn caused trouble,
he executed the sons of Zhào Dùn.
Shuò died,
but his wife was pregnant with a posthumous child.
When Àngǔ heard of this,
he searched the palace.
The mother placed the child in her trousers,
praying:
"If the Zhào lineage is to perish,
then you should cry;
if it is not to perish,
then remain silent."
When they searched, he never cried,
and thus he escaped and survived.
Chéng Yīng carried him on his back,
hiding in the mountains.
By the time of Duke Jǐng,
Hán Jué spoke to Duke Jǐng,
who then joined Hán Jué
in establishing the orphaned Zhào,
continuing the Zhào lineage,
who became Lord Wén.
When the orphaned Zhào made no sound,
it was as if someone covered his mouth.
Thus it is said,
the establishment of Lord Wén of Zhào
was fate.
Emperor Gāozǔ's mother was named Liú Ăo,
who once rested by the bank of a great marsh,
and dreamed of encountering a god.
At that time,
there was thunder, lightning, and darkness,
with a dragon above.
When he was born, he possessed fine qualities. He
was fond of drink,
and often bought wine on credit from
Wáng Ăo and Wǔ Fù.
When he drank to drunkenness
and lay down to sleep,
Ăo and Fù saw his body
often surrounded by divine wonders.
Whenever he stayed to drink,
wine sales multiplied several times.
Later, while walking in the marsh,
he killed a great serpent with his hand,
and an old woman blocking the path wept,
saying:
"The son of the Red Emperor has killed my son."
This omen became widely known.
Qín Shǐhuáng often said:
"There is the aura of a Son of Heaven in the southeast."
So he traveled east to suppress it.
When Gāozǔ rose to power,
he hid with Empress Lǚ
in the mountains and marshes of Máng and Dàng.
When Empress Lǚ and others searched for him,
they often saw a vapor rising straight above him,
and going to seek him, they always found him there.
Later, he made a pact with Xiàng Yǔ:
whoever entered the passes of Qín first would be king.
Gāozǔ arrived first,
and Xiàng Yǔ resented it.
Fàn Zēng said:
"I sent someone to observe his aura,
and it transformed into dragons,
forming five colors.
This is the aura of a Son of Heaven,
attack him quickly."
Gāozǔ went to apologize to Xiàng Yǔ,
who plotted with Yàfù to kill Gāozǔ,
ordering Xiàng Zhuāng to draw his sword and dance.
Xiàng Bó learned of this,
and rose together with Xiàng Zhuāng,
and whenever a sword was aimed at Gāozǔ,
Xiàng Bó would cover Gāozǔ's body with his own,
so the sword could not descend,
and the killing attempt failed.
There came the rescue of Zhāng Liáng and Fán Kuài,
ultimately enabling his escape,
and thus he became king of the world.
When she was first pregnant, there was the divine presence of a flood dragon;
after his birth,
the wine shop witnessed strange clouds and vapors;
he beheaded a snake while traveling at night,
and an old woman mourned and wept for the snake;
Qín Shǐhuáng and Empress Lǚ
saw the luminous aura;
Xiàng Yǔ plotted to kill him,
but Xiàng Bó shielded him,
foiling the conspiracy,
and he encountered Liáng and Kuài,
all signs of his destined wealth and honor,
where the aura appeared and things responded,
with people aiding and supporting him.
The brother of Empress Dowager Dòu
named Guǎngguó,
at four or five years old,
from a poor family,
was abducted and sold,
and his family did not know his whereabouts.
He was resold over ten times,
until reaching Yíyáng,
where he entered the mountains to make charcoal for his master.
One cold evening,
as over a hundred people lay beneath the charcoal pile,
it collapsed,
crushing all to death,
but Guǎngguó alone escaped.
He divined that within days he would become a marquis.
He followed his family to Cháng'ān.
Hearing that Empress Dòu had newly been installed,
and her family was from Guānjīn in Qīnghé,
he submitted a petition stating his case.
Empress Dowager Dòu spoke to Emperor Jǐng of Wén,
who summoned and questioned him,
confirming his identity,
and richly rewarded him.
When Emperor Jǐng of Wén ascended,
he appointed Guǎngguó as Marquis of Zhāngwǔ.
Thus, when the charcoal pile collapsed,
and over a hundred people died,
Guǎngguó alone escaped,
his fate destined for wealth and honor,
not only surviving,
but also enfeoffed as a marquis.
Yú Zǐdà,
from Hūn in Dōngguǎn, Chénliú,
was born at night,
just delivered from his mother,
when she saw above him
a vapor like a bolt of silk,
ascending to the sky.
At dawn, she asked others,
and all said:
"Auspicious. Noble."
The vapor connected with heaven,
and when he grew up, he became an official,
rising to the position of Minister over the Masses.
Guǎng Wénbó, from Púbǎn in Hédōng,
was also born at midnight,
just delivered,
when someone called his father's name from the door,
his father went out to answer,
but saw no one,
only a wooden staff planted by the door,
fine and exceptional.
His father brought the staff inside
to show others,
and they interpreted it:
"Auspicious."
Wénbó grew up and became an official,
rising to Governor of Guǎnghàn.
Wénbó was destined for wealth and honor,
so his father received the gifted staff,
the interpretation being:
"The staff signifies the strength you will gain from your son."
Emperor Guāngwǔ
was born in the first year of Jiànpíng
on the jiǎzǐ day of the twelfth month
in the second inner chamber of the rear hall of the Jìyáng Palace,
his late father being the magistrate of Jìyáng.
That night, without any fire,
the room illuminated itself.
His late father found it strange,
and immediately summoned the records official Chōng Lán,
sending him to consult a diviner.
Lán went with the groom Sū Yǒng
to the diviner Wáng Zhǎngsūn.
Zhǎngsūn divined,
and told Yǒng and Lán:
"This is an auspicious matter,
say no more."
That year,
grain grew on the palace roof, warding off fire,
three stalks from one stem with nine ears,
taller than regular grain by a foot or two,
truly auspicious grain.
In the early years of Emperor Āi,
a phoenix descended on Jìyáng Palace,
hence to this day there is a Phoenix Hut there.
When he first rose with Lǐ Fù and others,
reaching the boundary of Chái,
they encountered rebel troops
and fled in panic to the old hut in Jìyáng.
Upon arrival, they saw a light like fire, crimson,
south of the path to the old hut,
shining brilliantly up to the sky,
and after a while, it vanished.
During Wáng Mǎng's time,
the court attendant Sū Bó'ā could read auras,
and when sent past Chūnlíng,
he saw the city lush and vibrant.
When Emperor Guāngwǔ reached Héběi,
he met Bó'ā,
and asked:
"When you passed Chūnlíng before,
how did you know its aura was excellent?"
Bó'ā replied:
"I saw it lush and vibrant."
Thus, when Heaven's mandate was to rise,
and a sage king was to emerge,
the auras foretold it,
clearly and vividly.
Successors upholding culture,
building on former foundations,
imbued with heavenly light and vapor,
need little proof.
But founders rising like dragons,
from lowly origins in turmoil,
such as Gāozǔ and Guāngwǔ,
have they not always had signs of celestial, divine, and luminous wonders?
Fate
governs fortune and misfortune,
the way of nature,
the numbers of chance,
not due to other vapors or external forces
suppressing or influencing
to make it so.
The world says Wǔ Zǐxū fell on his sword,
and Qū Yuán drowned himself,
because Zǐ Lán and Zǎi Pǐ slandered them,
and the rulers of Wú and Chǔ wrongfully killed them.
But coincidentally, both men's fates were to end,
Zǐ Lán and Zǎi Pǐ happened to slander,
and King Huái and Fūchāi happened to believe the treachery.
The rulers happened to be unwise,
the ministers happened to slander,
the fates of the two
coincidentally were not long,
two chances and three concurrences,
seeming as if intended,
but in reality natural,
not caused by others.
The courts of Xià and Yīn happened to decline,
while Jié and Zhòu's evils ripened;
the fortunes of Shāng and Zhōu arose,
while Tāng and Wǔ's virtues flourished.
Guān Lóngpáng was killed,
Jīzǐ and Bǐgān imprisoned and died,
just as Jié and Zhòu's wickedness peaked,
coinciding with the end of the two men's fates.
Heeding Yī Yǐn's words,
adopting Lǚ Wàng's counsel,
was when Tāng and Wǔ were to rise,
and also when the two ministers were to be employed.
Ministers' fates have fortune and misfortune,
and worthy or unworthy rulers meet them.
When King Wén's time was to prosper,
Lǚ Wàng's fate was noble;
when Gāozōng's rule was to be peaceful,
Fù Yuè's virtue was to flourish.
It was not that King Wén and Gāozōng were born for the two ministers,
nor Lǚ Wàng and Fù Yuè
produced for the two rulers.
With enlightened rulers and worthy ministers,
their radiance illuminates each other,
the upper cultivate, the lower govern,
and their measures align.
When Yán Yuān died,
the Master said:
"Heaven is destroying me."
When Zǐlù died,
the Master said:
"Heaven is cursing me."
These were Kǒngzǐ's words of self-pity,
not statements of actual truth.
Kǒngzǐ was fated not to become king,
and these two disciples were fated not to have long lives.
Not becoming king and not having long lives -
what they received was different,
yet their predetermined measures coincided,
making them correspond appropriately.
When the omen of the two dragons was due to manifest,
King Lì of Zhōu happened to open the box;
when Bāo Sì was destined to cause the downfall of the Zhōu state,
King Yōu happened to have a naturally wicked disposition.
It wasn't that the two dragons made King Lì unleash the calamity,
nor that Bāo Sì caused King Yōu's foolishness and confusion -
they encountered each other
and naturally matched.
When the children's rhyme was due to be verified,
the cockfighting disturbance happened to arise;
when the omen of the mynah bird was due to be fulfilled,
Duke Zhāo of Lǔ's wickedness happened to mature.
It wasn't that the children's rhyme caused the fighting,
nor that the mynah bird attracted the ruler's wickedness -
the destined time arrived by itself,
and human actions happened to coincide.
When Yáo was destined to abdicate to Shùn,
Dān Zhū happened to be unprincipled;
when the Yú succession was due to pass to Xià,
Shāng Jūn happened to behave unlawfully.
It wasn't that Shùn and Yǔ, being destined to gain the empire,
caused these two sons to be wicked -
the good and evil, right and wrong
simply happened to meet.
When Mars and the Pleiades rise and set,
when the Pleiades are low Mars rises,
when the Pleiades appear Mars hides -
this is not because Mars's nature suppresses the Pleiades,
but because their timings happen not to coincide,
their cycles being out of phase.
When the first month establishes Yín,
the Dipper's handle points to Shěn -
this is not because Yín's establishment makes Shěn be pointed at,
but the turning scale of revolution
happens to correspond naturally.
When a father dies and the son succeeds,
when a mother-in-law dies and the daughter-in-law replaces her -
this is not because the son and daughter-in-law's replacement causes the father and mother-in-law's death,
but because old and young generations naturally succeed each other.
People say that autumn's energy strikes down grain and grass,
that grain and grass cannot withstand it and wither away to death.
This statement misses the truth,
for things are born in spring and grow in summer,
ripening and aging by autumn,
naturally drying up and dying
just as yin energy happens to be strong,
meeting with them.
How can this be verified?
There are things that do not die in autumn,
because their life nature has not reached its limit.
Humans live to a hundred years and then end,
things live one year and then die -
if we say things die because yin energy kills them,
then when humans end, what energy do they encounter that causes death?
Some theorists still say ghosts cause their death.
But when humans die ghosts come,
when things die cold arrives -
these are all coincidental encounters.
Humans end and ghosts appear,
yet sometimes ghosts appear but people don't die;
things die when encountering cold,
yet sometimes they encounter cold but don't wither.
Those crushed by collapsing houses,
those fallen from crumbling cliffs -
it is not that house spirits or cliff energies killed these people,
but that houses aged and cliffs crumbled,
and people with ill-fated lives
happened to be in the wrong place.
When the moon wanes in heaven,
snails diminish in the deep.
Wind follows the tiger,
clouds follow the dragon.
Like kinds communicate through energy,
natures mutually influence.
But when events encounter each other,
good and bad fortune occurring simultaneously,
this is accidental meeting,
not energy influence.
Those who kill people receive the punishment of death.
The killer's
crime deserves severity,
the dead person's
life was due to end.
Thus when harmful energy descends,
those with ill fate are first affected;
when sage kings bestow virtue,
those with abundant blessings are first encountered.
Therefore when virtue decrees descend in the court hall,
long-term prisoners emerge from their cells.
Heaven doesn't issue virtue decrees because the prisoners
shouldn't yet die and the sage king sends them forth -
the sage king happens to issue pardon,
and the confined prisoners happen to be due for reprieve.
This is like people sleeping at night and rising by day:
when night comes moonlight ends,
work cannot be done,
human strength is exhausted,
wanting unified rest;
when daytime brings light,
sleeping people wake,
strength is restored.
It's not that Heaven makes them work by day
and rest by night -
work corresponds with day,
rest matches with night.
When wild geese gather at Kuàijī,
leaving to avoid Jiéshí's cold,
they come encountering people's harvested fields,
treading on people's farmland,
pecking at grass and grain.
When the grain is exhausted and food depleted,
spring rain happens to come,
they avoid the heat flying north,
returning to Jiéshí.
The elephants plowing at Línglíng
were also like this.
The tradition says:
"When Shùn was buried at Cāngwú,
elephants plowed for him;
when Yǔ was buried at Kuàijī,
birds tilled for him."
This misses the factual truth,
being empty false words.
A man having short-lived features
will inevitably marry a wife destined to early widowhood;
an early-widowed wife
will similarly marry a husband destined to early death.
People say:
"When men and women die early,
the husband harms the wife,
the wife injures the husband."
This is not mutual harm,
but natural fate.
If you set fire burning,
then pour water on it,
you could say water harms fire.
But if the fire happens to go out by itself,
and water happens to spill by itself,
both separately fail,
not harming each other.
The early death of men and women today
is not like water pouring on fire,
but like these self-extinguishing examples.
Sons who harm fathers,
younger brothers who obstruct elder brothers -
share the same causation.
Living in the same household,
energies press upon each other,
causing emaciation and decline,
leading to death -
this could be called mutual harm.
But if someone dies abroad a thousand miles away,
by weapon fire, crushing, or drowning,
with energies not interacting -
how can this be mutual harm?
Wáng Mǎng's aunt Zhèngjūn,
betrothed to two husbands,
both husbands died, and when due to marry Zhào, the king died.
Without energies interacting,
she harmed three families from afar -
how grievous!
Huáng Cìgōng married the neighborhood shaman's daughter,
people said the woman's features indicated nobility,
so Cìgōng reached the position of chancellor.
Actually this was not so -
Cìgōng was due for nobility,
his path met the woman;
the woman also had self-dignity,
thus entering Cìgōng's household.
They happened coincidentally
to encounter each other,
this was timing.
Those without official emolument—
merchants who make no profit,
farmers who have nothing to sow—
it is not that their nature damages wealth
or their fate hinders grain.
It is because their fate is poor
that they dwell with unprofitable goods;
because their emolument is bad
that they cultivate ungerminating grain.
The world says dwellings have auspicious and inauspicious aspects,
and moving has yearly and monthly taboos.
But in actual fact this is not so.
The Way of Heaven is hard to know,
but supposing it exists,
people with inauspicious fate,
families facing decline,
will inevitably build houses on inauspicious sites
and move at times that violate yearly and monthly taboos.
If one family violates a taboo,
involving perhaps a dozen people,
those who end up dying
are inevitably persons with declining emolument and thin fate.
Extending this argument,
advancement or retreat in official career, promotion or transfer,
can likewise be understood.
When the time is right for retreat,
the ruler will listen to slanderous mouths;
when the time is right for rise,
worthy men will recommend oneself.
Thus, when one is about to obtain office,
gentlemen assist the good;
when one is about to lose position,
petty men destroy the extraordinary.
When Gōngbó Liáo slandered Zǐlù before Jìsūn,
Confucius spoke of fate;
when the Lǔ man Zāng Cāng defamed Mèngzǐ before Pínggōng,
Mèngzǐ spoke of Heaven.
When the Way is not yet to be practiced,
one encounters slander;
when Heaven has not yet granted one's purpose,
evil men employ their mouths.
Thus Confucius spoke of fate
and did not resent Gōngbó Liáo;
Mèngzǐ spoke of Heaven
and did not blame Zāng Cāng,
truly knowing that timing and fate accord
with what is natural.
Extending this argument,
the ruler's governance, achievements, and transformations
can likewise be explained.
When fate dictates nobility,
the times happen to be peaceful;
when the era is destined for chaos,
emolument meets decline.
The timing of order and chaos, success and failure
coincides with people's rise and fall, auspiciousness and inauspiciousness.
From this perspective, the successive emergence of sages and worthies
also belongs to this category.
A sage ruler surges forth abruptly,
and excellent ministers are elevated through opportune encounters.
The world says that Hán Xìn and Zhāng Liáng assisted the King of Hàn,
thus Qín perished and Hán arose,
and Gāozǔ obtained kingship.
But Gāozǔ's fate destined him to become king on his own,
and men like Hán Xìn and Zhāng Liáng were destined to rise in their own time;
the two encountered each other
as if they had long sought one another.
Therefore, when Gāozǔ rose from Fēng and Pèi,
many young men from Fēng and Pèi became wealthy and noble—
not because Heaven used these young men to assist Gāozǔ,
but because their fates and physiognomies, whether great or small, happened to correspond.
When Zhào Jiǎnzǐ deposed his crown son Bólǔ
and established the lesser son Wúxù,
Wúxù encountered worthiness,
and his fate also destined him to rule Zhào.
The world says Bólǔ was unworthy,
not equal to Wúxù.
Bólǔ's fate was base,
and his wisdom and thoughts were largely confused.
When Hán Shēng's official career reached Grand Tutor,
the world said it was due to Ní Kuān,
but in reality it was not so;
the Grand Tutor was destined for nobility
and happened to encounter Ní Kuān.
When Zhào Wǔ was hidden in trousers,
he did not cry all day—
not because someone covered his mouth
or stifled his sound,
but because his fate and timing destined him to live,
and he happened to be born while lying asleep.
Thus, marquises by military merit
must behead those destined to die in battle;
merchants of wealthy families must seize
the wealth of poor households.
Those who lose territory and are stripped of marquisates,
or are dismissed from ministerial posts,
have clear crimes and laws,
and their emoluments and ranks have reached their limits.
Thus, when vicious energies strike,
they inevitably afflict those with short-lived fate;
when famine years occur,
they inevitably starve households that are depleted and empty.
People say fate is hard to know.
But fate is very easy to know—
how can it be known?
By using the bones and body.
Since human fate is endowed by Heaven,
there are outward signs manifested in the body.
Examining outward signs to know fate
is like examining a dou or hu measure to know its capacity.
What are outward signs?
They are what is called bone physiognomy.
Tradition says Huángdì had a dragon's forehead,
Zhuānxū bore a shield on his head,
Dìkù had double teeth,
Yáo had eyebrows of eight colors,
Shùn had double pupils,
Yǔ had three perforations in his ears,
Tāng had double elbows on his arms,
King Wén had four nipples,
King Wǔ had a gaze facing the sun,
the Duke of Zhōu had a hunched back,
Gāoyáo had a horse's mouth,
and Confucius had a recessed forehead.
These twelve sages
all held the position of emperor or king,
or assisted rulers and worried about the world,
as known to the world
and recounted by Confucians,
recorded in classics and commentaries,
clearly evident and credible.
As for brief texts and common records, writings on bamboo and silk,
not seen by Confucians,
they are numerous and varied.
Cāngjié had four eyes
and became Huángdì's historian.
Prince Chóng'ěr of Jìn had fused ribs
and became hegemon among the feudal lords.
Sū Qín had a prominent nose bone
and became chancellor of the six states.
Zhāng Yí had fused ribs
and also became chancellor of Qín and Wèi.
Xiàng Yǔ had double pupils
and was said to be a descendant of Emperor Shùn,
dividing the world with Gāozǔ as kings.
Chén Píng was poor and had insufficient food,
yet his appearance and body were handsome,
so people found it strange,
saying,
"What does Píng eat to be so fat?"
When Hán Xìn was recognized by Lord Téng
and spared from execution,
it was also because his facial features were extraordinary.
A robust, plump, and handsome face
is also a kind of physiognomy.
Gāozǔ had a prominent nose bridge, dragon forehead, and beautiful beard,
with seventy-two black moles on his left thigh.
Lǚ Gōng of Shànfǔ was skilled in physiognomy
and saw Gāozǔ's form and appearance,
finding it extraordinary.
Thus he married his daughter to Gāozǔ—
this was Empress Lǚ,
who later gave birth to King Xiàohuì
and Princess Lǔyuán.
When Gāozǔ was the station chief of Sìshàng,
he once took leave to return to the fields
and lived in the fields with Empress Lǚ and their two children.
An old man passed by
and asked for a drink,
then read Empress Lǚ's physiognomy, saying,
"Madam,
you are a noble person of the world."
He was asked to read the two children's physiognomy.
Seeing Xiàohuì, he said,
"The reason for Madam's nobility is this boy."
Reading Lǔyuán's physiognomy,
he said,
"Both are noble."
After the old man left,
Gāozǔ came from outside,
and Empress Lǚ told him about it.
Gāozǔ caught up with the old man
and stopped him to have his own physiognomy read.
The old man said,
"Earlier, the physiognomy of the lady and the infants both resembled you, sir.
Your physiognomy, sir, is noble beyond words."
Later, Gāozǔ obtained the world,
just as the old man had said.
Extending this to infer
all members of a household, they all had physiognomies of wealth and nobility.
Those of similar qi and equal disposition,
their inherent natures and physical forms are naturally alike.
Even those with different qi and distinct kinds
may also encounter each other.
A wealthy and noble man
marries a wealthy and noble wife,
and a woman likewise finds a wealthy and noble man.
If two with incompatible dispositions meet,
it may result in immediate death;
if they have not yet matched,
there is the calamity of premature demise.
Wáng Mǎng's aunt, Zhèng Jūn, was betrothed,
but when the time came for the wedding,
her husband repeatedly died.
This happened twice.
Then she was offered to the King of Zhào,
but before the King could take her,
he passed away.
Nán Gōng Dàyǒu from Qīnghé,
who was a friend of Zhèng Jūn's father, Zhì Jūn,
encountered and assessed Zhèng Jūn, saying:
"You are destined to be the mother of the realm."
At that time,
during Emperor Xuān's reign,
with Emperor Yuán as the crown prince,
Zhì Jūn then through
the commandant of Wèi Commandery presented her to the crown prince,
who favored her,
and she gave birth to Jūn Shàng.
When Emperor Xuān passed away,
the crown prince ascended the throne,
Zhèng Jūn became empress,
and Jūn Shàng became crown prince.
After Emperor Yuán's death,
the crown prince succeeded him,
becoming Emperor Chéng,
Zhèng Jūn became empress dowager,
ultimately becoming the mother of the realm.
Thus, Zhèng Jūn's physiognomy destined her to be the mother of the realm,
while the two families she was previously betrothed to and the King of Zhào
lacked the physiognomy to be the father of the realm,
hence both husbands died before the wedding,
and the King of Zhào passed away.
This proves that the two husbands and the King of Zhào
lacked the great mandate to be emperors,
and Zhèng Jūn was not meant
to be with any of the three families.
Chancellor Huáng Cìgōng,
formerly a patrol officer in Yáng Jiǎ,
was traveling in the same carriage with a skilled physiognomist
when they saw a woman, about seventeen or eighteen years old.
The physiognomist pointed at her and said:
"This woman is destined for great wealth and nobility,
to be the wife of a marquis."
Cìgōng stopped the carriage,
and examined her closely.
The physiognomist said:
"If this woman does not become wealthy and noble,
then physiognomy books are useless."
Cìgōng inquired about her
and found she was the daughter of a shaman from a neighboring village,
so he married her.
Later,
Cìgōng indeed achieved great wealth and nobility,
rising to the position of chancellor,
and was enfeoffed as a marquis.
Since Cìgōng was destined for wealth and nobility,
and the woman was fated to match him,
they indeed met,
and both attained wealth and nobility.
Had Cìgōng been destined for a lowly fate,
unable to have such a woman as his mate,
if it were not the right time for them to be husband and wife,
then the calamities of the two husbands and the King of Zhào would have occurred.
Only when a family collectively possesses the fate for wealth and nobility
can they undertake matters leading to wealth and nobility.
If bone structure and physical form do not correspond,
separation and death are inevitable,
preventing long enjoyment of great blessings.
Thus, in wealthy and noble households,
the servants and slaves,
the oxen and horses raised,
must have qualities that set them apart from the ordinary.
Servants and slaves may have the physiognomy avoiding early death,
oxen and horses may have the nature to bear multiple offspring,
farmlands may have grains that sprout
and ripen quickly,
merchants may possess goods stored well
that sell rapidly.
Therefore, those who understand fate
can foresee wealth and nobility in poverty and lowliness,
and discern poverty and lowliness amidst wealth and nobility.
By examining the principles of bone structure
and observing the patterns of the skin,
to assess a person's innate nature and fate,
there are no cases that do not correspond.
Zhào Jiǎnzǐ sent Gūbù Zǐqīng to assess his sons by physiognomy;
none were deemed auspicious
until he reached Wú Xù, son of a Dí maid,
and considered him noble.
Wú Xù was the most virtuous
and also had a noble physiognomy;
Jiǎnzǐ later deposed the crown prince and established Wú Xù,
who eventually became a feudal lord,
known as Xiāngzǐ.
A physiognomist assessed Qíng Bù,
predicting he would first be punished and then become a king;
he was later punished and indeed enfeoffed as a king.
Wèi Qīng's father, Zhèng Jì,
had an affair with Wèi Ǎo, a servant of Princess Yáng Xìn,
and Wèi Qīng was born.
While at Jiànzhāng Palace,
a convict in fetters assessed his physiognomy,
saying:
"You are destined to be noble, reaching the rank of marquis."
Wèi Qīng replied:
"As a man born into servitude,
to escape whipping and scolding is enough;
how dare I aspire to be a marquis?"
Later, Wèi Qīng became a military officer,
achieved merit in numerous battles,
was promoted and his fief increased,
eventually becoming a grand general,
enfeoffed as a marquis of ten thousand households.
When Zhōu Yàfū had not yet been enfeoffed as a marquis,
Xǔ Fù assessed his physiognomy,
saying:
"You will become a marquis in three years.
Eight years after becoming a marquis, you will be a general and chancellor,
holding the reins of state,
extremely noble and powerful,
unmatched among subjects.
Nine years after that, you will starve to death."
Yàfū laughed and said:
"My elder brother has already inherited our father's marquisate;
if our father passes away, my brother should succeed him;
how can I become a marquis?
But even if I become as noble
as you say,
why would I starve to death?
Show me."
Xǔ Fù pointed to his mouth
and said:
"There is a vertical line entering your mouth,
indicating:
this is the mark of starvation."
Three years later,
his brother, Marquis of Jiàng, Shèng Zhī, committed a crime,
and Emperor Wén selected the worthiest son of the Marquis of Jiàng;
all recommended Yàfū,
so he was enfeoffed as Marquis of Tiáo,
succeeding the Marquis of Jiàng.
In the sixth year of Emperor Wén's later reign,
the Xiōngnú massively invaded the border,
and Yàfū was appointed general.
By Emperor Jǐng's time,
Yàfū became chancellor,
but later was dismissed due to illness.
His son purchased for Yàfū
five hundred sets of armor and shields from the imperial workshop
suitable for burial,
but exploited the laborers,
not paying them.
The laborers, knowing he had illicitly purchased government equipment,
resented this and reported his son.
Emperor Jǐng handed him over to officials for interrogation;
as a result, he refused food for five days,
vomited blood, and died.
When Dèng Tōng was favored by Emperor Wén,
his status surpassed that of ministers and high officials,
he received rewards amounting to vast sums,
and stood equal to the emperor.
A physiognomist assessed him and said:
"You will end up in poverty and lowliness, starving to death."
After Emperor Wén's death,
Emperor Jǐng ascended the throne,
and Dèng Tōng was accused of illegally minting coins;
Emperor Jǐng investigated,
Dèng Tōng fled,
lodged in someone's home and died there,
without a single coin to his name.
When Hán, the Grand Tutor, was still a student,
he went to the market, borrowed fifty coins from a physiognomist,
and went with him into the Imperial Academy,
to assess which students were destined for nobility.
The physiognomist pointed to Ní Kuān and said:
"That student is destined for nobility,
his rank will reach the Three Excellencies."
Hán Shēng dismissed the physiognomist,
sent his card to Ní Kuān,
forged a bond as strong as glue and lacquer,
exerted the utmost reverence of his strength,
moved his dwelling to follow Kuān,
deeply attaching and accommodating himself.
When Kuān once fell gravely ill,
Hán Shēng nursed him with the demeanor of a servant,
his kindness deeper than that of flesh and blood.
Later, his name became known throughout the world.
Ní Kuān's position rose to Grandee Secretary,
and upon the summons and recommendation by provincial and commandery officials, he was promoted and employed at the imperial court,
eventually reaching the rank of Grand Tutor.
Thus, the physiognomist who examined the钳徒, Xǔ Fù,
and those who read the appearances of Dèng Tōng and Ní Kuān,
can be called masters who understood destiny.
Therefore, those who understand destiny through physiognomy,
examining the evidence in bone structure,
perceive wealth, honor, poverty, and baseness
just as people see vessels like plates and bowls,
knowing their intended uses.
Fine vessels are surely used by the noble,
while crude ones are inevitably assigned to the lowly.
A revered tripod does not belong beside a latrine,
nor a gourd in the hall of a palace—
this is clear.
The bones of the wealthy and noble
do not endure the hardships of poverty and baseness;
the appearance of the poor and lowly
does not encounter the joys of wealth and honor—
it is also like this.
Just as a vessel's capacity for holding things
has measures in dou and shi,
so too do human ranks have levels of high and low.
If a vessel exceeds its capacity,
the contents overflow and are discarded;
if a rank oversteps its level,
death and loss follow.
Those who discuss destiny, comparing it to vessels
and applying the method of examining bone structure,
thus determine that destiny lies in bodily form—
this is settled.
Not only do wealth, honor, poverty, and baseness have bone structures,
but pure and turbid conduct also follow principles.
Nobility, baseness, poverty, and wealth
are matters of destiny;
pure and turbid conduct
are matters of nature.
Not only does destiny have bone patterns,
but nature also has bone patterns.
Yet only the clear signs of destiny are known,
while the bone patterns of nature go unrecognized—
this is seeing the outward signs of destiny
but missing the verifications of nature.
When Fàn Lǐ left Yuè,
he sent a letter from Qí to Minister Wén Zhǒng, saying:
"When the flying birds are gone,
the good bow is stored away;
when the cunning hares are dead,
the hunting hounds are cooked.
The King of Yuè has a long neck and a beak-like mouth—
he can share hardships with others,
but cannot share prosperity and joy.
Why do you not leave?"
Minister Zhǒng could not bring himself to go,
pleaded illness and did not attend court,
and was given a sword to die.
Wèi Liáo of Dàliáng
advised Qín Shǐ Huáng
on strategies to unite the world.
The First Emperor followed his plans,
treated him with equal courtesy,
and shared clothing, food, and drink alike.
Liáo said:
"The King of Qín's appearance—
with a prominent nose, long eyes,
a hawk-like chest, and a jackal's voice—
shows he has little kindness
and the gaze of a tiger, the heart of a wolf.
In hardship, he easily humbles himself before others;
in success, he likewise looks down on them.
I am but a commoner,
yet when he sees me,
he often personally demeans himself.
If truly the King of Qín achieves his ambition,
all under heaven will become his captives.
One cannot associate with him."
Thereupon, he fled.
Thus, Fàn Lǐ and Wèi Liáo,
perceiving the evidence of nature and conduct,
thereby determined the reality of future events—
indeed, there was proof,
matching their physiognomic readings.
From this, it is clear that
nature and destiny are tied to physical form.
Based on records in texts,
commonly seen in the world,
and comparing past and present,
those unheard of are certainly numerous and not few,
yet all have their reality.
Receiving qi from heaven,
establishing form on earth—
by examining the form on earth,
one can know the destiny from heaven;
none fail to grasp the reality.
There are accounts of Confucius misjudging Dàntái Zǐyú's physiognomy
and Táng Jǔ's reading of Cài Zé
proving inaccurate—
this error lies in lack of thoroughness. Why?
Because subtle, hidden signs were overlooked.
Physiognomy may lie internally,
or externally;
in physical form,
or in voice and breath.
Those examining the outside miss the inside;
those focused on form neglect voice and breath.
When Confucius went to Zhèng,
he became separated from his disciples,
and stood alone at the eastern gate of Zhèng.
A man of Zhèng asked Zǐgòng:
"There is a man at the eastern gate—
his head resembles Yáo's,
his neck is like Gāo Yáo's,
his shoulders are similar to Zǐchǎn's.
Yet from the waist down,
he falls three inches short of Yǔ,
weary and dejected like a homeless dog."
Zǐgòng reported this to Confucius,
who cheerfully laughed and said:
"The physical description is off,
but 'like a homeless dog'—
indeed! Indeed!"
As for Confucius's appearance,
the man of Zhèng missed the reality.
The man of Zhèng lacked clarity,
his method shallow.
Confucius's misjudgment of Zǐyú,
Táng Jǔ's confusion over Cài Zé—
were like the Zhèng man's reading of Confucius,
unable to fully see the reality of form.
Judging by looks,
one errs with Zǐyú;
judging by words,
one errs with Zǎi Yǔ.
For humans, whose nature and destiny entail wealth and honor,
they initially receive the natural qi,
are nurtured and grow up,
and the destiny of wealth and honor manifests.
When King Wén obtained the red sparrow,
and King Wǔ the white fish and red crow,
Confucian scholars debated it,
considering the sparrow as King Wén receiving the mandate,
and the fish and crow as King Wǔ receiving the mandate—
that Kings Wén and Wǔ received heaven's mandate,
and heaven used the sparrow, fish, and crow to bestow it.
Heaven used the red sparrow to mandate King Wén;
King Wén did not accept it,
so heaven again used the fish and crow to mandate King Wǔ.
In such cases, it is said that
originally there was no mandate from heaven,
but through self-cultivation and good deeds,
the good deeds reached heaven's awareness,
and heaven then conferred the imperial mandate.
Thus, the sparrow, fish, and crow
were heaven's envoys for the kingly mandate,
which the king upheld to carry out punishments.
In truthful discussion,
this is not destiny.
Destiny
refers to what is received at birth.
Humans receive their nature
and thereby receive their destiny.
Nature and destiny are both endowed,
obtained simultaneously—
not first receiving nature
and later receiving destiny.
How to clarify this?
Qì served Yáo as Minister of War,
held the office of Jì,
hence becoming Hòu Jì.
His great-grandson Gōng Liú resided in Tái,
later moving to Bīn.
A later descendant, Gǔgōng Dǎnfǔ, had three sons:
Tàibó,
Jìlì gave birth to King Wén, Chāng.
While Chāng was still in swaddling clothes,
sagely omens appeared.
Thus Gǔgōng said:
"Our lineage must have one who will flourish,
surely it is Chāng!"
Thereupon Tàibó, knowing this,
departed for Wú,
tattooed his body and cut his hair,
to yield the throne to Wáng Jì.
King Wén received the Mandate,
which is said to be at this time,
that Heaven's Mandate resides in human essence,
which Tàiwáng Gǔgōng recognized early.
Yet this was still not the beginning,
for King Wén had already received the Mandate
while still in his mother's womb.
When a true king receives the Mandate once,
internally it becomes his nature,
externally it forms his physique.
The physique,
the bone structure of the face and cheeks,
is endowed at birth.
Officials of rank one hundred shí and above,
from nobles and marquises downward,
court officers, generals, senior officials, down to primary officers,
externally including regional inspectors and grand administrators,
those who hold salaried positions,
are endowed with the fate of wealth and honor,
born with signs visible on their faces.
Thus Xǔ Fù and Gūbù Zǐqīng
consistently witnessed these verifications.
Officials advance according to their ranks,
and those who are promoted
may reach the highest ministers,
their fate and emolument being noble and honored,
their positions and prestige lofty and great.
The true king is the pinnacle of nobility
and the utmost of loftiness.
Born with a lofty and great fate,
his body then possesses noble and honored marvels.
Gǔgōng knew this,
seeing the anomaly of the four breasts.
The four breasts
are evidence of a sage,
while in the mother's body,
endowed with Heaven's sagely mandate.
How could it be that after growing up,
cultivating moral conduct,
the four breasts then appeared?
Using the four breasts to discuss gazing afar,
we also know that during gestation
he had already received it.
When Liú Āo rested by the great marsh,
she dreamed of encountering a spirit,
and subsequently gave birth to Emperor Gāozǔ,
at which time he had already received the Mandate.
When Emperor Guāngwǔ was born in the Jìyáng Palace,
at midnight without any fire,
the interior was illuminated.
The soldier Sū Yǒng
said to the official clerk Chōng Lán:
"This is an auspicious event,
say no more!"
At this time he had already received the Mandate.
To say that only King Wén and King Wǔ
received the Mandate upon obtaining the red sparrow and the fish with crow
is incorrect.
Heaven mandates once,
and the true king then rises;
it does not mandate again.
Having obtained the great fate of wealth and honor,
he naturally becomes king.
How can this be verified?
The old man of a wealthy family,
whose assets accumulate to a thousand gold,
is born with the bones of wealth.
Managing livelihood and accumulating goods,
until old age,
he becomes a wealthy old man.
The true king
is the elder of the world,
his mandated fate determined within his person,
just as birds are distinguished as male or female
within the eggshell.
The eggshell nurtures and male or female is born;
with the passing of days and months, the bones and joints strengthen.
When strong, the male naturally leads the female.
The male does not, after growing up,
have something teach it to be male,
and only then dare to lead the female.
This vigorous nature
is naturally so.
The true king
is the male of the world;
his fate is to be king.
The kingly mandate is determined during pregnancy,
just as the bones of wealth and honor are present at birth,
and the male bird is formed in the egg.
It is not only with humans and birds;
all things are like this.
Grasses and trees grow from seeds and pits,
emerging from the earth as sprouts and shoots,
gradually growing stems and leaves,
becoming long or short, large or small,
all originating from the seed or pit.
The true king
is the greatest in size and stature.
The stem of the vermilion grass is like a needle,
the sprout of the purple fungus is like a bean,
yet they become auspicious signs.
The true king is endowed with vital energy at birth,
also just like this.
Some say:
"The true king is born endowed with the Heavenly Mandate,
and when he is about to become king,
Heaven mandates him again.
It is like officials below the highest ministers
who dare assume their positions
only after receiving edicts of appointment.
The red sparrow and the fish with crow
are Heaven's mandates of appointment.
Heaven's way and human affairs
have the principle of mandated direction."
Spontaneity and non-action
are the way of Heaven.
To mandate Wén with a red sparrow
and Wǔ with a white fish
is to have action.
When Guǎn Zhòng and Bào Shū
divided wealth and Guǎn took more,
Bào Shū did not refuse,
and Guǎn Zhòng did not ask;
within, there was mutual understanding.
Seeing the other as oneself,
he took without hesitation.
The sage's rise to kingship
is like Guǎn's taking of wealth.
Between friends, the other and self
have no principle of giving and receiving.
Heaven is spontaneous;
if there were evidence of mandated direction,
then the Heavenly way would have action,
and friendship would be spontaneous.
When Hàn Gāozǔ slew the great serpent,
who directed him to slay it?
Could it be that Heaven's way arrived first,
and only then did he dare to slay it?
Courageous spirit stirred itself;
his nature was spontaneous.
The slaying of the great serpent,
the destruction of Qín,
and the killing of Xiàng
are of the same reality.
The receiving of the Mandate by Zhōu's Wén
and Wǔ to attack Yīn
is also the same principle.
Since Gāozǔ did not receive a mandate directing his actions,
to say that only Wén and Wǔ
received the mandate of the sparrow and fish
is erroneous.
An objection states:
"The 'Announcement to Kāng Shū' says:
'He was heard by the Lord on High,
the Lord was pleased,
and Heaven then greatly mandated King Wén.'
If there were no mandate history,
why would the classic say
'Heaven then greatly mandated King Wén'?"
What is called
"greatly mandated"
does not mean Heaven mandated King Wén;
rather, the sage's actions
accord with Heaven's Mandate's intent,
in harmony with Heaven,
as if Heaven directed him.
The "Book" was exhorting Kāng Shū,
urging him to do good;
therefore it says that King Wén practiced the way,
which was heard above by Heaven,
and Heaven then greatly mandated him.
The "Book of Songs" says:
"Then [Heaven] turned its gaze westward,
this, it considered, was my abode."
This has the same meaning.
Heaven has no head or face;
how could it gaze and turn?
Humans have looking and turning;
using humans to model Heaven,
the matter becomes easy to see,
hence it says "gazed and turned."
"Heaven then greatly mandated King Wén"
has the meaning of gazing and turning,
but in reality, Heaven did not mandate.
How can this be verified?
"The great man aligns his virtue with heaven and earth,
matches his brightness with the sun and moon,
conforms his order with the four seasons,
and harmonizes his fortune and misfortune with the spirits.
He precedes heaven, yet heaven does not oppose him;
he follows heaven, yet adheres to its timing."
If one must wait for heaven's mandate
to act,
how could there be preceding and following heaven?
Because he does not await heaven's mandate,
but acts directly from his heart,
thus there is the effort of preceding and following heaven;
his words align with heaven's timing,
hence there is the principle of not opposing and serving heaven.
The Analects say:
"How great was Yáo as a ruler!
Only heaven is great,
and only Yáo modeled himself after it."
The king modeling himself after heaven
without opposition embodies the meaning of serving heaven.
Extending the natural disposition,
harmonizing with heaven,
this is what is called "the great mandate to King Wén."
From King Wén's own intention,
King Wén acted on his own,
not that heaven drove a red sparrow
to inform King Wén
that he should become king,
and only then did he dare to rise.
Thus, King Wén's red sparrow
and King Wǔ's white fish
were not heaven's mandate,
but auspicious blessings.
When virtuous people undertake affairs,
everything is favorable.
People arrive without being summoned,
auspicious omens come without being invited,
silently harmonizing,
as if something guides them.
Stepping out, one hears good news;
looking around, one sees goodness;
this is the natural way.
King Wén was destined to rise,
and the red sparrow happened to come;
fish leaping, birds flying,
King Wǔ chanced to see them;
it was not that heaven sent the sparrow or the white fish,
but that auspicious creatures moved and the sages encountered them.
When the white fish jumped into the king's boat,
Wáng Yáng said:
"It was merely coincidental."
When the Grand Master of the Palace, Liú Kūn,
was previously the Governor of Hóngnóng,
and a tiger crossed the river,
Emperor Guāngwǔ said:
"It was naturally coincidental,
not directed by anything."
Thus, Wáng Yáng's word "coincidental"
and Guāngwǔ's term "chance"
can be said to align with nature.
Emotions and nature
are the foundation of human governance,
from which rites and music arise.
Therefore, to trace the extremes of emotions and nature,
rites are established as restraints,
and music as moderation.
Nature includes humility and deference,
so rites are created to suit its appropriateness;
emotions involve likes, dislikes, joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure,
so music is composed to express reverence.
What rites regulate
and music creates
are emotions and nature.
Former scholars and classicists,
in their writings,
all discussed this,
yet none could definitively establish it.
Shì Shuò of the Zhōu dynasty
believed that human nature has both good and evil;
cultivating a person's good nature
and nurturing it
makes goodness grow;
if the nature is evil, nurturing it
makes evil grow.
Thus,
emotions and nature each have their yīn and yáng,
and good or evil depends on cultivation.
Hence, Master Shì wrote one chapter of "The Book of Cultivation."
Mìzǐjiàn, Qīdiāo Kāi,
and followers of Gōngsūn Nízi,
also discussed emotions and nature,
differing slightly from Master Shì,
all stating that nature has both good and evil.
Mèngzǐ wrote his "On the Goodness of Nature,"
believing that "human nature is all good,
and when it becomes not good,
it is disturbed by external things."
He said humans are born between heaven and earth,
all endowed with good nature,
but as they grow and interact with things,
they become indulgent and rebellious,
and not goodness arises daily.
According to Mèngzǐ's words,
in early childhood,
none are not good.
Wēizǐ said:
"I long said of the child,
the prince would not emerge."
When Zhòu was a child,
Wēizǐ saw his不善 nature;
his evil nature did not stand out among the masses,
yet growing up, he became rebellious unchanged,
hence the statement.
When Yángshí Shíwǒ was first born,
Shū Jī saw him,
and upon reaching the hall,
heard his cry and turned back,
saying: "His voice
is like that of a wolf,
savage and unaffectionate.
None but he will destroy the Yángshí clan."
She then refused to see him.
When he grew up,
Qí Shèng started a rebellion,
and Shíwǒ was involved.
The people killed Shíwǒ,
and the Yángshí clan was thus destroyed.
Zhòu's evil
was present in his childhood;
Shíwǒ's rebellion
was evident in his birth cry.
A child at birth,
not yet in contact with things,
who causes his rebellion?
Dān Zhū was born in the Táng palace,
Shāng Jūn in the Yú chamber,
during the times of Táng and Yú,
when one could be ennobled house by house,
those they interacted with
must have been mostly good,
and beside the two emperors,
there must have been many worthies,
yet Dān Zhū was arrogant,
Shāng Jūn cruel,
both losing the imperial lineage,
serving as warnings through the ages.
Moreover, Mèngzǐ judged people by their pupils,
clear pupils indicating a pure heart,
cloudy pupils a turbid heart.
People's eyes are either cloudy or clear at birth,
cloudiness or clarity is endowed by heaven,
differing in vital energy,
not that they are clear in childhood
and become cloudy only after growing up and interacting with others.
Nature is inherently natural,
good and evil have their substance,
Mèngzǐ's discourse on emotions and nature
is not accurate.
Yet the theory of innate goodness
also has its basis.
Some are benevolent, some righteous,
due to differences in natural disposition.
Movements and gestures
vary with innate awareness.
Complexions may be fair or dark,
bodies tall or short,
until old age and death,
unalterable,
such is heavenly nature.
All know that water, soil, objects, and vessels
differ in form and nature,
yet few recognize that good and evil are endowed differently.
A one-year-old infant
has no heart for contention,
but upon growing up,
some gradually seek profit and pleasure,
with wild hearts and rebellious actions,
arising therefrom.
Gàozǐ, contemporary with Mèngzǐ,
argued that nature has no distinction of good and evil,
comparing it to rushing water:
channel it east, it flows east;
channel it west, it flows west.
Water has no inherent east or west,
just as humans have no inherent good or evil.
What Gào Zǐ said
means that human nature is like water.
If nature were like water,
one could use water to analogize nature,
just as metal is metal,
and wood is wood.
Humans are good because of goodness,
and evil because of evil,
initially endowed with natural dispositions,
receiving pure and undivided substance,
thus at birth signs appear,
and good and evil can be observed.
Those undifferentiated between good and evil,
who can be shifted,
are called average people,
neither good nor evil,
requiring education to become so.
Therefore, Confucius said:
"Those above average
can be told of higher things;
those below average
cannot be told of higher things."
Gào Zǐ's analogy of channeling water
only refers to average people,
not pointing to the extremely good or extremely evil.
Confucius said:
"By nature, they are close;
through practice, they drift apart."
The nature of average people
lies in what they practice;
practicing good makes them good,
practicing evil makes them evil.
As for the extremely good or evil,
it is no longer a matter of practice,
hence Confucius said:
"Only the highest wisdom and the lowest stupidity do not change."
Nature has good and not good,
and even sage transformation and worthy teaching
cannot change them.
Confucius, the ancestor of morality,
the most outstanding among the various masters,
said, "The highest wisdom and the lowest stupidity do not change,"
thus we know Gào Zǐ's words
are not accurate.
Gào Zǐ's words
also have some basis.
The Book of Songs says:
"That fine son,
how can I give to him?"
Its commentary says:
"It is like silk threads:
dye them blue, and they become blue;
dye them red, and they become red."
Channeling water to make it flow east or west
is like dyeing silk threads to make them blue or red.
Dān Zhū and Shāng Jūn
were already influenced by the transformations of Táng and Yú,
yet Dān Zhū was arrogant and Shāng Jūn cruel,
because their extremely evil substance
did not accept the changes of blue or red.
Xún Zǐ opposed Mèng Zǐ,
writing the chapter "Human Nature is Evil,"
believing that "human nature is evil,
and goodness is artificial."
Those who hold nature is evil
think that humans are born with evil nature,
and artificiality means
that after growing up,
they are compelled to do good.
According to Xún Zǐ's words,
humans in infancy have no goodness.
Hòu Jì as a child
played at planting trees;
when Confucius could walk,
he played with ritual vessels.
Stones are hard from birth,
orchids are fragrant from birth.
Endowed with good qi at birth,
they mature as they grow,
hence the play of planting trees
made him the Minister of War of Táng;
the play with ritual vessels
made him the sage teacher of Zhōu,
endowed with the nature of orchids and stones,
thus proving their hardness and fragrance.
Xún Zǐ's words
are not accurate.
However, the claim that nature is evil
also has some basis.
A one-year-old infant
has no sense of deference;
seeing food,
it cries wanting to eat it;
seeing something nice,
it wails wanting to play with it.
After growing up,
it restrains emotions and curbs desires,
striving to do good.
Liú Zǐ Zhèng criticized this, saying:
"If so,
then heaven has no qi.
If yīn and yáng, good and evil, do not correspond,
then how does human goodness arise?"
Lù Jiǎ said:
"Heaven and earth give birth to humans
with the nature of ritual and righteousness.
If humans can reflect on how they receive this mandate, they follow it;
following it is called the Way."
Lù Jiǎ knew that humans have ritual and righteousness as their nature,
and that humans can reflect on how they receive the mandate.
Those with good nature
are good without needing reflection,
while those with evil nature
may reflect on it,
yet still oppose ritual and righteousness.
Righteousness is drawn from goodness,
and they cannot achieve it.
Thus, the greedy can speak of integrity,
and the disorderly can speak of order.
Dào Zhí criticized others for stealing,
Zhuāng Qiā condemned others for excess,
showing they can reflect on themselves,
and their mouths can discuss virtue,
but with evil nature, they do not act on it;
what good does it do for goodness?
Lù Jiǎ's words
are not accurate.
Dǒng Zhòng Shū, reviewing the books of Xún and Mèng,
wrote the theory of "Emotions and Nature," saying:
"Heaven's great constants
are one yīn and one yáng;
humans' great constants
are one emotion and one nature.
Nature is born from yáng,
emotion is born from yīn.
Yīn qi is base,
yáng qi is benevolent.
Those who say nature is good
see its yáng aspect;
those who say it is evil
see its yīn aspect."
According to Dǒng Zhòng Shū's words,
Mèng Zǐ saw its yáng,
and Xún Zǐ saw its yīn.
To say that both schools have their insights
is acceptable;
but to not address that human nature
has both good and evil
is inadequate.
Human nature and emotions are both born from yīn and yáng,
and being born from yīn and yáng,
they vary in intensity and purity.
Jade is born from stone,
with pure and impure parts;
emotions born from yīn and yáng,
how can they be purely good?
Dǒng Zhòng Shū's words
are not accurate.
Liú Zǐ Zhèng said:
"Nature
is what one is born with,
residing in the body and not manifested;
emotion
is what arises from contact with things,
taking form externally.
External form is called yáng,
while what is not manifested is called yīn."
Liú Zǐ Zhèng's words
mean that nature is in the body and not manifested.
Emotion connects with things,
taking form externally,
hence it is called yáng;
nature is not manifested,
not interacting with things,
hence it is called yīn.
According to Liú Zǐ Zhèng's words,
emotion is yáng, and nature is yīn.
This does not base on the origin of their emergence,
but arbitrarily uses external manifestation and non-manifestation
to determine yīn and yáng.
If external manifestation must be yáng,
nature also interacts with things;
in haste, it is present,
in turmoil, it is present.
Compassion and inability to bear suffering
are the qi of benevolence;
humility and deference
are the manifestation of nature,
occurring through interaction,
hence compassion and humility
take form externally.
To say nature is internal and does not interact with things,
This likely does not reflect the truth.
Without discussing whether human nature is good or evil,
merely debating external and internal, yin and yang,
the principle is difficult to grasp.
Following Zǐ Zhèng's words,
taking nature as yin,
emotions as yang,
humans are endowed with emotions—
can they truly have both good and evil?
From Mèngzǐ down to Liú Zǐzhèng,
great Confucian scholars and erudite individuals,
have seen and heard much,
yet in discussing nature and emotions,
there is still no definitive conclusion.
Only Shì Shuò,
Gōngsūn Nízǐ and their followers,
somewhat grasped the correct view.
From this perspective,
facts are easy to know,
but the Way is hard to discuss.
Elaborate writings and abundant records,
flourish like glorious blossoms;
witty banter and lively talk,
sweet as syrup and honey,
yet they may not capture reality.
In reality,
human nature includes both good and evil,
just as talent varies in high and low.
The high cannot be made low,
nor the low made high.
To say nature has no good or evil
is to claim talent has no high or low.
Endowed nature and received fate
are of the same essence.
Fate has nobility and baseness,
nature has good and evil.
To say nature has no good or evil
is to claim human fate has no nobility or baseness.
The nature of the land across the nine provinces
is uneven in quality,
hence distinctions of yellow, red, and black,
and gradations of upper, middle, and lower;
waters differ in flow,
hence clear and turbid streams,
tending east, west, north, or south.
Humans receive the nature of heaven and earth,
harbor the energy of the five constants,
some benevolent, some righteous,
due to divergent nature and methods;
in movement and demeanor,
some heavy, some light, due to deceptive nature and awareness.
Complexions may be fair or dark,
bodies tall or short,
and until old age and death,
these cannot change,
for such is innate nature.
All know that water, soil, objects, and vessels differ in form and nature,
yet few recognize the variations in endowed good and evil.
I firmly believe Mèng Kē's claim that human nature is good
refers to those above average;
Xún Qīng's that it is evil
to those below average;
Yáng Xióng's that it is a mix of good and evil
to the average person.
If opposing the classics yet aligning with the Way,
it may serve as teaching;
but to exhaust the principle of nature,
it does not suffice.
Confucian scholars argue:
"Heaven and earth intentionally created humans."
This statement is false.
When heaven and earth combine their energies,
humans arise spontaneously;
just as when husband and wife unite their energies,
a child is born naturally.
In the union of husband and wife,
it is not that they intend to have a child at that moment;
desires stir, they unite,
and a child is born.
Since husband and wife do not intentionally produce a child,
we know heaven and earth do not intentionally create humans.
Thus, humans are born from heaven and earth
like fish in deep waters,
or lice on humans,
arising from energy,
reproducing within their kinds.
All things born between heaven and earth
share the same reality.
The tradition says:
"Heaven and earth do not intentionally create humans;
humans arise spontaneously."
If so,
why do discussers of matters say:
"Heaven and earth as the furnace,
all things as the bronze,
yin and yang as the fire,
creation as the artisan"?
Consider that potters and smiths use fire
to melt bronze and bake vessels,
doing so intentionally;
yet it's said "heaven and earth do not intentionally create humans,
humans arise spontaneously"—
can we then say potters and smiths
do not intentionally make vessels,
and vessels form by themselves?
Such comparisons do not match the facts,
and cannot be called apt;
if the writing does not correspond to reality,
it cannot be deemed correct.
It is said:
This metaphor illustrates that humans receive energy
not purely uniform,
like bronze cast into molds,
or vessels fired with heat,
not that heaven and earth creating humans
is identical to potters' work.
In raising metaphors,
people often cite human affairs.
Human affairs have their structure,
which cannot be severed.
Using the eyes to look at the head,
the head must move;
using hands to touch feet,
the feet must shift.
Eyes and head share the same form,
hands and feet belong to the same body.
Now, potters and smiths,
initially kneading clay to make vessels,
must use molds for shape,
hence they make them intentionally;
lighting charcoal to generate fire,
they must adjust the furnace and stove,
hence they do so intentionally.
But when bronze is melted, it may not all form perfectly,
vessels fired may not all turn out well,
they are not intentionally produced in that state.
Since heaven cannot intentionally create humans,
then in producing all things,
it also cannot do so intentionally.
When heaven and earth combine energies,
things arise spontaneously.
Plowing, weeding, and sowing seeds
are done intentionally;
but whether they mature or not,
is a matter of spontaneous nature.
How to verify this?
If heaven intentionally created all things,
it should make them love one another,
not harm each other.
Some say:
The energy of the five phases
is how heaven generates all things.
Since all things contain the five phases' energy,
and these energies harm each other in turn.
I say:
Heaven should use the energy of a single phase
to generate all things,
making them love one another,
not let the five phases' energies
cause mutual harm instead.
Some say:
To be of use,
they are made to harm each other;
harm leads to mutual completion.
Thus, heaven uses the five phases' energies
to generate all things,
and humans use all things to accomplish all tasks.
Without mutual control,
without mutual direction;
without mutual harm,
they cannot become useful.
If metal does not harm wood,
wood cannot be used;
if fire does not melt metal,
metal cannot be made into tools.
Hence, all things harm and benefit each other.
Blood-containing creatures
that overcome, subdue, bite,
and devour each other—
it is all due to the five phases' energies
making it so.
I say:
If heaven generated all things
intending them to be useful to each other,
and thus had to make them harm one another,
then creating tigers, wolves, vipers, and stinging insects like bees and scorpions,
all of which harm humans—
did heaven also intend for humans to be of use to them?
Moreover, within a single person's body,
the energies of the Five Phases are contained,
thus a person's conduct
manifests the virtues of the Five Constants.
The Five Constants—
they are the way of practicing the Five Phases' conduct.
The five organs reside within,
and the energies of the Five Phases are all present.
If we follow the argument of the theorists,
that creatures with blood,
harboring the energies of the Five Phases,
constantly harm each other;
then in a single person's body,
with the five organs in the chest,
would they harm each other?
In a person's conduct,
with a heart for righteousness and duty,
would they harm themselves?
Moreover, if the energies of the Five Phases harm each other,
and creatures with blood overcome and subdue one another,
where is the evidence for this?
It is said:
Yín belongs to Wood,
and its animal is the tiger.
Xū belongs to Earth,
and its animal is the dog.
Chǒu and Wèi also belong to Earth,
Chǒu's animal is the ox,
Wèi's animal is the sheep.
Wood overcomes Earth,
thus dogs, oxen, and sheep are subdued by the tiger.
Hài belongs to Water,
and its animal is the pig.
Sì belongs to Fire,
and its animal is the snake.
Zǐ also belongs to Water,
and its animal is the rat.
Wǔ also belongs to Fire,
and its animal is the horse.
Water overcomes Fire,
thus pigs eat snakes;
Fire is harmed by Water,
thus horses eat rat droppings and suffer bloated bellies.
It is questioned:
If we carefully consider the theorists' words,
there is also evidence that creatures with blood do not overcome each other.
Wǔ is the horse,
Zǐ is the rat,
Yǒu is the chicken,
Mǎo is the rabbit.
Water overcomes Fire,
so why don't rats chase horses?
Metal overcomes Wood,
so why don't chickens peck rabbits?
Hài is the pig,
Wèi is the sheep, Chǒu is the ox,
Earth overcomes Water,
so why don't oxen and sheep kill pigs?
Sì is the snake,
Shēn is the monkey.
Fire overcomes Metal,
so why don't snakes eat macaques?
Macaques—
they fear rats.
What bites macaques—
is the dog.
Rat belongs to Water,
macaque belongs to Metal.
Water does not overcome Metal,
so why do macaques fear rats?
Xū belongs to Earth,
Shēn belongs to Monkey.
Earth does not overcome Metal,
so why do monkeys fear dogs?
The East belongs to Wood,
its constellation is the Azure Dragon;
the West belongs to Metal,
its constellation is the White Tiger;
the South belongs to Fire,
its constellation is the Vermilion Bird;
the North belongs to Water,
its constellation is the Black Tortoise.
Heaven has the essences of these four constellations,
which descend to give birth to the forms of the four creatures,
and among creatures with blood,
these four creatures are the chiefs.
The four creatures contain the energies of the Five Phases
most prominently,
yet consider
the dragon and tiger interact without harming each other,
the bird and tortoise meet without injuring one another.
Using the four creatures as evidence,
and testing with the animals of the twelve earthly branches,
the idea that creatures of the Five Phases overcome each other based on energy and nature
is particularly inconsistent.
In general, when all things overcome and harm each other,
and creatures with blood overcome and subdue one another,
when it comes to eating each other,
it depends on their teeth being sharp or blunt,
the superiority or inferiority of their tendon strength,
the agility or clumsiness of their movements,
and the bravery or cowardice of their spirit and momentum.
Just as people in the world,
if their momentum is not equal,
and their strength not balanced,
naturally overcome and subdue each other.
To subdue by strength,
is to harm with weapons.
When people harm each other with weapons,
it is like creatures using teeth, horns, claws, and fangs
to attack and pierce.
With strong force and sharp horns,
fierce momentum and long teeth,
one can overcome;
with weak energy and short claws,
timid courage and blunt spurs,
one submits and fears.
People have bravery and timidity,
thus in battle there are victories and defeats,
the victor does not necessarily receive Metal energy,
the defeated does not necessarily obtain Wood essence.
Kǒngzǐ feared Yánghǔ,
retreating with sweat flowing,
yet Yánghǔ's complexion was not necessarily white,
and Kǒngzǐ's face was not necessarily green.
When hawks strike turtledoves and sparrows,
and owls peck swans and wild geese,
it is not necessarily that hawks and owls are born in the South,
and turtledoves, sparrows, swans, and wild geese are produced in the West;
it is naturally due to tendon strength, bravery, and timidity determining victory and submission.
In a single hall,
there must be debaters;
in a single village,
there must be litigants.
In litigation, there must be right and wrong,
in debate, there must be truth and falsehood,
the false and wrong lose,
