the true and right win.
Sometimes, one with a sharp tongue and eloquent speech,
with metaphors flowing unrestrained, wins;
sometimes, one who is halting and stuttering,
stammering and incoherent, loses.
Arguing and litigating with the tongue
is like fighting with swords and halberds.
With sharp swords and long halberds,
and nimble hands and feet, one wins;
with blunt knives and short spears,
and slow hands and feet, one loses.
Now, when things overcome each other,
it may be by tendon strength,
or by momentum and spirit,
or by skill and agility.
If the small have momentum,
and their mouths and feet are agile,
they can use smallness to control the large;
if the large lack bone strength,
and their horns and wings are not vigorous,
then the large submit to the small.
Magpies eat hedgehog skin,
shrikes eat snakes,
because hedgehogs and snakes are not agile.
The strength of mosquitoes and horseflies is less than that of oxen and horses,
yet oxen and horses are troubled by mosquitoes and horseflies,
because mosquitoes and horseflies have momentum.
A deer's antlers are enough to gore a dog,
a monkey's hands are enough to fight a rat,
yet deer are controlled by dogs,
and monkeys submit to rats,
because their antlers and claws are not effective.
Thus, a bull that can withstand a siege for ten years
is driven by a shepherd boy,
an elephant several ren tall
is hooked by a Yuè youth,
due to lack of agility.
Therefore, if one has agility,
then the small can overcome the large;
if one lacks agility,
then the strong submit to the weak.
Confucian scholars claim that when a sage is born,
it is not through human energy,
but rather they receive essence from Heaven.
Yǔ's mother swallowed a Job's tear and gave birth to Yǔ,
thus the Xià surname is Sì;
Xiè's mother swallowed a swallow's egg and gave birth to Xiè,
thus the Yīn surname is Zǐ;
Hòujì's mother
stepped in a giant's footprint and gave birth to Hòujì,
thus the Zhōu surname is Jī.
The Book of Songs says:
"Without splitting or tearing."
This refers to the birth of Hòu Jì.
Commentators further state:
"Yǔ and Xiè were born contrary,
emerging by opening their mothers' backs;
Hòu Jì was born smoothly,
without splitting or tearing.
He did not disturb his mother's body,
hence it is said 'without splitting or tearing'.
Those born contrary have descendants who die violently,
those born smoothly have descendants who perish naturally.
Thus Jié and Zhòu were executed,
while King Nǎn lost his cities."
The argument appears complete,
so people believe this explanation;
when supported with apparent evidence,
people accept its validity.
Apocryphal texts also claim:
"Yáo's mother Qìngdū went into the wilderness,
where a red dragon moved her,
and thus she gave birth to Yáo."
The "Basic Annals of Gāozǔ" records:
"Liú Āo once rested by a large marsh's bank,
dreaming of encountering a deity.
At that time
thunder flashed and darkness fell,
when Tàigōng went to look,
he saw a dragon above her.
She later conceived,
and thus gave birth to Gāozǔ."
These accounts seem divinely verified,
and are clearly recorded in texts,
so Confucian scholars
all accept them as true.
But examining them realistically,
they are false statements.
The Book of Songs mentioning "without splitting or tearing"
to indicate no disturbance to the mother's body
is acceptable;
but claiming emergence through the mother's back
is absurd.
When cicadas are born from nymphs,
they emerge through the back.
Would heaven's birth of sage sons
follow the same principle as cicadas?
Hares conceive by licking rooster feathers,
and when their young are born,
they emerge from the mouth.
Considering
Yǔ's mother swallowing coix seeds,
and Xiè's mother swallowing swallow eggs,
these are similar to the hare licking feathers,
so Yǔ and Xiè's mothers giving birth
should both be through the mouth,
not through the back.
Thus,
the theory of back-opening
is ultimately false.
Many die by the sword in this world,
yet their ancestors
when first born as humans
were not necessarily born contrarily.
When Qín lost the empire,
Yán Lè beheaded Húhài,
Xiàng Yǔ executed Zǐyīng,
but could Bóyì, Qín's ancestor,
have been born contrarily?
Therefore, using the smooth/contrary birth theory
to examine the ancestors of these three houses
is mistaken.
Moreover, coix seeds
are plants,
swallow eggs
are from birds,
and giant footprints
are of earth.
These three all have form,
not being ethereal essence,
how could they produce humans?
Those discussing sages believe
they receive heaven's subtle essence,
hence possessing extraordinary wisdom.
Now the births of these three houses
involve grass, birds, and earth -
can these be called subtle?
By nature's principle,
humans alone are noble,
while other things are base.
If noble human essence
receives base things' energy,
how could it remain subtle?
If sparrows mated with swans,
they could never produce offspring -
why?
Because sparrows' bodies are small,
while swans' forms are large.
Now swallows measure under five inches,
coix stalks reach only several feet,
yet two women swallowed their eggs and seeds -
how could these form seven-foot human bodies?
Melting a cauldron of copper
to cast a coin-sized mold
cannot fill the cauldron - this is clear.
Now they claim the giant was celestial,
hence his footprint was huge.
The giant-footed person
resembles the melted cauldron of copper;
Jiāng Yuán's body
is like the coin-sized mold.
If the giant emitted essence into Jiāng Yuán,
given her small body,
how could she receive all his essence?
Without receiving all his essence,
Hòu Jì could not become fully human.
If Yáo and Gāozǔ were truly dragons' sons,
sons' nature should resemble fathers',
and since dragons ride clouds,
Yáo and Gāozǔ should also do so.
All things born from earth
resemble their original kinds.
Those unlike earth
were not born from earth itself,
earth merely nurtured them.
A mother bearing children
resembles earth nurturing things.
If Yáo and Gāozǔ's mothers
received dragons' essence,
like earth receiving sown seeds,
things born resemble their kinds,
so these two emperors should resemble dragons.
Moreover, among blooded creatures,
when males and females mate,
their union
involves seeing their own kind,
with essence moved by desire
before they can procreate.
If stallards see cows,
or cock birds see hens,
they do not mate -
because they are different species.
Now dragons differ from humans,
how could they move humans and emit essence?
Some say:
"During Xià's decline,
two dragons fought in the court,
spitting saliva on the ground.
The dragons left but saliva remained,
stored in a casket.
Until King Yōu of Zhōu
opened the dragon saliva,
which transformed into a dark turtle,
entering the rear palace,
mating with a maiden,
thus giving birth to Bāo Sì.
The dark turtle differed from humans,
how could it move the maiden and emit essence?"
The dark turtle's mating was improper,
hence Bāo Sì brought disaster,
and the Zhōu state perished.
When different species mate improperly,
they produce disorderly offspring.
Now if Yáo and Gāozǔ's mothers
mated improperly,
why were these two emperors wise and sagely,
unlike Bāo Sì?
Some say:
"When Jiǎnzǐ of Zhào fell ill,
for five days he lacked consciousness.
Upon waking he said
he visited the emperor's place,
where a bear approached,
the emperor ordered him to shoot it,
he hit the bear,
and it died;
then a brown bear approached,
he shot again,
hit the brown bear,
and it died.
Later he asked a ghost blocking the way,
the ghost said:
'The bears
were ancestors of Jìn's two ministers.'
Bears are animals,
different from humans,
how could they emit essence to humans
to become the ministers' ancestors?"
The bears Jiǎnzǐ shot
represented the two ministers' impending fall,
and Jiǎnzǐ's rise - an omen.
Jiǎnzǐ saw them
as in a dream.
The appearance of emptiness
need not have substance.
Suppose there were such cases—
perhaps bears and brown bears first transformed into humans,
then gave birth to the two ministers.
In Lǔ, Gōngniú Āi fell ill and transformed into a tiger.
Humans transforming into beasts
is just like beasts becoming humans.
When the black turtle entered the rear palace,
it likely first transformed into a human.
Between heaven and earth,
creatures of different kinds
engaging with each other
has never occurred.
Heaven and humans share the same principle,
with aligned likes and dislikes.
If humans do not favor different kinds,
then heaven also does not interact with them.
Though humans are born from heaven,
just as lice are born from humans,
humans do not favor lice,
so why would heaven without reason wish to be born from humans?
Why so?
Different kinds have distinct natures,
and their desires are incompatible.
Heaven and earth
are like husband and wife;
heaven bestows vital energy upon earth to produce things.
Humans reproduce among themselves,
with the essence refined into sages,
all due to the father's energy,
without further receiving it elsewhere.
If receiving additional energy made one a sage,
then Xiè and Hòujì
would not be sages.
If all sages must receive additional energy,
then the twelve sages were not all so.
What energy did the mothers of Huángdì, Dìkù,
Zhuānxū, and Shùn
receive?
What did the mothers of Wénwáng, Wǔwáng,
Zhōugōng, and Kǒngzǐ
sense or swallow?
Perhaps upon seeing the surnames of three clans,
namely Sì,
Zǐ, and Jī,
people then imitated and fabricated,
creating absurd tales out of nothing,
just as upon seeing the land of Dǐnghú,
they invented the story of Huángdì ascending to heaven.
Losing the meaning of the Way,
they reverted to the characters.
When Cāngjié created writing,
it was connected to events.
Jiāngyuán trod in the giant's footprint;
"footprint" means foundation,
so the surname should have been "qí" below "tǔ",
yet it became
"nǚ" beside "yǐ",
not the character for foundation or footprint.
It does not match the original event,
casting doubt on its truth.
Using Zhōu's "Jī" to compare with Xià and Yīn, we also know that "Zǐ" and "Sì"
are not swallows or coix seeds.
Perhaps when the mothers of Yǔ, Xiè, and Hòujì
were about to conceive,
they happened to swallow coix seeds, swallow eggs,
or tread in a giant's footprint.
The world favors the strange,
a sentiment shared across ages;
without witnessing the unusual,
they deem virtue unremarkable,
hence adopting it as surnames.
The world, in its sincerity,
thus accepted it as true;
sages, cautious in doubt,
did not seek to rectify it;
scholars, with shallow discourse,
did not attempt to discern it;
Confucians, revering antiquity,
thus perpetuated these tales.
That line in the Shī,
"unbroken, unsevered,"
refers to Hòujì's birth
not harming his mother's body.
Confucians, forcing interpretations,
thus fabricated tales of Yǔ and Xiè being born unusually.
"Moved by the dragon,"
"dreaming of encountering a spirit,"
are of the same nature.
When the mothers of Yáo and Gāozǔ
were about to conceive,
they encountered thunder dragons riding clouds and rain;
people saw their forms
and thus claimed it so.
Dreaming of encountering a spirit
symbolizes receiving a sage child.
Dreaming of union with a ghost—
is that not dreaming of encountering a spirit?
How can we ascertain the truth?
"Going out to the wilds and moved by a dragon,"
and "a dragon residing above,"
perhaps because Yáo and Gāozǔ
received destinies of wealth and honor,
and the dragon, as an auspicious creature,
appeared upon them,
serving as an auspicious omen
and proof of their mandated rule.
When Emperor Guāngwǔ was born in Jìyáng Palace,
phoenixes gathered on the ground,
and bountiful grain grew on the roof.
The birth of sages
involves rare birds and auspicious objects as portents.
If one must claim that upon seeing strange auspicious things,
the child born is deemed their offspring,
then was Emperor Guāngwǔ the essence of bountiful grain
or the energy of a phoenix?
Consulting the "Dì Xì" chapter
and the "Sāndài Shì Biǎo",
Yǔ is the son of Gǔn;
Xiè and Jì are both sons of Dìkù,
their mothers all consorts of Dìkù,
and Yáo too is a son of Kù.
How could the consorts of emperors
venture into the wilderness?
Though ancient times were simpler,
rituals were already established;
why would an emperor's consort
bathe in open waters?
Thus,
the claim that sages receive additional energy from heaven
or that mothers sensed or swallowed things
is mere fallacy.
In reality,
sages have their own lineages,
as with Wén and Wǔ,
each with their kind.
Kǒngzǐ, by blowing pitch-pipes,
knew himself to be a descendant of Yīn;
Xiàng Yǔ, with double pupils,
knew himself to be a scion of Yú Shùn.
The Five Emperors and Three Sovereigns
all traced their ancestry to Huángdì;
Huángdì, a sage,
inherently possessed a noble destiny,
hence his descendants all became emperors.
The birth of emperors
must involve strange wonders;
if not manifested in objects,
then it appears in dreams.
The world believes in fallacious texts,
thinking that what is recorded on bamboo and silk
is all transmitted by sages and worthies,
with nothing untrue,
thus trusting and affirming it,
reciting and reading it;
yet upon seeing true accounts that contradict these fallacious texts,
they dismiss them as "short writings"
unworthy of credence.
If the realities of the obscure can still be known,
and hidden sentiments can still be determined,
then explicit texts and clear writings,
whose right and wrong are easily seen,
when lumped together and transmitted as non-factual,
it is due to inattentive scrutiny
and lack of reflection on matters.
The transmitted texts and sayings of various masters in the world
often aim to establish novelty and create strangeness,
proposing startling theories
to shock the common people;
crafting deceptive writings
to gain fame for uniqueness.
Transmitted texts say:
Yánlíng Jìzǐ was traveling
when he saw lost gold on the road.
It was summer, the fifth month,
and there was a man gathering firewood while wearing a fur coat.
Jìzǐ called to the firewood gatherer, "Pick up that gold from the ground."
The firewood gatherer threw his sickle to the ground,
glared, waved his hand, and said:
"How can you, living so high,
see so low,
with such dignified appearance,
yet speak so rudely?
I, in the summer's fifth month,
wear a fur coat to gather firewood—
do you think I'd take gold?"
Jìzǐ apologized to him
and asked for his name.
The woodcutter said:
"You are a scholar who judges by appearances!
Why bother telling you my name?"
He then left without looking back.
The world accepts this as true,
but it's likely a fabricated tale.
Now, Jìzǐ was ashamed of Wú's turmoil,
and though the people of Wú wanted to jointly establish him as ruler,
he ultimately refused to accept,
went to Yánlíng,
and never returned for life,
demonstrating conduct of integrity and humility
that remained consistent from start to finish.
XǔYóu declined the empire,
not suspected of coveting a marquisate;
Bóyí abandoned his state and starved to death,
not suspected of coveting trifles.
Acts of integrity and humility
can be extrapolated from great to small,
but not easily from small to great.
Since Jìzǐ could decline the throne of Wú,
why suspect him of coveting gold left on the ground?
When Jìzǐ was on a mission to the central states,
he passed through Xú,
where the lord of Xú admired his precious sword,
but Jìzǐ didn't give it to him immediately.
Upon his return, the lord of Xú had died,
so he untied the sword and hung it on a tree by the grave before leaving,
showing a heart of integrity and humility,
ashamed to betray his previous intent.
If Jìzǐ wouldn't betray the dead,
even abandoning his precious sword,
why suspect him of scolding a living person to pick up gold from the ground?
Before leaving Wú,
he was a noble scion;
after leaving Wú,
he was the lord of Yánlíng.
Whether as a scion or a lord,
he had attendants before and behind,
with chariots and followers,
making it clear
he couldn't travel the roads alone.
If he wasn't ashamed to take the gold,
why hesitate to have his attendants do it?
And why trouble the fur-clad woodcutter?
The world praises Liǔxià Huì's conduct,
saying he could cultivate purity
in obscurity.
Worthy men share similar virtues,
hence their aspirations connect across millennia.
If placed in a dark, secluded spot,
Jìzǐ still wouldn't take the gold,
let alone in broad daylight,
with his retinue complete,
picking up gold on the road—
that's not in Jìzǐ's character.
Perhaps Jìzǐ did see the lost gold,
pitied the fur-clad woodcutter, and wanted to benefit him;
or perhaps when he spoke of taking the gold from the ground,
he intended to give it to the woodcutter,
not to take it himself.
But in popular tales,
they say Jìzǐ took the lost gold.
Some records say:
Yán Yuān and Confucius
ascended Mount Tài in Lǔ together,
Confucius looked southeast, and outside the Chāng Gate of Wú
there was a tethered white horse,
so he led Yán Yuān
to point it out, saying:
"Do you see Wú's Chāng Gate?"
Yán Yuān said: "I see it."
Confucius asked:
"What's outside the gate?"
He replied:
"Something like the shape of a tied silk ribbon."
Confucius covered his eyes to stop him,
and they descended together.
After descending, Yán Yuān's hair turned white and teeth fell out,
and he eventually died of illness.
It's said that because his spirit couldn't match Confucius's,
he strained himself to the limit,
exhausting his essence,
thus dying young.
When people hear this,
they all believe it.
But judging by reality,
it's probably a false tale.
Examining the text of the Analects,
this statement isn't found;
checking the commentaries on the Six Classics,
there's no such account either.
If Yán Yuān could see a thousand lǐ away,
matching the sage,
why would Confucius and others avoid mentioning it?
The human eye's sight
doesn't exceed ten lǐ;
beyond that, it can't see,
not because it lacks acuity,
but due to distance.
A record says:
"Mount Tài stands lofty,
but from a hundred lǐ away,
one can't see
a clod of earth—it's too far."
Now, Lǔ is over a thousand lǐ
from Wú;
even if Lí Zhū were to look,
he couldn't see it,
let alone Yán Yuān—
how could he discern it?
If his talent approached that,
with vision surpassing others,
the world should call him second to the sage,
not just mention Lí Zhū.
In human vision,
large objects are easy to detect,
small ones hard to discern.
If Yán Yuān stood outside the Chāng Gate,
looking at Mount Tài's form,
he still couldn't see it,
let alone from atop Mount Tài,
trying to see a white horse's color?
He couldn't see the color,
that's clear.
Not only Yán Yuān couldn't see it,
Confucius couldn't either.
How to verify this?
The functions of ears and eyes
are similar.
If eyes can't see a hundred lǐ,
then ears can't hear that far either.
Lù Jiǎ said:
"With Lí Lóu's keen sight,
he couldn't see through curtains;
with Shī Kuàng's sharp hearing,
he couldn't hear beyond a hundred lǐ."
The distance from Chāng Gate to Mount Tài
isn't merely within curtains
or just a hundred lǐ away.
When King Wǔ of Qín and Mèng Yuè
lifted a cauldron but couldn't bear the weight,
his tendons snapped and he died.
Lifting a cauldron uses strength,
strength comes from sinews,
if the sinews can't endure,
they snap and cause death—
that's logical.
But Yán Yuān using his eyes to see far,
if his eyes couldn't handle the strain of distance,
he should have gone blind,
not had white hair and lost teeth—
that's not the result.
White hair and lost teeth
come from exhausting spirit in study,
laboring without rest,
until energy is depleted,
leading to death.
Bó Qí was exiled,
and his hair turned white early;
the Book of Songs says:
"Worry makes one old."
Bó Qí aged from worry,
while Yán Yuān supposedly from using his eyes—
a brief, sudden glance—
how could that cause this?
Confucian texts say:
Shùn was buried in Cāngwú,
Yǔ in Kuàijī,
because they were on inspection tours, old,
and died in borderlands.
Sages consider the world their home,
not distinguishing far or near,
not separating inner from outer,
so they were buried where they died.
That Shùn and Yǔ
died there is true;
but that they were on tour
is likely false.
Shùn and Yáo,
both being emperors,
shared a domain of five thousand lǐ,
and ruled the same realm within the Four Seas;
the ways of these two emperors
were interconnected and not different.
In the chapter "Yáo Diǎn",
it is recorded that Shùn made an inspection tour east to Dài Zōng,
south to Huò Shān,
west to Tài Huá,
and north to Héng Shān.
These were considered the Four Sacred Mountains,
central to the four directions,
where feudal lords would come
and gather at the foot of the mountains,
so that whether from remote or nearby places,
none would be unseen.
When sages undertake actions,
they seek what is appropriate and fitting.
King Yǔ followed Shùn's example,
changing nothing in the affairs,
and the places he toured
were again the same as Shùn's.
That Shùn went to Cāngwú
and Yǔ reached Kuàijī
is not the truth.
In reality, during the times of Shùn and Yǔ,
the great flood had not yet been controlled.
Yáo passed the throne to Shùn,
who accepted it as emperor,
and together with Yǔ, divided the regions
to manage and control the great flood.
After Yáo passed away,
Shùn grew old
and also passed the throne to Yǔ.
Shùn went south to control the floods
and died in Cāngwú;
Yǔ went east to control the floods
and died in Kuàijī.
Wise sages considered the world as their home,
hence they were buried where they died.
Wú Jūngāo explained:
Kuàijī was originally a mountain's name,
where Xià Yǔ during his inspection tour
held financial audits on this mountain,
thus naming the commandery after it,
hence called Kuàijī.
To say the commandery was named after the mountain is acceptable;
but to say Yǔ held audits on this mountain during his inspection tour
is false.
His inspection tour did not actually reach Kuàijī,
so how could he have held audits there?
If we follow Jūngāo's explanation,
indeed
it
is "Kuàijī" meaning "audit",
but when Yǔ went south,
what audits could he have held?
If Yǔ started east and died in Kuàijī,
and Shùn also toured to Cāngwú,
where did they hold audits?
When the hundred kings had stabilized their rule, they went on inspection tours,
and on tour, they would conduct audits;
then all mountains in the four directions would have been audit sites.
When the hundred kings achieved peace,
they ascended Tài Shān to perform fēng sacrifices.
On Tài Shān,
seventy-two fēng altars are visible,
while countless others
have been lost or destroyed.
If indeed emperors
conducted audits during their tours,
then places of audit
like the fēng sites on Tài Shān
should be numerous in all directions.
The naming of commanderies and states,
like the names of all things,
cannot be fully explained.
Why single out Kuàijī for explanation?
In the Zhōu dynasty, the old names were Wú and Yuè;
to establish names for Wú and Yuè,
where did they come from?
The six states had their names;
what should their origins be like?
There are nearly a hundred commanderies and states in the empire,
over ten thousand counties and towns,
with villages, hamlets, and neighborhoods all having names,
which even the talents of sages cannot fully explain.
Jūngāo could explain Kuàijī,
but could not determine the origins of other names;
thus his audit theory
cannot be followed.
Inspection tours were to examine and correct laws and measures;
in Yǔ's time,
Wú was a land of bare-bodied people,
with cut hair and tattooed bodies,
making inspections useless there—
what audits could be held?
Historical texts say:
When Shùn was buried in Cāngwú,
elephants plowed the land for him;
when Yǔ was buried in Kuàijī,
birds tilled the fields for him.
This was supposedly due to their sage virtue,
with heaven sending birds and beasts to reward and protect them.
The world generally accepts this.
But if we examine the truth,
it is likely a false statement.
The virtue of Shùn and Yǔ
could not surpass that of Yáo.
Yáo was buried in Jìzhōu,
or some say on Chóng Shān.
In Jìzhōu, birds and beasts did not plow,
yet they alone plowed for Shùn and Yǔ;
how partial and inconsistent is heaven's favor?
Some say:
"Shùn and Yǔ
controlled the floods,
never resting in peace,
so Shùn died in Cāngwú,
Yǔ died in Kuàijī.
Their toil and merit
moved heaven to reward them;
being far from the central states,
heaven pitied them."
But if heaven rewarded Shùn and Yǔ
by having birds and elephants till fields,
what benefit was that to them?
If heaven wished to reward Shùn and Yǔ,
it should have made Cāngwú and Kuàijī regularly offer sacrifices to them.
Having birds and beasts plow fields
cannot make people offer sacrifices;
sacrifices would honor Shùn and Yǔ's tombs,
while the tilling benefited the people's homes—
is heaven's way of rewarding sages
so clumsy?
And indeed, of no benefit!
Thus, it can be said
that birds and elephants tilling fields
as a reward for Shùn and Yǔ
is not the truth.
In reality,
Cāngwú is a land with many elephants,
and Kuàijī is where numerous birds dwell.
The "Yǔ Gòng" says:
"Pénglǐ became a marsh,
where the sunny birds dwell."
This is the nature of heaven and earth,
the behavior of birds and beasts.
Elephants naturally tread the earth,
birds naturally peck at grass;
when the soil is turned and grass cleared,
it resembles plowed fields,
with soil soft and mud easy,
people then sow seeds—
common folk call them Shùn and Yǔ's fields.
In Hǎilíng, the fields where elk roam
look like elephant-plowed fields;
has any emperor ever been buried in Hǎilíng?
Historical texts say:
King Fūchāi of Wú killed Wǔ Zǐxū,
boiled him in a cauldron,
then put his body in a leather sack
and threw it into the river.
Zǐxū, filled with rage,
drove the waters to form waves,
drowning people.
Now, in the great river at Kuàijī Dāndū,
and in the Zhèjiāng at Qiántáng,
temples to Zǐxū have been erected.
This is to appease his resentful spirit
and calm his fierce waves.
That King Wú killed Zǐxū
and threw him into the river
is true;
but that his rage drove the waters to form waves
is false.
Qū Yuán, bearing resentment,
threw himself into the Xiāng River,
yet the Xiāng River did not surge;
Shēntú Dí jumped into the Yellow River and died,
yet the Yellow River did not surge.
People might say:
"Qū Yuán and Shēntú Dí were not as brave and fierce,
their anger not as powerful as Zǐxū's."
But when Wèi minced Zǐ Lù's body,
Wǔ Zīxū was brave and fierce,
but not surpassing Zǐlù or Péng Yuè.
Yet these two men could not vent their anger
from within the cauldron,
using boiling soup and pickled juices
to splash upon bystanders.
Wǔ Zīxū was the same;
he first entered the cauldron,
and only afterward entered the river.
While in the cauldron,
where was his spirit dwelling?
Was he perhaps timid in the boiling water
but brave in the river?
Why is it that his wrath
does not match from before to after?
Moreover, into which river was he thrown?
There is the great river at Dāntú,
the Zhèjiāng at Qiántáng,
and the Tōnglíng River in Wú.
Some say he was thrown into the great river at Dāntú,
but it has no tidal bores.
If one claims he was thrown into the Zhèjiāng at Qiántáng,
the Zhèjiāng, Shānyīn River,
and Shàngyú River all have tidal bores.
If these three rivers have bores,
could it be that his body was divided in a sack
and scattered into the three rivers?
If a person holds hatred,
and the enemy is not yet dead,
with descendants remaining,
it is understandable.
But now the state of Wú has perished,
Fūchāi has no heirs,
Wú became the Kuàijī commandery,
established with a governor.
What resentment and bitterness
does the spirit of Wǔ Zīxū still have?
Why does he create unceasing bores,
what is he seeking?
In the time of Wú and Yuè,
they divided the Kuàijī commandery,
with Yuè governing Shānyīn,
and Wú's capital at present-day Wú.
Yújì and south belonged to Yuè,
Qiántáng and north belonged to Wú.
The river at Qiántáng
was the border between the two states.
Shānyīn and Shàngyú were within Yuè's territory.
If Wǔ Zīxū entered the river of Wú to create bores,
they should cease at the border of Wú.
Why would they enter the land of Yuè?
To resent the king of Wú
yet vent anger in the river of Yuè
defies reason—
proof that there is no such spirit.
Moreover, water is hard to drive,
but people are easy to influence.
In life, one relies on physical strength,
in death, on the essence and soul.
When Wǔ Zīxū was alive,
he could not use the living
to protect his own body,
leading to his death.
His strength extinguished,
his essence and soul scattered,
how could he create bores?
Even if there were hundreds or thousands
of beings like Wǔ Zīxū
crossing the river by boat,
they could not traverse the water;
with just Wǔ Zīxū's own body,
boiled in a cauldron,
his bones and flesh dissolved,
turned into soup and pickles,
how could he cause harm?
When King Xuān of Zhōu killed his minister Dù Bó,
and Duke Jiǎn of Yān
killed his minister Zhuāng Zǐyì,
later Dù Bó shot King Xuān,
and Zhuāng Zǐyì harmed Duke Jiǎn.
Though it seems plausible,
it is still a baseless tale.
Now, Wǔ Zīxū, with his body incomplete,
could not do as Dù Bó or Zǐyì did
to take revenge on the king of Wú,
yet he drives water back and forth—
is this the principle of vengeance, proof of awareness?
Common sayings, unfounded,
become recorded in texts,
and such writings
even confuse the wise and sages!
Just as the earth has its hundred streams,
so humans have blood vessels.
Blood flows,
rising and falling in motion,
with its own rhythm.
So too the hundred streams;
their ebb and flow
are like human breathing, the inhale and exhale.
It is the nature of heaven and earth,
existing since ancient times.
The Classic says:
"The Jiāng and Hàn rivers flow to the sea as to a court."
Before the time of Táng and Yú,
when they emerged from the sea,
they merely rippled and flowed;
entering the three rivers,
where it is narrow and shallow,
the water churns and boils up,
hence surging into bores.
The curved river at Guǎnglíng has bores,
which literati have described in rhapsodies.
The great river is vast and wide,
yet the curved river has bores
precisely because it is narrow.
If Wú killed him,
why create bores at Guǎnglíng?
The spirit of Wǔ Zīxū
must be unaware indeed.
In deep valleys and streams,
the flow is calm and broad;
where shallow with sand and stones,
it churns into rapids.
Bores and rapids
are of the same nature.
If Wǔ Zīxū is blamed for bores,
then who creates the rapids in the valleys?
Consider:
when bores enter the three rivers,
the banks seethe and surge,
while the center is silent.
If it must be Wǔ Zīxū causing bores,
does his body gather at the banks?
The rise of bores
follows the moon's wax and wane,
varying in size and fullness.
If Wǔ Zīxū makes the bores,
does his anger
pace itself by the moon?
When winds blow on the three rivers,
the waves of Yánghóu also drown people.
Is the spirit of Wǔ Zīxū
also creating the wind?
When Qín Shǐhuáng crossed the Xiāng River
and encountered a storm,
he asked what shrine was on Xiāng Mountain.
His attendants replied:
"The daughters of Yáo,
wives of Shùn."
The First Emperor was enraged,
sent three thousand convicts
to cut down the trees of Xiāng Mountain and trample them.
To say Wǔ Zīxū's spirit makes bores
is like saying the two women's essences make the wind.
The transmitted texts say:
Confucius was buried facing the Sì River,
and the Sì River receded.
This claims Confucius's virtue
could make the water retreat,
not erode his tomb.
The world believes it.
Hence, Confucian scholars in their discourses
all say that Confucius deserved enfeoffment posthumously,
citing the Sì River's recession as proof.
But upon examination,
it is likely a falsehood.
In death, how does Confucius compare to his living self?
In life, he could conduct himself,
carefully follow the Way, and respond to Heaven;
in death, his conduct ceases.
Heaven blesses ultimate virtue.
Thus, the Five Emperors and Three Kings attracted auspicious signs
all during their lifetimes,
not after death.
When Confucius was alive,
he was pushed aside and not accepted,
hence he sighed:
"The phoenix does not come,
the river gives forth no chart—
it is all over with me!"
If he had no blessing in life,
would he have retribution after death?
Confucius's death
is like that of the Five Emperors and Three Kings.
If they had no posthumous blessing,
how could Confucius alone receive heavenly reward?
Would that mean Confucius's soul is divine,
while the essences of the Five Emperors are not?
The Sì River, unknowing,
receded for Confucius—
was it made by a heavenly god?
Then why, when
Confucius was alive,
did the heavenly spirits not make people revere him?
As for the Sìshuǐ River flowing backward,
if Heaven wished to enfeoff Confucius' descendants,
Confucius during his lifetime, with virtues matching Heaven's will,
why would Heaven not enfeoff him personally,
but instead desire to enfeoff his descendants?
This was probably just the river occasionally flowing backward on its own.
The flow of rivers
has places where it reverses;
the courses of all streams
sometimes change paths and alter routes,
no different from flowing backward.
Thus the Sìshuǐ flowing backward
cannot be considered supernatural.
Transmitted texts claim:
The virtue of Lord Wèi Gōngzǐ
was benevolent and gracious to subordinates,
extending even to birds and beasts.
While drinking with guests,
a hawk attacked a dove;
the dove fled
and circled under the lord's table.
The hawk pursued and struck,
killing it before the lord.
The lord felt shamed by this,
immediately had many nets set up,
captured dozens of hawks,
and reproached them for the crime of attacking the dove.
The hawk that had attacked the dove
bowed its head, not daring to look up,
so the lord killed it.
People praised him, saying:
"Lord Wèi avenged the dove."
This is false.
Now hawks are animals
with different natures and minds;
their sounds and language are unintelligible.
Even sages cannot make birds and beasts act according to moral principles.
What kind of person was the lord,
that he could make hawks bow their heads and confess?
Hawks number
in the tens of thousands - if they had flown away after attacking the dove,
how could they be caught again?
If they could bow their heads and confess,
they would be sage birds;
if they understood the lord's words,
they would have known his character.
Knowing his character,
they would not have attacked the dove before him.
Even humans struggle to correct their faults;
birds differ from humans -
to claim they can repent
is merely vulgar talk
that misses the truth about creatures.
Perhaps the lord actually captured hawks,
and when caught,
people held their heads,
bending and breaking their necks,
causing them to droop in pain,
unable to look up.
Because the lord was a benevolent man,
people praised him,
saying the hawks admitted their fault.
In the course of storytelling,
empty false praises arise;
beneath fame and achievement,
often untruthful additions accumulate.
Transmitted texts say:
Duke Huán of Qí married seven of his aunts and sisters.
This is false.
To disrupt kinship bonds,
violate relatives,
and lack proper hierarchy
is the nature of beasts,
who disrupt relationships unknowingly.
Consider:
Duke Huán assembled the feudal lords nine times,
unifying the world once,
guiding with virtue,
leading with authority,
thus making the feudal lords submit,
none daring to disobey -
this couldn't be done by one consumed with bestial nature and internal disorder.
To lead feudal lords in serving the royal house
shames those above without power and below without propriety.
If he felt shame externally about lost propriety,
why would he internally violate propriety and undermine himself?
If external and internal didn't match,
his achievements would fail and authority wouldn't stand.
People speak of the evils of Jié and Zhòu,
but never mention incest with relatives.
Truthful accounts say
Jié and Zhòu's evils were lesser than the fallen Qín's,
the fallen Qín's faults slighter than Wáng Mǎng's,
yet none are accused of sexual impropriety.
If Duke Huán married seven aunts and sisters,
his evil would exceed Jié and Zhòu's,
and his faults outweigh Qín and Wáng Mǎng's.
The Spring and Autumn Annals records tiny virtues
and condemns minute faults;
if Duke Huán's evil was great,
why wasn't he condemned?
Wén Jiāng of Lǔ
was Duke Xiāng of Qí's sister,
with whom Duke Xiāng had an affair.
The Spring and Autumn Annals states:
"In winter of the second year of Zhuāng, the Lady Jiāng met the Marquis of Qí at Gào."
Why did the Spring and Autumn Annals blame Duke Xiāng,
recording his adultery?
Why spare Duke Huán,
concealing and not censuring him?
If the classic omitted this,
why did commentators like Zuǒ Qiūmíng, Gōngyáng, and Gǔliáng also avoid mentioning it?
Examining Duke Huán's faults: he had many consorts,
six favored ladies treated as wives.
Five sons contended for succession,
Qí fell into chaos,
and his death was announced only three months later.
People heard of six favored ladies
and unclear distinctions between primary and secondary wives,
then exaggerated it to seven aunts and sisters.
Transmitted texts say:
Duke Huán of Qí carried a woman on his back while receiving feudal lords.
This suggests extreme lewdness and impropriety in Duke Huán.
Now, during grand audiences,
if he carried a woman on his back,
what worse could he do
during banquets and excursions?
While cultivating scholarly rites
and promoting solemn respect,
how could he lead feudal lords
in serving the royal house with a woman on his back?
At the Kuíqiū assembly,
Duke Huán acted arrogantly,
and nine states rebelled then.
If mere displeasure
made nine states rebel,
how much more would they reject carrying a woman and lewd behavior?
Some say:
"Guǎn Zhòng told the feudal lords
'My lord has a boil on his back;
without a woman,
the sore won't heal.'
The feudal lords believed Guǎn Zhòng,
so none rebelled."
But in a village of ten households,
there must be loyalty and honesty like Confucius.
Among the feudal lords then, with over a thousand men,
some must have known methods
to cure boils without women -
Guǎn Zhòng was covering for his lord.
If the lords knew Guǎn Zhòng was deceiving them for his lord,
they would have angrily rebelled;
how then could he long assemble them
and achieve hegemony?
Some say:
"Duke Huán was truly unprincipled,
but employed the worthy minister Guǎn Zhòng,
thus hegemoning the world."
But unprincipled people
differ little from madmen;
they trust slanderers, shun the worthy,
and harm benevolence and righteousness -
how could such employ Guǎn Zhòng?
Could they nurture people
and accomplish deeds? Consider:
Jié executed Guān Lóngpáng,
Zhòu killed Prince Bǐgān.
Unprincipled rulers cannot employ the worthy.
Had Guǎn Zhòng been worthy,
Duke Huán couldn't have used him;
since he used Guǎn Zhòng,
we know Duke Huán had no disorderly conduct.
Where there are wise rulers,
there are loyal ministers.
Ministers' worthiness
proves rulers' wisdom;
how can this be called disorder?
The objection states:
"Duke Líng of Wèi was an unprincipled ruler,
yet he recognized worthy ministers in his time.
With Guǎn Zhòng as his minister,
how can one claim Duke Huán did not engage in disorderly conduct?"
Now, Duke Líng being unprincipled,
employed three ministers
merely to avoid losing his state,
which was not a true achievement.
Duke Huán honored the man who knew the multiplication table,
raised Níng Qì from beneath a cart,
demanded the tribute of bundled thatch grass,
deployed troops to attack Chǔ,
nine times assembled the feudal lords,
and unified the world under one standard—
a ruler who appears once in a thousand generations.
Yet it is said he carried a woman on his back—
this is false.
Commentators on the Shàngshū say:
"When the Duke of Zhōu acted as regent,
he wore the sash of the Son of Heaven,
donned the crown of the Son of Heaven,
and faced south with his back to the yǐ screen to receive the feudal lords in audience."
The space between the door and window is called yǐ,
the position for the south-facing seat.
To sit facing south with one's back to the yǐ screen
means the screen is behind.
When Duke Huán received the feudal lords,
he sometimes sat facing south,
with a woman standing behind him.
When transmitted in popular accounts,
it became 'carrying a woman on his back.'
This is like the sayings about Kuí having one foot or Sòng Dīnggōng digging a well and getting a person.
In the time of Táng and Yú,
Kuí served as a senior official,
naturally knowledgeable in music,
and skilled at creating moving melodies.
People of that time said:
"For tuning music, one Kuí is enough."
Popular tradition then spread:
"Kuí had one foot."
Consider that when the position of Zhìzōng was vacant,
Emperor Shùn broadly sought candidates,
and the multitude recommended Bó Yí,
but Bó Yí bowed and yielded to Kuí and Lóng.
The Zhìzōng is a ministerial post,
equivalent to the Zōngzhèng in Hàn times.
Having a severed foot
does not fit with reason.
Moreover, what use is a one-footed man
for walking about?
When Xiàhòu Kǒng Jiǎ was hunting at Fù Mountain in Dōngyáng,
the sky darkened with rain,
and he entered a commoner's home,
where the host was giving birth.
Some said:
"Since the ruler has come, this child will surely be noble."
Others said:
"If he cannot endure it, this child will surely be lowly."
Kǒng Jiǎ said:
"As my child,
who could make him lowly?"
So he took the child away with him.
When splitting rafters,
an axe cut the child's foot,
and he ended up as a gatekeeper.
Kǒng Jiǎ's desire to ennoble the child
had ample power behind it;
but with a severed foot, it was inappropriate,
so he became a gatekeeper.
Now if Kuí had one foot,
unable to walk,
he could still sit and tune music—
that would be feasible;
but for the post of Zhìzōng,
one foot is unsuitable,
just as a gatekeeper with a severed foot
cannot be ennobled.
Thus, Kǒng Jiǎ could not ennoble his child,
and Bó Yí could not have yielded to Kuí.
As for Sòng Dīnggōng,
he was a man of Sòng.
Before digging his well,
he often had to fetch water from others,
which, by calculation,
cost him one person's labor each day.
After digging his own well,
he no longer needed to fetch water elsewhere,
which, by calculation,
saved him one person's labor each day.
Hence it was said:
"Sòng Dīnggōng dug a well and got one person."
But popular tradition says:
"Dīnggōng dug a well and got a person from inside the well."
Now people are born from people,
not from the earth.
Digging into the earth to make a well
cannot produce a person.
Extending this reasoning,
the tale of carrying a woman
is of the same kind.
If he sat with a woman behind him,
it was said she was on his back;
knowing that having a woman on his back is improper,
then arose Guǎn Zhòng's words about using a woman to treat an abscess.
Supposing Duke Huán used a woman to remove his undergarments,
with the woman on his back,
female energy could cure the sore—thus using a woman to treat an abscess.
But while receiving the feudal lords,
Duke Huán wore heavy robes,
the woman was covered by skirts,
the female energy was separated,
so what good would carrying her do?
Duke Huán longed for scholars,
lighting courtyard torches and sitting late into the night
to attract them with his thoughts;
would he instead carry a woman in broad daylight to meet the feudal lords?
Transmitted texts say: Niè Zhèng assassinated the King of Hán for Yán Wēngzhòng.
This is false.
In Niè Zhèng's time,
the ruler of Hán was Marquis Liè.
In the third year of Marquis Liè,
Niè Zhèng assassinated the Hán minister Xiá Lěi.
In the twelfth year
Marquis Liè died,
so from the time of Niè Zhèng's killing of Xiá Lěi
seventeen years had passed;
yet it is said Niè Zhèng assassinated the King of Hán—
such brief texts and minor traditions
are ultimately false and unreliable.
Transmitted texts also say:
Yān Prince Dān sent the assassin Jīng Kē to kill the King of Qín, but he failed,
and was executed.
Later, Gāo Jiànlí again saw the King of Qín by playing the zhù,
and the King of Qín was pleased with him;
learning he was a retainer of Prince Dān of Yān,
he had his eyes put out,
and made him play the zhù.
Gāo Jiànlí then placed lead in the zhù to make it heavy,
and when playing it,
as the King of Qín leaned forward on his knees,
unable to restrain himself,
Gāo Jiànlí struck the King of Qín's forehead with the zhù.
The King of Qín was wounded and ill, and died after three months.
Now, that Gāo Jiànlí struck the King of Qín with the zhù
is true;
but that he hit the King of Qín, who was wounded and died after three months,
is false.
For the King of Qín
was Qín Shǐ Huáng.
In the twentieth year of his reign,
Prince Dān of Yān sent Jīng Kē to assassinate Shǐ Huáng,
and Shǐ Huáng killed Kē—this is clear.
In the twenty-first year,
he sent General Wáng Jiǎn to attack Yān,
and obtained the prince's head;
in the twenty-fifth year,
he then attacked Yān and captured King Xǐ of Yān.
Later, it is unclear in which year,
Gāo Jiànlí struck Shǐ Huáng with the zhù but missed,
and was executed.
In the thirty-seventh year,
while touring the empire,
he reached Kuàijī,
went to Lángyá,
north to Láo and Shèng Mountains,
along the sea,
west to Píngyuán Ford, where he fell ill,
reached Shāqiū Flat Terrace,
and Shǐ Huáng passed away.
Now, prognostic texts say Shǐ Huáng returned
and died at Shāqiū;
transmitted texts also say he was ill from the zhù wound for three months and died in Qín.
For one person, Shǐ Huáng,
some say he died at Shāqiū,
others say he died in Qín,
and regarding his death, they consistently mention the sore.
The words of transmitted texts
often lose touch with reality,
and ordinary people cannot ascertain the truth.
Transmitted texts say:
In the time of Duke Jǐng of Sòng,
Mars guarded the Heart constellation.
The duke, afraid,
summoned Zǐ Wéi and asked him:
"Mars is in the Heart—
Zǐ Wéi said:
"The Mars,
is Heaven's punishment;
the Heart constellation,
corresponds to the territory of Sòng,
the calamity should befall the ruler.
Nevertheless,
it can be transferred to the prime minister."
The Duke said:
"The prime minister is appointed to govern the state,
to transfer death onto him,
is inauspicious."
Zǐ Wéi said:
"It can be transferred to the people."
The Duke said:
"If the people die,
whom would I be ruler over?
I would rather die alone!"
Zǐ Wéi said:
"It can be transferred to the harvest."
The Duke said:
"If the people starve, they will surely die.
For a ruler to seek to kill his people to save himself,
who would then accept me as their ruler?
This means my fate is indeed at its end,
you need not speak further!"
Zǐ Wéi stepped back,
faced north and bowed twice, saying:
"I dare to congratulate you, my lord.
Heaven, though high, hears what is below;
you have spoken three times as a true ruler should,
Heaven will surely reward you thrice.
Tonight, the star will certainly move three lunar mansions,
and you will extend your life by twenty-one years."
The Duke said:
"How do you know this?"
He replied:
"You have uttered three benevolent statements,
hence there will be three rewards,
the star must move three times,
three moves cover seven stars,
each star represents one year,
three times seven makes twenty-one,
thus your life is extended by twenty-one years.
I request to kneel at the foot of the steps
to observe it;
if the star does not move,
I am willing to die."
That night,
the Mars indeed moved three lunar mansions.
If Zǐ Wéi's words are true,
then the extension of life was indeed twenty-one years.
If the star's movement is certain, then life is extended;
if life extension is clear, then Duke Jǐng did good,
and Heaven blessed him.
Then, if people in the world
can act as Duke Jǐng did,
they must receive the same blessings as Duke Jǐng.
But these words are false.
Why so?
If August Heaven transferred its anger,
making Mars target Duke Jǐng personally
due to his own misdeeds, then even listening to Zǐ Wéi's advice,
would be of no avail.
If it were not for Duke Jǐng's actions,
then even ignoring Zǐ Wéi's words,
would cause no harm.
When Duke Jǐng of Qí saw a comet,
he sent someone to perform an exorcism.
Yàn Zǐ said:
"It is useless,
only self-deception.
The Way of Heaven is not obscure,
it does not change its decrees,
how can exorcism alter it?
Moreover, the comet in heaven
serves to sweep away filth.
If you have no corrupt virtue,
why exorcise it?
If your virtue is corrupt,
what good is exorcism?
The Book of Songs says:
'Only this King Wén,
was cautious and reverent,
clearly serving God,
thus securing much happiness;
his virtue was without deviation,
so he received the states from all quarters.'
If you have no deviant virtue,
the states will come to you,
why worry about a comet?
The Book of Songs also says:
'I have nothing to mirror,
but the Xià and Shāng dynasties;
due to their disorder,
the people ultimately fled.'
If virtue is deviant and chaotic,
the people will flee,
and the prayers of priests
cannot remedy it."
The Duke was pleased,
and stopped the ritual.
The ruler of Qí wishing to avert the comet's omen,
is like Zǐ Wéi wanting to transfer Mars's calamity;
the Sòng ruler not heeding him,
is like Yàn Zǐ refusing to comply.
Thus, the Qí ruler acted as Zǐ Wéi did,
and Yàn Zǐ as the Sòng ruler.
Facing similar omens and calamities,
the same situation with two individuals,
if Heaven favored the Sòng ruler,
making Mars move three mansions,
extending his life twenty-one years,
why not also praise Yàn Zǐ,
causing the comet to vanish and increasing his lifespan?
Why does Heaven's blessing of the good
appear so inconsistent and uneven?
If a ruler has good words and deeds,
good deeds arise from the heart,
good words come from intent,
sharing the same source and root,
of one vital breath without difference.
Duke Jǐng of Sòng uttered three good statements,
so before these three statements,
he must have had good conduct.
Having good conduct,
he must have had good governance.
With good governance, auspicious signs gather,
and blessings arrive;
then Mars would have no reason to target the Heart constellation.
If Duke Jǐng had erroneous conduct,
leading to bad governance,
with bad governance emerging,
then monstrous anomalies appear,
and Mars
targeting the Heart,
is like grain growing in the court.
King Gāo Zōng eliminated the omen of the mulberry and grain,
through governance, not words;
Duke Jǐng repelling the Mars anomaly,
should also be by action.
If Duke Jǐng had bad conduct,
hence Mars targeted the Heart.
Without reforming governance and conduct,
merely uttering three good statements,
how could that move Heaven?
Why would Heaven respond?
How to verify this?
If Duke Jǐng had uttered three evil statements,
could that make Mars target the Heart?
If three evil statements cannot make Mars target the Heart,
how can three good ones make Mars retreat three mansions?
If three good statements grant twenty-one years,
then with a hundred good statements,
would one gain a thousand-year lifespan?
This is not the intent of Heaven blessing the good,
nor the reality of sincerity bringing fortune.
Zǐ Wéi's words:
"Heaven, though high, hears what is below;
you have spoken three times as a ruler should,
Heaven will surely reward you thrice."
But Heaven is a physical body,
no different from Earth.
All physical beings
have ears attached to their heads.
For a body and ears to be separate,
has never been.
Heaven's distance from humans,
is tens of thousands of miles high;
even if ears were attached to Heaven,
to hear words from tens of thousands of miles away,
would be impossible.
If one sits in a tower,
observing ants on the ground,
one cannot even see their bodies clearly,
how could one hear their sounds?
Why so?
Ants' bodies are tiny,
unlike human forms in size;
their sounds and breath cannot travel far.
Now Heaven's loftiness is far greater than a tower;
the human body compared to Heaven,
is not like ants to humans.
To claim Heaven is not like ants to humans, yet say Heaven hears human words,
and responds with fortune or misfortune based on good or evil,
is erroneous.
When barbarians enter the central states,
they communicate through interpreters.
Though of similar form and breath,
their language is not understood;
even the Five Emperors and Three Kings,
could not understand barbarians without interpreters,
let alone Heaven and humans
having different bodies, and sounds distinct from humans?
If humans do not understand what Heaven does,
how can Heaven know human conduct?
If Heaven has a physical body,
its ears are too high to hear human speech;
if Heaven is composed of qì,
qì is like clouds and smoke—
how could it listen to human words?
Proponents of calamity theories claim:
"Humans between Heaven and Earth
are like fish in water.
Their ability to affect Heaven and Earth through actions
resembles fish stirring and rippling water.
When fish move, water trembles, and qì changes."
This is not factual.
Even if it were true,
it couldn't reach Heaven.
A foot-long fish
moving in water
disturbs only the surrounding water
within a few feet.
At most comparable to humans,
the ripples extend merely a hundred paces,
while beyond one lǐ, the water remains calm and clear—
due to the distance.
Now if human conduct alters qì, the range
should match that of fish;
qì responding to changes
should be analogous to water.
With a seven-chǐ delicate form
and subtle qì within,
it's no more than steam from a cauldron's fire—
to change the august Heaven from below—
how impossibly lofty!
Moreover, Duke Jǐng was a worthy man,
whose conduct
fell short of sages above
but exceeded villains below.
Among sages, none surpass Yáo and Shùn;
among villains, none exceed Jié and Zhòu.
Yáo and Shùn's conduct was mostly virtuous,
yet it never shifted Mars' course;
Jié and Zhòu's governance was mostly evil,
but contrary evidence exists like Duke Jǐng escaping harm.
Duke Jǐng uttered three good statements,
gaining twenty-one years of life—
then Yáo and Shùn should have obtained millennia,
while Jié and Zhòu should have died young.
Yet reality differs:
each followed their natural lifespan,
Yáo, Shùn, Jié, and Zhòu all lived nearly a century.
This proves Zǐwéi's words false
and the life-extension claim groundless.
Furthermore, Zǐwéi stated:
"Mars
is Heaven's envoy;
the Heart constellation
governs Sòng's domain,
so disaster befalls the ruler."
If so,
when Heaven sent Mars
to inflict disaster on Duke Jǐng,
how could it be transferred to generals or ministers,
or to the year and citizens?
Heaven possessing Mars
is like the king having feudal lords.
If a vassal lord commits a capital crime,
the king sends lords to besiege his state.
Should the ruler inquire about blame among subjects,
and subjects clarify the ruler's guilt,
even then,
could it be shifted to ministers or people?
Suppose the ruler accepts
their words,
ordering subjects to blame the state.
Would the feudal lords, hearing this,
consent to their plea,
pardon the ruler's crime,
and transfer it to the citizens?
If the lords refuse,
it's the ruler's own fault,
not the people's innocence.
Since lords won't comply due to the ruler's guilt,
how would Mars shift disaster to the people?
Thus, Zǐwéi's words are absurd.
It is said:
"Had Duke Jǐng heeded the words,
how could it move Heaven?"
If a vassal lord ignores his minister's advice
and takes the blame himself,
would the feudal lords, upon hearing,
pardon him and depart?
If they don't pardon the lord's crime,
how would Mars retreat three segments?
Whether heeding or not,
neither brings blessing—
the claim of Mars moving
is unreliable.
Heaven and humans share principles,
with similar likes and dislikes;
if human principles don't apply,
then Heaven's are unverifiable.
When Sòng, Wèi, Chén, and
Zhèng suffered disasters together,
qì changes appeared in Heaven.
Zǐshèn recognized it
and appealed to Zǐchǎn for remedies,
but Zǐchǎn refused.
Heaven's way was inevitable;
human efforts couldn't avert it.
Had Zǐchǎn heeded Zǐshèn,
could the four states avoid disaster?
When Yáo faced great floods,
there must have been ministers like Zǐshèn or
Zǐwéi in wisdom,
yet they didn't prevent it—
for Yáo and Zǐchǎn were of like mind.
Examining Zǐwéi's words:
"Mars is Heaven's envoy;
the Heart constellation
governs Sòng's domain,
so disaster befalls the ruler."
If this holds true,
disaster is unavoidable,
and the star unstoppable.
As for imbalances in cold and heat,
or untimely winds and rains,
governance theorists
attribute them to faults,
claiming good governance and virtuous acts
can restore them.
But if Mars stations in Heart,
impending death or ruin,
how can disaster be removed?
Can improving governance and conduct
repel it?
If even good governance and virtuous acts
cannot avert it,
then uttering three empty words,
claiming the star recedes and disaster lifts,
prolonging life,
enjoying lasting fortune—
is erroneous.
Considering Zǐwéi's words to Duke Jǐng,
the disaster from Mars
isn't like weather changes
but an omen of death and demise.
When a state nears collapse,
and a ruler approaches death,
ominous signs appear in Heaven,
and complexion shows on the face.
Once the face bears this hue,
even good conduct cannot erase it—
the death omen is already visible.
As bodily signs
can't be removed by words or deeds,
how can celestial portents
be eliminated through governance?
When a person is ill and dying,
with signs on the face,
some might say:
"This is a sure sign of death.
Nevertheless,
it can be transferred to five neighbors
or to servants."
But a doomed person's
fate cannot be averted—
would the complexion fade due to good words,
and would the doomed life be extended?
Qì cannot be erased,
life cannot be prolonged—
so how could Mars be repelled?
How could Duke Jǐng's life be extended?
Hence, it follows that
Mars stationing in Heart
had unknown causes,
so Duke Jǐng did not die.
Moreover, what does
"the star moved three segments" mean?
Did the star move three times within one segment,
or once across three segments?
Zǐwéi stated:
"If the ruler speaks three ruler-like words,
Heaven will reward him thrice.
Tonight, the star will move three segments."
Thus, the star moved three segments outright.
If Duke Jǐng, in one session,
uttered three good statements
and the star moved three segments,
would ten good statements
make it move ten segments?
If Mars stationing in Heart
retreats due to good words,
should Duke Jǐng utter three evil statements,
would Mars devour the Heart constellation?
When good words are spoken, it retreats;
when evil words are spoken, it advances.
If there are neither good nor evil words,
where does the Mars reside without moving?
Sometimes Mars lingers near the Heart constellation, causing drought,
but not necessarily the death of the ruler.
Zǐ Wéi did not understand this,
mistaking it as an omen of death,
believing in the popular notion of sincere influence.
The position of Mars
among the stars would inevitably shift on its own;
Lord Jǐng did not die naturally,
so the world assumed Zǐ Wéi's words were accurate
and Lord Jǐng's sincerity moved heaven.
Alternatively, perhaps Zǐ Wéi
knew the star's course would naturally shift,
and attributed it to his own wisdom,
highlighting the mutual deference between ruler and minister.
Observing the star moved seven lunar lodges,
he claimed it retreated seven lodges,
thus granting twenty-one more years of life.
Using the star's lodges to calculate years
is no different from the diviner of Qí.
Lord Jǐng of Qí asked his diviner:
"What can your art achieve?"
The diviner replied:
"I can make the earth shake."
Yànzǐ went to see the lord,
who said:
"I asked the diviner,
'What can your art do?'
He replied,
'I can make the earth shake.'
Can the earth truly be shaken?"
Yànzǐ remained silent without answering.
Upon leaving, he met the diviner and said:
"Previously, I saw the Hooked Star
between the Room and Heart constellations,
will the earth shake then?"
The diviner said:
"Yes."
After Yànzǐ left,
the diviner hurried to see the lord,
saying: "I cannot actually shake the earth;
the earth was going to move on its own."
Thus, Zǐ Wéi's claim about the star moving
is like the diviner's claim about the earth shaking.
The earth was about to move anyway,
yet the diviner said he could shake it;
the star was destined to shift on its own,
yet Zǐ Wéi claimed the ruler could move it.
Had Yànzǐ not mentioned the Hooked Star between Room and Heart,
the diviner's deceitful response would have gone unnoticed.
Sòng lacked a minister as wise as Yànzǐ,
so Zǐ Wéi's single statement
succeeded in his deception.
Examining Zǐ Wéi's "Shū Lù Xù Zòu",
it also states: "Zǐ Wéi said,
'If the lord utters three good statements,
Mars ought to move.'
They then awaited it,
and it indeed shifted lodges."
It does not mention "three".
Perhaps the star was going to leave on its own,
and Zǐ Wéi took it as verification,
claiming it actually moved away from its lodge.
Later generations added the word "three".
Not only did they falsely increase it to three lodges,
but also fabricated twenty-one years of extended life.
During the time of Emperor Gāozōng of Yīn,
mulberry and grain trees grew together in the court,
reaching full arm-span in seven days.
Gāozōng summoned his minister to inquire,
who said:
"Although I know,
I cannot speak of it."
He then asked Zǔ Jǐ.
Zǔ Jǐ said:
"Mulberry and grain trees
are wild grasses,
yet they grow in the court.
Does this mean the court will perish?"
Gāozōng was frightened,
humbled himself and practiced virtuous governance,
reflecting on the policies of former kings,
clarifying the principles of honoring the elderly,
restoring destroyed states,
continuing severed lineages,
and reinstating neglected people. The mulberry and grain then vanished.
Three years later,
six states came to pay tribute through interpreters,
and he enjoyed blessings for a hundred years.
Gāozōng was a worthy ruler,
moved by the growth of mulberry and grain
to consult Zǔ Jǐ.
He followed Zǔ Jǐ's advice,
improved governance and amended conduct,
causing the ominous sign to disappear,
and secured long-lasting tribute from feudal lords.
His dedication to virtuous acts was profound,
hence the auspicious response and abundant blessings.
This is a false account.
Zǔ Jǐ claimed
the court would perish!
But if a court is destined to fall,
it is like a person destined to die.
When a person nears death,
strange occurrences appear;
when a state nears collapse,
its time is up.
Once a person dies, life ends;
death cannot be reversed,
nor can a perished state be restored.
What benefit could Zǔ Jǐ's political advice
have in preventing destruction?
How could Gāozōng's self-improvement
avert disaster?
If a commoner sees omens and cultivates goodness,
it cannot bring good fortune;
if Gāozōng sees a portent and reforms governance,
how could it eliminate calamity?
If it cannot even remove calamity,
how could it attract six states
and extend life for a hundred years?
Thus, a person's life or death
depends on their destined lifespan,
not on the goodness or evil of their actions;
a state's survival or fall
depends on the length of its allotted time,
not on the merits or faults of its governance.
Consider
Zǔ Jǐ's divination:
the mulberry and grain were omens of destruction,
the signs of ruin had already appeared.
Even if filial conduct were cultivated,
what good would it do?
How can this be verified?
During the time of Duke Zhāo of Lǔ,
magpies came to nest,
and Shī Jǐ recalled nursery rhymes from the eras of Dukes Wén and Chéng that mentioned magpies.
Seeing the nesting as fulfillment,
he interpreted it as an ill omen.
Later,
Duke Zhāo was expelled by the Jì family,
fled to Qí,
and the state indeed became empty.
The capital had signs of emptiness,
hence wild birds came to nest;
Shī Jǐ assessed it,
and the disaster unfolded as divined.
Had Duke Zhāo heard Shī Jǐ's words
and cultivated virtue, reformed governance for the better,
emulating Gāozōng's conduct,
it still would not have averted the outcome.
Why?
The omen of the magpies had already emerged,
the calamity of exile was already destined.
The sign of the magpies
had already appeared in the eras of Dukes Wén and Chéng.
If the root exists,
how can the leaves not flourish?
If the source flows,
how can the stream not widen?
This example is relatively recent,
but insufficient to fully illustrate the point.
When the Xià dynasty was declining,
two dragons fought in the courtyard,
spewed saliva and left.
The Xià king stored it in a case.
After Xià fell, it passed to Yīn;
after Yīn fell, it passed to Zhōu,
none opening it.
Until King Yōu's time,
it was opened and viewed,
the saliva flowing into the courtyard,
transforming into a black turtle,
entering the rear palace,
mating with a woman,
and thus Bāo Sì was born.
The silk threads are like yin and yang,
and the silk fabric is like ripe grain.
Giving someone silk is not considered bad;
so why is it considered inauspicious when Heaven grants grain?
The auspiciousness or inauspiciousness of raining grain cannot be determined,
and the claims about mulberry and grain are not necessarily reliable.
If the chàng grass had grown during the Zhōu dynasty,
when the world was at peace,
and the Wō people came to present chàng grass,
chàng grass is also a wild plant—
how is it different from the mulberry and grain?
If it is considered auspicious because barbarians offered it,
but had the chàng grass grown in the Zhōu court,
would it have been deemed inauspicious?
Chàng grass can be used for brewing,
and its fragrance spreads widely; before sacrifices, it is used to pour libations and invite the spirits.
If it had grown naturally in the Zhōu court,
it would have been no different from auspicious grain, vermilion grass,
and the calendrical plant.
Moreover, mulberry leaves feed silkworms,
silkworms produce silk,
silk becomes fabric,
fabric becomes clothing,
and clothing is worn in ancestral temples as court robes—
no different from chàng grass.
Why then is it called inauspicious?
When the crown prince of Duke Xiàn of Wèi went to the Língtái,
a snake coiled around the left wheel of his carriage.
The driver said:
"Your Highness, dismount and bow.
I have heard that when a snake coils around the left wheel of a carriage for the son of a ruler,
he will quickly gain the state."
The crown prince then did not proceed
and returned to his residence.
The driver went to see the crown prince,
and the crown prince said:
"I have heard that as a son,
one should be completely obedient to the ruler,
not act on personal desires,
respectfully carry out commands,
and not disrupt the ruler's peace.
If I were to gain the state now,
it would mean the ruler loses his peace.
To seek the state's benefit
and forget the ruler's peace
is not the way of a son;
to gain the state by bowing
is not the ruler's wish.
To abandon the way of a son is unfilial;
to oppose the ruler's wish is disloyal.
To ask me to do this
is likely because you desire our state's peril to be evident."
He drew his sword to kill himself,
and though his driver tried to stop him, he could not prevent it;
thus, he fell on his sword and died.
If the snake coiling around the left wheel
truly meant the crown prince would quickly gain the state,
then the crown prince should not have died,
and Duke Xiàn should have swiftly passed away.
But Duke Xiàn did not die,
and the crown prince fell on his sword;
thus, the driver's prediction
was a false popular belief.
Perhaps the snake was an omen of the crown prince's impending death,
but the driver, trusting the common divination,
misjudged the reality of auspiciousness and inauspiciousness.
The appearance of mulberry and grain
is similar to the snake coiling around the left wheel.
The snake was actually inauspicious,
but the driver thought it auspicious;
the mulberry and grain were actually auspicious,
but Zǔ Jǐ considered them inauspicious.
When Yǔ crossed the river southward,
a yellow dragon bore the boat on its back,
and the people in the boat
turned pale with fear.
But Yǔ laughed and declared:
"I have received my mandate from Heaven,
striving to toil for the myriad people.
Life is but a sojourn;
death is a return home.
Death is a return home;
why should it disturb harmony?
I see the dragon as no more than a lizard."
The dragon left, and no disaster occurred.
Consider that
throughout history, the appearance of a dragon has always been auspicious,
yet Yǔ alone called the yellow dragon inauspicious
because he saw it bearing the boat
and the fear of the people aboard.
Comparing mulberry and grain to the dragon,
though their auspiciousness is opposite,
the situations are similar.
Wild plants growing in the court
are still considered inauspicious,
perhaps because, like the strange event of the yellow dragon bearing the boat,
they were actually auspicious, and thus the Yīn dynasty did not fall.
When Duke Wén of Jìn was about to battle
King Chéng of Chǔ at Chéngpú,
a comet appeared over Chǔ,
and Chǔ held its handle.
He asked Jiù Fàn about it.
Jiù Fàn replied:
"In fighting with a comet,
the one who turns it upside down will win."
Duke Wén dreamed he was wrestling with King Chéng,
and King Chéng was on top,
sucking his brains.
He asked Jiù Fàn,
and Jiù Fàn said:
"You have gained Heaven's favor,
and King Chéng is submitting to his crime;
you will surely win the battle greatly."
Duke Wén followed his advice
and severely defeated the Chǔ army.
Had he consulted a mediocre minister instead,
the answer would surely have been
that he could not win.
Why?
Because comets are not auspicious,
and being pinned in wrestling is not inauspicious.
The divination about mulberry and grain,
interpreted as inauspicious,
is like Jìn facing the comet's tail and being pinned down as inauspicious.
Yet it turned auspicious,
perhaps due to a clever response like addressing the comet or seeing Heaven's favor,
so King Gāozōng reigned long,
and the Yīn dynasty did not fall.
If Duke Wén had not consulted Jiù Fàn,
and Jiù Fàn had not clarified the auspiciousness,
and he still won the battle greatly,
people would have said:
"Duke Wén, with his supremely virtuous character,
defeated Chǔ's unprincipled rule;
though Heaven showed omens
and he had inauspicious dreams,
he still eradicated the omens and dispelled the inauspiciousness to obtain blessings."
But Yīn lacked a discerning mind like Jiù Fàn's
and had only Zǔ Jǐ's reliance on conventional divination.
Therefore, the account of the mulberry and grain
has been passed down through generations without end;
while the saying of turning calamity into blessing
remains unverified to this day.
Confucian texts record:
"In Yáo's time,
ten suns appeared together,
scorching all things.
Yáo shot at the ten suns from below,
nine vanished,
and one sun remained as usual."
This statement is false.
A person's shooting range
does not exceed a hundred paces,
for beyond that, the arrow's force is exhausted.
The sun's course
follows the degrees of the celestial stars;
the distance from Heaven to humans
is counted in tens of thousands of miles.
How could Yáo, shooting from below,
possibly reach the sun?
If in Yáo's time,
Heaven and Earth were close,
no more than a hundred paces apart,
then Yáo shooting at the sun
might have reached it with an arrow;
but beyond a hundred paces,
he could not have hit it.
Even if in Yáo's time
Heaven and Earth were close,
and Yáo shot and hit the sun,
he still could not have harmed it.
If it wasn't harmed, why would it leave?
Why?
The sun is fire;
take a fire on Earth,
like a torch,
and shoot at it from the side—
even if hit, how could it be extinguished?
Earthly fire is not extinguished by being shot at,
so why would heavenly fire leave upon being shot?
This intends to say
that Yáo shot it with utmost sincerity,
and where sincerity is applied,
even metal and stone can be worn away—
for where there is sincerity, nothing is too hard,
and thus nothing is too far.
Now, water and fire
each have their own nature;
If one could shoot fire to extinguish it,
then one should shoot water to eliminate it.
During the flood era,
it inundated the Central Plains,
causing great calamity for the people—
why did Yáo not exert his utmost sincerity to shoot and eliminate it?
Yáo could shoot the suns,
preventing fire from causing harm,
but could not shoot the river,
to keep water from being a menace.
Since shooting water cannot repel it,
then we know the tale of shooting the suns
is false, not real.
Some say:
"The sun is composed of qì;
even if the arrow does not reach it,
sincere intent can extinguish it."
Now, heaven is also distant;
if it were made of qì,
it would be the same as the sun and moon;
if it had substance,
it would be like metal or stone.
With Yáo's utmost sincerity,
capable of extinguishing the sun and damaging metal or stone,
would shooting upward at the sun pierce heaven?
The world speaks of the wickedness of Jié and Zhòu,
shooting at heaven and striking the earth;
it praises the virtue of Gāozōng,
whose governance caused the mulberry and grain anomalies to disappear.
Now, Yáo could not use virtue to eliminate the ten suns,
but insisted on shooting them—
this shows his virtue was inferior to Gāozōng's,
and his wickedness akin to Jié and Zhòu's.
How could he
obtain heaven's response with sincere intent?
The transmitted texts say:
"When King Wǔ attacked Zhòu,
crossing the Mèngjīn River,
the waves of Yánghóu surged against the current,
with fierce winds and darkness,
obscuring men and horses.
Thereupon, King Wǔ held a yellow battle-axe in his left hand,
a white yak-tail banner in his right,
glared and waved it, saying:
'While I am here,
who under heaven dares oppose my will!'
Then the winds calmed and the waves ceased."
This statement is false.
When King Wǔ crossed Mèngjīn,
his troops were joyous,
singing and dancing before and after,
in harmony with heaven.
For men to rejoice while heaven rages
is not fitting in reality.
The singing and dancing
may not be factual;
waving to stop the wind
seems nearly fictitious.
Now wind is qì;
commentators consider it
heaven and earth's command.
If King Wǔ's execution of Zhòu was right,
heaven should have been tranquil to support him.
If it was wrong,
then heaven's wind showed anger.
King Wǔ, not heeding heaven's command,
seeking to justify his faults,
glared and declared:
"While I am here,
who under heaven dares oppose my will!"
This aggravated heaven's anger,
adding to his own wickedness—
why would the wind stop?
If parents are angry,
and a child does not amend his errors,
but glares and boasts,
would the parents forgive him?
If the wind is heaven's doing,
a natural calamitous qì,
it lacks consciousness,
and would not cease due to glaring and waving.
Wind is like rain;
could King Wǔ glare and wave his banner
to stop the rain?
If he could not stop rain,
then he could not stop wind either.
Perhaps when King Wǔ waved,
the wind coincidentally ceased,
and the world, praising his virtue,
claimed he could halt the wind.
The transmitted texts say:
"Lǔyáng Gōng battled Hán,
in the heat of combat at dusk,
he raised his spear and waved it,
and the sun retreated three shè for him."
This statement is false.
If a person can move heaven with sincere intent,
they must concentrate wholeheartedly,
set aside affairs, and accumulate spirit,
connecting profoundly with heaven—
then heaven might change.
Yet even that cannot be assured.
Lǔyáng Gōng's mind was on battle;
with one wave at dusk,
how could he make the sun retreat?
Even if a sage waved at the sun,
it would not retreat;
what kind of man was Lǔyáng Gōng,
to make the sun retreat?
The Hóng Fàn says:
"Some stars favor wind,
some stars favor rain.
The movement of the sun and moon
brings winter and summer.
When the moon follows the stars,
there is wind and rain."
Now stars share essence with the sun and moon;
if the sun and moon do not follow the stars,
the stars change accordingly.
This shows the sun and moon move by fixed measures,
not yielding to the stars' preferences;
how could they obey Lǔyáng Gōng's desires?
Stars in heaven
serve as lodgings for the sun and moon,
like post stations on earth
for officials' offices.
The twenty-eight lodgings have divisions in degrees;
one shè is ten degrees,
sometimes more or less.
To say the sun retreated three shè
means thirty degrees.
The sun travels one degree per day;
in the time of one wave,
could it revert thirty days' travel?
If shè means degrees,
three degrees equal three days' journey;
in one wave,
could the sun be pushed back three days?
When Duke Jǐng of Sòng expressed sincerity
with three virtuous statements,
Mars moved three shè,
yet true critics still call it false.
Lǔyáng Gōng, in conflict,
resented the dusk,
and with one spear wave,
lacking sincere intent or good words,
made the sun retreat—
is that not improbable?
Moreover, the sun is fire;
even a sage waving at fire
could not repel it;
how could Lǔyáng Gōng's wave
make the sun reverse?
Perhaps during battle, it was just mǎo hour,
and in the fray's confusion,
he thought it was dusk.
Waving, he turned left
on a curved path, making the sun seem to retreat.
The world favors the supernatural,
thus calling it a reversal,
not understanding the reality.
The transmitted texts say:
"When Jīng Kē plotted for Prince of Yān
to assassinate the King of Qín,
a white rainbow pierced the sun.
When Master Wèi for Qín
devised the Chángpíng strategy,
Venus eclipsed the Pleiades."
This claims sincere intent moved heaven,
causing heaven to change.
Now, to say
a white rainbow pierced the sun
or Venus eclipsed the Pleiades
is factual.
But to say Jīng Kē's plot
or Master Wèi's strategy
moved the august heaven,
thus causing the white rainbow to pierce the sun
and Venus to eclipse the Pleiades,
is false.
Using chopsticks to strike a bell
or a counting rod to beat a drum
won't produce sound—
because what strikes them
is too small.
Now, a human body is no more than seven chǐ;
with the spirit within this seven-chǐ form
wishing to act,
even with accumulated determination,
it's like chopsticks on a bell or a rod on a drum—
how could it move heaven?
It is not that their essence was insincere,
but what they moved with it was small.
Moreover, what they intended to harm were people;
if people cannot be moved,
how could Heaven be moved instead?
Someone asks:
"When a person's harmful qi
can it move each other?"
The reply:
"It cannot."
"When Yù Ràng intended to harm Zhào Xiāngzǐ,
Xiāngzǐ's heart was moved;
when Guàn Gāo intended to assassinate Gāozǔ,
Gāozǔ's heart was also moved.
These two men harbored essence,
therefore both rulers trembled with feeling."
The reply:
When calamitous change is about to arrive,
one's body naturally has portents,
it is not what someone else can move.
How to verify this?
Sometimes one encounters a madman on the road,
who presses a blade against oneself;
the madman may not necessarily intend to harm one's person,
yet one's own person had already beforehand experienced strange phenomena.
From this perspective,
the arrival of strange phenomena
is an omen of naturally occurring calamitous change,
not the doing of those who wish to harm oneself.
Moreover, when unlucky people
divine and get bad omens,
perform milfoil divination and get inauspicious hexagrams,
go out and see unlucky things,
observe prognostications of danger and perceive calamitous qi.
Calamitous qi appears on the face,
just as white rainbows and Tàibái stars appear in the sky.
Changes appear in Heaven,
portents emerge among humans,
above and below correspond appropriately,
naturally resonating with each other.
Transmitted texts say:
"When Yān Crown Prince Dān was at court in Qín,
he could not leave,
so he begged the Qín king to let him return.
The Qín king detained him,
making an oath with him:
'Only when the sun stands at noon twice,
when Heaven rains grain,
when crows turn white-headed,
when horses grow horns,
when the wooden elephant at the kitchen gate grows flesh feet,
may you return.'
At that time,
Heaven and Earth protected him,
the sun stood at noon twice,
Heaven rained grain,
crows turned white-headed,
horses grew horns,
the wooden elephant at the kitchen gate grew flesh feet.
The Qín king considered him sage,
and thus sent him back."
These words are false.
What kind of person was Yān Crown Prince Dān,
that he could move Heaven?
When sages were detained,
