they could not move Heaven;
Crown Prince Dān was a worthy man,
how could he achieve this?
If Heaven could protect the Crown Prince,
producing various auspicious signs to save him,
then it could have harmonized the Qín king's intentions to resolve his difficulties.
To end one matter of detention is easy,
to produce five auspicious matters is difficult.
To abandon the easy single matter
and undertake the difficult five matters—
why would Heaven not fear such labor?
When Tāng was trapped in Xiàtái,
King Wén was confined in Yǒulǐ,
and Confucius was distressed in Chén and Cài,
these three sages in困境,
Heaven could not protect them,
making their captors see protection and recognize their sageliness,
so they would release and honor them.
Some say:
"Those who detained the three sages did not make three oaths with them,
the three sages' hearts did not wish for it,
therefore the auspicious signs protecting sages had no cause to arrive.
Heaven's protection of people
is like lending people vessels:
if people do not seek them,
then it does not give."
The reply:
When the Crown Prince wished for heavenly auspicious signs,
did he necessarily use words?
He merely wished in his heart.
Yet when Tāng was imprisoned in Xiàtái
and King Wén confined in Yǒulǐ,
their hearts also wished to escape;
when Confucius was distressed in Chén and Cài,
his heart wished for food.
Why did Heaven not cause the locks of Xiàtái and Yǒulǐ to break,
allowing Tāng and King Wén to walk out;
or rain grain in Chén and Cài,
so Confucius could eat his fill?
Grand Historian Sīmǎ Qiān said:
"What the world calls Crown Prince Dān's command
that Heaven rained grain and horses grew horns,
are largely false words."
Grand Historian Sīmǎ Qiān recorded Hàn dynasty factual matters,
yet said "false words"
—this is close to being untrue.
Transmitted texts say:
"When Qǐ Liáng's wife cried facing the city wall,
the wall collapsed for her."
This means Qǐ Liáng
joined the army and did not return,
his wife grieved for him,
cried facing the city wall,
with utmost sincerity and悲痛,
her essential qi moved the wall,
therefore the wall collapsed for her.
That she cried facing the wall
is true;
that the wall collapsed for her
is false.
In mournful crying, no one surpasses Yōngménzǐ.
When Yōngménzǐ cried before Mèngchángjūn,
Mèngchángjūn sighed deeply for him.
Because his crying was sincere and essential,
therefore those facing him felt凄愴 and were moved.
Though Yōngménzǐ could move Mèngchángjūn's heart,
he could not affect Mèngchángjūn's clothing,
because clothing knows no compassion
and does not connect with human hearts.
Now a city wall is earth,
and earth is like clothing—
it has no heart or belly to store feelings,
how could it collapse from being moved by悲哭?
If utmost sincere sounds could move earthen walls,
then if one cried facing forests,
could one break grass and split wood?
If one wept facing fire and water,
could one make water surge or extinguish fire?
Grass, trees, water, and fire are no different from earth,
thus clearly
Qǐ Liáng's wife could not collapse the city wall.
Perhaps the wall happened to collapse by itself,
and Qǐ Liáng's wife happened to be crying;
later generations love the虚,
not examining the facts,
therefore the story of the collapsing wall
has not perished to this day.
Transmitted texts say:
"Zōu Yǎn, though innocent,
was detained in Yān.
During summer in the fifth month,
he looked up to Heaven and sighed,
and Heaven shed frost for him."
This is no different from
Qǐ Liáng's wife's crying that collapsed the city wall.
That he was innocent and detained,
and sighed looking up to Heaven in summer,
is true;
that Heaven shed frost for him
is false.
Even if ten thousand people raised their voices
and sighed together, they still could not move Heaven;
how could Zōu Yǎn alone,
with one sigh of冤, bring down frost?
Zōu Yǎn's冤
was no greater than Zēngzǐ's or Bó Qí's.
When Zēngzǐ was doubted, he chanted;
when Bó Qí was expelled, he sang.
Doubt and expulsion are the same as detention,
chanting and singing are equivalent to sighing—
Zēngzǐ and Bó Qí could not bring cold,
what kind of person was Zōu Yǎn,
that he alone could make frost fall?
The冤 of expulsion
is still not worth mentioning.
Shēnshēng fell on his sword,
Wǔ Zǐxū cut his own throat—
truly filial, yet given death;
sincerely loyal, yet executed.
Moreover, when facing death, both had vocal expressions.
When these expressions left their mouths,
it was no different from sighing to Heaven—
Heaven was not moved for these two men,
yet moved only for Zōu Yǎn.
Does Heaven pity detention but not grieve bloodshed?
Though Bó Qí's grievance was similar,
how could their effects differ?
Take a single torch flame to heat a cauldron of water—
it will not grow hot all day;
place a foot-long piece of ice in the kitchen—
it will not turn cold overnight.
Why?
Because tiny stimuli cannot move massive objects.
Now Zōu Yǎn's lament
was no more than that torch or piece of ice,
while August Heaven's immensity
far surpasses a cauldron or kitchen's humble likeness.
Yet one sigh heavenward
made Heaven shed frost—
how could Heaven be so easily moved,
frost so readily descend?
Grief and joy share nature,
as do delight and anger.
Had Yǎn stirred joy instead of pain,
making frost fall across the land,
and were he granted unexpected reward,
looking up to laugh at heaven,
could he make winter heat arise?
Proponents of cosmic response claim:
"If rulers reward in autumn, warmth comes;
if they punish in summer, cold arrives."
But cold unprolonged brings no frost;
warmth undoubled melts no ice.
One man's lament with one sigh
causing instant frostfall—
how could ethers shift so easily,
seasons turn so lightly?
Cold and heat follow their own seasons,
contradicting these theorists' claims.
Even by response doctrine,
perhaps when King Yān favored harsh punishments,
cold ethers were due to arrive;
as Yǎn, imprisoned, sighed,
frost chanced to descend at that moment.
The world, seeing sigh and frost coincide,
attributed it to Zōu Yǎn's lament.
Historical texts record:
"When Shī Kuǎng played the 'White Snow' melody,
divine beings descended,
storms burst forth,
Duke Píng fell ill therefrom,
and Jìn state's fields lay barren."
Others say:
"At Shī Kuǎng's 'Pure Angle' tune—
first played, clouds rose northwest;
played again, great winds came;
rains followed,
tore curtains,
shattered ritual vessels,
toppled corridor tiles.
Listeners fled scattered,
Duke Píng trembled with fear,
crouching in hallway chambers.
Jìn suffered great drought,
barren lands for three years,
Duke Píng chronically ill."
Now 'White Snow' and 'Pure Angle'
may be one tune with dual names,
their disasters sharing one reality.
Text transmitters
record this as truth;
common sight
accepts it as fact.
Examining its substance,
it seems empty words.
What sound could 'Pure Angle' hold
to cause such effects?
They say:
"'Pure Angle' is wood's tone,
thus summoning wind and rain.
If wood generates wind,
rain accompanies it."
But three feet of wood,
few strings' vibration,
moving heaven and earth—
how miraculously!
This repeats the wall-collapsing weep
and frost-bringing sigh tropes.
Had Shī Kuǎng truly played 'Pure Angle',
he must have received transmission,
not born with innate skill.
When first learning it,
he practiced constantly,
not just once or twice.
If texts be accurate,
during his study of 'Pure Angle',
storms should have arrived then.
Texts also claim:
"When Hù Bā played se,
deep fish surfaced to listen;
when Shī Kuǎng played qín,
horses raised heads from fodder."
Others say:
"At Shī Kuǎng's 'Pure Angle'—
first played, sixteen black cranes
flew from south,
perched on corridor eaves;
played again, they formed ranks;
played thrice, they stretched necks singing,
spread wings dancing,
tones matching shāng and gōng pitches,
voices crying to heaven.
Duke Píng greatly pleased,
all listeners delighted."
The Shàng Shū states:
"Strike stone chimes,
all beasts dance following."
Though wondrous,
this remains credible.
Why?
Beasts love mournful sounds,
their ears like human ears.
Seeing humans eat,
they too wish to eat;
hearing human music,
why not rejoice?
Yet "fish listening", "horses raising heads",
"cranes stretching necks", "beasts dancing"
may hold some truth,
while storms arriving, Jìn's great drought,
barren lands three years, Duke Píng's illness—
likely empty words.
Perhaps when 'Pure Angle' played,
heaven chanced storms;
after storms,
Jìn chanced drought;
Duke Píng, loving music,
laughed beyond measure,
chancing chronic illness.
Text transmitters,
believing it true,
and common observation
made it seem factual.
In truth, music cannot cause this.
How tested?
Sudden storms
mean yīnyáng disruption.
If music disrupts yīnyáng,
it could also harmonize it.
Why would kings need self-cultivation,
widespread benevolent rule?
Let them play yīnyáng-harmonizing tunes—
harmonious ethers would come,
peace establish itself.
Texts record:
"Tāng suffered seven-year drought,
prayed beneath mulberry groves,
confessing six faults,
whereupon heaven rained."
Some say five years.
His prayer went:
"If I alone have sinned,
let not multitudes suffer;
if multitudes sin,
blame rests on me.
Heaven, for one man's folly,
should not let spirits harm people's lives."
Then he cut his hair,
bound his hands,
offering himself as sacrifice
to beg blessings from God.
God greatly pleased,
timely rain then fell.
That Tāng prayed beneath mulwoods confessing,
or cut hair, bound hands,
offering self as sacrifice
to beg God's blessings—
may be true.
But that rain came
because Tāng prayed confessing—
likely empty words.
When Confucius fell ill,
Zǐ Lù sought to pray for him.
Confucius asked:
"Is this proper?"
Zǐ Lù replied:
"Yes;
the Lěi says:
'Pray for you to heaven and earth spirits.'"
Confucius said:
"I've prayed long already."
Sages cultivate virtue,
having prayed long since;
heaven, earth, and spirits
know their innocence,
hence "prayed long already."
The Book of Changes says:
"The great man aligns his virtue with heaven and earth,
his brightness with the sun and moon,
his order with the four seasons,
and his fortune with the spirits and gods."
This speaks of the sage sharing the same virtue
as heaven, earth, and the spirits.
Yet if one must pray to obtain blessings,
this indicates a lack of alignment.
Both Tāng and Confucius were sages,
and both had long practiced regular prayer.
Confucius did not allow Zǐlù to pray to cure illness,
so how could Tāng obtain rain through prayer?
Though Confucius regularly prayed,
he still fell ill;
though Tāng also regularly prayed,
drought still occurred.
Thus, just as humans have illnesses,
heaven and earth have floods and droughts.
Illness cannot be cured by self-reproach,
nor can floods and droughts be removed by prayer and atonement—
this is clear.
Did Tāng cause the drought
through some fault?
Then he did not share virtue with heaven and earth.
If he did not cause the drought through fault,
then self-reproach and prayer
would still be futile.
The human body stands seven feet tall,
containing the five constant virtues within.
When afflicted with feverish illness,
even deep self-chastisement
cannot cure it—
how much less could Tāng, using his seven-foot body
and the sincerity within it,
through self-reproach and prayer,
obtain rain from the vast heaven
with its inherent fluctuations of flood and drought?
If a person stands on a high tower,
and another below kowtows
begging for something from above,
the person on the tower may hear the plea
and pityingly grant it;
but if unheard,
no matter how earnest the plea,
it will never be granted.
Heaven's distance from humanity
far exceeds that of a high tower.
Though Tāng blamed himself,
how could heaven hear and grant him rain?
Drought is a fiery anomaly;
inundation is a watery aberration.
Yáo encountered great floods—
a true inundation—
yet he did not practice self-reproach or bodily prayer,
but necessarily assigned Shùn and Yǔ to control it,
knowing water anomalies require governance.
Since inundation isn't removed by prayer,
drought should be likewise.
Thus it follows that
Tāng's prayers could not bring rain.
Perhaps the drought had lasted long enough
and rain was due naturally;
Tāng, due to the prolonged drought,
happened to engage in self-reproach at that time.
People saw rain fall
following Tāng's self-accusation,
and thus claimed Tāng obtained rain through prayer.
Transmitted texts say:
"When Cāngjié created writing,
grain rained from heaven,
and ghosts wept at night."
This means that with the rise of writing,
disorder gradually appeared,
hence these eerie manifestations
causing grain to rain and ghosts to weep.
That grain rained and ghosts wept
may be true,
but attributing it to Cāngjié's invention of writing
is false.
When the river produced the Diagram
and the Luò River produced the Writing,
these were auspicious responses to sage emperors and enlightened kings.
How do these diagrams and writings differ from what Cāngjié created?
Heaven and earth produced diagrams and writings,
while Cāngjié created characters—
his work aligned with heaven and earth,
his intent harmonized with spirits and gods.
What transgression or evil
could cause the anomalies of grain-rain and spirit-weeping?
If heaven, earth, and spirits hated humans having writing,
then their production of diagrams and writings
would be wrong;
if heaven does not hate humans having writing,
why should creating writing provoke such anomalies?
Perhaps Cāngjié happened to create writing
while grain chanced to rain from heaven
and ghosts coincidentally wept at night.
The grain-rain
and spirit-weeping
had their own causes,
but people saw them correspond with writing's appearance
and claimed writing produced omens of chaos and decay,
responding to events through action.
"Grain raining from heaven"—
commentators say it falls from the sky above,
emerging in response to change.
But considering clouds and rain,
the anomaly of grain-rain
is not so strange.
How to verify this?
Clouds and rain emerge from hills and mountains,
descending and dispersing as rain.
People see it fall from above
and call it rain from heaven.
In summer it rains water,
in winter's cold, rain congeals as snow,
all arising from vapor over hills and mountains,
not descending from heaven to earth—
this is clear.
Grain-rain
is likewise like clouds spreading—
it also rises from the earth,
carried by strong winds,
mingling with the sky,
and gathering on the ground.
People see it fall from above
and call it "grain raining from heaven."
In the thirty-first year of the Jiànwǔ era,
grain rained in Chénliú,
covering the ground.
Examining the grain's form,
it resembled cí but black,
similar to barnyard grass seeds.
This might have been grain
from barbarian lands,
where people don't eat grains;
this grain grew in wilderness grasses,
ripened and drooped to the ground,
when a strong wind arose
lifting and blowing it aloft,
until the wind calmed and it fell in the central states.
People there saw it
and called it "grain raining from heaven."
How to confirm this?
When wild fires blaze through mountains and marshes,
burning all plants
and turning leaves to ash,
a strong wind may rise,
lifting the ash
skyward,
until the wind drops and it settles
on roads.
"Grain raining from heaven"
is like these blown, burnt leaves gathering—
yet people take it as grain-rain,
and transmitted texts deem it anomalous.
Heaven governs the dispersal of vapor,
earth governs the production of things.
All that has leaves, fruits, or can be pecked and eaten
is born from earth,
not made by heaven.
Now grain isn't produced from vapor alone
but requires soil to form.
Though called anomalous,
anomalies follow their kinds.
Can things born from earth
truly gather from heaven?
Can things born from heaven
emerge from earth?
Earth having all things
is like heaven having stars.
Stars aren't reborn from earth;
how could grain alone be born from heaven?
Transmitted texts also say:
"When Bó Yì dug wells,
dragons ascended to dark clouds,
and spirits dwelled on Kūnlún."
This means wells harmed dragons,
hence dragons and spirits manifested anomalously.
That dragons ascended to dark clouds
may be true.
It is said that the deity dwells on Kūnlún,
and also that because a well was dug,
the dragon ascended and the deity departed,
which is false.
Now, digging a well to drink
and plowing fields to eat
are of the same nature.
Bó Yì dug a well,
causing changes to occur,
but those who first began plowing and weeding—
why did they experience no changes?
Shénnóng bent wood to make plows,
teaching the people to plow and weed,
so the people began to eat grain,
and grain started to be sown.
Tilling the soil to make fields,
excavating the earth to dig wells,
wells bring forth water to quench thirst,
fields yield grain to relieve hunger—
these are what Heaven, Earth, and the ghosts and spirits desire to accomplish.
Why then would the dragon ascend to the dark clouds?
Why would the deity dwell on Kūnlún?
Now, the dragon's ascent to the dark clouds
has occurred in both ancient and modern times;
it did not begin with Bó Yì's well-digging that it then ascended.
In the height of summer now,
thunderstorms occur seasonally,
and dragons often ascend the clouds.
Clouds, rain, and dragons correspond to each other;
dragons ride on clouds and rain to travel—
things of the same category attract one another,
it is not due to any deliberate action.
In the time of Yáo,
the world was greatly harmonious,
the common people had no troubles,
and there were elderly people striking clods on the roadside.
An onlooker said:
"How great is the virtue of Yáo!"
The clod-striker replied:
"I rise at sunrise to work,
rest at sunset,
dig wells to drink,
plow fields to eat—
what strength has Yáo to do with this?"
Thus, wells already existed in Yáo's time.
In the eras of Táng and Yú,
there were dragon-keepers and dragon-drivers;
dragons were often at court.
By the end of the Xià dynasty, governance declined,
and the dragons then went into hiding—
it was not due to Bó Yì's well-digging
that the dragons ascended the clouds.
As for the so-called deity,
which deity is it?
If it refers to all deities,
why would all deities detest people digging wells?
If we suppose deities are like humans,
then they too should have the desire to drink.
Having the desire to drink,
yet hating wells and leaving—
this is not in accordance with reality.
It is likely that Bó Yì did not dig wells,
dragons did not ascend clouds due to well-digging,
and deities do not dwell on Kūnlún;
the transmitted texts are willfully erroneous,
fabricating these tales.
The transmitted texts say:
"When Mount Liáng collapsed,
blocking the river, so it did not flow for three days,
the ruler of Jìn was troubled by it.
Jìn's Bó Zōng, based on the words of a carriage-puller,
had Duke Jǐng don plain white mourning clothes and weep for it,
and the river water then flowed through."
This is a false statement.
Now, a mountain collapsing and blocking a river
is like a person having a boil or swelling,
where the blood vessels are blocked.
Can one treat a boil or swelling
by again using plain clothes and the sound of weeping to cure it?
In Yáo's time,
the floodwaters reached the heavens,
surrounding mountains and engulfing hills;
Emperor Yáo sighed deeply,
broadly seeking worthy individuals.
The water disaster was more severe than a blocked river,
and Yáo's worry was deeper than Duke Jǐng's;
we have not heard that plain white mourning clothes and the sound of weeping
could suppress it.
Did Yáo lack a worthy like the carriage-puller's method?
Or was it that the flood disaster was too great,
and could not be removed by sounds and attire?
If "donning plain white and weeping"
means repenting of faults and blaming oneself,
Yáo and Yǔ's flood control used labor conscription,
not self-blame.
Mount Liáng
existed in Yáo's time;
the blocked river
was the river of Yáo's time.
The mountain collapsed and the river was blocked,
heaven rained and the waters surged—
the two disasters were not different in nature.
Yáo and Yǔ controlled the flood with labor conscription,
while the carriage-puller treated the blocked river with self-blame;
the disasters were similar but the treatments different,
the men equivalent but the responses distinct—
this is likely not the reality of how sages respond to and reverse changes.
Generally, the way of responding to and reversing changes
relies on the ability to mutually stimulate and move,
through the categories of things.
If there is cold, one counters it with warmth;
if there is warmth, one dispels it with cold.
Thus, using dragons to bring rain,
or using punishments to drive away heat,
all depend on the qì of the Five Phases,
employing mutual stimulation and overcoming.
A mountain collapses and blocks a river;
donning plain white and weeping for it—
what principle does that follow?
Perhaps at the time the river was blocked,
the mountain had just collapsed,
soil had accumulated,
and the water was not yet abundant.
Three days later,
the water swelled and the soil dispersed, gradually breaking down.
As it broke down, the water flowed,
eventually pouring eastward.
It happened that Bó Zōng obtained the carriage-puller's words,
and because of donning plain white and weeping,
the weeping coincided with the flow;
when it flowed, it was said the river's change arose from this and was reversed.
But in reality, it was not so.
How can this be verified?
If the mountain constantly collapses by itself,
donning plain white and weeping is of no benefit.
If it was a heavenly change responding to it,
the governance should have been reformed.
By donning plain white and weeping,
what governance was reformed to reverse the heavenly change?
The transmitted texts say:
"Zēngzǐ's filial piety
made him share the same qì with his mother.
When Zēngzǐ was out gathering firewood in the wild,
a guest came and was about to leave.
Zēng's mother said:
'I wish you to stay;
Shēn will arrive shortly.'
She then pinched her left arm with her right hand.
Zēngzǐ's left arm immediately hurt,
and he rushed home to ask his mother,
saying: 'Why does my arm hurt?'
His mother said:
'Just now a guest came and was about to leave,
so I pinched my arm to call you.'
It is because his utmost filial piety
made him share the same qì with his parents,
so that if their bodies had an illness or pain,
his spirit would immediately sense it."
I say:
This is false.
Now, "the ultimate in filial piety and fraternal duty
penetrates to the divine and luminous"
means that moral transformation reaches Heaven and Earth.
Common people use this to explain,
saying that at the ultimate of filial piety and fraternal duty,
essential qì mutually moves.
If Zēng's mother's arm hurt,
and Zēngzǐ's arm also immediately hurt,
then if Zēng's mother fell ill, would Zēngzǐ also immediately fall ill?
If Zēng's mother died,
would Zēngzǐ also immediately die?
Examining the facts,
Zēng's mother died first,
and Zēngzǐ did not die.
This shows that essential qì can cause minor mutual movements,
but cannot cause major mutual sensations.
The world recounts that Shēn Xǐ heard his mother singing at night,
felt a stirring in his heart,
opened the door and asked who the singer was,
and it was indeed his mother.
It was because he heard his mother's voice;
voices and sounds mutually stir,
his heart grieved and his mind was moved,
so he opened the door and asked—
this is probably true.
Now, Zēng's mother was at home,
Zēngzǐ was in the wild,
not hearing any cries or calls—
A mother pinching her own arm slightly,
how could that move her child?
I suspect that people's praises are formed by convention,
hearing of Zēngzǐ's filial piety, unparalleled in the world,
then they fabricate the tale of a mother pinching her arm.
It is said in the world:
Zhuō Gōng of Nányáng, as magistrate of Gōushì,
locusts did not enter his jurisdiction.
This is attributed to his worthiness, wisdom, and utmost sincerity,
so that calamitous insects would not invade his county.
This is also false.
Now, the transformative power of worthiness, wisdom, and utmost sincerity
communicates with beings of the same kind,
enabling mutual understanding of hearts,
and only then admiration and submission follow.
Locusts,
belonging to the same category as mosquitoes and horseflies,
what knowledge or perception do they have? How could they recognize the transformative influence of Zhuō Gōng?
If a worthy person dwelled in the deep wilderness,
could mosquitoes and horseflies avoid entering his dwelling?
If mosquitoes and horseflies cannot avoid the dwelling of a worthy person,
how could locusts avoid entering Zhuō Gōng's county?
If one claims that locusts are transformed beings, different from mosquitoes and horseflies,
consider that cold and warmth are also calamitous changes;
if a whole commandery turns cold,
and a worthy person governs one county,
could the boundaries of that one county alone remain warm?
If cold and warmth cannot avoid the county of a worthy person,
how could locusts avoid entering Zhuō Gōng's boundaries?
Thus being the case,
it was merely by chance that locusts did not enter the boundaries,
and Zhuō Gōng's reputation for worthiness happened to be praised in the world;
then the world claims he was able to repel locusts.
How can this be verified?
When locusts gather in the fields,
they cannot universally cover the entire ground;
often they accumulate more in some places and less in others.
The places where they do not accumulate
are not necessarily where a robber like Dào Zhí resides;
the fields with fewer locusts
are not necessarily where a virtuous person like Bó Yí dwells.
The gatherings vary in density,
and cannot completely cover the land.
Since the gatherings on the ground vary in density,
then as they pass through counties, some areas are left with more, others with less.
The density
cannot serve to verify good or evil,
and the presence or absence
how can it clarify worthiness or unworthiness?
It was likely that the locusts happened to pass by,
and it is clear that it was not because they avoided the boundaries of a worthy person.
The world argues that those who do good will have blessings arrive,
and those who do evil will have calamities come.
The response of blessings and calamities
all comes from Heaven;
humans act,
and Heaven responds.
Visible kindness,
is rewarded by the ruler for one's conduct;
hidden virtue,
is repaid by Heaven and Earth for one's moral character.
Regardless of nobility, baseness, wisdom, or foolishness,
no one says it is not so.
Merely seeing recorded events in texts and traditions,
and also seeing good people occasionally encountering blessings,
thus they believe it,
and say it is truly so.
Such words might sometimes be because sages wished to encourage people to do good,
so they set down definitive statements
to clarify the repayment of virtue;
or perhaps blessings happened to coincide, and those who encountered them considered it true.
If we discuss it based on reality,
how can there be such blessings and protection?
King Huì of Chǔ ate cold pickles and found a leech,
so he swallowed it,
and then had abdominal pain and could not eat.
The Prime Minister entered and asked,
saying:
"How did Your Majesty contract this illness?"
The King said:
"I ate cold pickles and found a leech.
If I considered reprimanding but did not enforce the punishment,
that would mean the law is abandoned and authority not established,
and it is not something to let the people of the state hear.
If I reprimand and execute,
then the cooks and supervisors of the food would, by law, all deserve death,
but my heart cannot bear it.
I feared my attendants would see it,
so I swallowed it."
The Prime Minister left his mat, bowed twice, and congratulated him, saying:
"Your servant has heard that the Way of Heaven is impartial,
and only supports those with virtue.
Your Majesty has humane virtue,
which Heaven upholds,
so the illness will not harm you."
That evening,
after King Huì relieved himself, the leech came out,
and his long-standing ailment of abdominal masses was completely cured.
So, does not Heaven's care for the virtuous
seem quite evident?
I say:
This is a false statement.
Consider King Huì swallowing the leech—
he was an unworthy ruler.
Having unworthy conduct,
Heaven would not protect him.
Why?
King Huì could not bear to reprimand over the leech,
fearing that the cooks and supervisors would all be executed by law.
The ruler of a state
holds exclusive power over rewards and punishments;
to pardon
is an action of the ruler.
Had King Huì thoroughly investigated why there was a leech in the pickles,
and the cooks and supervisors deserved to face the law,
yet he ultimately refrained from executing anyone over food matters,
pardoning and not punishing,
his kindness would have been immense.
The cooks' offense discovered but not punished,
they would reform and change thereafter;
King Huì pardoning a minor fault and sparing the humble,
he would have remained safe and healthy.
But instead, he did not do so;
he forcibly ate a harmful object himself,
preventing the supervising ministers from hearing of their fault,
losing the authority to control his subordinates,
lacking the heart to guard against wrongdoing—
this is the first instance of his unworthiness.
Had the cooks and supervisors failed in harmonizing flavors,
if, say, dust and soil fell into the pickles,
as small as lice and nits,
beyond intentional detection,
invisible to the eye,
and judging by intent to determine guilt,
their fault might not be clear,
that could be called kindness.
But this leech had measurable width,
and length in inches,
in the cold pickles,
even a person with poor eyesight would see it.
The ministers showed no fear or respect,
selection and washing were not careful,
their offense was extremely grave,
yet King Huì did not reprimand them—
this is the second instance of his unworthiness.
There should not be a leech in the pickles;
if not eaten, it should be thrown to the ground;
if fearing his attendants might see it,
concealing it in a hidden place
would suffice to keep the leech unseen,
why necessarily eat it?
If it was an inedible object
mistakenly in the pickles,
should one still hide it and forcibly eat it?
This is the third instance of his unworthiness.
Having unworthy conduct,
yet Heaven protected him,
that would mean Heaven rewards and protects unworthy people.
His inability to bear reprimanding over the leech
is called worthiness by the world,
but if the conduct of the worthy
is often like swallowing leeches,
and swallowing leeches leads to Heaven curing their illness,
then the worthy would always be free from illness.
If the virtuous are of meager virtue,
they are not worth mentioning.
But sages, pure in the Way,
with conduct rarely faulty,
acting out of不忍之心 (bù rěn zhī xīn, compassionate heart),
tolerating others' faults,
must be numerous indeed.
Yet King Wǔ fell ill,
Confucius suffered from disease;
does Heaven's protection of people not hold true?
Perhaps when King Huì swallowed the leech,
the leech happened to come out on its own.
All living things that are eaten die,
due to the heat in the abdomen.
When first swallowed, the leech
was not yet dead,
and with the abdominal heat,
the leech moved,
causing abdominal pain.
Shortly, the leech died
in the abdomen, and the pain ceased.
The nature of leeches is to consume blood,
and King Huì's abdominal masses
were likely accumulations of blood.
So when the blood-consuming insect died,
the illness of accumulated blood was cured.
Just as the nature of a cat is to eat mice,
when a person suffers from a rat-related ailment,
swallowing a cat can cure it by itself,
as creatures overcome each other,
and remedies work through mutual influence.
If one swallows a leech and recovers from illness,
why find it strange?
No living being swallowed survives,
and none fails to be expelled after death;
when the leech is later expelled,
how can it be considered divine protection?
The Prime Minister, seeing King Huì's compassionate virtue,
knew the leech in his stomach would die and be expelled.
The minister thus bowed twice,
congratulating that the illness would not cause harm,
displaying his foresight
to comfort King Huì's heart.
This is no different from Zǐwéi's claim about the star shifting
or the Grand Diviner's assertion of an earthquake.
A man from Sòng was devoted to good deeds,
unwavering for three generations.
Unexpectedly, his black cow bore a white calf,
so he consulted Confucius.
Confucius said:
"This is auspicious,
use it to sacrifice to the ghosts and deities."
They then sacrificed the calf.
A year later,
the father went blind for no reason.
The cow bore another white calf,
and the father again sent his son to ask Confucius.
Confucius said:
"It is auspicious,
use it to sacrifice to the ghosts and deities."
They again sacrificed the calf.
A year later,
the son also went blind without cause.
Later, Chǔ attacked Sòng,
besieging its city.
At that time,
people exchanged children to eat,
and dismantled bones to cook.
Only because both father and son were blind
were they exempt from defending the city walls.
When the army withdrew and the siege lifted,
both regained their sight.
This was seen as the effect of divine reward for accumulated good deeds.
I say:
This is a false tale.
If the Sòng father and son cultivated goodness so diligently,
why would the deities reward them
by first blinding them and then restoring their sight?
Could they not have been protected while retaining their vision?
If the deities cannot protect the sighted,
then they cannot protect people through blindness either.
Had the rulers of Sòng and Chǔ
clashed in fierce battle,
with bloodshed and fallen corpses,
soldiers captured,
and deaths unreturned,
then escaping due to blindness
and avoiding conscription
might be called divine reward.
But in the actual conflict between Sòng and Chǔ,
before the armies engaged,
Huà Yuán and Zǐ Fǎn negotiated a truce and withdrew;
both forces
returned intact,
with weapons unused.
Though there was a siege,
there was no risk of death.
Was the reward for goodness merely avoiding wall duty?
Had they not been blind,
they would still not have died.
Blind or not,
all would have been spared;
what good did divinely caused blindness do for virtue?
When Sòng faced food shortages,
were the blind family's stores
any richer?
They too had to exchange children and dismantle bones like other besieged families,
yet suffered the added hardship of blindness without sight.
If this is divine reward,
it mistakes good and evil.
The father and son in Sòng likely went blind earlier due to a chill,
and after the siege,
their blindness coincidentally healed.
The world, seeing their goodness,
their sacrifice of two white calves,
their exemption from wall duty during the war,
and their regained sight post-siege,
called it a reward for virtue and divine protection.
When Chǔ's Prime Minister Sūnshū Áo was a child,
he saw a two-headed snake,
killed and buried it,
then returned home crying to his mother.
She asked why,
and he replied:
"I've heard that seeing a two-headed snake means death.
Earlier, when I went out,
I saw one,
and I fear I'll die and leave you, Mother,
hence my tears."
His mother said:
"Where is the snake now?"
He answered:
"I feared others might see it,
so I killed and buried it."
His mother said:
"I've heard that those with hidden virtue
are always rewarded by Heaven.
You will not die;
Heaven will surely reward you."
Sūnshū Áo indeed did not die
and became Prime Minister of Chǔ.
Burying one snake
brought double blessings;
Heaven's reward for goodness is clear.
I say:
This is a false tale.
That seeing a two-headed snake causes death
is a folk belief;
that hidden virtue brings heavenly reward
is a common saying.
Sūnshū Áo believed the folk tale and buried the snake,
his mother trusted the saying and expected reward,
implying life and death are not fated
but hinge on a snake's death.
Mèngcháng Jūn of Qí, Tián Wén, was born on the fifth day of the fifth month.
His father Tián Yīng reproached his mother:
"Why did you rear him?"
Wén asked:
"Why do you not rear children born in May?"
Yīng said:
"A child born in May will grow as tall as the door,
and kill his parents."
Wén replied:
"Is life decreed by Heaven
or by the door?
If by Heaven,
why worry?
If by the door,
then raise the door higher;
who could reach it then?"
Later, Wén grew as tall as a door,
yet Yīng did not die.
Thus, the taboo against rearing May-born children
has no proof.
The dread of seeing a two-headed snake
is like that of birthing in May.
Since a May-born child
does not kill the father,
then seeing a two-headed snake
brings no disaster.
Thus,
seeing a two-headed snake does not cause death,
regardless of burial.
If burying one snake
brings two blessings,
how many would burying ten bring?
He buried the snake to prevent others from seeing it—
this was virtuous of Sūnshū Áo.
But do the deeds of the virtuous
consist only of burying a snake?
Before burying the snake,
he had already done many good acts.
Endowed with a heavenly good nature,
his actions were consistently virtuous.
Such a person
should encounter auspicious signs,
not a deadly snake.
Could it be that before seeing the snake, he had faults,
and Heaven meant to kill him,
but seeing him bury the snake,
pardoned his errors
and spared him?
A stone is hard by nature,
an orchid fragrant by birth.
To say Sūnshū Áo's virtue began with burying the snake
denies his innate endowment.
Dǒng Wúxīn of the Confucian school
and Chán Zǐ of the Mohist school
met to debate doctrines.
Chán Zǐ praised the Mohist reverence for ghosts and deities,
citing Duke Mù of Qín's bright virtue,
for which the God on High granted him nineteen extra years.
Dǒng Zǐ countered that Yáo and Shùn were not given extra years,
nor did Jié and Zhòu die young.
Yáo and Shùn, as well as Jié and Zhòu, are still too distant to consider,
so let us take Duke Mù of Qín and Duke Wén of Jìn as closer examples.
Now, posthumous titles are traces of one's conduct,
based on actions during life, used to assign names after death.
"Mù" signifies a name of error and chaos,
while "Wén" represents a manifestation of virtue and benevolence.
Yet one with erroneous and chaotic deeds
was granted long life by Heaven;
while one with virtuous and benevolent character
had his life taken by Heaven—how can this be?
Examining Duke Mù's hegemony, it did not surpass that of Duke Wén of Jìn;
yet Duke Wén's posthumous title is more honorable than Duke Mù's.
Heaven did not extend Duke Wén's lifespan,
but uniquely bestowed years upon Duke Mù—
this suggests Heaven rewards error and chaos,
aligning with Duke Mù's case.
In the world, good people are few,
while wicked people are many.
Good people follow the Way,
wicked people defy Heaven.
Yet the lives of the wicked are not short,
nor are the years of the good long.
Why does Heaven not decree that good people always enjoy a century of life,
while the wicked die young or badly?
The world claims those who receive blessings
do so due to their good deeds;
and those who suffer calamities
are said to have hidden wickedness and concealed faults,
for which Heaven and Earth punish them,
and ghosts and spirits exact retribution.
Punishments by Heaven and Earth,
whether great or small, will be inflicted;
retributions by ghosts and spirits,
whether near or far, will arrive.
The "Zhuàn" records:
"Zǐxià lost his son and then his eyesight.
Zēngzǐ went to console him,
and wept.
Zǐxià said:
'Heaven!
I am without fault!'
Zēngzǐ angrily replied:
'Shāng!
How can you claim to be without fault?
You and I studied under our Master between the Zhū and Sì rivers,
then you retired to grow old by the Western Hé,
causing the people there to compare you to our Master—
that is your first fault.
When you lost your parent,
you let the people hear nothing exceptional—
that is your second fault.
Losing your son,
you also lost your sight—
that is your third fault.
And you say you are without fault?'
Zǐxià threw down his staff and bowed,
saying:
'I was wrong!
I was wrong!
I have lived apart from the group, in solitude,
for too long!'"
When Zǐxià lost his sight,
Zēngzǐ reproached him with faults,
and Zǐxià threw down his staff and accepted Zēngzǐ's words—
believing Heaven truly punished his errors,
thus causing his blindness;
since he truly possessed them,
he bowed and accepted his faults.
Upon first hearing or brief reflection,
all may think this correct.
But upon careful examination,
it is empty falsehood.
Losing eyesight is like losing hearing:
losing sight is blindness,
losing hearing is deafness.
One does not say deafness results from fault,
yet claims blindness comes from crime—
this is confusion.
For ailments of eyes and ears
are like ailments of heart and belly.
If losing sight or hearing
is called criminal,
then having heart or belly illness
could be called faulty?
Bóniú fell ill;
Confucius took his hand through the window,
saying:
"It is over—
such is fate!
That such a man should have such a disease!"
Considering Confucius's words,
he meant Bóniú was unfortunate,
thus grieving for him.
If Bóniú's illness came from faults,
and Heaven repaid with misfortune like Zǐxià,
Confucius should have listed his errors,
as Zēngzǐ did with Zǐxià.
Yet he spoke of "fate"—
and fate is not fault.
Moreover, when Heaven punishes people,
it is like a ruler sentencing subjects.
If the punished admit guilt,
the ruler pardons them.
Zǐxià admitted his faults,
bowed in self-reproach—
if Heaven's virtue is supremely bright,
it should have cured his blindness.
If Heaven did not fault him,
then Zǐxià's loss of sight
had nothing to do with three crimes.
And compare the ailment of blindness
to that of leprosy:
if blindness warrants three crimes,
does leprosy warrant ten faults?
Yán Yuān died young,
Zǐlù was minced into paste—
early death and mincing
are the ultimate calamities under Heaven.
If judged by blindness's standard,
Yán Yuān and Zǐlù had a hundred crimes each.
Thus, from this perspective,
Zēngzǐ's words were mistaken.
Now, Zǐxià's blindness
came from losing his son.
Sons are universally cherished in human emotion;
parents are those whom one strives to repay.
Losing a parent, he let no one hear of it;
losing a son, he lost his sight—
this shows reduced gratitude toward parents, but increased love for his son.
Increased love leads to endless weeping,
and frequent weeping induces wind-stroke,
causing loss of eyesight.
Zēngzǐ, following common opinion,
attributed three crimes to Zǐxià.
Zǐxià, also influenced by popular belief,
accepted the blame due to his blindness.
Zēngzǐ and Zǐxià had not transcended convention,
so in Confucius's school, their conduct was not ranked among the highest.
King Xiāng of Qín bestowed a sword upon Bái Qǐ,
who leaned on it to commit suicide,
saying:
"What crime have I committed against Heaven?"
After a long pause, he said:
"I surely deserve death.
At the Battle of Chángpíng,
several hundred thousand Zhào soldiers surrendered,
and I deceitfully had them all buried alive—
this is enough to die for."
Thereupon he killed himself.
Bái Qǐ knew his former crime
and accepted the subsequent punishment.
But Bái Qǐ knew why he was guilty,
not why the Zhào soldiers were buried.
If Heaven truly punishes those with faults,
what had the surrendered Zhào soldiers done to offend Heaven?
If it was reckless injury and killing in war,
then among the four hundred thousand, some must have been innocent;
those innocent ones—
why were they buried despite their good conduct and lack of crime?
They could not receive Heaven's protection for their goodness,
so why was Bái Qǐ alone punished by Heaven for his crime?
From this perspective,
Bái Qǐ's words were mistaken.
Qín Èrshì sent an envoy with an edict to execute Méng Tián.
Méng Tián sighed deeply, saying:
"What have I done against Heaven?
To die without crime!"
After a long while,
he slowly said:
"Tián's crime indeed warrants death!
From Líntáo to Liáodōng,
I built a wall ten thousand lǐ long,
and in doing so, I must have severed the earth's veins.
This is my crime!"
He then took poison and killed himself.
Grand Historian Sīmǎ Qiān criticized this, saying:
"When Qín first eliminated the feudal lords,
the hearts of the people were unsettled,
wounds had not yet healed,
and Méng Tián, as a famous general,
did not forcefully remonstrate at that time,
relieving the people's distress,
caring for the aged and pitying the orphaned,
cultivating harmony among the masses,
but instead flattered and pursued ambitious projects.
That he and his brothers met with execution
was not fitting?
Why instead blame the earth's veins?"
Since Méng Tián's statement was incorrect,
but Sīmǎ Qiān's criticism of it is also not right.
Why so?
Méng Tián severed the earth's veins,
a crime deserving death.
The earth nurtures all things,
what wrong has it done to humans,
that Méng Tián severed its veins?
Méng Tián knew he had the crime of severing earth's veins,
but did not understand the fault that caused the earth's veins to be severed.
If he did not reflect on this himself,
how is it different from not reflecting at all?
Sīmǎ Qiān criticized Méng Tián as a famous general
who failed to offer strong remonstrance,
thus bringing this disaster upon himself.
When one should remonstrate but does not,
it leads to suffering death and execution.
Yet Sīmǎ Qiān himself vouched for Lǐ Líng,
and was punished with castration in the silkworm chamber.
According to his own logic,
recommending an unfit person
resulting in mutilating punishment
must be due to Heaven's mandate.
If he criticizes Méng Tián for not remonstrating strongly enough,
thus causing his misfortune,
then his own castration
must also be subject to criticism.
If he himself is blameless,
then his criticism of Méng Tián
is wrong.
When writing the "Biography of Bó Yí",
he listed examples of good and evil conduct, saying:
"Among the seventy disciples,
Confucius particularly recommended Yān Yuān as fond of learning.
Yet Yán Huí often lived in poverty,
not even having enough chaff and husks to eat,
and died young.
How does Heaven reward good people?
Robber Zhí killed innocent people daily,
ate human livers,
was cruel and tyrannical,
gathered followers numbering thousands,
rampaged across the world,
yet eventually died of old age.
Why did he alone follow such a path?"
Speaking like this,
Yán Huí should not have died young,
and Robber Zhí should not have lived out his life.
Not finding it strange that Yán Huí died untimely,
but alone claiming Méng Tián deserved death,
is mistaken.
Hàn general Lǐ Guǎng once conversed with diviner Wáng Shuò, saying:
"Since Hàn began attacking the Xiōngnú
I have always been involved,
yet officers below me,
with talent inferior to average,
have dozens become marquises through military achievements against the Hú,
while I never lag behind others,
yet ultimately have not achieved the slightest merit
to obtain a fiefdom.
Why is this?
Is my physiognomy unfit for marquisate,
or is it simply fate?"
Shuò said:
"General, search your conscience,
have you ever done anything you deeply regret?"
Guǎng said:
"When I was governor of Lǒngxī,
the Qiāng often rebelled,
I tricked eight hundred into surrendering;
then deceitfully had them all killed the same day.
To this day I regret it,
only this matter."
Shuò said:
"No misfortune greater than killing those who have surrendered,
this is why you cannot become a marquis."
Lǐ Guǎng agreed,
and listeners believed it.
Not becoming a marquis
is like not becoming king.
Why regret not being marquis?
What failure is not becoming king?
Confucius never became king,
yet critics don't call it failure;
Lǐ Guǎng never became marquis,
yet Wáng Shuò says he has reason for regret.
Thus Wáng Shuò's words
lose touch with reality.
Commentators believe: human enfeoffment
follows Heaven's mandate,
the signs of which
appear in bone structure.
When General Wèi Qīng was at Jiànzhāng Palace,
a convict in fetters read his face:
"You will become noble, even a marquis."
Later he indeed merited enfeoffment as a ten-thousand-household marquis.
Before Wèi Qīng had achievements,
the convict saw evidence he should be enfeoffed.
Thus,
marquisate is fated,
not obtainable through personal conduct.
The convict's words proved true and effective;
Wáng Shuò's words empty and unverified.
Many tyrants escape disaster,
while followers of the Way miss blessings,
Wáng Shuò's theory
resembles Bái Qǐ's self-blame and Méng Tián's self-condemnation.
In chaotic times,
many kill for wealth.
Sharing carriage or boat,
traveling thousands of lǐ as merchants,
reaching remote places,
they murder companions and seize their property.
Corpses abandoned uncollected,
bones exposed unburied,
becoming food for fish and turtles in water,
or ants and insects on land.
Lazy people
who neither farm diligently nor trade hard,
to store grain and goods,
encounter famine years,
go hungry unfed,
butcher people like livestock,
carving and eating them.
Regardless of gentleman or commoner,
all become meat,
unknown to others,
undetected by officials.
Over a thousand,
under ten thousand people -
in one settlement,
only one in hundred survives,
nine in ten die.
This can be called ruthless, extremely tragic,
yet perpetrators prosper, wealthy and content.
Heaven doesn't punish their lack of benevolence,
their mutual slaughter,
nor their laziness leading to cannibalism in crisis,
adding heavy punishment,
cutting short their lives,
revealing hidden crimes,
clearly showing the world
proof that wrongdoing brings retribution - why?
Wáng Shuò's words
may not be accurate.
Historical records state: "Lǐ Sī envied equal talent,
imprisoned and killed Hán Fēi in Qín,
later suffered dismemberment by cart;
Shāng Yāng betrayed old friend,
captured Prince Áng of Wèi,
later received execution."
They mean harming worthies and deceiving friends
brings retributive disaster.
What wrong did Hán Fēi commit to be imprisoned by Lǐ Sī?
What crime did Prince Áng commit to be captured by Shāng Yāng?
Dismemberment and execution,
harming worthies and betraying friends -
but what caused the imprisonment and capture?
How did these come about?
If Hán Fēi and Prince Áng had evil,
Heaven sent Lǐ Sī and Shāng Yāng to punish them,
then Lǐ Sī and Shāng Yāng acted as Heaven's agents,
should receive rewards,
not suffer disaster;
if Hán Fēi and Prince Áng were innocent,
not Heaven's targets,
Lǐ Sī and Shāng Yāng couldn't have imprisoned or captured them.
Commentators explain:
"Hán Fēi and Prince Áng had hidden wickedness and unexposed crimes,
unknown to people,
but Heaven alone knew,
thus they suffered execution."
But all guilty people
either harm worthies or oppose the Way.
If harming worthies,
what did the victims do wrong?
If opposing the Way,
what fault lies with the Way opposed?
Human suffering or success, disaster or blessing
largely depends on destiny,
minorly on timing.
Lǚ Shàng was poor and lowly,
met King Wén of Zhōu and was enfeoffed;
Nìng Qì lived in obscurity and hardship,
encountered Duke Huán of Qí and became official.
It is not that poverty and obscurity are inherently wrong,
nor that receiving titles and official positions are inherently right.
Success and failure depend on timing,
encounters and experiences are determined by fate.
Tàigōng and Nìng Qī were virtuous men,
yet they could still be said to have experienced wrongdoing.
Sages are those of pure virtue.
Yú Shùn was harmed by his father and brother,
nearly dying multiple times.
When he encountered Táng Yáo,
Yáo abdicated the throne to Shùn.
Before becoming emperor,
he suffered harm,
yet this was not wrong;
after being established as emperor,
this was not right.
Earlier, the time had not come;
later, fate and timing arrived.
Consider ancient rulers and ministers who experienced hardship and poverty,
later achieving success and recognition;
it is not necessarily that they initially had evil, with heaven bringing disaster upon them earlier,
nor that they eventually had goodness, with spirits blessing them later.
In one's lifetime conduct,
and in the integrity of one's actions,
from youth until death,
there is no difference between before and after;
yet one succeeds while another fails,
one advances while another retreats,
one is impoverished while another prospers,
one is preserved while another is ruined,
this is because encounters happen by chance,
with fate and timing aligning appropriately.
During midsummer,
lightning strikes and breaks trees,
destroys houses and rooms,
commonly said to be heaven taking dragons.
It is said that dragons hide within trees,
and conceal themselves between houses and rooms,
so when lightning breaks trees,
and destroys houses,
the dragons appear outside,
and when dragons appear,
lightning takes them to ascend to heaven.
Regardless of foolish or wise, virtuous or unworthy in the world,
all say this is so.
But if we examine the truth,
this is false talk.
Now when heaven takes dragons, what is the meaning?
If dragons as divine beings are heaven's envoys,
like virtuous ministers serving their ruler,
they would report back at times,
with no need to be taken.
If dragons escape and do not return,
this is not the behavior of divine beings,
and heaven would have no use for them.
If dragons by nature belong in heaven,
those in heaven should naturally bear offspring there,
with no need to be on earth again.
If dragons have ascents and descents,
and descending dragons bear offspring on earth,
when the offspring grow up,
heaven takes them,
then the world calls lightning heaven's anger,
but taking dragon offspring
should not involve anger.
Moreover, where dragons reside
is usually in marshes and waters,
not in trees or between houses.
How do we know this?
Shū Xiàng's mother said:
"Deep mountains and great marshes
truly produce dragons and snakes."
The Records say:
"When mountains reach their height,
clouds and rain arise there;
when waters reach their depth,
jiāo dragons are born there."
The Records also say:
"When Yǔ crossed the river,
a yellow dragon carried the boat."
"Jīng Cìfēi crossed the Huái,
with two dragons encircling the boat."
"On the Eastern Sea, there was Qiū Xīn,
brave and strong,
who went out and passed a divine abyss,
ordering his driver to water the horse,
but the horse sank while drinking.
Xīn angrily
drew his sword, entered the abyss chasing the horse,
saw two jiāo eating his horse,
and struck them with his sword, killing both jiāo."
From this we say,
jiāo and dragons often dwell in deep waters,
not in trees or between houses, this is clear.
In deep waters,
they are like fish and turtles,
creatures like fish and turtles,
why would they ascend to heaven?
Why would heaven need to take dragons?
If heavenly gods ride dragons to travel,
gods are formless and elusive,
entering and exiting without doors,
they wouldn't need to ride dragons.
If immortals ride dragons,
and heaven takes dragons for immortals,
then immortals contain heaven's essential energy,
their forms light enough to fly,
like swans and geese,
they wouldn't need to ride dragons.
The world claims Huángdì rode a dragon to ascend to heaven,
but this saying is probably false,
like today's claim that heaven takes dragons.
Moreover, when the world says dragons ascend to heaven,
they must mean dragons are divine.
If not divine,
they cannot ascend to heaven;
ascending to heaven
is proof of divinity.
By nature of heaven and earth, humans are most noble,
so dragons are inferior.
If the noble are not divine,
would the inferior instead be divine?
If dragons' nature includes being divine or not,
the divine ones ascend to heaven,
the non-divine cannot,
then turtles and snakes also have divine and non-divine,
would divine turtles and snakes also ascend to heaven?
And what energy do dragons receive to be uniquely divine?
Heaven has the forms of Azure Dragon, White Tiger, Vermilion Bird, and Black Tortoise,
earth also has creatures of dragon, tiger, bird, and turtle.
The essence of the four stars
descends to birth the four beasts,
yet tiger, bird, and turtle are not divine,
why would dragon alone be divine?
Humans are the head of naked creatures,
dragons are the head of scaly creatures,
both are heads of creatures,
if dragons ascend to heaven,
do humans also ascend to heaven?
Dragons and humans are similar,
yet only dragons are said to ascend to heaven,
meaning dragons are divine.
Some say sages are divine and know in advance,
like saying divine dragons can ascend to heaven.
Thus they attribute sages with foreknowledge,
discussing dragons' capability,
saying dragons ascending to heaven is therefore fitting.
Between heaven and earth,
elusive and formless,
the energies of cold, heat, wind, and rain are considered divine.
Now dragons have form,
having form means they move,
moving means they eat,
and eating is the nature of creatures.
By nature of heaven and earth,
those with physical form,
creatures that move and eat,
cannot be divine.
How do we say this?
Dragons have bodies.
The Records say: "There are three hundred scaly creatures,
and dragons are their head."
Since dragons head the scaly creatures,
how can they be without bodies?
How do we say this?
Dragons move and eat.)
Confucius said:
"Dragons eat in clear waters,
and swim in clear waters;
turtles eat in clear waters,
but swim in turbid waters;
fish eat in turbid waters,
but swim in clear waters.
I, above, do not reach dragons,
below, am not like fish,
perhaps in the middle, like the turtle!"
The Classic of Mountains and Seas says: Beyond the four seas,
there are people who ride dragon-snakes.
Common drawings of dragons
have horse heads and snake tails.
From this we say,
they are like horses and snakes.
Shènzǐ said:
"Flying dragons ride clouds,
soaring snakes swim in fog,
but when clouds disperse and fog clears,
they are the same as earthworms and ants."
Hánzǐ said:
"The dragon as a creature,
when tame, can be approached and ridden,
but under its throat are inverted scales over a foot long,
if anyone touches them,
it will certainly kill the person."
Comparing them to earthworms and ants,
and further stating that insects can be tamed and ridden,
clearly places snakes and horses in the same category.
The Commentary states:
"When King Zhòu made ivory chopsticks, Jīzǐ wept."
The reason for his weeping
was grief over the extremity of it.
For where there are ivory chopsticks,
there must be jade cups;
what fills the jade cups
and is lifted by the ivory chopsticks
must surely be dragon livers and leopard fetuses.
Now, dragon liver may be edible,
but dragons are hard to obtain;
being hard to obtain causes distress among the people, and distress among the people breeds calamity,
hence his consequent grief.
If the dragon were divine,
its body could not be killed,
so how could its liver be obtained for eating?
The livers and fetuses of birds and beasts are not unique,
yet "dragon liver and leopard fetus" are mentioned
because people have eaten them and know their delicious taste.
During the Spring and Autumn period,
a dragon appeared in the suburbs of Jiàng.
Wèi Xiànzǐ asked Cài Mò, saying:
"I have heard that
no insect is wiser than the dragon,
because it is never captured alive.
Is it true, then, to call it wise?"
He replied:
"It is actually humans who lack knowledge,
not that the dragon is truly wise.
In ancient times, dragons were reared,
so there were states with Dragon-Keepers
and Dragon-Handlers."
Xiànzǐ said:
"These two, I have also heard of,
but do not know the details.
What does this refer to?"
He replied:
"Formerly, Liù Shū'ān
had a descendant named Dǒng Fù,
who was exceedingly fond of dragons,
and could seek out their preferences to feed them;
thus, many dragons came to him.
He then tamed and reared dragons,
serving Shùn with them,
and was granted the surname Dǒng,
and the clan name Huànlóng (Dragon-Keeper),
enfeoffed at Zōngchuān;
the Zōngyí clan are his descendants.
Thus, under Emperor Shùn's line, dragons were reared for generations.
By the time of the Xià dynasty,
Kǒng Jiǎ pleased the emperor,
who bestowed upon him riding dragons,
two from the Hé River and two from the Hàn River,
each pair male and female.
Kǒng Jiǎ could not feed them,
and had not yet obtained a Dragon-Keeper.
After the Táotáng clan declined,
their descendant Liú Lěi learned dragon-taming from the Dragon-Keepers,
and served Kǒng Jiǎ,
able to feed the dragons.
The Xià sovereign praised him,
granting him the clan name Yùlóng (Dragon-Handler),
replacing the line of Shǐwéi.
When one female dragon died,
he secretly made it into minced meat and fed it to the Xià sovereign.
The Xià sovereign ate it,
and later sent for more.
Fearing and unable to obtain it,
he moved to Lǔ County.
The Fàn clan are his descendants."
Xiànzǐ said:
"Why are there none today?"
He replied:
"For all things, there are officials in charge,
who cultivate their methods,
pondering them day and night.
If one day they neglect their duties,
death befalls them;
losing their office, they lose their sustenance.
When officials reside in their profession,
the things they manage thrive;
if they abandon them,
the things decline and lie dormant,
stifled and unable to grow."
From this, it is said
that dragons can be reared and also eaten.
What can be eaten
cannot be divine.
As the world lacks such officials,
and also lacks people like Dǒng Fù or Liú Lěi,
dragons lie hidden and concealed,
appearing rarely;
and when they emerge, they ride clouds,
taking paths different from humans,
so people call them divine.
If such officials and people existed,
then dragons
would be like oxen,
what divinity would they have?
Considering the Shānhǎijīng,
corroborating with Shènzǐ and Hánzǐ,
testing with common paintings,
verifying with Jīzǐ's weeping,
and discussing with Cài Mò's response,
it is clear that dragons cannot be divine,
cannot ascend to heaven,
and heaven does not take dragons with thunder and lightning,
evidently.
The common saying that dragons are divine and ascend to heaven
is false.
Common sayings,
however, have some basis.
Short texts state: "Without a foot of wood,
the dragon cannot ascend to heaven."
It also says "ascend to heaven",
and mentions "a foot of wood",
meaning the dragon ascends from within the wood.
Those authors of short texts,
being common people,
see that when thunder and lightning occur,
dragons rise with them,
and when thunder strikes trees,
dragons happen to be beside the trees with the thunder,
and when the thunder departs,
the dragons follow it upward,
hence they say they ascend from within the trees.
In reality, thunder and dragons are of the same kind,
attracting each other through shared energy,
thus the Yìjīng says:
"Clouds follow the dragon,
wind follows the tiger."
It also says:
"When the tiger roars, the valley wind arrives;
when the dragon rises, the auspicious clouds gather."
Dragons and clouds attract each other,
as tigers and wind do.
Therefore, Dǒng Zhòngshū's method for rain sacrifices
involved setting up earthen dragons to induce this.
In high summer, the Great Yang prevails,
but clouds and rain interfere.
The Great Yang is fire,
clouds and rain are water;
when fire and water clash, they roar and become thunder.
Dragons, hearing the thunder, rise,
and as they rise, clouds gather;
with clouds present, dragons ride them.
Clouds and rain attract dragons,
and dragons also stir clouds to ascend.
The sky is extremely high with thunder,
and when clouds disperse, they descend again.
People see them riding clouds and say they "ascend to heaven";
they see heaven with thunder and lightning and think "heaven takes the dragons".
Confucian scholars reading the Yìjīng
and seeing the Commentary's words
all know that dragons are of the same category as clouds.
But constrained by common opinions,
they cannot fully explain it;
and with short texts as evidence,
they thus claim "heaven takes the dragons".
Heaven does not take dragons,
and dragons do not ascend to heaven.
When Qiū Xīn killed two flood dragons,
he grabbed their tails,
dragged them out to beyond the abyss,
and thunder and lightning struck them.
Flood dragons are of the same kind as dragons;
when flood dragons appear, clouds and rain come,
and with clouds and rain comes thunder and lightning.
If heaven truly took dragons,
and dragons served heaven,
why would it take a dead flood dragon?
Moreover, fish in water
also follow clouds and rain, flying
and riding clouds and rain, but not ascending to heaven.
Dragons,
being of the same category as fish,
riding thunder and lightning is like fish flying.
Fish following clouds and rain are not called divine,
yet dragons riding thunder and lightning are uniquely called divine;
this common saying
loses the truth.
Things in the world
each have their means of conveyance:
fish ride water,
snakes ride mist,
dragons ride clouds,
birds ride wind.
To see dragons riding clouds
and uniquely call them divine
is to lose the reality of dragons
and misrepresent their ability.
Thus, the reason the dragon is considered divine
lies in its ability to contract and extend its body,
causing its form to appear or vanish.
Yet merely contracting and extending its body,
making its form appear or vanish,
is insufficient to deem it divine.
Yù Ràng swallowed charcoal,
lacquered his body to appear leprous,
and people failed to recognize his form;
Zǐgòng shaved his beard to become a woman,
and others were unaware of his true appearance;
the dragon alters its form to conceal itself,
and humans likewise cannot detect it—
such transformation and hiding are skillful.
Creatures also possess innate natures:
the xīngxīng knows the past,
the magpie knows the future,
the parrot can speak;
these three marvels compared to the dragon
exhibit natures of transformation.
If skillfulness defines divinity,
then Yù Ràng and Zǐgòng would be divine.
Confucius said:
"Swimming creatures can be caught with nets,
flying ones with arrows.
But as for the dragon,
I know not how it rides wind and clouds to ascend!
Today I see Lǎozi,
is he not like the dragon?"
Now the dragon rides clouds upward,
and descends when clouds disperse;
its category as a creature can be discerned,
its ascent and descent can be known—
yet it's claimed Confucius did not know it.
With Confucius' sageliness,
he still did not comprehend the dragon,
let alone ordinary people of shallow wisdom,
who possess a nature curious for marvels
but lack a mind seeking substantiation,
calling the dragon divine and sky-ascending—
this is hardly surprising.
In midsummer's season,
thunder and lightning strike swiftly,
splitting trees,
destroying houses,
sometimes killing people.
Common belief holds that "splitting trees and destroying houses"
signifies Heaven seizing dragons;
while "killing people"
is said to punish hidden faults.
Those who serve unclean food and drink
provoke Heaven's wrath, struck dead.
The rumbling sound
is Heaven's angry voice,
like human roaring.
None, foolish or wise,
dispute this.
Yet applying human principles to discuss it,
reveals these as empty falsehoods.
When thunder occurs,
it's one breath, one sound.
Tree-splitting and house-wrecking also kill;
when killing occurs, trees and houses are also damaged.
To claim solely that tree-splitting and house-wrecking
mean Heaven takes dragons,
while killing people
punishes hidden faults—
assigning different auspicious or ominous meanings to dragon-seizing—
though simultaneous and sharing one sound,
is unfounded.
Some argue the "rumbling"
is Heaven's roaring anger.
This suits punishing faults,
but not seizing dragons.
Punishing faults
with Heaven's anger is plausible;
but seizing dragons—
what fault justifies anger at them?
If dragons are divine,
Heaven taking them
shouldn't involve anger;
if dragons have faults,
sharing guilt with humans,
Heaven should simply kill them,
why "take" them?
Killing humans
with anger is understandable;
but seizing dragons—
what fault warrants anger at them?
Killing humans
doesn't involve "taking,"
yet killing dragons
does—
how do human and dragon crimes differ?
And how does their killing differ?
Thus, the dragon-seizing theory is untenable,
and the fault-punishing claim likewise unworthy of belief.
How to verify this?
Consider thunder's sound during its swift strike:
people fall dead on the ground,
the rumbling noise overhead
causes their death.
Is the rumbling truly Heaven's anger?
Anger uses the mouth; can mouth-anger kill?
The breath of an angry mouth
—how can it kill people?
Those killed by thunder
upon examination of their bodies
show burn marks.
If Heaven uses mouth-anger,
does an angry mouth produce fire?
Moreover, the mouth attaches to the body,
its movement aligns with the body.
When striking and splitting occurs,
the sound touches the ground;
as it fades,
the sound reaches heaven.
If so,
when the sound touches ground,
the mouth must reach ground,
and so must the body.
Yet during thunder's swift strike,
looking upward,
one doesn't see heaven descending.
Not seeing heaven descend,
means the rumbling sound
is not heaven's anger.
Heaven's anger would resemble humans'.
When humans are angry,
closeness makes the sound swift,
distance makes it faint.
Now the sound is near,
but its body distant—
this contradicts anger's reality.
Moreover, during thunder's swift strike,
the sound moves east-west or north-south.
If heaven's angry body moved,
with mouth pointing directions,
looking up, heaven should shift directions too.
Some say:
"Heaven already moves east-west or north-south,
but clouds and rain darken the sky,
so people cannot see it."
But winds differ within a thousand lǐ,
thunder varies within a hundred lǐ.
The Yìjīng says:
"It shocks a hundred lǐ."
Where thunder and lightning strike,
with dark stormy weather,
beyond a hundred lǐ where no rain falls,
one should see heaven shifting directions.
The mouth attaches to heaven,
so heaven should follow the mouth;
one mouth-movement should shift the entire sky,
not just thunderstorm areas—
heaven moving with the mouth.
And who is supposedly angry?
A celestial deity?
Or the vast blue sky?
If a deity,
divine anger is soundless;
if the blue sky,
as a physical body, it cannot be angry—
anger requires a mouth.
Furthermore, heaven and earth coexist
as husband and wife,
thus acting as parents to the people.
If a child errs,
the father angrily
beats them to death—
would the mother not weep?
Now if heaven angrily kills,
earth should weep for it.
Yet we only hear heaven's anger,
not earth's weeping.
If earth cannot weep,
then heaven cannot be angry either.
Moreover, with anger comes joy.
People have hidden faults,
but also hidden virtues.
For hidden faults,
heaven angrily kills;
if there are hidden virtues,
heaven should joyfully reward them.
Rumbling is called heaven's anger;
so heaven's joy should sound like hearty laughter.
Humans have joy and anger,
hence attributing them to heaven.
To infer Heaven through humans,
knowing Heaven is rooted in humanity,
if humans do not feel anger,
then there is no basis to claim Heaven is angry.
To understand Heaven through humans,
one should fully comprehend human nature.
When humans are angry, they sigh and groan;
when joyful, they sing and laugh.
Yet we often hear of Heaven's anger,
rarely of its joy;
often see Heaven's punishments,
seldom its rewards.
Could it be that Heaven is angry but not joyful,
sparing in rewards but eager to punish?
Why do anger and punishment manifest,
while joy and rewards show no evidence?
Moreover, when thunder strikes,
"splitting trees and destroying houses,"
"sometimes killing people,"
it is taken as Heaven's anger.
Yet sometimes thunder occurs
without causing damage,
nor killing anyone—
is Heaven angry for no reason?
A ruler does not express empty joy or anger;
joy and anger must entail rewards or punishments.
To be angry without punishment is futile—
this would make Heaven capricious.
Caprice loses authority,
which is not Heaven's way.
Those who study governance
take cold and warm air as signs of joy or anger,
claiming the ruler's joy brings warmth,
his anger brings cold.
On days of thunder and lightning,
Heaven must be cold.
Before Gāozǔ's birth, his mother Liú Āo
once rested by a marsh's bank,
dreaming of encountering a spirit,
while thunder darkened the sky.
Heaven was bestowing its energy,
a time of joy;
why then the angry thunder?
If destruction indicates anger,
and its absence indicates joy,
then the rumbling sound
should not be the same.
Humans express anger and joy with different sounds;
if Heaven's anger and joy share one sound,
contradicting human nature,
how can we call it Heaven's anger?
Moreover, "feeding someone unclean food"
is a minor offense.
For the most exalted being
to personally punish such a small fault
is unbefitting.
The exalted do not personally punish faults,
hence kings do not personally execute criminals.
If Heaven is superior to kings,
yet personally punishes minor errors,
then its virtue is inferior to a king's.
Furthermore, Heaven's intent
resembles human intention.
When a ruler hears of a crime,
initially
he condemns it in anger,
but when executing punishment,
he feels sorrow and pity.
Thus the *Analects* say:
"If you uncover the truth,
feel compassion, not joy."
Zhòu was utterly wicked,
yet King Wǔ, preparing to punish him,
felt sorrow and pity,
as the *Shàngshū* states:
"I follow compassion for you."
A ruler punishes evil
with pity in killing;
Heaven punishes faults
with angry strikes—
thus Heaven lacks kindness while humans show more mercy.
Those who discuss rain say it is Heaven bestowing energy.
Heaven bestows energy,
which condenses into rain,
thus rain nurtures all things,
called a blessing.
If humans are not joyful,
they do not bestow favors;
if Heaven is displeased,
it does not send rain.
To call thunder
Heaven's anger,
and rain
Heaven's joy,
yet thunder often comes with rain,
as theorists claim
Heaven is both angry and joyful.
A ruler does not reward and punish on the same day,
but Heaven's anger and joy occur simultaneously,
contradicting human ways,
making rewards and punishments inconsistent.
Moreover, expressing both anger and joy causes chaos.
To punish evil-doers for chaos
with chaotic methods
is not Heaven's conduct.
Winter thunder is called yang energy leaking;
spring thunder, yang energy emerging;
summer thunder is not called yang energy flourishing,
but labeled Heaven's anger—
mere empty words.
Humans in the world
are beings;
other creatures are also beings.
What animals eat,
Heaven cannot know;
what humans eat,
Heaven alone knows.
All things under Heaven
are its children.
Parents toward children
show equal kindness—
would they favor the noble and wise,
while neglecting the lowly and foolish?
Why then does Heaven scrutinize humans so clearly,
yet remain blind to other creatures?
Pigs eat filth
given by humans,
and Heaven does not strike them dead.
If humans are esteemed and uniquely forbidden,
then when rats contaminate food,
humans unknowingly
eat it by mistake,
yet Heaven does not kill them.
If Heaven can forgive rats,
it can forgive humans.
If someone unintentionally feeds another unclean food,
and it is eaten unknowingly,
how could it be deliberately offering filth?
If done deliberately,
the person would not eat it.
Empress Lǚ severed Lady Qī's hands,
gouged out her eyes,
and placed her in a latrine,
calling her a "human pig."
People shown this
were heartbroken.
Emperor Huì saw it,
fell ill and could not rise.
Lǚ did this deliberately,
yet Heaven did not punish her;
humans err unknowingly,
and Heaven kills them.
Failing to pardon mistakes while forgiving intent—
Heaven's governance is perverse.
When people eat unclean things,
their mouths do not perceive the filth;
if they eat knowingly,
it is called gut filth.
Lady Qī was thrown into a latrine,
her body
defiled—
how does defilement differ from filth?
How do guts differ from the body?
To care for guts but not the body,
to harm filth but not shame—
this is not Heaven's intent.
Hearing of someone eating unclean food,
one remains calm;
witnessing Lady Qī's fate,
none are unmoved.
If humans grieve,
Heaven should feel sorrow.
To pity Lady Qī is to resent Lǚ.
Yet when Lǚ died,
there was likely no thunder.
The sorcerer Liú Chūn misled King Yīng of Chǔ,
making him eat unclean food.
Chūn died
without encountering thunder.
In the fourth year of Jiànchū, summer sixth month,
thunder killed five sheep in Kuàijī, Yín, that ate unclean food—
all died.
What hidden fault had the sheep, that thunder killed them?
If a boatman pollutes upstream,
and others drink downstream,
the boatman is not struck dead.
Heavenly spirits reside above,
as kings dwell in palaces.
Kings live behind layered gates,
so heavenly spirits should dwell in secrecy;
kings inhabit palaces,
thus Heaven has its seats in Tàiwēi, Zǐgōng, Xuānyuán, and Wénchāng.
The ruler is far removed from the people,
unaware of their hidden wrongdoings;
the celestial deities reside within the four palaces,
how could they perceive humanity's covert faults?
When a ruler learns of people's errors,
it is through human means;
if Heaven knows of human wickedness,
it should likewise rely on spirits.
Should Heaven inquire about faults through spirits,
then when executing punishment,
it ought to employ spirits;
but if spirits are employed,
then the anger belongs to spirits,
not to Heaven.
Moreover, rulers administer punishments in autumn,
while Heaven employs killing in summer—
this shows rulers contradict celestial timing in applying penalties.
To follow Heaven's way,
their executions
should emulate the celestial model.
Heaven kills in summer,
rulers punish in autumn—
this divergence between Heaven and humanity
violates the principle of serving Heaven.
Some argue:
"Defiling human food and drink
is Heaven's gravest abomination,
and eradicating great evils
requires no seasonal restriction."
For rulers, great evils are
treason and gross immorality;
for Heaven, the great evil is
defiling human nourishment—
what Heaven detests
shows disproportionate severity.
If scales were equal,
rulers should imitate Heaven
by establishing capital punishment for food defilement.
Yet when sage kings governed the realm,
their penal codes omitted this law—
does this mean sage kings were negligent
and committed oversights?
Others contend:
"Spirits govern the hidden realm,
while rulers govern the visible.
Covert transgressions escape human detection,
hence spirits are assigned to oversee them."
The response:
Hidden faults are numerous—
why not eliminate them all?
Punishing only selected offenses
contradicts the principle of governing the hidden.
Heaven's wrath allows no delay,
human resentment brooks no respite.
When people commit covert wrongs,
some occur in winter—
not exclusively in summer.
If winter offenses
are not immediately punished,
but deferred until summer,
this violates the principle of immediacy.
Painters and illustrators
depict thunder's form
as layered spheres resembling connected drums.
They further portray a figure
with a mighty warrior's appearance,
calling him Léi Gōng,
showing him pulling linked drums with his left hand
while pushing with his right,
as if striking them.
Their conception implies
the rumbling thunder
stems from these drums colliding;
the sudden cracking sounds
come from hammer strikes;
when it kills people,
it's through dragging and striking
with these connected drums.
People believe this
without questioning.
But examining its origins
reveals a false image.
Now thunder
must be either sound or energy.
How can sound or energy
be pulled and pushed into drum shapes?
If truly tangible,
then it becomes physical.
Objects that clang when struck
are either drums or bells.
Is the rumbling noise
from drums or bells?
If so,
bells and drums cannot hang unsupported—
they require stands
to be secured
before sounding.
Yet these thunder-drums hang from nothing,
and Léi Gōng's feet
touch no surface—
how then does thunder occur?
Some say:
"This confirms his divinity.
If he required support
and footing like humans,
how could he be divine?"
The response:
Divine beings
are formless and elusive,
passing without portals,
boundless in movement—
hence called divine.
Now Léi Gōng has form
and thunder has physical instruments—
