how can this be divinity?
If formless,
he couldn't be depicted;
if having form,
he cannot be called divine.
When people speak of divine dragons ascending,
skeptics deny it
because humans occasionally see dragon forms.
Since their form appears,
people paint ascending dragons;
because they can be painted,
they possess non-divine substance.
Objection:
"People also see ghost forms—
are ghosts then divine?"
Response:
People sometimes see ghosts,
but do they see Léi Gōng?
Ghosts are called spirits
yet walk the ground
like humans.
Léi Gōng's head hangs not from heaven,
his feet touch not the earth—
how can he be Léi Gōng?
All flying creatures have wings;
wingless flying beings
are called immortals.
When painting immortals,
artists give them wings.
If Léi Gōng resembles immortals,
he should have wings.
If Léi Gōng doesn't fly,
thunder-artists err in claiming flight;
if he truly flies,
they err in omitting wings.
Thus,
those depicting thunder
create false images.
Furthermore,
thunder-theorists
call thunder
Heaven's angry exhalation;
while thunder-artists
call it Léi Gōng pulling drums.
If theorists are correct,
artists are wrong;
if artists are correct,
theorists err.
The two conflict,
yet accepting both
obliterates truth and falsehood.
Without this distinction,
reality cannot be determined.
Unable to resolve doubts,
false theories prevail.
The Lǐ Jì states:
"Carve wine vessels into thunder shapes."
Emerging and receding,
bending and stretching—
when interlocking they resonate.
This interlocking pattern
resembles swirling accumulations.
Here lies the symbolic representation.
When energies interlock and split,
the rumbling sound
is this interlocking noise.
The sudden cracking
is energy喷射的声音,
and when this energy strikes people,
they perish.
To speak truthfully,
thunder is the agitated energy of the sun.
How can this be proven?
In the first month, yang energy stirs,
thus thunder begins in the first month;
in the fifth month, yang energy is at its peak,
thus thunder is swift in the fifth month;
in autumn and winter, yang energy declines,
thus thunder lies dormant in autumn and winter.
During the height of summer,
the sun governs affairs,
and yin energy takes advantage of this.
When yin and yang struggle against each other,
they clash and grind,
and this grinding produces violent projections,
which become poisonous,
striking people and causing instant death,
striking trees and breaking them,
striking houses and destroying them.
If a person is beneath a tree or inside a house,
they may be struck accidentally and die.
How can this be verified?
Try pouring a dou of water onto a foundry fire:
the steam bursts forth with a cracking sound,
resembling the noise of thunder.
If one approaches it,
it will certainly scorch the human body.
Heaven and earth serve as the furnace, vast indeed;
yang energy is the fire, fierce indeed;
clouds and rain are the water, abundant indeed.
When they struggle and project violently,
how could it not be swift?
When it strikes and injures the human body,
how could it not cause death?
When a smelters melt iron,
they use clay molds;
if the mold is dry, the iron flows smoothly,
otherwise, it splashes and shoots out.
If it hits a person's body,
the skin is scorched and peeled.
The heat of yang energy
is not merely as intense as molten iron;
when agitated by yin energy,
it is not merely like damp clay;
when this agitated energy strikes a person,
the pain is not just that of scorching and peeling.
Now thunder
is fire,
and fire energy scorches people,
leaving marks on them.
If the scorched area resembles writing,
people see it
and say that Heaven has recorded their faults
to show the common people.
This is again false and baseless.
If everyone had faults,
and Heaven used thunder to kill people,
it should reveal their evils
to warn those who come after,
clearly displaying the writing,
not leaving it obscure.
The "Diagram" emerged from the River,
the "Book" emerged from the Luo,
the Hé Tú and the Luò Shū
were acts of Heaven and Earth,
and people could read and understand them.
Now, if the writing on those killed by thunder
is also an act of Heaven,
why is it hard to understand?
If one argues that human skin cannot be written on,
consider Zhòngzǐ, wife of Duke Huì of Lǔ,
daughter of Duke Wǔ of Sòng,
born with writing on her palm,
saying, "She will be the wife of the ruler of Lǔ."
The writing was clear and understandable,
so Zhòngzǐ went to Lǔ.
If thunder writing is not clear,
it is hard to use it as a warning.
Thus,
the marks of fire scorching
are not carved by Heaven.
Some may exaggerate the words if there is a slight mark,
or invent tales where there is none.
Such baseless customs
delight in creating strange wonders.
How can it be verified that thunder is fire?
When a person is struck by thunder and dies,
examine the body:
if the head is struck, the hair and beard are burned;
if the body is struck, the skin is scorched;
approach the corpse and smell the fire energy—
this is the first verification.
Practitioners of the arts
heat stones until they turn red
and throw them into a well;
the stones are hot, the well is cold,
causing a loud, agitated sound
resembling thunder—
this is the second verification.
When a person is injured by cold,
and cold energy enters the abdomen,
where it is normally warm,
the struggle between warm and cold
produces an agitated, thunder-like sound—
this is the third verification.
When thunder occurs,
lightning is often seen
as a great fire, blazing like a person's shine—
this is the fourth verification.
When thunder strikes,
at that moment,
it may burn people's houses, as well as trees and grass on the ground—
this is the fifth verification.
To argue that thunder is fire, there are five verifications;
to say thunder is Heaven's anger, there is not one proof.
Therefore, to claim thunder is Heaven's anger
is a false and baseless statement.
Though some may object:
The "Lúnyǔ" says:
"When a rapid thunderclap or fierce wind occurs, one must change demeanor."
The "Lǐjì" states:
"If there is a violent wind, rapid thunder, or heavy rain, one must change demeanor,
even at night, one must rise,
dress, don the cap, and sit upright."
This is for fear of Heaven's anger,
dreading punishment upon oneself.
If thunder is not Heaven's anger,
and its strikes are not punishment for faults,
then why would the nobleman change demeanor and sit formally in court dress at the sound of thunder?
The response is:
Heaven's relation to humans is like that of father and son;
if the father changes,
how can the son remain indifferent?
Thus, when Heaven changes,
one should also change.
This is顺应天时,
showing that one does not defy it.
When people hear a dog barking outside,
they are all startled,
straining their bodies and ears to listen carefully;
how much more so when they hear the abnormal sound of Heaven's change,
the roaring and rapid noise?
What the "Lúnyǔ" refers to
and the "Lǐjì" speaks of
concern the nobleman.
The nobleman is cautious and prudent,
knowing he has no fault, like the eclipses of the sun and moon;
he does not harbor dark, unclean deeds that harm others,
introspects without fear,
so why should he fear thunder?
If indeed he does not fear thunder,
then his change in demeanor cannot serve as proof of Heaven's anger.
Why?
Because it is not for his own sake.
If indeed he fears thunder,
it still does not prove punishment for hidden faults.
Why?
Because those struck by thunder
are often without fault;
the nobleman fears encountering it by chance,
hence his fearful change in demeanor.
Thus,
the nobleman's change in demeanor
cannot prove that thunder is Heaven's anger,
but instead highlights thunder's indiscriminate striking.
Indiscriminate striking does not punish faults,
so people fear it.
If it truly punished faults,
only those with faults should fear it,
and the nobleman would have no reason to fear.
King of Sòng asked Táng Yāng:
"I have killed many people,
yet my ministers grow less fearful;
what is the reason?"
Táng Yāng replied:
"Those whom you punish, King,
are all the wicked.
Punishing the wicked,
why should the good fear?
If you want your ministers to fear,
it is better not to distinguish between good and wicked but to punish them arbitrarily from time to time.
In this way, your ministers will fear."]
The King of Sòng followed his advice,
the ministers became fearful,
and the state of Sòng was greatly terrified.
The King of Sòng punished arbitrarily,
so the state of Sòng was greatly terrified;
fearing the indiscriminate strikes of thunder and lightning,
the nobleman changes his demeanor.
The nobleman's change in demeanor
is akin to the great terror in the state of Sòng.
The Confucian texts say:
Huángdì mined copper from Shǒushān,
and cast a tripod at the foot of Jīngshān.
Once the tripod was completed,
a dragon descended with its beard hanging down to welcome Huángdì.
Huángdì mounted the dragon,
and over seventy ministers and consorts followed him up,
whereupon the dragon ascended.
The minor officials who could not get on
all grabbed the dragon's beard.
The beard was pulled out,
and Huángdì's bow fell.
The people looked up and saw that Huángdì had already ascended to heaven,
so they clutched his bow and the dragon's beard, wailing and crying.
Hence, later generations named the place "Dìnghú,"
and the bow "Wūhào."
The Records of the Grand Historian, in eulogizing the Five Emperors, also states:
After Huángdì performed the Fēng and Shàn sacrifices,
he became an immortal and departed,
and his ministers paid homage to his clothes and crown.
They were then buried.
I say:
This is a false tale.
What exactly is "Huángdì"?
A title?
Or a posthumous name?
If it is a posthumous name,
it is what the ministers eulogized and listed,
based on his deeds in life to give him the name.
Huángdì loved the Way,
and thus ascended to heaven;
if his ministers eulogized him,
they should have used
"Xiān" or "Shēng,"
not "Huáng" as his posthumous name.
The Rules for Posthumous Names state:
"Bringing peace to the people and establishing laws is called Huáng."
"Huángdì" is
a posthumous name for pacifying the people,
not a title for attaining the Way.
The posthumous names of the hundred kings:
if civil, they are called "Wén,"
if martial, they are called "Wǔ."
Wén and Wǔ do not lose their truth,
thus encouraging conduct and behavior.
If in Huángdì's time it was simple,
were there no posthumous names?
Calling him "Huángdì," from which generation's people was he?
If Huángdì's ministers knew their lord;
if later generations traced his deeds—
in Huángdì's era,
whether titles or posthumous names existed is uncertain,
but it is clear that "Huáng" is not a term for ascending as an immortal.
Dragons do not ascend to heaven;
if Huángdì rode one,
it shows he did not ascend to heaven.
Dragons stir clouds and rain,
riding them to travel;
when clouds disperse and rain stops,
they descend back into the abyss.
If Huángdì truly rode a dragon,
he would have drowned in the abyss with it.
Consider that Huángdì was buried at Qiáoshān,
yet it is said his ministers buried his clothes and crown.
If he truly rode a dragon and ascended to heaven,
his clothes would not leave his body;
if after the Fēng and Shàn sacrifices, he became an immortal and left,
his clothes and crown should not have been left behind.
If Huángdì truly became an immortal, did not die, and ascended to heaven,
it would have been witnessed by his ministers and people.
Seeing him ascend,
they would know he did not die, necessarily.
Burying the clothes of one who did not die
is no different from burying an actual dead person,
not the sincere heart of ministers dealing with facts,
nor distinguishing between life and death.
Those recorded on Mount Tài, seventy-two lords,
all toiled in spirit and strained their thoughts,
worried about royal affairs,
and only then achieved merit and established deeds,
bringing order and great peace.
With great peace, the world is harmonious and safe,
then they ascend Mount Tài to perform the Fēng and Shàn sacrifices.
Cultivating the Way to seek immortality
is different from worrying about duties and laboring at affairs.
Focusing on the Way, one forgets affairs;
worrying about affairs harms one's nature.
It is said Yáo was like dried meat,
Shùn like preserved meat,
their hearts troubled and bitter,
their bodies emaciated and haggard.
If Huángdì brought about great peace,
his body should have been like Yáo and Shùn's.
Yáo and Shùn did not attain the Way,
yet Huángdì ascended to heaven—
that is not the truth.
If Huángdì neglected affairs to cultivate the Way,
then his mind would be harmonious,
his body robust and strong,
different from Yáo and Shùn.
Different, thus his achievements would not be the same.
With different achievements,
the world not at peace, yet he ascended to perform Fēng—
again, not true.
Among the Five Emperors and Three Sovereigns, all had superior sage virtue,
yet Huángdì is not among the highest.
If all sages became immortals,
then Huángdì would not be the only one;
if sages do not become immortals,
why did Huángdì alone become one?
The world sees Huángdì loved esoteric arts,
and esoteric arts are the work of immortals,
so they say Huángdì became an immortal.
They also see the name "Dìnghú,"
and say Huángdì mined copper from Shǒushān to cast a tripod,
and a dragon hung its beard to welcome him.
This is no different from the tale of Mount Kuàijī.
The mountain is named "Kuàijī,"
so it is said Xià Yǔ toured and inspected,
and held accounts on this mountain,
hence called "Kuàijī."
But Yǔ went to Kuàijī
to control floods, not to tour,
just as Huángdì loved esoteric arts but did not ascend to heaven.
There was no accounting event,
just as there was no reality of casting a tripod and a dragon hanging its beard.
A village named "Shèngmǔ,"
can it mean a son truly surpassed his mother?
A town named "Cháogē,"
can it mean the people sing when they rise in the morning?
The Confucian texts say:
Huáinán Wáng studied the Way,
summoning all who had the Way in the world.
He lowered the dignity of a whole state
to approach masters of esoteric arts,
so those masters
all gathered in Huáinán,
and extraordinary methods and unusual arts
vied to emerge.
The king then attained the Way,
and his whole family ascended to heaven.
Even the livestock became immortals,
dogs barked in the sky,
chickens crowed among the clouds.
This says the elixir of immortality was abundant,
dogs and chickens ate it,
and followed the king up to heaven.
Those who love the Way and study immortality
all say it is so.
This is a false tale.
Humans
are beings,
though noble as kings or marquises,
their nature is no different from other beings.
Beings all die;
how can humans become immortals?
Birds have feathers,
can fly, but cannot ascend to heaven.
Humans have no feathers;
how can they fly up?
If they had feathers,
they would only be like birds,
let alone without them—
how could they ascend to heaven?
Consider that beings able to fly and ascend
are born with signs of feathers;
beings able to run
are born with hooves or feet.
Runners cannot fly up;
flyers cannot run;
endowed nature and received qi
make forms distinct.
Now humans have the nature to run,
so born without signs of feathers,
growing to old age,
never showing marvels.
Loving the Way and studying immortality,
mid-life growing feathers,
finally flying up—
if the nature of beings could change,
could metal, wood, water, fire
be transformed?
Toads turning into quails,
sparrows entering water becoming clams—
Knowing that one would inevitably be blamed by the world,
one resorts to exaggerated and fabricated tales,
claiming to have encountered a certain scholar.
The implication is that there are immortals,
and failing to find them
is merely due to the destined time not yet arriving.
Liú Ān, the King of Huáinán, was executed for rebellion,
known throughout the land,
witnessed by contemporaries,
yet Confucian texts still say he attained the Way and ascended as an immortal,
with his chickens and dogs rising to heaven too.
How much more so for Lú Áo alone,
traveling to remote, untrodden places,
could he not fabricate tales of the netherworld?
This is no different from the story of Xiàng Màndū from Púbǎn in Hédōng.
Màndū loved the Way and sought immortality,
abandoned his family and fled,
returning after three years.
His family asked about his experience,
and Màndū said:
"When I left, I didn't realize it myself;
suddenly I felt as if lying down,
and several immortals
took me up to heaven,
stopping a few miles from the moon.
I saw the moon above and the darkness below,
the darkness where I couldn't tell east from west.
Living beside the moon,
the cold was desolate.
When I was hungry and wanted to eat,
the immortals would give me a cup of flowing rosy clouds to drink.
Each time I drank a cup,
I wouldn't feel hungry for months.
I don't know how many years passed,
or what I did wrong,
but suddenly I felt as if lying down again,
and descended back here."
In Hédōng, he was called the Rejected Immortal.
Those who examine facts heard this
and knew it wasn't true.
If Màndū could ascend to heaven,
why wasn't he an immortal?
After three years,
why did he return?
When one leaves the human world
and ascends to the highest heavens,
their essence, energy, form, and body
should change from their former state.
All things that transform
never return to their original form.
The pupa transforms into a cicada;
once its wings are fully grown,
it cannot turn back into a pupa.
Beings that can ascend
all have wings;
if they ascend and then descend again,
their wings should remain as before.
If Màndū's body had wings,
his words might be credible;
but without wings,
his tale is false.
Its falseness makes it of the same nature as Lú Áo's story.
Perhaps Màndū, fond of the Way,
secretly left his family,
wandered to distant lands,
gained nothing in the end,
exhausted and hopeless,
silently returned home,
ashamed and speechless,
so he claimed to have ascended to heaven.
He meant to say the Way can be learned,
and immortals truly exist,
but he himself must have erred,
hence achieving but then being rejected,
ascending but then descending.
Confucian texts say:
The King of Qí had an illness,
so he sent someone to Sòng to fetch Wén Zhì.
When Wén Zhì arrived,
he examined the king's illness
and said to the crown prince:
"The king's illness
can certainly be cured.
However,
once the king is cured,
he will surely kill me."
The crown prince asked:
"Why?"
Wén Zhì replied:
"If I don't anger the king,
his illness cannot be treated.
If the king gets angry,
I will certainly die."
The crown prince kowtowed and urgently pleaded:
"If you can cure the king's illness,
I and my mother will plead with the king even at the risk of death;
the king will surely favor us.
I beg you, sir, not to worry."
Wén Zhì said:
"Very well,
I will risk death for the king."
He made an appointment with the crown prince,
but when the time came, he failed to appear three times,
so the King of Qí was already enraged.
When Wén Zhì finally arrived,
he did not remove his shoes before climbing onto the bed, stepped on the king's clothes,
and asked about his illness.
The king was angry and did not speak to him.
Wén Zhì then used harsh words to further provoke the king's anger.
The king shouted and rose,
and his illness was thus cured.
The king, furious and displeased,
ordered Wén Zhì to be boiled alive.
The crown prince and queen urgently pleaded for him but failed,
and indeed Wén Zhì was boiled alive in a cauldron.
After being cooked for three days and three nights,
his complexion did not change.
Wén Zhì said:
"If you truly wish to kill me,
why not cover the cauldron
to cut off the yin and yang energies?"
The king had it covered,
and only then did Wén Zhì die.
Now, Wén Zhì
was a man of the Way,
who could enter water without getting wet,
enter fire without being burned,
hence remaining in the cauldron for three days and three nights
with his complexion unchanged.
This is a false tale.
If Wén Zhì could be boiled for three days and three nights
without his complexion changing,
yet died from suffocation just by being covered once,
that is not proof of attaining the Way.
All living beings that breathe
die when their breath is cut off;
dead creatures,
when boiled, will rot.
If a living being is placed in a sealed container,
with its opening covered,
and gaps painted shut with lacquer,
cutting off inside and outside air,
preventing breath from escaping,
it will die shortly.
If placed in a pot of boiling water,
it would rot immediately.
Why?
Because their bodies and breath are alike,
endowed with nature from heaven,
belonging to the same category.
Did Wén Zhì not breathe?
If he were like metal or stone,
not rotting in boiling water,
that would be consistent;
but if Wén Zhì breathed,
how could boiling not kill him?
It couldn't.
Consider Wén Zhì's speech:
speaking requires sound,
sound relies on breath.
The movement of breath
depends on the flow of blood and energy.
The flow of blood and energy
is attached to bones and flesh.
Beings of bone and flesh,
when boiled, will die.
To say boiling didn't kill him
is the first falsehood.
If he could survive boiling,
he would be a true immortal,
like metal or stone.
Whether metal or stone is covered
or not makes no difference.
Yet they say covering killed Wén Zhì,
that's the second falsehood.
Placing a person in cold water,
without the heat of fire or boiling water,
if their nose and mouth are blocked from the outside,
in a short while,
they will suffocate and die.
If drowning in cold water
can kill,
how much more in boiling water
with the fury of fierce fire?
To claim he didn't die in boiling water
is the third falsehood.
When submerged in water,
the mouth isn't visible from outside,
and speech cannot be heard clearly.
When Wén Zhì was boiled,
his body must have been submerged in the cauldron. Submerged, his mouth wouldn't be visible,
If the mouth is unseen, words cannot spread.
Wén Zhì's claims
are the fourth fabrication.
Boiling a man who should have died instantly,
for three days and three nights,
without his complexion changing—
even foolish and ignorant people
would recognize this as strange.
Had King Qí been unaware,
the crown prince and his ministers should have witnessed this marvel.
Finding Wén Zhì extraordinary,
they would have requested his release, honored and revered him,
and followed him to learn the Way.
Yet it is said that after three days and three nights,
no minister or son pleaded for his release—
this is the fifth fabrication.
Perhaps it was heard that Wén Zhì was truly boiled,
and died immediately upon boiling,
but the world, seeing him as a Daoist practitioner,
fabricated tales of his immortality.
Just as Huángdì actually died,
yet legends say he ascended to heaven;
or as Huáinán rebelled,
but texts claim he transcended the world.
The world delights in spreading falsehoods,
hence Wén Zhì's story has passed down to this day.
The world lacks evidence of anyone attaining the Way,
yet there are long-lived individuals.
When people see those who live long,
practice Daoism to become immortals,
and surpass a hundred years without dying,
they collectively call them immortals.
How can this be proven?
During Emperor Wǔ's time,
there was Lǐ Shàojūn, who presented methods for worshiping the stove, abstaining from grains, and preventing aging to the emperor,
who esteemed him highly.
Shàojūn concealed his age and origins,
often claiming to be seventy,
yet capable of manipulating objects and halting aging.
He traveled among feudal lords with his arts.
He had no wife or children.
People heard he could control things and remain ageless,
so they bestowed gifts upon him, leaving him with surplus money, gold, clothing, and food.
All thought he did not work yet lived abundantly,
and not knowing his background,
they believed more fervently, vying to serve him.
Shàojūn possessed a talent for formulas,
skilled at clever revelations and astonishing accuracy.
Once drinking with Wǔ'ān Hóu,
among the guests was a man over ninety,
and Shàojūn mentioned a place where he had roamed and hunted with the man's grandfather.
The old man, as a child,
had followed his grandfather
and recognized the spot.
The entire assembly was astounded.
When Shàojūn met the emperor,
the emperor had an ancient bronze vessel,
and asked Shàojūn about it.
Shàojūn said:
"This vessel was displayed by Duke Huán of Qí in the fifteenth year at Bó Qǐn."
Later, checking the inscription,
it indeed was Duke Huán's vessel,
astonishing the whole court,
who deemed Shàojūn divine, a man of centuries.
After some time,
Shàojūn fell ill and died.
Those called Dao-attainers today
are like Lǐ Shàojūn.
Shàojūn died among people,
who saw his corpse,
hence it's known he was naturally long-lived.
Had he been in the mountains and forests,
in untrodden wilderness,
dying alone among rocks,
his body eaten by tigers, wolves, or foxes,
the world would again deem him a true immortal who departed.
Daoist learners today lack Shàojūn's longevity,
not reaching a hundred years,
dying alongside others,
yet ignorant fools
still call it 'corpse liberation,' claiming
they did not truly die.
What is meant by 'corpse liberation'?
What is it?
Does it mean the body dies and the spirit departs?
Or that the body doesn't die but sheds its skin?
If it means the body dies and the spirit leaves,
that's no different from death,
and everyone would be an immortal.
If it means not dying but shedding the skin,
then all Daoist learners who die have bones and flesh intact,
no different from ordinary corpses.
Consider the cicada leaving its nymph shell,
the turtle shedding its scutes,
the snake sloughing its skin,
the deer casting its antlers—
shelled and skinned creatures shed their coverings,
taking their bones and flesh away;
this could be called corpse liberation.
But those who die learning the Dao
have corpses similar to cicada nymphs,
yet cannot be said to have undergone corpse liberation.
Why?
For when the cicada leaves its nymph shell,
it's no more divine than the nymph;
how much less so for those unlike the nymph—
to call it corpse liberation
is but another falsehood distorting reality.
Grand Historian Sīmǎ Qiān lived in the same era as Lǐ Shàojūn;
though he wasn't present at
Shàojūn's deathbed,
he sufficiently witnessed the truth.
Had Shàojūn not truly died,
but been liberated from his corpse,
the Grand Historian should have recorded the event,
not stated he died.
The incident with the ninety-year-old who recalled his childhood
is proof of Shàojūn's advanced age.
Perhaps Shàojūn was fourteen or fifteen,
and the old man was a child,
accompanying his grandfather.
If Shàojūn died at two hundred,
why wouldn't he recognize him?
Emperor Wǔ's time was far from when Duke Huán cast the bronze vessel,
which Shàojūn couldn't have witnessed.
Maybe he heard of old vessels in the palace,
or someone checked the inscription and told him,
so he knew upon seeing it.
Similarly, enthusiasts today
seeing old swords or hooks
can often name them,
but can we say they witnessed their making?
Some say: Dōngfāng Shuò was also a Daoist,
surnamed Jīn,
styled Mànqiàn,
changing his name and surname,
serving in the Hàn court.
Outwardly an official,
inwardly a transcendent.
This too is false.
Shuò and Shàojūn were contemporaries under Emperor Wǔ,
both seen by the Grand Historian.
Shàojūn had methods for grain abstinence, stove worship, and aging prevention,
identified Duke Huán's cast tripod,
and knew where the old man's grandfather roamed—
yet even he had no proof of attaining the Way,
merely being long-lived and slow to die.
How much less for Shuò, who lacked Shàojūn's arts and evidence,
what did people see
to call him a Dao-attainer?
Consider Emperor Wǔ's time:
Daoists like Wén Chéng and Wǔ Lì
went to sea seeking immortals,
searching for elixirs of immortality,
showing evidence of Daoist arts,
hence trusted by the emperor.
Shuò had no missions to the sea,
no wondrous feats.
Had he any marvels,
they'd be like Shàojūn's or Wén Chéng and Wǔ Lì's,
yet how could he be called enlightened?
Perhaps he occasionally resembled Shàojūn,
hiding his origins,
so courtiers didn't know the truth;
Shuò boasted of his great age,
but people saw his youthful appearance,
his calm disposition,
his dislike for officialdom,
his skill in divination and guessing hidden objects as amusing tricks—
thus the world deemed him a Dao-attainer.
Some believe Lǎozi's Way can transcend the world,
through calmness and desirelessness,
nurturing essence and cherishing energy.
For humans, spirit determines lifespan;
if spirit is unharmed, life is long and deathless.
Fact is:
Lǎozi practiced this,
lived over a hundred years, transcending the world,
becoming a true immortal.
But in calmness and few desires,
how do humans compare to birds and beasts?
They too grow old and die.
Birds and beasts have emotions and desires,
somewhat similar to humans',
but that's not sufficient to discuss.
What emotions or desires do plants have?
Yet they are born in spring and die in autumn.
Plants and trees have no desires,
yet their lifespan does not exceed a year;
humans have abundant emotions and desires,
yet their lifespan reaches a hundred years.
This shows that those without emotions and desires die young instead,
while those with emotions and desires live long.
If this is so,
then Lǎozi's method of attaining longevity and transcending the world through tranquility and desirelessness
is again false.
Perhaps Lǎozi
and people like Lǐ Shàojūn
practiced the way of tranquility,
and coincidentally their natural lifespan was long.
The world saw their long life
and heard of their tranquility,
so they claimed Lǎozi used techniques to transcend the world.
Some in the world consider those who abstain from grains as practitioners of Daoist arts,
saying that figures like Wángzǐ Qiáo,
by not eating grains
and having a different diet from ordinary people,
thus had a different lifespan from ordinary people,
exceeding a hundred years to transcend the world,
and became immortals.
This is also false.
In human life,
we are endowed with the nature of eating and drinking,
so above the body there are mouth and teeth,
and below the body there are orifices.
The mouth and teeth are for chewing food,
the orifices are for excretion.
Following this nature is to accord with the true way of heaven;
going against this nature is to violate what we are endowed with.
If one loses the original vital energy from heaven,
how can they attain long life?
If Wángzǐ Qiáo were born without mouth, teeth, or orifices,
then his endowed nature would differ from humans.
If his endowed nature differed from humans,
it still couldn't be called longevity,
let alone when the physical form is identical but practices differ?
To say he transcended the world
is not the reality of human nature.
Humans not eating
is like the body not wearing clothes.
Clothes warm the skin,
food fills the stomach,
when skin is warm and stomach full,
the spirit becomes clear and vigorous.
If hungry but not full,
cold but not warm,
then there will be harm from freezing and starvation;
those who freeze and starve,
how can they live long?
Moreover, in human life,
food serves as energy,
just as plants grow with earth as energy.
Uproot plants from the ground,
separating them from soil,
and they wither and die early;
close human mouths,
preventing them from eating,
and they starve and don't live long.
Daoists boast saying:
"True humans consume energy."
Using energy as food,
thus the tradition says:
"Those who consume energy live long without dying."
Though not full from grains,
they are filled with energy.
This is also false.
What energy is this?
If referring to yīn-yáng energy,
yīn-yáng energy cannot fill people.
Some people swallow energy,
their stomachs bloated with energy,
but not satiated.
If referring to the energy of various medicines,
some people take medicine,
eating one portion of powder,
swallowing dozens of pills,
the medicinal power is strong,
causing turmoil and toxicity in the chest,
unable to fill people.
Those who consume energy must mean breathing exercises,
exhaling old and inhaling new air;
in the past Péng Zǔ practiced this,
yet couldn't live long,
fell ill and died.
Some Daoists use energy guidance to nurture life,
claiming to transcend the world without death.
They believe blood vessels in the body,
if not moved or stretched,
become blocked and impassable;
blocked accumulations
lead to illness and death.
This is also false.
The human form
is like the body of plants.
Plants on mountain peaks,
struck by strong winds,
shaking day and night—
can they surpass those hidden in valleys,
sheltered from strong winds?
Examining plant growth,
those that shake are damaged and don't thrive;
why would humans doing guiding exercises and shaking their bodies
live long without dying?
Blood vessels hidden in the body
are like rivers flowing through land.
River flows
are turbid, not clear;
blood vessel movements
are also disturbed and unsettled.
Being unsettled
is like people suffering hardship without relief,
how can they live long?
Some Daoists use ingested medicines
to lighten the body and boost energy,
prolonging life to transcend the world.
This is also false.
Taking medicines
to lighten the body and boost energy
has some evidence.
But as for prolonging life to transcend the world,
the world shows no such effect.
Medicines cure diseases,
after recovery energy is restored,
and with restored energy the body lightens.
All humans by nature
have bodies naturally light
and energy naturally long,
but affected by wind-dampness,
various illnesses harm them,
so the body becomes heavy and energy poor.
Taking good medicine,
body and energy return to original state—
it's not that original energy was scarce or body heavy,
then medicine made energy long and body light;
during endowment,
these were originally present.
So taking medicines to cure diseases
and make body light and energy long
restores original nature—
how can this prolong life to transcend the world?
All beings with blood vessels
are born without exception;
being born, none avoid death.
Because they live,
we know they will die.
Heaven and earth are not born,
so they don't die;
yīn and yáng are not born,
so they don't die.
Death
is the proof of life,
life
is the evidence of death.
What has a beginning must have an end,
what has an end must have a beginning.
Only what has neither end nor beginning
can be immortal.
Human life
is like ice.
Water freezes into ice,
energy accumulates to form humans.
Ice lasts through winter then melts,
humans complete a hundred years then die.
If humans could be made deathless,
could ice be made unmeltable?
Various studies of immortality arts
are bound to fail,
just as ice cannot be made to never melt.
The tradition says:
Sages worry about the world,
think deeply and work diligently,
disturb their spirits,
and affect their bodies,
hence it is said:
"Yáo looked like dried meat,
Shùn like preserved fowl;
while tyrants like Jié and Zhòu
had hanging fat over a foot long."
To say that sages worry about the world and care for people,
and thus their bodies become emaciated and frail,
unable to be plump and glossy,
is acceptable;
but to claim that Yáo
and Shùn were like dried meat and jerky,
while Jié and Zhòu had excess fat hanging over a foot long,
is an exaggeration.
Duke Huán of Qí stated:
"Before obtaining my uncle-guiding minister, it was extremely difficult;
after gaining him, it became very easy."
Duke Huán was inferior to Yáo
and Shùn, and his minister was no match for Yǔ
or Qì. If Duke Huán's situation turned easy,
how could Yáo and Shùn's be反而 difficult?
Since Duke Huán easily obtained Guǎn Zhòng,
we know that Yáo
and Shùn obtaining Yǔ
and Qì was not hard.
Where things are easy, there is less worry;
less worry means less distress;
less distress then the body does not become emaciated.
Shùn inherited Yáo's peaceful reign,
with Yáo and Shùn continuing virtuous rule,
their achievements extended to remote regions,
yet Yáo still had worries,
so how could Shùn be entirely free of troubles?
Therefore the Classic says:
"God leads them to ease."
This refers to Yú Shùn.
Shùn inherited stability and continued orderly governance,
appointing the worthy and employing the capable,
respectfully refraining from action yet the world was well-governed.
Thus Confucius said:[37"How majestic!
Shùn and Yǔ possessed the world,
yet did not interfere with it!"
Now
"not interfering"
is described as being as lean as jerky;
if one's virtue is inferior and inherits decline,
like Confucius rushing about anxiously,
traveling everywhere responding to invitations,
finding no personal acceptance,
his Way unable to be implemented,
could he have become skeletal and lame,
collapsing on the road?
Zhòu engaged in all-night drinking,
with mounds of dregs and ponds of wine,
immersed in alcohol,
without ceasing day or night,
this would certainly lead to illness.
Illness then causes loss of appetite,
loss of appetite
means excess fat couldn't reach a foot in length.
The Classic says:
"Only pursuing excessive pleasure,
thus none achieved long life."
Prince Wújì of Wèi engaged in all-night drinking,
and died from the poisoning effects.
Although Zhòu didn't die immediately,
he should have been emaciated and lean.
Now since Jié
and Zhòu acted similarly,
they should have suffered the same illness;
to say his hanging fat exceeded a foot
is not only exaggeration,
but also contrary to fact.
Traditional accounts also claim:
"Zhòu's strength could twist iron and straighten hooks,
and replace beams and pillars."
This speaks of his great strength.
"Fēilián,
Èlái and their followers,
all enjoyed favor and宠爱."
This shows that rulers who appreciate physical prowess
attract men of strength and skill.
Some say:
"When King Wǔ attacked Zhòu,
his blades were not stained with blood."
Now with strength to twist iron and straighten hooks,
aided by Fēilián
and Èlái's followers,
facing the Zhōu army in battle,
even with King Wǔ's abundant virtue,
he couldn't have overcome Zhòu's long-trusted supporters' loyalty;
though Zhòu was evil,
he wouldn't lack companions who shared his ways.
Even if captured by King Wǔ,
he should have killed or wounded scores of men.
Now to claim
"blades not bloodied"
contradicts Zhòu's great strength
and Fēilián
and Èlái's assistance to Zhòu.
Examining King Wǔ's auspicious signs,
they don't surpass Gāozǔ's.
King Wǔ had the white fish
and red crow's blessings,
Gāozǔ had the omen of cutting the great serpent
and the old woman weeping on the road.
King Wǔ had eight hundred feudal lords' assistance,
Gāozǔ had the world's righteous troops' support.
King Wǔ's physiognomy
showed merely gazing-at-sheep eyes;
Gāozǔ's countenance
had dragon forehead,
prominent nose bridge,
purple neck,
beautiful beard,
with seventy-two black moles on his body.
Gāozǔ also hid from Empress Lǚ in the marshes,
where she consistently saw cloud-qi manifestations above him;
no such thing is heard of King Wǔ.
His physiognomy surpassed the gazing-at-sheep eyes,
his omens outshone the fish
and crow, the world's righteous troops all gathered to Hàn,
providing stronger support than the feudal lords.
King Wǔ succeeded Zhòu,
Gāozǔ inherited from Qín,
the Second Emperor's wickedness
exceeded Zhòu's,
the world's rebellion against Qín
should have been greater than against Yīn.
Consider Gāozǔ attacking Qín,
then defeating Xiàng Yǔ,
battlefields flowing with blood,
tens of thousands of corpses exposed,
armies defeated and troops lost,
nearly dying more than once,
before gaining the world;
military hardship was severe,
suppressing chaos was intense.
To claim only Zhōu's troops had "blades not bloodied"
is untrue to facts.
To say it was easy
is acceptable;
but to claim
"blades not bloodied"
is exaggeration.
Examining when Zhōu conquered Yīn,
according to Tàigōng's "Secret Plans" text,
they fed children cinnabar,
teaching them to say
"Yīn perishes."
When troops reached Mùyě,
they raised torches at dawn.
Investigating the "Wǔ Chéng" chapter,
the battle of Mùyě
had "blood flowed enough to float pestles,"
and barren land for thousands of miles.
From this perspective,
Zhōu's conquest of Yīn
was the same case as Hàn
and Qín.
Yet to say conquering Yīn was easy,
"blades not bloodied,"
praising King Wǔ's virtue,
exaggerates the facts.
All matters under heaven
cannot be exaggerated or diminished;
investigate what precedes and follows,
evidence naturally appears,
once it appears,
the truth of right and wrong becomes determined.
The world claims Zhòu could twist iron and straighten hooks,
and also says King Wǔ attacked him with blades not bloodied.
Now with strength to twist iron facing others,
this would match Mèng Bēn
and Xià Yù's caliber;
with virtue of not bloodying blades conquering others,
this would rank with the Three Sovereigns
and Five Emperors.
With iron-twisting strength,
he shouldn't have been captured;
with non-bloodying virtue,
there shouldn't have been fierce combat.
Now praising Zhòu's strength
diminishes King Wǔ's virtue;
commending King Wǔ
reduces Zhòu's strength.
Iron-twisting
and non-bloodying
cannot coexist;
descriptions of Yīn
and Zhōu cannot both be fully true.
Not both fully true,
then necessarily one is false.
Confucius said:
"The wickedness of King Zhòu
was not as extreme as it is made out to be.
Hence, the gentleman dislikes being in a low position,
for all the evils of the world are attributed to him."
Mencius said:
"Regarding the 'Wǔ Chéng' chapter,
I only accept two or three strips of it.
When the most benevolent attacks the unbenevolent,
how could there be blood enough to float pestles?"
According to Confucius's words,
this nearly refutes the floating pestles;
according to Mencius's words,
it approaches bloodless blades.
Floating pestles exaggerate the reality,
while bloodless blades also miss the truth.
One sage and one worthy,
discussing the same King Zhòu,
differ in the weight of their descriptions,
and vary in the substance of their accounts.
King Zhòu's evil was not as great as Wáng Mǎng's.
Zhòu killed Bǐ Gān,
while Mǎng poisoned Emperor Píng;
Zhòu inherited the throne legitimately,
while Mǎng stole the Hàn position.
Killing a sovereign is worse than executing a minister,
and legitimate succession is more proper than usurpation.
The rebellion of the scholars and masses
should have been more severe against Zhòu.
When Hàn executed Wáng Mǎng,
the battle stalled at Kūnyáng,
with tens of thousands dead,
and when the army reached the Jiàntái,
blood flowed deep enough to submerge feet.
Yet it is said that Zhōu took the world
with blades unstained by blood,
which is not the reality.
A tradition states:
"King Wén drank a thousand zhōng,
and Confucius a hundred gū."
This intends to say that the sages' virtue was so abundant
that they could control wine with their virtue.
But if one could sit and drink a thousand zhōng or a hundred gū,
this would be a drunkard,
not a sage.
Drinking has its measures;
the capacity of chest and belly
is similar among humans.
Drinking a thousand zhōng
should require consuming a hundred cattle,
and a hundred gū should need ten sheep.
Considering a thousand zhōng with a hundred cattle
or a hundred gū with ten sheep,
only if King Wén's body were like that of the Lord of Fángfēng,
and Confucius's frame like that of the Chángdí people,
could they endure it.
But examining King Wén's
and Confucius's bodies,
they could not match the Fángfēng
or Chángdí;
with their short and small statures,
consuming so much food and drink
would detract from King Wén's breadth
and diminish Confucius's loftiness.
Consider the "Jiǔ Gào" chapter:
"Morning and evening, it is said:
'Only use wine in sacrifices.'"
This shows King Wén cautioned against wine.
If he was cautious morning and evening,
the people would be transformed.
To outwardly preach caution
while inwardly drinking a thousand zhōng
would mislead the people and set a poor example;
how could that achieve transformation?
Inheriting Zhòu's hated practices,
how could he distinguish himself?
Moreover, what purpose would
the feat of a thousand zhōng
or the test of a hundred gū serve?
Did King Wén
and Confucius use wine for sacrifices?
Then the blessed offerings would not satisfy their hunger.
Did they use it for banquets and archery rites?
Banquets and archery drinking
have their own rituals and rules.
Or was it for private feasts and rewards?
Then reward drinking
should be equal with subordinates.
Before a superior, after three cups one should retire;
exceeding three cups
leads to drunkenness and disorder.
King Wén
and Confucius
were people who followed rites;
if rewarding their attendants
led to drunken chaos,
and they themselves drank a thousand zhōng or a hundred gū,
on a large scale, they would be like Jié
or Zhòu, on a small scale, mere drunkards.
How could they then establish virtue, accomplish transformation,
and make their names renowned for posterity?
The world hears
the saying "Virtue controls without drunkenness,"
and seeing that sages have the effect of abundant virtue,
they fictitiously increase King Wén to a thousand zhōng
and emptily add to Confucius a hundred gū.
A tradition states:
"Zhòu immersed himself in wine,
made mounds of dregs,
and turned wine into a pool,
with three thousand people drinking like cattle,
holding all-night drinking parties,
losing track of the days."
Now, though Zhòu was fond of wine,
he also sought pleasure in it.
If the wine pool was in the central courtyard,
then it shouldn't be called an all-night drink.
Sitting in deep chambers,
with windows closed and candles lit,
is why it's called all-night.
If they sat in rooms,
each time drinkers had to
rise and go to the courtyard,
then return to their seats,
it would be troublesome and uncomfortable,
not very pleasurable.
If the pool was in deep chambers,
then the three thousand should sit by the pool.
Leaning forward to drink from the pool,
then leaning back to eat dishes,
with music and performers in front,
that would be pleasurable.
But if they truly sat by the pool,
drinking forward would interfere with eating,
and the performers' acts
couldn't be in front.
Since their eating and drinking lacked ritual,
drinking like cattle by the pool,
then they likely ate meat without cups,
and should have devoured fish and meat like tigers;
thus, we know the wine pool and cattle drinking
are not factual.
The tradition also says:
"Zhòu hung meat to form a forest,
and had men and women run naked through it."
This implies drunken pleasure, debauchery, and lack of restraint.
Now, meat should enter the mouth,
and what the mouth eats
should be clean, not defiled.
To say men and women ran naked there—
how clean is that?
If drunk, they disregarded cleanliness,
they should have bathed in wine.
Yet they ran naked among the meat;
why wouldn't they bathe in wine?
Since bathing in wine isn't mentioned,
we know they didn't run naked among the meat.
Some accounts say:
"Carts served wine,
riders served roasted meat,
and a hundred twenty days made one night."
Now, to say
"used wine as a pool"
contradicts
"carts served wine";
to say
"hung meat as a forest"
contradicts
"riders served roasted meat."
Perhaps when Zhòu was indulging in drink,
he overturned the wine,
which poured profusely onto the ground,
and it was said that he made a pond of wine;
when the dregs of brewing wine accumulated,
it was said that they formed a hill;
when meat was hung in the woods,
it was said that it was a forest of meat;
in the deep shade of the woods,
people sometimes ran and played within,
and it was said that they chased each other naked;
perhaps when wine was transported on deer-drawn carts,
it was said that carts moved the wine,
and riders carried the roasts;
perhaps when it lasted for over ten nights,
it was said to be a hundred and twenty;
perhaps when he was drunk and lost track of the days,
it was said that he forgot the calendar.
When the Duke of Zhōu enfeoffed Kāngshū,
he warned him about Zhòu's use of wine,
hoping to reach the extreme,
intending to caution him,
yet he did not mention a hill of dregs,
a pond of wine,
a forest of hanging meat,
drinking through the long night,
or forgetting the calendar.
Since the sage did not speak of it,
it is likely not true.
The tradition says:
"Zhòu once drank like cattle with three thousand people at the wine pond."
Now, the Xià dynasty had a hundred officials,
the Yīn two hundred,
and the Zhōu three hundred.
Those with whom Zhòu enjoyed himself
must have been either commoners or officials,
either minor officials or high-ranking ones,
but their number could not have reached three thousand.
The writers of traditions wished to vilify Zhòu,
so they spoke of three thousand people,
exaggerating the reality.
The tradition states:
"The Duke of Zhōu held gifts and visited scholars in humble cottages."
This means he paid them respect.
Now, the Three Dukes,
the pillar ministers,
are the steadfast supports of the king;
scholars in humble cottages
are the lowly and insignificant in the alleys.
For the Three Dukes to lower their pillar-like dignity,
holding gifts to wait upon scholars in humble cottages,
is not realistic.
Perhaps he treated scholars with humility and respect,
not arrogant toward those in humble cottages,
and people then said he went to visit them;
or perhaps he raised up scholars from humble cottages,
welcoming them with jade discs as a礼节,
and people then said he held gifts to wait at their homes.
The tradition states:
"Yáo and Shùn were so frugal
that their thatched roofs were not trimmed,
and their rough wood rafters were not carved."
Now, to say
"thatched roofs"
and "rough wood rafters"
is acceptable;
but to say
"not trimmed"
and "not carved"
is an exaggeration.
The Classic says:
"He completed the fivefold robes."
The fivefold robes
are robes of five colors.
To wear robes of five colors,
yet have thatched roofs
and rough wood rafters—
how inconsistent are the palace and clothing!
Wearing five colors,
decorated with sun, moon, and stars,
yet having thatched roofs
and rough wood rafters—
this is not realistic.
The tradition states:
"Qín Shǐ Huáng burned the Books of Songs and Documents,
and buried the Confucian scholars alive."
To say he burned the Books of Songs and Documents
means he destroyed the texts of the Five Classics;
to say he buried the Confucian scholars alive
means they were all people who carried the classics and texts.
Burning their books
and burying the people—
the Songs and Documents were cut off.
To say he burned the Books of Songs and Documents
and buried the Confucian scholars alive
is true;
but to say he intended to destroy the Songs and Documents,
hence burying the people,
is not sincere,
and again an exaggeration.
In the thirty-fourth year of Qín Shǐ Huáng,
he hosted a banquet at the Xiányáng Terrace,
and seventy Confucian scholars came forward to offer toasts.
The Captain of Attendants, Zhōu Qīngchén, praised the virtue of the First Emperor.
Qí's Chúnyú Yuè admonished the First Emperor for not enfeoffing his sons, brothers, and meritorious officials,
to serve as branches of support,
and criticized Zhōu Qīngchén for flattery.
The First Emperor referred the matter to Chancellor Lǐ Sī.
Lǐ Sī criticized Chúnyú Yuè, saying:
"These scholars do not follow the present but study the past,
to criticize the current age,
confusing and misleading the common people.
I request to order the historiographers
that all records not of Qín be burned;
except for those held by the Erudites,
anyone in the empire daring to hide the Books of Songs,
Documents,
the Hundred Schools' texts, or various penal codes;
must all be delivered to the prefects
and commandants for mixed burning;
anyone daring to discuss the Songs
or Documents in pairs shall be executed in the market;
those using the past to criticize the present shall be exterminated with their clans;
officials who know of it but do not report shall share the crime."
The First Emperor approved it.
The next year,
the thirty-fifth year,
many of the scholars in Xiányáng
spread seditious words.
The First Emperor ordered the Censors to investigate the scholars,
and those who implicated each other in succession,
voluntarily exposing four hundred sixty-seven offenders of the禁令,
were all buried alive.
The burning of the Songs and Documents
arose from Chúnyú Yuè's admonition;
the burying of Confucian scholars
arose from the scholars spreading seditious words,
with four hundred sixty-seven people buried.
The tradition exaggerates by saying he buried Confucian scholars
to destroy the Songs and Documents,
and also says he buried them all—
this is not true,
and again an exaggeration.
The tradition states:
"As flat as the neighborhood of Jīng Kē."
This means Jīng Kē, who attempted to assassinate the King of Qín for Prince Dān of Yān,
later had his nine clans executed,
and afterward, due to unceasing rage,
his entire village was also wiped out.
The whole village was destroyed,
hence it was called flat.
This statement is exaggerated.
Though Qín was without virtue,
it would not wipe out Jīng Kē's entire village.
When the First Emperor visited the Liángshān Palace,
he saw from the hill that Chancellor Lǐ Sī's carriage and horsemen were very numerous,
became angry, and spoke critically of it.
Afterward,
his attendants informed Lǐ Sī,
and Lǐ Sī immediately reduced his carriage and horsemen.
The First Emperor knew his attendants had leaked his words,
but not knowing who,
arrested and killed all those nearby.
Later, a falling star landed in Dōngjùn,
reaching the ground as a stone.
Some people carved on the stone:
"The First Emperor dies,
and the land divides."
The First Emperor heard of it,
ordered the Censors to investigate thoroughly,
but no one confessed,
so he had all the people near the stone executed.
When the emperor executed those accompanying him at Liángshān Palace,
and killed the bystanders by the stone,
he wanted to find those who leaked words
and carved the stone,
but could not identify them precisely,
so he killed them all.
As for the neighborhood of Jīng Kē,
what crime did they commit against Qín to be entirely executed?
If the assassination of the Qín king occurred within the neighborhood,
and it was unknown who did it,
killing everyone
might be justified;
but Jīng Kē was already dead,
and the assassin was identified,
so why should all the residents of the neighborhood
be punished for it?
In the twentieth year of Qín Shǐ Huáng,
Yān sent Jīng Kē to assassinate the Qín king,
the king detected it,
dismembered Kē's body as a warning,
but did not mention executing his entire neighborhood.
Perhaps he executed Kē's nine clans,
and since the nine clans were numerous,
residing in the same neighborhood,
executing them
would nearly empty the area,
leading those fond of exaggerating events
to claim it was utterly devastated.
Confucian texts claim:
"Yáo
and Shùn's virtue
was supremely excellent and great,
bringing peace to all under heaven,
with not a single person punished."
They also say:
"The prosperity of Wén
and Wǔ
extended to Chéng
and Kāng's eras,
where punishments were set aside unused for over forty years."
and Shùn, and extol Wén
and Wǔ.
If words do not exaggerate,
then beauty is insufficiently praised;
if writing is not embellished,
then deeds are inadequately extolled.
Though Yáo and Shùn were excellent,
they could not prevent a single person from being punished;
though Wén and Wǔ were prosperous,
they could not make punishments unnecessary.
To say that few broke the law,
and punishments were rarely applied,
is acceptable;
but to claim not one person was punished,
or that punishments were unused,
is an exaggeration.
If one could prevent a single person from being punished,
then one could prevent a state from being attacked;
if punishments could be set aside unused,
then armies could be disbanded and not deployed.
Yet records show Yáo attacked Dānshuǐ,
Shùn campaigned against the Yǒumiáo,
the four criminals were subdued,
and punishments and armies were employed.
In King Chéng's time,
four states rebelled and usurped,
with Huáiyí
and Xúróng
both causing harm.
Punishing people uses blades,
attacking people uses armies,
convicting offenders employs laws,
executing people relies on force.
Force and law are not different,
armies and blades are alike—
those skilled in argument
cannot distinguish them.
Virtue being deficient leads to using armies,
lawbreaking necessitates applying punishments.
Punishments and armies
are like legs and wings:
walking uses legs,
flying uses wings;
though their forms differ,
their function for movement is the same.
Punishments and armies
both preserve order and suppress evil—
their essence is identical.
To claim armies are unused
or punishments unapplied
is like a person missing an ear but having intact eyes,
and calling them whole based on the eyes—
this cannot be accepted.
One brave in stabbing tigers
but timid in attacking people
cannot be called courageous
based on tiger-stabbing alone—
this is unreliable.
Only when the body is unblemished
and courage never falters
can one be considered complete.
Now, praising
"not a single person punished"
without mentioning no armies used;
extolling
"punishments set aside unused"
without stating no one rebelled—
this does not prove excellence,
nor can it be called prosperity.
Confucian texts claim:
"Chǔ's Yǎng Yóujī was skilled in archery,
shooting at a single poplar leaf,
he could hit it a hundred times out of a hundred."
This praises his archery skill.
To say he hit the leaf at that moment
is plausible;
but to claim a hundred shots and a hundred hits
is exaggerated.
A single poplar leaf,
once shot and hit,
after a few hits,
would be torn and unusable for further shooting.
If the leaf were hung on a tree for shooting,
even without aiming for it,
amid dense poplar foliage,
he might hit it accidentally.
This would require taking leaves from above,
placing them one by one on the ground to shoot—
shooting several tens of rows
would suffice to show skill;
observers familiar with archery
would know it couldn't reach a hundred,
clearly.
Those narrating events like to exaggerate skill,
so tens of hits
become a hundred hits.
Hundred and thousand
are large numbers—
intending to say
"ten"
they say
"hundred,"
and "hundred"
becomes
"thousand."
This matches the Shū's
"harmony of ten thousand states"
and the Shī's
"descendants numbering thousands of millions,"
sharing the same intent.
Confucian texts say:
"Wèi had a loyal minister Hóng Yǎn,
sent as an envoy by Duke Āi of Wèi,
before his return,
the Dí people attacked and killed Duke Āi,
eating all his flesh,
but sparing only his liver.
When Hóng Yǎn returned,
he reported his mission to the liver.
Grieving Duke Āi's death,
with his body's flesh gone,
and the liver unattached,
he drew a knife to cut open his own abdomen,
removed all his internal organs,
and placed Duke Āi's liver inside before dying."
This story aims
to praise his loyalty.
To say he cut himself open
and died with Duke Āi's liver inside
is acceptable;
but claiming he removed all his organs to insert the liver
is an exaggeration.
When a person is stabbed with a blade,
piercing the five organs leads to death.
Why is that?
The five organs
are the masters of vital energy,
just as the head
is the convergence point of blood vessels.
Once the head is severed,
one cannot take another's head and attach it to the neck;
how then could one first remove the contents of their own abdomen
and then insert Duke Āi's liver?
Once the abdominal contents are removed,
death follows immediately,
and the hand can no longer grasp anything.
If one were to insert Duke Āi's liver first
and then remove the abdominal contents,
the text should have stated
"insert Duke Āi's liver,
then remove the abdominal contents."
Now it first says
"completely remove the abdominal contents,
then insert Duke Āi's liver,"
and further uses
"completely,"
exaggerating the facts.
Confucian texts claim:
"When Chǔ's Xióng Qúzǐ went out,
he saw a recumbent stone,
mistook it for a crouching tiger,
drew his bow and shot at it,
the arrow sank up to its feathers."
Some say:
"When Yǎng Yóujī saw a recumbent stone,
he thought it was a rhinoceros,
shot at it,
and the arrow pierced deep with its feathers submerged."
Others mention
"Lǐ Guǎng."
Even if the names—
Xióng Qúzǐ, Yǎng Yóujī,
or Lǐ Guǎng—are uncertain,
it does not harm the account.
Some thought it was
a "tiger,"
others believed it was
a "rhinoceros,"
but both are fierce creatures,
the essence is the same.
Some say
"sank to the feathers,"
others say
"submerged the feathers,"
feathers refer to the same part,
just phrased differently.
The key point is that the recumbent stone resembled a tiger
or rhinoceros, causing heightened focus due to fear,
leading to the arrow penetrating deeply.
To say they mistook the stone for a tiger
and shot an arrow that sank in
is plausible;
but to claim it submerged the feathers
is an exaggeration.
When seeing something like a tiger,
the mind believes it real,
drawing the bow to shoot,
with intense concentration and effort,
then the perception
is no different from a real tiger.
Shooting at a stone resembling a tiger,
if the arrow sank to the feathers,
were it a real tiger's body,
would the arrow pierce through?
Stone is hard to penetrate,
flesh is easy.
If shooting the hard submerged the feathers,
then shooting the easy should pierce through,
without doubt.
A skilled archer can hit distant, tiny targets,
without missing by a hair's breadth,
but how can they make the bow exert more force?
When Yǎng Yóujī served in the army,
he shot the Marquis of Jìn in the eye.
For a commoner to shoot a ruler of ten thousand chariots,
his focus and doubled strength
must equal shooting at the recumbent stone.
Hitting the Marquis's eye,
could it also pierce through to the neck?
If it pierced through to the neck,
the Marquis should have died.
Even with a cart-mounted crossbow of ten shí strength,
it likely couldn't penetrate an inch;
the arrow would shatter into three,
let alone with a single person's strength,
drawing a weak bow,
even with utmost focus,
how could it submerge the feathers?
Human essence is vital energy,
and energy is strength.
In emergencies like fire or flood,
panic and fear arise,
moving objects,
with extreme sincerity,
one who usually lifts one shí
may lift two shí.
However,
seeing a recumbent stone and shooting,
with doubled sincerity,
it might penetrate no more than an inch;
how can it be called submerging the feathers?
If a skilled swordsman,
seeing a recumbent stone,
fearfully strikes it,
can it be said he cut the stone?
Or a brave man who fights tigers bare-handed,
suddenly seeing a recumbent stone,
strikes it with his hand—
can he leave a mark on the stone?
The essence of a skilled person
is the same as an unskilled one;
the sincerity of ancient people
is no different from today's.
Have a modern archer
shoot at wild animals,
desiring to hit them—
wouldn't they spare no effort?
Yet when they hit the animal,
it penetrates only a few inches.
If they mistakenly hit a stone,
the tip won't enter,
and the arrow breaks.
Thus,
the Confucian texts' accounts of Chǔ's Xióng Qúzǐ,
Yǎng Yóujī,
and Lǐ Guǎng shooting recumbent stones,
with arrows submerging feathers,
are all exaggerations.
Confucian texts praise:
"The ingenuity of Lǔ Bān
and Mòzǐ,
who carved wooden kites
that flew for three days without landing."
To say they made wooden kites that flew
is acceptable;
but to claim they flew for three days without landing
is an exaggeration.
Carving a wooden kite
to resemble a kite's shape—
how could it fly without landing?
Even if it could soar,
how could it last three days?
If it truly had mechanisms,
once flown, it kept soaring,
unable to descend,
then it should be described as
"flew away,"
not as
"three days."
Similarly, a legend says:
"Lǔ Bān's cleverness
caused him to lose his mother."
It claims the skilled craftsman
made a wooden carriage and horse for his mother,
with a wooden driver,
fully equipped with mechanisms,
placed his mother on it,
and it drove off never to return,
thus he lost his mother.
If the wooden kite had full mechanisms,
like the wooden carriage,
then it should have flown away without landing.
If the mechanisms lasted only a short while,
not exceeding three days,
then the wooden carriage should have stopped on the road in three days,
not gone straight off to lose his mother.
Both tales must be untrue.
Texts say:
"Confucius was not tolerated in his time,
traveling around to persuade over seventy states,
never finding peace."
To say he traveled without being accepted
is plausible;
but to claim he visited seventy states
is an exaggeration.
Examining the chapters of the Analects,
and the texts of various scholars,
it is recorded that Confucius returned to Lǔ from Wèi,
was cut off from provisions in Chén,
had his traces erased in Wèi,
forgot the taste of food in Qí,
and witnessed trees being felled in Sòng.
Including Fèi and Dùnmóu,
he did not reach even ten states.
Yet tradition claims seventy states,
which is not factual.
Perhaps he visited over ten states,
but the "seventy states" narrative
was transmitted through documents,
thus leading to the assertion of seventy states.
The Analects states:
"Confucius asked Gōngmíng Jiǎ about Gōngshū Wénzǐ:
'Is it true
that your master does not speak,
does not laugh,
and does not take?'
Gōngmíng Jiǎ replied:
'Those who told you this exaggerated.
My master speaks only at the proper time,
so people never tire of his words;
he laughs only when joyful,
so people never tire of his laughter;
he takes only what is righteous,
so people never tire of his taking.'
The Master said:
'How could this be so?
How could this be so?'"
Now Gōngshū Wénzǐ indeed spoke at the right time,
laughed when joyful,
and took righteously,
yet in popular accounts,
he was described as not speaking,
not laughing,
and not taking—
a clear case of exaggeration by common speech.
Historical texts claim:
"When Duke Mù of Qín attacked Zhèng,
he passed through Jìn without seeking permission,
whereupon Duke Xiāng of Jìn led the Jiāngróng tribes to ambush him at the Xiáo Pass,
leaving not a single horse or chariot wheel to return."
Yet at that time, Qín sent three commanders—Mèngmíng Shì,
Xīqí Shù,
and Báiyǐ Bǐng—
all of whom managed to return alive.
Since these three commanders returned,
their chariots and horses must have followed—
thus the text's claim
"not a single horse or chariot wheel returned"
exaggerates the reality.
Texts also state:
"Lord Mèngcháng of Qí,
Lord Xìnlíng of Wèi,
Lord Píngyuán of Zhào,
and Lord Chūnshēn of Chǔ
treated scholars with humility,
gathering talents from all directions,
each hosting three thousand retainers."
This aims to emphasize their extreme deference to scholars
and the multitude who flocked to them.
To say they had many retainers is acceptable;
but to claim three thousand
is an exaggeration.
Though these four lords cherished scholars,
and though many came,
their numbers likely did not exceed a thousand each—
yet the texts insist on three thousand.
For crowds, people insist on thousands;
for scarcity, they claim none—
such is the nature of worldly accounts,
a distortion in narrating events.
The Chronicles record:
"When Gāo Zìgāo lost his parents,
he wept tears of blood,
and for three years never revealed his teeth—
a feat gentlemen considered difficult."
It was deemed difficult precisely because it was exceptional.
Yet instead of recognizing it as unreal,
they called it difficult—
a mistaken judgment by gentlemen.
That Gāo Zì wept blood
may well have happened.
Why?
When Jīng Hé presented treasure to Chǔ,
his feet were amputated,
grieving that the treasure went unaccepted
and his feelings unheard,
he wept tears,
and when tears dried, blood followed.
Similarly, Gāo Zì, mourning his parents,
with grief extreme and tears exhausted,
might have shed blood—
this is plausible.
But to say
"he never revealed his teeth for three years"
is an exaggeration.
Claiming
"never revealed his teeth"
implies he neither spoke nor laughed.
A filial son in mourning
may refrain from laughter,
but how could he not speak?
And if he spoke, how could his teeth not show?
Confucius said:
"Speech should not be ornate."
Perhaps he sometimes remained silent,
and the Chronicles exaggerated it to "never revealing his teeth";
or perhaps
the Chronicles extended it to three years.
Emperor Gāozōng observed the mourning hut,
remaining silent for three years.
Even as an honored Son of Heaven, his silence
was recorded merely as
"not speaking"—
already suspected of exaggeration—
so how much more for Gāo Zì, a man of low status,
to claim
"never revealed his teeth"
must be an embellishment.
Confucian texts say:
"Qín Xī recommended Bǎilǐ Xī,
but Duke Mù did not heed him,
so Qín Xī blocked the gate,
dashed his head, shattered his skull, and died.
The duke, grief-stricken,
then employed Bǎilǐ Xī."
This story praises a worthy recommending talent
without regard for his life,
dying by dashing and shattering his head
to aid his friend.
Scholars stir each other with such tales,
and texts transmit them
as if unquestionably true.
That one might dash his head to recommend another
has occurred in past and present;
Qín Xī's head-dashing
may be factual,
but claiming he shattered his skull in death
is exaggerated.
When a person kowtows,
intense pain may draw blood,
but even in fury, fear, or desperation,
none shatter their own skulls.
Not that the skull cannot break,
but human strength alone cannot achieve it.
Slitting one's throat with a blade
or impaling the chest on a spear—
such acts require the aid of sharp edges
for the limbs to exert force.
Had Qín Xī wielded a hammer to strike himself,
skull-shattering would be unsurprising;
but dashing his head to splinter it
exceeds natural strength.
Some may die from kowtowing,
but none from self-inflicted skull-shattering.
Perhaps Qín Xī kowtowed to recommend Bǎilǐ Xī,
and tradition falsely added his death;
or if he did die kowtowing,
tradition falsely added the skull-shattering.
Confucian texts claim:
"Jīng Kē, on behalf of Prince Dān of Yān, attempted to assassinate the King of Qín,
wielding a dagger,
but failed in the strike.
The king drew his sword to counterattack.
Jīng Kē threw the dagger at the king,
missed,
hit a bronze pillar,
and it penetrated a foot deep."
This aims to highlight the dagger's sharpness
and Jīng Kē's formidable force,
suggesting he thrust a sharp blade into a solid pillar—
praising Jīng Kē's courage
by exaggerating the event.
That the dagger entered the bronze pillar
is true;
but to say it penetrated a foot deep
is an exaggeration.
Although bronze is not as hard as a dagger,
it would only allow penetration of a few inches,
hardly reaching a foot.
To claim it entered a foot—
supposing it hit the King of Qín,
would the dagger have pierced through him?
Even a crossbow drawn with a force of ten shí,
shooting at a wooden target on a wall,
cannot penetrate a foot deep.
With the strength of Jīng Kē's hand,
throwing a light, small dagger,
its blade forged from the essence of swords like Lóngyuān,
penetrating a hard bronze pillar—
this would mean Jīng Kē's strength
surpassed that of a ten-shí crossbow,
and the bronze pillar's hardness
was less than that of a wooden target.
The world praises Jīng Kē's courage,
but not his immense strength.
As for men of great strength,
none surpass Mèng Bēn.
If Mèng Bēn were to strike a bronze pillar,
could he pierce through it a foot?
Perhaps the dagger was as sharp as Gānjiàng
and Mòyé,
piercing whatever stood before it,
striking down all in its path,
hence the effect of penetrating a foot.
But to speak of Gānjiàng
and Mòyé
is also to exaggerate their reality.
Claims of piercing without hindrance
or striking all down are like the story of penetrating the bronze pillar a foot.
Confucian texts say:
"Dǒng Zhòngshū read the 'Spring and Autumn Annals,'
focusing his mind entirely on it,
with no other thoughts,
for three years without glancing at the garden vegetables."
That he did not look at the garden vegetables
is true;
but to say it was for three years
is an exaggeration.
Although Zhòngshū was diligent,
he must have taken breaks at times.
During such breaks,
he would likely stroll near his courtyard,
and if he could reach the courtyard,
why would he avoid looking at the garden vegetables?
It is said that those who concentrate intensely
may not see what they observe,
losing themselves in the pursuit of the Way,
but never that they do not go to the courtyard,
sitting in thought for three years
without a glance at the garden.
The "Book of Documents: Against Idleness" states:
"The gentleman avoids idleness in his station,
first understanding the toil of farming,
then finds rest."
Rest means
relaxation.
Human tendons and bones,
unlike wood or stone,
cannot avoid relaxation.
Thus, to be always tense without relaxation,
King Wén did not do;
to be always relaxed without tension,
King Wén did not practice;
alternating tension and relaxation,
King Wén took as the norm.
Even sages, with their superior talent,
had periods of relaxation and tension;
Zhòngshū's ability was inferior to the sages',
how could he concentrate without rest for three years?
Confucian texts say:
"When the Xià dynasty was flourishing,
distant lands depicted their strange creatures,
the nine provinces offered metal,
cast into cauldrons bearing images of these creatures,
thus preparing against them,
so that entering mountains and marshes,
one would not encounter evil beings,
using them to ward off divine malevolence,
thereby harmonizing above and below,
to receive heaven's blessings."
Now, the nature of metal
is material;
using that offered from distant lands may be fine,
casting it into cauldrons,
using it to represent the wonders of all things—
how could it prevent encountering evil beings in mountains and marshes,
or ward off divine malevolence?
In the Zhōu era, when the world was at peace,
Yuècháng presented white pheasants,
and the Wō people offered fragrant grass.
Eating the white pheasants
or using the fragrant grass
did not avert calamities;
how could bronze cauldrons
ward off malevolence?
Moreover, the coming of the Nine Cauldrons
was an omen of virtuous prosperity.
Bearing such auspicious responses
cannot bring fortune.
Men wear jade,
women wear pearls,
yet pearls and jade,
for humans, cannot ward off evils;
if rare treasures
were made into orchid ornaments
or ivory adornments,
some might claim benefits,
as with the tales of the Nine Cauldrons.
Since the Nine Cauldrons could not ward off evils,
yet the tradition claims they warded off divine malevolence,
this is the texts exaggerating the account.
Common tradition says:
"The Zhōu cauldrons boiled without fire,
without adding anything,
things emerged on their own."
This is the tradition exaggerating the tale,
and the texts embellishing the record,
thus making the Nine Cauldrons seem divine without cause.
Moreover, to claim the Zhōu cauldrons were divine—
how can this be verified?
The metal for the Zhōu cauldrons
came from distant tributes,
which Yǔ obtained to cast into cauldrons.
As cauldrons,
they bore images of all things.
If considered divine because of the distant tributes,
how could distant things be divine?
If considered divine because Yǔ cast them,
Yǔ was a sage,
but not divine himself.
If a sage's person cannot be divine,
how could his cast vessels be divine?
If considered divine because metal is divine,
then metal
is of the same category as stone;
if stone cannot be divine,
how can metal be divine?
If considered divine because they bore images of all things,
then the images of all things
are like the thunder wine vessel;
the thunder vessel is carved with clouds and thunder patterns,
clouds and thunder are in heaven,
more divine than all things,
yet the images of clouds and thunder are not divine—
how can the images of all things be divine?
The tradition says:
"When Qín destroyed Zhōu,
Zhōu's Nine Cauldrons went to Qín."
Examining the historical facts,
during the time of King Nǎn of Zhōu,
King Zhāo of Qín sent General Jiū to attack King Nǎn.
King Nǎn, in fear, fled to Qín,
kowtowed to accept blame,
and offered all his thirty-six cities
and thirty thousand people.
Qín accepted the offering
and returned King Nǎn.
After King Nǎn's death,
the King of Qín took the Nine Cauldrons and treasures.
Thus,
the Nine Cauldrons were in Qín.
In the twenty-eighth year of Qín Shǐ Huáng,
he traveled north to Lángyá,
returned via Péngchéng,
fasted, prayed, and sacrificed,
wishing to retrieve the Zhōu cauldrons,
sending a thousand men to dive into the Sì River,
but they failed to find them.
Considering the timeline,
after King Zhāo,
three generations passed to Shǐ Huángdì.
Since Qín had no disasters or chaos,
the cauldrons should not have been lost;
they were likely lost in Zhōu's time.
The tradition says:
"King Nǎn fled to Qín,
and Qín took the Nine Cauldrons."
This may be an error.
The Book of Songs says:
"The crane cries in the ninefold marsh,
its voice is heard in heaven."
This means the crane cries in the winding marsh,
yet its voice can still be heard in heaven,
metaphorically illustrating that a nobleman cultivating virtue in remote obscurity,
his reputation can still reach the imperial court.
To say its sound is heard from a high distance,
is acceptable;
but to say it is heard in heaven,
is an exaggeration.
That statement about the voice being heard in heaven
comes from seeing cranes cry among the clouds,
and listening from the ground,
estimating that if their cries reach the ground,
they should also be heard in heaven.
When cranes cry among the clouds,
people hear the sound and look up to see them,
their eyes perceiving their forms.
Eyes and ears work together -
when ears hear the sound,
then eyes see the form.
However, what ears and eyes can perceive
does not exceed ten li;
even if there were cries reaching heaven,
people could not hear them.
Why?
Because heaven is tens of thousands of li distant from people,
so eyes cannot see it,
nor ears hear it.
When cranes cry now,
we hear them from below,
meaning the cranes are crying nearby.
To hear their sound from below
and claim they cry from the ground,
then should also be heard in heaven,
loses touch with reality.
If cranes cry among the clouds,
and people hear from below;
if they cry in the ninefold marsh,
with no one in heaven above,
how can we know their sound reaches heaven?
There's no way to know -
this is just conjecture based on analogy.
The poet might not have known the truth,
and sincerely believed it;
or might have known,
but wanted to use it metaphorically,
thus exaggerating it.
The Book of Songs says:
"Of Zhou's black-haired people,
there is not a single one left."
This refers to King Xuān of Zhōu's time,
when they suffered great drought disaster.
The poet grieved over the severe drought,
how people suffered from it,
saying there wasn't a single person left untouched by sorrow and pain.
That the drought was severe,
is true enough;
but to say not a single person remained,
is exaggeration.
The people of Zhōu
were like people today.
If people today
suffered great drought disaster,
the poor and weak without savings
would pray desperately for rain;
but those rich with abundant grain,
with full granaries,
with neither hunger nor thirst,
what sorrow would they have?
During heavenly drought,
forests and mountains don't wither completely,
just as during floods,
hills and mounds aren't completely submerged.
In forests and mountains,
there must be some wealthy people who escape harm,
yet it says
"there is not a single one left",
exaggerating the text,
to emphasize the drought's severity.
The Book of Changes says:
"He enlarges his house,
shades his family,
peeps through his door,
quietly without anyone."
This doesn't mean there are no people,
but no worthy people.
The Book of Documents says:
"Do not leave the multitude of offices empty."
Empty means vacant,
multitude means many.
Not to leave many offices empty
means if filled with unsuitable people,
it's no different from being empty,
hence called empty.
