Even the unworthy possess the five constant virtues,
though their ability is inferior,
not making them pure worthies,
they are not madly stubborn and ignorant,
completely devoid of knowledge.
Virtue varies in degree,
ability varies in level,
those holding office and managing duties
all wish to diligently serve in their positions.
The officials in the Book of Documents,
the household in the Book of Changes,
can still be beneficial -
how can they be called empty and without people?
The Book of Songs says:
"With many officials gathered,
King Wén found peace."
This means King Wén obtained many worthy men,
and few unworthy ones.
Now the Book of Changes should say
"quietly with few people",
the Book of Documents should say
"not without numerous officials".
Using
"few"
would be acceptable;
but saying empty without people
is too extreme.
The five grains for people
can all satisfy hunger when eaten.
The taste of rice and millet
is sweet and rich;
beans and wheat, though coarse,
can also relieve hunger.
Those eating beans and wheat
all call them coarse and not sweet,
but none say their stomachs are empty with nothing to eat.
Bamboo and wooden staffs
can all support the sick.
The strength of bamboo staffs
is weaker than wood.
Those using bamboo staffs
all say they're not strong,
but none say their hands are empty without support.
Unworthy ministers
are like beans, wheat,
and bamboo staffs.
The Book of Changes, referring to incompetent ministers present,
says
"without anyone"
because it detests them extremely.
The Book of Documents' numerous officials
could also include minor talents,
yet saying
"do not leave empty"
criticizes them severely.
The Analects say:
"Great indeed
was Yáo as sovereign!
So vast that people could find no name for it."
The tradition says:
"There was a fifty-year-old man playing earthen drums by the road,
when a spectator said:
'Great indeed
is Yáo's virtue!'
The drum player said:
'I rise with the sun
and rest at sunset,
dig wells to drink,
plow fields to eat -
what has Yáo to do with it?'"
This illustrates the effect of being too vast to be named.
To say "vast"
is acceptable;
but to say people could find no name for it
is exaggeration.
Vast as the four seas may be,
numerous as the myriad people are,
to claim none can describe Yáo's virtue
is likely untrue.
Those beating the soil sang:
"What strength had Yáo?"
meaning the people could not name it;
yet observers exclaimed:
"How great!
Yáo's virtue!"
This
"what"
folk
could still understand it.
Since some truly knew,
to say
"none"
is an exaggeration.
Confucian texts also state:
"Yáo and
Shùn's people
could be enfeoffed house by house."
Meaning every household had conduct of a gentleman,
all fit for office.
To say they could be enfeoffed
is plausible;
but "house by house"
is exaggerated.
At fifty, one becomes a father;
if a father knows not his ruler,
how can he guide his son?
In an age of peace,
homes nurture gentlemen,
people uphold courtesy and duty;
fathers observe rites,
sons uphold conduct.
Those with conduct have understanding;
none know a ruler like his ministers;
worthy ministers can know their ruler,
and knowing him,
thus govern the people.
If one cannot know Yáo,
how could they be enfeoffed?
At fifty, beating soil on roads,
mingling with unformed youths,
what worthiness is this?
When Zǐlù made Zǐgāo steward of Hòu,
Confucius deemed it improper,
for he had not learned,
and knew nothing.
If soil-beaters are ignorant,
how appoint them?
To praise Yáo's magnanimity
cannot justify enfeoffing house by house;
to claim worthies could be thus enfeoffed
cannot excuse their folly and ignorance.
Soil-beaters hardly suit "house by house,"
nor does "house by house" match magnanimity;
both are exaggerations.
Their origin
lies in extolling Yáo's virtue.
The Shàngshū states:
"Zǔ Yī admonished Zhòu:
'Now our people all desire your fall.'"
"Wǎng" means none,
that all under heaven wish the king's demise.
To say some desired the king's fall
is plausible;
but "all"
is exaggerated.
Though Zhòu was wicked,
not all subjects were ungrateful;
yet Zǔ Yī exaggerated
to frighten Zhòu.
Hence it is said:
"Words unenhanced,
hearts unshaken;
hearts unshaken,
deeds unchanged."
Exaggerating words
aims to instill fear,
hoping for awakening.
Sū Qín told the King of Qí:
"In Línzī,
chariot hubs clash,
shoulders rub,
raised sleeves form curtains,
joined lapels make screens,
sweat flung becomes rain."
Though Qí was prosperous,
it was not so;
Sū Qín exaggerated
to rouse the king.
Zǔ Yī's admonition to Zhòu
resembles Sū Qín's persuasion.
Sages exaggerate texts
for outward purpose,
not necessarily reflecting truth.
How to prove this?
The "Wǔchéng" chapter
says
"King Wǔ attacked Zhòu,
blood flowed enough to float pestles."
Many joined the battle,
hence such bloodshed.
But all desired Zhòu's fall;
with collapse imminent,
who would fight hard?
Thus Zǔ Yī's claim
"all desired"
is like Sū Qín's hyperbole.
The "Wǔchéng" saying
"blood floated pestles"
is also excessive.
The dead's blood flowing
could not float pestles.
Consider Wǔ attacking Zhòu at Mùyě:
Héběi's land is high,
soil dry everywhere;
weapons bloodied,
it soaked into earth—
how could pestles float?
Moreover, Zhōu and
Yīn soldiers
carried provisions,(
or dry rations),
needing no pestle and mortar,
so what pestles floated?
Speaking of floating pestles
aims to convey
the battle's fierceness and casualties,
hence the hyperbole.
The Chūnqiū
"Duke Zhuāng's seventh year,
summer, fourth month, Xīnmǎo,
midnight,
fixed stars unseen,
stars fell like rain."
The Gōngyáng Zhuàn says:
"'Like rain'
means what?
Not rain.
Not rain,
why say
'like rain'?
The unrevised Chūnqiū said:
'(As)
rain stars,
not reaching a foot down, returned.'
The gentleman revised it:
'Stars fell like rain.'"
"Unrevised Chūnqiū"
means the Lǔ Historical Records before revision,
stating:
"Rain stars,
not reaching a foot down, as if returning."
"Gentleman"
refers to Confucius.
Confucius revised it to:
"Stars fell like rain."
"Like rain"
means resembling rain's appearance.
Mountain mist forms clouds,
not reaching heaven above,
descending as(
cloud) rain.(
Star) stars fall not reaching earth,
returning to heaven above,
hence called
"like rain."
This is Confucius's correct phrasing.
When stars fall, sometimes they reach the ground,
and sometimes they do not;
it is difficult to ascertain the exact distance in feet or zhang.
The Records of the Historian states
"a foot,"
which is also an exaggeration.
The earth has towers, terraces, mountains, and hills—
how can one speak of
"a foot"?
Confucius said
"like rain,"
which captures the reality.
Confucius composed the Spring and Autumn Annals,
so he correctly stated
"like rain."
If Confucius had not composed it,
the phrase
"not reaching the ground by a foot"
would have been transmitted down to the present day.
During the time of Emperor Guāngwǔ,
the court gentleman Bēn Guāng from Rǔnán submitted a memorial stating:
"During the reign of Emperor Wén of the Hàn,
he resided in the Míngguāng Palace,
and only three legal cases were adjudicated in the empire."
He praised Emperor Wén,
presenting his achievements as facts.
Emperor Guāngwǔ said:
"During Emperor Wén's time,
he did not reside in the Míngguāng Palace,
and more than three legal cases were adjudicated.
He accumulated goodness and cultivated virtue,
and his fine reputation spread far and wide.
This is why a gentleman dislikes being in a lowly position."
Now, Bēn Guāng submitted his memorial during the Hàn dynasty,
and the Hàn is a recent era;
yet he exaggerated the merits and virtues,
still surpassing the reality.
How much more so for ancient emperors from remote antiquity?
When worthies and scholars praise and recount them afterward,
they lose touch with reality and stray from the truth,
and this alone is already excessive.
Had it not been for Emperor Guāngwǔ's critique,
a thousand generations later,
the affairs of Emperor Wén,
recorded in the classical texts,
would have been taken by people without knowing they were exaggerated,
and his residing in the Míngguāng Palace
with only three legal cases adjudicated
would have been accepted as factual.
Scholars of the world
are fond of trusting their teachers and esteeming antiquity,
believing that everything spoken by sages and worthies is without fault.
They concentrate solely on studying and reciting,
without knowing how to question or challenge.
When sages and worthies take up the brush to compose texts,
their intentions are careful and thorough,
yet it still cannot be said that they fully capture reality.
How much more so for words spoken hastily?
How can they all be correct?
If they cannot all be correct,
people of the time do not know how to challenge them;
or if they are correct,
but the meaning is obscure and difficult to discern,
people of the time do not know how to inquire.
Examining
the words of sages and worthies,
there are often contradictions between the higher and lower;
their texts
frequently have inconsistencies between the earlier and later parts.
Yet scholars of the world
are unable to perceive this.
Commentators all say:
"The disciples of Confucius' school,
the seventy disciples in talent,
surpass the scholars of today."
This statement is absurd.
They see Confucius as a teacher,
a sage transmitting the Way,
who must have taught exceptional talents,
and therefore call them extraordinary.
But the talents of ancient people
are the talents of modern people.
What we today call outstanding and heroic,
in antiquity were regarded as sages and divine.
Thus, the seventy disciples are considered rare throughout the ages.
If there were a teacher like Confucius in the present day,
then the scholars of this era
would all be like Yán Huí and Mǐn Sǔn.
If there were no Confucius,
then the seventy disciples
would be the scholars of today.
How can this be verified?
By the fact that when studying under Confucius,
they were unable to question exhaustively.
The words of the sage
could not be fully understood;
when expounding the Way and presenting principles,
they could not be immediately clarified.
If they could not be immediately clarified,
one should ask to elucidate them;
if they could not be fully understood,
one should challenge to exhaust them.
When Gāo Yáo presented the Way before Emperor Shùn,
it was shallow and brief, not exhaustive.
Yǔ questioned and challenged him,
causing shallow words to deepen,
and brief points to become detailed.
It is through questioning and challenging
that explanations are stimulated to become profound and incisive,
and touched upon to become clear and evident.
Confucius laughed at Zǐyóu's playing of the zither and singing,
and Zǐyóu cited earlier words to refute Confucius.
Now, examining the text of the Analects,
Confucius' words are often like those laughing at the zither and singing,
but few disciples are like Zǐyóu in challenging him.
Thus, Confucius' words
become entangled and unresolved.
Since the seventy disciples could not challenge him,
the scholars of the world
are unable to truly discern right and wrong.
In all methods of learning,
the difficulty lies not in lacking talent,
but in challenging the teacher,
examining the Way and verifying principles,
and determining right and wrong.
The way of questioning and challenging
does not necessarily require facing the sage during his lifetime.
Those in the world who explain and comment on people
do not necessarily need the sage to instruct them
before they dare to speak.
If there are questions that are not understood,
pursuing and challenging Confucius—
what harm is there to righteousness?
If one truly possesses the knowledge to transmit the sage's teachings,
and critiques Confucius' doctrines—
what violation of principle is there?
To question Confucius' words,
and challenge the passages that are not understood—
if in the world there are born those of great talent and broad knowledge,
people capable of answering questions and resolving difficulties,
they will surely commend the right and wrong of the challenging questions in our world.
Mèng Yìzǐ asked about filial piety,
and the Master said:
"Do not disobey."
When Fán Chí was driving the carriage,
the Master told him:
"Mèngsūn asked me about filial piety,
and I replied:
'Do not disobey.'"
Fán Chí said:
"What does that mean?"
The Master said:
"While they are alive, serve them according to ritual;
when they die, bury them according to ritual;
and sacrifice to them according to ritual."
The question is:
Confucius' words "do not disobey"—
what is not to be disobeyed is ritual.
A filial son should also anticipate his parents' wishes and comply with their intentions,
and should not disobey his parents' desires.
Confucius said "do not disobey,"
but did not say "do not disobey ritual."
When Mèng Yìzǐ heard Confucius' words,
would he not suspect that it meant not to disobey his parents' wishes?
Fán Chí asked
what it meant,
and only then did Confucius say
"while they are alive, serve them according to ritual;
when they die, bury them according to ritual;
and sacrifice to them according to ritual."
If Fán Chí had not asked,
the meaning of "do not disobey" would have remained unknown.
Mèng Yìzǐ's talent
was no greater than Fán Chí's.
Thus, in the chapters of the Analects, his words and actions are not recorded.
If Fán Chí did not understand,
would Mèng Yìzǐ necessarily have understood?
Mèng Wǔbó asked about filial piety,
and the Master said:
"Parents are only anxious about their children's illnesses."
Wǔbó was good at worrying about his parents,
so he said
"only anxious about their illnesses."
Wǔbó worried about his parents,
while Yìzǐ disobeyed ritual.
Addressing their shortcomings,
he replied to Wǔbó, saying
"parents are only anxious about their children's illnesses."
To Yìzǐ, he should also have said
"only in cases of fire or flood should one disobey ritual."
The Duke of Zhōu instructed those of minor talent in detail,
but treated those of great talent briefly.
Fán Chí was of great talent,
yet Confucius instructed him in detail;
while Yìzǐ was of minor talent,
yet he was answered briefly,
contrary to the Duke of Zhōu's intent.
To attack Yìzǐ's shortcomings,
violates the principle of appropriateness,
and yet the disciples did not find it difficult—
why is that!
If it was because Yìzǐ held high authority,
and he dared not speak exhaustively,
then in his reply to Wǔ Bó, he should have merely said "do not worry" and that's all.
Both were sons of the Mèng family,
their authority and status equal,
yet he instructed Wǔ Bó in detail but treated Yìzǐ briefly—
the reason for this is unclear.
Had Confucius spoken exhaustively to Yìzǐ,
telling him not to violate ritual,
what harm could there have been?
No one in Lǔ held more power than the Jì family,
yet he criticized their eight rows of dancers in the courtyard,
and reproached their offering sacrifices to Tàishān—
he did not fear the harm of arousing the Jì family's hatred with his lack of concealment and taboo,
yet he alone feared the crime of answering Yìzǐ with exhaustive words—
why is that?
Moreover, those asking about filial piety were not few,
and all had attendants present,
but when he spoke to Yìzǐ,
not only was he convinced in heart and willing in mind,
hence he told Fán Chí.
Confucius said:
"Wealth and honor
are what people desire,
but if they are not obtained by the right way,
they do not abide with them;
poverty and lowliness
are what people dislike,
but if they are not obtained by the right way,
they do not avoid them."
This means that one should obtain through moral principles,
and should not seize improperly;
one should maintain integrity and be content with poverty,
and should not improperly avoid it.
Now, to say that if wealth and honor are not obtained by the right way, one does not abide with them—
that is acceptable;
but what about not obtaining poverty and lowliness by the right way?
Wealth and honor can indeed be avoided,
but where would one go to avoid poverty and lowliness?
To avoid poverty and lowliness
is to obtain wealth and honor;
if one does not obtain wealth and honor,
one does not avoid poverty and lowliness.
If it means that if wealth and honor are not obtained by the right way,
then one does not avoid poverty and lowliness?
Then what is obtained is wealth and honor,
not poverty and lowliness.
Why then should poverty and lowliness be spoken of as "obtained"?
It should instead be said:
"Poverty and lowliness
are what people dislike,
but if they are not avoided by the right way,
then they do not avoid them."
It should say "avoid,"
not "obtain."
"Obtain"
applies to gaining something.
Now, when avoiding them,
how can one say
"obtain"?
Only wealth and honor should be spoken of as "obtained."
Why?
Because obtaining wealth and honor
means avoiding poverty and lowliness.
Then, how does one "avoid" poverty and lowliness by the right way?
By cultivating oneself and practicing the Way,
serving in office to obtain rank, emolument, wealth, and honor—
obtaining rank, emolument, wealth, and honor,
then one avoids poverty and lowliness.
And how does one "avoid" poverty and lowliness not by the right way?
Resenting the bitterness of poverty and lowliness,
one turns to treachery and theft,
amasses goods and wealth,
and arbitrarily assumes official ranks—
this is not by the right way.
Since the seventy disciples did not ask about this,
and scholars of the time also did not question it,
this statement's meaning remains tangled and unresolved, and the text unclear—
this would mean Confucius could not articulate clearly;
if the meaning is tangled and the text also unclear,
then Confucius did not instruct thoroughly.
The disciples did not ask,
the world did not question—
why is that?
Confucius said:
"Gōngyě Cháng is fit to be given a wife,
though he was in bonds,
it was not his crime."
And he gave him his own daughter in marriage.
The question is:
On what basis did Confucius give his daughter to Gōngyě Cháng?
What evidence did he see?
Was it based on his being thirty years old and fit to marry?
Or did he see his virtuous conduct as fit for marriage?
If it was based on his being thirty,
he should not have mentioned his being in bonds;
if he saw his virtuous conduct,
he also should not have mentioned his being in bonds.
Why?
All who entered Confucius's school
had good conduct,
hence they were deemed fit to serve as disciples.
Among the disciples, if one had no wife,
he would be given a wife,
with no need for special mention.
If many among the disciples had no wives,
and Gōngyě Cháng was especially virtuous,
so he alone was given a wife,
then in praising him, his conduct should have been listed,
not his being in bonds mentioned.
Why?
In the world, many are wrongly accused,
but they are not necessarily all virtuous.
Ordinary people suffer injustice,
and they are numerous and varied.
If being wrongly accused made one fit for Confucius to give his daughter,
then Confucius did not marry his daughter to the virtuous,
but to the wronged.
Consider:
In Confucius's praise of Gōngyě Cháng,
there is mention of his being wronged,
but no text about his conduct or ability.
If he was truly not virtuous,
and Confucius gave him his daughter,
that was wrong;
if he was truly virtuous,
and Confucius's praise was incomplete,
that was also wrong.
It would have been like his saying of Nán Róng:
"When the state has the Way, he is not cast aside;
when the state is without the Way, he avoids punishment and execution."
There, he praised him fully.
Confucius said to Zǐgòng:
"You and Huí—
who is superior?"
He said:
"How dare I compare myself to Huí?
Huí hears one and understands ten;
I hear one and understand two."
The Master said:
"You are not equal to him,
I and you are both not equal to him."
This was praising Yán Yuān, testing by questioning Zǐgòng.
The question is:
What Confucius taught
was ritual and humility.
When Zǐlù governed a state with ritual,
his words lacked humility,
and Confucius criticized him.
If Zǐgòng was truly superior to Yán Yuān,
and Confucius asked him,
he should still say he was not equal;
if he was truly inferior,
he should also say he was not equal.
Not that his answer deceived his teacher,
but words of ritual humility should be modest and humble.
Now, in speaking thus,
what was Confucius aiming at?
If Confucius knew Yán Yuān was superior to Zǐgòng,
then there was no need to ask Zǐgòng;
if Confucius truly did not know,
and asked Zǐgòng,
Zǐgòng's modest humility would not reveal the truth either.
If Confucius merely wanted to praise Yán Yuān's goodness,
to say Yán Yuān was virtuous,
and no disciple could match him,
there were many ways to do so by name,
why need he ask Zǐgòng?
The Master said:
"Virtuous indeed is Huí!"
He also said:
"I talked with Huí all day,
and he never disagreed, as if he were stupid."
He also said:
"Huí!
His heart does not turn away from benevolence for three months."
These three passages all praise directly,
without using others to provoke,
yet in this one passage,
he alone used Zǐgòng to provoke—
why is that?
Some say:
"This was meant to restrain Zǐgòng.
At that time,
Zǐgòng's reputation surpassed that of Yán Yuān,
and Confucius feared Zǐgòng would become arrogant and complacent,
so he restrained him."
But having a reputation above Yán Yuān
was due to contemporary evaluations,
not because Zǐgòng sought to surpass him.
What was Zǐgòng's actual wisdom like?
If Yán Yuān's talent was superior to his own,
he would naturally acknowledge it,
needing no restraint;
if Zǐgòng lacked self-awareness,
even if Confucius spoke,
he would think Confucius merely wanted to restrain him.
From this perspective,
whether he asked or not,
could neither restrain nor praise.
Zǎi Wǒ slept during the day,
and the Master said:
"Rotten wood cannot be carved,
a wall of dung cannot be plastered.
As for Yǔ, what is there to criticize?"
This expressed disgust at Zǎi Wǒ's daytime sleeping.
The question arises:
Sleeping during the day is a minor fault;
rotten wood and dung walls
are utterly ruined, beyond repair,
representing major faults.
To reprove a minor fault with major faults,
how can that convince anyone?
If Zǎi Wǒ's nature was bad,
like rotten wood or dung walls,
he shouldn't have been admitted to Confucius' school,
listed among the four disciplines;
if his nature was good,
and Confucius disliked him,
the dislike was excessive,
a fault itself.
"When people are unvirtuous,
and you detest them excessively,
it causes disorder."
Confucius' detestation of Zǎi Yǔ
could be considered excessive.
If an ignorant person faces a minor offense,
and the official sentences them to execution,
would they feel wronged and resentful?
Or accept and blame themselves?
If Zǎi Wǒ was foolish,
he would react like the minor offender;
if Zǎi Wǒ was virtuous,
understanding Confucius' reproof,
he would subtly reform himself.
Clear words to inform him,
spread remarks to fault him,
served to show the issue, and he would reform himself.
Self-reform depends not on the words' severity,
but on whether Zǎi Yǔ could change.
The principle of the Spring and Autumn Annals
praises hair-thin goodness,
condemns tiny faults.
To praise minutely with grandeur,
or condemn minutely with gravity—
considering the Annals' principle,
would it endorse this?
If not,
then Zǎi Wǒ didn't accept it;
not accepting it,
Confucius' words were discarded.
A sage's words match his writings,
words from the mouth,
texts on bamboo slips,
both originate from the heart,
their essence is one.
When Confucius composed the Spring and Autumn Annals,
he didn't condemn small faults with major ones,
yet in criticizing Zǎi Yǔ,
he used major faults for minor ones,
contradicting his writings,
how could that convince?
The Master said:
"Initially, towards people,
I'd listen to their words and trust their actions;
now, towards people,
I listen to their words and observe their actions.
It is because of Yǔ that I have changed."
This originated from Zǎi Yǔ's daytime sleeping,
revising the method of judging people.
The question arises:
How can daytime sleeping
suffice to ruin one's conduct?
Those who ruin their conduct
may not sleep day or night,
how does that make them good?
To judge people's goodness by daytime sleeping,
can that capture the truth?
Consider
Zǎi Yǔ, in Confucius' school,
ranked among the four disciplines,
placed above Cì.
If his nature was lazy,
incapable of cultivation,
how did he achieve this?
If Zǎi Wǒ reached this despite daytime sleeping,
his talent far surpassed others.
If he was unaccomplished,
but considered himself sufficient,
lacking self-awareness,
it was unclear understanding,
not evil conduct.
Admonishment would suffice,
no need to change methods.
If he knew his inadequacy,
and slept from exhaustion,
it was mental depletion.
Mental depletion can lead to death,
how is sleeping alone significant?
Moreover, in evaluating people,
if we value actions, we disregard words,
if we value words, we disregard actions.
Now Zǎi Yǔ, though lacking in action,
had words.
Using his words,
despite his action's shortcomings,
gives one measure.
Now Confucius, prompted by Zǎi Yǔ's sleeping,
listened to his words,
observed his actions,
seeking correspondence between them,
then called him virtuous—
this shows Confucius expected completeness in people.
How then to apply the principle
"Do not expect perfection from anyone"?
Zǐzhāng asked:
"Língyǐn Zǐwén took office three times as Prime Minister
without showing pleasure;
was dismissed three times,
without showing resentment.
The policies of the former administration
he always reported to the new Prime Minister.
What do you think?"
The Master said:
"He was loyal."
Zǐzhāng said:
"Was he benevolent?"
The Master said:
"I do not know;
how could he be benevolent?"
Zǐwén had recommended Chǔ Zǐyù to succeed him, who attacked Sòng,
and with a hundred chariots was defeated, losing his troops.
Not knowing this,
how could he be benevolent?
The question arises:
Zǐwén recommended Zǐyù,
showing poor judgment of character.
Wisdom and benevolence
are unrelated.
Having a flaw in understanding
does not hinder benevolent conduct.
The five constant virtues
are benevolence, righteousness, propriety, wisdom, and faithfulness.
These five are distinct,
not interdependent for fulfillment,
so there are wise people and benevolent people;
proprietous people and righteous people.
A faithful person may not be wise,
a wise person may not be benevolent,
a benevolent person may not be propriety,
a propriety person may not be righteous.
Zǐwén's wisdom was clouded regarding Zǐyù,
how does that damage his benevolence?
To call him benevolent,
why is it unacceptable?
Moreover, loyalty
is厚 (thickness/generosity),
being厚 to others
is benevolence.
Confucius said:
"Observe a person's faults,
and you will know his benevolence."
Zǐwén had the substance of benevolence.
For Confucius to say loyalty is not benevolence
is like saying parents are not one's two progenitors,
or a spouse is not one's husband or wife.
Duke Āi asked:
"Which of your disciples would you consider fond of learning?"
Confucius replied:
"There was one Yán Huí
who never transferred his anger
nor repeated a fault.
Unfortunately, his life was short and he died!
Now there is none,
and I have not heard of anyone fond of learning."
Now, the reason for Yānyuān's death—
what exactly was its cause?
If we say he died young by nature,
it is like Bóniú having an illness.
Human life receives its mandate,
and all ought to be whole and pure.
But if one has a vile disease,
we say 'he has no mandate.'
Human life should all receive Heaven's long mandate,
yet if one gets a 'short life,'
it should also be said 'he has no mandate.'
If Heaven's mandate has short and long,
then it also has good and evil.
To say Yānyuān had a 'short life'
then one should say Bóniú had an 'evil fate';
to say Bóniú 'had no mandate'
then one should say Yānyuān 'had no mandate.'
One died, one fell ill,
both lamented as matters of fate,
yet what they received was no different—
the wording differs,
and I do not understand the reason.
Duke Āi asked Confucius who was fond of learning,
and Confucius replied:
"There was Yán Huí who was fond of learning,
but now there is none.
He never transferred his anger,
nor repeated a fault."
Why is that?
The answer:
"It was to criticize Duke Āi's nature of
transferring anger and repeating faults.
Taking advantage of the question,
he answered with both points,
thereby attacking the ruler's shortcomings
without incurring punishment."
It is asked:
Kāngzǐ also asked about fondness for learning,
and Confucius also answered with Yānyuān.
Did Kāngzǐ not also have shortcomings?
Why not answer to criticize Kāngzǐ as well?
Kāngzǐ was no sage;
his conduct still had failings.
For instance:
Kāngzǐ was troubled by thieves,
and Confucius replied:
"If you yourself were without desire,
even if you rewarded them, they would not steal."
From this it is said,
Kāngzǐ's shortcoming was desire—
why not criticize him?
Confucius visited Nánzǐ,
and Zǐlù was displeased.
The Master said:
"If I have done anything vile,
may Heaven reject me!
May Heaven reject me!"
Nánzǐ was the wife of Duke Líng of Wèi;
she summoned Confucius,
and Zǐlù was unhappy,
thinking Confucius was involved in licentiousness.
Confucius explained, saying:
"If what I did was base,
may Heaven strike me down!"
He swore with utmost sincerity,
to assure Zǐlù.
It is asked:
Could Confucius's self-justification
truly resolve the matter?
If ordinary people had base behavior
and Heaven indeed struck them down,
one could invoke that to swear.
Hearing it, Zǐlù
might believe and be appeased.
But there has never been anyone struck down by Heaven for such;
to say "Heaven rejects me"—
would Zǐlù believe it?
Consider:
lightning strikes people dead,
water and fire drown or burn people,
walls and houses collapse and crush people.
If one said,
"May lightning strike me,
may water and fire drown or burn me,
may walls and houses crush me,"
Zǐlù might somewhat believe it.
But to invoke a never-before-seen calamity
to swear to Zǐlù—
how could Zǐlù be appeased and believe it?
Consider also:
there are those who die in their sleep without waking—
can we say Heaven rejected them?
Examining those who die thus,
not all were base.
Though Zǐlù's understanding of the Way was shallow,
he still knew the facts of matters.
If the matter was untrue,
and Confucius swore by it,
Zǐlù would certainly not be appeased.
Confucius once said:
"Death and life are decreed,
wealth and honor depend on Heaven."
That being so,
human life and death have their own long or short span,
not depending on the goodness or evil of one's conduct.
For instance:
Yānyuān died early,
and Confucius called it a short life—
from this we know those who die young
need not have had evil conduct.
Though Zǐlù's understanding was shallow,
hearing Confucius's words,
he knew the reality of life and death.
When Confucius swore,
saying, "If I have done anything vile,
may Heaven reject me,"
why did Zǐlù not say:
"If your fate was not due to die,
how could Heaven strike you down?"
Thus,
swearing to Zǐlù with "Heaven rejects me"
would never be believed.
If not believed,
then Confucius's self-justification
would ultimately fail.
The Shàngshū says:
"Do not be like Dānzhū in his arrogance,
devoted only to idleness and pleasure."
This refers to Emperor Shùn admonishing Yǔ
not to give [the throne] to an unworthy son.
He emphasized the Mandate of Heaven,
fearing Yǔ would favor his son,
so he cited Dānzhū to warn him.
Yǔ said:
"I married at the time of
Xīn-Rén;
when Qǐ was born crying,
I did not treat him as a son."
He recounted his own actions, using the past to infer the future,
revealing the hidden through the evident,
to show he dared not favor an unworthy son.
He did not say "Heaven rejects me,"
knowing that common people swear, fond of invoking Heaven.
Confucius, suspected by Zǐlù's doubts about his conduct,
did not cite his actions to prove he was not base,
but said "Heaven rejects me"—
how does this differ from commoners resolving suspicions by invoking curses to Heaven?
What distinction is there?
Confucius said:
"The phoenix does not come;
the river gives forth no chart—
I am finished!"
The Master lamented that he would not become king.
Had he become king,
he would have brought about great peace,
and with great peace, the phoenix would come,
and the river would produce the chart.
Now, unable to become king,
the auspicious responses did not appear;
with a grieving heart he lamented,
hence saying, "I am finished."
It is asked:
What exactly is the basis for the phoenix and river chart?
If based on the beginning of a reign,
at that initial time,
the bird and chart had not yet arrived.
If based on great peace,
emperors of great peace
did not necessarily always bring the phoenix and river chart.
The Five Emperors and Three Sovereigns
all achieved great peace,
yet examining their auspicious signs,
the phoenix was not always an inevitable omen.
For great peace,
the phoenix is not a necessary response;
Confucius, a sage,
lamented over what was not inevitable—
that should not have been his response.
Moreover, when Confucius said "Heaven is destroying me,"
it was because Yán Yuān was virtuous.
Consider:
virtuous individuals in the world
are not necessarily destined to become advisors.
That the virtuous may not become advisors
is like sages not necessarily receiving the Mandate.
Some emperors are not sagely,
some advisors are not virtuous.
Why so?
Because official rank and bone structure differ from talent.
From this perspective,
Yán Yuān alive might not have become an advisor,
his death need not constitute a loss,
yet Confucius said "Heaven is destroying me"
—on what basis did he perceive this?
Furthermore, if Heaven prevented Confucius from being king,
what was its original intent?
Was it that at the conferral of his nature and destiny,
Heaven did not make him king?
Or did it intend to make him king,
but later regretted it?
If originally not making him king,
why consider Yán Yuān's death
a loss?
If originally making him king,
but later regretting it,
this king lacked the bone structure,
which should rather reside with Heaven's autonomy.
Moreover, what goodness did it originally see to make him king?
What evil did it later hear
to regret and not mandate?
Are the discussions of celestial spirits mistakenly unclear?
When Confucius went to Wèi,
he encountered the funeral of his former hostel keeper,
entered and wept for him.
Upon exiting, he had Zǐgòng unharness a side horse to contribute to the funeral.
Zǐgòng said:
"For disciples' funerals,
you've never unharnessed a horse;
to unharness one for a former hostel keeper,
isn't that excessive?"
Confucius said:
"When I entered and wept for him,
I met with grief and shed tears.
I detest tears without accompanying action,
so, my disciple, carry this out!"
Confucius unharnessed the horse for the former keeper
to avoid emotion not matching ritual.
Ritual performed with genuine emotion
arises from feeling and moves with kindness.
When ritual and emotion correspond,
the gentleman acts accordingly.
When Yán Yuān died,
the Master wept with deep grief.
A disciple said:
"You are grieving excessively!"
"If I don't grieve for this man, for whom should I?"
Such grief
is the peak of sorrow.
Weeping for Yán Yuān with deep grief
distinguished him from other disciples,
showing extreme pain.
He had a coffin but no outer coffin,
Yán Lù requested the carriage to make one,
but Confucius did not give it,
as a senior official cannot go on foot.
Mourning the former keeper, he unharnessed a horse as contribution,
detesting tears without action;
weeping for Yán Yuān with deep grief,
he refused the carriage request,
leaving grief unaccompanied.
Are tears and grief different,
or horses and carriages distinct?
There, ritual and emotion matched;
here, kindness and duty were inconsistent.
I don't understand Confucius's intent in ritual.
Confucius said:
"When Lǐ died,
he had a coffin but no outer coffin,
I didn't go on foot to provide one."
His kindness to Lǐ was deeper than to Yán Yuān,
yet Lǐ died without an outer coffin,
due to the senior official's protocol
prohibiting going on foot.
Lǐ was his son,
Yán Yuān was of another surname.
He didn't provide full rites for his own son's death,
how much less for someone of another surname?
It is said:
"This shows Confucius's practical application of kindness."
Matching emotion for the former keeper,
but not equating kindness for his son—
was it because he was previously a scholar,
later a senior official?
If formerly a scholar,
scholars rode two horses;
if a senior official,
senior officials rode three.
A senior official cannot leave his carriage to walk;
why not sell two horses to make the outer coffin,
and ride the remaining one?
As a scholar, riding two horses,
he unharnessed one for the former keeper;
why not now sell two to match kindness,
riding one to avoid going on foot?
Not unharnessing a horse for the keeper
might not disrupt rules;
but burying a son without an outer coffin
violates rites and damages norms.
Confucius valued matching kindness for an old acquaintance
over lightly discarding burial rites for his son,
gaining ritual propriety with others
but losing regulation with his own child.
Then, Confucius not selling his carriage for Lǐ's outer coffin—
how to explain his fear of losing office without a carriage?
He himself said, "The gentleman sacrifices life to achieve benevolence,"
why hesitate to resign to fulfill rites?
Zǐgòng asked about governance,
the Master said:
"Sufficient food, sufficient arms,
and the people's trust."
Asked:
"If forced to discard one,
which of these three comes first?"
Said:
"Discard arms."
Asked:
"If forced to discard another,
which of the two remains?"
Said:
"Discard food.
Since ancient times, all die,
but without trust, people cannot stand."
Trust is most important.
I ask:
if governing a state without food,
people starve,
they abandon ritual and duty.
With ritual and duty abandoned,
where does trust stand?
The Tradition says:
"Granaries full,
then know ritual decorum;
food and clothing sufficient,
then know honor and shame."
Courtesy arises from surplus,
strife from insufficiency.
Now, to discard food
—how can trust be achieved?
During the Spring and Autumn period,
during wartime famines,
people exchanged children to eat,
dismembered skeletons for fuel.
Mouths starving, with no food,
they had no leisure to consider kindness and duty.
The kindness between father and son
is trustworthy indeed,
yet starvation made them abandon trust,
using children as food.
Confucius taught Zǐgòng to discard food and preserve trust—
how is this tenable?
Discard trust, preserve food,
and even if unwilling to trust,
trust naturally arises;
discard food, preserve trust,
and even if wanting to be trustworthy,
trust cannot stand.
When the Master went to Wèi,
Rǎn Zǐ drove for him.
The Master said:
"How populous!"
Asked:
"Since populous,
what next?"
Said:
"Enrich them."
Asked:
"Since enriched,
what next?"
Said:
"Educate them."
Telling Rǎn Zǐ to enrich first then educate,
but teaching Zǐgòng to discard food and preserve trust—
what difference between food and enrichment?
What distinction between trust and education?
Two disciples, different teachings,
emphases unlike,
in governing a state, Confucius's
intent—how was it determined?
Qú Bóyù sent an envoy to Confucius,
and Confucius asked:
"What is your master engaged in?"
The envoy replied:
"My master wishes to reduce his faults but has not yet succeeded."
After the envoy left,
Confucius remarked:
"What an envoy! What an envoy!"
This was a criticism.
Commentators on the *Analects* say:
"The criticism was directed
at his excessive humility on behalf of his master."
Now, when Confucius asked the envoy,
"What is your master doing?"
he was inquiring about his administrative duties,
not his moral conduct.
Given Confucius's question,
the envoy should have answered:
"My master is handling such-and-such affairs,
governing such-and-such policies."
Instead, he replied
"wishes to reduce his faults but has not yet succeeded."
How can we know that his response missed the point,
and that Confucius was criticizing him?
Moreover, why did Confucius actually criticize the envoy?
Was it for his excessive humility?
Or was it because his answer missed the point?
There must be a concrete reason for the criticism,
yet the fault remains unclear,
and he merely said, "What an envoy! What an envoy!"
This leaves later generations puzzled,
unable to discern the envoy's specific error.
Hán Zǐ said:
"When writings are concise, disciples debate their meaning."
Confucius's words "What an envoy!"
how concise they were!
Some say:
"According to the principles of the *Spring and Autumn Annals*,
we conceal faults for the worthy.
Since Qú Bóyù was worthy,
his envoy's fault was concealed."
But to know the son, look at his friends;
to know the ruler, look at his envoys.
If Bóyù were unworthy,
then his envoy would indeed be at fault.
The principle of the *Spring and Autumn Annals*
is to conceal faults for the worthy,
yet it also condemns even minor wrongdoings.
If no criticism is made and faults are concealed,
how can minor condemnations be applied?
If Confucius intended to conceal for Bóyù,
he should have remained silent.
Instead, he exclaimed aloud:
"What an envoy! What an envoy!"
ensuring that everyone knew he was criticizing.
Speaking in such a manner,
what good does it do for concealment?
When Fú Xī summoned him,
Confucius considered going.
Zǐlù was displeased,
saying:
"Previously,
I heard you, Master, say:
'A gentleman does not join those who personally engage in wrongdoing.'
Fú Xī is rebelling from Zhōngmóu;
why would you go to him?"
The Master said:
"I did say that.
But is it not said,
'What is hard cannot be worn thin by grinding'?
Is it not said,
'What is white cannot be blackened by dyeing'?
Am I a bitter gourd?
How can I be hung up without being eaten?"
Zǐlù cited Confucius's past words
to criticize him.
Earlier, when Confucius spoke those words,
he intended his disciples to emulate and practice them.
Zǐlù cited them in remonstrance;
Confucius explained,
not calling his earlier words "a joke"
or "incorrect" and "impracticable,"
but acknowledging "I did say that,"
affirming their validity and applicability.
"Is it not said,
'What is hard cannot be worn thin by grinding';
is it not said,
'What is white cannot be blackened by dyeing'?"
Did these words of Confucius
resolve Zǐlù's objection?
"A gentleman does not join those who personally engage in wrongdoing."
To explain, he should have said:
"Fú Xī has not actually done wrong,
so it is still permissible to join him."
Instead, he said:
"What is hard cannot be worn thin;
what is white cannot be blackened."
According to Confucius's words,
one with hard and white virtue may join such company.
Does a "gentleman's" conduct
become soft and easily tarnished?
Why then specifically "not join"?
Confucius would not drink from the Dào Quán,
and Zēngzǐ would not enter Shèngmǔ's lane,
avoiding evil and filth
because of the dishonor in their names,
even if not based on true morality.
Dào Quán and Shèngmǔ had only empty names,
yet Confucius and Zēngzǐ were ashamed of them;
Fú Xī had actual evil deeds,
yet Confucius considered joining him.
If not drinking from Dào Quán was right,
then wanting to go to Fú Xī was wrong.
"Wealth and honor obtained through unrighteousness
are to me as floating clouds."
To distort principles and accept the salary of a rebel—
is this not what "floating clouds" refer to?
Some say:
"He was adapting to the times to practice the Way."
Even if adapting to practice the Way,
when Zǐlù objected,
he should have said "to practice the Way,"
not "to eat."
One may adapt to practice the Way,
but not to seek food.
"Am I a bitter gourd?
How can I be hung up without being eaten?"
Comparing himself to a bitter gourd
means that one should serve in office to earn a salary.
"I am not a bitter gourd hung up without being eaten"—
this did not address Zǐlù's point.
Zǐlù's criticism of Confucius
was not that he should not serve at all,
but that he should choose a good state to join.
By comparing himself to a bitter gourd,
Confucius showed his desire for sustenance.
Moreover, his words
how vulgar they were!
Why reduce office-holding to mere eating?
A gentleman should not speak thus.
A bitter gourd hung up without being eaten
is equivalent to being hung up without serving.
To rebut Zǐlù, he could have said:
"Am I a bitter gourd,
hung up without serving?"
But he said "hung up without being eaten,"
implying that his purpose in office
was not to practice the Way,
but merely to seek food.
When people take office,
their main aim is to greedily seek salary;
but in terms of ritual and righteousness,
they claim it is to practice the Way.
It is like marriage:
the main desire is lust,
but in terms of ritual and righteousness,
it is to continue the family line.
If office can be bluntly said to be for food,
can marriage be bluntly said to be for lust?
Confucius's words
revealed his true feelings without pretense,
unadorned by righteous principles—
this makes him a common man,
not a gentleman.
Confucian scholars claim that Confucius traveled around
responding to invitations without success,
lamenting that the Way was not practiced—
this misrepresents Confucius's true intentions.
When Gōngshān Fúrǎo rebelled from Bì and summoned him,
Confucius considered going.
Zǐlù said:
"There is no need!
Why must you go to Gōngshān?"
The Master said:
"Would he summon me for nothing?
If someone employs me,
could I not establish a Eastern Zhōu?"
"Establish a Eastern Zhōu"
means to practice the Way.
Both Gōngshān and Fú Xī were rebels;
yet with Gōngshān, he spoke of practicing the Way,
while with Fú Xī, he sought food—
Confucius's words lacked a consistent direction.
If his words lacked consistency,
then his actions had no constant purpose.
That he traveled around without being employed—
was there not a reason for it?
Yáng Huò wished to see him, but he would not see him;
summoned him to office, but he would not take office.
How pure he was!
When Gōngshān and Fú Xī called him, he wished to go.
How impure he was!
Gōngshān Bùrǎo and Yáng Hǔ both rebelled,
seized Jì Huánzǐ.
Both men shared the same wickedness,
their summonses were equally courteous,
yet he responded only to Gōngshān,
and refused to see Yáng Hǔ.
Was it that Gōngshān was still acceptable,
but Yáng Hǔ was not?
Zǐlù challenged the summons of Gōngshān,
so Confucius should have explained that Gōngshān and Fú Xī were not extremely wicked.
The methods of Hánzǐ
emphasized clear laws and valued achievement.
If the worthy brought no benefit to the state, they received no reward;
if the unworthy did no harm to governance, they incurred no punishment.
He demanded achievement and valued rewards,
employed penalties and used executions.
Thus, in his assessment of the Confucians,
he called them those who eat without plowing,
comparing them to parasites;
in discussing the beneficial and the useless,
he compared them to deer and
horses. A horse resembling a deer is worth a thousand pieces of gold,
for there are horses worth a thousand pieces of gold in the world,
but no deer worth a thousand pieces of gold.
Deer are useless,
while horses are useful.
Confucians are like deer,
while useful officials are like horses.
Now Hánzǐ knew how to use deer and
horses as metaphors,
but did not know how to use caps and
shoes as analogies.
If Hánzǐ did not wear a cap,
but only wore shoes to court,
I would listen to his words.
But with a cap on his head standing in court,
wearing useless garments,
adding to the useless officials,
his words contradict his attire,
his actions oppose his methods,
therefore I criticize his words and do not employ his methods.
Nothing wearies the human body more,
with no benefit to the person,
than kneeling and bowing.
If Hánzǐ met people without bowing,
saw his lord or father without kneeling,
it would not necessarily harm his body.
Yet bowing and kneeling are required to honor one's elders,
for ritual and righteousness are most important,
and must not be neglected.
Thus, with ritual and righteousness in one's person,
the body may not necessarily become fat;
but if ritual and righteousness leave the person,
the body may not necessarily become lean and degenerate.
If one claims what is beneficial,
ritual and righteousness are not as good as food and drink.
If Hánzǐ were given food before his lord or father,
and he took it without bowing,
would he be willing to do so?
Bowing and kneeling are the manifestations of
ritual and righteousness,
not substantial benefits to the body,
yet Hánzǐ never neglects them,
for he does not abandon ritual and righteousness for mere physical gain.
Now Confucian scholars represent
ritual and righteousness,
while farming and warfare represent
food and drink.
To value farming and warfare and despise Confucian scholars
is to discard ritual and righteousness in pursuit of food and drink.
If ritual and righteousness are abandoned,
order collapses,
the hierarchy becomes chaotic, and yin and yang go awry,
floods and droughts occur at the wrong times,
the five grains do not ripen,
the myriad people starve to death,
farmers cannot plow,
soldiers cannot fight.
When Zǐgòng wanted to abolish the sacrificial lamb for the first day of the month,
Confucius said:
"Cì!
You love the lamb,
but I love the ritual."
Zǐgòng disliked wasting the lamb,
while Confucius valued preserving the ritual.
Thus, to consider old dikes useless and remove them
will surely lead to floods;
to consider old rituals useless and abolish them
will surely bring chaos and calamity.
Confucians in the world
are the old dikes of ritual and righteousness.
Having them may not bring benefit,
but not having them brings harm.
The establishment of schools
has existed since ancient times,
to honor fundamentals and respect origins,
thus officials are appointed and clerks installed.
Officials cannot be abolished,
the Way cannot be discarded.
Confucian scholars are
the officials of the Way,
to consider them useless and abolish them
is to discard the Way.
The Way brings no tangible results to people,
yet tangible results require the Way to be achieved.
Just as one walks by treading on a path,
the path trodden
requires the untrodden parts;
the body moves using hands and feet,
yet relies on what does not move.
Thus, some things may seem useless,
but the useful depend on them;
they may show no effect,
but the effective await them.
Confucian scholars are
what farming and warfare depend upon.
To discard and not preserve them,
how can that be?
Hánzǐ criticized the Confucians,
saying they are useless and harmful,
probably referring to vulgar Confucians without conduct or integrity,
whose actions do not value ritual,
who bear the name of Confucians but act vulgarly,
engaging in practical studies but with false teachings,
greedy for office and honor,
thus not worthy of respect.
But those with pure aspirations and illustrious conduct,
who do not covet ranks and emoluments,
who discard high ministerial positions as if taking off sandals,
who hold office and perform duties,
though they may not achieve merit,
these are the ones who uphold ritual and righteousness.
What preserves the state
is ritual and righteousness.
If the people lack ritual and righteousness,
the state will topple and the ruler be endangered.
Now the conduct of Confucians,
valuing ritual and cherishing righteousness,
guides those without ritual,
inspires those without righteousness,
leading the people to goodness,
and loving their ruler.
This is also beneficial.
Those who hear of Bó Yí's influence
become廉洁 from greed,
the懦夫 gain determination;
those who hear of Liǔxià Huì's influence
become sincere from shallowness,
the narrow-minded become broad-minded.
This is transformation from above,
not something people can see.
Duàngàn Mù shut his door and did not go out,
yet Wèi Wén honored him,
erected a marker at his lane,
and when the Qín army heard of it,
they ultimately did not attack Wèi.
Had Wèi not had Duàngàn Mù,
the Qín troops would have entered the border,
and the territory would have faced peril and destruction.
Qín was a strong state,
its troops ever victorious.
When its army advanced against Wèi,
Wèi would surely have been crushed,
its three armies defeated,
with bloodshed spanning a thousand miles.
Now because Wèi Wén honored the recluse behind closed doors,
he repelled the strong Qín army,
preserved the territory of Wèi,
and saved the masses of the three armies.
No merit is greater than this,
no reward should come before this.
In Qí, there were men of high principle named Kuáng Jué
and Huá Shì.
These two men
were brothers,
righteously not lowering their aspirations,
not serving a lord who was not their own.
When Tàigōng was enfeoffed in Qí,
he considered these two men disrupted and discouraged the Qí populace,
opening a path of not being used by the ruler,
and executed them simultaneously.
Hánzǐ approved of this,
thinking these two were useless and harmful.
As for Kuáng Jué and
Huà Shì,
they were of the same kind as Duàn Gān Mù.
Tài Gōng executed them,
yet achieved nothing to repel;
Marquis Wén of Wèi honored Duàn Gān Mù's dwelling,
and repelled the powerful Qín, preserving Wèi—
whose achievement was greater?
If Hán Zǐ approved of Gān Mù shutting his door and maintaining high integrity,
then Marquis Wén of Wèi honoring him was right;
but the conduct of Kuáng Jué and
Huà Shì
was of the same integrity as Gān Mù's,
so approving of Tài Gōng executing them
is wrong.
If Hán Zǐ disapproved of Gān Mù's behavior,
and looked down on Marquis Wén's gesture of respect,
then Gān Mù's conduct was beneficial,
and Marquis Wén's act of honor brought merit—
this means Hán Zǐ fails to reward merit and
respect what is beneficial.
Some critics argue:
"When Marquis Wén of Wèi honored Duàn Gān Mù's neighborhood,
the Qín army did not advance because of it,
but this was not an achievement of laws and institutions.
It was a singular success,
not something that can be consistently applied;
even if it benefited the whole state,
it is not to be highly valued."
Now, the achievements of laws and institutions—
what do they refer to?
Nourishing the soldiers of the three armies,
clarifying the commands of rewards and punishments,
enforcing strict penalties and harsh laws,
enriching the state and strengthening the military—
these are the methods of laws and institutions.
Consider the strength of Qín—
would they yield to this?
The six states perished,
all annihilated by Qín's troops.
The armies of the six states were not unsharp,
the strength of their masses not unforceful,
yet they were defeated,
leading to their destruction—
because the strong and weak were mismatched,
the many and few differed.
Even with clear laws and institutions,
what good would it do?
If a child provoked Mèng Bēn's anger,
and Mèng Bēn raged,
the child wielding a blade
to fight Mèng Bēn
would surely not win,
for his strength is inferior.
But if Mèng Bēn was angry,
and the child cultivated courtesy and showed utmost respect,
Mèng Bēn would not bear to harm him.
Qín versus Wèi
is like Mèng Bēn versus a child.
If Wèi had laws and institutions,
Qín would not necessarily fear them,
just as the child wielding a blade
would not make Mèng Bēn retreat.
But honoring scholars and respecting the wise in their neighborhoods
is not merely a child's courtesy and respect.
When strength is small, one cultivates virtue;
when the military is strong, one exerts might.
Qín, with its military might,
was invincible in power.
That they withdrew their army and turned back,
not violating Wèi's borders,
was due to the integrity of the worthy Gān Mù
and the high respect shown by Marquis Wén of Wèi.
Respecting the worthy
is the method for a weak state,
a powerful aid when strength is lacking.
To say this is not an achievement of laws and institutions—
how can that be?
When Emperor Gāo considered deposing the crown prince,
Empress Lǚ was troubled,
so she summoned Zhāng Zǐfáng for advice.
Zǐfáng taught her to respectfully invite the Four Haos and treat them with great honor.
When Gāozǔ saw them,
his resolve weakened and his intention faded,
and the crown prince was thus secured.
If Hán Zǐ had advised Empress Lǚ,
at best, he would have strongly remonstrated,
at worst, exerted forceful effort—
relying on this for self-preservation
would have been a path to execution;
how could it have been merely easy?
The crown prince's respect and generosity toward the Four Haos
dissolved Gāozǔ's intention,
just as Marquis Wén of Wèi honoring Duàn Gān Mù's neighborhood
repelled the powerful Qín army.
The way to govern a state
involves nurturing two aspects:
first, nurturing virtue,
second, nurturing strength.
Nurturing virtue means
supporting people of high reputation,
to demonstrate the ability to honor the worthy;
nurturing strength means
supporting men of physical power,
to show the ability to employ military force.
This is what is called the simultaneous application of civil and martial arts,
ensuring both virtue and strength are complete.
Some matters can be won over by virtue,
others must be crushed by force.
Externally, rely on virtue to stand firm;
internally, use strength for self-defense.
Those who admire virtue will submit without a fight,
while those who violate virtue will fear the military and retreat.
Xú Yǎn Wáng cultivated benevolence and righteousness,
and thirty-two states came to pay homage on land,
but when the powerful Chǔ heard of it,
they raised an army and destroyed him.
This is a case of having virtuous conduct
but no preparation of strength.
Virtue alone cannot be relied upon to govern a state,
nor can strength alone be used to fend off enemies.
Hán Zǐ's method neglects nurturing virtue,
while Xú Yǎn Wáng's conduct lacked reliance on strength—
both are one-sided and flawed,
each with its shortcomings.
Xú Yǎn Wáng suffered the disaster of lacking strength,
so we know Hán Zǐ must face the peril of lacking virtue.
All people are endowed with nature,
pure or turbid, greedy or廉洁,
each with their own conduct,
just as plants and trees differ in essence,
and cannot be changed again.
Kuáng Jué and
Huà Shì did not serve in Qí,
just as Duàn Gān Mù did not serve in Wèi.
Their nature and actions were pure and honest,
not coveting wealth or rank,
disdaining the times and detesting the world,
righteously refusing to serve carelessly.
Even if such people are not executed,
their behavior cannot be followed by others.
Tài Gōng executed them,
and Hán Zǐ approved of it—
this implies that people have no inherent nature or conduct,
like plants and trees without substance.
Tài Gōng killed these two men,
but if there were others like them in Qí,
they would not necessarily purify themselves
just because these two were executed;
if there were no others like them,
even if nurtured,
they would never be transformed.
Yáo did not execute Xǔ Yóu,
yet the people of Táng did not all nest in trees;
King Wǔ did not execute Bó Yí,
yet the people of Zhōu did not all starve in seclusion;
Marquis Wén of Wèi honored Duàn Gān Mù's neighborhood,
yet not everyone in Wèi shut their doors.
From this, it follows that
had Tài Gōng not executed the two men,
not everyone in Qí would have refused to serve.
Why?
Because pure and honest conduct
is something not everyone can achieve.
What people cannot do,
even if nurtured to do it,
cannot make them diligent;
what people can do,
even punished to prohibit it,
cannot make them stop.
Thus, Tài Gōng executing the two men
did not benefit transformation,
but only killed innocent people.
Rewarding the unmerited
and killing the innocent
are what Hán Zǐ disapproves of.
Tài Gōng killed the innocent,
yet Hán Zǐ approved of it—
this means Hán Zǐ's method involves killing the innocent.
As for those who insist on not taking office,
they may not necessarily have committed any proper crime,
yet Tàigōng executed them.
If someone takes office but has not achieved merit,
would Tàigōng be willing to reward them?
Rewards must be bestowed based on merit,
and punishments administered only when there is a crime.
If Tàigōng did not reward those who took office without merit,
then his execution of commoners who did not take office without any crime
is wrong,
yet Hánzǐ approves of it—
this is a mistaken statement.
Moreover, those among the people who do not take office
have a nature of integrity and few desires;
those who are fond of taking office
have a nature of greed and many profits.
If profit and desire do not reside in the heart,
then they regard ranks and emoluments as dung and soil.
With integrity, they are frugal and limitless in restraint;
with greed, they are extravagant and never cease.
If extravagance does not cease,
then what they desire
will not shy away from opposing their ruler.
Examining the ancient ministers who usurped and rebelled,
few were pure and honest, incorruptible individuals.
Being greedy, they were thus able to achieve merit;
being arrogant, they were thus able to hold life lightly.
They accumulated merit to seek great rewards,
and were extravagant to covet the ruler's position.
Tàigōng left behind this method and departed,
hence Qí had the disaster of the Chén clan's seizure and murder.
Tàigōng's technique
is a method that leads to seizure and murder.
Hánzǐ praises it,
meaning Hánzǐ's technique is also one of peril and ruin.
When Zhōugōng heard that Tàigōng had executed two men,
he disapproved and did not affirm it,
instead personally holding gifts to visit scholars in humble cottages.
The scholars in humble cottages
are of the same kind as those two men.
Zhōugōng treated them with courtesy,
while Tàigōng executed them—
which of the two's conduct
is the correct one?
There was a man of Sòng who drove horses;
if a horse did not advance,
he would draw his sword, cut its throat, and abandon it in a ditch.
He harnessed another horse,
and again the horse did not advance,
so he again cut its throat and abandoned it in a ditch.
This happened three times.
Using this to intimidate the horses
was extreme,
but it was not the method of Wáng Liáng.
When Wáng Liáng mounted the carriage,
the horses were never worn out or inferior;
when Yáo and Shùn governed the world,
the people were not reckless or rebellious.
Wáng Liáng tamed the hearts of the horses,
and Yáo and Shùn followed the will of the people.
Humans share the same nature,
while horses are of a different kind.
Wáng Liáng could harmonize horses of a different kind,
yet Tàigōng could not lead scholars of the same nature.
Thus, Zhōugōng's humbling himself before the humble cottages
is like Wáng Liáng's taming of horses;
Tàigōng's execution of the two men
is like the man of Sòng's cutting the horses' throats.
If we present Wáng Liáng's method and the man of Sòng's conduct
for Hánzǐ to judge,
Hánzǐ would certainly affirm Wáng Liáng and reject the man of Sòng.
Wáng Liáng preserved the horses,
while the man of Sòng harmed them.
For a horse to be harmed
is not as good as for it to be preserved;
then likewise,
for the people to die
is not as good as for them to live.
If Hánzǐ were to reject Wáng Liáng,
aligning himself with the man of Sòng,
he would be harming good people.
If he rejects the man of Sòng,
yet the man of Sòng's technique is the same as Tàigōng's,
then by rejecting the man of Sòng
and affirming Tàigōng,
Hánzǐ's likes and dislikes have no consistency.
Governing a state is like governing one's own person.
In governing one's own person,
if one reduces acts of kindness and virtue
and increases conduct that causes harm,
then one's circle of friends will drift apart and sever ties,
and shame and disgrace will come to oneself.
Extending the governance of one's person to illustrate the governance of a state,
the way to govern a state
should rely on virtue.
Hánzǐ relies on punishment
alone to govern the world—
this is like a person governing themselves
by embracing harm.
How could Hánzǐ not know that relying on virtue is good?
He believed that the world had declined and affairs had changed,
the people's hearts were fickle and shallow,
so he created methods and techniques,
focusing solely on punishment.
But the world is not lacking in virtue,
just as the year never ceases to have spring.
To say that a declining age is difficult to govern with virtue—
can one say that a chaotic year should not have spring?
A ruler governs a state
just as heaven and earth give life to all things.
Heaven and earth do not abandon spring because of a chaotic year,
and a ruler should not discard virtue because of a declining age.
Confucius said:
"These are the people
through whom the Three Dynasties were able to proceed by the straight path."
In the age of King Mù of Zhōu,
it could be said to have been a decline,
yet he governed with punishment,
resulting in chaos and no achievement.
Fǔhóu admonished him,
and King Mù preserved virtue,
enjoying a long reign,
with his merits passed down through the ages.
King Mù's governance
was chaotic at first and well-ordered in the end—
not because his wisdom was dim before
and superb later,
but because earlier he employed the punishments of Chīyóu,
and later he followed the words of Fǔhóu.
In governing people, one cannot forsake kindness;
in governing a state, one cannot discard virtue;
in nurturing things, one cannot remove spring.
How can Hánzǐ wish to rely solely on punishment and execution?
What is to be done?
Duke Mù of Lǔ asked Zǐsī:
"I hear that Páng Dùn's son is unfilial.
Being unfilial,
what is his behavior like?"
Zǐsī replied:
"A gentleman honors the worthy to exalt virtue,
and promotes the good to encourage the people.
As for wrongful conduct,
that is what petty people take note of—
I do not know of it."
After Zǐsī left,
Zǐfú Lìbó had an audience.
The ruler asked about Páng Dùn's son.
Zǐfú Lìbó reported his faults,
all of which the ruler had never heard before.
From then on,
the ruler esteemed Zǐsī and looked down on Zǐfú Lìbó.
When Hánzǐ heard of this,
he criticized Duke Mù,
believing that an enlightened ruler should seek out the wicked and punish them.
Zǐsī did not report the wickedness,
while Lìbó reported the wickedness in his reply—
thus Lìbó should be esteemed,
and Zǐsī should be looked down upon.
Now Duke Mù esteemed Zǐsī
and looked down on Lìbó,
violating the proper order of esteem and disdain,
so Hánzǐ criticized him.
What Hán Zǐ esteemed
were laws and regulations.
When people did good,
the laws rewarded them;
when they did evil, the laws punished them.
Even without hearing about good or evil from outside,
good and evil were regulated.
To punish based solely on hearing about evil
is like rewarding based solely on hearing about good.
Not reporting wrongdoers due to personal considerations
is not in line with Hán Zǐ's methods.
If Hán Zǐ heard of a good deed,
he would surely test it;
only after it proved effective
would he reward it.
Not immediately rewarding upon hearing of good
is because empty words may not be trustworthy.
In this case,
whether one hears of good or not
makes no difference.
If good deeds are not immediately rewarded,
then evil deeds are not immediately punished either.
Upon hearing of good, one must test it;
upon hearing of evil, one must investigate it;
only after testing proves effective should rewards be given,
and only after investigation confirms guilt should punishment be imposed.
Mere hearsay and empty sightings,
without solid verification,
should not lead to rewards or punishments.
Without rewards or punishments,
good and evil remain undetermined.
For undetermined matters,
proper methods are needed to resolve them;
thus, relying solely on what one hears
is incorrect.
When Zǐ Chǎn of Zhèng went out in the morning,
passing by the workshop of Dōng Jiàng,
he heard a woman weeping.
He grasped his servant's hand and listened.
After a while,
he had an official arrest and interrogate her,
and it turned out she had murdered her husband with her own hands.
The next day,
his servant asked:
"How did you know, Master?"
Zǐ Chǎn replied:
"Her voice was fearful.
Generally, when people are with their loved ones,
they worry when they know they are ill,
fear when they are near death,
and grieve after they have died.
Now, she was weeping for her already deceased husband,
but instead of grief, there was fear,
so I knew there was wrongdoing."
Hán Zǐ heard of this and criticized it, saying:
"Was Zǐ Chǎn not being overly meddlesome?
If wrongdoing must await what one's own ears and eyes perceive to be known,
then those caught for wrongdoing in Zhèng State would be few.
Not relying on the officials in charge of the city,
nor examining the evidence through cross-referencing,
failing to clarify standards,
but instead exhausting one's own senses
and straining one's intellect to uncover wrongdoing—
is that not a lack of method?"
Hán Zǐ's criticism of Zǐ Chǎn
is correct;
but his criticism of Mù Gōng
is not.
The woman's lack of grief
is like Páng Dùnshì's son being unfilial.
To criticize Zǐ Chǎn for relying on his senses to detect wrongdoing,
yet alone expect Mù Gōng to determine truth through questioning—
Zǐ Chǎn did not rely on city officials,
but used what he heard to establish facts;
Mù Gōng also did not rely on officials,
but used oral inquiries to ascertain truth.
Hearing with one's ears
and asking with one's mouth
are of the same nature;
both do not rely on officials,
neither involves cross-examination.
Lì Bó's testimony cannot establish facts,
just as the woman's weeping cannot confirm truth.
If it cannot confirm truth,
why have officials arrest and interrogate?
If it cannot establish facts,
why not have officials investigate,
but instead trust solely Lì Bó's words
to condemn unexamined wrongdoing—
how is this justified?
Hán Zǐ said:
"Zǐ Sī did not report faults,
yet Mù Gōng honored him;
Zǐfú Lì Bó reported wrongdoing,
yet Mù Gōng looked down on him.
Human nature favors honor and dislikes disgrace,
so the turmoil of the Jì family escalated unreported,
which is why the ruler of Lǔ was usurped."
Was the ruler of Lǔ usurped
because laws were unclear?
Or because he failed to hear of wrongdoing early?
If laws are clear,
even without hearing of wrongdoing,
wrongdoing has no means to arise;
if laws are unclear,
even daily searches for wrongdoing
are like trying to stop a flood's source
with the palm of one's hand.
A driver without reins
sees the horse about to bolt,
with no means to control it.
If Wáng Liáng holds the reins,
the horse has no desire to bolt,
for driving requires skill.
Now, instead of saying the ruler of Lǔ lacked method,
Hán Zǐ says he did not hear of wrongdoing;
instead of emphasizing the need to clarify laws,
he says the ruler failed to understand his subjects' sentiments.
Hán Zǐ's criticism of Mù Gōng
contradicts the essence of statecraft.
Páng Dùnshì's son was unfilial,
Zǐ Sī did not report it,
yet Mù Gōng honored him.
Hán Zǐ criticized this,
believing that
"an enlightened ruler seeks out the good to reward them,
and seeks out the wicked to punish them."
An unfilial person
is of the lowest folly.
The lowest folly, lacking propriety,
follows base desires,
akin to birds and beasts.
To call this evil
is acceptable;
to call it wrongdoing
is not.
Wrongdoers appear good outwardly but are evil within,
stern in appearance but weak inside,
their actions and demeanor
mimic virtuous conduct,
aiming for advancement,
flattering superiors—
how would they commit unfilial acts,
openly displaying evil,
risking condemnation and rejection?
Páng Dùnshì's son may be called unfilial,
but not a wrongdoer.
Hán Zǐ calling him a wrongdoer
misses the true nature of wrongdoing.
Hán Zǐ said:
"Common cloth and silk,
ordinary people do not fuss over;
but glowing gold worth a hundred yì,
even the robber Zhí would not snatch."
From this perspective,
if laws are clear,
people dare not violate them.
If clear laws are established in the state,
those with thieving intentions
dare not act,
and the undetectable
dare not emerge.
With wicked thoughts hidden in their hearts,
they dare not break the law,
for the law deters them.
Deterred by clear laws,
there is no need to investigate wrongdoing or seek out evil among the people.
If laws are strict,
people will not commit wrongs;
if laws are not strict,
people will often do wrong.
Yet instead of advocating the clear laws and severe punishments of enlightened kings,
Hán Zǐ speaks of seeking out wrongdoing to punish it.
To speak of seeking out wrongdoing
implies laws are not strict enough,
and people might still violate them.
If the world does not focus on clarifying laws,
but instead concentrates on seeking out wrongdoing,
then Hán Zǐ's words
contradict the purpose of law.
When people clear out ditches and canals,
they know they will drown themselves;
those who do not block the ditches but repair boats and oars
understand that water's nature cannot be obstructed,
and its force is bound to drown people.
The nature of ministers and sons to deceive their rulers and fathers
is like water's nature to drown people.
Not teaching the means to prevent deceit,
yet blaming them for not being aware,
is like not preparing tools against water,
and merely wishing to know in advance that water will drown people.
When drowned by water,
one does not blame the water but faults oneself,
for having failed to take precautions.
Thus, if a ruler is coerced by his ministers,
he has lost the law.
Preparing against drowning does not mean blocking the water's source;
preventing coercion does not require investigating ministers' deceit—
this is what Hán Zǐ should have taught himself.
Water's nature overcomes fire,
but if wrapped in a cauldron,
the water boils and cannot overcome it—
this is certain.
The ruler is like fire,
ministers are like water,
laws and measures
are the cauldron.
Fire does not seek out water's deceit;
the ruler should not seek out ministers' crimes either.
Mèngzǐ visited King Huì of Liáng.
The king said:
"Venerable sir!
Not minding the thousand lǐ distance, you have come—
what will you use to benefit my state?"
Mèngzǐ said:
"Benevolence and righteousness alone—
why must you speak of benefit?"
Now benefit has two kinds:
there is the benefit of goods and wealth,
and there is the benefit of safety and auspiciousness.
When King Huì said:
"How to benefit my state?"
how do we know he did not desire the benefit of safety and auspiciousness,
yet Mèngzǐ directly challenged him with the benefit of goods and wealth?
The Yì Jīng says:
"It is beneficial to see the great man."
"It is beneficial to cross the great river."
"Qián:
originating, penetrating, beneficial, and steadfast."
The Shàng Shū says:
"Do the common people also still have benefit?"
These all refer to the benefit of safety and auspiciousness.
Practicing benevolence and righteousness yields the benefit of safety and auspiciousness.
Mèngzǐ should have first questioned King Huì:
"What do you mean by
'benefit my state'?"
If King Huì spoke of the benefit of goods and wealth,
then he could have answered accordingly.
Now, the intent of King Huì's question is unknown—
yet Mèngzǐ directly answered with the benefit of goods and wealth.
If King Huì indeed asked about goods and wealth,
Mèngzǐ had no way to verify it;
if he asked about the benefit of safety and auspiciousness,
and Mèngzǐ answered with the benefit of goods and wealth,
then he missed the ruler's point
and violated the reality of principle.
King of Qí asked Shí Zǐ:
"I wish to grant Mèngzǐ a residence in the central state,
support his disciples with ten thousand zhōng,
so that all the high officials
and the people of the state may have a model to emulate.
Why don't you speak to him for me?"
Shí Zǐ then told Mèngzǐ through Chén Zǐ.
Mèngzǐ said:
"How does Shí Zǐ know it cannot be done?
If I desired wealth,
would I decline a hundred thousand and accept ten thousand—
is that desiring wealth?"
Now, Mèngzǐ declining the hundred thousand
violates the principle of humility and deference.
Wealth and honor
are what people desire;
if not obtained by the right way,
they do not dwell in it.
Thus, regarding ranks and emoluments, the gentleman
sometimes declines them,
sometimes does not.
How can one, on the grounds of not being greedy for wealth and honor oneself,
refuse a gift that ought rightly to be accepted?
Chén Zhēn asked:
"In Qí,
the king offered a hundred yì of double-refined gold, yet you did not accept;
in Sòng,
they gave seventy yì and you accepted;
in Xuē,
they gave fifty yì and you accepted.
If the previous non-acceptance
was right, then the present acceptance
is wrong;
if the present acceptance
is right, then the previous non-acceptance
is wrong.
You, sir,
must be in one of these cases."
Mèngzǐ said:
"Both are right.
When in Sòng,
I was about to travel far,
and travelers must have traveling funds—
they said:
'Presenting traveling funds.'
Why should I not accept?
When in Xuē,
I had a wary heart,
and they said:
'Hearing of your wariness,
we present this for military preparedness!'
Why should I not accept?
As for in Qí,
there was no reason.
Without a reason to give it,
is to bribe me—
how can a gentleman be bought with goods?"
Now, when gold is given,
whether accepted or not,
there are always reasons;
it is not that at the time of acceptance one was greedy,
or at the time of non-acceptance one was not greedy.
Gold has principles of
acceptance and non-acceptance,
and a residence should also have principles of
acceptance and non-acceptance.
Now, not saying
"I have no merit"
or
"having retired from office,
accepting a residence is unreasonable,"
but saying
"I am not greedy for wealth and honor,"
citing the previous decline of a hundred thousand to compare with the later ten thousand—
if he ought to have accepted the large sum of a hundred thousand before,
how could he decline it?
Péng Gèng asked:
"With dozens of carriages following behind,
and hundreds of followers,
eating successively among the feudal lords—
is that not excessive?"
Mèngzǐ said:
"If not according to the Way,
then even a single basket of food cannot be accepted from others;
if according to the Way,
then Shun accepting the world from Yáo
is not considered excessive."
Accepting Yáo's world—
how does that compare with a hundred thousand?
Shun not declining the world
was because it was according to the Way.
Now, not saying
"accepting a hundred thousand was not according to the Way,"
but saying
"I am not greedy for wealth and honor,"
lacks humility and deference—
how can that serve as a warning?
Shěn Tóng privately asked:
"Is Yān permissible to attack?"
Mèngzǐ said:
"Yes.
Zǐ Kuài should not have given Yān to another,
and Zǐ Zhī should not have received Yān from Zǐ Kuài.
Suppose there is a scholar here,
and you like him,
and without informing the king, privately give him rank and emolument.
That scholar,
also without the king's command, privately accepts it from you—
is that permissible?
How is this different from that?"
The people of Qí attacked Yān.
Someone asked:
"Did you encourage Qí to attack Yān,
is that true?"
The reply was:
"No.
Shěn Tóng said:
'May Yān be attacked?'
I responded to him:
'It may!'
Thereupon he attacked it.
If he had said:
'Who may attack it?'
Then I would have responded:
'One who is Heaven's official may attack it.'
Now suppose there is a murderer,
and someone asks:
'May the man be executed?'
Then one would respond:
'He may!'
If he then said:
'Who may execute him?'
Then one would respond:
'The chief judge may execute him.'
Now with Qí attacking Yān,
why would I encourage it?"
Someone asked whether Mèngzǐ encouraged the king to attack Yān,
was this not indeed the case?
Shěn Tóng asked whether Yān could be attacked;
this concealed his private desire to attack it himself.
Knowing that his intention was inclined toward this,
he should have said:
"Although Yān may be attacked,
one must be Heaven's official,
then one may attack it."
Shěn Tóng's intention would then have been cut off,
and there would have been no plan to attack Yān.
Not knowing of this private intention and directly responding to him,
not examining his words,
this is not knowing speech.
Gōngsūn Chǒu asked:
"May I ask what your strong points are?"
Mèngzǐ said:
