"I know speech."
He asked further:
"What is meant by knowing speech?"
The reply was:
"With biased words, I know wherein the mind is beclouded;
with extravagant words, I know wherein the mind is sunk;
with evil words, I know wherein the mind has departed from principle;
with evasive words, I know wherein the mind is at its wit's end.
From the heart growing,
they are harmful to government;
when manifested in government,
they are harmful to practical matters.
Though a sage should again arise,
he would certainly agree with my words."
Mèngzǐ,
is one who knows speech,
and also knows the disasters arising from speech,
and the ultimate harm it can cause.
Seeing that question,
he should have known what the phrasing aimed at,
and knowing its aim,
he should have known the ultimate harm it would cause.
Mèngzǐ once said:
"The people would all be at peace,
and the king would perhaps change!
I daily hope for this."
The king whom Mèngzǐ left,
was he not the same king he had previously refused to attend?
If so,
why did he previously regard him so lightly,
and later so heavily?
If it was not the former king,
why did he not leave before,
but
left later?
If this later king was more unworthy than the former,
and he left,
lingering for three nights,
while for the former, less unworthy,
he did not attend court but lodged at Jǐng Chǒu's house.
Why was Mèngzǐ's conduct
different before and after?
In his dealings with the king,
why was he not consistent from start to finish?
Moreover, when Mèngzǐ was in Lǔ,
Duke Píng of Lǔ wished to see him.
The favorite Zāng Cāng slandered Mèngzǐ,
and stopped Duke Píng.
Yuèzhèngzǐ reported this.
Mèngzǐ said:
"To act,
something causes it;
to stop, something prevents it.
To act or stop,
is not within human power.
That I did not meet with the marquis of Lǔ,
is due to Heaven."
Not meeting earlier in Lǔ,
and later not meeting in Qí,
there is no difference.
Previously he attributed it to Heaven,
now he attributes it to the king.
Mèngzǐ's statements and claims,
after all, how are they fixed?
That he did not succeed in Qí,
that the king did not employ him,
was like Zāng Cāng and his kind slandering him;
this too is
"to stop,
something prevents it."
All are due to Heaven's decree not to meet,
not within human power.
When leaving, why did he not go directly,
but remained for three nights?
If Heaven's decree was that he should not meet with Qí,
and the king did not use his words,
would Heaven within three days
change its decree to make them meet?
In Lǔ he attributed it to Heaven,
cutting off hope without expectation;
in Qí he attributed it to the king,
still having some expectation.
Thus,
the discussion of not meeting
depends entirely on the person.
Some say:
"When first leaving,
he could not yet determine Heaven's decree.
Hoping within three days,
the king might recall him;
Heaven's decree might sometimes lie within three days,
so it was permissible."
Such being the case,
when the king of Qí first made him leave,
was that not Heaven's decree?
If Heaven's decree could change within three days,
if Duke Píng of Lǔ had waited three days,
he might have discarded Zāng Cāng's advice,
and used Yuèzhèngzǐ's words instead,
to go see Mèngzǐ.
Why then did Mèngzǐ attribute it to Heaven
so early?
If within three days,
the duke had seen Mèngzǐ,
what would Mèngzǐ have done with his previous words?
When Mèngzǐ left Qí,
Chōng Yú asked him on the way:
"Master, you seem to have an unhappy countenance.
The other day,
I heard you say:
'The superior man does not murmur against Heaven,
nor grumble against men.'"
Mèngzǐ said:
"That was one time,
this is another.
Every five hundred years a true king should arise,
and in that period there would be those renowned in their generation.
From the Zhōu dynasty onwards,
over seven hundred years have passed.
Judging by the number,
it is overdue;
judging by the timing,
it is possible.
Does Heaven not wish to pacify and govern the world?
If it wishes to pacify and govern the world,
in the present age,
who is there but me?
Why should I be unhappy?"
Mencius stated that
"every five hundred years a true King should arise,"
how can this be seen?
Emperor Kù was a King,
and Yáo also ruled the world;
Yáo passed it to Shùn,
and Shùn ruled the world;
Shùn passed it to Yǔ,
and Yǔ ruled the world.
These four sages ruled the world,
rising one after another.
From Yǔ to Tāng was nearly a thousand years;
from Tāng to the Zhōu dynasty was also the same.
It began with King Wén,
and eventually passed to King Wǔ.
After King Wǔ's death,
King Chéng
and the Duke of Zhōu jointly governed the world.
From the Zhōu dynasty to Mencius's time,
another seven hundred years had passed without a King.
Where is the evidence that
every five hundred years there must be a King,
in which era?
Saying
"every five hundred years there must be a King,"
who said this?
The argument does not examine factual evidence,
but believes in extravagant and baseless words.
When Mencius left Qí,
he had a displeased expression,
which is not the effect of a worthy man like Mencius,
showing no difference from common scholars.
"Five hundred years"
is considered the period Heaven sets for a sage to emerge.
He also said that
"Heaven does not yet wish to bring peace and order to the world,"
meaning that if Heaven wished to bring peace and order to the world,
it should produce a sage King within five hundred years.
According to Mencius's words,
this means Heaven intentionally creates sages.
Then, is five hundred years
the period set by Heaven for producing a sage?
If this is the period,
why doesn't Heaven produce a sage?
Since no sage King was born within that period,
yet Mencius still believed in it,
Mencius did not understand Heaven.
"Since the Zhōu dynasty,
over seven hundred years have passed.
By the count, it has exceeded,
but by the timing, it is acceptable."
What does
"the count has exceeded" mean?
What does
"the timing is acceptable"
mean? The count is the timing,
and the timing is the count.
"The count has exceeded"
means exceeding five hundred years.
From the Zhōu dynasty to now,
over seven hundred years have passed,
surpassing by more than two hundred years.
If a King were born out of time,
then saying
"the timing is acceptable,"
what does that mean?
Saying
"every five hundred years a King must arise,"
and also saying
"in between, there must be those renowned in their age,"
are these
"renowned in their age"
the same as
"Kings,"
or different?
If the same,
why say it twice?
If different,
what kind of people are
"those renowned in their age"?
Are they like Confucius's disciples,
or Mencius's peers,
teaching the younger generation,
enlightening the stubborn and ignorant?
Confucius already existed,
and he himself was also born.
If referring to sage ministers,
they should appear at the same time as sage Kings;
when a sage King emerges,
sage ministers appear.
Saying
"five hundred years"
is enough,
why mention
"in between"?
If not referring to the five-hundred-year mark,
does it mean the interim period?
That would be two or three hundred years,
when sages do not coincide with the five-hundred-year sage King.
If so,
when Mencius said
"in between, there must be those renowned in their age,"
who exactly did he mean?
"Heaven does not yet wish to bring peace and order to the world.
If it did, who else but me?"
Speaking like this,
he did not claim to be the King himself,
but if there were a King,
he would serve as a minister.
To be a minister to a King
is also decreed by Heaven.
If his own fate was not to bring peace and order to the world,
he should have been content in Qí without resentment,
yet he harbored displeasure and a resentful expression,
which was a mistake.
Péng Gèng asked:
"Is it acceptable for scholars to eat without working?"
Mencius said:
"Without exchanging labor and goods,
using surplus to make up for deficits,
then farmers would have excess grain,
and women excess cloth.
If you facilitate exchange,
then carpenters and carriage-makers can all eat from you.
Suppose there is someone here
who is filial at home,
respectful abroad,
upholds the ways of the ancient kings,
and instructs later learners,
yet cannot eat from you.
Why do you honor carpenters and carriage-makers
but slight those who practice benevolence and righteousness?"
Péng Gèng said:
"Carpenters and carriage-makers
work with the intent to earn food.
When gentlemen pursue the Way,
is their intent also to earn food?"
Mencius said:
"Why consider their intent?
If they benefit you,
they deserve to be fed.
Moreover, do you feed based on intent
or on merit?"
Péng Gèng said:
"Based on intent."
Mencius said:
"Suppose someone here
breaks tiles and scribbles on walls,
with the intent to earn food,
would you feed them?"
Péng Gèng said:
"No."
Mencius said:
"Then you do not feed based on intent,
but on merit."
Mencius cited the example of breaking tiles and defacing walls,
intending to challenge Péng Gèng's words.
Knowing that breaking tiles and defacing walls are without merit yet done with intent,
Péng Gèng certainly would not offer food for such acts.
Even so,
citing the example of breaking tiles and defacing walls
is not the way to challenge Péng Gèng.
Why is that?
Among all those who intend to seek food,
those who break tiles and deface walls are not among them.
Not being among them,
then it is difficult to use this to challenge someone.
If a person breaks tiles and defaces walls without reason,
this is either due to madness or playful mischief.
Those who are mad,
do not intend to seek food;
those engaged in playful mischief,
also do not seek food.
Those who seek food
all engage in activities that benefit many people,
selling what they produce in the market,
obtaining payment to bring back,
only then do they get to eat.
Now, breaking tiles and defacing walls
brings no benefit to others,
what intent could there be?
Those who are knowledgeable,
knowing it brings no benefit,
certainly would not do it;
those who are ignorant,
comparable to the mad,
certainly have no such intent.
Breaking tiles and defacing walls
is like children striking clods in the road—
how is it different?
Those striking clods in the road,
do they intend to seek food?
These are merely children,
who have no such intent.
Grown men gambling,
are also similar to defacing walls.
Those who gamble,
do they intend to seek food?
Gamblers
may still seize each other's money and wealth;
if money and wealth are plentiful,
they themselves can also obtain food,
and sometimes may have such intent.
Throwing stones and leaping over distances,
are also similar to defacing walls.
Those who throw stones and leap over distances,
do they have the intent to seek food?
If so, then Mencius's challenge to Péng Gèng
was not entirely accurate.
If Péng Gèng followed Mencius's words,
it could be said
"to refute others with a ready tongue."
Kuāng Zhāngzǐ said:
"Is Chén Zhòngzǐ not truly a man of integrity?
He lived in Wūlíng,
went three days without eating,
until his ears could not hear,
and his eyes could not see.
There was a plum tree by the well,
with more than half the fruit eaten by grubs;
he crawled over,
and was about to eat them.
After three swallows,
then his ears could hear
and his eyes could see."
Mencius said:
"Among the scholars of Qí,
I must consider Zhòngzǐ as a thumb!
Even so,
how can Zhòngzǐ be considered of integrity?
To fulfill Zhòngzǐ's principles,
one would have to be an earthworm to do so.
Now the earthworm
eats the dry soil above,
and drinks from the yellow springs below.
The house Zhòngzǐ lives in,
was it built by a Bó Yí?
Or was it built by a Dào Zhí?
The grain he eats,
was it planted by a Bó Yí?
Or was it planted by a Dào Zhí?
This is unknowable."
[Kuāng Zhāngzǐ] said:
"What harm is there in that?
He himself weaves sandals,
his wife spins hemp,
to exchange for them."
[Mencius] said:
"Zhòngzǐ
belongs to a noble family of Qí;
his elder brother Dài
enjoys an emolument of ten thousand zhōng.
Considering his brother's emolument as unrighteous,
he does not eat from it;
considering his brother's house as unrighteous,
he does not live in it.
Avoiding his brother and leaving his mother,
he resides in Wūlíng.
One day returning,
there was someone who had given his brother a live goose;
he frowned and said:
'What use is this cackling thing for?'
Another day,
his mother killed this goose
and gave it to him to eat.
His brother, coming in from outside,
said:
'This is the meat of that cackling thing.'
He went out and vomited it up.
From his mother, he would not eat,
yet from his wife, he eats;
his brother's house he will not live in,
yet in Wūlíng he resides.
Is this still fulfilling his kind of principle?
As for Zhòngzǐ,
one must be an earthworm to fully realize his principles."
Now Mencius's criticism of Zhòngzǐ
did not grasp Zhòngzǐ's shortcoming.
Zhòngzǐ found the goose strange and vomited it—
was it really because he would not eat from his mother?
Rather, he had previously condemned the goose, saying:
"What use is this cackling thing for?"
Another day,
his mother killed it to feed him,
and his brother said:
"This is the meat of that cackling thing."
Zhòngzǐ, ashamed to contradict his former words,
immediately vomited it out.
Had his brother not told him,
he would not have vomited;
not vomiting,
then he would have eaten from his mother.
To say
"from his mother he would not eat"
misses the point.
If Zhòngzǐ held to not eating from his mother,
when the goose meal arrived,
he should not have eaten it.
Now that he had already eaten it,
and upon learning it was goose,
found it strange and vomited,
thus Zhòngzǐ's vomiting the goose
was due to shame at eating something that did not align with his stated intent,
not because he rejected the kindness of his mother,
nor because he wished to refuse food from her.
It is also said,
"How could Zhòngzǐ be considered incorrupt?
To fulfill Zhòngzǐ's integrity,
one would have to become an earthworm.
Now the earthworm
feeds on dry soil above
and drinks from the yellow springs below."
This implies that the earthworm represents ultimate incorruptibility,
suggesting Zhòngzǐ must be like an earthworm
to be deemed pure.
Now, if the house he inhabits
was built by Bóyí,
and the grain he eats
was grown by Bóyí,
then for Zhòngzǐ to live and eat thus
could be considered incorrupt.
But if he were to eat grain grown by Dào Zhí
or dwell in a house built by Dào Zhí,
it would taint his integrity.
To criticize Zhòngzǐ on this basis
is again mistaken.
The house was inherited,
the grain obtained through exchange of sandals and hemp,
even if it were planted or built by thieves,
he would not be aware.
Now, his brother's lack of righteousness
is evident in his conduct,
which is visible to all,
clearly discussed,
so Zhòngzǐ avoided it by living in Yùlíng,
not residing in his brother's house,
weaving sandals and hemp,
not consuming his brother's provisions.
To expect Zhòngzǐ to stay in Yùlíng,
avoid his brother's house,
and spurn his brother's provisions,
with clear knowledge
and no doubt,
it is evident he would not reside or eat there.
Clearly,
in Yùlíng, the house
does not reveal who built it;
the grain, unknown who planted it,
so how can he be sure when occupying the house?
How can he be sure when eating the grain?
Mèngzǐ's criticism
is overly demanding.
If the place Zhòngzǐ lived
was perhaps built by thieves,
and he dwelled there unknowingly,
to say he fails in integrity,
only an earthworm would suffice.
But in the ground of a thief's house,
there are earthworms too,
feeding on the dry soil of the thief's abode,
drinking from its yellow springs,
how can the earthworm be deemed acceptable?
To fulfill Zhòngzǐ's integrity
and satisfy Mèngzǐ's critique,
one would have to be a fish.
For fish dwell in rivers and seas,
feeding on the soil there,
seas not dug by thieves,
soil not gathered by them.
Thus, Zhòngzǐ has major faults,
but Mèngzǐ's criticism
misses the mark.
Zhòngzǐ left his mother and avoided his brother,
living alone with his wife in Yùlíng,
considering his brother's house unrighteous,
his brother's provisions unrighteous,
hence he did not reside or eat there,
achieving utmost integrity.
Yet, when he returned from Yùlíng to visit his mother,
he should have brought his own food.
When goose delicacies were offered,
they must have come with meals.
The meals his mother prepared
were from his brother's provisions,
clearly, she did not have private grain to feed Zhòngzǐ,
it's evident.
Thus, Zhòngzǐ did consume his brother's provisions.
Bóyí did not eat the grain of Zhōu,
starving to death at the foot of Shǒuyáng Mountain,
how could one bite of Zhōu's grain defile his purity?
Zhòngzǐ's integrity,
though not as high as Bóyí's,
and Mèngzǐ comparing him to an earthworm,
misrepresents the proper measure of his integrity.
Mèngzǐ said:
"Nothing is not ordained by Heaven's mandate,
accept it rightly.
Therefore, those who know fate
do not stand under a precarious wall.
Those who die fulfilling their path
have a proper fate;
those who die in shackles
do not have a proper fate."
Mèngzǐ's words
imply that humans lack a fate of chance encounters.
Following moral conduct leads to a proper fate,
reckless actions lead to an improper fate,
thus fate depends on conduct.
But Confucius did not become king,
Yán Yuān died young,
Zǐxià lost his sight,
Bóniú suffered from leprosy,
were their actions not upright?
Why did they not receive a proper fate?
Bǐ Gān was disemboweled,
Wǔ Zǐxū was boiled,
Zǐlù was minced,
these are extreme punishments,
not just shackles.
If shackles signify an improper fate,
then Bǐ Gān,
Wǔ Zǐxū acted improperly.
Humans are endowed with fate and nature,
some are destined to be crushed, drowned, killed in war, or burned,
even if they cautiously cultivate virtue,
what good does it do?
Dòu Guǎngguó lay with a hundred others under a pile of charcoal,
the charcoal collapsed,
all hundred died,
only Guǎngguó survived,
his fate destined him to become a marquis.
How is a pile of charcoal different from a precarious wall?
If fate dictates not to be crushed,
even if the mountain collapses,
one with Guǎngguó's fate
would still escape.
To act, something may drive it;
to stop, something may hinder it.
If fate dictates being crushed,
one might still be made to stand under the wall.
The son of the host where Kǒng Jiǎ stayed,
destined by fate to be lowly,
even if taken into the palace,
remained a guard.
Not standing under a precarious wall
and Kǒng Jiǎ taking the son into the palace
share the same truth.
Confucian texts say:
"Gònggōng contended with Zhuānxū to be Son of Heaven, and failing,
in anger struck Mount Bùzhōu,
causing the pillar of heaven to break,
and the cords of earth to snap.
Nǚwā smelted five-colored stones to mend the blue sky,
and cut off the legs of a giant turtle to set up the four pillars.
The sky is insufficient in the northwest,
hence the sun and moon move there;
the earth is insufficient in the southeast,
hence all rivers flow into it."
This is an ancient text,
accepted as truth in the world.
Refined scholars,
find it strange but cannot refute it,
or if they doubt, cannot disprove it,
fearing it might be true,
dare not dispute it directly.
Judging by the way of heaven and human affairs,
it is likely a false tale.
Contending with another to be Son of Heaven, and failing,
in anger struck Mount Bùzhōu,
causing the pillar of heaven to break,
the cords of earth to snap,
with such strength,
he would be invincible under heaven.
With such power,
fighting against three armies,
the soldiers would be like ants,
weapons like fine hairs,
how could he bear the regret of defeat,
and angrily strike Mount Bùzhōu?
Moreover, nothing is as solid and heavy as a mountain;
with the strength of ten thousand men,
pushing together a small hill,
it cannot be moved.
As for Mount Bùzhōu,
it is a great mountain.
If it were the pillar of heaven?
Breaking it would be difficult indeed;
if it were not the pillar of heaven?
Striking Mount Bùzhōu to break the pillar of heaven
is also hard to believe.
If Zhuānxū contended with him,
mobilizing all under heaven's troops,
gathering everyone within the seas,
they could not withstand him,
how could he not have won?
Now, regarding heaven—
is it composed of qi,
or is it a solid body?
If it were like qi,
no different from clouds and smoke,
how could it have pillars that break?
Nǚwā patched it with stones,
indicating it is a solid body.
If this is indeed the case,
then heaven must be of the same category as jade and stone.
But stone is heavy in substance,
and if a pillar stood every thousand miles,
it could not bear the weight.
If the peaks of the Five Sacred Mountains
do not reach heaven to serve as pillars,
then how could Mount Bùzhōu,
touch the heavens?
Mount Bùzhōu was broken by Gònggōng,
and at that time,
heaven was damaged.
If it was truly damaged,
what was used to support it?
"She cut off the legs of the giant turtle
to set up the four pillars."
Commentators say:
"The turtle
was a giant beast of antiquity,
with four long and large legs,
so its legs were cut off to establish the four pillars."
Now, Mount Bùzhōu
is a mountain,
while the turtle
is an animal.
If heaven originally used mountains as pillars,
and Gònggōng broke them,
replacing them with animal legs,
bones decay over time,
how could they stand for long?
Moreover, if the turtle's legs could pillar heaven,
its body must have been enormous,
too large to be contained between heaven and earth.
Even if Nǚwā was a sage,
how could she kill it?
If she could kill it,
what means did she use?
If its legs could pillar heaven,
then its hide would be like iron or stone,
impervious to swords, spears, and halberds,
and even strong crossbows and sharp arrows could not pierce it.
Observing that heaven is now very high above the earth,
the heavens of antiquity were no different from today's.
When Gònggōng damaged heaven,
heaven did not fall to the earth.
Nǚwā
was a human,
and though humans may be tall,
none can reach heaven.
When she patched heaven,
how did she climb and perch to repair it?
Could it be that in ancient times, heaven was like the shape of a house's roof,
not far from people,
so Gònggōng could damage it,
and Nǚwā could patch it?
If this were truly the case,
before Nǚwā's time,
among humans,
the Human Sovereign was the earliest.
During the Human Sovereign's era,
was heaven like a canopy?
Commentators on the "Yì" say:
"Before the primordial qi divided,
all was a chaotic unity."
Confucian texts also state:
"Vast and misty, indistinct and boundless,
it was the state before the qi separated.
When it separated,
the clear became heaven,
the turbid became earth."
According to these commentators and Confucian texts,
when heaven and earth first separated,
their forms were still small,
and they were close to each other.
Being close, heaven may have rested on Mount Bùzhōu,
allowing Gònggōng to break it,
and Nǚwā to patch it.
All things containing qi
grow without exception.
Heaven and earth,
being natural entities containing qi,
since their establishment,
have passed many years,
so the distance between heaven and earth,
in breadth and narrowness, far and near,
can no longer be calculated.
The words of the Confucian texts
may have some basis.
But their accounts of striking Mount Bùzhōu and breaking the pillar of heaven,
severing the cords of the earth,
smelting five-colored stones to patch the azure sky,
and cutting off the turtle's legs to set up the four pillars,
are still fanciful.
Why?
Even if the mountain shook,
Gònggōng's strength could not break it.
Could it be that when heaven and earth first separated,
the mountains were small and humans large?
How could they strike and break it?
Using five-colored stones to patch heaven
might be compared to using medicinal stones to cure illness.
But as for cutting off the turtle's legs to set up the four pillars,
it is hard to justify.
It has been a long time since Nǚwā's era,
yet the four pillars stand firm as ever—
are they really the turtle's legs?
Zōu Yǎn's writings claim:
"The world has nine continents,
and what the 'Yǔ Gòng' describes is one of these nine."
The nine provinces in the "Yǔ Gòng"
are but one continent.
Beyond the "Yǔ Gòng," there are nine such.
The nine provinces of the "Yǔ Gòng"
are the nine provinces of the present world,
located in the southeast corner,
named Chìxiàn Shénzhōu.
Beyond this, there are eight other continents,
each surrounded by a sea,
called the Bì Sea.
Outside these nine continents,
lies the Yíng Sea.
These claims are bizarre,
startling to hear,
yet none can verify their truth,
so people follow along, reading and discussing them.
Thus, both true and false accounts
are passed down through the ages,
without distinction between genuine and fabricated.
People are confused by this,
making it difficult to judge.
Consider that Zōu Yǎn's knowledge did not surpass Yǔ's.
When Yǔ controlled the floods,
he had Yì as his assistant.
Yǔ took charge of water management,
while Yì recorded things.
They spanned the breadth of heaven,
traversed the length of earth,
identified lands beyond the four seas,
reached beyond the four mountains,
documenting thirty-five regions,
including birds, beasts, plants, trees, metals, stones, water, and soil,
all meticulously recorded,
with no mention of additional continents.
Huáinán King Liú Ān summoned scholars like Wǔ Bèi and Zuǒ Wú,
filling his palace,
to compose texts on arts and methods,
discussing matters of the world.
In the "Topography" chapter,
he described exotic creatures,
foreign curiosities,
listing the wonders of thirty-five countries,
yet did not mention additional continents.
Zōu Yǎn's travels did not match Yǔ's or Yì's,
his knowledge no greater than Bèi's or Wú's,
his talent not that of a sage,
his information not divinely granted—
how could he make such claims?
Examining Yǔ's "Shān Hǎi Jīng"
and Huáinán's "Topography,"
compared to Zōu Yǎn's writings,
they are false and baseless.
Grand Historian Sīmǎ Qiān said:
"The 'Yǔ Běn Jì' states:
'The Kūnlún mountains are over 2,500 lǐ high,
where the sun and moon take turns hiding and shining.
On them are the Jade Spring and Magnificent Pool.'
But since Zhāng Qiān's mission to Dàxià,
and the exploration of the Yellow River's source,
where is the Kūnlún described in the 'Běn Jì'?
Thus, for the nine provinces' mountains and rivers,
the 'Shàng Shū' is more reliable.
As for the monsters in the 'Yǔ Běn Jì' and 'Shān Hǎi Jīng',
I dare not speak of them."
His reluctance to speak
implies they are unreal.
The height of Kūnlún,
the Jade Spring and Magnificent Pool,
are widely known,
yet Zhāng Qiān personally traveled and found no evidence.
Consulting the "Yǔ Gòng,"
it details the nine provinces' mountains, rivers, strange wonders, and precious metals and jades,
all thoroughly recorded,
but says nothing of Jade Spring or Magnificent Pool on Kūnlún.
Based on Sīmǎ Qiān's words,
the "Shān Hǎi Jīng"
and "Yǔ Běn Jì"
are false and baseless.
All matters are difficult to know,
right and wrong are hard to discern.
The celestial pole is at the center of heaven,
yet the present world lies south of Yǔ's domain,
so north of the celestial pole must still have many people.
The "Tribute of Yǔ" states:
"To the east, it reaches the sea,
to the west, it extends to the flowing sands."
This does not represent the ultimate boundaries of heaven and earth.
The sun's apparent diameter spans a thousand lǐ,
yet now, from the eastern sea's shore,
at Kuàijī, Yín, and Mào,
observing the sun at its first emergence measures only two chǐ in diameter—
evidence that it is still far away.
If it is far, then the eastern lands must still be extensive.
If the eastern lands are still extensive,
then north of the celestial pole,
heaven and earth are broad and long,
beyond measure.
If this is so,
then Zōu Yǎn's words cannot be faulted,
while the "Records of Yǔ," "Classic of Mountains,"
and "Huáinánzǐ's Topography" cannot be trusted.
Zōu Yǎn said:
"The present world lies in the southeast of the earth,
named Chìxiàn Shénzhōu."
The celestial pole is the center of heaven;
if the present world were in the southeast of the earth,
viewing the pole should place it in the northwest.
Yet now it is directly to the north,
indicating the present world is south of the pole.
Speaking in terms of the pole,
it is not in the southeast;
thus, Zōu Yǎn's words are incorrect.
If it were in the southeast,
close to where the sun rises,
when the sun emerges,
its light should be great.
But now, observing the sun from the eastern sea,
and viewing it from the land of flowing sands,
its size is the same.
Though separated by ten thousand lǐ,
its size does not change—
proof that the present world
occupies but a small part of the earth's breadth.
Luòyáng
is the center of the nine provinces.
Looking north from Luòyáng,
the pole is directly to the north.
From the eastern sea,
three thousand lǐ from Luòyáng,
the pole is also seen to the north.
Extending this reasoning,
from the land of flowing sands
viewing the pole, it must also be to the north.
The eastern sea and flowing sands
mark the eastern and western bounds of the nine provinces;
though ten thousand lǐ apart,
the pole is still seen to the north—
this shows the land is small and narrow,
unable to extend beyond the pole.
In the Rìnán commandery,
nearly ten thousand lǐ from Luòyáng,
returning migrants
report that
at midday,
their location
is not yet directly under the sun.
Estimating another ten thousand lǐ south,
the sun would be to the north of them.
Thus, twenty thousand lǐ from Luòyáng would be truly "south of the sun."
Now, judging the sun's distance from Luòyáng,
it is not the same as the pole's,
for the pole is farther.
If one traveled north thirty thousand lǐ,
they would not reach directly under the pole.
If they did arrive,
that would be called the base of the pole.
Extending to fifty thousand lǐ south of the sun,
it would also be fifty thousand lǐ north of the pole.
With fifty thousand lǐ north of the pole,
it would be fifty thousand lǐ east and west as well.
Thus, east-west spans one hundred thousand lǐ,
north-south one hundred thousand lǐ,
totaling one million square lǐ.
Zōu Yǎn claimed:
"Between heaven and earth,
there are nine realms like this world."
According to the Zhōu dynasty's nine provinces,
five thousand lǐ east-west,
and five thousand lǐ north-south,
five times five is twenty-five,
so one province is twenty-five thousand square lǐ.
If the world is nine times this,
multiplying by twenty-five thousand lǐ
yields two hundred twenty-five thousand lǐ.
Yet per Zōu Yǎn's writings,
if this is considered vast,
measured and verified,
it turns out to be small instead.
Confucian scholars say:
"Heaven
is qì,
so it is not far from humans.
When people have right or wrong,
and secretly commit virtuous or harmful acts,
heaven knows of it,
and responds accordingly—
proof of its proximity to humans."
In truth,
heaven is a substance,
not qì.
Humans are born under heaven;
why suspect heaven lacks qì?
Yet it is a substance above,
distant from humans.
Secret texts say: Heaven is over sixty thousand lǐ from the earth.
Astronomers calculate
three hundred sixty-five degrees in a celestial circuit.
Below, there are degrees of circumference;
above, measurements in lǐ.
If heaven were truly qì,
qì like clouds and smoke,
how could it have lǐ and degrees?
Also, using the twenty-eight constellations as evidence—
they are lodgings for the sun and moon,
just as the earth has post stations for officials' offices.
Post stations are fixed on earth,
as star lodgings are fixed in heaven.
Examining transmitted texts,
heaven has form,
their basis is not empty.
Considering this,
there is no ambiguity; it is clear.
Confucian scholars say:
"The sun appears at dawn,
emerging from yīn;
it vanishes at dusk,
entering yīn.
Yīn qì is dark and obscure,
so it disappears from sight."
In truth,
it does not emerge from or enter yīn.
How to prove this?
Night
is yīn,
and qì is also dark.
Yet if one lights a fire at night,
its light is not extinguished.
The yīn of night
is like the yīn of the north;
the sun at dawn
is like a lit fire.
If a fire lit at night
does not lose its light,
why does the sun at dusk vanish,
becoming unseen?
This disproves the qì theory.
Observe the sun's path in winter:
it emerges southeast at dawn,
and sets southwest at dusk.
Southeast and southwest are not yīn;
why then say it emerges from and enters yīn?
Moreover, small stars remain visible,
while the large sun vanishes—
the arguments of worldly scholars
are ultimately false.
Confucian scholars say:
"Winter days are short,
summer days long,
also due to yīn and yáng.
In summer, yáng qì is abundant,
yīn qì scarce;
yáng qì is bright,
shining like the sun,
so the sun rises unobstructed.
In winter, yīn qì is dark,
obscuring the sun's light;
though the sun rises,
it remains hidden,
hence winter days are short,
with more yīn and less yáng,
opposite to summer."
In truth,
the length of daylight
does not depend on yīn and yáng.
How can this be verified?
Consider again the stars of the northern direction,
the shadow of the north,
which is the shadow of the winter sun.
The shadow of the north
does not obscure the starlight;
the shadow of the winter sun,
why then does it alone extinguish the sunlight?
From this perspective,
those who explain with yīn and yáng
lose sight of the reality.
In reality,
in summer the sun is in Dōngjǐng,
in winter the sun is in Qiānniú.
Qiānniú is far from the celestial pole,
so the sun's path is short;
Dōngjǐng is near the pole,
so the sun's path is long.
In summer it reaches Dōngjǐng to the north,
in winter it reaches Qiānniú to the south,
thus at the solstices of winter and summer,
both are called 'arrivals';
in spring and autumn it has not yet arrived,
so they are called 'equinoxes'.
Some say:
"In summer the yáng energy is abundant,
yáng energy resides in the south,
so heaven is lifted high;
in winter the yáng energy declines,
heaven is pressed down low.
High, the sun's path is more,
so the days are long;
low, the sun's path is less,
so the days are short."
If yáng energy is abundant,
heaven lifts the south and the sun's path is long,
then the moon should also be long.
Yet in summer when days are long,
the sun rises in the northeast,
while the moon rises in the southeast;
in winter when days are short,
the sun rises in the southeast,
the moon rises in the northeast.
If in summer heaven lifts the south,
both sun and moon should rise in the northeast,
and in winter when heaven is pressed down,
both should rise in the southeast.
From this perspective,
in summer heaven does not lift the south,
in winter heaven is not pressed down.
Thus, the length of summer days
is due to the stars appearing in the north;
the shortness of winter days
is due to the stars appearing in the south.
A question arises:
"When in summer, the fifth month, days are long, the sun is in Dōngjǐng,
Dōngjǐng is near the pole,
so the sun's path is long.
Now observe the fifth month:
the sun rises at Yín,
sets at Xū.
The sun's path is long,
far from people,
how then can it be seen rising at Yín and setting at Xū?"
When the sun is in Dōngjǐng,
it is close to people and the pole.
Dōngjǐng is near the pole,
if the pole rotates,
people would often see it.
If Dōngjǐng were beside the pole,
wouldn't night often become day?
The sun travels sixteen parts by day and night,
people often see it,
it does not rise or set.
Some scholars say:
"The sun and moon have nine paths,
hence it is said: 'The sun's travel has near and far,
days and nights have long and short.'"
Again, in the fifth month,
day is eleven parts,
night five parts;
in the sixth month,
day ten parts,
night six parts;
from the sixth to the eleventh month,
each month decreases one part.
This shows the sun travels, the moon follows one part of the path;
annually, the sun travels sixteen paths in heaven,
how can it be only nine paths?
Some say:
"Heaven is high in the south, low in the north.
The sun rises high, so it is visible;
sets low, so it is not seen.
Heaven's position is like a leaning lid,
so the pole is north of people,
this is the evidence.
The pole is at the center of heaven,
now it is north of people,
clearly, it is like a leaning lid."
Since heaven is compared to a leaning lid,
it should resemble the shape of a lid.
The pole star is north above,
like the knob of a lid;
south below,
if there is something like the stem of a lid,
where exactly is it?
A lid leaned on the ground cannot move;
set upright and planted, then it can rotate.
Now heaven rotates,
if its northern edge does not touch the ground,
what would it bump against to move?
From this perspective,
heaven is not like a leaning lid,
and the sun's rising and setting do not follow heaven's height, clearly.
Some say:
"Heaven's northern edge dips into the earth,
the sun follows heaven into the earth,
the earth densely blocks and hides it,
so people do not see it.
Yet heaven and earth
are like husband and wife,
joined as one body.
Heaven is within the earth,
earth combines with heaven,
heaven and earth merge their energies,
thus they can generate things.
The north is yīn,
combined body and merged energy,
so it resides in the north."
Does heaven run within the earth?
Or else, is the northern land low and uneven?
If it truly runs within the earth,
dig one zhàng into the ground,
and you'll see water sources appear;
does heaven run in the earth,
entering and exiting water?
If the north is low and uneven,
then the nine rivers flowing north
could not fill it full.
In reality,
heaven is not within the earth,
nor does the sun follow heaven into hiding,
heaven is level and even, no different from earth.
Yet the sun appears to rise above and set below
because it follows heaven's rotation,
viewing heaven like an overturned bowl,
so the sun seems to move up and down,
as if entering and exiting the earth.
Thus, when the sun appears,
it is near,
when it disappears, it is far,
no longer seen,
so it is called 'setting'.
When it moves into view in the east, near,
it is called 'rising'.
How can this be verified?
Tie a bright pearl to the rib of a carriage canopy,
rotate it and spin it around,
does the bright pearl spin askew?
Human sight does not extend beyond ten lǐ,
where heaven and earth seem to meet;
far away, they do not actually meet.
Now when we see the sun set,
it is not entering,
but far away.
When the sun sets in the west,
the people below would call it midday.
From where the sun sets,
looking east at the present world,
sometimes heaven and earth may seem to meet.
Thus, the current world is in the south,
so the sun rises in the east,
sets in the west.
In northern lands,
the sun rises in the north,
sets in the south.
Each place calls the near direction 'rising',
the far direction 'setting'.
In reality, it does not enter, but is far.
Stand by the shore of a great lake,
look at the edges on all sides joining heaven;
in reality, they do not join,
but from afar, they seem to join.
The sun seems to enter because it is far,
the lake seems to join heaven because it is far,
the principle is the same.
There is land at the lake's edge,
people look but do not see it.
The land is there,
but observed, it seems absent;
the sun is also there,
This is all due to the effect of distance.
Mount Tài's height,
reaches the sky and enters the clouds,
yet from a hundred lǐ away,
it appears no larger than a clod of earth.
If from a hundred lǐ away
one cannot see Mount Tài clearly,
how much more so for the sun, which is thousands of lǐ distant from humans?
The evidence from Mount Tài
is thus already clear.
Try having someone carry a large torch and walk at night on a road,
level and without obstacles,
less than a lǐ away from a person,
and the torchlight will seem to vanish.
It is not extinguished,
but appears so due to distance.
That the sun turns westward and is no longer seen
is not because it has entered somewhere.
A question asks:
"The sky is level and even, no different from the earth.
Yet now, looking up at the sky,
observing the movement of the sun and moon,
the sky seems high in the south
and low in the north.
Why is that?"
The answer:
Currently, the land under heaven lies to the southeast,
making the sky appear high.
The paths of the sun and moon are to the south of people,
and now the land under heaven is below these paths,
so when observing the movement of the sun and moon,
it seems as if the south is high and the north low.
How to verify this?
If the sky is high in the south, then the stars in the south
should also be high.
But now, looking at the southern stars, they appear low,
so how can the sky be low in the south?
When observing the sky's position, what is near seems high,
and what is far seems low.
The people at the extreme north think it is high,
and the south low.
At the extreme east and extreme west,
it is also like this.
Everywhere, what is near seems high,
and what is far seems low.
From the northern frontier, looking up close at the Dipper and Polaris,
they appear above people.
North of the Xiōngnú,
at the border of the earth,
looking northward at the sky,
the sky again seems high in the north and low in the south,
and the paths of the sun and moon
are also above there.
Standing on Mount Tài,
Mount Tài is high;
but ten lǐ away from its base,
Mount Tài appears low.
The height and lowness of the sky
are like how one perceives Mount Tài.
Level and even,
the height is the same in all four directions and the center.
That the four edges of the sky now seem low
is not actually so,
but an effect of distance.
Not only do they seem low,
but as if merging together.
Some Confucian scholars think the sun is near at dawn and dusk when rising and setting,
and far at noon;
others think it is near at noon,
and far when rising and setting.
Those who say it is near at sunrise and sunset,
and far at noon,
base it on seeing the sun large at rise and set,
and small at noon.
Observing objects, near ones appear large,
far ones small,
hence they say it is near at rise and set,
and far at noon.
Those who say it is far at rise and set,
and near at noon,
base it on feeling warmth at noon,
and cold at rise and set.
Since fire feels warm when near people,
and cold when far,
they thus say it is near at noon,
and far at rise and set.
Both views have their observations,
so right and wrong are not yet determined.
In truth,
the sun is near at noon and far at rise and set.
How to verify this?
By erecting a pole under a roof.
If the roof is three zhàng high,
and the pole is under the roof beam,
set upright,
its top touching the beam,
its bottom on the ground,
then the beam is three zhàng from the ground.
If the pole is tilted sideways,
its top will slant away,
not touching the beam,
making it more than three zhàng from the ground.
At noon,
the sun is directly overhead,
like the pole set upright
three zhàng from the ground.
At sunrise and sunset,
it slants beside people,
like the pole tilted sideways
more than three zhàng from the ground.
Thus,
it is clear that the sun is near at noon
and far at rise and set.
This can be known,
evident.
Try also sitting one person in the hall of a house,
with another walking on the roof.
When the walker is in the middle of the roof,
directly above the seated person,
the person on the roof
and the seated person below
are three zhàng apart.
If the person on the roof is at the east or west eaves,
the distance from the seated person below
is more than three zhàng.
Noon is like the person being directly on the roof;
sunrise and sunset
are like the person at the east or west eaves.
At noon, the sun is near, hence warm;
at rise and set, far, hence cold.
Yet at noon, the sun appears small,
and at rise and set, large.
This is because at noon, the light is bright, so it appears small;
at rise and set, the light is dim, so it appears large.
Just as observing fire by day, the light seems small;
observing it at night, the fire seems large.
Using fire as evidence,
and stars for verification:
stars are not seen by day
because the sunlight obscures them;
at night, with no sunlight,
stars become visible.
The sun and moon
are of the same category as stars.
At dawn and dusk, their light fades,
so they appear large.
Confucian scholars argue:
"The sun rises from Fúsāng at dawn,
and sets at Xìliǔ in the evening.
Fúsāng
is an eastern land,
Xìliǔ
a western wilderness.
Fúsāng and Xìliǔ
mark the boundaries of heaven and earth,
the usual places where the sun and moon rise and set."
A question asks:
In the second and eighth months,
the sun rises due east,
and sets due west,
so one could say it rises from Fúsāng
and sets at Xìliǔ.
But in summer, when days are long,
the sun rises in the northeast,
and sets in the northwest;
in winter, when days are short,
it rises in the southeast,
and sets in the southwest.
In winter and summer,
the sun rises and sets at the corners;
then where exactly are Fúsāng and Xìliǔ?
The argument made
only refers to spring and autumn,
not winter and summer.
In truth,
the sun does not rise from Fúsāng
or set at Xìliǔ.
How to verify this?
It follows the sky's rotation;
near, it is seen;
far, it is not.
When it is at Fúsāng or Xìliǔ,
for the people of Fúsāng or Xìliǔ,
it is noon.
At that time,
observing from Fúsāng or Xìliǔ,
it might be sunrise or sunset for them.
Everyone considers what is above them as center,
and the sides as dawn or dusk;
how can it be said to rise from Fúsāng and set at Xìliǔ?
Confucian scholars argue:
"The sky rotates leftward, but the movement of the sun and moon
is not tied to the sky;
they each rotate on their own."
An objection was raised:
If the sun and moon move on their own,
not tethered to the heavens,
with the sun moving one degree
and the moon thirteen degrees,
then when the sun and moon appear,
they should advance eastward;
why do they instead turn westward?
They are tethered to the heavens,
following the heavens as they revolve through the four seasons.
The analogy is like ants crawling on a millstone:
the sun and moon move slowly, while the heavens move swiftly;
the heavens carry the sun and moon in their revolution,
so although the sun and moon actually move eastward,
they appear to spin westward.
Someone asked:
"The sun, moon, and heavens all move,
but their speeds differ.
How can the slowness or swiftness of these three
be verified by human or natural phenomena,
and what analogy can be used?"
The reply:
The heavens
complete one revolution.
The sun moves one degree, covering two thousand lǐ,
traveling one thousand lǐ by day
and one thousand lǐ by night.
A fine steed
also travels one thousand lǐ in a day.
Thus, the sun's speed,
resembles that of a steed's pace.
The moon moves thirteen degrees,
ten degrees being twenty thousand lǐ,
three degrees six thousand lǐ,
so the moon travels twenty-six thousand lǐ in a day and night,
similar to the flight of a morning wild duck.
The heavens move through three hundred sixty-five degrees,
totaling seven hundred thirty thousand lǐ.
Their motion is extremely swift,
with no direct means of verification;
perhaps it is comparable to the rotation of a potter's wheel
or the flight of an arrow from a crossbow?
The heavens move swiftly,
but being high and distant from people,
they appear slow.
When observing distant objects,
movement seems like non-movement,
motion seems like stillness.
How can this be verified?
Aboard a ship on a river or sea,
driven by a favorable wind,
near the shore it seems fast,
far from the shore it seems slow.
The ship's speed is constant,
yet it appears fast or slow
due to the perspective of distance.
Looking up at the motion of the heavens,
it does not seem as fast as a steed galloping with the sun,
yet by dusk, the sun remains ahead.
Why?
The steed is near, while the sun is far.
Distance makes it seem slow,
closeness makes it seem fast;
over a distance of sixty thousand lǐ,
it is hard to grasp the reality of motion.
Confucian scholars claim:
"The sun moves one degree,
while the heavens move three hundred sixty-five degrees in a day and night.
The heavens move left,
the sun and moon move right,
meeting the heavens."
The question:
The motion of the sun and moon
is tied to the heavens.
The sun and moon attach to the heavens to move,
not moving independently.
How can this be argued?
The Yì Jīng says:
"The sun, moon, and stars adhere to the heavens,
fruits and plants adhere to the earth."
To adhere
means to attach;
attached to the heavens, they move,
like humans attached to the earth moving in circles,
the analogy being ants crawling on a millstone.
The question:
"How do we know they do not separate from the heavens to move independently?"
If the sun could move on its own,
it should travel eastward;
why would it follow the heavens westward?
The moon's motion is the same as the sun's,
both attached to the heavens.
How can this be verified?
Verified by clouds.
Clouds do not attach to the heavens;
they often stay in place.
If the sun were not attached to the heavens,
it should also remain stationary.
Thus,
it is clear the sun moves attached to the heavens.
The question:
"The sun
is fire.
Fire on earth does not move;
why does the sun in the sky
move?"
The reply:
Qi attached to the heavens moves,
qi attached to the earth does not.
Fire attaches to the earth,
and the earth does not move,
so fire does not move.
Objection:
"If qi attached to the earth does not move,
how does water move?"
Reply:
Water moves
by flowing east to the sea.
The northwest is high,
the southeast low;
water's nature is to seek the low,
just as fire's nature is to rise.
If the earth were not high in the west,
water would not flow east.
Objection:
"If qi attached to the earth does not move,
why do humans, attached to the earth, move?"
Reply:
Human movement
seeks purposeful action.
Human principles involve action,
so they move in pursuit.
In ancient times, people were simple;
neighboring states shared borders,
the sounds of chickens and dogs were heard,
yet they never interacted in their lifetimes.
Objection:
"If qi attached to the heavens moves,
why do the stars not move?"
Reply:
The stars are fixed in the heavens,
and the heavens already move;
following the heavens in revolution,
they too are moving.
Objection:
"Human principles involve action, hence movement;
why do the heavenly principles, without purpose, move?"
Reply:
The movement of the heavens
is the natural emission of qì;
emitting qì, things generate spontaneously,
not intentionally emitting qì to produce things.
Without movement,
qì is not emitted;
without qì emission,
things do not generate,
differing from human movement.
The movements of the sun, moon, and five planets
all involve emitting qì.
Confucian scholars say:
"There is a three-legged crow in the sun,
and a hare and toad in the moon."
Now, the sun
is the fire of the heavens,
no different from fire on earth.
Earthly fire contains no living creatures;
why would heavenly fire have a crow?
Fire has no living beings;
if a living being entered fire,
it would burn and die;
how could a crow stand there?
The moon
is water.
Water contains living creatures,
but not a hare or toad.
A hare or toad长时间 in water
would inevitably die.
The sun and moon perish in the heavens,
while clams and mussels dwell in the depths;
their shared qì nature is evident.
Are the so-called hare and toad
somehow akin to clams and mussels?
Moreover, ask the scholars:
Are the crow, hare, and toad
dead or alive?
If dead,
long in the sun and moon,
they would be charred and decayed;
if alive,
during a solar eclipse when the sun is obscured,
or at the moon's dark phase when it vanishes,
where do the crow, hare, and toad go?
The crow, the rabbit, and the toad are
the vital energies of the sun and moon,
much like the internal organs of humans,
or the heart and spine of all things.
The moon can still be observed;
when people observe the sun, none fail to be dazzled,
unable to discern exactly what energy it is,
so how can they claim to see a creature called a crow within it?
If one cannot see the form of the crow upon careful examination of the sun,
how can they claim to see it has three legs?
This is already not factual.
Moreover, listening to the Confucian scholars' words,
there are many kinds of creatures,
so why would there be a "crow" in the sun?
Why would there be
a "rabbit" or "toad" in the moon?
The Confucian scholars say
"it is an eclipse of the sun or moon."
They observe that solar eclipses often occur on the last and first days of the lunar month,
when the moon and sun conjoin,
hence they can eclipse each other.
During the Spring and Autumn period,
solar eclipses were frequent.
The classics say:
"On the first day of such-and-such month,
the sun was eclipsed."
When it says the sun was eclipsed,
it does not necessarily mean by the moon.
If they knew the moon caused the eclipse,
why avoid mentioning the moon?
Some explain:
"The phenomenon of solar eclipse
is due to yang being weak and yin strong."
Beings in the world,
when their vital force is vigorous and strong,
can then overcome others.
Consider that the moon's light fades at the end of the month,
and at the new moon it is as if extinguished,
being extremely faint,
how could it overcome the sun?
As for the eclipse of the sun,
and that of the moon.
A solar eclipse is said to be caused by the moon,
but who causes the lunar eclipse?
Nothing eclipses the moon;
it diminishes by itself.
Arguing from the moon to the sun,
we also know that in solar and lunar eclipses,
the light diminishes on its own.
Roughly every forty-one or forty-two months, there is one solar eclipse;
every hundred and eighty days, one lunar eclipse.
Eclipses occur at fixed times,
occurring out of time is an anomaly,
and when such anomalies happen,
it is due to natural energy fluctuations.
If it always happens at the new moon,
does the moon cause it again?
The sun should be full and solid,
and its waning is a change;
if one insists something eclipses it,
then when mountains collapse and the earth shakes,
who is the eclipser?
Some say:
"A solar eclipse is
the moon covering it.
The sun is above,
the moon below,
obscured by the moon's form.
When the sun and moon conjoin and overlap,
if the moon is above and the sun below,
it cannot cover the sun.
When the sun is above,
and the moon below the sun,
obscured by the moon,
the moon blocks the sunlight,
hence it is called an eclipse.
Being obscured by the moon
is like when dark clouds hide the sun or moon from view.
When their edges meet,
that is when an eclipse occurs.
When they align perfectly like overlapping jade discs,
that is a total solar eclipse."
The sun and moon conjoin at the new moon,
which is a regular celestial event.
That a solar eclipse is
the moon blocking sunlight
is incorrect.
How to verify this?
If the sun and moon conjoin,
and the moon blocks sunlight,
the initial point of eclipse should alternate with the point of recovery at dawn.
Suppose the sun is in the east,
the moon in the west,
the moon moves swiftly,
catches up to the sun from the east,
covers the sun's edge,
soon passes the sun and moves east,
the western edge initially covered should recover its light,
while the eastern edge not yet covered should be eclipsed.
But observing a solar eclipse,
the western edge loses light;
upon recovery,
the western edge regains light,
passing from covering the eastern edge back to the western edge—
how can this be called overlapping cover and obstruction?
Confucian scholars say: "The bodies of the sun and moon are perfectly round."
They see their shapes from below,
like the form of a dipper or basket,
appearing perfectly round.
But this is not observing the distant light and energy,
for the energy itself is not round.
The sun and moon are not round;
they look round
because they are far from people.
How to verify this?
The sun is
the essence of fire,
the moon is
the essence of water.
On earth, fire and water are not round;
in heaven, why would fire and water alone be round?
The sun and moon in heaven are like the five planets,
the five planets are like the other stars,
the other stars are not round,
but their shining appears round
because they are far from people.
How to demonstrate this?
During the Spring and Autumn period,
a star fell in the capital of Sòng,
people went to see it,
it was a stone,
not round.
From the star not being round,
we know the sun, moon, and five planets are also not round.
Confucian scholars discussing the sun, and the craftsmen experts,
all regard the sun as one.
Yǔ and Yì's "Shānhǎi Jīng" says:
"There are ten suns.
They are overseas. In the east is Tānggǔ,
above which is Fúsāng,
where ten suns bathe in the water;
there is a great tree,
nine suns reside on the lower branches,
one sun on the upper branch."
The "Huáinán Shū" also says: "It illuminates ten suns.
In Yáo's time, ten suns appeared together,
scorching all things,
so Yáo shot down nine suns."
Hence, they do not appear simultaneously now.
Common custom also names the heavenly stems as days,
from jiǎ to guǐ making ten days;
having ten suns
is like having five planets.
Learned debaters,
finding it hard to know,
refuse to clarify,
hence texts pass down two versions unsettled,
the world has two sayings without a definitive one.
Truly speaking,
there are not ten.
How to verify this?
The sun is like the moon;
if there are ten suns,
are there twelve moons?
There are five planets,
essences of the five phases,
metal, wood, water, fire, and earth, each with different light colors.
If there were ten suns,
their energies must differ.
But observing sunlight shows no differences;
examining their size, they appear the same before and after.
If their energies truly differed,
their light and color should vary;
if they were the same energy,
they should merge into one,
not remain ten.
Testing with a yang-sui mirror,
fire comes from the sky.
The sun is heavenly fire.
Observe fire on earth—
it is one energy;
if there are not ten fires on earth,
how can there be ten suns in heaven?
Thus, the so-called ten suns
probably refer to other things,
with substance and light like the sun,
residing in the waters of Tānggǔ,
sometimes perched on Fúsāng,
which Yǔ and Yì saw,
hence recorded as ten suns.
Various experts measure the sun's light,
count the sun's substance,
estimating its diameter at a thousand lǐ.
If the sun that rises is the one on the Fúsāng tree,
then the Fúsāng tree must cover ten thousand lǐ
to hold it.
Why so?
In one day it travels a thousand lǐ,
in ten days it should travel ten thousand lǐ.
The distance between Heaven and humans
is over sixty thousand lǐ.
Looking up to observe it,
the sunlight dazzles and glares.
The firelight is intensely bright,
making it unbearable.
If the sun that rises were the sun on the Fúsāng tree,
even Yǔ and Yì, upon seeing it,
would not recognize it as the sun.
Why so?
Observing one sun from below,
the eyes are still dazzled,
how much more so observing ten suns?
When Yǔ and Yì saw it,
it resembled the shape of a dipper or basket,
hence they named it "sun."
Now, something as large as a dipper or basket,
viewed from sixty thousand lǐ away,
is not the form
of an object observed up close.
From this perspective,
what Yǔ and Yì saw
likely resembled the sun but was not the sun.
Between Heaven and Earth, objects and energies resemble each other,
but many that appear so are not genuine.
Southwest beyond the seas, there is a pearl tree;
upon inspection, it appears to be pearls,
yet they are not pearls from oysters.
The ten suns are like the pearls of the pearl tree;
the pearl tree resembles pearls but they are not real pearls,
the ten suns resemble the sun but are not true suns.
When Huáinán saw the "Classic of Mountains and Seas,"
he falsely stated that "the true man illuminated ten suns,"
and erroneously recorded that "in Yáo's time, ten suns appeared together."
Moreover, the sun
is fire,
and Yángǔ
is water.
Fire and water harm each other;
thus, if ten suns bathed in Yángǔ,
they should be extinguished and destroyed.
Fire burns wood;
Fúsāng
is wood,
and with ten suns resting upon it,
it should be scorched and withered.
Yet now, bathing in Yángǔ, their light is not extinguished,
and perched on Fúsāng, its branches are neither scorched nor withered,
similar to today's sun rising—
this does not align with the Five Phases,
thus we know the ten suns are not true suns.
Furthermore, when Yǔ and Yì saw the ten suns,
it was certainly not at night.
If it were during the day,
then with one sun out,
the other nine should remain hidden;
how could all ten appear together?
If at dawn the sun has not yet risen,
and Heaven's motion has its measures,
with the sun following Heaven's rotation,
how could it linger among the branches of Fúsāng
or bathe in the waters of Yángǔ?
Lingering would disrupt its course and measure,
causing discrepancies in its path, making it inconsistent.
If the sun that appears differs from the ten suns,
then it resembles the sun but is not the sun.
"The Spring and Autumn Annals": "In the seventh year of Duke Zhuāng,
in the summer, fourth month, on Xīnmǎo,
at midnight, the fixed stars were not seen,
and stars fell like rain."
The "Gōngyáng Commentary" says:
"What does 'like rain' mean?
It was not rain.
If it was not rain, then why call it 'like rain'?
The unrevised 'Spring and Autumn Annals' said:
'Rain stars,
not reaching within a chǐ of the ground before returning.'
The gentleman revised it to say:
'Stars fell like rain.'"
The unrevised "Spring and Autumn Annals"
refers to the "Records of Lǔ" before the revision of "Spring and Autumn Annals,"
which said, "Stars fell like rain,
not reaching within a chǐ of the ground before returning."
The gentleman
was Confucius.
Confucius revised it to say: "Stars fell like rain."
Confucius' intention was that the earth has mountains, mounds, and towers,
and saying "not reaching within a chǐ of the ground"
might lose accuracy;
thus he corrected it to say: "like rain."
"Like rain" means
that as rain falls from the sky to the ground,
stars also fall from Heaven and return,
being similar,
hence the term "like."
Although Confucius did not say "within a chǐ of the ground,"
but only "like rain,"
what he referred to as falling
were all stars.
Though Confucius did not fix their positions,
he recorded the text,
calling the falling objects stars,
aligning with the historian.
Looking from level ground to the summit of Mount Tài,
a crane appears like a crow,
a crow like a sparrow,
because Mount Tài is high and distant,
distorting the true size of objects.
Heaven is over sixty thousand lǐ from Earth,
far higher and more distant than just the peak of Mount Tài.
Stars are attached to Heaven,
and when humans observe them,
they lose the true appearance of the stars,
not merely like viewing cranes or crows.
Estimating the substance of stars to be a hundred lǐ,
their bodies large and light brilliant,
thus they can radiate splendor.
When people see them from afar,
they look like phoenix eggs,
due to distance, losing their true form.
If the falling stars were truly
stars in Heaven, falling to Earth,
people would not recognize them as stars.
Why?
Their size when falling differs from when in Heaven.
Now, if falling stars are seen as they appear in Heaven,
they are not stars;
if not stars,
then it is energy causing this.
When people see ghosts resembling the dead,
they are actually energy manifestations,
not real deceased persons.
Thus, the form of falling stars
is indeed not stars.
Confucius did not explicitly state that the falling objects were not stars,
but only corrected the text to say "like rain" and not rain,
likely missing the true nature of the stars.
"The Spring and Autumn Annals' Zuǒ Commentary":
"On the fourth year, Xīnmǎo,
at midnight, the fixed stars were not seen,
because the night was bright;
stars fell like rain,
together with rain."
It says the night was bright,
hence they were not seen,
similar to the "Yì Jīng's" statement "seeing the Dipper at midday."
Seeing the Dipper at midday
indicates darkness and lack of light;
at midnight, stars not being seen
indicates the night is bright.
Events differ but the principle is the same,
likely reflecting the truth.
Its statement "together with rain"
refers to their gathering.
Now, on the Xīnmǎo night, it was bright,
so stars were not seen;
brightness is evidence of no rain,
as rain brings cloudy darkness—how could it be bright?
If bright, there is no rain,
how could it be "together with rain"?
Thus,
the statement "together with rain" is not factual.
Moreover, saying the night was bright and stars were not seen,
how could one see stars together with rain?
Also, in the sixteenth year of Duke Xī, first month, Wùshēn,
five stones fell in Sòng.
The "Zuǒ Commentary" says:
"They were stars."
Calling falling stones stars
means calling falling stars stones.
On the Xīnmǎo night,
if falling stars were stars,
then they were actually stones.
On the Xīnmǎo night,
if falling stars were such stones,
and the earth had towers,
the towers would collapse.
Although Confucius did not appropriately say "within a chǐ of the ground,"
surely the ground must have a definite measure;
the Lǔ historian witnessed it,
not speaking baselessly.
Saying "together with rain,"
rain gathers on the ground,
stones should do the same.
If they reached the ground without damaging towers,
they were clearly not stars.
Moreover, Zuǒ Qiūmíng called stones stars;
how can this be verified?
At that time, the stones fell lightly.
How could they have fallen from Heaven?
In Qín times, three mountains vanished;
what vanishes does not dissipate,
and when they gathered below, there must have been sounds.
When it sometimes gathers over the mountains of barbarians and descends upon Sòng,
and Sòng hears of stones falling,
they call them stars.
Zuǒ Qiūmíng, upon reflection,
also called them stars.
Now stars,
being the essence of all things,
are akin to the sun and moon.
Those who discuss the five planets
say they are the light of the essence of the five elements.
The five planets and the multitude of stars share the same radiance;
to single out the constellations as stones
is likely to miss the truth.
In reality, on the night of Xīnmǎo,
the falling stars were like rain but were not stars,
just as the ten suns of Tānggǔ,
though sun-like, were not true suns.
Confucian scholars also say:
"Rain falls from the sky."
Meaning it descends directly from heaven.
But to discuss it truthfully,
rain originates from the earth, not from the sky.
Seeing rain gathering from above,
they say it falls from heaven,
yet its source is earthly.
Moreover, it emerges from the earth, starting at mountains.
How can this be proven?
The "Spring and Autumn Annals" states:
"It emerges upon touching the stones,
coalesces within inches,
and before the morning is over, rains all over the land,
but only from Tài Shān."
Tài Shān rains upon the world,
while smaller mountains rain upon a single state,
each according to size and distance as a gradient.
When rain issues from mountains,
some say clouds carry it along,
and when clouds disperse, water falls,
named as rain.
Now, clouds bring rain,
and rain comes from clouds.
Initially emerging as clouds,
they thicken into rain.
When excessive, it muddies and soaks clothes,
resembling the form of rain.
It is not that clouds accompany it;
rather, clouds bear the rain aloft.
Some say:
"The 'Shàng Shū' states:
'When the moon follows the stars,
it brings wind and rain.'
The 'Shī Jīng' says:
'When the moon clings to Bì,
it causes pouring rain.'
Both classics affirm this;
if it's said not to be from heaven, how so?"
Now, rain arises from mountains,
and when the moon passes by or clings to Bì,
that time is due for rain.
If it doesn't rain then,
the moon doesn't cling,
and mountains lack clouds,
it's because heaven and earth, above and below, respond to each other naturally.
The moon clinging above,
and mountains steaming below,
their energies coincidentally combine,
following the natural way.
Clouds and mist
are signs of rain;
in summer, they become dew,
in winter, frost,
in warmth, rain,
in cold, snow.
Rain, dew, and frozen condensates
all emanate from the earth,
not descend from heaven.
Someone asks:
"Virtuous individuals practice the Way,
gaining high office and ample salary; why
must one flatter to attain wealth and honor?"
The reply:
Flatterers know that practicing the Way can bring wealth and honor,
yet they resort to flattery for rank and salary
because they cannot restrain their desires.
Just as one knows that diligent farming yields grain,
and earnest trade brings goods,
but still some steal,
it's due to uncontrollable passions and desires.
Advancing and retreating with ritual,
all people value it,
yet many violate ritual,
few uphold righteousness,
because their hearts crave greed,
and their minds are disordered and addicted.
Flatterers and the virtuous have the same talent,
but flatterers ruin themselves through their passions;
thieves and farmers or merchants share the same knowledge,
yet thieves bring about their own downfall through their desires.
The question:
"If flatterers and the virtuous have the same talent,
their abilities and conduct should be equal,
so why do flatterers alone ruin themselves through passion?"
The answer:
Wealth and honor are what all people desire;
even those with noble conduct
still have feelings of hunger and thirst.
The noble person can use ritual to guard against passions,
and righteousness to cut off desires,
thus they follow the Way,
and following the Way brings no calamity;
petty individuals indulge in greedy desires,
overstep ritual and violate righteousness,
so in advancement, they resort to reckless flattery,
and reckless flattery incurs guilt.
Now, the virtuous
are noble persons,
while flatterers
are petty persons.
Noble and petty persons fundamentally differ in conduct and action,
with distinct choices and rejections.
The question:
"Are flatterers and slanderers of the same path?
Or do they differ?"
The reply:
Slanderers and flatterers
are both petty persons,
sharing the same path but differing in talent,
both possessing a nature of envy,
yet differing in how they act and instigate.
Slanderers harm others with their mouths,
flatterers endanger others through deeds;
slanderers do not deviate from straightforward ways,
while flatterers prevaricate and conceal their tracks;
slanderers lack cunning schemes,
but flatterers employ tactics and calculations.
Therefore, rulers can all distance slanderers and befriend the benevolent,
but none can recognize the virtuous and distinguish flatterers.
An objection:
"Rulers can all distance slanderers and befriend the benevolent,
yet cannot recognize the virtuous and distinguish flatterers;
does that mean flatterers' intentions are unknowable?"
The reply:
Flatterers can be known,
but rulers fail to know them.
Mediocre rulers
cannot recognize the virtuous;
unable to recognize the virtuous,
they cannot identify flatterers.
Only sagely and virtuous individuals,
using the nine virtues to examine conduct,
and testing words against actual outcomes,
can tell: if conduct doesn't match the nine virtues,
and words aren't verified by results,
the person is either not virtuous or a flatterer.
Knowing flatterers helps know the virtuous,
and knowing the virtuous helps know flatterers;
knowing flatterers makes the wise self-aware,
knowing the virtuous exposes the crafty and flattering.
Virtuous and flattering conducts differ;
examine them with one test,
their inner feelings differ,
observe them with one reality.
The question:
"The method of the nine virtues
has long been established,
and those who study it
all seem to understand,
like using a dou or hú to measure volume,
or a scale to weigh lightness and heaviness.
Yet why do rulers who govern states and lands often have treacherous, flattering ministers,
and often face deception and delusion?"
The reply:
The worry isn't lacking a dou or hú,
but measuring the wrong grain;
not lacking a scale,
but weighing the wrong object.
Those in rulership
all know the nine virtues can examine conduct,
and outcomes can reveal true feelings,
yet they are confused and unable to see,
due to a lack of keen observation.
Some cannot act,
but all actions can be examined;
some cannot test,
but all feelings can be known.
The question asks:
"If one's conduct does not align with the nine virtues,
their achievements are not verified through merit evaluation,
and they advance by drawing near to those who are not virtuous—
not being virtuous means they are crafty.
But those of mediocre talent,
lacking profound wisdom, cannot reach the level of the virtuous.
If they fail to demonstrate the merits of the virtuous
or embody their conduct,
can they be called crafty?"
The response:
Talents may not match,
conduct may not follow,
and achievements may not be inherited.
If wisdom cannot be passed down,
and human talents differ by tens or hundreds,
then choices should be uniform.
The virtuous and the crafty have distinct behaviors;
affirming the right and denouncing the wrong,
their true names and realities are both established,
yet the outcomes of their efforts may succeed or fail.
Statements of right and wrong may both be appropriate,
but achievements can be upright or wicked.
If words align but actions contradict,
reputation thrives while conduct decays,
that is a crafty person.
The question asks:
"If conduct aligns with the nine virtues, one is virtuous;
if not, one is crafty.
But among those in the world who uphold conduct, can all be called crafty?"
The response:
All that is not virtuous is evil,
and the most rebellious among evils
is called unprincipled;
the most cunning among evils
is called a crafty person.
When sage kings impose punishments,
craftiness lies within evil;
when sage kings reward and encourage,
virtue lies within goodness.
The purely virtuous,
exceptionally high among the good,
are sages among the virtuous;
the greatly crafty among evils,
are the champions of wickedness.
Thus it is said:
"Observe virtue through goodness,
detect craftiness through evil."
Once good and evil are determined,
virtue and craftiness take form.
The question asks:
"Intelligence can be obscured,
actions can be erroneous.
Now, to deem those in the right as virtuous
and those in the wrong as crafty—
is this not missing the true essence of virtue?"
The response:
Obscured intelligence
and erroneous actions
are human shortcomings.
Hence it is said:
"Punish intent regardless of scale,
pardon mistakes regardless of magnitude."
Sage rulers examine intentions and reflect on motives,
thus punishing deliberate acts while forgiving errors.
Deliberate harm aggravates,
mistaken acts mitigate—
this can be decided by any prison official,
and the virtuous recognize it without doubt.
The question asks:
"If words and actions yield no results,
can one be called crafty?"
The response:
Sū Qín allied the six states in a vertical pact,
so the powerful Qín dared not send troops beyond the pass;
Zhāng Yí formed horizontal alliances,
and the six states dared not jointly attack within the pass.
When the six states united vertically,
Qín feared them and the six states grew strong;
when the three Qín proclaimed horizontal alliances,
Qín strengthened and the world weakened.
Their achievements were prominent and effects clear,
recorded in bamboo and silk texts.
How could even the virtuous surpass this?
Sīmǎ Qiān narrated the tales of many virtuous figures,
including chapters on Yí and Qín,
with no text expressing envy or malice.
Their merits equaled and reputations rivaled,
no different from the virtuous.
That achievements cannot prove virtue
is like names not matching reality.
Yí and Qín
were resolvers of crises,
thriving in tumultuous times,
practicing strategies of assessment and persuasion.
In that era,
even Jì and Xiè could not outmatch their schemes,
nor could Yǔ or Gāo Yáo compare in effectiveness.
As for the harmony of yīn and yáng,
timely winds and rains,
abundant harvests of the five grains,
the decline of banditry,
people practicing honesty and deference,
and households upholding moral deeds—
such fortunes and noble blessings
are brought by methods and calculations,
not achieved through morality alone.
Sīmǎ Qiān recorded achievements,
thus elevating those of high merit,
documenting completed deeds
to highlight clear effects and proofs,
gathering accounts of excellence.
Due to Yí and Qín's admirable accomplishments,
he detailed their actions.
From this perspective,
crafty individuals can also achieve merits through tactical persuasion.
Without such achievements,
one cannot be deemed crafty.
An objection raises:
"Those who achieve merits within evil are called crafty.
Those capable of such deeds
possess high talent and clear wisdom.
Those with far-reaching thoughts
must align with righteousness and benevolence,
rivaling the great virtuous.
Thus, the essay 'Detecting Craftiness' states:
'If the ruler enjoys debate,
the crafty speak of profit;
if the ruler appreciates refinement,
the crafty use elegant rhetoric.'
Hearts and minds in accord,
they coincidentally please the ruler.
If their persuasion shows no faults,
how can one detect their falseness and uncover their treachery?"
The response:
This refers to a mediocre ruler,
of low talent and clouded wisdom,
obscured and deluded, unable to see.
But a sage ruler,
examining with clarity and precision,
can see as if looking at meat on a cutting board,
point to the lines in their palm,
count the pieces on a game board,
or select horses from a carriage shaft.
Fish and turtles hide in deep waters,
yet fishermen know their sources;
beasts conceal themselves in mountains,
yet hunters discern their trails.
Crafty individuals act differently in the world,
yet the world fails to notice—
this is due to mediocre rulers,
lacking people of high capability.
The objection continues:
"If the ruler enjoys debate,
the crafty speak of profit;
if the ruler appreciates refinement,
the crafty use elegant rhetoric.
When their words and conduct match,
how can they be detected?"
The response:
The "Wén Wáng's Method for Evaluating Officials" states:
"Infer their future words from their past actions,
reflect on their past actions from their present words;
observe their outward display to examine their hidden motives,
scrutinize their interior to gauge their exterior.
Thus, those feigning virtue and setting up false integrity can be known,
those adorned with insincerity and devoid of true feeling can be distinguished,
those genuinely sincere and dwelling in goodness can be identified,
and those embodying loyalty and upholding integrity can be perceived."
If people's inherent nature lacks eloquence,
but the ruler enjoys debate,
the crafty learn to迎合 the superior.
If people's original abilities lack refinement,
but the ruler appreciates elegance,
the crafty aim to praise the superior.
If the superior is extravagant,
they wear luxurious clothes;
if the superior is frugal,
they refrain from adornment.
Their current conduct differs from the past,
their court behavior contrasts with their home life.
By examining their traces in the village,
verifying their actions at court,
observing the integrity of their close relationships,
and clarifying their conduct in serving the ruler—
if inner and outer do not align,
name and reality do not match,
then when opportunities arise, their craftiness will be exposed.
The question asked:
"People's conduct is not constant,
adapting to circumstances as needed.
The trustworthy deceive others,
the straightforward bend.
With the application of expedient measures,
their actions differ before and after;
responding to situations,
their words vary left and right.
The Confucian texts record
various instances of expediency.
Now if we examine them by their original principles,
wouldn't that be losing touch with reality?"
The reply:
The worthy employ expediency,
the cunning also employ expediency.
When the worthy employ expediency,
there are subsequent responses;
when cunning people employ expediency,
it also goes against the norm,
with subsequent harm.
Thus the expediency of the worthy
serves affairs and the state;
the expediency of the cunning
serves themselves and their families.
Observing their expedient measures,
worthiness and cunning can be distinguished;
