examining their motivations,
wickedness and righteousness can be identified.
The question asked:
"Do cunning people like to slander others?
Is this true?"
The reply:
Cunning people do not slander others.
If they slandered others,
they would be calumniators.
Why is this?
Cunning people seek profit,
so they do not slander others.
If it benefits themselves,
why would they slander?
If it doesn't benefit themselves,
slandering brings no advantage.
They use schemes to seek convenience,
employ strategies to gain profit.
When profit is obtained,
they envy others sharing their work,
then they endanger others.
When they endanger others, it's not through slander;
when they harm others, it's not through obvious means.
They praise while endangering,
so people don't realize it;
they treat generously while harming,
so people don't suspect.
Thus when cunning people endanger others, people are endangered without resentment;
when they harm others, people are ruined without enmity,
because they conceal their true feelings and intentions
in their actions.
If they slandered others,
others would also slander them,
the masses wouldn't be close,
scholars wouldn't adhere,
how could they then find acceptance in the world and gain profit from superiors?
The question asked:
"If cunning people don't slander others in ordinary circumstances,
do they slander before generals?"
The reply:
Cunning people use others to deceive generals,
they don't slander people before generals.
"Then what do cunning people do?"
The reply:
When cunning people ruin others,
they praise them;
when they endanger others,
they make them feel secure.
How do they ruin and endanger?
Suppose A has outstanding conduct and exceptional wisdom,
his reputation is widely known,
and the ruler might summon him for questioning,
supporting him to surpass oneself,
so one wishes to deliberately neglect mentioning him,
but constantly praises him instead.
When many recommend him,
and the ruler considers employing him,
asking the cunning person;
the cunning person will certainly reply:
"A is worthy and should be summoned.
Why?
A doesn't wish to remain in the county,
I've heard him say so before,
his ambition wants to enter the prefecture,
in the commandery he aspires to enter the province.
With high ambitions, his conduct differs from others,
with distant aspirations, his mind doesn't consider the near.
If employed in a humble position,
his heart will be dissatisfied,
otherwise he'll feign illness.
If given a lowly appointment, it hurts the worthy,
otherwise it damages authority.
Thus what causes rulers to lose reputation and suffer disgrace
is keeping such ministers as regular officials.
If you can tolerate being beneath him,
you may employ him;
if you judge you cannot be beneath him,
employing him is inconvenient.
Employing him doesn't benefit both sides,
dismissing him doesn't harm both sides."
The ruler fears his ambition,
believes the cunning person's words,
and thus sets him aside unused.
The question asked:
"Do cunning people simply rely on great talent and broad knowledge to surpass previous generations?
Or do they have teachers and learning to check them?"
The reply:
Cunning people use their own knowledge to deceive others,
and when persuading rulers,
they need techniques to move superiors,
just as warriors use their own courage to intimidate others,
but when fighting battles,
they need military strategy to advance troops.
Their techniques involve vertical and horizontal alliances,
their teacher is Guǐgǔ.
The tradition says:
"Sū Qín and Zhāng Yí studied vertical and horizontal alliance techniques under Guǐgǔ Xiānshēng,
who dug a pit in the ground, saying:
'Descend,
if your persuasion moves me to tears,
then you may share the rulers' lands.'
Sū Qín descended,
and his persuasion made Guǐgǔ Xiānshēng's tears wet his lapel.
Zhāng Yí was not his equal."
Sū Qín became chancellor of Zhào,
and concurrently chancellor of six states.
When Zhāng Yí was poor and humble
and went to join him, Sū Qín
seated him in the lower hall,
fed him servants' food,
repeatedly reproached and provoked him,
wanting him to become chancellor of Qín.
Yí, angry and resentful,
then went west to enter Qín.
Sū Qín had people richly escort him.
Later Yí realized,
saying:
"This was within his strategy,
I didn't know it,
this is where I fall short of Lord Sū."
With deep knowledge and possessing techniques,
expedient measures emerging sharply,
thus they achieved尊贵荣显,
becoming heroes of their age.
Deep strategies and clear techniques,
depth and shallowness cannot proceed together,
brightness and darkness cannot be known simultaneously.
The question asked:
"Do cunning people cultivate reputation to appear lofty?
Is this true?"
The reply:
Cunning people seek profit and monopolize power,
they don't cultivate reputation to appear lofty.
By coveting power and occupying ordinary positions,
lofty reputation naturally establishes itself.
Praised by petty people,
but not practiced by gentlemen.
Why?
Profit and righteousness conflict,
upright and wicked oppose each other.
Righteousness moves gentlemen,
profit moves petty people.
Cunning people covet the prominence of profit and fame,
making rulers uneasy. Otherwise they endanger themselves.
All cunning people in the world
bring disaster to the masses.
Unable to nurture their own persons,
how can they nurture their reputation?
Early historical biographies record those who abandoned clan to nurture themselves,
renounced profit to pursue fame,
as recorded in bamboo and silk texts:
Bóchéng Zǐgāo abandoned his state to farm,
Yúlíng Zǐ resigned his position to garden.
In recent times, Lánlíng's Wáng Zhòngzǐ,
Dōngjùn's Xīlú Jūnyáng,
who long feigned illness in their positions,
not responding to imperial summons,
could be said to cultivate reputation.
Those who don't advance by the Way,
certainly won't establish themselves by the Way;
those who don't stop by righteousness,
certainly won't establish reputation by righteousness.
Cunning people harbor greedy, profit-seeking hearts,
take disasters lightly but value themselves heavily,
would rather die than be disgraced,
what reputation do they cultivate?
With righteousness abandoned and virtue ruined,
conduct following disgrace,
how can they be called lofty?
The question asks:
"Are great flatterers easy to recognize?
Or are petty flatterers easy to recognize?"
The reply:
Great flatterers are easy to recognize,
while petty flatterers are difficult to detect.
Why is this?
Great flatterers possess superior talent,
making their traces easily observable;
petty flatterers have inferior wisdom,
making their effects hard to perceive.
How can this be demonstrated?
Consider established facts:
Petty thieves are difficult to discover,
while great robbers are easy to know.
When attacking cities and seizing towns,
plundering and capturing loot,
once the deed is done, it becomes known,
and everyone on the roads knows they are robbers;
but those who bore through walls,
sneaking like foxes and stealing like rats,
none know who they are.
Someone says:
"Great flatterers are deeply cunning, deceiving and confusing people.
If great flatterers were easy to recognize,
what difficulty would rulers have?
The Book of Documents says:
'To know men is wisdom,
which even the Emperor found difficult.'
Yú Shùn was a great sage,
while Huān Dōu was a great flatterer.
If a great sage found it difficult to know a great flatterer,
and a great flatterer did not worry about a great sage,
how could they be easy to recognize?"
The reply:
This refers to being known from below,
and being known from above.
When known from above, the great are difficult and the petty easy;
when known from below, the great are easy and the petty difficult.
Why is this?
Great flatterers have superior talent,
their arguments are elegant and beautiful,
and through these elegant and beautiful discourses,
they exploit the ruler's authority,
so people's minds cannot hold them accountable,
and knowledge may fail to detect them.
Petty flatterers have inferior talent,
their responses reveal omissions,
their interactions lack secrecy,
so the ruler becomes alert and awakened,
discovering the reason.
Thus the great are difficult and the petty easy.
When the roof leaks from above,
those who know are below.
If the leak is large,
those below see it clearly;
if the leak is small,
those below see it faintly.
Someone said:
"Yǒng is benevolent but not eloquent."
Confucius said:
"What use is eloquence?
Using quick speech to oppose others
often makes one hated by the people."
Mistakenly devising schemes,
harassing farmers and merchants,
harming those below to benefit those above,
distressing the people to please the ruler.
Harming those above to benefit those below
is the argument of loyal ministers;
harming those below to benefit those above
is the principle of flatterers.
"Jì Shì was wealthier than the Duke of Zhōu,
yet Qiú collected taxes for him to increase his wealth.
My disciples, you may beat the drums and attack him.
Tax collection—
Jì Shì did not know its evil,
nor did he know the common resentment against it.
Critics often say that Confucian scholars are inferior to those clerks,
seeing the clerks' advantages and convenience, while Confucian scholars decline,
then they slander Confucian scholars as shallow and limited,
praising clerks as profound and capable.
This shows they neither understand Confucian scholars,
nor do they understand clerks.
Both Confucian scholars and clerks have talent and wisdom;
it is not that clerks have superior talent while Confucian scholars have inferior wisdom.
Clerks have practical experience,
while Confucian scholars are not trained in it.
To say clerks have experience
while Confucian scholars are untrained
is acceptable;
but to say clerks are profound
and Confucian scholars are shallow
is clearly wrong.
Common opinion universally disparages Confucian scholars,
and even among Confucian scholars themselves, they belittle each other.
Why is this?
Because all desire official positions and bureaucratic learning,
using clerks as the standard.
When Confucian scholars have shortcomings,
common opinion universally disparages them;
when clerks make errors,
common opinion dares not criticize them.
Blame is attributed to Confucian scholars,
while credit is given to clerks.
Now Confucian scholars' talent is not inferior to clerks',
nor are their learned professions inappropriate,
yet common opinion universally disparages them
because they see that officials do not favor employing them.
The reason officials do not favor employing them
is that many affairs they cannot manage themselves
require clerks to handle them.
When discussing good planning and talent,
applying accumulated abilities,
the expectation is to be beneficial.
Clerks manage complexities,
their bodies bound to duties,
tasks accomplished and merits established,
so officials respect their abilities.
Confucian scholars are cautious and fearful,
unable to handle intense tasks;
when officials face complicated doubts,
they cannot provide effective service.
When their strength brings no benefit to the times,
official positions do not come to them.
Officials use positions to test talent,
talent is verified through official performance,
hence common opinion often elevates clerks
and demeans Confucian scholars.
The lowness of Confucian scholars
and the highness of clerks
ultimately stem from incapable officials.
Common opinions
follow officials' preferences and aversions.
Today's officials,
if highly talented and deeply knowledgeable,
comprehensive in all matters,
grasping the key points and maintaining control,
will settle affairs without uncertainty;
their employment of clerks
merely fills quotas and completes staff,
sufficient to support their own intentions.
If their intention lies in cultivating virtue,
devoted to establishing transformation,
then clerks are like tiles and stones,
while Confucian scholars are pearls and jades.
Though clerks can break through difficulties and manage complexities,
they cannot guard their own character;
[cannot guard] their character,
thus they cannot assist officials either.
Confucian scholars may be untrained in duties,
but excel in correction and rescue;
when officials deviate,
they remonstrate without fear.
Indeed,
those in the world who can establish unwavering integrity,
achieve the principle of repeated remonstration,
compelling officials to examine themselves and reform,
daring not to be corrupt,
are mostly Confucian scholars.
Those who flatter to seek favor,
when officials are about to err,
lower their heads and remain silent,
are mostly clerks.
Clerks excel in affairs,
but fail in loyalty;
Confucian scholars excel in integrity,
but are inferior in duties.
These two have strengths and weaknesses,
each fitting different purposes;
officials in the world
each make their choices accordingly.
Those who choose Confucian scholars
must be those who follow virtue and establish transformation;
those who choose clerks
must be those who prioritize managing affairs and controlling chaos.
If talent cannot accomplish things alone, then assistance is needed;
needing assistance requires relying on strength.
The establishment of assistant officials
is due to insufficient strength;
the employment of capable clerks
is due to inadequate talent.
When the sun illuminates darkness,
no lamp or candle is needed;
when Bēn and Yù face enemies,
no assistance is required.
If officials' strength were like the sun illuminating darkness,
or Bēn and Yù's ability to face enemies unaided,
then clerks' abilities would have no use.
When illness strikes, doctors are employed;
when disaster arises, shamans are used.
If one could personally follow prescriptions and mix medicines,
enter rooms to seek out evil spirits,
then doctors would have no market and shamans would not be advanced.
Bridges are built because
feet cannot leap across ditches;
carriages and horses are used because
running cannot chase far.
If feet could leap across ditches,
and running could chase far,
then bridges would not be built, nor carriages and horses used.
The phenomena of heaven and earth,
which people value and respect,
all stem from the limits of their strength and knowledge,
requiring reliance on them for fulfillment.
Nowadays, generals and ministers
do not blame themselves for their incapabilities,
but belittle Confucian scholars for their lack of practice;
they do not examine the origins of what clerks gain and use,
yet respect their talent, calling them capable officials.
Without clerks,
worries would not be removed;
without clerks,
crises would not be rescued.
Therefore, in selecting officials, they stick to convention,
and in evaluating clerks, they seek those who cause no harm.
Confucian scholars lack influential backgrounds,
and their abilities cannot handle complex tasks,
so they are overlooked in elections,
and neglected in the court.
The clever and quick-witted,
adapting to the times,
learn clerical duties,
then follow in the footsteps of clerks,
yet fail to earn a reputation for excellence.
Those who uphold antiquity and follow their aspirations,
adhering to rituals and cultivating righteousness,
are often deemed unfit by generals and ministers,
and mocked by clerks.
Not being appointed leads to waning determination and withdrawal,
being mocked causes loss of morale,
so they lack diligence in office,
and are imprecise in examining affairs,
thus being deemed incapable,
and rejected for inexperience.
Those with vulgar talent but no refinement,
learning clerical duties,
disrupt the ranks of clerks,
observe what the generals know,
cater to urgent needs,
shift their goals and change their tasks,
studying day and night,
without shame or disgrace,
aiming only to become renowned for their clerical skills.
Those with high aspirations and noble conduct,
ashamed to lower their intentions or diminish their dignity,
to flatter for advancement,
deeply despise Confucian scholars of talent.
When they enter the category of clerks,
they firmly hold to their high ideals,
unwilling to learn from those below.
Sometimes, due to lack of familiarity or oversight,
their attention is scattered and not meticulous,
failing to recognize issues in handling affairs;
they make errors in responses,
are awkward in bowing and rising,
and lose propriety in advancing and retreating;
in submitting reports and discussing matters,
they cover up recommendations and explain faults,
citing ancient principles;
they bluntly critique desires,
speaking directly and pointedly,
touching on taboos and offending sensitivities;
in sealing and binding documents,
simplifying regulations and endorsing,
they fail to follow procedures;
their language is peculiar,
diverging from reality with sharp criticism,
and twisting without aligning with righteousness.
Thus, they are belittled by the common world,
looked down upon by clerks,
and despised by generals and ministers.
Therefore, those who pursue learning in the common world
are unwilling to thoroughly study the classics and understand scholarship,
or deeply grasp past and present,
but rush to master the chapters and sentences of one school.
With a superficial grasp of principles,
they hastily turn to studying official documents,
reading laws and reciting decrees,
practicing drafting petitions and memorials,
learning how to respond,
and smoothly executing bows and kneels,
until they master it at home,
and are immediately capable when appointed.
They follow the present without regard for antiquity,
chase profit without preserving their aspirations,
compete for advancement without adhering to rituals,
and abandon the classics without considering learning.
Thus, ancient classics are discarded and not cultivated,
old learning fades into obscurity,
Confucian scholars languish in empty rooms,
while clerks clamor in the court.
Those with talent and ability
gallop along with the times;
those with integrity and principles
guard narrow paths and hide away.
The galloping grow more cunning by the day,
while the hiding grow more clumsy.
It is not that their talent is dull or knowledge insufficient,
but that they rarely see or do,
and are not accustomed to it.
For if feet have never walked, even Yáo or Yǔ would ask about the twists and turns;
if eyes have never seen, even Kǒngzǐ or Mòzǐ would inquire about forms.
In Qí Province, embroidery is common,
and ordinary women are all skilled;
in Xiāngyì, weaving brocade is customary,
and even clumsy women become adept.
They see it with their eyes,
do it daily,
and their hands become familiar.
If a talented man has never seen it,
or a skilled woman has never done it,
faced with strange tasks and unfamiliar hands,
briefly attempting or glimpsing,
even easily achievable things
would leave them confused.
Nowadays, in evaluating affairs, they do not attribute it to lack of experience,
but say the talent is not sharp;
not that they have never done it,
but that their knowledge is inadequate,
which misses the truth.
Confucian scholars' talent is not incapable of sharpness,
their studies not incapable of mastery,
but their will is unwilling to act.
Now, common views see inexperience and call it incapability;
see inaction and call it inadequacy.
Using categories to assess cumulative ability,
thus clerks come first,
Confucian scholars last,
as judged by the court.
If evaluated from the Confucian hall,
then Confucian scholars would rank above,
and clerks below.
Discuss farming from a farmer's perspective,
and the farmer excels;
discuss trade from a merchant's view,
and the merchant is superior;
now, from the court's standpoint,
clerks are deemed so.
Those of the court
start as junior clerks in youth,
treating the court as their fields,
the pen as their plow,
documents as their crops,
much like family children growing up in the estate,
who know its twists and turns better than guests.
Guests arrive briefly,
even with the talent of Kǒngzǐ or Mòzǐ,
cannot discern it all.
Confucian scholars are like guests,
clerks like family children.
Judging by the children,
then clerks are more aware than Confucian scholars,
and Confucian scholars are less aware than clerks.
Today's generals and ministers,
know that family children consider clerks long-practiced as wise,
but do not realize clerks rely on familiarity for ability;
they know guests briefly present as unsteady,
but do not understand Confucian scholars are deemed clumsy due to rarity,
being confused and obscured,
failing to see the analogy.
The talent of a county assistant clerk
can serve as a commandery clerk;
the ability of a commandery cultivator
can qualify as a provincial attendant.
Yet commanderies do not summon county assistants,
nor provinces take cultivators,
preferring the skillfully practiced and harmless.
Literary skill is scant, but virtue high.
The five ministries have their own regulations,
records and documents their own precedents,
through diligent effort and manipulation,
one becomes a clever clerk,
but is that truly praiseworthy?
Wise and enlightened generals,
measure clerks by their material,
not seeking highly practiced debaters,
but valuing those who preserve aspirations over literary skill.
They call good officials loyal,
and loyalty's proof
lies not in records.
For affairs can be learned and known,
rituals practiced and mastered,
but loyalty, integrity, and public spirit
cannot be instantly established.
Both civil clerks and Confucian scholars have their aspirations,
yet Confucian scholars strive for loyalty and virtue,
while civil clerks focus on administrative affairs.
If one achieves loyalty and virtue,
even if clumsy in practical matters,
it does not diminish their nobility.
Critics argue that Confucian scholars lack proficiency in documentation,
thus relegating them to lower ranks.
Laws and regulations
are adjudicated by clerks.
When civil clerks handle affairs,
they must consult legal experts.
In governmental matters,
nothing surpasses the importance of laws.
If official duties are deemed the highest standard,
then legal experts should be ranked foremost.
Some say:
"Indeed.
Laws and decrees
are the classics of the Hàn dynasty,
decided through clerical deliberation.
Matters settled by law
are truly clear."
I respond:
The Five Classics were also established by the Hàn dynasty,
and Confucian scholars excel in governance, with great principles
all deriving from them.
Dǒng Zhòngshū demonstrated the principles of the Spring and Autumn Annals,
aligning them with legal codes,
without any discrepancy.
Thus, the Spring and Autumn Annals
are the classics of Hàn,
authored by Confucius,
and passed down to the Hàn dynasty.
Critics merely honor legal experts,
without elevating the Spring and Autumn Annals,
which is blindness.
The Spring and Autumn Annals and the Five Classics share interconnected principles;
since it is the Spring and Autumn Annals,
not elevating the Five Classics
is ignorance.
The Five Classics prioritize the Way,
while affairs are secondary to the Way;
when the Way prevails, affairs are established,
without the Way, nothing is accomplished.
Thus, what Confucian scholars learn
is the Way;
what civil clerks learn
is affairs.
If talents are equal,
priority should be given to the Way.
Comparing them to civil clerks,
washing mud requires water,
roasting raw meat uses fire;
water and fire
are the Way,
while their application is affairs,
with affairs being secondary to the Way.
Confucian scholars govern the root,
civil clerks manage the branches;
comparing the root of the Way to the branches of affairs,
the hierarchy of nobility and baseness
can be determined.
Yáo, with his splendid virtue, brought harmony to the common people.
Confucius said:
"The utmost in filial piety and fraternal duty
penetrates to the divine and luminous."
Zhàng Shìzhī said:
"The Qín dynasty employed petty clerks skilled in documentation,
leading to decline by the second generation,
and the empire collapsed."
Zhāng Tāng and Zhào Yǔ,
capable officials of Hàn,
were listed by Grand Historian Sīmǎ Qiān in the category of cruel officials,
leading to collapse. How can they compare to penetrating the divine and luminous,
filling people with admiration?
If generals and ministers understand classical learning and the supreme Way,
yet do not respect classical scholars,
it is because they see that these scholars' abilities fall short of administrative clerks.
An ox-knife can slaughter a chicken,
but a chicken-knife can hardly slaughter an ox;
an embroidery master
can sew ceremonial robes,
while a seamster
cannot weave brocade;
Confucian scholars can perform the tasks of civil clerks,
but civil clerks cannot establish the learning of Confucian scholars.
The abilities of civil clerks
are truly inferior;
what Confucian scholars do not practice,
they excel at but do not engage in.
When Yǔ tamed the rivers,
he did not carry hoes and spades;
when the Duke of Zhōu built Luòyáng,
he did not grasp construction tools.
Writing brushes, ink, and documents
are like hoes, spades, and tools;
to expect those devoted to the great Way to handle them personally
is like making a general fight battles or a master craftsman do carving.
A scholar versed in one classic,
assigned to manage one department's affairs,
can learn it in ten days or a month;
a clerk in charge of one department,
tasked with learning one classic,
cannot master it in a year.
Why?
Clerical tasks are easy to grasp,
while classical learning is hard to comprehend.
Confucian scholars study the classics,
exhaustively seeking the sages' intent;
civil clerks wield brushes,
examining traces of civil affairs.
To understand the great sages' intent
or to grasp the common people's sentiments—
which is more difficult?
With the talent to master the difficult,
embracing texts and commentaries
exceeding a hundred thousand words,
they still have energy to spare.
Learned in ancient and modern times,
the wisdom in their minds
overflows beyond a hundred thousand words.
What civil clerks know
is merely deciphering documents.
Accumulating wealth of a thousand gold
—how does it compare to assets worth a hundred or ten?
Granaries piled high like hills
—how do they compare to small heaps like mounds?
The world praises talent as a precious vessel,
and a large vessel holds more.
Thus, what Confucian scholars possess
can be said to be abundant.
Weeds growing among hemp
straighten without support;
white silk entering black dye
darkens without staining.
This illustrates how learned habits
transform one's nature:
the nature of Confucian scholars
is not inherently all good,
but clad in the sages' teachings,
reciting day and night,
they attain the sages' conduct.
Civil clerks, from youth, handle brushes and ink,
practicing with their hands,
without reciting texts
or hearing words of benevolence and righteousness.
Growing up to become officials,
they manipulate documents and laws cunningly,
serving selfish ends,
striving for power and profit;
investigating matters, they accept bribes;
governing the people, they exploit them;
in high positions, they abuse power;
favored by superiors, they betray commanders;
once in office,
they don sharp crowns and swords;
after a year in charge,
they amass fields and estates.
Their nature is not all evil,
but their learned actions defy the sages' teachings.
Thus, trained in the Confucian path of goodness,
they turn toward transformation and admire righteousness,
their will and conduct inspired to rise high.
Enlightened leaders, recognizing this,
prominently employ Confucian scholars.
Zōng Shūxiáng, Chancellor of Dōnghǎi,
widely summoned the reclusive,
holding spring and autumn feasts,
establishing three categories,
appointing officials by rank,
so that nine-tenths of his staff
were Confucian scholars.
Chén Zǐyǔ, Governor of Chénliú,
expanded the Confucian path,
with departmental officers
all capable of teaching;
document-handling clerks
made up only one or two in ten.
Both leaders understood the principles of the Way and affairs,
grasping the measure of much and little,
thus the world praised their names,
and records accumulated their deeds.
What "Assessing Talents" discusses
concerns ability and conduct,
not yet addressing the uniqueness of learning and knowledge.
The reason Confucian scholars surpass civil clerks
lies in their daily increasing learning,
refining their nature,
and honing their talents.
Therefore, scholars are those who return to their innate dispositions and cultivate their nature,
fully developing their talents and completing their virtue.
When talents are fully developed and virtue is completed,
compared to clerical officials, they are like carved jades,
their measure and substance are far greater.
When a poor person and a rich person
both contribute a hundred coins
as funeral gifts for a bereaved family,
those who understand know that the poor person can barely manage the hundred coins,
while considering the rich person to have abundant surplus and extraordinary means;
those who do not understand,
seeing both contribute a hundred coins,
think that the wealth and possessions of poor and rich are equal.
Clerical officials and Confucian scholars are similar to this.
Both serve as subordinate officers,
and both administer a department.
Those who understand
know that while clerical officials and Confucian scholars wield the same brush,
the knowledge stored in the Confucian scholars' minds
still contains much extraordinary surplus;
those who do not understand,
thinking they are all officials,
consider their depth and abundance to be of the same measure,
which is greatly mistaken about reality.
The nature of earth is to grow grasses,
the nature of mountains is to grow trees.
But if the earth is planted with sunflowers and leeks,
and the mountains are covered with jujube and chestnut trees,
they are called beautiful gardens and lush forests,
and are no longer comparable to ordinary land and common mountains.
Clerical officials and Confucian scholars
are similar to this.
Both have talent and ability,
and both use brush and ink,
but Confucian scholars uniquely possess the Way of the ancient kings.
The Way of the ancient kings
is not merely the equivalent of sunflowers, leeks, jujubes, or chestnuts.
The hands of ordinary women
spin, weave, and manage warp threads.
But if one has extraordinary skill,
weaving brocade or embroidering,
she is called outstanding and exceptional,
and is no longer classified with ordinary women.
When Confucian scholars and clerical officials are measured for talent,
the Confucian scholars abundantly possess the learning of classics and commentaries,
just like the extraordinary skill of women weaving brocade and embroidery.
That poor people tend to be unrestrained while rich people uphold integrity
is because poor people lack sufficiency and rich people have abundant surplus.
That Confucian scholars do not do wrong while clerical officials are prone to deceit
is because clerical officials lack moral virtue and Confucian scholars abound in benevolence and righteousness.
When poor people and rich people
both act as guests,
receiving gifts from their host,
the rich feel no shame while the poor often feel ashamed
because the rich have something to reciprocate with,
while the poor have nothing to return.
Confucian scholars and clerical officials
both regard high officials as their hosts.
Confucian scholars receive salaries from high officials
and repay them with the Way;
clerical officials have empty minds, without the learning of benevolence and righteousness.
Holding positions and consuming salaries,
they ultimately have nothing to contribute,
being what is called "corpse occupants consuming meals for nothing."
"Sù"
means empty,
empty and devoid of virtue,
consuming others' salaries,
hence called "sù cān."
Without the craft of the Way and arts,
ignorant of governance,
silently sitting in court,
unable to discuss affairs,
no different from a corpse,
hence called "corpse occupant."
Thus, clerical officials are what is called "corpse occupants consuming meals for nothing."
Holding high positions and enjoying fine emoluments,
seeing their superiors about to err,
how could they present records and articulate gains and losses?
Firstly, they cannot discern right from wrong;
secondly, they fear punishment and dare not speak directly.
The Rites say:
"Emotions and desires require skill."
Those capable of speaking forthrightly,
if their writing is unrefined,
having bone but no flesh,
lacking richness and smoothness,
offending the intentions of generals and ministers,
will then face gaps and estrangements.
Those who fight for territory cannot achieve merit and fame;
those greedy for titles and salaries cannot remonstrate with superiors.
Clerical officials, greedy for titles and salaries,
once in office for a day,
immediately seek to plot for profit to cover expenses,
infringing and preying for personal gain,
not acting to display righteousness for their generals and officials.
Even if they see evils as great as Mount Tài,
how would they be willing to raise even a hair's breadth of criticism?
Since affairs and principles are like this,
how can they excuse themselves from being "corpse occupants consuming meals for nothing"?
Confucian scholars learn the great principles,
serve their generals with the Way,
and desist if it is not acceptable,
having the ambition of great ministers.
Urged by the classics to maintain a fair and upright conduct,
they dare to speak out,
yet their positions are also distant and remote.
To advise closely while being distant
is called flattery in the Rites.
This is why the halls of commandery and county governments are often empty and unmanned.
Some say:
"Clerical officials have the skill of brush and documents,
settling accounts and managing records,
examining and handling troublesome matters.
Although without the learning of the Way,
their strength and talent are fully exerted in the court;
this is also evidence of repaying their superiors."
The response is:
This is similar to a poor person bearing heavy official debts.
Being poor and unable to repay,
they then perform labor for the government,
until the debt is fully settled.
Government labor
involves either buildings or walls.
For buildings, axes are used;
for walls, tampers and shovels are used.
Carrying axes,
gripping tampers and shovels—
how is that different from holding knives and brushes?
If managing documents is considered evidence of repaying superiors,
then those building houses and walls
also repay superiors.
Both perform government labor;
knife-brushes, axes, tampers, and shovels are equivalent.
Holding cloth to exchange for silk,
trading what one has for what one lacks,
each gets what they desire.
Confucian scholars hold the Way to trade for emoluments;
clerical officials have nothing to hold,
so what do they use to trade?
Farmers and merchants have different occupations;
the goods they accumulate
cannot be the same.
Assessing their refinement and coarseness,
measuring their quantity,
those with surplus are called rich people.
Rich people in the world
are admired in their villages.
But the Way of the ancient kings
is not merely the goods of farmers and merchants;
it enables high officials to achieve merits and accomplish transformation,
not just the glory of abundant surplus.
Moreover, the vocation of Confucian scholars,
is it merely about having surplus?
Their persons are trained and refined,
their knowledge and thoughts are bright,
their discernment of right and wrong is precise—
this is especially extraordinary.
Firewood has the same material as the timber of ordinary mountains.
Cut to become firewood,
heated with fire,
blazing hot and leaping high, its
color and luster moist and glossy,
burning in the hall,
its radiance vast and wide—
this is the added effect of the fire and stove.
Before embroidery is stitched,
before brocade is woven,
ordinary silk and common cloth—
how are they different?
But when the skill of five colors is applied,
and the adornment of needle and engraving is added,
the patterns become dazzling,
with axe-shaped patterns, adorned with brilliant birds,
mountains, dragons, sun, and moon.
Scholars who have the learning of literary patterns
are like silk and cloth possessing the skill of five colors.
Their inherent substance may not surpass others,
but through accumulated learning,
they exceed by far.
Things without a core are called uncultivated;
those without the carving of axe and knife are called unadorned.
Clerical officials do not learn; the teaching of the world
lacks a core.
Uncultivated and unadorned people—
how can they be measured?
Bone is called cut;
ivory is called polished;
jade is called carved;
stone is called ground.
Cutting, polishing, carving, and grinding
then produce precious vessels.
Human learning and knowledge, the achievements of wisdom and ability,
are like bones, ivory, jade, and stones that are cut, polished, carved, and refined.
Even if one wishes not to employ them,
would a wise ruler discard them?
Sūn Wǔ and Hé Lǘ,
were masters of military strategy in their time.
It is known that those who study their methods
are certain to be victorious in battle.
Those who do not understand formations of squads and companies,
or the techniques of striking and thrusting,
if forcibly sent to the army,
will lead to the defeat of regiments and collapse of divisions,
due to the lack of such methods.
When grain first ripens, it is called sù (unhusked millet).
Pounded in a mortar,
winnowed of its husks and chaff,
steamed in a zèng (earthenware pot),
cooked over fire,
it matures into rice,
then becomes sweet and edible.
When edible and consumed,
it produces flavor, nurtures flesh, and enriches the body.
If sù has not been hulled into rice,
or rice not cooked into meal,
its energy is raw and uncooked,
and eating it harms people.
Similarly, if a person does not study,
it is like grain not yet hulled into sù,
or rice not yet made into meal.
With a disordered and deficient mind,
it is like eating raw grain,
whose energy injures people.
Scholars who refine themselves through learning,
and mature under teachers,
benefit their persons,
just as grain becomes rice,
and eating it generates flesh and enrichment.
Before copper and tin are mined,
they reside among ordinary stones.
Craftsmen quarry and dig them out,
smelt them in furnaces with bellows, then cast them into vessels.
If not processed through furnace and bellows,
they are called accumulated stones.
Such accumulated stones are no different from tiles by the roadside or gravel in the mountains—all of the same substance.
Thus, grain unhusked and unsteamed is called sù,
copper unsmelted and uncast is called accumulated stone,
and a person unlearned and uninquiring is called méng (ignorant).
The méng
are akin to bamboo and wood.
Bamboo grows in the mountains,
trees flourish in the forests,
not yet knowing their purpose.
Cut bamboo into tubes,
split them into slips,
add traces of brush and ink,
and they become writing,
large ones for classics,
small ones for commentaries and records.
Cut wood into tablets,
split them into boards,
apply effort to scrape and polish,
and they become memorial tablets.
Bamboo and wood,
coarse and crude materials,
through carving, polishing, cutting, and scraping,
become useful vessels.
How much more so for humans, who embody the nature of heaven and earth,
and are the most noble of all!
If one does not enter the gate of a teacher,
lacking the instruction of classics and commentaries,
with the raw substance of uncultivated simplicity,
unaware of ritual and righteousness,
and is established in the court,
it is like erecting pillars or setting up markers—
what benefit is there?
When mountains and wilds are overgrown with grass,
hooked sickles cut and clear it,
then paths are formed.
If scholars have not entered the gate of the Way,
with evils not yet removed,
it is like the grasses and trees in the wilds not yet cut,
not forming a path.
Dyeing and refining cloth and silk,
they are called colorful fabrics,
used for auspicious and noble garments.
Without the process of dyeing and refining, they are called húcū (coarse cloth),
húcū is inauspicious,
and worn by mourners.
If a person lacks the learning of the Way,
yet serves in the court,
they cannot attract good fortune,
just as mourners wearing coarse cloth cannot attract auspiciousness.
One who can carve beams and pillars
is called a carpenter;
one who can dig pits and tunnels
is called an earthworker;
one who can engrave and compose documents
is called a clerk.
The learning of clerical officials,
which involves managing documents,
should be classified alongside carpenters and earthworkers;
how can they be measured against Confucian scholars?
When imperial censors handle documents,
they do not err by a fraction;
when officials arrange ritual vessels,
they do not mistake the order.
Such skillful practices
are also learned beforehand,
yet people do not value them,
considering them minor, lowly skills,
not esteemed or important duties.
Without the foundation of classical arts,
but possessing the trivialities of brush and ink,
the great Way is insufficient, while minor techniques are excessive.
Even if one claims to have much learning,
it is merely the addition of a censor or the favor of an official.
Those who eat fine millet are satisfied,
those who consume chaff and husks are full;
though both are called eating,
the nourishment differs.
Confucian scholars and clerical officials,
both are said to be learned,
yet their benefit to the court
is not equal.
When Zhèng Zǐpí appointed Yǐn Hé to governance,
Zǐchǎn compared it to giving a knife to one who cannot wield it for cutting.
When Zǐlù made Zǐgāo steward of Bì,
Confucius said:
"You are harming that man's son."
Both cases were due to lack of learning and ignorance of the great Way.
A physician without medical methods who says,
"I can cure illness,"
when asked,
"What do you use to cure illness?"
replies,
"I use my mind and intent."
The patient will certainly not believe him.
An official without classical learning who says,
"I can govern the people,"
when asked,
"What do you use to govern the people?"
replies,
"I use my ability."
This is like a physician without methods,
using mind and intent to cure illness;
how would the common people willingly trust and follow him,
and how would a ruler appoint and employ him?
If you go to the market with no money in hand
to buy goods, and the merchant asks,
"Where is your money?"
and you reply,
"I have no money,"
the merchant will certainly not give you the goods.
Similarly, to have no learning in one's breast
is like having no money in hand.
To desire the ruler to employ you,
and the people to trust and follow you—how is it possible?
In "Chéng Cái" and "Liàng Zhì,"
it is said that the abilities of Confucian scholars and clerical officials
do not surpass each other,
yet since Confucian scholars cultivate the great Way,
while clerical officials understand documents,
the Way surpasses mere affairs,
thus Confucian scholars are considered somewhat superior to clerical officials.
This is an external measurement and comparison of professions,
but internally each has their shortcomings,
which have not been sincerely acknowledged.
Confucian scholars who can expound one classic
consider themselves versed in the great Way and thus look down on clerical officials;
clerical officials who understand documents
consider themselves flawless in writing and thus mock Confucian scholars.
Each holds themselves full and self-concealed,
deeming the other wrong and themselves right,
unaware of their own shortcomings,
unenlightened about their own deficiencies.
The "Lùn Héng" responds to this,
intending to make each clearly aware of their lacks.
The shortcoming of Confucian scholars
is not merely their ignorance of documents;
the inferiority of clerical officials
is not merely their lack of understanding of the great Way.
Rather, both are hindered by闭塞 and fail to survey past and present,
unable to realize that their own professional knowledge is incomplete.
Both sides have shortcomings,
yet cannot recognize them themselves;
and commentators of the world
also fail to address this—
what is to be done?
The profession of Confucian scholars
is the Five Classics.
Facing south as teachers,
they lecture on chapters and sentences morning and night,
smoothly familiar with meanings and principles,
thoroughly mastering the Five Classics—
this is acceptable.
After the Five Classics,
the events of the Qin and Han dynasties
are all within their knowledge—
a shortcoming.
To know antiquity but not the present
is called being submerged in the past;
then Confucian scholars
are what is called submerged in the past.
Before the Five Classics,
back to the beginning of heaven and earth
and the initial establishment of emperors and kings, whose names were recorded—
Confucian scholars again do not know.
To know the present but not antiquity
is called being blind.
The Five Classics compared to high antiquity
are still considered contemporary.
Merely able to discuss the classics,
yet ignorant of high antiquity,
then Confucian scholars
are what is called blind.
Confucian scholars still say:
"High antiquity is long distant,
its events obscure and vague,
thus the classics do not record them and teachers do not speak of them."
Though the affairs of the Three Sovereigns are remote,
and though the classics do not record them,
their principles are interconnected,
and those specializing in the Five Classics ought to know them,
Confucian scholars ought to examine and discuss them.
From Yǔ establishing the state of Xià,
how many years passed until Yīn?
From Tāng of Yīn, how many sacrifices until Zhōu?
From King Wén of Zhōu, how many years until Qín?
Jié lost Xià, and Zhòu abandoned Yīn—
which king destroyed Zhōu?
If Zhōu is considered distant,
then Qín was overthrown by Hàn.
Xià began with Yǔ,
Yīn originated with Tāng,
Zhōu's ancestor was Hòujì—
who was Qín's first human founder?
Qín burned the Five Classics,
buried Confucian scholars alive—
this is well known among specialists of the Five Classics.
Why did Qín arise and burn the Five Classics?
What provoked them to bury Confucian scholars?
Qín is a previous dynasty,
while Hàn's state originates from Confucian families.
From Emperor Gāozǔ to the present court, how many generations?
From its establishment to now, how many years?
What mandate did it initially receive?
What auspicious signs did it obtain?
How does the difficulty of gaining the empire compare to Yīn and Zhōu?
If family children
study for several years,
and someone asks them:
"How many years has the residence stood?
What did the ancestors do?"
If they cannot answer,
they are foolish children.
Then Confucian scholars not knowing Hàn affairs
makes them the foolish and ignorant of the world.
Reviewing the old to understand the new
qualifies one to be a teacher;
knowing neither past nor present,
how can they claim to be teachers?
Those people say:
"The two-foot-four-inch texts,
containing the sage's literary words,
studied morning and night,
covering related principles—
thus we focus on knowing these.
Hàn affairs are not recorded in the classics,
deemed short writings on brief tablets,
compared to minor paths—
even if we could know them,
it is not what Confucians value."
Confucian scholars cannot fully comprehend past and present,
yet wish to separately explain their classics;
are classical affairs and principles
something where ignorance becomes valuable?
Not understanding affairs,
yet not considering it a shortcoming!
Let me again question Confucian scholars separately,
each regarding their classic and what they teach daily.
First ask the Yì specialists:
"Where did the Yì originally come from?
Who created it?"
They will respond:
"Fúxī made the Eight Trigrams,
King Wén expanded them to sixty-four,
Confucius wrote the Tuàn, Xiàng, and Xìcí.
Three sages' layered work
made the Yì complete."
Question them:
"The Yì has three versions:
one called Liánshān,
second called Guīcáng,
third called Zhōuyì.
Which did Fúxī create?
Which did King Wén make?
Liánshān?
Guīcáng? Zhōuyì?
Qín burned the Five Classics—
how did the Yì escape?
How many years after Hàn's rise was it reestablished?
During Emperor Xuān's time,
a woman in Hénèi broke down an old house
and found one chapter of the Yì—
which Yì was it?
Was the Yì complete by then?"
Ask the Shàngshū specialists:
"The twenty-nine chapters taught today—
there are oddly one hundred two chapters,
also one hundred chapters.
Where did the twenty-nine come from?
How were the one hundred two created?
When Qín burned the Shī and Shū,
where were all the Shàngshū chapters?
When Hàn arose,
which emperor first compiled the Shàngshū?
Who first received and studied it?"
Ask the Lǐ specialists:
"Before Confucius' time,
Zhōu had already established rites,
as had Yīn and Xià rites.
All Three Dynasties
modified according to the times,
chapters varying in number,
texts increasing or decreasing.
Do we not know if the current Lǐ
is Zhōu's?
Or Yīn's or Xià's?"
They will certainly say Hàn succeeded Zhōu,
thus claiming:
"Zhōu rites."
But the Zhōulǐ has six codes,
each with six subdivisions,
six sixes being thirty-six,
three hundred sixty total—
hence Zhōu had three hundred sixty offices.
Yet the current Lǐjīng shows no six codes,
no three hundred sixty offices,
nor does it mention the Son of Heaven—
when were the Son of Heaven's rites abandoned?
Was it Qín that destroyed them?
Under Emperor Xuān, a Hénèi woman broke an old house
and found a lost Lǐ chapter—
among the sixteen chapters,
which one was it?
Emperor Gāozǔ ordered Shūsūn Tōng to compile Yípǐn—
where are those sixteen chapters?
And why reestablish ceremonial rites?
The existing sixteen chapters
are remnants after Qín's burning—
before Qín's time,
how many chapters were there total?"
Ask the Shī specialists:
"During which emperor's reign was the Shī composed?"
They will say:
"The Shī was made when Zhōu declined,
around King Kāng's time.
King Kāng's virtue failed in the chamber,
ministers satirized his laxity—
thus the Shī was composed."
But the flourishing of Kings Wén and Wǔ peaked under Chéng and Kāng—
King Kāng had not declined;
how could the Shī then arise?
Zhōu had more than one king—
how do you know it was King Kāng?
The ends of both Xià and Yīn saw decline—
when Xià and Yīn declined,
why was the Shī not composed then?
The Shàngshū states:
"Poetry expresses intent,
songs chant words."
Thus poetry already existed then.
To truncate from Zhōu onward and claim it arose in Zhōu—
in antiquity, poems were collected;
poetry had written form.
Now the Shī lacks texts—
how do we know it wasn't that Qín burned the Five Classics,
and the Shī alone left no remnants?"
Ask the Chūnqiū specialists:
"When Confucius composed the Chūnqiū,
which Zhōu king's time was it?
After returning from Wèi to Lǔ,
he corrected music,
then composed the Chūnqiū.
Returning from Wèi to Lǔ
was during Duke Āi's time.
From Wèi—
which ruler was that?
What rites did he show Confucius,
that Confucius returned to Lǔ to compose the Chūnqiū?
Confucius compiled historical records to make the Chūnqiū—
were those records originally called Chūnqiū?
Did compiling them as a classic then make it belong to the Chūnqiū?"
The legal experts
are also Confucian scholars.
Someone asks:
"Who composed the 'Nine Chapters'?"
Hearing that Gāo Yáo established penal law,
they will certainly say:
"Gāo Yáo did."
I question them:
"Gāo Yáo
lived during the times of Táng and Yú,
when the punishments under Táng and Yú were the Five Punishments,
yet the current statutes contain no provisions for the Five Punishments."
Some say:
"Xiāo Hé did."
I question them:
"Xiāo Hé
served under Emperor Gāozǔ.
During Emperor Wén's reign,
Chúnyú Yì, the Grand Granary Official of Qí, committed a crime
and was summoned to Cháng'ān.
His daughter Tí Yíng petitioned the emperor on her father's behalf,
stating that once corporal punishment is applied,
it cannot be revoked.
Emperor Wén, moved by her words,
then abolished corporal punishment.
Now the current 'Nine Chapters' prescribe symbolic punishments,
not corporal punishments.
Emperor Wén came after Xiāo Hé's time,
showing that corporal punishment existed then.
How could what Xiāo Hé created
instead contain symbolic punishments?
How can one claim the 'Nine Chapters' were created by Xiāo Hé?"
The ancient rites numbered three hundred,
with three thousand detailed rules of conduct,
while penal law also had three hundred main statutes
and three thousand subsidiary clauses.
What violates the rites
falls under punishment;
what the rites reject,
punishment adopts,
hence their numbers correspond.
Now the Classic of Rites has sixteen chapters,
while Xiāo Hé's statutes have nine chapters -
they don't correspond, so why is this?
The chapters of the Five Classics
are all distinguished by their content and meaning,
yet even with rites and laws being like classics,
when titled,
why do rites speak of 'canonical rites'
while laws speak of 'laws against theft'?
Why?
When generally questioning Confucian scholars about ancient and modern principles,
they cannot answer;
when separately questioning them about matters in their respective classics,
they still cannot understand.
This results from stubbornly adhering to
their teachers' methods without broad learning.
Clerical officials claim to understand official affairs
and comprehend documents.
Question them:
"If you know these matters,
can you fully grasp their principles,
and thoroughly understand their meaning?"
The clerical officials will certainly be perplexed.
Ask them:
"In ancient times, feudal lords governed their own territories;
now we appoint governors and magistrates -
what principle underlies this?
The ancient well-field system
had people farming for the public;
now we measure land and hay taxes -
what is the reasoning?
Requiring people to do corvée labor one month annually -
what is the basis?
Registration at twenty-three,
taxation at fifteen,
head tax at seven -
what is the rationale?
The là sacrifice -
from which emperor's time does it originate?
Gates, doors, wells, stoves -
why are they established?
The Altars of Soil and Grain, First Farmer, and Ling Star -
what sacrifices are offered?
Year-end epidemic expulsion -
what is driven away?
Placing peachwood figures at gates -
what is the purpose?
Hanging reed ropes over doors,
painting tigers on gateposts -
what is being imitated?
Drawing fire-repelling figures on walls -
what is the origin?
The six-foot pace,
the six-inch cap -
what do they correspond to?
Having minor clerks and recorders,
but no senior assistants -
what system is this?
When two commanderies exchange documents, they write:
'We dare inform the commander';
but two counties don't mention this -
how to explain?
When commanderies report to the two ministries, they write
'We dare report';
the Minister of Works writes 'submit' -
what is the form?
Granting eight ranks of nobility to commoners -
what model follows?
Names like 'Ornamented Tassel' and 'First Creation' -
what do they mean?
Officials reporting merits as 'service records',
with names written in black -
what does this indicate?
Granting royal staffs at seventy -
where did this begin?
Placing a dove on the staff's end,
not other birds -
why this staff?
If the dove is considered good,
why not grant doves but dove staffs,
and not other birds?
How to explain?
Dividing the day into sixty parts,
the water clock counting to one hundred,
the drum beating five times -
what is the reason?
Officials wearing black clothes,
palace gates having red steps -
what caution signifies?
Wearing girdle pouches at the waist,
having decorated tips on shoes -
Wearing daggers on the right,
swords on the left -
Having hooks on shoes,
caps on heads -
what do they symbolize?
Officials dwelling in cities,
traveling by carriage,
sitting handling documents,
building city walls -
which king started this?
Making carriages -
which artisan began?
Domesticating horses -
where originated?
Creating writing -
who did it?"
Building city walls and horse domestication
are hard to know
being ancient matters.
But making carriages and creating writing
should be easy to understand.
They will certainly answer:
"Cāng Jié created writing,
Xī Zhòng made carriages."
I question them:
"What inspired Cāng Jié to create writing?
What motivated Xī Zhòng to make carriages?"
Again they don't know.
What clerical officials should know,
yet remain ignorant of,
also results from insufficient broad learning.
Confucian scholars who don't study past and present
know only to adhere to classical texts,
skillfully recite chapters and sentences,
analyze interlocking complexities,
and clarify contradictions.
Clerical officials who don't understand governance
can only handle legal cases and investigations,
transfer documents and issue orders,
respond smoothly to local matters,
yet lack comprehensive understanding.
All are superficial and inadequate,
biased and impure,
each having deficiencies -
how can they criticize each other?
The chapters "Assessing Abilities" and "Measuring Knowledge"
merely discuss knowledge and learning,
without addressing capability.
When people possess knowledge and learning,
they have capability.
Clerical officials consider administrative skill as capability,
while Confucian scholars regard learning as capability.
Someone asked Yáng Zǐyún:
"If one has strength to lift great tripods and raise grand banners,
does knowledgeable virtue also have such power?"
He replied:
"Equivalent to a hundred men's strength."
The power of knowledgeable virtue equaling a hundred men
can match those lifting great tripods and raising grand banners in assessing opponents.
As for strong men, those with great strength
can lift cauldrons and hoist banners;
among Confucian scholars, those with abundant strength
are erudite, penetrating, comprehensive, and thorough.
Thus, erudition, penetration, comprehensiveness, and thoroughness
are the strengths of Confucian scholars;
lifting heavy weights and pulling out solid objects
are the strengths of strong men.
The "Zǐ Cái" chapter says:
"The strong men assist the king in opening the way for the worthy,
and they lead in transforming the people."
This means that the worthy are also strong in ritual and righteousness,
thus they can open the way for the worthy,
and lead in transforming the people.
Transforming the people requires ritual and righteousness,
and ritual and righteousness require literary compositions.
"When you have energy to spare after action,
then use it to study literature."
Being able to study literature
is evidence of having strength.
Someone asks:
"Can a Confucian scholar who expounds on one classic
be considered a person of strength?"
The reply is:
They are not persons of strength.
Páng Shǎodū of Chénliú, whenever recommending scholarly candidates for official posts,
often said:
"Wáng Jiǎ and so-and-so have the talent and ability of a hundred men."
The governor, not believing in their ability,
did not respond.
Shǎodū then said:
"What I said is still an understatement.
Wáng Jiǎ and so-and-so
have the talent and ability of a million men."
The governor angrily said:
"My close officer speaks recklessly!"
Shǎodū said:
"Clerical officials do not comprehend a single passage of the classics,
nor do they quote a single saying from a master;
whereas the scholars can expound on a million chapters and sentences—
is that not talent and wisdom equal to a million men?"
The governor had no reply.
Now, Shǎodū's words
are true,
but still incomplete.
Why so?
Though scholars can transmit a million words,
if they cannot survey past and present,
and merely adhere strictly to their masters' methods,
even if their explanations are numerous,
they ultimately cannot be considered erudite.
Events before the Yīn and Zhōu dynasties
are largely recorded in the Six Classics,
which Confucian scholars can expound upon.
But matters of the Qín and Hàn dynasties,
Confucian scholars have not witnessed,
and their strength is too feeble to survey them.
Zhōu took the two previous dynasties as mirrors,
Hàn took Zhōu and Qín as mirrors;
yet regarding the period since Zhōu and Qín,
Confucian scholars are ignorant,
and when Hàn wishes to observe and survey it,
Confucian scholars lack the strength.
If a Confucian scholar can broadly observe and survey,
then they become a literary Confucian.
Literary Confucians
possess more strength than ordinary Confucian scholars.
According to Shǎodū's words,
literary Confucians have talent and ability equal to ten million men.
Zēngzǐ said:
"The scholar may not be without breadth of mind and strength of will,
for their burden is heavy and their road is long.
Taking benevolence as their own burden—
is that not heavy?
Only with death does it end—
is that not long?"
From this perspective,
what the Confucian carries in mind
is uniquely heavy indeed;
the destination of their aspirations
is uniquely distant indeed;
bearing such heavy responsibilities on their person,
until the end of their lives,
without weariness or decline—
their strength is uniquely great indeed.
Now, Zēngzǐ bore the burden of benevolence, while Confucian scholars bear the burden of learning;
what they bear is different,
but the weight is equal.
A weight of one dàn,
one person can lift;
but for ten dàn or more,
two people cannot raise it.
In the world, many can shoulder the burden of one dàn,
but few have the strength to lift ten dàn.
What Confucian scholars bear
is not merely the weight of ten dàn.
Where the land's fertility is abundant,
plants and trees grow luxuriantly;
the harvest from one mǔ
equals that from five mǔ of average fields.
In seedling fields,
people know that high grain output indicates rich land fertility,
but they do not realize that abundant literary output indicates flourishing talent and wisdom—
this misses the reality of the matter.
Now, the strength of literary Confucians surpasses that of ordinary Confucian scholars,
how much more so that of clerical officials?
The ability to recommend worthy men and scholars
is considered by the world as great strength.
However, the ability to recommend worthy men and scholars
involves submitting memorials and written reports.
Those capable of submitting memorials and written reports
are literary Confucians.
Literary Confucians are not necessarily those who are merely students;
any worthy and enlightened person who employs literature qualifies.
Gǔ Zǐyún and Táng Zǐgāo submitted hundreds of memorials,
their brushes still having energy to spare;
they expressed extreme views without taboo,
their writings never faltering or lacking—
this cannot be done without being persons of talent and wisdom.
Confucius,
a man of great strength in the Zhōu era,
composed the "Spring and Autumn Annals,"
edited the Five Classics,
and determined secret texts and subtle writings
without exception.
Great mountains have abundant clouds;
Mount Tài can rain upon all under heaven before the morning is over.
Thus,
the worthy possess the knowledge of clouds and rain,
so when they produce writings of ten thousand tablets or more,
they may truly be called men of great strength.
When the world speaks of strength,
they often praise Wū Huò;
then indeed, Dǒng Zhòngshū and Yáng Zǐyún
are the Wū Huò of literature.
King Wǔ of Qín and Mèng Yùe attempted to lift a cauldron but could not bear the weight,
their tendons snapped and they died.
Those with little literary ability,
if they were to pour out the thoughts in their breasts like Dǒng Zhòngshū,
would surely be unable to bear it,
and suffer the calamity of snapped tendons.
During Wáng Mǎng's time,
when the Five Classics' chapters and sentences were reduced, each to two hundred thousand characters,
the erudite disciple Guō Lù determined old interpretations by night,
and died beneath the candle,
his refined thoughts unable to bear the strain,
his tendons snapped and breath extinguished.
Yán Yuān,
who had once raced past Confucius on the road,
worn out and utterly exhausted,
his hair turned white and teeth fell out.
Even with his promising talent,
he still met with the disaster of collapse and exhaustion;
Confucius' strength was superior,
while Yán Yuān could not bear it.
When talent and strength are not equal,
then their wisdom and intelligence do not match either.
Forcing oneself to be ten or a hundred times better,
vomiting blood from the chest,
losing one's soul and going mad,
until one breathes one's last.
Writing a document of five lines,
or a report of ten submissions—
for those of inferior talent, the effort of brush and ink is especially difficult,
how much more so linking sentences to form chapters,
and composing essays reaching tens or hundreds!
Their strength is uniquely great indeed!
The waters of the great rivers,
rushing and surging, smooth and seeping,
spreading over the land far and long,
without drying up or exhausting their flow—
their source is abundant.
Knowing that the flow of the great rivers is long,
and the source within the earth is abundant,
yet not knowing that the person of ten thousand tablets
has flourishing talent in their breast—
this is delusion.
Thus, seeing the feet of a fine steed,
they appear no different from the hooves of ordinary horses;
but let it tread level ground and gallop,
and the traces of a thousand lǐ
become visible in a moment.
Now, a horse's feet and a man's hand
are of the same substance;
yet to praise the feet of a fine steed
and not recommend the hand of a literary man—
this is to lack understanding of categories.
Those who can discuss muscular strength to show comparisons and categories,
then can select persons of literary strength
and establish them in the court.
Thus, those with literary strength
rely on powerful leaders
to achieve merit through their abilities.
Having strength but no support
turns ability into disaster.
How can this be verified?
Large, massive objects
require strong individuals
to lift them.
Heavily laden carts
need powerful oxen
to pull them.
When a loaded cart ascends a slope,
a strong ox pulls from the front,
while strong men push from behind,
only then can it climb over.
If the ox is weak and the men exhausted,
the loaded cart will retreat,
fall back into ravines,
and suffer the disaster of breaking and overturning.
Literary scholars embracing the ways of ancient kings,
containing the teachings of various schools,
are difficult to promote and guide,
not merely as heavy as loaded carts.
Those who recommend them
being weak and powerless,
cause them to retreat and hide in mountain caves.
The Yellow River originates from Kūnlún,
the Yangtze arises from Mínshān,
their water power abundant,
with surging flows,
growing stronger as they descend,
yet without broad banks and low land,
they cannot flow into the Eastern Sea.
If the banks are narrow and the land elevated,
the channels burst and overflow,
scattering across hills and ruins.
The knowledge of literary scholars
is similar to this.
With overflowing writings,
if not met by powerful leaders who support and recommend,
they will be abandoned beneath humble gates,
how then could they ascend to the courts of sage rulers,
to discuss affairs of governance?
The light of a fire,
unraised, does not shine.
Suppose there is a person
whose wisdom is like a mound,
whose virtue is like a mountain,
too weighty to promote themselves,
needing others to lift them,
yet if none assist,
clutching their lofty strengths,
they remain hidden in deep alleys,
when will they ever achieve prominence?
Ào and Yù,
renowned strong men of old,
could carry loads of a thousand jūn,
their hands could break horns and straighten hooks,
yet asked to lift themselves,
they could not leave the ground.
Those filled with intelligence and capability,
though fit for royal courts,
require a three-inch tongue,
a one-foot brush,
to then take action,
unable to advance on their own,
and once advanced, cannot secure themselves,
needing others to move them,
and others to stabilize them.
Their principles are weighty, their knowledge vast,
making positions hard to suit.
Small stones attached to a mountain
can be supported by the mountain's strength;
amid sand dunes,
though small stones are light,
they can remain stable on their own.
But as for large rocks,
if sand and soil do not cover them,
and the mountain cannot hold them,
positioned on precarious cliffs,
they will inevitably collapse into ravines.
The weight of great wisdom,
encountering leaders of minor talent,
lacking the aid of surrounding support like sand and soil,
even if in prominent positions,
will not be sustained,
leading to the disaster of great rocks falling.
When gathering firewood in the mountains,
small, light trees
can be bundled together.
But as for large trees
over ten arm-spans around,
pulling cannot move them,
pushing cannot shift them,
so they are left in the forest,
and only the bundled small wood is taken back.
From this perspective,
those with great knowledge and ability
are like trees over ten arm-spans around;
human strength cannot lift or recommend them,
just as woodcutters cannot push or pull large trees.
Kǒngzǐ traveled from state to state,
with nowhere to stay,
not because his sage-like talent was unclear,
but because his Way was too great to be implemented,
and people could not employ him.
Thus, Kǒngzǐ
is of the category of a giant tree in the mountains.
Huán Gōng united the feudal lords nine times,
bringing order to the world,
through the strength of Guǎn Zhòng.
Guǎn Zhòng had the ability,
and Huán Gōng could elevate him,
which can be called robust and strong.
Wú could not use Zǐxū,
Chǔ could not use Qū Yuán,
both men were of great strength,
yet their rulers could not lift them.
If one cannot bear the weight of an object,
it is acceptable to drop it and leave.
But if sometimes in anger,
one chops it with an axe, causing damage,
then it is harmful, as happened to Zǐxū and Qū Yuán.
Fish in a pond
swallow each other in turn,
gauging what their mouths can hold
before swallowing;
if the mouth cannot accept it,
they choke and cannot swallow.
Thus, Shāng Yāng proposed three times to Xiào Gōng,
with the last proposal being adopted,
the first two were hard to use,
the last one easy to implement.
Examining Guǎn Zhòng's "Míng Fǎ"
and observing Shāng Yāng's "Gēng Zhàn",
it is clear that weak and inferior rulers could not employ them.
During the time of the Six States,
ministers of talent and virtue
entered Chǔ and Chǔ became weighty,
left Qí and Qí became light,
served Zhào and Zhào remained intact,
betrayed Wèi and Wèi was wounded.
Hán employed Shēn Bùhài,
implementing his "Sān Fú",
and no troops invaded their borders
for about fifteen years.
If not using such talents,
and not examining their writings,
led to military defeat and broken armies,
and the state being annexed by Qín.
In the eras of Yīn and Zhōu,
traces of chaos were continuous,
calamities of downfall were shoulder to shoulder,
was it that their hearts did not wish to govern well?
They were weak in strength and inferior in wisdom,
unable to accept profound advice.
Therefore, a heavy mortar
cannot be trodden by one person's step;
a large millstone
cannot be pushed by one person's hand.
Worthy ministers possess the advantage of robustness,
while foolish rulers have the flaw of incompetence;
matching them together
is like making birds and fish swim together.
The blade of a Gānjiàng sword,
if not wielded and thrust,
cannot even injure a gourd;
arrows of fine bamboo,
if not set and released by a crossbow mechanism,
cannot pierce Lǔ's thin silk.
It is not for lack of Gānjiàng or fine bamboo talent,
but for lack of a master to wield and launch them,
that gourds and silk remain unpierced;
how then can one hope for the feat of cutting banners and piercing leather?
Thus, the strength to draw a bow cannot draw a strong crossbow.
A crossbow requiring five shí of force,
if drawn with only three shí,
will have its string snap and bones break,
unable to be raised.
Therefore, if strength cannot bear forceful pulling,
there is the disaster of mutation and a broken spine;
if wisdom cannot employ the worthy,
there is the failure of damaged virtue and ruined reputation.
Those who discuss affairs do not say that talent is great and the Way heavy,
and thus the ruler cannot employ it,
but claim the unworthy cannot promote themselves.
Those who self-promote are like belts that snap without resistance,
those who boast of themselves are like goods too cheap to sell.
Consider all objects made for human use -
they require human utilization
before their efficacy is established.
The chisel penetrates wood
through the mallet's strikes;
the spade can break earth
because feet tread upon it.
All bladed instruments
that can cut, slash, and carve
rely on hands to grip them
and strength to push and pull them.
When Hán Xìn left Chǔ for Hàn,
Xiàng Yǔ couldn't secure his loyalty,
yet Gāozǔ could maintain his service.
Being able to employ his talents
and stabilize his position,
then one could measure his strength
and distinguish his achievements.
Although Fán and Lì had merits of storming cities and fighting battles,
when Gāozǔ distributed rewards,
he first reached Xiāo Hé,
comparing Xiāo Hé to a hunter,
while equating Fán and Lì to hounds.
Now Xiāo Hé sat peacefully,
while Fán and Lì raced about -
rewards not going to the runners but first to the sitter
because Xiāo Hé used wisdom as strength,
while Fán and Lì used physical force as merit.
The reason Xiāo Hé could command Fán and Lì
was through collecting documents when entering Qín.
While other generals gathered gold,
he alone gathered texts,
thus understanding Qín's situation while seated,
thereby able to plan its advantages and disadvantages.
The other generals who raced about -
Xiāo Hé directed them.
Thus when Shūsūn Tōng established rituals,
Gāozǔ gained respect;
when Xiāo Hé created laws,
the Hàn dynasty achieved peace.
Consider the achievements of rituals and laws -
they outweigh battlefield victories;
the strength of beheading enemies
cannot match honoring the sovereign.
Therefore, plowing fields and growing grain
is the farmer's strength;
fierce attack in battle
is the soldier's strength;
constructing and carving
is the artisan's strength;
managing documents and records
is the clerk's strength;
discussing principles and debating governance
is the worthy scholar's strength.
All humans possess strength,
but what constitutes strength
may be noble or humble.
Though Confucius could lift the beam of the North Gate,
he didn't display his physical strength,
knowing that muscular power
is less glorious than the power of benevolence and righteousness.
A rich man's house,
with one zhang of space as its interior,
contains within it
chests and boxes overflowing with
silks, cloths, and fine fabrics.
A poor man's house,
also with one zhang as interior,
stands empty inside,
with only bare walls standing,
hence called poor.
The learned are like the rich,
the unlearned like the poor.
Both have seven-foot bodies,
but the learned carry the words of hundred schools in their hearts,
while the unlearned have empty bellies without a single text memorized -
the poor man's interior
with only four walls standing.
Considering wealth and poverty are incomparable,
so too are the learned and unlearned unmatched.
People admire wealth without honoring learning,
feel shame at poverty but not at lack of virtue -
they fail to reason by analogy.
The reason the rich are admirable
is that abundant goods bring prosperity,
hence people admire them.
But the rich are inferior to Confucian scholars,
and Confucian scholars inferior to the learned.
The learned accumulate writings, over ten cases worth,
containing the words of sages,
the sayings of worthies,
from the earliest Huángdì
down to Qín and Hàn,
methods for governing states and enriching families,
words criticizing eras and satirizing customs - all complete.
They enable people to understand clearly and see broadly -
their value for honor
is not merely like silks and fine fabrics.
When Xiāo Hé entered Qín
and gathered documents,
the reason Hàn could control the nine provinces
was through the power of documents.
Governing the world through documents -
the wealth of the world -
how can family wealth compare?
Eyes that don't see colors are called blind,
ears that don't hear notes are called deaf,
noses that don't smell scents are called blocked.
The blocked, deaf, and blind
are not complete persons.
Those who don't read extensively
hear nothing of past and present,
see no categories of events,
know not right from wrong -
they are like the blind, deaf, and blocked.
If Confucian scholars don't read widely,
they remain in darkness,
let alone commoners without literary works,
knowing not right from wrong -
their darkness is extreme.
These are like earthen figures
with complete eyes and ears
that hear and see nothing.
Those wading shallow water see shrimps,
those going somewhat deeper observe fish and turtles,
those going deepest behold flood dragons.
Footprints differ in depth,
hence what they see varies.
The depth of entering the Way
is just like this.
The shallow see biographies and common writings,
the deep enter the sage's chamber to view secret texts.
Therefore, the deeper one enters the Way,
the greater what one sees.
When people travel,
they necessarily want to enter cities,
for cities have many marvelous sights.
Entering cities, they necessarily want to see markets,
for markets have many exotic goods.
The words of hundred schools,
deeds of past and present -
their marvels and wonders
are not merely those of cities and great markets.
Those wandering cities satisfy their minds,
those viewing great markets fill their thoughts -
how much more those wandering among the ways and arts!
Great rivers don't dry in drought
because they have many channels;
stagnant ponds, after days without rain,
soon show mud
because they have no outlets.
Therefore, great rivers connect with each other,
small streams link together,
flowing east to return to the sea -
hence the sea is great.
If the sea didn't connect with hundred rivers,
how could it gain the name "immense"?
People containing the words of hundred schools
are like the sea embracing the flows of hundred rivers.
Not calling them great
means calling the sea smaller than the rivers.
That the sea is greater than rivers
is known by all,
but the learned understanding more than the unlearned -
none can distinguish this.
Moistening below creates saltiness -
this is water's flavor.
The eastern sea's water is salty
because its flow is vast;
the western region's salt wells
have deep springs.
Some people eat without wells,
others dig wells but find no springs -
do they have the benefit of salt wells?
Not connecting with the sages' works,
yet hoping for fame surpassing the age -
how difficult!
Legal experts
who don't see actual cases
judge crimes inaccurately;
textual scholars
who don't read past and present
discuss events unrealistically.
Some say studying one classic is sufficient -
why need extensive reading?
Now in Confucius' school,
they taught and studied the Five Classics,
and mastering all Five Classics
made one a talent of high promise.
The officials of the counties and towns,
summoned to the jurisdiction of their superiors,
were questioned about governance and transformation.
The wise and intelligent officials
presented what they had seen and heard,
enabling the generals and ministers to awaken and realize,
thus allowing for the reform of governance
and emphasis on culture. The words and deeds of sages and worthies,
recorded in bamboo and silk texts,
temper people's minds,
and sharpen people's knowledge—
these are not merely dialogues between county officials and their superiors.
Yǔ and Yì both managed the great flood,
with Yǔ primarily governing the waters
and Yì recording unusual phenomena.
Beyond the seas and across the mountains,
no distance was too far to reach;
based on what they saw and heard, they composed the "Classic of Mountains and Seas."
Had Yǔ and Yì not traveled far,
the "Classic of Mountains and Seas" would not have been created.
