Thus, the creation of the "Classic of Mountains and Seas"
arose from witnessing a vast array of things.
Dǒng Zhòngshū observed the bird of recurring omens,
and Liú Zǐzhèng understood the corpse of Èrfù,
both having seen the "Classic of Mountains and Seas,"
thus enabling them to establish theories about these two matters.
If Yǔ and Yì had not traveled far,
they could not have written the "Classic of Mountains and Seas";
if Dǒng and Liú had not read the "Classic of Mountains and Seas,"
they could not have resolved these two doubts.
Regarding Shíchén and Táiyí,
Zǐchǎn, being knowledgeable about many things,
could thus speak of them;
when the dragon appeared in Jiàng's outskirts,
Cài Mò, skilled in divination,
could thus control it.
When fathers and elder brothers are a thousand miles away,
and near death,
they leave behind instructive writings.
Worthy sons and younger brothers seek out and read these texts,
holding them close without abandoning them,
honoring ancestors and respecting elders
with great caution;
the unworthy, however, treat them lightly and neglect them,
lacking any intention to examine their origins.
The writings left by ancient sages and worthies for later generations
are far more significant than just the books of fathers and elder brothers.
Some may read and adopt them,
while others discard and ignore them.
The difference in standing between these two types
can be discussed even by passersby;
how much more should those who discern truth and falsehood be able to distinguish them?
When Confucius fell ill,
Shāng Qú divined that he would die by noon.
Confucius said,
"Bring the books;
what else is there to do before noon arrives?"
The sage's love for learning
did not cease even at death's door.
His thoughts were on the classics,
not abandoning the ways and arts
because of impending death.
That he became a sage for a hundred generations,
a model for learning and emulation, is indeed no empty claim!
From Confucius down to the Hàn period,
those renowned for their talent and ability
were not ones who ate their fill all day without applying their minds.
If not discussing the Five Classics, they were reading historical texts.
The texts and records are vast,
making it difficult to master them fully.
Divining hexagrams and predicting good or bad fortune
are all part of the ways of King Wén and King Wǔ.
In the past, Shāng Qú could interpret hexagrams;
later, Dōngfāng Shuò and Yì Shǎojūn could excel in divination and guessing concealed objects.
Though these arts may be minor,
they are still techniques of the sages,
yet some remain unaware of this.
Humans are endowed with the nature of the five constants,
fond of the Way and devoted to learning,
thus distinguishing themselves from other beings.
Nowadays, it is not so;
people eat their fill and drink to satisfaction,
thinking deeply only about seeking rest,
their bellies becoming pits for rice,
their intestines sacks for wine—
this is to be like mere objects.
Among the three hundred naked creatures,
humans are the leaders.
"Of all beings heaven and earth give life to,
humans are the most noble"
because of their knowledge and awareness.
If now they are closed off and obstructed,
without any desires or passions,
how do they differ from the three hundred naked creatures?
How can they be called leaders and considered noble?
The reason the people of the central states are more esteemed than barbarians
is their understanding of the texts on benevolence and righteousness
and their knowledge of ancient and modern learning.
If they merely rely on their innate wit to secure food and clothing,
passing through the years
until old age and death,
remaining unenlightened till the end,
they are no better than barbarians.
Observe how spiders spin silk to trap flying insects—
can human creations
surpass this?
Relying on innate wit,
wielding deceit for power and profit,
to seek the joys of wealth and longevity
without knowledge of ancient and modern learning
makes one no different from a spider.
All blood-bearing creatures
avoid the peril of starvation,
as they can use their wits to seek food and drink.
Even those without learning
can support themselves;
serving as officials or clerks,
they may attain high positions.
Generals, ministers, and senior officials
are like our dignitaries and nobles—
how can one distinguish them?
Accumulating merits over time,
gaining office by fate,
ignorant of ancient and modern affairs,
deeming themselves worthy by position alone,
their methods differ from those of the learned.
How can they recognize the truly knowledgeable
and treat them with exceptional respect?
If generals, ministers, and senior officials
are not like Cài Bóxié of Yòufúfēng,
Zhāng Mèngcháng, governor of Yùlín,
or Lǐ Jìgōng, governor of Dōnglái, and their kind,
whose minds are naturally enlightened,
well-versed in ancient and modern times,
then they would respect the knowledgeable as if receiving honored guests.
Why did Yān Zhāo sweep the path for Zōu Yǎn?
What unique nature did he alone possess?
Dǒng Zhòngshòu, magistrate of Dōngchéng, knew he was an outstanding scholar,
renowned throughout the land as knowledgeable,
thus in his interactions, he could recognize the extraordinary.
Hence, Zhōnglí Chǎngōng, a commoner among the populace,
received the reverence due to jade and precious stones,
a testament to clear understanding.
Therefore, when one has understanding,
even ordinary stones emit light;
without understanding,
even gold and jade lack luster.
From Emperor Wǔ's reign to the present court,
numerous recommendations of worthy and talented individuals
have required them to answer policy questions in graded categories.
Like Dǒng Zhòngshū, Táng Zǐgāo,
Gǔ Zǐyún, and Dīng Bóyù,
their responses were substantial and accurate,
their writings elegant and excellent,
born from extensive learning and rich knowledge.
Had these four only been able to recite classics
or merely take notes,
without reading ancient and modern books,
how could they have established excellence in the court of a sage king?
During Emperor Míng's time in the Hàn,
upon reading the "Biography of Sū Wǔ,"
and seeing the official title "Supervisor of the Yízhōng Palace,"
he asked all officials about it,
yet none knew.
The "Cāngjié" primer,
a foundational text for elementary learning,
contains all the essential characters,
yet they could not answer the sovereign's question—
this shows that many in office are merely those who gained position through routine appointments.
If they cannot even recognize the character with "wood" and "many" beside it,
how can they hope to match Dǒng Zhòngshū's knowledge of recurring omens
or Liú Zǐzhèng's understanding of Èrfù? It is difficult indeed!
Some say,
"The posts for the knowledgeable,
like the Lántái court historians,
are tasked with collating texts and determining characters.
Compared to the Grand Historian or Grand Invocator,
their duties lie in documents,
with no role in governing the people,
thus offering no practical application.
Therefore, historians of the Lántái,
such as Bān Gù, Jiǎ Kuí, Yáng Zhōng, Fù Yì, and their peers,
though renowned for their fragrant names and beautiful writings,
accumulate without being bound,
are of little use to the world."
The response is:
This is not consistent.
In the Zhōu era, those of broad learning,
like Zōu Yǎn and his followers,
or Xúnzǐ and his contemporaries,
received the favor of the kings of their time,
honored and prominent in the world.
Though Dǒng Zhòngshū did not hold a position among the three highest ministers,
his wisdom surpassed that of the dukes and ministers.
The Zhōu dynasty modeled itself upon the two preceding dynasties,
and the Hàn dynasty modeled itself upon the Zhōu and Qín.
Thus, the officials of the Orchid Terrace
are those by whom the state examines successes and failures.
Just as the heart is like a pellet or egg,
serving as the inner store of the body;
and the pupils are like beans,
providing the body's light and clarity;
so, although the clerks and historians may be humble,
they oversee the state's repository of the Dào,
and it is through them that the learned men advance,
much like the academicians' office,
through which the Confucian scholars arise.
If their accumulated works remain unbound,
is it because the sage state neglects them?
It is probably because the writings are not yet finalized and their duties not yet completed.
Those who master over a thousand chapters of texts,
up to ten thousand scrolls,
who broadly comprehend the elegant and refined,
who critically examine and determine the readings of texts,
and who teach others as masters,
are learned men.
Those who weave together their meanings and purposes,
refining and editing their phrases,
and who present memorials and reports to the court,
or who initiate discussions, establish theories, and connect chapters into works,
are literary men and great Confucians.
Those who love learning and diligently exert themselves,
with broad knowledge and strong memory,
are abundant in the world;
but those who write books and express themselves in writing,
discussing and evaluating past and present,
are not one in ten thousand.
Thus, writing books and expressing in writing
are what the broadly learned can utilize.
Enter the mountains and see the trees:
their lengths and shortness, none unknown;
enter the wilds and see the grasses:
their sizes, none unrecognized.
Yet, if one cannot fell trees to build houses,
or pick herbs to compound prescriptions,
this is knowing the plants but being unable to use them.
Now, the learned man sees broadly and extensively,
but if he cannot extract and discuss,
this is to be a hidden owner of living books,
like what Confucius called, "Recite the three hundred Poems,
yet when entrusted with governance, cannot succeed,"
which is the same as being unable to fell or gather those plants.
Confucius obtained the Historical Records to compose the Spring and Autumn Annals,
and when he established principles and created ideas,
praising, blaming, rewarding, and condemning,
he no longer relied on the Historical Records,
for his subtle thoughts emerged from his own breast.
In general, what is valued in being learned
is the ability to use that knowledge.
If one merely recites and reads,
reciting poems and chanting techniques, even if over a thousand chapters,
it is like a parrot's ability to speak.
To elaborate on the meanings of transmitted texts,
and produce rich and elegant phrases,
requires extraordinary talent,
which not everyone can undertake.
Those who broadly survey
are relatively common in the world;
those who write literary works
are rare through the ages.
In recent times, Liú Xiàng and his son, Liú Xīn,
Yáng Xióng, and Huán Tán,
are like King Wén, King Wǔ, and the Duke of Zhōu
appearing together in one era;
others who are truly capable
are often like this,
comparable to pearls and jades, which cannot be abundantly found,
due to their rarity.
Therefore, those who can expound one classic are Confucian scholars;
those who broadly study past and present are learned men;
those who gather from transmitted texts to present memorials and reports are literary men;
those who can deeply ponder, write, and connect chapters are great Confucians.
Thus, Confucian scholars surpass common people,
learned men excel Confucian scholars,
literary men exceed learned men,
and great Confucians transcend literary men.
Therefore, the great Confucians
are what we call those who transcend and transcend again.
With the extraordinariness of their transcendence,
if compared back with Confucian scholars,
it is like an ornate carriage compared to a broken cart,
or brocade and embroidery compared to a wadded robe;
the gap between them is vast.
If compared with common people,
the peak of Tài Mountain and its base,
or the head and feet of the tall Dí people,
are not enough to illustrate it.
Thus, hills and mountains have earth and stone as their substance,
but if they contain copper or iron,
that is the extraordinariness of the mountain.
If copper and iron are extraordinary,
some may yield gold or jade.
Now, great Confucians
are the gold and jade of the world,
extraordinary and yet more extraordinary.
Extraordinary and yet more extraordinary,
their talents transcend and surpass,
each with degrees of difference.
Confucian scholars make a name in the Confucian school,
far surpassing common people.
Some cannot expound a single classic
or teach the younger generation.
Some gather disciples and crowds,
their discussions profound and overflowing,
and are called clear in the classics.
Some cannot complete a document
or develop a single theory.
Some can present successes and failures,
submit expedient proposals,
their words corresponding to classics and commentaries,
their writing like stars and the moon.
The highest among them, like Gǔ Yún
and Táng Zǐgāo,
expound texts in documents and memorials,
but cannot connect chapters into works.
Some draw upon and arrange past and present,
recording and describing events,
like Sīmǎ Qiān and Liú Xiàng and their peers,
accumulating chapters and volumes,
their writings numbering in the tens of thousands,
far surpassing Yáng Zǐyún
and Zǐgāo;
yet, they rely on completed records of the past,
without creation from their own breast.
As for Lù Jiǎ and Dǒng Zhòngshū, who discuss contemporary affairs,
their thoughts emerge from their intent,
without borrowing from external sources,
yet they are shallow and obvious,
and those who read them still call them biographies.
Yángchéng Zǐcháng composed the Classic of Music,
Yáng Zǐyún composed the Classic of the Supreme Mystery,
creating from subtle thought,
reaching the depths of the profound and obscure,
which cannot be accomplished
without near-sagely talent.
Confucius composed the Spring and Autumn Annals,
these two men composed two classics,
what we call toweringly following in Confucius's footsteps,
with grand and splendid talent matching that of the sages.
A noble asked Huán Tán about Yáng Zǐyún.
Jūnshān replied:
"Since the rise of the Hàn,
there has been no one like him."
Jūnshān's assessment of talent
can be said to have captured the reality of high and low.
The jade seeker's heart admires jade,
the tortoise shell diviner can know the divine through the tortoise.
To be able to assess the talents of many scholars,
rank them high and low,
is to be wiser than those ranked.
He also composed the New Discourses,
discussing worldly affairs,
distinguishing and illuminating right and wrong,
so that false and baseless words,
deceptive and embellished phrases,
are all verified and settled.
Among those like Zǐcháng and Zǐyún, who engage in discussions,
Jūnshān is the foremost.
Since Jūnshān's time,
all have been talents of profound subtlety,
hence there are excellent and fine writings.
If the brush can write,
then the mind can strategize and discuss,
writing emerges from the breast,
the mind expresses itself through writing.
Observing their writings,
extraordinary, grand, and unparalleled,
one can say they have mastered discourse.
From this perspective,
those with abundant writings
are the outstanding among men.
Just as there are roots and trunks below,
and flourishing leaves above;
as there are solid kernels within,
and husks and shells without;
so, literary compositions and rhetoric
are the flourishing leaves and husks of scholars.
Sincere substance lies in the breast,
literary ink is set on bamboo and silk,
the outer and inner, surface and core,
naturally correspond and match.
When intent is fervent, the brush flows freely,
so the writing reveals and the substance is exposed.
That humans possess writing
is like birds having feathers.
Feathers have five colors,
all growing from the body.
If there is literary form without substance,
it is like a bird of five colors
with feathers growing in vain.
Selecting scholars through archery,
one must have a calm mind and upright posture,
hold the bow and arrows steadily and firmly,
and only then can one hit the target.
The expression of discourse and argument
is like the release of a bow and arrows.
A theory conforming to reason
is like an arrow hitting the target.
Archery demonstrates skill through arrows hitting the mark,
while discourse proves its excellence through writing.
Both excellence and skill originate from the mind,
their essence is one.
Some writings contain profound intentions and grand strategies,
methods for rulers and ministers to govern,
which they cannot implement personally,
nor divulge verbally,
so they express their innermost thoughts
to demonstrate their capability to achieve them.
Confucius composed the "Spring and Autumn Annals"
to convey the kingly intent.
Thus, Confucius's "Spring and Autumn Annals"
is the work of an uncrowned king;
the writings of the various philosophers
are the affairs of uncrowned ministers.
Observe the "Spring and Autumn Annals" to see the kingly intent,
read the philosophers to perceive the ministers' purposes.
Hence it is said:
When Chén Píng divided the meat,
the makings of a chancellor were seen;
when Sūn Shū'áo dredged the Qīsī River,
the signs of a prime minister emerged.
Reading the texts of the philosophers,
their governance and administrative affairs,
are not merely omens like dividing meat or dredging rivers.
If the feet are not strong, the tracks will not go far;
if the blade is not sharp, the cut will not be deep.
Connecting chapters and composing texts
must be done by those of great wisdom and profound virtue.
Some say:
Those who write books,
being widely read and knowledgeable,
and skilled in learning,
can then infer categories and produce writing.
Writing arises from external influences,
and may not necessarily match true talent.
Moreover, superficial ideas in flowery words,
without deep roots,
fail to grasp the essence of the great Way,
hence few achieve merit.
In times of safety and danger,
literati do not participate,
having no proof of ability to achieve merit,
but only the effect of wielding the brush.
The response is:
This is not so.
In the Zhou dynasty, writers were all strategizing ministers;
in the Han dynasty, forthright scholars were all well-read officials.
How can one say that writing is not the growth of flowers and leaves,
pushed forth from roots?
Thoughts in the mind form plans,
collected on slips they become writing;
emotions appear in the phrasing,
intentions are verified in the words.
Shāng Yāng served as minister of Qín,
achieving success in hegemony,
and wrote the "Book on Plowing and War";
Yú Qīng for Zhào, having decided plans and established proposals that were implemented,
retired and composed the "Spring and Autumn Annals of Master Yú".
The thoughts in the "Spring and Autumn Annals" arose from debates within Zhào's walls;
the "Book on Plowing and War"
contained strategies from Qín's court.
Lù Jiǎ dispelled the plots of the Lǚ family,
with the same intent as in his "New Discourses";
Huán Jūnshān altered Cháo Cuò's policies,
sharing the same thought as in his "New Treatise".
Observing Gǔ Yǒng's submissions,
Táng Lín's straightforward words,
Liú Xiàng's critical discussions,
all based on knowledge as foundation,
their writings with brush and ink
were presented and conveyed—
how could they be merely carving patterns and adorning phrases,
recklessly producing flowery words?
Sincerity comes from within,
hence their words deeply move people.
Thus, when Lǔ Lián sent a swift letter,
the Yān general committed suicide;
when Zōu Yáng submitted a memorial,
Liáng Xiào opened the prison.
The meaning in letters and memorials,
wrenched from the liver and heart,
is not something that the merely well-read can create,
nor the merely skilled can produce.
Great Confucians are rare,
while literati are common;
should not generals, ministers, and senior officials
value them highly?
How can they only use their talents
to wander among documents and records?
When provinces and commanderies face troubles,
they can draft memorials and submissions,
resolve complexities and troubles,
leaving the provinces and commanderies without issues.
With officials like Táng Zigāo and Gǔ Ziyún,
who devote themselves fully to thought,
exhausting the power of brush and record,
how could there be troubles that remain unresolved?
In the distant ancient past,
with remote regions in all directions,
literate scholars
were rarely recorded,
but let us take closer, from Kuàijī, for example.
There was one Zhōu Chángshēng,
a hero among literary scholars,
in the province, he drafted submissions for Inspector Rèn Ān;
in the commandery, he wrote memorials for Grand Administrator Mèng Guān.
Affairs were resolved and worries removed,
the province and commandery were untroubled,
and both generals were preserved.
Chángshēng himself did not attain honor and prominence,
not because his talent and wisdom were lacking or his efforts weak,
but because the two generals held the principles of common men,
and could not value him.
Had he encountered a former age like that of Yān Zhāo,
then Chángshēng would have enjoyed the favor that Zōu Yǎn received.
After Chángshēng's death,
when provinces and commanderies faced troubles,
there were no officials to draft submissions,
hence affairs remained tangled and unresolved,
summonses and assignments followed one another,
literary standards were not honored,
and brush and memorial did not continue.
Was it that there were no officials concerned for their superiors?
Rather, their writing and brushwork were not adequate to emulate.
Chángshēng's talent
was not only sharp in documents and records;
he composed the "Comprehensive Calendar" in ten chapters,
covering from the Yellow Emperor above
down to the Hàn dynasty,
recording even matters as fine as hair and feathers,
similar to Grand Historian's "Tables" and "Annals".
Connecting above and reaching below,
hence it was called "Comprehensive Calendar".
Thus, Chángshēng was not merely a literatus,
but what is called a great Confucian.
In earlier times, there was Yán Fūzǐ,
later there was Wú Jūngāo,
and lastly there was Zhōu Chángshēng.
The white pheasant was tribute from Yuè,
the flourishing grass was offered from Yuān,
jade came from Yōng Province,
gold was produced in Jīng and Yáng.
Precious things are produced in the four distant quarters,
in remote and secluded lands—one cannot say there are no extraordinary people.
Confucius said:
"King Wén is gone;
is not culture (wén) now here?"
King Wén's culture lay in Confucius,
Confucius's culture lay in Dǒng Shū;
since Dǒng Shū has died,
does it not lie in followers like Chángshēng?
How exceptional their words are,
how beautiful their writing!
Táng Lè and Sòng Yù,
also literary men of Chǔ,
are not recorded in bamboo and silk
because Qū Yuán stands above them.
As for literary talent in Kuàijī, how could it reside solely in Zhōu Chángshēng?
The reason others are not discussed here
is that Chángshēng was especially outstanding.
Among the nine provinces are many mountains,
yet Huà and Dài are the sacred peaks;
in the four directions are many rivers,
yet the Jiāng and Hé are the great streams—
because Huà and Dài are high, and Jiāng and Hé are vast.
Chángshēng
is the high and vast one among provinces and commanderies.
If an elder of one's own clan is worthy,
yet one abandons him to praise an elder of another clan,
that is not right.
Chángshēng is the leading master of literary expression,
revered by all literati;
to record him alone
follows the principle of the "Spring and Autumn Annals" beginning its chronology with Lǔ.
The common tendency is to admire antiquity and praise what one has heard of it.
The works of earlier people,
even if they were like bland vegetables and fruits, are considered sweet;
while what later people newly create,
even if it were honeyed cheese, is deemed bitter and acrid.
Chángshēng lived in Kuàijī,
born in the present age;
although his writings are exceptional,
critics still say they are immature compared to those of earlier people.
Heaven endows the primal breath,
humans receive the essential spirit—
how can there be a degradation based on ancient versus modern times?
The superior is esteemed as high,
the enlightened is regarded as supreme.
Those who deal with facts,
who perceive the distinction between right and wrong,
upon seeing error,
push the former back and place it behind;
upon seeing truth,
promote the modern and advance it to the status of the ancient.
Their minds are clear and their understanding bright,
unswayed by common opinions.
Bān Shūpí continued the "Records of the Grand Historian" with over a hundred chapters,
recording events in detail and thoroughly,
with principles透彻 and reasoning complete.
Those who read it consider it first-rate,
while the Grand Historian's work is placed second.
His son Bān Gù, who served as a Secretary in the Imperial Secretariat,
in literary merit compared to Shūpí, is not merely a small fiefdom of five hundred li,
but rather like the states of Zhōu, Shào, Lǔ, and Wèi.
If one were to solely esteem antiquity,
then the Bān father and son would not be worth recording.
The Zhōu dynasty had its flourishing culture
at the end of a hundred generations.
The Hàn dynasty, coming after a hundred generations,
in its literary discussions and rhetorical expressions,
how could it not be lush?
Using the small to illustrate the large,
inferring from common people's affairs
to perceive the principles of the royal court.
When a house is first built,
and mulberries and hemp have just been planted,
after residing there for years,
with descendants continuing one after another,
peach, plum, apricot, and other trees
will cover the hills and fields.
With numerous roots and stems,
the flowers and leaves flourish abundantly.
The Hàn dynasty has long been stable in its governance,
with vast territory and a populous people;
righteous causes arise and events unfold—
how could the words, like flowers and leaves, not be plentiful?
Flowers and fruits are both produced together;
for fruit to grow without flowers
is rare among things.
If a mountain is bald,
how can it be lush?
If land is parched,
how can it be fertile?
The literary figures
who flourish in the Hàn court
are indeed an auspicious sign of the Hàn dynasty's prosperity.
When the sky is clear,
the constellations shine brilliantly;
during overcast rain,
the sun and moon are hidden.
The emergence of many literary talents today
is clear evidence of the Hàn dynasty's brilliance.
Emperor Gāozǔ read Lù Jiǎ's writings
and exclaimed in admiration, shouting "Long live!";
Xú Yuè and Zhǔfù Yǎn submitted memorials,
and were appointed as Imperial Attendants—
such things are not heard of now.
If a meal lacks bitter or sour dishes,
and the mouth finds no flavor pleasing,
one would not lift it to feed others.
Whenever an imperial edict is issued,
its literary meaning draws from the classics and the four disciplines;
the edicts are elegantly composed,
a clear testament to a love for refined culture.
If memorials lack substance and verification,
and writings have no moral purpose,
then the exclamation "Long live!"
and the favor of "appointment"
—from where would they arise?
All who adorn their faces wish to look beautiful,
but few can captivate the eye;
all who listen to music desire it to be moving,
but rare are those that startle the ear.
Before Lù Jiǎ's writings were presented,
and before the strategies of Xú Yuè and Zhǔfù Yǎn were heard,
the crowd of those who speak blindly,
with their crude and ugly discussions of affairs,
writings unrefined and unpolished,
failing to point to the intended meaning,
and language that is frivolous and slippery—
if they escape the condemnation of being like sand in the waves,
they are fortunate indeed!
How could they receive the honor of appointment as Imperial Attendants?
Considering the talent of worthy Confucians,
it already surpasses the standard.
People wonder why they do not advance in official posts,
remaining in low and minor positions.
That worthy talents are relegated behind common clerks
is indeed not surprising.
In this way,
it sufficiently reveals the distinction between the worthy and the unworthy,
showing the reality of who is high or low, and in what measure.
A turtle lives three hundred years,
growing as large as a coin,
swimming on lotus leaves.
At three thousand years, its edges turn green,
and it reaches over a foot in length.
The yarrow plant produces one stalk at seventy years,
and ten stalks at seven hundred years.
These are spiritual beings,
hence they grow slowly and linger,
passing through long years,
and thus can achieve clarity and discernment.
Truly, worthy Confucians in the world
are like the divine yarrow and the spiritual turtle.
Counting the days devoted to learning,
they have already spent half their lives.
Focused intently on the Way,
they thus have no greedy desire for office.
When they do take office,
they are purely upright and principled,
lacking the sharp edge for adaptation.
Hence, people find them slow to advance and difficult to promote.
What a needle or awl pierces
always passes through smoothly.
If the tip of a needle or awl were squared,
it could not penetrate an object even a tenth of an inch.
Worthy Confucians act with squared integrity,
without the sharpness of a needle or awl;
how could they possibly pierce through on their own and achieve smooth success?
Moreover, a steed that travels a thousand li in a day
carries no burden;
if made to pull a heavy cart,
it becomes like a common horse.
In the past, such a steed was once used to pull a salt cart,
hanging its head, sweating profusely,
unable to move forward.
When Bólè noticed it,
and Wáng Liáng drove it,
free and lightly galloping,
it then gained fame for a thousand li.
Now, worthy Confucians, possessing learning of past and present,
bearing the weight of ritual and righteousness,
internally burdened by the knowledge in their hearts,
externally toiling with the conduct of ritual righteousness,
dare not recklessly advance or seek gain improperly;
thus, they face the difficulty of delay.
Without the friendship of a Bólè,
or encountering a commander like Wáng Liáng,
how can they gallop in a clear and enlightened court and leave a thousand-li trail?
Furthermore, in the life of creatures with blood and breath,
when active, the back is above and the belly below;
when ill or dead,
the back is below and the belly above.
Why is that?
Because the back's flesh is thick and heavy,
while the belly's flesh is thin and light.
Worthy Confucians and common clerks
coexist in the present age,
resembling this.
When the Way is to be illuminated and practiced,
then common clerks carry worthy Confucians,
and worthy Confucians ride upon common clerks.
When the Way is to be obscured and abandoned,
then common clerks ride upon worthy Confucians,
with worthy Confucians in lower positions,
like objects harmed,
the belly above and the back below.
Moreover, the back models heaven and the belly models earth;
in life, activity follows the correct order,
so belly and back are in their proper places;
in sickness or death, the proper order is lost,
hence the belly turns and lies upon the back.
Not only the belly,
but in all things that fall and stiffen,
the feet are also above.
Worthy Confucians, unmet by opportunity,
fall and are cast aside in the world,
while restless-footed clerks
all stand above them.
Dōngfāng Shuò said:
"If the eyes are not on the face but on the feet,
one cannot even save them from being blinded by dust—
what can they see?"
Jí Àn said to Emperor Wǔ:
"Your Majesty's appointment of officials is like piling up firewood;
those who come later end up on top."
Reflecting on Jí Àn's words
and examining Dōngfāng Shuò's statement,
is it not that vulgar clerks gain positions, while worthy Confucians lose their posts?
Thus, in officialdom,
without position,
it is hard to observe virtue;
with position,
it is hard to detect incompetence.
Fame arises from high office, while slander springs from lowly status.
Lowly status is often where worthy Confucians reside.
Following rituals and adhering to principles,
cultivating oneself and upholding integrity,
they do not anxiously seek advancement when in humble positions,
hence they remain stagnant.
Stagnation lies in their ability to sustain themselves,
so they face unshakable obstacles.
They accumulate much learning within themselves,
thus their minds are steadfast.
Vulgar clerks have no means of self-cultivation;
though they may be promoted,
their greedy hearts waver,
leading to corrupt practices of exploitation.
Maple and tung trees,
growing rapidly,
have bark and wood that cannot become hard.
The sandalwood tree grows leaves in the fifth month,
later than trees that flourish in spring,
yet its timber is strong and resilient,
used for cart axles.
The mulberry and paper mulberry of the Yīn dynasty,
reached an arm's span in seven days,
growing too fast and violently,
thus became omens of abnormality.
Great vessels take time to complete;
treasured goods are hard to sell.
What is priced and sold in a single morning
are mere vegetables and fruits.
Thus, in a rushing stream,
sand and stones are carried along, but large rocks remain unmoved.
Why?
Because large rocks are heavy, while sand and stones are light.
Sand and stones accumulate over the large rocks,
burying them from sight.
Worthy Confucians and vulgar clerks,
both exist in the worldly sphere,
are similar to this.
When encountering ignorant high officials,
vulgar clerks are promoted, rising above worthy Confucians,
who remain in low positions,
tasked with menial errands,
or even dwelling in caves and cliffs,
unseen for life.
The fault lies with the high officials' inability to recognize worth,
and because the way of the worthy is vast,
their strength is too weak to uplift them.
As for lifting objects with fingers,
if one's strength is insufficient to raise them,
one dares not move them.
The way of worthy Confucians
is not merely the weight of objects.
Thus, metal and iron on the ground
cannot be moved by a whirlwind,
while feathers and dust among them can fly a thousand miles.
What worthy Confucians embody,
is like large rocks in water
or metal and iron on land.
Their advancement is not as swift as that of vulgar clerks
because high officials' strength is weak,
incapable of employing them.
Feathers and dust among iron and stones
can be blown by a single breath,
not necessarily a gale.
Vulgar clerks are easily promoted,
just as feathers and dust are easily blown.
Thus, what moves sand and stones
is the rushing stream;
what flies feathers and dust
is the whirlwind.
In calm water,
sand and stones do not move;
in gentle breeze,
feathers and dust stay still.
Commanders without principle,
with violent and base intentions,
do not scrutinize officials carefully,
promoting them recklessly,
granting offices and titles arbitrarily—
like fierce waters moving sand and stones,
or whirlwinds flying feathers and dust.
Thus, feathers and dust fly due to strange winds,
sand and stones are carried by violent currents,
and vulgar clerks are promoted under misguided commanders.
Moreover, round objects thrown to the ground
roll east, west, north, or south without restraint,
but stop with a slight tap of a cane.
Square objects land
and stay put with one throw;
to move them,
they require someone to lift them.
Worthy Confucians
are the square objects of the world;
hard to move,
they require human effort to shift.
Birds are more agile than humans,
covering long distances—
humans cannot match birds,
yet by the nature of heaven and earth,
humans are the most noble.
Locusts in flight
can travel ten thousand miles,
while qílín must be presented
to reach the palace gates;
yet locusts bring disaster,
and qílín are auspicious signs.
The qílín has four legs
but cannot reach on its own;
humans have two legs—
how can they reach by themselves?
Thus it is said:
"Swallows fly more lightly than fènghuáng,
hares run faster than qílín,
frogs leap more frantically than divine turtles,
snakes dart more swiftly than sacred dragons."
Followers of Lǚ Wàng
only gained fame in old age;
the wisdom of Bǎilǐ Xī
shone in his white-haired years.
Those who deeply plan for the state
and become royal assistants
are all people of substance, hard to advance.
Those who are frivolous and achieve early
face sudden disasters and rapid ruin.
Hence it is said:
"Those who advance sharply retreat quickly."
Warm weather and cold spells
take months to arrive;
disastrous auras
become omens in a single morning.
Thus, the freezing of a river
is not from one day's cold;
piling earth into a mountain
is not the work of a moment.
The sword Gānjiàng,
long in the furnace's fire,
with sharp blade and edge,
tempered a hundred times—
long forging reveals
its delayed completion;
slowness in making enables it to cut.
Flesh that grows rapidly is called a tumor;
a spring that bursts forth is called a gush;
wine that ferments quickly sours easily;
vinegar that turns sour rapidly spoils easily.
From this, it can be said:
the delay of worthy Confucians
all has its reasons.
What are these reasons?
Abundant learning and weighty principles become burdens to oneself.
Living plants and trees are moist,
and moist things are heavy;
dead ones are dry,
and dry things are light.
Dry, light things are easy to lift;
moist, heavy ones are hard to move.
Yet the vital energy resides
in the living, not the dead.
Thus, carts on land
and boats in canals—
the full and heavy move slowly,
the empty and light move swiftly.
The way of the ancient kings,
carried within the heart and mind,
is heavy, not just the load of boats and carts.
Bearing such weight,
their rapid advancement is difficult.
Stealing others' belongings—
the gain is not without speed,
yet it is not rightfully theirs,
acquired not by their own strength.
Those who gain high office early in life
may have glory,
but the slander of holding sinecures and feeding idly
is exceedingly loud.
Moreover, the reason virtuous Confucian scholars fail to advance
is that high officials and local administrators do not foster open communication.
When farmers transport grain to the capital
and merchants carry goods to distant lands,
they all seek to fulfill their aspirations.
If the city gates are closed and impassable,
or bridges are broken and uncrossable,
even with strenuous efforts to seize opportunities,
how could they arrive early to gain profit?
When administrators are jealous of the worthy
and incapable of tolerating goodness,
to escape the punishment of fetters and scarlet prison garments
is already fortunate.
How dare one hope for official promotion
or the early achievement of moral principles?
Those who explain the cold and warmth say:
"When the ruler is pleased, it becomes warm;
when angry, it turns cold."
Why so?
Because joy and anger emanate from within his breast,
then manifest outwardly,
resulting in rewards and punishments.
Rewards and punishments
are the effects of joy and anger,
hence extreme cold or warmth
withers things and harms people.
Yet the alternation of cold and warmth
occurs within a few days,
without the ruler necessarily having emotions of joy or anger arising in his breast
before manifesting intensely externally.
Observing the external cold or warmth,
one then knows the energy within his breast.
When the ruler experiences joy or anger,
the energy in his breast may not necessarily correspond to cold or warmth.
How does the energy in his breast
differ from the energy within the borders?
If the energy in his breast
does not change with joy or anger,
then how does the cold or warmth within the borders
come about?
During the era of the Six States,
and at the transition between Qín and Hàn,
when feudal lords attacked each other
and weapons filled the roads,
states harbored mutual aggression and anger,
generals possessed ambitions to conquer,
and soldiers had杀气,
yet the world at that time was not necessarily constantly cold.
In the peaceful age,
during the time of Táng and Yú,
when governance was proper and people tranquil,
and the ruler was consistently joyful,
with stringed music, songs, drumming, and dancing
found in every household,
the world at that time was not necessarily constantly warm.
Could it be that the energy of joy and anger
manifests for minor triggers but not major movements?
Why does it not align with actual events?
Now, proximity to water makes one cold,
proximity to fire makes one warm,
and the effect diminishes with distance.
Why?
Because the influence of energy
varies with distance.
Established facts:
Fire's position is in the south,
water's position is in the north,
hence the northern regions are cold,
and the southern extreme is hot.
Fire in a stove,
water in a ditch,
energy in a body—
their essence is the same.
When the ruler experiences joy or anger,
the energy of cold or warmth
should be strongest within the women's quarters
and faintest beyond the borders.
But examining cold and warmth, they are uniform inside and outside;
this is likely not caused by the ruler's joy or anger.
The explanations of contemporary Confucians
are thus mistaken.
The transformations of the king affect the entire world,
those of feudal lords affect their domains,
those of ministers and high officials affect their positions,
and those of commoners affect their households.
If households can induce changes,
then joy and anger should also be able to induce energies.
When father and son are angry with each other,
or husband and wife reprimand one another,
if anger should turn to joy,
or faults are condoned and wrongs concealed,
within that single room,
there ought to be corresponding cold or warmth.
From this perspective,
it is clear that changes are not produced by joy or anger.
Some say:
"It is attraction by category.
Joy is harmonious and warm,
harmony and warmth bring rewards,
the way of Yang bestows,
Yang energy is warm,
so warm energy responds to it.
Anger is resentment and fury,
resentment and fury lead to executions,
the way of Yin is severe and lethal,
Yin energy is cold,
so cold energy responds to it.
When a tiger roars, the valley wind arrives;
when a dragon rises, auspicious clouds gather.
Same energy, shared category,
movements attract each other,
hence it is said: 'The form chases the shadow,
the dragon brings rain.'
Rain comes in response to the dragon,
the shadow follows the form,
such is the nature of heaven and earth,
the way of spontaneity.
In autumn and winter, punishments are carried out,
minor cases are slightly reduced,
major executions peak in severe cold,
cold follows punishment—
the mutual attraction is evident."
Now, comparing cold and warmth to wind and clouds,
equating joy and anger with dragons and tigers,
same energy, shared category,
movements attracting each other—this is acceptable.
When a tiger roars,
wind arises from that valley;
when a dragon rises,
clouds form within a hundred lǐ.
Other valleys and different places
have no such wind or clouds.
But changes in cold and warmth
occur simultaneously everywhere.
If punishments are applied in one hundred lǐ,
cold pervades a thousand lǐ—
this is hardly verifiable.
Qí and Lǔ share a border,
yet if rewards and punishments are simultaneous,
suppose Qí rewards and Lǔ punishes,
the effects should differ;
could it be that Qí becomes warm and Lǔ turns cold at that moment?
Consider past users of punishment:
Chīyóu and the fallen Qín were extreme.
Under Chīyóu, the people
were chaotic and confused;
on the roads of fallen Qín,
red-clad convicts stood shoulder to shoulder,
yet the world then was not necessarily constantly cold.
In the capital's market,
where cattle and sheep are slaughtered
by the hundreds daily,
with executioners killing animals,
all having harmful intent,
the energy in the capital's market
does not turn cold.
Some say:
"Humans are nobler than things,
only humans can stir energy."
Is it the executioner who stirs the energy,
or the one being punished who causes the change?
If it's the executioner,
punishing people or killing animals
involves the same mindset.
If it's the one being punished,
humans and animals are both beings,
all part of the myriad things—
can a hundred lowly beings not equal one noble?
Some say:
"Only the ruler can stir energy,
the masses cannot."
If energy response must come from the ruler,
why does the world praise Zōu Yǎn?
Zōu Yǎn was a commoner,
one man stirring energy,
yet the world affirms it.
Does punishing one person make it cold,
or sparing one make it warm?
When amnesty decrees are issued far and wide,
and myriad punishments are all remitted,
the energy of that time does not warm.
In past years, when ten thousand households caught fire,
flames leapt to the sky;
when the river burst its banks for a thousand lǐ,
the view was boundless in all directions.
Fire shares the nature of warmth,
while water belongs to the category of cold.
When fires break out or rivers burst their banks,
there is neither cold nor warmth.
Thus, the arrival of cold and warmth
is hardly caused by governance.
Yet when cold and warmth arrive,
they coincide with rewards and punishments,
leading prognosticators
to associate them accordingly.
Spring brings warmth, summer heat,
autumn coolness, and winter cold—
even if rulers do nothing,
the four seasons proceed naturally.
Since the four seasons are not governed by policies,
how can cold and warmth alone respond to governance?
At the start of the first month,
after the New Year begins,
around the beginning of spring,
all punishments are concluded,
and prisons stand empty,
yet cold and warmth still alternate.
When it turns cold,
what punishment could have caused it?
When it turns warm,
what reward could have induced it?
From this perspective,
cold and warmth
are seasonal rhythms of heaven and earth,
not man-made—
this is clear.
When people suffer from chills or fever,
it is not due to their conduct.
Exposed to wind and elements,
their bodies develop cold or warmth.
Even if they change their behavior,
the cold or warmth remains.
If one cannot cure an ailment in one's own body,
how much less a distant state or city,
whose atmosphere could one regulate?
When a person is afflicted by cold,
they take medicine for relief,
and the discomfort gradually subsides;
if it turns into a warm illness,
swallowing sweat-inducing pills should cure it.
In Yān there was a cold valley
where no grains would grow.
Zōu Yǎn played his pitch pipes,
making the cold valley cultivable.
The people of Yān planted millet there,
naming it Millet Valley.
If this is true,
then for disasters of cold and warmth,
one could use pipe-playing to harmonize the climate,
so why would changing governance or conduct
be necessary to eliminate them?
Therefore, ailments of cold and warmth
require medicine to heal;
the climate of Millet Valley
needed pipes to harmonize.
When Yáo encountered the great flood,
he appointed Yǔ to control it.
Cold and warmth, like Yáo's flood,
are of the same nature.
Yáo did not alter governance or conduct,
knowing the flood wasn't caused by them.
Since the flood wasn't due to governance,
so too, cold and warmth aren't summoned by it.
Some may object:
The "Various Omens" in the Hóng Fàn state:
"Haste
brings constant cold;
leisure,
constant warmth."
Ruò means
compliance,
yù means
warmth,
héng means
constant.
If a ruler is hasty,
constant cold follows;
if leisurely,
constant warmth ensues.
If cold and warmth respond to haste and leisure,
how can they be unrelated to governance?
But does this mean haste doesn't bring cold or leisure warmth?
When haste or leisure in rulers coincides with cold or warmth,
it's mere chance, natural,
as if deliberately corresponding.
Like divination yielding omens or stalks yielding numbers,
people say heaven and earth answer queries,
but it's actually coincidental.
The response of cold and warmth to haste and leisure,
like omens and numbers to queries,
appears to correspond externally,
but is truly random.
How to verify this?
The way of heaven is natural,
and nature is non-action.
When commands and coincidences align,
it's happenstance, meeting by chance;
human affairs begin,
while heavenly conditions already exist—
hence it's called the Dào.
If they responded to governance,
it would be action, not nature.
In the Zhōu Yì, Jīng Shì arranged sixty-four hexagrams
across a year,
with six days and seven fractions
per governing hexagram.
Hexagrams have yīn and yáng,
energies rise and fall;
when yáng rises, warmth comes,
when yīn rises, cold arrives.
Thus,
cold and warmth follow the hexagrams,
not responding to governance.
Consider the response in the Yì's "No Falsehood" hexagram:
floods and droughts arrive
on their own schedule,
all disasters and changes
likely follow a similar pattern.
Prognosticators
doubt and may miss the truth.
Why the doubt?
The great person aligns virtue with heaven and earth,
preceding heaven without heaven contradicting,
following heaven while honoring its timing.
The Hóng Fàn says:
"Haste
brings constant cold;
leisure,
constant warmth."
If as the Hóng Fàn states,
heaven's climate changes with people,
it should be about preceding without contradiction,
so why also mention
"following heaven while honoring its timing"?
"Following" means
heaven has already brought cold or warmth before,
and people reward or punish after.
Hence,
human claims conflict with the Shàng Shū,
first doubt.
Jīng Shì attributes cold/warmth to yīn-yáng shifts,
prognosticators to punishments/rewards and emotions—
the two schools contradict,
second doubt.
Commoners divining cold/warmth
find cold today, warmth tomorrow;
frost at dawn,
bright skies by dusk;
rain in morning brings warmth,
sun in morning brings cold.
Now rain is yīn,
sunshine is yáng;
cold is yīn, warmth yáng.
Yet morning sun brings cold,
morning rain brings warmth,
not corresponding by category,
third doubt.
With three doubts unresolved,
the "natural"
theory remains unproven.
Those discussing portents claim ancient rulers misgoverned,
and heaven warned them with disasters.
Disasters vary,
with cold/warmth as evidence.
Untimely punishments bring cold,
ill-timed rewards bring warmth.
Heaven's warnings to rulers
resemble rulers reprimanding subjects.
Thus King Zhuāng of Chǔ said:
"If heaven sends no disasters,
has it forgotten me?"
Disasters serve as warnings,
so King Zhuāng feared and reflected.
I say:
This is doubtful.
States having disasters
is like households having anomalies.
If disasters
warn rulers,
do anomalies warn households too?
If households are clear,
one can analogize to the human body.
Sickness in the body
is like disasters in heaven.
Imbalanced blood and vessels
cause human illness;
disharmonious winds and energies
breed yearly disasters.
Disasters and anomalies are said to be Heaven's reprimands for misgovernment.
But do illnesses also represent Heaven's repeated reprimands to individuals?
When brewing wine in jars
or cooking meat in cauldrons,
one always desires harmonious flavors.
Occasionally, salty, bitter, sour, or bland tastes offend the palate,
just as when people improperly blend seasonings, losing the proper harmony.
That misgovernment has its disasters and anomalies
is like cooking and brewing having foul tastes.
If disasters and anomalies are claimed to be Heaven's reprimands,
then errors in cooking and brewing should also be seen as reprimands.
Inferring the great from the small,
clarifying through analogies of things and affairs,
is sufficient to understand Heaven.
If King Yǎn had wisdom like Confucius,
then his words would be credible.
The talents of hegemons in decadent times,
akin to those of the prognosticators of change and recovery,
may not necessarily be trustworthy,
hence they are doubted.
Now, the Way of Heaven is natural,
non-acting.
If it reprimands people,
that is acting,
not natural.
The Huáng-Lǎo school,
in discussing the Way of Heaven,
grasped its reality.
Moreover, if Heaven truly can reprimand rulers,
it ought to alter the ethers to awaken them.
If punishments are applied untimely,
the punitive ether being cold, Heaven should make it warm;
if rewards are bestowed out of season,
the rewarding ether being warm, Heaven should make it cold.
Changing their governance and altering the ethers,
thus the ruler can be awakened to recognize right and wrong.
But now it merely follows cold and warmth,
being cold or warm, which is not the intent of reprimand,
which should aim to prompt appropriate changes.
Great King Dǎnfù, believing Wáng Jì worthy of succession,
therefore changed his name to Lì.
"Lì" means
"to go to."
Tàibó, awakening to this,
went to Wú and Yuè to gather herbs,
to avoid Wáng Jì.
Had the Great King not changed Jì's name,
but still called him "Jì,"
would Tàibó have awakened and avoided him?
Now, when punishments and rewards deviate from the law,
if Heaven wishes to alter the governance,
it should produce anomalous ethers,
like the Great King changing Jì's name.
But instead, it reinforces the same ethers to reprimand,
so when will the ruler ever awaken
to see the errors in punishments and rewards?
When a zither player errs in stringing and setting bridges,
causing the notes to sound wrong,
the master, recognizing it,
changes the strings and moves the bridges.
That Heaven sees errors in punishments and rewards
is like the zither master seeing the faults in strings and bridges;
yet instead of altering the ethers to awaken the ruler,
it augments the ethers, aggravating the faults.
Thus, Heaven has no mind or intent,
but merely follows the ruler's errors and wrongs.
Zhòu indulged in all-night drinking,
while King Wén said morning and night:
"In sacrifices, use this wine."
Qí was extravagant in sacrifices,
so Yànzǐ, offering at the temple,
did not cover the sacrificial pig with the stand.
Why?
Not to criticize them,
but to have means to change them.
When sons and younger brothers are arrogant,
fathers and elder brothers teach them respectfulness;
when officials and people are unruly,
senior officials show them harmony and compliance.
Thus, Kāng Shū and Bó Qín, failing in their duties as younger relatives,
visited Zhōu Gōng,
and with arrogant behavior in bowing and rising,
were caned three times in three visits.
They went to see Shāng Zǐ,
who had them observe the catalpa and birch trees.
The two, seeing the trees,
felt awakened in heart,
and understood the rites between father and son.
Zhōu Gōng could have followed their arrogance,
Shāng Zǐ could have acquiesced to their disrespect,
but they had to apply caning
and teach through observing things,
hoping the two would see the difference,
and awaken themselves through the unusual.
Now, a ruler's misgovernment
is like the two's failure in the Way;
yet Heaven does not instruct on governance,
to awaken him,
as the two saw the catalpa and birch,
but instead follows the errors in punishments and rewards,
responding with cold and warmth.
This means Heaven and the ruler both err.
There is no sense of mutual awakening,
only an ether of mutual following,
not the intent of August Heaven,
nor the proper way of reprimanding from above.
Generally, things that can cut each other
must have different natures;
those that can complement each other
must share the same ether.
Hence, "Lí below, Duì above" is called "gé" (revolution).
Gé means
"to change."
Fire and metal have distinct ethers,
so they can revolutionize each other.
If both were fire or both metal,
how could they revolutionize?
Qu Yuán, distressed by Chǔ's stench and filth,
thus used fragrant and pure words;
the Fisherman, arguing against following customs,
thus presented words on bathing.
Generally, to deal with foulness,
some teach fumigation,
others order carrying pigs.
Of these two sayings for removing stench and filth,
which is right, which wrong?
Without change,
there is little benefit.
Using cold and warmth
instead of punishments and rewards,
can it bring change?
Xīmén Bào was impatient,
so he wore a leather girdle to remind himself of flexibility;
Dǒng Ānyú was slow,
so he wore a string to urge himself on.
These two worthies knew to wear objects that change themselves,
and thus correct their shortcomings.
Heaven is supremely bright;
yet when a ruler misgoverns,
instead of using other ethers to reprimand and change,
it follows his errors,
reinforcing the ethers.
This shows August Heaven's intent
is less discerning than the two worthies.
King Zhuāng of Chǔ loved hunting,
so Fán Jī refrained from eating bird and beast meat because of it;
Duke Mù of Qín loved excessive pleasure,
so Queen Huáyáng refused to listen to Zhèng and Wèi music because of it.
These two consorts, not being the two rulers,
thwarted their desires and did not follow their actions.
August Heaven, not being the rewards and punishments,
yet follows their conduct,
and intensifies the ethers.
This suggests August Heaven's virtue
is less worthy than these women.
Hence, remonstrance means
"to interpose."
Holding good to interpose against evil,
must be called ordering chaos.
King Mù of Zhōu relied on punishments;
the "Fǔ Xíng Piān" says:
"Repay cruelty with威慑."
Both威慑 and cruelty are evil.
Using evil to repay evil,
nothing is more chaotic.
Now, punishments and rewards being untrue
is evil,
and Heaven again uses evil to respond,
meaning August Heaven's conduct is the same as King Mù's.
Therefore, refuting evil with good,
using evil to instill fear of good,
is the principle of admonishing people,
the way to encourage goodness.
Shùn warned Yǔ, saying:
"Do not be like Dān Zhū in his arrogance."
Zhōu Gōng instructed King Chéng, saying:
"Do not be like King Zhòu of Yīn."
"Do not" means
to prohibit it.
Dān Zhū and Yīn Zhòu were extremely evil,
hence "do not" to prohibit them.
Saying "do not be like" —
how does it compare to saying "must be like"?
Thus, the two terms "do not" and "must,"
the sages examined carefully;
how much less would they reprimand wrong with wrong,
following people's faults to increase their evil?
Heaven and humanity share the same Way;
the great person aligns virtue with Heaven.
Sages and worthies use good to reverse evil,
while August Heaven uses evil to follow wrong —
is this the effect of sharing the Way, the verification of aligned virtue?
The proponents of change and retribution,
seeing falsehoods spoken of Heaven,
and calamitous anomalies occurring from time to time,
then generate statements of reproof and warning.
Examining antiquity to understand the present,
knowing Heaven through humans.
"He received the mandate in the temple of the Cultured Ancestor,"
does not say he received the mandate from "Heaven"—
this shows Yáo’s mind understood Heaven’s intent.
When Yáo conferred it,
Heaven also conferred it,
all officials and ministers turned toward Shùn.
Shùn’s conferral upon Yǔ,
Yǔ’s transmission to Qǐ,
all used human hearts to reflect Heaven’s will.
The "turning to look" in the Shī,
the "thunderous rage" in the Hóng Fàn,
all use human hearts to reflect Heaven’s intent.
When King Wén and King Wǔ died,
King Chéng was young,
the Way of Zhōu not yet established,
the Duke of Zhōu acted as regent—
was there then any teaching from the High Heaven?
The Duke of Zhōu extended his heart to match Heaven’s will.
The heart of High Heaven
resides in the sage’s breast,
and when it comes to reproof and warning,
it is in the sage’s mouth.
Not believing the sage’s words,
instead affirming the ether of calamitous anomalies,
seeking to fathom the intent of High Heaven—
how far off is that?
If the age lacks a sage,
how can one obtain the sage’s words?
The talent of a worthy approaching [the sage],
is next to that of a sage.
Those who discuss calamitous anomalies
already suspect that Heaven uses them to reprove and warn humans.
They further explain:
"When calamitous anomalies arrive,
it is likely that the ruler’s governance stirs Heaven,
and Heaven moves ether in response.
It is like striking a drum with an object,
or hitting a bell with a mallet:
the drum is like Heaven,
the mallet like governance,
the sound of bell and drum like Heaven’s response.
When the ruler acts below,
then Heaven’s ether follows the person and arrives."
I say:
This is also doubtful.
Heaven can move things,
but how can things move Heaven?
Why so?
Humans and things are tied to Heaven,
Heaven is the master of humans and things.
Hence it is said:
"When Wáng Liáng whips his horse,
chariots and cavalry fill the wilds."
It is not that chariots fill the wilds,
and then Wáng Liáng whips his horse.
Heaven’s ether changes above,
humans and things respond below.
Thus when Heaven is about to rain,
the shāngyáng bird dances;
it does not cause Heaven to rain.
The shāngyáng
is a creature that knows rain;
when Heaven is about to rain,
it bends one leg and dances.
Thus when Heaven is about to rain,
mole crickets and ants migrate,
earthworms emerge,
zither strings slacken,
chronic illnesses flare up—
this is proof that things are moved by Heaven.
Thus when Heaven is about to be windy,
nest-dwelling insects stir;
when about to rain,
burrow-dwelling creatures are disturbed—
the ether of wind and rain affects insects and creatures.
Thus humans between Heaven and Earth
are like fleas and lice inside clothing,
or mole crickets and ants in burrows and crevices.
Can the rebellion, compliance, or random movements of fleas, lice, mole crickets, and ants
cause the ether in clothing or crevices to change?
Fleas, lice, mole crickets, and ants cannot,
yet one claims humans alone can—
this fails to grasp the principle of things and ether.
When wind arrives, tree branches move;
tree branches cannot cause wind.
Thus in late summer
cicadas sing,
autumn insects cry,
sensing the yin ether.
Thunder claps and pheasants startle,
hibernation ends and snakes emerge,
roused by the yang ether.
Cranes call past midnight,
roosters crow near dawn—
though these are not anomalies,
they show Heaven’s ether moving things,
and things responding to Heaven’s ether.
One could say cold and warmth affect the ruler,
and the ruler stirs ether to reward and punish,
but to claim that rewards and punishments move the August Heaven,
and Heaven produces cold and warmth in response to governance—!
The Six Affections wind theorists say
that when wind arrives,
those prone to banditry are influenced and rise.
It is not that the essential ether of bandits influences Heaven
to make the wind come.
Wind arriving shakes unruly hearts,
and bandit tendencies are triggered.
How to verify this?
Bandits,
seeing objects, take them;
seeing foes, kill them—
all in fleeting, momentary shifts,
not necessarily planned long in advance,
yet Heaven’s wind has already come on a day of greed and treachery.
Those who use wind to predict rank and wealth
say wind from the direction of royal or ministerial influence brings honor,
from captivity or death direction brings lowliness.
Rank, wealth, and quantity
are matters of pecks and bushels.
When wind comes, grain sellers adjust prices high or low—
Heaven’s ether sways humans and things.
Thus grain prices fall and rise,
now high, now low.
The Tiān Guān text
uses the first month’s dawn to divine winds from four directions:
wind from south brings drought,
from north brings flood,
from east brings plague,
from west brings war.
Grand Historian Simǎ Qiān truly stated
that using wind to predict flood, drought, war, and plague
shows human fortunes are governed by Heaven.
What makes things live is spring;
what makes things die is winter.
Life in spring, death in winter—that is Heaven.
If one wished to kill in spring and give life in winter,
things would not ultimately die or live—
why?
Life of things is governed by yang,
death of things is tied to yin.
Thus blowing on a person with one’s breath
cannot make them cold;
breathing warm breath on them
cannot make them warm.
But let the person blown on
pass through winter or touch summer,
and they will suffer cold or heat.
The ether of cold and warmth
is tied to Heaven and Earth, governed by yin and yang—
how can human affairs or state governance move it?
Moreover, Heaven is fundamental, humans secondary.
Climb a tree and shake a branch—
you cannot move the trunk.
If you cut the trunk,
all stems wither.
Human affairs are like branches,
cold and warmth like roots and trunk.
Humans are born from Heaven,
contain Heaven’s ether,
take Heaven as master—
like ears, eyes, hands, and feet tied to the heart.
When the heart intends something,
ears and eyes see and hear,
hands and feet act.
To say Heaven responds to humans
is to say the heart is directed by ears, eyes, hands, and feet.
Banners with hanging tassels—
tassels tied to the pole.
If the pole moves east, tassels follow west.
If one claims cold and warmth follow punishments and rewards,
this makes Heaven’s ether the tied tassels.
When the Hooked Star is between Fáng and Xīn,
it portends earth’s shaking.
The Qí court diviner knew this,
told Duke Jǐng:
"I can move the earth."
Duke Jǐng believed him.
To say a ruler can cause cold and warmth
is like Duke Jǐng of Qí believing the diviner could move the earth.
Humans cannot move the earth,
and likewise cannot move Heaven.
Now, cold and warmth
are matters of celestial energy.
The heavens are supremely lofty and great,
while humans are extremely lowly and small.
A chopstick cannot make a bell chime,
and a firefly cannot boil a cauldron—
why is that?
Because the bell is long and the chopstick short,
the cauldron large and the firefly small.
With a slender form of seven feet,
to affect the great energy of the august heavens,
it is certain that there will not be the slightest evidence of it.
When a general is about to enter a city or town,
if the weather is cold, the general will be angry;
if warm, he will be pleased.
Now, anger and pleasure arise from events and are triggered,
but before he has entered the territory,
before he has seen the officials and people,
before right and wrong have been examined,
before anger or pleasure has been expressed,
the energies of cold and warmth have already arrived in advance.
If anger and pleasure cause cold and warmth,
then after the anger or pleasure occurs,
the energy should then arrive.
This means that the energies of cold and warmth actually cause the ruler to be angry or pleased.
Some say:
"It is because they are not utterly sincere.
If one acts
with utmost sincerity, like Zōu Yǎn calling to heaven and frost descending,
or Qǐ Liáng's wife weeping and the city wall collapsing—
how could celestial energy not be moved?"
Now, utmost sincerity
still depends on the likes and dislikes of the mind.
Take a fruit or melon,
placed before a person,
a foot away from the mouth;
if the mind desires to eat it,
and the breath from the mouth sucks at it, it cannot be obtained;
only when the hand picks it up and brings it to the mouth
can it then be acquired.
Now, with something as small as a fruit or melon,
round and easily rolled,
not far from the mouth,
even with utmost sincerity desiring it,
it cannot be obtained—
how much more so with heaven so high and far from humans,
its energy vast and boundless without beginning or end!
In the height of summer,
one may stand in the wind;
in the depth of winter,
sit facing the sun.
In summer, one desires cold, and in winter, warmth—
the sincerity is extreme.
For those who desire it intensely,
some even fan themselves in the wind,
or light stoves facing the sun,
yet heaven never changes its energy for winter or summer,
because cold and heat have their seasons,
and do not change for humans.
If even with correct desire one cannot attain it,
how much less when, through punishments and rewards,
the intention does not seek cold or warmth!
If ten thousand people sigh together,
they cannot move heaven,
how could the mouth of one Zōu Yǎn
cause frost to descend?
What was Zōu Yǎn's situation
compared to Qū Yuán's?
The injustice of being imprisoned—
how does it compare to drowning in a river?
The sorrow of "Lí Sāo" and "Chǔ Cí"—
how does it compare to a single sigh?
When Qū Yuán died,
there was no frost in the state of Chǔ—
this was during the time of King Huái and King Xiāng.
In the era of King Lì and King Wǔ,
Biàn Hé presented jade,
had his feet amputated,
wept as he held the jade,
tears exhausted, continued with blood.
How does Zōu Yǎn's sincerity
compare to Biàn Hé's?
The injustice of being imprisoned—
how does it compare to foot amputation?
Sighing while looking up at heaven—
how does it compare to weeping blood?
Surely, sighing is not as poignant as weeping,
imprisonment not as severe as amputation;
estimating the scale of injustice,
Zōu Yǎn does not match Biàn Hé,
yet at that time, no frost was seen in Chǔ.
When Lǐ Sī and Zhào Gāo falsely accused and killed Crown Prince Fúsū,
along with Méng Tián and Méng Ào,
they all uttered words of pain and suffering.
These were akin to sighs,
and moreover, the calamity led to death,
not merely imprisonment;
yet in the place where they died,
no cold energy arose.
When Qín buried alive the soldiers of Zhào at Chángpíng,
four hundred thousand men
fell together simultaneously.
At that time, there was wailing and crying,
not just sighing.
Though their sincerity may not have matched Zōu Yǎn's,
the injustice of four hundred thousand people
should equate to the pain of one worthy minister;
the cries from the burial pits
should surpass the calls of imprisoned men—
yet at that time, at Chángpíng,
no falling frost was seen.
The "Fǔ Xíng" says:
"The multitude, afflicted, widely proclaimed their innocence to the Heavenly Emperor."
This refers to the people of Chī Yóu being wronged,
proclaiming their innocence to heaven.
If the cries of the masses
cannot bring about frost,
then Zōu Yǎn's words
are probably false.
The south is extremely hot,
scorching sand and melting stones,
where fathers and sons bathe in the same waters;
the north is extremely cold,
with frozen ice and cracked earth,
where fathers and sons dwell in the same caves.
Yān is on the northern border;
in Zōu Yǎn's time,
the fifth month of the Zhōu calendar
was the third month of the regular year.
In the central regions, in the first and second months,
frost and snow often fall;
on the northern border, where it is extremely cold,
frost in the third month
is not unusual.
It is likely that on the northern border, it was still cold in the third month,
frost happened to fall,
and Zōu Yǎn happened to call out,
coinciding with the frost.
The "Zhuàn" says:
"In Yān, there was a cold valley
where the five grains did not grow;
Zōu Yǎn blew his pitch-pipes,
and the cold valley became warm again."
If he could make the energy warm,
he could also make it cold again.
How do we know that Zōu Yǎn did not, to make people aware of his injustice,
use the weather to display his sincerity,
secretly blowing his pitch-pipes in the Yān valley prison to make the energy cold
and then call out to heaven?
If not so,
why did frost fall?
Fàn Jū was slandered by Xū Gǔ,
and Wèi Qí punished him,
breaking his ribs and injuring his sides.
Zhāng Yí traveled in Chǔ,
where the Chǔ prime minister tortured him,
beating him until he bled.
These two men were wronged,
and Sīmǎ Qiān recorded their circumstances.
Zōu Yǎn being imprisoned—
is comparable to Fàn Jū and Zhāng Yí;
why then would Zǐcháng refrain from mentioning it?
Checking Zōu Yǎn's biography,
it does not mention that he caused frost to fall while imprisoned.
False writings and rumors
are like the tales of Crown Prince Dān making the sun stand still at noon again or heaven raining grain.
From this, it follows that
Zōu Yǎn's call causing frost to fall
is false!
Then, Qǐ Liáng's wife weeping and the city wall collapsing
is also unfounded!
When Dùnmóu rebelled,
Zhào Xiāngzǐ led troops to attack it.
When the army reached the city walls,
Dùnmóu's walls collapsed over ten zhàng,
and Xiāngzǐ sounded the gongs to retreat.
If Qǐ Liáng's wife weeping caused the city wall to collapse,
were there weepers in Xiāngzǐ's army?
When Qín was about to perish,
the capital's inner gates collapsed;
when Huò Guāng's family was near ruin,
the walls of their residence fell on their own—
who wept in the Qín palace
or cried in Huò Guāng's household?
Yet the gates collapsed and walls crumbled,
signs of Qín and Huò's downfall.
Perhaps the state of Qǐ was about to collapse,
and Qǐ Liáng's wife happened to weep beneath the wall,
just as Yān happened to be cold, and Zōu Yǎn chanced to call out.
Events of the same category follow each other in time,
and those who hear or see them may affirm them as such.
When a city wall ages and decays,
it may still collapse.
If one woman's weeping
could collapse a fifty-zhàng city wall,
that would be like a single finger toppling a pillar three rèn high.
During the Spring and Autumn period, mountains often changed.
Mountains and city walls
are of the same category.
If weeping could collapse a city wall,
could it also destroy a mountain?
A woman, clad in plain white, wept by the river,
and the river flowed freely.
If indeed weeping could collapse a city wall, it would be fitting.
However, consider Qǐ Liáng, who joined the army
and died,
not returning home.
His wife went to meet him,
and the Lord of Lǔ condoled with her on the road.
The wife did not accept the condolences,
and the coffin was brought home,
where the Lord of Lǔ then offered his condolences.
It is not mentioned that she wept beneath the city wall.
Originally, he died in the army,
and dying in the army does not occur within the city.
For his wife to weep facing the city
would be an inappropriate place.
Thus, the claim that Qǐ Liáng's wife wept and collapsed the city wall
is again a false statement.
By extension of this category,
when Jīng Kē attempted to assassinate the King of Qín, a white rainbow pierced the sun;
when Wèi Xiānshēng devised the Chángpíng strategy for Qín, Venus eclipsed the Pleiades—
these are also absurd claims.
Consider Yùzǐ, who plotted to assassinate Xiāngzǐ
and hid under a bridge.
When Xiāngzǐ reached the bridge, his heart stirred;
Guàn Gāo, intending to kill Gāozǔ,
concealed men within the walls.
When Gāozǔ arrived at Bó Rén, his heart also stirred.
These two men sought to assassinate two rulers,
and both rulers' hearts stirred.
In a factual discussion,
it is still said that it was not due to the spiritual influence of the two men,
so how could Jīng Kē's attempt to assassinate the King of Qín,
without the king's heart stirring,
cause a white rainbow to pierce the sun?
Thus, the white rainbow piercing the sun
was a natural celestial phenomenon,
not Jīng Kē's essence becoming a rainbow to pierce the sun.
When the Hooked Star appears between Fáng and Xīn,
it is an omen of impending earthquakes.
When an earthquake is imminent,
the Hooked Star responds in Fáng and Xīn.
As for Venus eclipsing the Pleiades,
it is like the Hooked Star in Fáng and Xīn.
To say that Wèi Xiānshēng's Chángpíng proposal
caused Venus to eclipse the Pleiades is doubtful!
When Jupiter harmed the tail of the Bird,
Zhōu and Chǔ suffered misfortunes;
when a reddish vapor appeared,
Sòng, Wèi, Chén, and Zhèng experienced disasters.
Yet at that time, Zhōu and Chǔ had done no wrong,
and Sòng, Wèi, Chén, and Zhèng had no evils.
However, Jupiter first guarded the tail,
and the calamitous qi manifested in the sky.
Later, Zhōu and Chǔ encountered disasters,
and Sòng, Wèi, Chén, and Zhèng all suffered simultaneously.
Jupiter's harm to Zhōu and Chǔ
was the celestial qi bringing disaster to the four states.
How can we know that the white rainbow piercing the sun did not lead to the attempt on the King of Qín,
or that Venus eclipsing the Pleiades did not cause the Chángpíng strategy to arise?
[Original text missing.]
Those who advocate transformation and response
attribute prolonged rain to excess water,
and prolonged sunshine to drought.
Drought corresponds to excessive yang,
while flooding corresponds to sinking and drowning.
Some object, saying:
"In the course of a year,
it rains once in ten days,
and winds blow once in five days.
If rain lingers excessively,
it is a sign of flooding;
if sunshine persists too long,
it is the onset of drought.
During floods,
the ruler may not be sinking or drowning;
during droughts,
there may not be excessive yang."
When a ruler governs,
his actions may be consistent throughout,
yet flooding and drought occur alternately—
this is due to the timing of qi.
Fàn Lǐ's Jì Rán states:
"When the Year Star is in water, there is destruction;
in metal, abundance;
in wood, famine;
in fire, drought."
Thus,
floods, droughts, famines, and abundance
are governed by the year's cycle.
When the year aligns with its cycle,
and the qi matches the era,
the transformation and response advocates point and name it.
If the ruler follows their words
and seeks to correct his faults,
prolonged sunshine will eventually turn to rain,
and prolonged rain to sunshine.
Then the transformation and response advocates
claim credit for the outcome.
The ruler agrees with them
and thus believes in their methods.
But suppose the ruler remains calm and secure, not seeking his own faults—
heaven will still bring rain on its own,
and rain will still turn to sunshine.
During the transitions between sunshine and rain,
if the ruler does nothing,
the transformation and response advocates
will still attribute it to their methods.
This implies that yin and yang qi
are governed by humans,
not controlled by heaven.
But humans cannot influence heaven through their actions,
nor does heaven respond to human deeds.
In the Spring and Autumn Annals, the Great Rain Sacrifice in Lǔ
was a ritual to pray for rain during drought.
When drought persists without rain,
people pray and offer sacrifices for blessings,
just as when humans fall ill, they sacrifice to spirits to avert misfortune.
This is the concept of transformation and response.
The Book of Songs says:
"When the moon passes through Bì,
heavy rain falls abundantly."
The Book of Documents states:
"When the moon follows the stars,
there will be wind and rain."
Thus, wind and rain follow where the moon passes.
The Fáng constellation has four markers and three paths.
The travels of the sun and moon
move along these three paths.
If they exit to the north, there is flooding;
if to the south, drought.
Some say exiting north brings drought,
and south brings flooding.
Consider that the moon foretells for all under heaven,
and Fáng serves as an indicator for the nine provinces.
The moon's movement north or south
is not solely for Lǔ.
When Confucius went out,
he had Zǐlù bring rain gear.
Shortly after,
heaven indeed poured heavy rain.
Zǐlù asked the reason,
and Confucius said:
"Last evening, the moon passed through Bì."
Another day,
the moon again passed through Bì.
Confucius went out,
and Zǐlù requested to bring rain gear,
but Confucius did not consent.
When they went out, there was indeed no rain.
Zǐlù asked the reason,
and Confucius said:
"Previously,
the moon passed through its yin side,
hence rain;
last evening,
it passed through its yang side,
hence no rain."
Thus,
rain in Lǔ naturally occurred due to the moon's passage,
how could it be due to governance?
If it were truly due to governance, then
the moon passing through Bì as a rain omen
should apply to all under heaven.
If it rained in Lǔ,
it should rain everywhere in the world.
During the time of the Six States,
governance varied,
and rulers' actions—rewards and punishments—differed in timing.
If rain were to respond to governance, then
the moon would need to pass through six or seven stars of Bì
to suffice.
During the time of Lǔ Mùgōng,
there was a year of drought.
Mùgōng asked Xiànzǐ:
"Heaven is dry without rain;
I wish to expose the shaman,
what do you think?"
Xiànzǐ did not agree.
"I wish to move the market,
what do you think?"
He replied:
"When the Son of Heaven passes away,
markets are held in alleys for seven days;
when a feudal lord dies,
markets are held in alleys for five days.
Would it not be appropriate to relocate the market for this purpose!"
According to Xiànzǐ's statement,
relocating the market brought rain.
Yet according to the texts of the Shī and Shū,
rain comes when the moon passes through Bì.
The movements of the sun and moon
follow constant rhythms;
would they really, because of relocating a market,
enter the shadowy part of Bì?
The moon and Bì
are observed throughout the world;
