how could moving the market in Lǔ
possibly shift the moon?
The moon traverses the heavens
and completes its cycle in thirty days.
Within one month,
it passes Bì once;
when it passes the sunny side, it is clear,
and when it passes the shadowy side, it rains. Even if the influence of relocating the market
could make the moon enter Bì's shadow,
would it rain precisely when the market was moved?
Thus, Xiànzǐ's words
cannot be relied upon.
Dǒng Zhòngshū sought rain,
expounding the principles of the Chūnqiū,
and establishing empty sacrifices.
A father does not accept offerings from collateral branches,
and Heaven does not accept them from lower lands;
the feudal lords perform the yú sacrifice—
what spirits are they worshipping?
If they are heavenly spirits,
only the king's offerings are enjoyed by Heaven;
feudal lords and current officials are not accepted by Heaven.
If spirits do not enjoy the offerings,
how can they be moved?
If it is the essence of
clouds and rain,
what need has it for offerings?
Clouds touch the rocks and emerge,
gathering inch by inch,
and within a morning, rain spreads across the land—
this is Mount Tài's doing.
Mount Tài rains upon the world,
while smaller mountains rain upon cities and towns.
If so, then what is the great yú sacrifice offering to?
Is it sacrificing to the mountains?
If that were truly the case,
it would still be ineffective.
How can this be proven?
Water resides in separate streams,
with differences in height by inches and fractions;
without a breach, it does not flow,
and without digging, it does not converge.
If a ruler were to pray and sacrifice by the water,
could he make water from a higher level flow and merge?
Even with visible water,
where the difference is slight,
if a ruler requests it,
it ultimately will not flow;
how much more so for rain, which has no visible form,
hidden deep within high mountains—
can a ruler obtain it through yú sacrifice?
How could it be achieved?
Rainwater in the space between heaven and earth
is like tears in a human body.
If one brings wine and food to beg before a kind person,
asking them to shed tears,
the kind person will not weep for it.
Since tears cannot be summoned by request,
how can rain be obtained by seeking?
When Yōngménzǐ wept in sorrow,
Mèngchángjūn shed tears for him;
when Sū Qín and Zhāng Yí spoke mournfully in the valley,
Guǐgǔ Xiānshēng's tears soaked his lapel.
Perhaps if one could emulate Yōngmén's voice
or deliver Sū and Zhāng's persuasions, it might move Heaven?
But Heaven's ears and eyes are lofty and distant,
and sound and breath do not reach it.
When Qǐ Liáng's wife wept in grief,
instead of rain, the city wall collapsed.
If so,
what ultimately should be done to bring rain?
Those who perform the yú sacrifice—
how do they move Heaven?
According to observation, when the moon emerges on the northern path
and passes through Bì's shadow,
it rarely fails to rain.
From this, it is said
that the northern path
is where the star Bì resides.
Would the stars of the northern path descend rain
because of the yú sacrifice?
When Confucius went out
and had Zǐlù bring rain gear,
Lǔ likely was not performing the yú sacrifice.
Without sacrifice,
rain fell abundantly on its own;
without seeking,
the skies cleared naturally.
Thus,
Heaven's clear and rainy weather
has its own timing.
Within a year,
clear and rainy days follow one another.
When it rains,
who sought it?
When it is clear,
who stopped it?
If a ruler heeds requests
to comfort the people and bestow grace,
he must not be virtuous.
Heaven is supremely virtuous;
if the time is not right for rain,
and false requests are made, causing rain to fall recklessly,
that would be like a ruler heeding such requests.
Those who deal with anomalies and responses
do not verify through analogy
but vainly promote methods
to delude rulers.
Sometimes, when rain is not due,
a virtuous ruler seeks it but does not get it;
sometimes, when rain is due naturally,
a wicked ruler seeks it
and happens upon the right time.
This causes the virtuous ruler to bear empty blame
and the wicked ruler to enjoy a false reputation.
It is said that the sage is pure and the worthy is mixed;
purity means conduct is without fault,
and without fault, governance is without error.
Yet among the sage rulers of history,
none compare to Yáo and Tāng.
Yáo encountered floods,
and Tāng encountered great drought.
If this was due to governance,
then Yáo and Tāng were wicked rulers;
if not due to governance,
then it was fate's cycle.
The cycle of fate has its timing;
how can it be sought by request?
Those who discuss such matters still say that Yáo and Tāng's floods and droughts were due to timing,
while minor droughts and excessive rains are due to governance.
If that were truly the case,
what causes excessive rain?
If it is indeed caused by governance,
without rectifying the errors that led to it,
and merely making requests,
how can it be restored?
If the world truly claims Yáo and Tāng's floods and droughts were Heaven's fate cycle,
not caused by governance,
then Heaven's fate cycle
occurs naturally in its time.
Even with yú sacrifices and requests,
there is ultimately no benefit.
Yet it is also said that Tāng prayed at Sānglín for five faults
and immediately obtained rain.
If one speaks of fate's cycle,
then the Sānglín account is refuted;
if one cites Sānglín,
then the theory of fate's cycle is negated.
What should those who make such claims ultimately follow?
What method should truly be used to counter floods and droughts?
Generally, there are two types of disasters and anomalies:
those due to governance,
and those that are unforeseen changes.
For disasters due to governance,
one must seek to address them.
Even if seeking does not achieve it,
the kindness of compassion and empathy,
the sentiment of having no alternative,
is like that of a loving father for his child
or a filial child for their parent.
Knowing the illness cannot be cured by worshipping spirits,
or pain relieved without medicine,
yet they never sit idly waiting for the end
but still divine for curses, call doctors, and mix medicines—
all out of heartfelt sorrow and earnest hope
for some effect.
After death, when breath is gone
and nothing more can be done,
they climb to the high point of the house,
waving clothes to summon the soul back,
grieving and longing,
hoping for a revival.
The intention behind the yú sacrifice
is the same as that of a loving father or filial child.
For unforeseen disasters,
the common people do not understand
and inevitably blame the ruler.
Those in governance, to appease the people's hopes,
thus also necessarily perform the yú sacrifice.
Question:
How can one distinguish between calamities due to governance
and unforeseen changes?
Answer:
When virtue is abundant and governance proper,
yet disasters still occur,
they are unforeseen;
when virtue declines and governance fails,
and changes respond accordingly,
they are due to governance.
In the latter case, one should conduct rain ceremonies externally and reform internally
to restore what is lacking;
in the former, one should maintain the old governance internally
and perform rain ceremonies externally
to comfort the people's hearts.
Thus, the qi of unforeseen events,
arriving through the ages,
should be met with steadfast consistency,
not by altering governance.
How can this be verified?
The Duke of Zhōu, in advising King Chéng on establishing governance, said:
"At times, things may interrupt it.
From every word and utterance, I shall not deviate,
but rely on virtuous talents to govern the people entrusted to me."
The Duke of Zhōu's establishment of governance
can be considered proper.
Knowing that extraordinary phenomena
do not come without cause,
he instructed King Chéng that from every word and utterance,
no aspect of governance should be at fault,
daring not to make changes.
Thus, when extraordinary changes occur,
the qi of unforeseen events
has arrived intermittently.
Flood qi interrupted Yáo's reign,
drought qi interrupted Tāng's.
King Xuān of Zhōu, being virtuous,
encountered a prolonged drought.
In the first year of the Jiànchū era,
the northern regions suffered consecutive droughts,
cattle died and people were destitute,
fleeing to seek cheaper lands.
The sage ruler above was lenient and enlightened,
the officials below fulfilled their duties—
a time of clear peace.
Though governance had no minor faults,
drought still occurred,
due to qi interrupting it.
The sage ruler understood this
and did not alter governance or conduct,
but transported grain for relief,
reducing abundance to aid depletion.
This shows his careful discernment,
enabling appropriate rescue measures.
When Duke Wén of Lǔ experienced a great drought one year,
Zāng Wénzhòng said:
"Repair the city walls,
reduce food and expenses,
promote frugality and encourage sharing."
Wénzhòng knew it was not due to governance,
so he only prepared defensively,
without changing governance.
Those who advocate change and restoration,
seeing anomalies, blame governance,
without considering that governance may be blameless;
fearing upon seeing omens,
they alter their conduct.
Changing what should not be changed
only invites disaster.
Why must rain ceremonies be held?
Answer:
The Spring and Autumn Annals records great rain ceremonies,
and commentators like Zuǒ Qiūmíng,
Gōngyáng, and Gǔliáng offer no criticism—
thus, rain ceremonies are justified.
Zēng Xī, speaking of his aspiration to Confucius, said:
"In late spring,
when spring garments are ready,
with five or six adults
and six or seven youths,
we bathe in the Yí River,
enjoy the breeze at the Rain Altar,
and return singing."
Confucius said:
"I agree with Diǎn."
Lǔ held rain ceremonies by the Yí River.
"Mù" means late,
"spring" refers to the fourth month.
"Spring garments are ready"
means the fourth-month garments are complete.
Adults and youths
are performers in the rain ceremony.
"Bathe in the Yí"
means wading across the river,
symbolizing the dragon emerging from water.
"Enjoy the breeze at the Rain Altar"
—"fēng" means singing.
"Return singing"
means singing while offering sacrifice,
performing the ceremony with song.
Interpreters of the Analects
think "bathing"
means washing in the Yí River;
"fēng" means drying the body.
But the fourth month in Zhōu calendar
corresponds to the second month of the year,
when it is still cold—
how could one bathe and dry outdoors?
Thus,
wading does not mean bathing,
confirming it as a rain ceremony.
The Zuǒ Zhuàn states:
"Hold rain ceremonies when insects awaken."
Also:
"Hold rain ceremonies when the dragon appears."
Both insect awakening and dragon appearance
occur in the second month.
Rain ceremonies in spring's second month
and autumn's eighth month
pray for spring rain
and autumn harvest.
The present-day Língxīng sacrifice
is the autumn rain ceremony.
Spring ceremonies are abandoned,
autumn ones remain,
so the Língxīng sacrifice
is the annual rain ceremony.
Confucius said,
"I agree with Diǎn,"
approving his words
to use rain ceremonies to balance yīn and yáng,
hence his agreement.
If rain ceremonies were improper,
and Diǎn proposed them,
Confucius should have criticized,
not agreed.
When Fán Chí accompanied him
and asked about the ceremony,
he criticized Lǔ for not cultivating virtue but relying on ceremonies.
Rain ceremonies have existed since antiquity,
so the Rites record:
"Rain and ancestral ceremonies
sacrifice for water and drought."
Thus, the rain ceremony is established,
so Confucius did not criticize it,
and Dǒng Zhòngshū elaborated.
Therefore,
rain ceremonies
are proper sacrifices.
If rain ceremonies are proper,
then for great floods, drumming and offering animals at the shrine
are also ancient rites.
Being proper and blameless,
rain ceremonies are justified—first reason.
Rites: sacrificing to the earth shrine
rewards its role in nurturing all things.
The land is vast and distant,
hard to worship entirely,
so the shrine is established as a focal point,
to focus reverence.
Water and drought
stem from yīn and yáng qi,
filling the cosmos, hard to worship fully,
so altars are built and positions set,
to respectfully pray,
emulating the earth shrine's principle,
as a way to counter disasters.
Extend service for the living to the dead,
human affairs to ghosts.
If the essence of yīn and yáng
could eat and drink like the living,
we offer fragrance,
present delicacies,
sincerely and earnestly,
hoping for a response.
By analogy with earth shrine sacrifices,
rain ceremonies are justified—second reason.
Even when the year's qi is harmonious
and disasters absent,
rain ceremonies are still held.
The present Língxīng sacrifice
is an ancient rite.
How much more when the year's qi changes,
water and drought strike unpredictably,
the ruler's fear
must be profound.
Even with the Língxīng sacrifice,
rain ceremonies are repeated,
fearing prior inadequacy,
following the principle of continuous sacrifice.
Hoping to remedy disaster's damage,
and gain abundant harvests,
third reason.
The heart of ritual is sincere devotion,
the essence of music is joyful delight.
Sincere devotion is manifested through jades and silks,
joyful delight is verified by bells and drums.
The rain sacrifice for supplication and prayer
reflects the ruler's utmost sincerity.
When utmost sincerity remains within,
with no means to manifest externally,
thus the rain sacrifice expresses one's fearful reverence,
channeling concentrated sincerity before the rain ceremony.
The significance of jades, silks, bells and drums
constitutes the fourth point.
When a minister offends his ruler,
or a son incurs fault against his father,
they should reform themselves
and offer apologies.
Fearful reverence toward drought, as if caused by misgovernment,
resembles ministers and sons admitting offenses and faults.
Silently reforming governance,
quietly changing conduct,
without external manifestation,
heaven's anger remains unappeased,
thus the rain sacrifice is necessary.
The significance of fearful reverence
constitutes the fifth point.
When the Hàn established academicians,
teachers and disciples debated each other,
seeking to exhaust the Way's profundity,
revealing the principles of right and wrong.
Without encountering harsh challenges,
one cannot attain persuasive arguments;
without posing difficult queries,
one cannot hear satisfying responses.
Winnowing rice by tossing it up and down,
seeks to obtain refined grain;
whetting stones against each other,
seeks to achieve sharpness.
Inferring the principles of the Spring and Autumn Annals,
seeking explanations for rain sacrifices,
verifying Confucius's intentions,
examining Dǒng Zhòngshū's meaning.
Since Confucius has passed away,
and Dǒng Zhòngshū has died,
among contemporary discussants,
who should be questioned?
Only those like Confucius's disciples,
Dǒng Zhòngshū's followers
can explain it.
The principle in the Spring and Autumn Annals
regarding great floods
states: "Beat drums and offer sacrifices at the altar of soil."
Commentators explain:
"Drumming
means to attack it."
Some say:
"To coerce it."
Coercing indeed means attacking.
When yin prevails,
attack the soil altar to rescue the situation.
Some object saying:
Attacking the soil altar implies gaining victory in contention,
yet fails to achieve the proper ritual decorum.
The ruler serves heaven as father,
and earth as mother.
If the mother's kind causes harm,
can one attack the mother to rescue it?
When governance errs,
causing yin-yang disorder,
the fault lies with the ruler.
Not rectifying oneself to restore order,
but instead violating hierarchy by offending superiors—
how would heaven and earth consent to assist?
If floodwaters harmed heaven itself,
not using earth to harm heaven,
attacking might be permissible.
But what floods actually damage
are creatures.
All creatures belong to earth,
which is humble.
Harming the supreme尊's substance
violates the Way.
Those discussing the Spring and Autumn Annals never raise this objection.
Consider: rain emerges from mountains,
flows into rivers;
floodwaters belong to
mountains and rivers.
During great flood disasters,
we don't attack mountains and rivers.
The soil altar represents earth,
but among the five phases' natures,
water and earth differ.
To attack earth because water causes harm—
earth conquers water—
this "attack the soil altar" principle
resembles modern craftsmen using hammer and chisel:
hammer strikes chisel
to make chisel penetrate wood.
So does attacking earth
mean to suppress water?
Moreover, the principle of attacking the soil altar
presumes attacking yin's category.
If person Jiǎ commits robbery,
harming people,
while Jiǎ remains unpunished,
ignoring Jiǎ to attack Yǐ's household—
would this stop Jiǎ?
Now rain
is water.
Water exists,
yet we don't attack water itself,
but instead attack the soil altar.
Observe: before heaven sends rain,
mountains first produce clouds,
clouds accumulate into rain,
rain flows as water.
Thus mountains are
parents,
water is
offspring.
Should severe punishment extend to family members?
Punish parents and children?
Or punish their companions?
Comparing mountains/water with the soil altar—
both relate to rain.
Which is closer?
The soil altar is earth,
of different phase energy from water,
far removed.
Under King Tàiwù of Yīn,
mulberry and grain grew together.
Some say King Gāozōng.
Alarmed,
he humbled himself and practiced the Way,
pondering ancient kings' governance,
restoring destroyed states,
continuing severed lineages,
elevating recluses,
clarifying elder care principles—
then mulberry and grain vanished,
and he long enjoyed sovereignty.
Spring and Autumn commentators all know this.
How do flood disasters differ from the mulberry-grain omen?
The Yīn king reformed governance,
while Spring and Autumn prescribes attacking the soil altar—
contradictory paths,
which should we follow?
Under King Chéng of Zhōu,
heaven sent great thunderstorms,
flattening crops and uprooting trees,
causing severe damage.
King Chéng unsealed the Metal-Bound Casket documents,
seeking past actions,
recognized the Duke of Zhōu's merits,
held the documents and wept over his errors—
rain ceased,
winds reversed,
crops and great trees restored.
Prolonged heavy flooding
is essentially the same.
King Chéng reformed his faults,
Spring and Autumn attacks the soil altar—
two classics, two principles,
how should we act?
Those who follow the Monthly Ordinances,
when insects devour grain crops,
take officials resembling the insects in kind,
whip, strike, humiliate, and disgrace them,
to eliminate the anomaly.
Those who discuss reality say this may not be truly justified.
Yet it is done,
to satisfy people's expectations.
Now, those responsible for bringing rain
are the governance,
the officials.
Without changing the governance,
without punishing the officials,
and merely attacking the altar of soil,
how can this remedy the situation?
If it is thought appropriate to attack their kind,
the essence of all yin
is the moon.
When the moon-mirror faces the moon,
water naturally descends.
When the moon passes through Bì,
or emerges north of Fáng,
it rarely fails to rain.
The creatures in the moon
are the hare and the toad.
Their counterparts on earth
are snails and clams.
When the moon wanes in the sky,
snails and clams shrink and hollow,
clearly showing they are of the same kind.
If rain persists without clearing,
to attack yin's kind,
one should capture and behead hares,
toads,
smash snails,
and clams, to address the reality.
When locusts arrive in season,
some fly, some settle,
and where they gather,
grains and grasses wither and dry up.
Officials, soldiers, and local people
dig trenches and pits,
drive them into the trenches,
and gather locusts by the thousands of hectoliters.
Directly attacking the locusts themselves,
the locusts still do not cease;
how much less effective is merely attacking yin's kind?
How could the rain then clear?
The "Shangshu Dazhuan" says:
"If the suburban and soil altars are not maintained,
mountains and rivers not prayed to,
wind and rain not timely,
frost and snow not falling,
blame falls on the Duke of Heaven.
If ministers often assassinate their lords,
concubines often kill the clan heads,
and the five relationships are not in order,
blame falls on the Duke of Men.
If city walls are not repaired,
moats and pools not maintained,
springs not flowing,
and water becomes a harm to the people,
blame falls on the Duke of Earth."
The king
and the three dukes each have their responsibilities;
feudal lords,
ministers, and officials each have their duties.
In great floods, why not blame the ministers and officials,
but instead beat drums and attack the altar of soil?
What is the reason?
If not,
it was because the state of Lǔ lost propriety,
and Confucius wrote the classic,
using it as a warning.
Gōngyáng Gāo could not verify it,
Dǒng Zhòngshū could not determine it,
so the rationale for attacking the altar
has been practiced again to this day.
If Gāo were still alive,
and Zhòngshū not dead,
one might challenge them, saying:
"Prolonged rain and flooding overflow—
who caused it?
If it is the ruler,
he should change governance and conduct
to remedy it;
if it is the officials,
he should punish those people
to appease Heaven for their faults.
If it is not due to ruler or officials,
but the interaction of yin and yang energies,
coinciding with the times,
then beating drums to attack the altar,
how can that stop it?"
The "Chūnqiū" commentary says:
"If the ruler is excessively yang, it causes drought;
if submerged in indulgence, it causes floods."
If so,
then for drought, it is due to excessive yang conduct,
for floods, it is due to indulgent behavior;
why attack the altar of soil?
Attacking the altar does not resolve it;
binding it with red silk
is also not understood.
Commentators believe
the altar is yin,
red is yang.
Water is yin;
using a yang color to bind it
aids the drums in rescue.
If a great mountain catches fire,
and you douse it with jar-water,
everyone knows it cannot extinguish it—
why?
The fire is strong, the water little,
the coolness cannot overcome it.
Now, the state flooded
is like a great mountain on fire;
using such thin silk threads,
binding the altar as rescue,
is like dousing a great mountain with jar-water.
To understand Heaven's mind through human intent,
or describe Heaven's governance through human affairs:
when people attack each other,
if their energies do not combine,
their weapons not superior,
they cannot win.
Now, for a whole state flooded,
if one truly wishes to attack yin to cut off its energy,
mobilize all the people of the state,
armed with knives and sticks to strike it,
like driving out pestilence at year's end,
then it might be feasible.
In the time between Chǔ and Hàn,
during the era of the Six States,
with armed conflicts and attacks,
the stronger in force won,
the weaker lost.
Attacking the altar,
with one person beating a drum,
lacking the might of arms,
how can it rescue from rain?
For one sunny day and one rainy day,
it is like one day and one night;
encountering floods like Yáo's
or Tāng's droughts,
is like one winter and one summer.
If one hopes to use human affairs and sacrifices to remedy the anomaly,
it is like seeking summer in winter,
or day at night.
How to prove this?
During prolonged rain without clearing,
try having the ruler lie back peacefully on his pillow;
the rain will stop by itself.
After stopping long enough,
until a great drought comes,
try having the ruler lie back peacefully on his pillow;
the drought will rain by itself.
Why?
When yang reaches its extreme, it turns to yin;
when yin reaches its extreme, it turns to yang.
So, when Heaven and Earth have flooding,
how do we know it is not like humans having water-related illness?
When there is drought,
how do we know it is not like humans having feverish disease?
Praying and seeking blessings
ultimately cannot cure it;
changing conduct and behavior
ultimately cannot save it.
Have a doctor administer medicine,
hoping for a cure;
when fate is exhausted and the time comes,
medicine is ineffective.
Yáo encountered floods,
the great floods recorded in the "Chūnqiū";
the sage ruler understood it,
did not pray to spirits,
did not change his governance,
but had Yǔ control it,
and all rivers flowed east.
Yáo having Yǔ control the waters
is like a water-diseased person having a doctor.
Thus, Yáo's floods
were Heaven and Earth's water illness;
Yǔ's water control
was the floods' good doctor.
How can commentators change this?
The principle of attacking the Earth Altar
is unjustifiable in practice.
When rain does not cease,
offering sacrifices to Nǚwā—
where is this seen in the rites?
Fúxī and
Nǚwā
were both sages.
Abandoning Fúxī to sacrifice to Nǚwā
is not mentioned in the Spring and Autumn Annals.
What then was Dǒng Zhòngshū's reasoning
for this?
Now, the Spring and Autumn Classic only says
"drumming,"
how could it mean
"attacking"
? Commentators, seeing the
"drumming"
text, then speak of
"attacking."
But drumming does not necessarily mean attacking;
the commentators' intent differs.
The Jì family was wealthier than the Duke of Zhōu,
yet Qiú still amassed taxes to increase their riches.
Confucius said:
"He is no disciple of mine.
My young friends, you may beat the drums and assail him,
that is permissible."
Here, "assail" means
to reprimand,
to reprove him.
The mutual attacks among the six warring states
cannot challenge this meaning.
This too is incorrect.
For the lowly to reprimand the noble
is rebellious.
Perhaps it is by appealing to Heaven that they reprove them.
The king serves Earth as a mother;
if the mother errs,
can the son rely on the father to reprimand her?
From subordinate to superior,
it is proper to speak of remonstrance.
In serving,
it is the ritual of ministers and sons;
reproving
is the ritual of superiors.
To act contrary to ritual meaning—
how can it be practiced?
In ritual, drums are used to aid shouting,
making the sound clear.
In ancient times, when a ruler was about to depart,
bells were struck and drums beaten
to alert those below.
If beating drums must be taken as attacking
the
Earth Altar, then the sound of bells and drums would be attacking superiors.
During great floods, drums are used,
perhaps to repeatedly inform the Earth Altar.
When yin is excessively dominant,
rain floods and does not cease,
yin strong and yang weak,
is not the proper way.
If oral prayers are insufficient,
drums are used for self-assistance,
sharing the same principle as
using drums and sacrificial animals at the Earth Altar during solar eclipses.
It is the same meaning.
Both are declarations of emergency,
revealing the dominance of yin.
For great and urgent matters, bells and drums are used;
for minor and less pressing matters, bells and small drums—
to manifest the emergency,
aiding the spoken word.
The ways of Heaven are hard to know;
when great floods long persist,
even if caused by misgovernment,
one first declares an emergency,
then implements corrective policies.
The outbreak of banditry
follows the same procedure.
Banditry too results from misgovernment;
comparing it to seeking faults,
one still first issues a declaration.
Using drums and sacrificial animals at the Earth Altar
is to reveal the situation.
The Earth Altar
is the chief of all yin forces,
so drums are beaten to make it aware.
Those explaining the drums consider it
"attacking,"
hence the difficulties of
"attacking the mother"
and "rebellious righteousness"
arise,
stemming from this.
Now, speaking of
"informing"
due to yin's dominance and yang's weakness,
how could the difficulty of attacking the noble
arise from this?
Moreover, informing suits the use of sacrificial animals,
but using animals does not suit attacking.
Informing with sacrificial animals
is ritual;
attacking with sacrificial animals—
where is this seen in ritual?
Vermilion silk threads like cords
symbolize yang.
As yang energy is truly weak,
subtle objects are used.
Inserting a one-inch needle,
applying a moxa pellet to the pathways of blood vessels,
can cure severe illness.
Vermilion silk threads are like the one-inch needle,
the moxa pellet.
When Wú attacked and defeated Chǔ,
King Zhāo fled,
Shēn Bāoxū hurried on foot to Qín,
weeping and pleading for help,
finally obtaining military aid,
repelling Wú and preserving Chǔ.
If the drum-beater
were truly like this.
If one were truly like Shēn Bāoxū,
one person's drumming could suffice.
Suppose one person beats the drum,
could it make the Earth Altar share the Qín king's empathy,
using earth's power to conquer water,
halting the clouds and rain?
If the clouds and rain could share Wú's fear,
dispersing into the mountains,
then the afflicted people
would receive clear skies,
gaining Chǔ's safety.
At sudden thunder and fierce winds,
the nobleman must change demeanor,
rising even at night,
sitting dressed and capped,
fearing the awe of anomalies.
Floods and droughts
are like thunder and winds;
even if the cycles are inevitable,
should the ruler recline on high pillows,
awaiting their time,
without compassionate concern for the people?
Yáo did not use sacrificial animals,
perhaps because ancient times were simpler.
Cāngjié created writing,
Xīzhòng made carts—
can we say that before their time, writing and
carts did not exist,
and they were not later developments?
Same era, different creations—
that can be challenged;
different eras, changed customs—
how can they be criticized?
Common depictions of Nǚwā's image
show her in woman's form,
and her title is
"Nǚ."
Dǒng Zhòngshū likely meant
that Nǚwā
was an ancient female sovereign.
Male is yang, female is yin;
when yin energy causes harm,
sacrificing to Nǚwā seeks blessings.
The Tradition also says:
"Gònggōng contended with Zhuānxū to be Son of Heaven,
was defeated,
angrily struck Mount Bùzhōu,
causing the pillars of Heaven to break,
and the cords of Earth to snap.
Nǚwā smelted five-colored stones to repair the blue sky,
severed the turtle's feet to set up the four pillars."
Dǒng Zhòngshū's sacrifice to Nǚwā
likely stemmed from this Tradition.
Since she had the divine power to mend the sky
and erect the four pillars,
when the weather is discordant,
and the yang path is overpowered,
perhaps Nǚwā could spiritually aid the sage king in stopping the flooding rains!
Dǒng Zhòngshū elaborated on the Spring and Autumn rain sacrifice,
setting up earthen dragons to summon rain,
intending that clouds and dragons attract each other.
The Yì Jīng says:
"Clouds follow the dragon,
wind follows the tiger."
Seeking by category,
thus earthen dragons are set up;
yin and yang follow their kinds,
clouds and rain come naturally.
Some Confucian scholars may ask:
When the Book of Changes says
"clouds follow the dragon,"
it refers to a real dragon,
how could it mean an earthen one?
Lord Shè of Chǔ loved dragons,
painting them on walls, plates, and vessels.
If resemblance must imply reality,
then Lord Shè's state should have constant rain.
The Book of Changes also says
"wind follows the tiger,"
meaning that when a tiger roars, valley winds arise.
Wind and tiger
share the same vital energy.
If we place an earthen tiger
in a valley,
can wind arrive?
Since an earthen tiger cannot summon wind,
how can an earthen dragon summon rain?
In ancient times, people kept dragons,
harnessing them to pull chariots,
hence there were dragon-tamers
and dragon-drivers.
At the court of the Xià sovereign,
two dragons often stayed;
in its declining years,
the two dragons lay low.
Even with real dragons on earth,
there was no rain,
let alone with artificial images?
In rituals, the thunder-wine vessel is shaped like thunder,
yet it never summons thunder;
how can earthen dragons stir rain?
Amber picks up mustard seeds,
lodestone attracts needles,
because they are genuine,
not by imitating other things.
Why is it that other things,
though similar in appearance,
cannot attract them?
Because their natures differ,
and they cannot influence each other.
When Liú Zǐjùn oversaw the rain sacrifice
and the earthen dragon ritual,
Huán Jūnshān challenged him, asking how,
if amber and lodestone were not genuine,
they could attract needles and mustard seeds?
Zǐjùn was at a loss for an answer.
Zǐjùn,
the wise counselor of the Hàn court,
a deep well of literary talent,
was left speechless—
surely because the matter was misunderstood,
and the true principle was not grasped.
I respond:
To challenge based on unreality
is correct,
but to deny the principle of resemblance
is wrong.
When the east wind blows, wine overflows.
For wine tastes sour,
belonging to the east and wood.
Its flavor is sour,
hence it overflows.
When a whale dies,
a comet appears.
Such is the way of heaven, natural,
not human affairs.
This is of the same nature
as clouds following the dragon.
The sun is fire,
the moon is water.
Fire and water interact
through true energy.
Now, artisans
cast burning mirrors to capture fire from the sun,
make moon mirrors to draw water from the moon—
not naturally,
yet by heaven's principle.
Earthen dragons are not real either,
so why can't they move heaven?
This is point one.
To take fire from the sky with a burning mirror,
one must smelt five minerals
at noon on the bǐngwǔ day in May,
casting them into a vessel
to obtain fire.
Yet even an ordinary crescent-shaped sword,
polished and facing the sun,
can also draw heavenly fire.
Since earthen dragons cannot compare to burning mirrors,
they should be likened to crescent swords.
This is point two.
When Mèngcháng Jūn of Qí fled Qín by night,
the pass was closed,
but his follower's cock-crow
drew real crows in response.
If fowl can be moved by artificial sounds,
then rain can be summoned by artificial images.
This is point three.
When Lǐ Zǐcháng governed,
to discern prisoners' guilt,
he carved figures from phoenix tree wood,
resembling the prisoners,
dug pits in the ground,
fenced them with reeds,
and laid the wooden prisoners inside.
If a prisoner was guilty,
the wooden figure stayed still;
if wronged,
it moved or emerged.
Was it the prisoner's spirit possessing the wooden figure,
or the energy of spirit moving it?
If spirit can move wooden figures,
why should it not respond to earthen dragons?
This is point four.
Shùn, with his sage virtue,
entered the wild forests,
where tigers and wolves did not harm him,
nor insects or snakes.
Yǔ cast a bronze tripod depicting all creatures,
and entering the mountains,
warded off calamities.
Critics say this is not true,
yet in antiquity's distant past,
the magic of the Zhōu tripods cannot be denied.
Metal and earth share the five phases;
if makers of earthen dragons had Yǔ's virtue,
they too would evidence clouds and rain.
This is point five.
Amber picks up mustard seeds,
but lodestone and magnetic rocks,
though not amber,
also attract them.
Earthen dragons are not real,
yet they belong to the same category
as lodestone and magnetic rocks.
This is point six.
Lord Shè of Chǔ loved dragons,
painting their images on walls and vessels,
and real dragons descended upon hearing.
Since dragons share energy with clouds and rain,
they can influence each other,
following by kind.
If Lord Shè's paintings drew real dragons,
why alone can they not draw rain?
This is point seven.
Spirits show people images,
not realities,
hence in dreams we see images of events.
When good fortune approaches,
auspicious images come;
when misfortune nears,
ominous ones arrive.
The energy of spirits
and the category of clouds and rain
are alike.
This is point eight.
There are fifteen evidences based on symbolic categories,
and four meanings conveyed through ritual expressions.
Dǒng Zhòngshū, with his profound and extensive insight,
established practices not without reason,
setting up the image of an earthen dragon,
which indeed had tangible form.
When the dragon briefly emerges from water,
clouds and rain follow.
In ancient times, when dragons were kept
and harnessed,
they remained constantly present,
yet without bringing clouds or rain.
Just as when old friends long separated
suddenly meet again,
they rejoice, sing, and laugh,
or even weep with emotion,
but after a short while of interaction,
their emotions gradually fade away.
The "Yì Jīng" says
"Clouds follow the dragon,"
not that the dragon follows the clouds.
If a wine vessel were carved with images of thunder and clouds,
would the dragon willingly come?
Given this,
how can the transmitters explain it?
Then Huán Jūnshān's objections can be addressed,
while Liú Zǐjùn could not respond,
being inferior,
and thus Dǒng Zhòngshū's theory of the dragon remains incomplete.
The "Lùn Héng" concludes it,
hence it is said
"Disorderly Dragons."
Disorderly Dragons—
disorder finds its resolution.
The experts on anomalies and their remedies
claim that when a tiger kills a person,
it is due to the misconduct of the Gōng Cáo.
They believe that the Gōng Cáo,
as the leader of officials,
and the tiger, as the strongest among beasts,
symbolize each other: if the Gōng Cáo is corrupt,
exploiting his subordinates,
then the tiger kills people
to reflect this.
Yet tigers kill people,
and people also kill tigers.
If saying the tiger kills people
symbolizes the Gōng Cáo's extortion from clerks,
then when people kill tigers,
does it mean clerks are exploited by the Gōng Cáo?
Consider that among honest and upright men,
not one in a hundred
holds the position of Gōng Cáo;
most harbor deceitful intentions,
favoring old acquaintances for personal gain;
bribes and gifts,
both large and small, are common.
If we insist tigers correspond to the Gōng Cáo,
then tigers in the wild should constantly harm people.
But tigers appear at certain times,
just as dragons reveal themselves periodically.
Yīn creatures emerge in winter,
yáng insects appear in summer.
Their emergence responds to the cosmic breath,
which activates their kind.
Shēn and Fá stars appear in winter,
Xīn and Wěi stars in summer.
Shēn and Fá correspond to the tiger constellation,
Xīn and Wěi to the dragon's image.
When the image appears, the creature is seen;
when the breath arrives, the kind is stirred—
this is the nature of heaven and earth.
Moving through forests and marshes,
if one encounters a tiger's attack,
it is due to the tiger's savage nature,
its greed and hunger,
striking at any who approach—
how could it not eat them?
Human strength
may be weak and unfit,
lacking skill or awareness,
so encountering a tiger leads to death.
If Mèng Bēn were to climb the mountain,
or Féng Fù enter the forest,
they would suffer no such harm.
When Confucius traveled through a forest in Lǔ,
he heard a woman weeping
most sorrowfully
and sent Zǐgòng to ask her:
"Why do you weep so sadly?"
She replied:
"Last year, a tiger killed my husband,
and this year, it killed my son,
hence my bitter tears."
Zǐgòng asked:
"If so,
why not leave this place?"
She answered:
"I appreciate the government's lack of harshness
and the officials' lack of cruelty."
Zǐgòng returned and reported to Confucius.
Confucius said:
"Remember this, my disciples!
Harsh governance
and cruel officials are worse than tigers!"
That tigers harm people
has been known since ancient times.
If the government is not harsh,
and officials are not cruel,
virtuous influence should suffice to repel tigers,
yet here, two people were killed in two consecutive years,
suggesting the beasts in the forest do not respond to good governance.
If they do not respond to integrity,
neither should they to corrupt officials.
Some say:
"The tiger responds to the Gōng Cáo's corruption,
but the good governance mentioned
does not involve the Gōng Cáo.
The woman
belongs to the district of an honest official;
even with good governance,
how could it transform the tiger?"
Now, Lǔ had no Gōng Cáo position;
the equivalent of Gōng Cáo
was the Prime Minister.
The Prime Minister of Lǔ
was hardly a Confucius
or a Mòzǐ, but surely one of the Three Families,
and as such, lacked virtuous conduct.
With an unworthy holding power,
his evil
must include corruption.
If we blame the Prime Minister's corruption
for the tiger's killing,
then tigers in Lǔ's wilderness should constantly prey on people.
Poisons in water
do not reach high ground,
and the vapors on high ground
do not enter the water;
each suffers calamity
according to its proximity.
Thus, fishermen do not die in mountains,
nor hunters drown in deep waters.
Those who venture deep into forests,
exploring remote and hidden places,
treading near tiger dens,
may be attacked and eaten—
why consider this an anomaly?
Gōngniú Āi of Lǔ, after an illness, turned into a tiger
and killed his own brother.
When transformation occurs among humans,
it is not deemed strange,
yet when one enters forests and marshes
and is harmed by a tiger,
it is considered anomalous—
this is incorrect.
Vipers are fierce and violent,
able to harm people too.
If bitten by a viper in the mountains,
which official does it correspond to?
Bees and scorpions harm people,
poisonous gases harm people,
fire and water harm people.
If stung by bees or scorpions,
affected by poisonous gas,
burned by fire,
or drowned in water,
who is to blame for these?
If beasts are said to reflect officials' conduct,
then in the mountains and forests,
deer, wild boars,
bison, elephants, bears, and brown bears,
jackals, wolves, and apes
all also kill people.
If eating people is considered an anomaly,
then mosquitoes and gadflies all bite people,
but due to human robustness,
it rarely leads to death.
In times of turmoil,
when grain is scarce and expensive,
and people starve,
they may resort to cannibalism—
an anomaly worse than tiger attacks.
Yet the experts on anomalies and remedies
do not attribute this to harsh governance.
Moreover, what tigers devour
is not limited to humans alone;
blood-bearing birds
and formed beasts
are all preyed upon by tigers.
If devouring humans corresponds to the wickedness of the merit officials,
then when they eat other birds and beasts,
which officials does that correspond to?
Now tigers
are furred creatures,
while humans are naked creatures;
when furred creatures are hungry,
they eat naked creatures—
what anomaly is there in that?
Beyond the four barbarian regions,
the great eat the small;
tigers and the barbarians
share the same inherent nature.
On level plains and broad metropolises,
tigers do not roam;
in mountain forests and marshy grasslands,
tigers are born and thrive.
If it must be claimed that tigers eating people corresponds to the wickedness of merit officials,
then in counties of level plains and broad metropolises,
the merit officials should always be virtuous;
while in towns of mountain forests and marshes,
the merit officials should constantly face execution.
If tigers devouring people in the wild
corresponds to the wickedness of merit officials,
then when tigers occasionally enter towns
and walk among the people,
are the merit officials roaming the alleys and lanes?
In truth,
tigers harming people in the wild
does not correspond to governance;
their appearance in cities and towns
is what constitutes an anomaly.
Now tigers,
beasts of the mountain forests,
are untamed creatures,
often dwelling in grassy wilderness,
not domesticated animals,
much like the mice in human homes,
hiding and rarely emerging,
not commonly seen.
When fate is auspicious and dwelling secure,
mice do not cause disturbance;
when fortune declines and dwelling is perilous,
mice bring calamitous changes.
So it is with tigers as well:
when the town or county is auspicious and peaceful,
and the chief officials are free from trouble,
tigers hide unseen;
when the chief officials face peril,
then tigers enter the town,
walking among the people.
Why is this?
Because the radiant energy of the chief officials has already faded,
and the land of the city
becomes equal to the wilderness.
Extending this reasoning,
those whom tigers devour
also have their fate and timing.
When fate is exhausted and times decline,
radiant energy leaves the body,
making the flesh appear as a corpse,
so tigers eat them.
Heaven's way coincidentally converges:
tigers happen to devour people,
chief officials encounter misfortune,
thus it is called an anomaly,
but it corresponds not to the faults of superiors.
Throughout history, ominous signs
are not limited to tigers alone;
wild creatures all behave similarly.
When King Yīng of Chǔ's palace tower was unfinished,
a deer ascended the steps,
and later he indeed passed away.
When Duke Zhāo of Lǔ was about to depart,
mynas came to nest,
and later Jì Shì expelled Duke Zhāo,
who fled to Qí,
ultimately dying without return.
When Jiǎ Yì was tutor to the King of Chángshā,
an owl perched in his residence;
he consulted the texts for divination,
which said:
"The master will depart."
Later he was transferred to be tutor to the King of Liáng.
Since King Huái enjoyed horseback riding,
he fell from his horse and died;
Jiǎ Yì grieved over this,
and also fell ill and died.
During the time of the King of Chāngyì,
wild doves gathered under the palace hall,
and the king shot them,
then asked Lángzhōnglìng Gōng Suì about it.
Gōng Suì replied:
"Wild doves are birds of the field;
entering the palace
portends loss."
Later, the King of Chāngyì indeed perished.
When Tián Guāng, magistrate of Lúnú, conspired with Gōngsūn Hóng and others to rebel,
just before their plot was discovered,
a fox cried on the roof of Guāng's house,
and Guāng felt troubled by it.
Later the affair was uncovered,
and he was executed.
When Lǐ Wénbó was Dūwèi of the Eastern Division of Kuàijī,
a goat lay in the hall,
and later he was promoted to Tàishǒu of Dōnglái.
When Wáng Zǐfèng was Dūwèi,
a river deer entered the government office,
and later he was promoted to Tàishǒu of Dānyáng.
Now auspicious and ominous signs share the same interpretation,
promotion and dismissal are one verification,
both symbolizing emptiness and loss,
the essence and energy fading away.
Thus, when a person is about to perish,
wild birds enter the dwelling;
when a city is about to be emptied,
grass insects enter the town.
Such examples are numerous,
occurrences stand shoulder to shoulder,
so I briefly cite the more notable ones
to establish factual verification.
Those who interpret changes and cycles
claim that insects devouring grain
are caused by local officials.
If they are greedy and encroach,
then insects eat the grain.
If the body is black and the head red,
they say it corresponds to military officials;
if the head is black and the body red,
they say it corresponds to civil officials.
If punishment is imposed on the officials symbolized by the insects,
then the insects will vanish
and not reappear.
Now if a red head signifies military officials,
and a black head signifies civil officials,
what if sometimes the head is red and the body white,
or the head black and the body yellow,
or both head and body yellow,
or both head and body blue,
or all white like fish or meat insects—
which officials do they correspond to?
What if sometimes powerful commoners in white cloth
or crafty officials punished and seeking loans
have more authority than officials,
and take more than clerks—
what would the insects symbolizing them look like?
The disappearance of insects
is always due to wind and rain.
Consider that when insects vanish,
the officials may not necessarily be punished.
In dry fields, there are often rats;
in paddy fields, there are fish, shrimp, crabs, and such,
all harmful to grain.
Some may appear rarely and cause temporary harm,
others are constant and create disasters,
with many similar types—
which officials do they correspond to?
When Duke Xuān of Lǔ implemented the field-acre tax,
in response to the times, there were those who said young locusts appeared,
some claiming they were like locusts.
When locusts arrive in season,
they obscure the sky like rain,
gathering on the ground to eat things,
not distinguishing between grain and grass.
Observe their heads and bodies—
what officials do they resemble in form?
Those who interpret changes and retributions—
what response do they say the locusts signify?
In the thirty-first year of the Jiànwǔ era,
locusts arose in Tàishān Commandery,
traveling southwest past Chénliú,
Hénán,
and then entered the lands of the barbarians.
The villages and counties where they gathered
numbered in the hundreds and thousands,
yet the officials of those villages and counties at the time
had not all implemented the field-acre tax.
The locusts ate grain and grass,
and after several days grew old and exhausted;
some flew away,
others stopped and died dried up.
The officials of those villages and counties at the time
did not necessarily all admit their guilt.
Now, when insects eat grain,
it naturally has an end date;
just as silkworms eating mulberry leaves
naturally have their fill in time.
They are born on certain days,
and die exhausted in certain months;
when their time ends, they transform—
they do not remain insects forever.
If the ruler does not blame his officials,
the insects will still vanish on their own.
Now insects
are born from wind and qi,
as Cāng Jié knew;
thus
the character for
"insect"
combined with
"wind"
forms the character
They take qi from the wind,
so they transform in eight days.
Things born in spring and summer
may eat the five grains,
or may eat various grasses.
If eating the five grains
symbolizes officials accepting money and grain,
then when they eat other grasses,
what are they receiving from people?
There are three hundred types of naked creatures,
and humans are their chief.
From this perspective,
humans are also insects.
Humans eat what insects eat,
and insects also eat what humans eat;
all being insects that eat each other's food—
why find it strange?
If insects had consciousness,
they might also criticize humans, saying:
"You eat what Heaven produces,
and I eat it too;
you call me an aberration,
but do not call yourselves a disaster."
Among all breathing creatures,
what they find sweet and crave
does not differ in mouth and belly.
Humans relish the five grains,
yet hate insects for eating them;
they themselves live between Heaven and Earth,
yet detest the emergence of insects.
If insects could speak,
using this to criticize humans,
we would have no way to refute them.
When insects are among things,
the wise do not find it strange;
when they eat all things,
it is not called a disaster.
Things that are sweet, fragrant, and rich in flavor
often produce many insects;
thus among grains, the one with many insects
is millet.
Rice sometimes has insects,
but wheat and beans have none.
If one must blame the responsible officials for having insects,
then the officials in millet-producing regions would always be admitting guilt.
Shénnóng
and Hòu Jì's methods for storing seeds,
such as boiling horse dung to soak the seeds in its juice,
were to prevent the grain from having insects.
If someone used horse dung to soak seeds,
then the officials of their village
would be like Bào Jiāo
and Chén Zhòngzǐ.
Thus, if the methods of Hòu Jì
and Shénnóng were applied,
then the local officials could avoid being corrupt.
Why so?
Insects would have no way to arise,
and superiors would have no basis for investigation.
When insects eat other grasses,
it is considered normal and not strange;
but when they eat the leaves of the five grains,
it is called a disaster.
Cinnamon has borers,
mulberry trees have caterpillars;
cinnamon is used in medicine,
and mulberry feeds silkworms—
their uses are also crucial,
no different from grain.
Borers and caterpillars are not considered strange,
yet only insects eating grain are called a disaster—
this shows a lack of understanding of the reality of things,
and ignorance about the nature of disasters and changes.
Grain insects are called "insects,"
while grain moths are like moths.
Millet and rice when heated and spoiled produce moths.
Now, when moths eat millet and rice,
it is not called a disaster;
but when insects eat sprouts and leaves,
it is attributed to governance.
As those who interpret insects would say,
this values the sprouts over the grain.
The types of insects
are numerous and not uniform.
Rotting fish and meat have insects;
unsealed vinegar and sauce have insects;
warm, damp cooked rice has insects;
unopened scrolls have insects;
folded, unhung clothes have insects;
sores, ulcers, abscesses, and tumors have insects.
Some are white, some black;
some long, some short;
large and small, thick and thin,
not resembling each other;
all are born from wind and qi,
and all die connected to it.
They are born without choosing a day,
and if their life is short,
they are seen and then quickly perish.
Those who interpret changes and retributions,
seeing them appear rarely,
and then eating things when they emerge,
call it a disaster.
If a disaster emerges, there must be someone to blame,
so they follow the resemblance to officials
and explain it accordingly.
In the human abdomen, there are three worms;
in the marshes below ground,
their insect is called a leech.
Leeches eat at people's feet,
while the three worms eat the intestines.
Those who explain by resemblance—
what will they say the three worms resemble?
Throughout Heaven and Earth,
what is born from yīn and yáng—
creatures like centipedes and pinworms,
and categories like insects and maggots—
are born breathing qi,
and open their mouths to eat.
Whether their food is sweet or not,
their hearts and desires are equal;
the strong eat the weak,
and the wise oppress the dull.
When other creatures, large and small, continuously bite and devour each other,
it is not called a disaster;
yet only when insects eat grain is it said to reflect governance—
this loses the reality of principle,
and fails to understand the nature of things and qi.
If no birds follow it,
it might be a phoenix;
if flocks of birds follow it,
it might not be one.
When a noble person exists in the world,
they uphold their pure integrity,
not widely gathering followers;
in their comings and goings and actions,
people do not follow them.
Cunning and powerful individuals,
who practice chivalry and act on impulse,
in their interactions and movements,
attract crowds like gathering clouds.
Now, the phoenix
is like the noble person;
if one must judge a phoenix by the number of followers,
then these cunning individuals would be considered noble persons.
The more exquisite the song,
the fewer those who can harmonize with it;
the purer one's conduct and integrity,
the fewer companions one will have.
Birds and beasts are the same.
If one must judge a phoenix by the followers it attracts,
that would be like judging a fine song by the number of people who can sing along.
The dragon and the phoenix are often compared.
During the reign of Emperor Xuān,
a yellow dragon appeared in Xīnfēng,
yet no snakes followed it.
The divine sparrow
and the luán bird
are both leaders among birds;
though their benevolence and sageliness may not match that of the phoenix,
they should still be followed by dozens of birds.
Lord Xìnlíng
and Lord Mèngcháng
had three thousand retainers,
and were called virtuous lords;
yet the Hàn generals Wèi Qīng and Huò Qùbìng
had no retainers at their gates,
and were also renowned as great generals.
Grand Historian Sīmǎ Qiān said:
"Robber Zhí rampaged,
gathering a gang of several thousand;
while Bóyí
and Shūqí
lived in seclusion on Shǒuyáng Mountain."
The nature of birds and beasts
is similar to that of humans.
If having many followers among people
is not enough to distinguish the virtuous,
then how can judging a phoenix by the birds that follow it
be valid?
Some say:
"The phoenix
and the qílín
are omens of peace.
In times of peace,
they appear and arrive.
Yet there are also instances when they arrive without peace prevailing.
If birds and beasts have extraordinary bones and unusual feathers,
uncommonly卓越,
then they are such creatures;
why would they be unrecognizable?"
Do the phoenix
and qílín
always arrive in times of peace?
During the Spring and Autumn period,
a qílín once appeared, which was misinterpreted by King and troubled Confucius.
Emperor Guāngwǔ was born in Jìyáng,
and a phoenix came to gather there.
Now, when Guāngwǔ was born,
it was during the era of Emperors Chéng and Āi,
a time not yet peaceful,
yet the phoenix arrived.
If it is said that it came because Guāngwǔ possessed sage virtue,
then this would be an omen for the birth of a sage king,
not a response to peace.
Auspicious signs may sometimes respond to peace,
or sometimes to a birth,
their true nature is hard to discern.
If we judge solely by their appearance in peaceful times,
how reliable is that?
Some say:
"Phoenixes and qílín
are born with their own kinds,
just as turtles and dragons have their kinds.
Turtles naturally beget turtles,
dragons naturally beget dragons,
their forms, colors, and sizes
no different from their predecessors.
Seeing the father,
one can observe the offspring;
why would they be unrecognizable?"
Now, ordinary things have kinds,
but auspicious omens have no fixed species and arise appropriately,
hence it is said
"virtue responds,"
and so it is with turtles and dragons.
Do people see
"divine"
turtles
or "numinous"
dragons and recognize them?
During the time of King Sòng Yuán,
a fisherman netted a divine turtle,
yet the fisherman did not know it was divine.
The Confucian scholars of today
are like that fisherman.
If the fisherman did not know the divine turtle,
then we also know that people of the world do not recognize the numinous dragon.
Sometimes a dragon may resemble a snake,
and sometimes a snake may resemble a dragon.
Hán Fēizǐ said:
"A horse that resembles a deer is worth a thousand in gold."
A fine horse may resemble a deer,
and a divine dragon may sometimes resemble a snake.
If they truly have kinds,
their forms and colors should not differ.
During Wáng Mǎng's time, there was a large bird like a horse,
with five-colored dragon patterns,
that gathered with dozens of other birds
in Qí County of Pèi State.
During Emperor Xuān's time, a phoenix gathered on the ground,
five feet tall,
and it was said
"like a horse,"
their heights were the same;
its patterns were five-colored,
and it was said
"five-colored dragon patterns,"
their appearances were equal;
"dozens of other birds"
and it was said
"gathered together,"
"followed,"
and so on.
If based on the body and color of the phoenix in Emperor Xuān's time,
and the birds following it, we judge it to be a phoenix,
then the bird attracted by Wáng Mǎng
was also a phoenix.
If it truly was,
then Wáng Mǎng attracted it,
which would mean it was not an auspicious omen.
If it was not a phoenix,
why were its body color
and followers
identical?
Moreover, auspicious omens all arise from harmonious energy,
born among ordinary kinds,
yet possessing extraordinary qualities,
thus they are considered auspicious.
Therefore, the arrival of a phoenix
is like the gathering of red crows.
To say the phoenix has a kind,
do red crows also have a kind?
Bountiful grain,
sweet springs,
and sweet dew
—bountiful grain grows among ordinary grain,
with stalks different from the rest,
and is called bountiful grain.
Sweet springs
and sweet dew
emerge sweet and exquisite;
they are all produced from springs
and dew,
not because there is a kind of sweet dew in heaven
or a type of sweet spring underground.
It is when sage governance is fair and just
that they moisten and produce below.
The calendrical plant
and vermilion grass
also grow on the earth,
among the grasses,
without permanent roots,
temporarily produced,
withering and breaking in ten days or a month,
hence they are called auspicious.
Now, the phoenix
and qílín
are also auspicious;
how could they have kinds?
In the case of the Zhou dynasty's great peace,
Yuècháng presented a white pheasant.
The white pheasant—
it is a pheasant born with white feathers,
not from a distinct breed of white pheasants.
The people of Lǔ obtained a river deer with horns,
calling it a qílín,
which might also occasionally be born among river deer,
not from a distinct category of qílín.
From this perspective,
the fènghuáng might also occasionally be born among swans or magpies,
with extraordinary feathers and unique plumage,
standing out among other birds,
thus being called a fènghuáng;
how could it be of a species entirely different from other birds?
Yǒuruò said:
"The qílín among beasts,
the fènghuáng among birds,
Mount Tài among hills,
rivers and seas among puddles—
are of the same categories."
Then, the fènghuáng
and qílín,
are all of the same categories as birds and beasts,
only their forms and colors are extraordinary!
How could they be of different species?
Of the same category yet possessing uniqueness,
the unique is not common in the world,
the uncommon is hard to verify,
how can one recognize it?
Yáo gave birth to Dānzhū,
Shùn gave birth to Shāngjūn.
Shāngjūn
and Dānzhū
are of the same category as Yáo and Shùn,
only their bone structures and natures are different.
Gǔn gave birth to Yǔ,
Gǔsǒu gave birth to Shùn.
Shùn and Yǔ,
are of the lineage of Gǔn and Gǔsǒu,
yet their wisdom and virtue are exceptional.
Try planting seeds of fine grain,
but one cannot always obtain fine grain.
Often seen among millet and sorghum,
are stalks and ears that are strangely unique.
People saw Shūliáng Hé,
but did not know he was Confucius's father;
they saw Bóyú,
but did not know he was Confucius's son.
Zhāng Tāng's father was five chǐ tall,
while Tāng grew to eight chǐ,
and Tāng's grandson was six chǐ tall.
During Xiàoxuān's reign, a fènghuáng was five chǐ tall,
the bird from which it came might have been two chǐ tall,
and later-born birds might be one chǐ tall—
how can there be a constant breed?
Species and categories are not fixed,
thus Zēngxī gave birth to Shēn,
whose temperament was unparalleled,
Yán Lù produced Huí,
unmatched through ancient and modern times.
Horses capable of traveling a thousand lǐ
are not necessarily foals of qíjì;
birds possessing benevolence and sageliness
are not necessarily chicks of the fènghuáng.
Streams on mountain peaks,
unconnected to rivers and lakes,
yet contain fish—
the essence of water spontaneously produces them.
Abandoned courtyards and ruined halls,
with grass growing on their foundations—
the earth's energy spontaneously brings them forth.
Consider the fish in stream waters,
the grass on hall foundations—
they appear without specific categories,
auspicious responses arise spontaneously;
heaven and earth may not have fixed species.
Now, auspicious responses are like calamitous changes.
Auspicious signs respond to goodness,
calamities respond to evil;
though good and evil are opposites,
their responses are the same.
Calamitous changes have no fixed seed,
auspicious responses also have no fixed category.
The energies of yīn and yáng—
are the energies of heaven and earth—
encountering goodness become harmonious,
meeting evil turn into change;
could it be that heaven and earth administer policies of good and evil,
then generate energies of harmony and change?
Thus, the emergence of auspicious responses
likely has no fixed species,
but arises due to goodness,
born from harmonious energy.
Or perhaps when governance is peaceful and energy harmonious,
all things undergo transformations,
just as in spring, hawks change into turtledoves,
in autumn, turtledoves transform into hawks;
snakes and rats may turn into fish and turtles,
toads become quails,
sparrows transform into clams.
Things change according to energy,
one cannot say it does not happen.
A yellow stone turned into an old man,
handed a book to Zhāng Liáng,
then departed and became stone again—
confucian scholars know this.
Perhaps in times of great peace and harmonious energy,
river deer become qílín,
swans become fènghuáng.
Following their original natures,
they change with the times—
how must there always be constant categories?
Bāosì
was the child of a black turtle,
or the saliva of two dragons.
The two ministers of Jìn—
were descendants of bears and brown bears.
Tales of swallowing swallow eggs,
coix seeds,
or stepping in giant footprints—
people of the world believe them;
why then insist that auspicious signs have constant categories?
Considering things have no fixed seeds,
discussing humans have no fixed classes,
arguing that forms undergo changes—
the fènghuáng
and qílín are born without constant categories;
then why should their shapes and colors necessarily be the same?
Examining the "Chapter on Auspicious Mandates" in the Lǐjì, it states:
"The male is called fèng,
the female is called huáng.
The male's call is 'jí jí,'
the female's call is 'zú zú.'"
The Shījīng says:
"The wútóng tree grows,
on that high ridge.
The fènghuáng cries,
facing the morning sun.
Lush and luxuriant,
harmonious and melodious."
Both the "Auspicious Mandates" and the Shījīng
speak of the fènghuáng's cry,
yet the "Auspicious Mandates" says
"jí jí, zú zú,"
while the Shījīng says
"yōng yōng, jiē jiē"—
these sounds differ.
If the sounds were precise,
then the forms would differ;
if the sounds were the same,
the Shījīng and Lǐjì would not conflict.
The transmitted accounts of the fènghuáng's cry
thus invite doubt.
The Spring and Autumn Annals states:
"During a western hunt, a dead qilin was captured,
and people showed it to Confucius.
Confucius said:
'Why have you come?
Why have you come?'
He turned his sleeve to wipe his face,
weeping until tears soaked his lapel."
Confucian scholars explain this,
believing Heaven sent the qilin to mandate Confucius,
yet Confucius
was a sage without kingship.
Now the qilin came for sage kings,
but Confucius considered himself unworthy of kingship,
while the contemporary ruler of Lǔ lacked the virtue to attract the qilin.
Perplexed by its arrival and unaware of its purpose,
he therefore said:
"Why have you come?
Why have you come?"
Knowing it came not for prosperous governance
but because his Way was exhausted,
he felt despair and heartfelt sorrow,
hence weeping until tears soaked his lapel.
From Confucius' words
"Why have you come?"
they know the qilin came for sage kings.
I say: Before Confucius' time,
Confucian scholars already transmitted this theory.
When Confucius heard this theory,
he rarely witnessed such creatures.
Seeing the qilin's arrival,
he wondered about its purpose.
In reality,
the qilin's coming had no special purpose -
it was merely a common creature
wandering through the marshes of Lǔ
that happened to be spotted by the people of Lǔ
and captured by chance.
When Confucius saw the captured qilin,
captured and already dead,
he identified himself with the qilin,
believing his Way was cut off and would not prevail again,
fearing he would be captured by petty men.
Thus Confucius wept upon seeing the qilin
because he witnessed its capture and death,
not because of its original purpose for coming.
Then the qilin's arrival
was merely joining other animals in gathering,
its death
caused by human killing.
If the qilin had intelligence
and came for sage kings,
since there were no sage kings at that time,
why would it come?
If it could think deeply
and avoid harm from afar,
why was it captured and killed by Lǔ?
Since the qilin came when no sage kings existed,
we know it didn't come for sage kings;
since it was captured and killed by Lǔ,
we know it couldn't avoid harm from afar.
If holy beasts cannot escape misfortune,
neither can sages avoid calamity.
Disasters and difficulties
cannot be avoided even by sages,
yet they claim phoenixes
and qilins think deeply
and avoid harm from afar -
this is absurd.
Moreover, phoenixes
and qilins aren't born in foreign lands -
they come only when China has sage kings.
Born in China,
raised among mountain forests,
with pure natures rarely seen,
they cannot be harmed by humans,
thus deemed deep-thinking
and harm-avoiding.
Born contemporaneously with sage kings,
appearing during prosperous governance,
the world calls them auspicious signs of sage kings,
claiming they come for sages.
When nests are destroyed and eggs broken,
phoenixes refuse to soar;
when forests are burned for hunting
and ponds drained for fishing,
turtledragons refuse to swim.
Phoenixes,
turtledragons and their kind
are all born in China,
living close to humans.
When nests break and eggs smash,
they hide and refuse to soar;
when forests burn and ponds drain,
they conceal themselves and refuse to swim.
There's no record of them going far away -
how do we know they're in foreign lands?
Turtledragons
and phoenixes
belong to the same category.
If rarity and harmlessness
mean they're in foreign lands,
then since turtledragons are rarely seen,
they must be in foreign lands too.
During Emperor Xuān of Hàn's reign,
phoenixes,
qilins,
yellow dragons,
and divine sparrows all appeared.
Their simultaneous arrival
indicates similar natures and behaviors,
thus they should originate from similar habitats.
If dragons aren't born in foreign lands,
yet foreign lands also have dragons;
if phoenixes and qilins aren't born abroad,
yet foreign lands also have them.
Then China has them too,
not necessarily meaning foreign phoenixes and qilins.
People see phoenixes and qilins rarely,
so say they're in foreign lands;
see them during peace times,
so say they come for sage kings.
Now the arrival of phoenixes
and qilins
resembles sweet springs emerging
and vermilion grass growing.
If phoenixes are in foreign lands,
hearing of virtuous ways to come,
how do sweet springs
and vermilion grass know to appear during peaceful times?
Sweet springs
and vermilion grass
are born of harmonious energy,
thus phoenixes
and qilins
are also born of harmonious energy.
Harmonious energy produces sages,
yet sages are born in decadent ages.
Creatures appear as auspicious signs,
humans are born as sages -
simultaneous occurrences,
growing with time,
they eventually meet.
Decadent ages also have harmonious energy,
which occasionally produces sages.
Sages born in decadent ages,
decadent ages also occasionally have phoenixes
and qilins.
Confucius was born in late Zhōu's decadence,
qilins appeared in Lǔ's western marshes;
Emperor Guāngwǔ was born between Chéng and Āi's reigns,
phoenixes gathered in Jìyáng territory.
Sages and holy creatures appear in both prosperous
and decadent ages.
When sage kings emerge,
holy creatures appear -
encountering holy creatures
resembles fortunate people meeting auspicious signs:
their actual meeting
isn't deliberately arranged.
Confucian scholars discuss the auspicious signs of great peace,
all claiming that the ethers and objects are exceptionally outstanding,
such as vermilion grass,
sweet springs,
soaring phoenixes,
sweet dew,
auspicious stars,
fine grains,
shà fǔ plant,
míng jiá plant,
and qū yì grass;
they also say that chariots appear from mountains,
horses emerge from marshes,
men and women walk on separate paths,
markets have no dual pricing,
farmers yield field boundaries,
travelers give way to each other,
the grey-haired carry no burdens,
passes and bridges remain unbarred,
roads witness no plunder,
winds do not make branches whistle,
rains do not break clods of earth,
wind blows once every five days,
rain falls once every ten days;
the most flourishing among these
bring forth yellow dragons,
qílín,
and fènghuáng.
Now the words of Confucian scholars
contain exaggerated praise beyond reality.
As for these auspicious response objects,
some may exist while others may not.
Speaking of fènghuáng,
qílín, and the like,
these great auspicious signs are relatively clear
and cannot be embellished further;
but the minor auspicious signs and responses
are likely mostly untrue.
Now winds, ethers, rains, and dews
ought to be harmonious and moderate by nature;
to say that the winds soar and dews are sweet,
that winds do not make branches whistle,
and rains do not break clods
is acceptable;
but to claim wind blows once every five days
and rain falls once every ten days
is an exaggeration.
Even if winds and rains are moderate,
they cannot precisely follow a five- or ten-day cycle.
To say that men and women do not interfere with each other
and market prices are not deceptive
is acceptable;
but to claim they walk on separate paths
and there is no dual pricing
is an exaggeration.
In times of great peace,
would separate roads be built for men and women?
If no separate roads are built,
and everyone walks the same path,
how could they be separated?
In times of great peace,
if there were no merchants, it might be possible,
but if there are,
they would surely seek convenience for their livelihood,
so how could buyers not seek lower prices?
How could sellers not seek higher prices?
With the desire for high and low prices,
there must be talk of dual pricing.
These all have some basis in fact
but are exaggerated beyond reality.
As for shà fǔ,
míng jiá,
qū yì, and the like,
they probably do not exist.
How can this be verified?
By examining reality,
great peace does not have such things.
Confucian scholars claim that shà fǔ grows in kitchens,
meaning that meat-like strips naturally grow there,
thin as shà leaves,
swaying and fanning to produce wind,
cooling food
to prevent spoilage.
Now, even if the ether of great peace is harmonious,
it cannot make kitchens produce meat-shà
to provide cooling.
If it could do this,
then it could make the five grains grow spontaneously,
without human effort.
If it could make kitchens produce meat-shà naturally,
why not make rice steam itself in pots,
or fire ignite itself on stoves?
Generally, what produces shà
aims to fan food with wind;
why not make the food not spoil by itself?
Why must shà grow to fan it?
If kitchens can naturally produce shà,
then why would ice houses still cut ice to cool things?
In summer, people holding shà
must shake it by hand
to generate wind.
Held in the hand,
facing a strong wind,
the shà also flutters.
To say that shà fǔ fans itself
is acceptable,
but it requires wind to flutter;
without wind, it does not move.
If wind comes from hand-shaking,
it alone is enough to cool things in the kitchen;
what need is there for shà fǔ?
It is said that Prince Dān of Yān made the sun stand at noon twice,
heaven rained grain,
crows turned white-headed,
horses grew horns,
and kitchen door statues grew fleshy feet.
Since these accounts are false,
then tales of shà fǔ
and the five responses
likely have no basis in reality.
Confucian scholars also say
that in ancient times, míng jiá grew flanking the steps,
with one pod sprouting on the first day of the month,
reaching fifteen pods by the fifteenth day;
from the sixteenth day onward,
one pod falls daily,
until the month's end,
when all pods are gone.
On the first day of the next month,
one pod sprouts again.
The king, facing south, observes the pods' sprouting and falling
to know the number of days,
without the trouble of consulting a calendar.
Now, if heaven can make pods to indicate days,
why not have the pods bear day names,
so the king looking at the characters on the pods
could know the current day's name?
Merely knowing the day count
without knowing the day names
still requires checking a calendar to find out,
thus when the king observes the days,
it becomes more troublesome and unclear;
how can the growth of míng jiá
bring any benefit?
Now míng jiá
is the fruit of a plant,
like the pods of beans;
it does not grow in spring or summer,
but must sprout by late autumn.
In winter's severe cold,
with frost and snow falling,
all things wither;
would Confucian scholars dare say míng jiá alone survives through winter?
If it lives and dies with all other things,
and the pods form by late autumn,
then one can examine the pods only in late autumn,
but not in spring, summer, or winter.
Moreover, with fifteen pods by the fifteenth day,
and pods falling from the sixteenth day,
six pods fallen by the twenty-first day,
the fallen pods decay and are lost,
making them uncountable;
one would still have to count the remaining pods to know the days,
which is laborious and distressing,
not a divine blessing.
Even if the pods grew in the hall,
with the ruler sitting by the window,
observing the pods' growth
to know the day count,
it would not be considered good.
Now it is said
"flanking the steps they grow,"
meaning they grow below the hall.
The hall of a king,
as Mòzǐ described Yáo's
and Shùn's halls as three chǐ high,
Confucians consider too low.
Suppose it were so,
a hall three chǐ high,
with míng jiá growing below the steps;
if the king wishes to see the pods,
he cannot see them from the window;
he must go to the hall to observe them
to learn the pod count.
Now, rising to see the pods below the hall—
how does that compare to hanging a calendar by the throne,
where a glance reveals the date?
If heaven produces auspicious signs
to delight the king;
requiring him to rise and observe to know the day count
is creating a nuisance to burden him.
Moreover, the calendrical plant is
merely a grass.
In the hall of a king,
where he sits day and night,
even in ancient times when simplicity prevailed,
within the palace chambers,
any grass that grew would be weeded out immediately—
how could the calendrical plant grow there for people to count over months?
Furthermore, the purpose of counting days one by one
is to record and identify events.
In ancient times, there were historiographers in charge of calendars and days—
why would a king personally count the calendrical plants?
Yáo observed the equinoxes and solstices,
commanding Xī
and Hé to examine the four stars to determine the seasons and weather.
The four stars were extremely important,
yet he did not inspect them personally;
would he instead examine the calendrical plant to count the days?
Confucian scholars also say that
in times of great peace,
Qūyì grows at the edge of the courtyard,
resembling grass in form,
and it points out flatterers.
When a flatterer enters the court,
the Qūyì at the courtyard's edge points at them,
and the sage king then knows where the flatterers are.
If Heaven could intentionally create this thing to point out flatterers,
why not endow the sage king with the innate ability to know them himself?
Or if flatterers did not emerge at all,
must Heaven create another object to indicate them?
Why would Heaven go to such trouble?
No sage kings surpass Yáo
and Shùn; under Yáo
and Shùn’s rule,
it was the most peaceful.
If Qūyì had already grown at the edge of the courtyard,
and when flatterers came,
it pointed them out for recognition,
then why would Shùn have found it difficult to identify flatterers,
leading him to have Gāo Yáo expound methods for knowing people?
The Classic says:
"To know people is wisdom,
which even the Emperor found difficult."
Humans embody the five constant virtues,
and through sound and breath, they communicate,
yet they still cannot fully understand each other.
Qūyì,
being grass,
how could it know flatterers?
If we follow the Confucians' words,
then in times of peace,
plants and trees surpass the worthiness of sages.
In legal disputes, there are rights and wrongs;
in human feelings, there are straight and crooked.
Why not also have Qūyì point out the wrong and unjust,
instead of necessarily judging cases by heart,
with three men deciding lawsuits?
Thus, the Qūyì grass
might not have existed at all but was merely claimed to grow,
or it might have existed but its pointing ability was falsely attributed.
Suppose it could point;
perhaps it was the grass's nature to move when people approached.
Ancient people were simple and unsophisticated;
seeing the grass move,
they said it could point;
since it could point,
they claimed it pointed out flatterers.
The spoon of the south-pointing chariot,
when placed on the ground,
its handle points south.
Insects from fish and meat,
gathering on the ground, move north—
such is the nature of these insects.
Now if grass can point,
it is also its innate nature.
The sages, because the grass could point,
declared:
"At the courtyard's edge, there is Qūyì,
which can point out flatterers."
Then officials and subjects with deceitful hearts
would each change their nature and conduct,
acting with loyalty and integrity.
This is like today's government courts painting images of Gāo Yáo
and Xièzhì.
Confucian scholars explain:
Xièzhì
is a one-horned goat,
green in color with four legs,
