some say resembling a bear,
able to discern right from wrong,
and intuitively know the guilty.
When Gāo Yáo tried cases,
if someone's guilt was in doubt,
he would have the goat butt them.
If guilty, it would butt;
if not, it would not.
This was supposedly a heaven-sent one-horned sacred beast
to assist in trials as evidence,
so Gāo Yáo revered the goat,
rising and sitting to serve it.
This falls into the category of miraculous auspicious responses.
It is said:
This tale of Xièzhì is again like that of Qūyì.
Goats originally have two horns;
Xièzhì having one horn
means its body is impaired compared to the herd,
inferior to other kinds—
how can that be considered extraordinary?
A turtle with three legs is called 'néng',
a tortoise with three legs is called 'bēn'.
Consider that 'néng' and 'bēn' are no more divine than four-legged turtles and tortoises;
how can a one-horned goat be wiser than two-horned animals?
The xīngxīng knows the past,
the magpie knows the future,
and the parrot can talk.
Each has one innate ability,
not two.
Perhaps Xièzhì's nature was merely to butt people,
not necessarily to know the guilty.
Gāo Yáo wanted to use divine means to aid governance,
disliking that the accused might not submit to the verdict,
so he used Xièzhì's butting to condemn them,
hoping to deter people from crime through fear,
so that the families of the convicted
would harbor no resentment for life.
Each creature has its own innate knowledge;
if butting by Xièzhì is called divine,
then creatures like the xīngxīng
would all be considered divine.
Shamans know fortune and misfortune,
predicting people's woes and blessings,
and none fail in this.
If Xièzhì is considered akin to a shaman,
then what makes shamans so extraordinary as to be deemed good?
These are all cases of people wanting to use divine matters to establish influence.
Shī Shàngfǔ served as the Grand Marshal of Zhōu,
leading troops to attack Zhòu,
and when they reached the banks of Mèng Jīn,
holding his battle-axe and banner,
he shouted to his troops:
"Cāngsì!
Cāngsì!"
Cāngsì
is a creature of the water,
skilled at capsizing boats.
Using the divine to transform,
he wanted them to cross quickly,
implying that if they did not hurry,
Cāngsì would harm them—
this is again like the case of Xièzhì.
If there were such a strange creature in the river,
occasionally surfacing and floating,
with one body and nine heads,
people would fear and loathe it,
but it might not necessarily capsize boats.
Shàngfǔ, knowing of this oddity in the river,
used it to intimidate the masses.
Xièzhì butting the guilty
is like Cāngsì capsizing boats—
both have a false reputation
without real effect.
People fear the strange and unusual,
hence empty praise and exaggeration arise.
They also say that in times of peace, there is a jǐngxīng.
The Shàngshū Zhōnghòu states:
"In Yáo's time, the jǐngxīng appeared in the Zhěn constellation."
Now the jǐngxīng
might be one of the five planets.
The larger ones
are Jupiter
and Venus.
Perhaps at that time, Jupiter
and Venus were moving through the Zhěn constellation;
the ancients, being simplistic, could not calculate the motions of the five planets,
and did not know what Jupiter
and Venus looked like.
Seeing a large star, they called it the jǐngxīng.
The Book of Songs also states:
"In the east there is Qǐmíng,
in the west there is Chánggēng."
These may sometimes refer to Jupiter
and Venus respectively.
Sometimes appearing in the west at dusk,
sometimes emerging in the east at dawn,
the poets, not knowing this,
named them Qǐmíng
and Chánggēng.
Thus Chánggēng is the same as the Auspicious Star,
both being among the five planets.
In times of peace,
the sun and moon are brilliant.
The five planets
belong to the same category as the sun and moon.
If peace brings the Auspicious Star,
could it also bring additional suns and moons?
The poets were common people;
the era of the Zhōnghòu,
was an unrefined age,
where none knew the stars.
During Wáng Mǎng's time,
Venus crossed the sky,
shining like a half-moon.
Had those ignorant of stars seen it,
they would have again called it the Auspicious Star.
The Ěryǎ's "Explanation of the Four Seasons" chapter says:
"Spring is called Fāshēng (growth),
summer is Chángyíng (flourishing),
autumn is Shōuchéng (harvest),
winter is Ānníng (tranquility).
When the four energies harmonize, it produces the Auspicious Star."
According to the Ěryǎ's words,
the Auspicious Star is merely the name for harmonious seasonal energies,
likely not referring to a great star in the sky.
The Ěryǎ's text
and the commentaries on the Five Classics
are studied by all Confucian scholars,
yet they do not believe or follow them,
instead calling a great star the Auspicious Star.
How could the Auspicious Star described in the Ěryǎ
differ from what Confucian scholars claim?
The Ěryǎ further states:
"When sweet dew falls timely,
all things become excellent -
this is called Lǐquán (sweet spring)."
Lǐquán here refers to sweet dew.
Modern scholars explain it
as a spring emerging from the earth,
with a taste as sweet as sweet wine,
hence called Lǐquán.
These two interpretations are far apart,
and the truth is unknowable.
Examining the Ěryǎ's "Explanation of Waters
(Springs)" chapter:
"A spring that appears and disappears is Jiān.
Jiànquán emerges uprightly.
Upright emergence
means gushing out.
Wòquán hangs suspended.
Suspended emergence
means flowing downward."
Thus different types of spring emergence
receive different names.
If during peaceful times
there were indeed Lǐquán emerging from the earth,
it should be mentioned in this chapter.
Why instead place it in the "Explanation of Four Seasons" chapter,
calling sweet dew Lǐquán?
Thus,
the scholars' claim that Lǐquán emerges from earth
and that sweet dew has a very sweet taste
cannot be accepted.
Scholars say:
"When the Way reaches heaven,
the sun and moon shine brilliantly,
stars do not stray from their courses,
soaring winds arise,
and sweet rain falls."
Rain that clears and moistens is called sweet rain,
not because the rainwater tastes sweet.
Extending this argument,
sweet dew must refer to dew that falls
just when it properly moistens and nurtures all things,
not necessarily meaning the dew tastes sweet.
There is also dew sweet as syrup or honey,
both being responses to great peace,
but not the sweet dew that nurtures all things.
How to prove this?
Observe that dew sweet as syrup or honey
adheres to trees
but not to the five grains.
That dew which is not sweet
falls at such times
that the earth becomes moist and damp,
and all things are thoroughly soaked.
From this perspective,
the Ěryǎ is closer to the truth.
Testing the Ěryǎ's words
against physical evidence,
sweet-tasting dew falling on trees
shows that the trees it lands on
do not grow more luxuriantly than those it misses.
Yet what we now call sweet dew
likely differs from the Ěryǎ's definition.
To verify the Ěryǎ's sweet dew,
observe abundant harvests
and absence of disasters -
this demonstrates sweet dew has fallen.
When sweet dew descends,
this then is Lǐquán.
The world claims that when ancient rulers were virtuous,
their moral influence spread,
leading to successful governance and stability;
when rulers were unworthy,
moral influence collapsed,
leading to failure and chaos.
Throughout history, commentators
all affirm this view.
Why?
They see Yáo and Shùn's virtue bringing peace,
while Jié and Zhòu's wickedness brought chaos and execution.
But in truth,
it is the natural course of fate,
not moral transformation.
Officials of all ranks,
from minor functionaries upwards,
holding positions to govern people,
administering policies and education -
whether teachings succeed or fail,
whether people are orderly or chaotic,
all depends on fate.
Some with high talent and pure conduct
fail in their positions;
others with shallow wisdom and corrupt character
succeed in governing people.
In ancient times, promotions and demotions,
evaluations of merit,
rewards for achievement,
and punishments for failure
were actually measuring fate and prolonging fortune,
not assessing true ability and substantial competence.
Commentators, using these evaluation methods
and judging by results to determine virtue,
claim that orderly people and stable nations
result from virtuous rulers,
while chaotic people and endangered nations
come from wicked rulers' actions.
Thus when danger and chaos occur,
commentators blame the ruler,
attributing fault to improper governance.
Rulers accept this self-blame,
torment their spirits with bitter thoughts,
and exhaust their bodies,
yet the danger and chaos
never diminish.
This only embitters rulers' hearts,
causing wise rulers
to bear empty accusations -
such is the effect of worldly discussions and traditions.
Virtuous rulers can govern already peaceful people,
but cannot transform destined chaotic times.
Good doctors can apply acupuncture and medicine,
making their methods effective
when treating living people with curable diseases.
But when fate is exhausted and illness critical,
even Biǎn Què could do nothing.
That incurable critical illness
resembles ungovernable chaotic people;
medicine's healing power
resembles education's pacifying effect.
All depend on fate and timing,
beyond human effort to change.
When Gōngbó Liáo slandered Zǐlù to Jìsūn,
Zǐfú Jǐngbó reported this to Confucius.
Confucius said:
"Whether the Way will prevail -
that is fate!
Whether the Way will fail -
that is fate!"
Thus we see
that the success or failure of teaching,
the safety or danger of nations,
all depend on fate and timing,
not human power.
In times of societal chaos and rebellious people,
the state faces peril,
with disasters tied to heaven's will,
yet the virtue of a wise ruler
cannot dispel them.
The Book of Songs recounts how King Xuān of Zhōu encountered a great drought.
The Book of Songs says:
"The remnant people of Zhōu,
none were left unscathed."
This means not a single person escaped harm.
King Xuān was a worthy ruler,
yet some suspect his virtue was insufficient;
but those with the greatest benevolence,
none surpassed Yáo
and Tāng, yet Yáo faced floods,
and Tāng suffered a great drought.
Floods and droughts
are among the severest disasters,
and these two sages encountered them—
could it be that they were caused by the governance of these two sages?
It is simply the natural course of heaven and earth's cycles.
Using the floods and droughts of Yáo
and Tāng
as a standard for the disasters of all kings,
they are not caused by governance.
If not caused by governance,
then blessings and protection
are not achieved through virtue either.
A wise ruler governing a state
is like a kind father managing a household.
A kind father can enforce fair teachings and clear orders,
but cannot ensure all descendants are filial and good.
If descendants are filial and good,
the household prospers;
if the people are peaceful and secure,
the state thrives.
But prosperity must decline,
and rise must fall.
Rise and prosperity are not achieved by virtue alone,
so decline and fall are not caused by a lack of virtue.
Prosperity, decline, rise, and fall
all depend on the timing of heaven.
This is the reality of good and evil,
not to mention the effects of suffering and joy.
Household peace and human happiness
come from abundant wealth and sufficient resources.
Consider that abundance
results from thick fate,
not from worthiness or kindness.
People all know that those living in wealth and comfort have thick fortune,
but do not realize that a state's peace and orderly transformation stem from auspicious cycles.
Thus, societal order is not the merit of sages,
and decline and chaos are not due to lack of virtue.
When a state is destined to decline and chaos,
even sages cannot make it prosper;
when the time is ripe for order,
evil people cannot disrupt it.
The order or chaos of an era
lies in timing, not governance;
the safety or peril of a state
lies in fate, not instruction.
Whether a ruler is worthy or not,
whether governance is enlightened or not,
cannot increase or decrease this.
It is said that in the time of the Five Emperors,
the world was at peace,
households had ten years' stores,
and people conducted themselves as gentlemen.
Perhaps it was not so,
and later ages enhanced its beauty;
or perhaps it was true,
but not due to governance.
How can we verify this?
Is not the reason for societal chaos
that bandits and thieves abound,
arms and conflicts arise together,
people abandon ritual and righteousness,
and betray their superiors?
If so,
it stems from a lack of grain and food,
making hunger and cold unbearable.
Few can refrain from wrongdoing when hunger and cold strike together,
yet few fail to do good when warmth and fullness coexist.
The Tradition says:
"When granaries are full,
people know ritual and礼节;
when food and clothing are sufficient,
people know honor and shame."
Courtesy arises from surplus,
strife springs from insufficiency.
With ample grain and food,
hearts for ritual and righteousness grow;
with rich rituals and strong righteousness,
the foundation for peace is laid.
Thus, in the spring of a lean year,
one does not share food with relatives;
in the autumn of a abundant year,
one invites even distant neighbors.
Not sharing with relatives
is evil conduct;
inviting neighbors
is good and righteous.
Whether one acts good or evil
does not depend on human nature,
but on whether the year is lean or abundant.
From this perspective,
the practice of ritual and righteousness
depends on sufficient grain.
Consider that the success or failure of grain
naturally follows the year's conditions.
Years of floods or droughts,
where the five grains fail,
are not caused by governance,
but are due to the cycles of time.
If one insists floods and droughts
result from governance,
then the worst rulers were Jié
and Zhòu, and in their times,
there should have been constant floods and droughts.
Yet records show in Jié
and Zhòu's eras,
there were no famine or depletion disasters.
Disasters come by their own fate,
sometimes even in the times of sage rulers.
Historical accounts say Yáo's floods
and Tāng's great drought
were both encountered events,
not caused by poor governance.
To speak of the harms of all kings
and attribute them solely to responses to evil
is to see Yáo
and Tāng as virtuous and superior,
and all other kings as inferior.
Examining one case can reveal a hundred,
clarifying evil can illuminate good.
Yáo and Tāng serve as evidence for all kings:
when all kings encounter changes,
it is not due to governance.
Using changes to discern fortune and misfortune,
the Five Emperors achieving great peace
was not accomplished through virtue—
this is clear.
When a person dies of febrile disease,
ominous signs first appear on the face.
The illness
encounters pathogenic influences.
If the illness does not heal,
leading to death,
it is because lifespan has ended.
A state's chaos and downfall
share the same evidence.
Changes seen in heaven and earth
are like a person dying of febrile disease,
with signs showing on the face.
Having floods or droughts as disasters
is like a person falling ill from influences.
If disasters are not eliminated,
leading to the state's fall,
it is like an illness not healing,
resulting in death.
Critics claim changes indicate governance issues,
but if a worthy person has ominous signs from febrile disease,
can it be said to arise from their conduct?
To say floods and droughts
result from lack of virtue,
while a worthy falls ill—
can it be said they gained it without cause?
To say those who perish are extremely evil,
yet a worthy dies—
can it be said their crimes are heavy?
Some worthies fall ill and die young,
while evil people remain strong and live long;
human illness and death
do not stem from conduct or evil deeds.
Thus, a state's chaos and downfall
do not lie in the right or wrong of governance.
Evil people being strong and long-lived
does not mean governance is peaceful and enduring.
From this perspective,
calamities and changes are insufficient to prove evil,
and auspicious signs are inadequate to signify good—
this is clear.
In the changes of heaven,
there are solar and lunar eclipses.
In forty-two months, a solar eclipse occurs once;
in fifty-six months,
a lunar eclipse also occurs once.
Eclipses follow constant patterns,
unrelated to governance.
Hundreds of changes and thousands of disasters,
all share the same nature;
they are not necessarily caused by the ruler's policies or teachings.
When the Year Star harms the Bird Net,
Zhōu and Chǔ face calamity;
when baleful qi appears,
Sòng, Wèi,
Chén, and Zhèng all suffer disasters.
At such times,
the governance of these six states may not necessarily have been at fault.
The capital of Lìyáng
sank overnight to become a lake,
yet the officials of Lìyáng at the time were not necessarily deceitful or reckless.
Success and failure are tied to heaven,
fortune and misfortune are determined by timing.
Before human affairs take action,
celestial signs have already appeared—
is this not due to timing?
The five grains grow on earth,
sometimes abundant, sometimes scarce;
grains sold in the market
are sometimes expensive, sometimes cheap.
Abundance does not necessarily mean cheapness,
nor scarcity necessarily expensiveness.
Abundance and scarcity vary by year,
expensiveness and cheapness change with time.
When the time calls for high prices,
even abundant grains become dear;
when the time calls for low prices,
even scarce grains drop in value.
The price of grain does not depend on abundance or scarcity,
just as a state's order or chaos does not depend on good or evil.
When a worthy ruler ascends,
it happens to be in an era destined for order.
His virtue shines from above,
and the people naturally become good below;
the age is peaceful, the people secure,
auspicious signs and blessings arrive together,
and the world attributes it to the worthy ruler.
When a ruler without virtue
happens to be born in an era destined for chaos,
the times are turbulent, customs disordered,
disasters never cease,
leading to the destruction of the state, loss of life, and extinction of lineage,
and the world attributes it all to his evil.
In this way,
people see only the outward appearance of good and evil,
but fail to perceive the inner reality of fortune and misfortune.
Fortune and misfortune do not lie in good or evil;
the proof of good or evil is not in fortune or misfortune.
When an official assumes office,
before taking any action,
following previous policies and teachings
without any changes,
yet bandits may increase or decrease,
disasters may be absent or present—
why is this?
If an official's rank is noble,
he should ascend through peace and stability;
if his fate is base and unfit,
he should be demoted through danger and chaos.
Comparing today's officials
to ancient rulers,
we can discuss safety and danger, survival and perishability.
Heaven and earth combine their qi,
and all things are born spontaneously,
just as husband and wife combine qi,
and a child is born naturally.
In the birth of all things,
creatures with blood
know hunger and cold.
Seeing the five grains can be eaten,
they take and eat them;
seeing silk and hemp can be worn,
they take and wear them.
Some say that heaven produces the five grains to feed people,
and generates silk and hemp to clothe people.
This claims that heaven acts as a farmer
or silkworm girl for humans,
which does not accord with nature,
so the idea is doubtful
and cannot be followed.
Let us try reasoning according to the Daoist school.
Heaven
universally bestows qi within all things;
grains alleviate hunger, silk and hemp relieve cold,
so people eat grains
and wear silk and hemp.
Heaven does not intentionally produce the five grains, silk, and hemp to clothe and feed people,
just as it does not use disasters to reprimand humans.
Things grow spontaneously,
and people clothe and feed themselves with them;
qi changes naturally,
and people fear it.
With this explanation,
it satisfies the human mind.
If heavenly auspicious signs were intentional,
where would nature be?
What place would non-action have?
How do we know heaven is natural?
Because heaven has no mouth or eyes.
Consider those who act purposefully—
they belong to the category with mouths and eyes.
The mouth desires to eat, the eyes to see;
with cravings within,
they express them outwardly,
the mouth and eyes seek,
obtaining benefits,
which is the nature of desire.
Now, without the desires of mouth and eyes,
and no demands upon things,
what would it do?
How do we know heaven has no mouth or eyes?
We know from the earth.
Earth's body is made of soil,
and soil fundamentally has no mouth or eyes.
Heaven and earth
are like husband and wife;
since earth's body has no mouth or eyes,
we know heaven has none either.
If heaven has a body,
it should be like earth.
If heaven is qi,
qi is like clouds and smoke;
how could clouds and smoke
have mouths and eyes?
Some say:
"All things that move and act
originally have no purposeful action.
They move due to desires,
and movement entails purposeful action.
Now, heaven's movements and actions resemble humans';
how can it be without purposeful action?"
The response: Heaven's movement and action
involve the emission of qi.
As the body moves, qi emerges,
and things are born.
Similarly, when humans emit qi,
as the body moves, qi comes out,
and a child is born.
When humans emit qi,
it is not with the intent to bear a child;
qi is emitted, and the child is born spontaneously.
Heaven moves not intending to produce things,
yet things are born spontaneously—
this is nature.
Emitting qi without intent to create things,
yet things come into being on their own—
this is non-action.
Why call heaven natural and non-acting?
Because of qi.
Serene and without desires,
non-acting and without affairs—
this is why Lǎo Dān attained longevity.
Lǎo Dān received this from heaven;
if heaven lacked this qi,
how could Lǎo Dān have received this nature?
A teacher without a doctrine, yet the disciple speaks alone—
such a thing has never existed.
Someone reported to Duke Huán,
and the duke said:
"Inform Zhòngfù."
His attendants said:
"First it's Zhòngfù,
then it's Zhòngfù again;
being a ruler is so easy!"
Duke Huán replied:
"Before I obtained Zhòngfù,
it was difficult;
now that I have Zhòngfù,
why would it not be easy?"
Duke Huán, having obtained Zhòngfù,
entrusted him with tasks,
delegated governance to him,
and no longer involved himself.
If the August Heaven, with its most excellent virtue,
followed royal governance to reprimand and warn,
then heaven's virtue would be inferior to Duke Huán's,
and the conduct of a hegemon ruler would surpass that of the Supreme Deity.
Some say:
"Duke Huán knew Guǎn Zhòng was worthy,
hence entrusted him with authority;
had it not been Guǎn Zhòng,
he would have issued warnings and reprimands.
If Heaven had sent Yáo or
Shùn, there would certainly have been no warnings or reprimands."
I respond: If Heaven can warn and reprimand rulers,
then it could also deliberately appoint sage rulers,
select talents like Yáo and
Shùn, bestow upon them the kingly mandate,
entrust them with royal affairs,
and no longer intervene.
But now it is not so;
it produces mediocre rulers,
who lose the Way and abandon virtue,
then follows them with warnings—
why would Heaven not dread such toil?
When Cáo Cān was chancellor of Hàn,
he indulged in wine and song,
paying no heed to governance.
His son admonished him,
and he caned him two hundred strokes.
Yet at that time, the world was free from turmoil and disorder.
In Huáiyáng, counterfeit coins were cast,
and officials could not stop it.
When Jí Àn became grand administrator,
he did not destroy a single furnace,
nor punish a single person,
but rested high on his pillow in peace,
and Huáiyáng's governance became clear.
Now Cáo Cān as chancellor
was as if he were not chancellor;
Jí Àn as grand administrator
was as if the commandery had no one.
Yet the Hàn court had no troubles,
and Huáiyáng saw punishments set aside,
because Cáo's virtue was superior and Jí's authority was weighty.
Consider Heaven's power and virtue—
how do they compare with Cáo Cān's or
Jí Àn's?
To say that Heaven participates in royal governance
and follows it with warnings
is to claim that Heaven's virtue is not as generous as Cáo Cān's
and its authority not as weighty as Jí Àn's.
When Qú Bóyù governed Wèi,
Zǐgòng sent someone to ask him:
"How do you govern Wèi?"
He replied:
"By governing it through not governing."
Governing through not governing
is the Way of non-action.
Some say:
"The response of great peace
is the River producing the Diagram,
and the Luò producing the Writing.
They do not appear without being drawn,
nor accomplished without being made.
Heaven and Earth produced them,
which is evidence of purposeful action.
When Zhāng Liáng wandered by the Sìshuǐ river,
he met the Old Man of the Yellow Stone,
who bestowed upon him the Tàigōng's Text.
It seems Heaven aided Hàn to destroy Qín,
so it commanded a divine stone to become a ghostly text given to a person—
again, evidence of purposeful action."
I respond: These are all natural occurrences.
How could Heaven use brush and ink to create diagrams and writings?
Heaven's Way is natural,
so diagrams and writings form spontaneously.
When Jìn's Shū Yú
and Lǔ's Jì Yǒu were born,
patterns appeared on their hands,
hence Shū was called Yú,
and Jì was called Yǒu.
When Sòng's Zhòngzǐ was born,
there was writing on her hand,
saying:
"Become the夫人 of Lǔ."
In all three cases, while still in the womb,
the written characters were already formed.
To say that Heaven made the writing
while they were in the womb—
did Heaven send a spirit with a stylus, ink, to carve their bodies?
The transformations of nature
are inherently difficult to comprehend;
outwardly they may seem purposeful,
but inwardly they are truly natural.
Thus, when Grand Historian Sīmǎ recorded the Yellow Stone affair,
he doubted it and could not verify it.
When Jiǎnzǐ of Zhào dreamed of ascending to Heaven,
he saw a man beside the Emperor.
Later, going out,
he saw someone blocking the road,
who was the very man he had dreamed of beside the Emperor.
Commentators considered this an omen of Zhào's impending prosperity.
The Yellow Stone bestowing a book
was also an omen of Hàn's rise;
uncanny energy becomes ghosts,
ghosts take human form—
this is the natural Way,
not something made by anyone.
When plants and trees grow,
their blossoms and leaves are lush,
all with twists and turns,
resembling patterns and designs.
Would you say Heaven makes writing
and also makes blossoms and leaves?
A man of Sòng once carved a wooden leaf,
taking three years to complete it.
Confucius said:
"If Heaven and Earth took three years to make one leaf,
then few things in the world would have leaves."
As Confucius said,
the leaves of all things grow by themselves.
Growing by themselves,
they can all form together.
If Heaven made them,
the delay would be like the Sòng man carving the leaf.
Observe the feathers of birds and fur of beasts,
the colors of their feathers—
could these be made?
Birds and beasts are not fully understood.
In spring, observe the birth of all things;
in autumn, observe their maturity.
Does Heaven and Earth make them?
Or do things happen naturally?
If you say Heaven and Earth make them,
making them should require hands;
how could Heaven and Earth have countless thousands of hands,
making countless thousands of things simultaneously?
All things exist between Heaven and Earth
like a child in its mother's womb.
The mother nurtures the child's vital energy,
and after ten months it is born,
with nose, mouth, ears, eyes,
hair, skin, fur, texture,
blood vessels, fat, flesh,
bones, joints, nails, teeth.
Do these form naturally in the womb?
Or does the mother make them?
There may be thousands of figurines,
but they are not called human—
why?
Because their noses, mouths, ears, and eyes are not naturally endowed.
When Emperor Wǔ favored Lady Wáng,
and Lady Wáng died,
he longed to see her form.
A Daoist used arts to create Lady Wáng's form,
and when it was completed,
it moved in and out of the palace gates.
Emperor Wǔ was greatly startled,
stood to welcome it,
but suddenly it vanished.
It was not the truth of nature,
but the artifice of a cunning magician;
thus, once glimpsed, it blurred
and dissipated into nothing.
Transformations made by purposeful action
cannot long endure,
just as Lady Wáng's form could not long be seen.
When Daoists discuss nature,
they fail to cite actual events to verify their words,
so their theory of nature is not trusted.
Yet although it is natural,
it still requires purposeful action as aid.
Plowing with the lěisì,
sowing seeds in spring—
these are human actions.
But once the grain enters the earth,
growing day and night,
humans cannot make it.
Those who try to force it
follow the path to ruin.
A man of Sòng, distressed that his sprouts were not growing,
went and pulled them up,
and the next day they withered and died.
Those who wish to act upon nature
are of the same kind as the man of Sòng.
The question asks:
"Humans are born between Heaven and Earth,
yet Heaven and Earth act through non-action,
and since humans receive their nature from Heaven,
they too should practice non-action.
Why then do they engage in action?"
The response is:
Individuals of utmost virtue and purity,
who receive abundant heavenly energy (qì),
are able to emulate Heaven,
naturally practicing non-action.
Those who receive meager energy,
do not follow the Dào and virtue,
and do not resemble Heaven and Earth,
are thus called 'unworthy'.
'Unworthy' means
not resembling.
Not resembling Heaven and Earth,
nor akin to sages and worthies,
they therefore engage in action.
Heaven and Earth serve as the furnace,
creation as the craftsman;
since the endowments of energy vary,
how can all be worthy?
The purest among the worthy
are Huáng and Lǎo.
Huáng refers to
Huángdì,
Lǎo to
Lǎozi.
The conduct of Huáng and Lǎo
embodies inner tranquility and simplicity;
their governance is non-action,
rectifying themselves and maintaining composure, thus harmonizing yīn and yáng naturally,
without intent to act, yet all things transform on their own,
without desire to generate, yet all things accomplish themselves.
The Yì Jīng states:
"Huángdì,
Yáo, and Shùn let their robes hang down, and the world was governed."
Letting robes hang down means
ruling with folded hands through non-action.
Confucius said:
"How great was
Yáo as a ruler!
Only Heaven is great,
and only Yáo emulated it."
He also said:
"How majestic!
Shùn and Yǔ possessed the world,
yet did not interfere with it."
The Duke of Zhōu said:
"Shàngdì leads in ease."
Shàngdì here refers to
Shùn and
Yǔ.
Shùn and Yǔ inherited peace and continued governance,
employing the worthy and capable,
humbling themselves in non-action, and the world was governed.
Shùn and Yǔ succeeded to the tranquility of Yáo,
who followed Heaven's way in action,
not striving for achievements or seeking fame;
the transformation through non-action occurred naturally,
hence it is said:
"So vast and boundless,
the people could find no name for it!"
Fifty-year-olds played earthen games on the roads,
unaware of Yáo's virtue,
for it was the transformation of spontaneity.
The Yì Jīng says:
"The great person's virtue aligns with that of Heaven and Earth."
Huángdì,
Yáo,
and Shùn are great persons;
their virtue aligns with Heaven and Earth,
thus they understood non-action.
The way of Heaven is non-action;
thus spring does not cause birth,
nor summer growth,
autumn completion,
nor winter storage.
Yáng energy arises spontaneously,
and things grow on their own;
yīn energy emerges naturally,
and things store themselves.
Drawing water from wells or opening dams
to irrigate gardens and fields
also makes things grow.
When rain pours down abundantly,
the stems, leaves, roots, and tips of all things are thoroughly moistened.
Comparing the measure of this rainfall
to drawing from wells or opening dams—which is greater?
Thus, the non-action of action is vast.
Not seeking merit from the outset,
merit is thereby established;
not pursuing fame from the beginning,
fame is thereby achieved.
The abundant rain
has great merit and fame,
yet Heaven and Earth do not act for it;
energies harmonize, and rain gathers naturally.
The Ru school speaks of the way of husband and wife,
modeling it on Heaven and Earth.
They know that husband and wife emulate Heaven and Earth,
but fail to extend the way of husband and wife
to discuss the nature of Heaven and Earth—
this can be called delusion.
Heaven covers above,
Earth supports below;
the lower energy steams upward,
the upper energy descends downward,
and all things are born spontaneously between them.
When they are born,
Heaven need not intervene further,
just as a child in its mother's embrace
is unknown to the father.
Things are born on their own,
children mature by themselves;
what do Heaven, Earth, or parents
have to do with knowing it?
Once born,
human ways involve teaching and guidance.
But Heaven's way is non-action,
allowing nature free rein;
thus, fish are released into rivers,
beasts set free in mountains,
following their innate desires.
Why not drive fish onto hills
or chase beasts into abysses?
Because
it would contradict their nature,
depriving them of what suits them.
The common people
are like fish and beasts;
ruling with superior virtue
is like cooking a small fish—gently—
sharing the same conduct as Heaven and Earth.
When Shāng Yāng altered Qín's laws,
seeking extraordinary achievements,
he ignored Zhào Liáng's advice
and met the disaster of being torn apart by chariots—
a case of meager virtue and many desires,
leading to mutual hatred between ruler and minister.
In Dàoism, virtue is深厚,
subordinates support their superiors,
superiors secure their subordinates;
in pure simplicity and non-action,
what need is there for admonition?
Hence it is said:
"In ideal governance,
ruler and minister forget each other in order;
fish forget each other in water,
beasts in the forest,
humans in the world—
this is called Heaven's way."
Confucius said to Yán Yuān:
"I am so attuned to you that
I forget;
you, in following me,
also forget."
With Confucius as ruler
and Yán Yuān as minister,
admonition was still unnecessary;
how much more so with Lǎozi as ruler
and Wénzǐ as minister?
Lǎozi and
Wénzǐ
resemble Heaven and Earth.
Strong wine tastes sweet;
those who drink it become intoxicated without awareness of each other.
Weak wine is sour and bitter;
host and guest frown in discomfort.
Mutual admonition
is evidence of a shallow Dào.
To speak of Heaven's admonition—
would one claim Heaven's virtue is inferior to strong wine?
Rites are
the attenuation of loyalty and trustworthiness,
and the beginning of chaos.
When people criticize each other with rites,
they consequently engage in mutual reproof and admonition.
In the era of the Three Sovereigns,
those sitting were content and at ease,
those walking were simple and unadorned,
at times considering themselves horses,
at times considering themselves oxen.
With pure moral conduct, the people were innocent and ignorant;
minds of cleverness and cunning had not yet taken shape.
At that time, there were no calamities or anomalies either.
Even if there were calamities or anomalies,
they were not called reproof and admonition.
Why so?
Because people of that time were simple and foolish,
and did not know how to hold each other accountable.
In the decadent and declining end times,
superiors and subordinates fault each other,
and when calamities and anomalies occur frequently,
then arise the words of reproof and admonition.
Now the Heaven of today
is the same as the Heaven of antiquity.
It is not that the Heaven of antiquity was generous
while the Heaven of today is harsh.
The emergence of reproof and admonition in the present age
is because people measure and analogize it with their own minds.
Covenants and oaths did not reach the Five Emperors,
compelled alliances did not reach the Three Kings,
exchanging hostages did not reach the Five Hegemons;
the thinner the virtue, the weaker the trust.
With treacherous hearts and perverse conduct,
they violate covenants and betray teachings.
When teachings and covenants are not upheld,
they reprove and admonish each other.
If reproof and admonition do not bring change,
they raise arms to destroy one another.
From this perspective,
the words of reproof and admonition
are the language of decline and chaos,
yet they are attributed to the actions of Heaven above;
this is precisely what raises doubts.
Moreover, all those who speak of reproof and admonition
verify it by human principles.
According to human principles,
the ruler reproves and admonishes the ministers,
thus Heaven above reproves and admonishes the ruler,
and calamities and anomalies are considered reproof and admonition.
But in human principles,
ministers also remonstrate with the ruler;
if calamities and anomalies are taken as reproof and admonition,
then the king should also have the duty to remonstrate with Heaven above at times.
Where is the evidence for this?
If it is said that Heaven's virtue is superior,
and humans cannot remonstrate with it,
then a superior virtue should also be silent and profound,
and ought not to reprove and admonish.
When Wànshí Jūnzǐ had faults,
he did not speak of them,
but faced his desk without eating—
this is evidence of utmost superiority.
If even a superior human can refrain from speaking,
how much more so
the greatly virtuous August Heaven—
how can it be said to reprove and admonish?
Heaven is non-active,
therefore it does not speak.
When calamities and changes occur timely,
it is the qì acting on its own.
Heaven and Earth cannot act,
nor can they know.
When there is cold in the abdomen,
or pain and illness in the belly,
it is not caused by humans,
but the qì acts on its own.
The space between Heaven and Earth
is like the inside of a person's back and abdomen.
To say that Heaven creates calamities and changes,
and all kinds of strange phenomena,
regardless of size, slightness, or severity,
are all acts of Heaven—
when an ox gives birth to a horse,
or a peach tree bears plums,
according to the theorists' words,
does a heavenly spirit enter the ox's belly to make a horse,
or place plum fruits among peach branches?
Láo said:
"The Master said:
'I was not employed,
therefore I acquired many arts.'"
He also said:
"When I was young, I was of low status,
therefore I acquired many menial skills."
When humans are lowly and not employed for great tasks,
they generally possess many skills.
Heaven, being honorable, noble, and lofty,
how could it contrive calamities and changes to reprove and admonish people?
Moreover, auspicious and ominous changing complexions appear on the face,
humans cannot create them,
the colors arise spontaneously.
Heaven and Earth are like the human body,
changes in qì are like changing complexions.
Humans cannot create changing complexions;
how can Heaven and Earth create changes in qì?
Thus, the appearance of qì changes
is probably natural.
Changes appear by themselves,
colors arise spontaneously;
diviners and prognosticators
thereupon make their statements.
As for cold and warmth,
reproof and admonition,
changes and movements,
and induction,
these four doubts have all been discussed.
Reproof and admonition are particularly contrary to the Way of Heaven,
hence it is discussed again,
for it is difficult to distinguish in discourse.
Theories may accord with human affairs,
but not with the intent of the Way.
Following the Way and not conforming to affairs,
though it may contradict Confucian theories,
accords with the principles of Huáng
and Lǎo.
When yīn and yáng are not harmonious,
calamities and changes arise;
sometimes they are remnants of faults from previous generations,
sometimes the qì acts naturally.
Sages and worthies, sensing the categories,
feel remorseful and fearful, reflecting on themselves—
why have these calamitous changes and ominous signs
come about?
They attribute faults to themselves and engage in self-reproach,
fearing they may be guilty,
with a mind of caution and fear;
but there may not necessarily be actual facts.
How to clarify this?
By the example of Tāng encountering drought and reproaching himself for five faults.
A sage is perfectly complete,
his conduct without flaw or omission;
why would he reproach himself for five faults?
Yet as the Shū says:
"Tāng reproached himself,
and Heaven responded with rain."
If Tāng originally had no faults,
yet reproached himself for five faults,
why did Heaven then send rain?
If drought occurred despite no faults,
it is also known that self-reproach cannot bring rain.
From this perspective,
the drought did not come because of Tāng,
nor did the rain respond to self-reproach.
Rather, the earlier drought and later rain
were due to natural qì.
These words
are from the Shū.
Objection is raised:
The Spring and Autumn records the great rain sacrifice,
Dǒng Zhòngshū set up earthen dragons;
both were for a temporary period.
When it did not rain for a time,
they feared and performed the rain sacrifice,
seeking yīn and requesting blessings,
out of concern for the common people.
Tāng encountered drought for seven years;
reproaching himself for five faults—
at what time is this said?
Did he reproach himself immediately upon encountering drought for a time?
Or when the drought reached seven years,
then he reproached himself?
If it is said he reproached himself immediately for a time,
yet rain came only after seven years,
then Heaven's response, if sincere,
how could it be so delayed?
If it is said he reproached himself only after seven years,
then his concern for the common people—
how could it be so belated?
It does not match the method of rain sacrifice,
nor satisfy the principle of caring for the people.
The words of the Shū
cannot be trusted.
From this discussion,
the thunder and wind at the time of King Chéng of Zhōu
are also of this category.
The "Jīn Téng" says:
"In autumn, when the grain was fully ripe but not yet harvested,
there came a great thunderstorm with wind.
All the grain was laid flat,
and large trees were uprooted.
The people of the state were greatly terrified."
At this time,
the Duke of Zhōu died.
Confucian scholars explain it,
believing that King Chéng was hesitant about how to bury the Duke of Zhōu.
If he wished to bury the Duke with the rites of the Son of Heaven,
the Duke was a subject;
if he wished to bury the Duke with the rites of a subject,
the Duke had achieved kingly merits.
While hesitating over the burial of the Duke of Zhōu,
a great thunderstorm occurred,
displaying Heaven's anger as a portent,
to manifest the sage's merit.
The Old Text school holds that when King Wǔ passed away,
the Duke of Zhōu acted as regent,
Guǎn and Cài spread rumors,
causing the king to doubt the Duke of Zhōu,
so the Duke fled to Chǔ,
hence Heaven sent thunder and rain,
to awaken King Chéng.
Now, the phenomenon of thunder and rain
is interpreted by some as due to burial doubts,
by others as due to believing slanders;
the two schools cannot be verified.
Let us examine the theory of burial doubts.
Between summer and autumn,
the yang energy is still strong,
and thunder and rain are not uncommon,
but the uprooting of trees and flattening of grain
is rather extraordinary.
During the thunderstorm,
King Chéng felt fear and awe,
opened the "Jīn Téng" document,
saw the merits of the Duke of Zhōu,
held the document and wept over his fault,
deeply blaming himself.
As soon as he blamed himself,
Heaven coincidentally reversed the wind;
the "Shū" scholars then say Heaven was angry for the Duke of Zhōu.
Throughout countless autumns and summers,
thunder and rain never cease.
If thunder and rain are said to be Heaven's anger,
then the August Heaven is angry every year.
In the first month, yang energy emerges,
and thunder begins to sound;
in autumn and summer, yang reaches its peak and thunder bursts forth.
If the thunder of autumn and summer is said to be Heaven's great anger,
is the thunder of the first month Heaven's slight anger?
Thunder is Heaven's anger,
rain is its benevolent gift.
If Heaven was angry for the Duke of Zhōu,
it should only have thundered,
not rained.
Now that both thunder and rain came,
was Heaven both angry and pleased?
"On the day the Master did so,
he would not sing if he had wept."
The "Zhōu Lǐ" says:
"On zǐ and mǎo days,
millet and vegetable soup are eaten."
Sorrow and joy do not coexist.
If sorrow and joy do not coexist,
can anger and joy appear together?
When Qín Shǐ Huángdì sealed Tài mountain in the east,
a sudden thunderstorm arose.
When Old Woman Liú rested in the marsh,
thunder and rain darkened the sky.
Qín Shǐ Huángdì was unprincipled,
yet compared himself to former sages,
claiming peace in times of chaos;
Heaven's anger here is understandable.
But when Old Woman Liú rested in the marsh,
dreamed of meeting a deity,
and gave birth to Gāozǔ,
why would Heaven be angry at the birth of a sage and send thunder and rain?
In Yáo's time, great winds caused harm,
and Yáo subdued the great wind in the wilds of Qīngqiū.
When Shùn entered the great forest,
fierce winds and thunderstorms occurred.
Yáo and Shùn were exemplary rulers of their age;
what fault had they against Heaven,
that Heaven sent wind and rain?
During great droughts,
the "Chūnqiū" records rain sacrifices;
also, Dǒng Zhòngshū set up earthen dragons,
to attract energy through resemblance.
If Heaven responds to rain sacrifices
and dragons, it must bring thunder and rain.
Why?
Because autumn and summer rains
come with thunder.
If we follow the methods of the "Chūnqiū"
and Dǒng Zhòngshū,
then do great rain sacrifices
and dragons seek Heaven's anger?
When Shī Kuàng played the "White Snow" melody,
lightning struck down;
when he played the "Clear Horn" music,
wind and rain suddenly arrived.
If thunder and rain are Heaven's anger,
why would Heaven detest the "White Snow"
and "Clear Horn"
and be angry at Shī Kuàng for playing them?
This is the difficulty with the thunder and rain theory.
Further questioning says:
"If King Chéng did not bury the Duke of Zhōu with Son of Heaven rites,
Heaven sent thunder and wind,
flattening grain and uprooting trees.
When King Chéng realized his error,
held the document and wept over his fault,
Heaven then reversed the wind,
and the flattened grain stood again.
Why did it not quickly reverse the wind to raise the large trees,
but required the people to rebuild them?"
The response says:
"Heaven could not."
The question:
"Then is there something Heaven cannot do?"
The response:
"Yes."
The objection:
"When Mèng Bēn pushes a man,
the man falls;
when he helps him up,
he helps him stand.
If Heaven can uproot trees,
but cannot raise them again,
then Heaven's strength is inferior to Mèng Bēn's.
When three mountains disappeared in Qín times,
it was said Heaven moved them.
How does the weight of trees
compare to three mountains?
If it can move three mountains,
but cannot raise large trees,
this is not consistent with Heaven's power.
If the three mountains were not moved by Heaven,
then is thunder and rain alone Heaven's doing?"
The response says:
"Heaven wished King Chéng to bury the Duke of Zhōu with Son of Heaven rites,
because the Duke had sage virtue,
because the Duke had kingly merits.
The classic says:
'The king then obtained the account of how the Duke of Zhōu offered himself as substitute for King Wǔ.'
Now Heaven moved its majesty,
to manifest the virtue of the Duke of Zhōu."
The objection was raised:
"Yī Yǐn assisted Tāng in attacking the Xià,
bringing benefits to the people and eliminating harms,
achieving great peace under heaven.
After Tāng's death,
he again assisted Tàijiǎ.
When Tàijiǎ became negligent and pleasure-seeking,
Yī Yǐn exiled him to the Tóng Palace,
governing as regent for three years,
before withdrawing and restoring him to the throne.
The Duke of Zhōu said:
'Yī Yǐn moved the August Heaven.'
Heaven should have made this manifest.
When Yī Yǐn died,
why didn't Heaven create thunder and rain?"
The reply came:
"According to the 'Hundred Chariots Chapters' it says:
'When Yī Yǐn died,
there was heavy fog for three days.'"
Heavy fog for three days
indicates disordered energy,
not the transformation of Heaven's anger.
Zhāng Bà of Dōnghǎi fabricated the 'Hundred Chariots Chapters',
his words cannot be trusted,
but let me use them to ask:
"When Heaven created thunder and rain to awaken King Chéng,
did the thunder and rain stop before King Chéng opened the golden casket?
Or did it stop only after he opened the golden casket?"
The reply was:
"The thunder and rain stopped before he opened the golden casket.
When he opened the casket and obtained the documents,
saw the Duke's achievements,
awakened and wept over his errors,
he decided to bury the Duke with imperial rites.
Going to the suburbs to observe the changes,
heaven stopped the rain and reversed the wind,
and the grain all stood up again.
From this we can say,
before King Chéng awakened,
the thunder and rain had already ceased."
The objection continued:
"When Yī Yǐn died,
there was fog for three days.
Why didn't Heaven create three days of thunder and rain,
waiting until King Chéng awakened to stop it?
During Tàiwù's time,
mulberry and paper-mulberry trees grew in the court,
reaching full size in seven days.
Tàiwù reflected on improving his governance,
and the mulberry trees vanished.
During Duke Jǐng of Sòng's time,
Mars remained in the Heart constellation,
he uttered three good statements,
and Mars moved from its station.
Had Tàiwù not reflected on governance,
had Duke Jǐng not uttered the three good statements,
the mulberry trees would not have vanished,
Mars would not have moved.
Why is this?
Disasters and anomalies serve as warnings and reprimands,
if the warning is unheeded,
the disaster is not removed,
this is Heaven's ultimate intent.
Now if Heaven's anger manifested as thunder and rain
to reprimand King Chéng,
yet before King Chéng awakened,
the thunder and rain ceased,
why so early?"
Another question was raised:
"According to ritual,
sons of feudal lords are called gōngzǐ,
grandsons of feudal lords are called gōngsūn,
both receive fiefs,
distinguishing them from commoners.
Why is this?
Gōngzǐ and gōngsūn,
being kin and honored,
deserve the title 'gōng',
and receive fiefs,
so name and reality correspond,
just as substance and refinement match.
Since Heaven manifested the Duke of Zhōu's achievements,
causing King Chéng to bury him with imperial rites,
why didn't Heaven have King Chéng title the Duke of Zhōu as King of Zhōu,
to match the imperial rites?"
The reply was:
"The title 'king'
is an honorific name,
not to be used by ministers."
The objection continued:
"Can ministers properly be called kings?
Is this ritual?
When King Wǔ attacked Zhòu,
he descended his chariot and posthumously honored Tàiwáng,
Wáng Jì,
and Wénwáng as kings.
These three men
were feudal lords,
also ministers,
yet the kingly title was bestowed upon them.
Why was this permissible for the three kings,
but not for the Duke of Zhōu?
If Heaven's intent was to manifest the Duke of Zhōu,
could this not be made clear?
Was it because the kingly way originated with these three?
Yet the kingly achievement was also completed by the Duke of Zhōu.
The Jiāng River rises in the Mín Mountains,
flowing to become rapids and torrents.
Compare the flow of rapids and torrents
with the source from which it first arose.
Was it due to the three kings
that the black millet wine arrived,
the white pheasants came?
Or was it due to the Duke of Zhōu?
The Duke of Zhōu's merit and virtue surpassed the three kings,
yet he was not given the kingly title.
Does Heaven detest people falsely claiming titles?
When Zhōu declined,
the six states declared themselves kings,
Qí and Qín alternately called themselves emperors,
yet Heaven showed no prohibitive anger or anomalies.
The Duke of Zhōu not being buried with imperial rites,
Heaven created thunder and rain to reprimand King Chéng.
Why is Heaven's likes and dislikes not consistent?"
Another question was raised:
"Jì Sūn of Lǔ gifted Zēngzǐ a mat,
Zēngzǐ, ill, lay on it.
A youth said:
'Ornate and bright,
this is a senior official's mat.'
Zēngzǐ felt ashamed,
and ordered his son Yuán to change the mat.
According to ritual,
a senior official's mat
cannot be used by a scholar.
Now the Duke of Zhōu,
being a minister,
was buried with imperial rites.
If his soul is aware,
would he be at ease with this?"
The reply was:
"What King Chéng did
was granted by Heaven,
why would he not be at ease?"
The objection continued:
"The senior official's mat gifted by Jì Sūn,
was it something Zēngzǐ made himself?
Why was he alone not at ease?
When the Master was seriously ill,
Zǐlù had disciples act as retainers.
When the illness eased,
he said:
'Long has Yóu practiced deceit!
Having no retainers, he acted as if he had.
Whom do I deceive?
Do I deceive Heaven?'
Thus Confucius blamed Zǐlù.
Not being a ruler himself,
Zǐlù had disciples act as retainers,
contrary to Heaven's will,
and presumptuously did this,
which was deceiving Heaven.
The Duke of Zhōu was also not the Son of Heaven.
Using Confucius' mindset to consider the Duke of Zhōu,
the Duke of Zhōu would certainly not be at ease.
When the Jì family made offerings to Tàishān,
Confucius said:
'Do you think Tàishān is less discerning than Lín Fàng?'
Considering Zēngzǐ's minor status,
he still rejected what was ritually improper.
The Duke of Zhōu, being a supreme sage,
how could he be at ease with an imperial burial?
Do you think the Duke of Zhōu was less discerning than Zēngzǐ?
From this we deduce,
the Duke of Zhōu would not be at ease.
Great men share virtue with Heaven and Earth.
If the Duke of Zhōu was not at ease,
Heaven would also not be at ease.
Why then create thunder and rain to reprimand King Chéng?"
Another question was asked:
" 'Life and death are fated,
wealth and honor lie with Heaven.'
King Wǔ's destiny,
how could it be substituted?"
The response was:
"The dream of nine ages,
Heaven took years from King Wén to add to King Wǔ.
When two years had passed after conquering Yīn,
the nine ages had not yet been completed,
King Wǔ fell ill,
then the request was made.
Human life cannot be requested,
only for King Wǔ could it be done.
It was not the usual way of the world,
thus it was hidden in the 'Metal-Bound Coffer';
it could not be done again,
so it was concealed and not seen."
An objection was raised:
"In the dream of nine ages,
had King Wǔ already received King Wén's years or not?"
The response was:
"He had already received them."
The objection continued:
"Since he had already received King Wén's years,
his destiny should have extended naturally.
Two years after conquering Yīn,
even if ill, he would not have died;
why did the Duke of Zhōu request to substitute for him?"
The response was:
"When a ruler appoints someone to an official position,
after deliberation is settled,
it is not immediately granted;
documents are prepared and recorded,
only then can it be approved.
Although Heaven took years from King Wén to add to King Wǔ,
it still required the Duke of Zhōu's request,
to be able to obtain it.
The numbers of destiny are subtle and precise,
not something a single dream can fully secure."
The response added:
"The dream of nine ages could secure it."
The objection argued:
"In the dream of nine ages,
King Wén dreamed of giving King Wǔ nine ages,
King Wǔ dreamed that the Emperor granted him nine ages;
Heaven had already given it,
King Wǔ had already received it,
why was there still a need to request?
If a person is to receive an official post,
first dreams of obtaining the rank,
and later is not recommended,
he may still get the position.
Why so?
The omen appears first,
its fulfillment is bound to come.
In ancient times, years were called 'ages';
having obtained nine ages,
is like a person dreaming of receiving a rank.
If the Duke of Zhōu relied on a dream that was certain to be fulfilled,
and requested it from Heaven,
how great could his merit be?"
Another question was asked:
"Merit has no size,
virtue has no measure;
if people must rely and depend on it,
then it is commendable.
Had the Duke of Zhōu not substituted for King Wǔ,
and King Wǔ died of illness,
could the Duke of Zhōu and King Chéng still bring about peace under Heaven?"
The response was:
"As a matter of record,
the Duke of Zhōu assisted King Chéng and the world did not fall into chaos.
Had King Wǔ not been substituted for,
and his illness progressed to death,
why doubt that the Duke of Zhōu could have brought peace?"
An objection was raised:
"If so,
then King Wǔ's life brought no benefit,
his death caused no loss;
the Duke of Zhōu's merit was what accomplished it.
When the Zhōu declined,
the feudal lords rebelled,
Guǎn Zhòng nine times assembled the feudal lords,
unifying and rectifying the world.
Confucius said:
'Without Guǎn Zhòng,
we would be wearing our hair loose and folding our robes to the left.'
Had there been no Guǎn Zhòng,
the feudal lords would not have been united,
the barbarians would have invaded repeatedly,
and the Central States would have perished;
this shows the harm without Guǎn Zhòng.
Evaluating the benefits,
Guǎn Zhòng's merit
is comparable to that of the Duke of Zhōu.
When Guǎn Zhòng died,
Duke Huán did not bury him with the rites of a feudal lord;
comparing him to the Duke of Zhōu,
Heaven should also have been angered,
yet not even a slight thunder or light rain occurred;
why is that?
Is it because the Duke of Zhōu was a sage and Guǎn Zhòng was not virtuous?
Now, Guǎn Zhòng had the reversed platform,
and the three returns,
Confucius criticized him,
considering him not virtuous.
The reversed platform,
three returns,
are rites for feudal lords;
burial with the rites of a Son of Heaven,
is the institution for a king;
both, as ministers,
should not have done so.
The great man is in harmony with Heaven and Earth in virtue;
Confucius,
being a great man,
criticized Guǎn Zhòng for overstepping rites;
if the August Heaven desired the Duke of Zhōu to infringe upon institutions,
it would not be a sign of harmony in virtue;
the explanations from the Shū school,
cannot be considered correct."
Seeing bird tracks, one knows writing;
seeing flying thistledown, one knows the cart;
Heaven did not command Cāng Jié with bird tracks,
nor order Xī Zhòng with flying thistledown.
Xī Zhòng was inspired by flying thistledown,
and Cāng Jié initiated from bird tracks.
When Duke Wén of Jìn returned to his state,
he ordered the removal of soot and ink,
Jiù Fǎn felt it in his heart,
and resigned his position to return home.
Duke Wén's removal of soot and ink
was not intended to dismiss Jiù Fǎn;
Jiù Fǎn felt ashamed,
identifying himself with the soot and ink.
When Huá Chén of Sòng weakened his clan,
he sent six household assassins
to kill Huá Wú with spears behind the left marshal's residence in Sòng.
The left marshal feared, saying:
"This old man is innocent."
Later, the left marshal resented Huá Chén,
and Huá Chén took precautions.
When the people were chasing a mad dog,
the mad dog entered Huá Chén's gate.
Huá Chén thought the left marshal was coming to attack him,
and fled by climbing over the wall.
Huá Chén himself killed Huá Wú, and the left marshal feared;
the people chased a mad dog, and Huá Chén fled on his own;
King Chéng's fear
was of a similar kind.
His heart was suspicious about not burying the Duke with the rites of a Son of Heaven,
and when the thunderstorm suddenly arrived,
he feared and was apprehensive of his fault.
Now, the arrival of the thunderstorm
may not necessarily have been Heaven reprimanding King Chéng.
The thunderstorm came,
and King Chéng feared and blamed himself.
Inspiration is like the hearts of Cāng Jié
and Xī Zhòng;
fear is like the minds of the left marshal
and Huá Chén.
Harboring suspicious thoughts,
encountering a sudden violent atmosphere,
with omens appearing by analogy,
the effect of Heaven's anger was thus realized.
Seeing omens in solitude,
one can still be moved and fearful;
how much more with the roaring sound of thunder and rain,
could King Chéng hardly avoid being startled?
At sudden thunder and fierce wind,
Confucius would always change countenance.
According to rites, a gentleman hearing thunder,
even at night,
sits up dressed and capped,
to show respect for thunder and fear of agitated energy.
Sages and gentlemen have no doubts about the Way,
yet still comply with Heaven's changes;
how much more for King Chéng, who had doubts about the Duke of Zhōu,
upon hearing the change of thunder and rain,
could he not be shaken with fear?
Thus, the arrival of thunder and rain
was probably due to natural weather;
King Chéng's fear
was likely a response to the omens."
The Way of Heaven is non-action.
If Heaven were to reprimand humans with thunder and rain,
it could also use thunder and rain to kill the unprincipled.
In ancient times, there were many unprincipled individuals;
why not strike them dead with thunder and rain,
instead of commanding sages to raise armies and mobilize troops,
halting soldiers and injuring officers?
It is difficult to execute punishment with a single thunderclap,
yet easy to conquer enemies with three armies—
why does Heaven not avoid such trouble?
Some say:
"Zhòu's father, Dì Yǐ,
shot at the sky and kicked the earth,
frolicked between the Hé
and Wèi rivers,
and was struck and killed by lightning.
This is an example of Heaven using thunder and lightning to punish the unprincipled."
How do Dì Yǐ's evils
compare to those of Jié
and Zhòu? Zōu Bóqí argued that the evils of Jié
and Zhòu were less than those of the fallen Qín,
and the fallen Qín's were less than Wáng Mǎng's,
yet Jié,
Zhòu, Qín,
and Wáng Mǎng did not die
by thunder and lightning.
When Confucius composed the "Spring and Autumn Annals,"
he highlighted goodness as fine as a hair
and condemned evils as slight as a speck,
praising goodness without exceeding its merit,
and condemning evil without inflating its fault.
To blame the small with the standards of the great—
no one does that.
When King Chéng had a minor doubt,
Heaven sent great thunder and rain.
If it were determined that a minister buried a duke,
how could the omen exceed this?
The "Hóng Fàn" examines doubts,
and those who do not understand calamities and anomalies—
human talent cannot fully comprehend them,
so Heaven does not hold people accountable for their doubts.
King Chéng's mind was unsettled and undecided;
for Heaven to reprimand him with great thunder and rain
is hardly the intent of the August Heaven.
The explanations by the Shū school
likely miss the truth.
It is said that people of high antiquity
were tall and handsome,
strong and long-lived,
reaching around a hundred years;
whereas people of later ages
are short, ugly,
and die young prematurely.
Why is that?
Because high antiquity had harmonious and pure vitality,
marriages occurred at the right time,
people were born imbued with good energy,
their lives were unharmed,
their bones and joints firm,
hence they grew tall and long-lived,
with beautiful appearances.
Later ages are the opposite,
so people are short and die young,
with ugly forms and faces.
This statement is absurd.
The rulers of high antiquity
were sages,
and the rulers of later ages
were also sages.
The virtue of sages
does not differ between earlier and later times;
thus, their governance of the world
is no different across ages.
The Heaven of high antiquity
and that of later ages are the same;
Heaven does not change,
and the vital energy does not alter.
The people of high antiquity
and those of later ages
all receive the primordial energy.
The primordial energy is pure and harmonious,
unchanged from ancient to modern times;
then why would those who receive it as their form
be different?
If the energy received is equal,
then the nature embraced is uniform;
if the nature is uniform,
then the forms are identical;
if the forms are identical,
then ugliness and beauty are even;
if ugliness and beauty are even,
then early death and longevity are appropriate.
One heaven, one earth,
together give birth to all things.
The life of all things
all comes from one energy.
The thickness or richness of this energy
remains the same for ten thousand generations.
Emperors and kings govern the world,
following the same path for a hundred generations.
People marry and wed,
at the same time and with shared rites.
Although it is said that men marry at thirty
and women at twenty,
when laws and institutions are established,
they are not necessarily followed.
How can this be verified?
By the fact that they are not followed today.
The systems of rites and music
still exist today,
but would the people of today
willingly practice them?
If people today refuse to practice them,
the ancients would also have been unwilling to uphold them.
We can understand the people of antiquity
by the people of today.
Humans
are beings,
and things are also beings.
A person lives one lifetime,
with a lifespan up to a hundred years.
When born as a ten-year-old child,
the things seen on earth
change greatly between life and death.
By the time they reach a hundred years,
near death,
the various things they see
are no different
from what they saw at ten years old.
If the people of high antiquity and later ages
are no different,
then within a hundred years,
it is enough for divination.
The length of domestic animals,
the size of the five grains,
insects, plants, and trees,
metals, stones, pearls, and jades,
flying and crawling creatures,
those that walk on feet and breathe through beaks—
there are no differences;
this shows the forms do not vary.
The water and fire of antiquity
are the water and fire of today.
If the energy now forms water and fire,
and if the energy were different,
would the water of antiquity be clear and the fire hot,
while today's water is turbid and the fire cold?
Humans grow to six or seven feet tall,
with a girth of three or four spans,
faces with five colors,
and lifespans up to a hundred years—
this does not change for ten thousand generations.
If the people of high antiquity
were tall and handsome,
strong and long-lived,
and later ages are the opposite,
then when heaven and earth were first established,
and humans began to exist,
would they have been as tall as the Lord of Fángfēng,
as fair as Sòng Cháo,
and as long-lived as Péng Zǔ?
And from now until a thousand generations later,
would people be as tall as bean pods,
as ugly as Mómǔ,
and as short-lived as morning ephemerals?
In the time of Wáng Mǎng,
there was a tall man who grew to ten feet,
named Bà Chū.
During the Jiànwǔ era,
Yǐngchuān's Zhāng Zhòngshī was two feet two inches tall.
Zhāng Tāng was over eight feet tall,
while his father was less than five feet.
All exist in the present age—
some tall, some short.
The claims of the Confucians
are ultimately mistaken.
It is said that in high antiquity, people were employed appropriately:
the hunchbacked guarded gates,
dwarves became entertainers.
If all were tall and handsome,
how could there be hunchbacks
or dwarves?
It is said that people of ancient times
were simple and easily guided;
people of later ages
were ornate and difficult to govern.
Thus the Book of Changes states:
"In high antiquity, knotted cords were used for governance;
in later ages, these were replaced by written contracts."
The earlier knotted cords
demonstrate the ease of guidance;
the later written contracts
show the difficulty of governance.
Therefore, before Fú Xī's time,
people were extremely simple,
sleeping peacefully,
sitting contentedly,
living in groups,
knowing their mothers but not recognizing their fathers.
By Fú Xī's time,
people had become rather ornate,
the clever seeking to deceive the foolish,
the brave seeking to intimidate the timid,
the strong seeking to oppress the weak,
the many seeking to abuse the few,
so Fú Xī created the Eight Trigrams to govern them.
By the Zhōu period,
people had become ornate and shallow,
making the Eight Trigrams difficult to continue using,
so King Wén developed them into sixty-four hexagrams,
exhausting their variations,
to keep the people from wearying.
By the Zhōu period,
people had long been shallow,
so Confucius composed the Spring and Autumn Annals,
gathering hair-fine virtues,
condemning thread-thin evils,
declaring:
"The Zhōu surveyed the two preceding dynasties,
how resplendent was its culture!
I follow the Zhōu."
Confucius knew the age was gradually deteriorating,
ornate and difficult to govern,
so he added dense nets,
established minute prohibitions,
restrained and maintained,
making preparations extremely thorough.
These claims are false.
People of ancient times
possessed the five constant virtues;
people of later ages
also possessed the five constant virtues.
Both embracing the way of the five constants,
sharing the same vital energy at birth,
why were ancient people simple?
Why are later people ornate?
They see ancient people
drinking blood and eating raw meat,
lacking the five grains for food,
while later people dug wells in the ground,
tilled soil to grow grain,
drank from wells and ate millet,
having regulated water and fire;
they also see ancient people dwelling in caves,
clothed in animal skins,
while later people replaced these with houses,
having cloth and silk for adornment,
then claim ancient times were simple,
later ages ornate.
Though tools and practices change,
human nature remains unchanged,
yet there is talk of simplicity
and ornate shallowness because
ages have prosperity and decline,
and prolonged decline leads to deterioration.
Just as clothing and food for people:
when newly made, fresh and intact,
when first cooked, fragrant and clean,
after brief use, worn and damaged,
after days, stinking and rotten.
The patterns of substance and ornamentation
are common to all ages, ancient and modern.
One substantial, one ornate,
one declining, one flourishing -
this has existed since antiquity,
not only in the present.
How to verify this?
The Tradition states:
"The kings of the Xià dynasty taught loyalty.
When superiors taught loyalty,
gentlemen were loyal,
but the failing was
that commoners became crude.
To rescue crudeness, nothing better than reverence,
so the kings of the Yīn dynasty taught reverence.
When superiors taught reverence,
gentlemen were reverent,
but the failing was
that commoners became superstitious.
To rescue superstition, nothing better than culture,
so the kings of the Zhōu dynasty taught culture.
When superiors taught culture,
gentlemen were cultured,
but the failing was
that commoners became shallow.
To rescue shallowness, nothing better than loyalty."
Those succeeding Zhōu as kings
should teach loyalty.
The Xià succeeded the Táng
and Yú's shallow teachings,
so they taught loyalty.
If Táng and Yú taught culture,
then what they succeeded had superstitious failings.
People seeing present ornate shallowness
disparage and criticize it,
then claim ancient times were simple,
later ages ornate,
just as when family members behave carelessly,
they claim other families' members are careful and good.
It is said that ancient people
valued righteousness over life,
encountering matters of loyalty and righteousness,
when clearly required to sacrifice themselves,
would march through boiling water and rush toward spears,
dying without regret.
Thus the integrity of Hóng Yǎn,
the righteousness of Chén Bùzhàn,
deeds of similar kind,
recorded in books,
sacrificing life and abandoning self,
were numerous and varied.
Now people pursue profit and cling to life,
abandon righteousness and seek gain recklessly,
not encouraging each other with righteousness,
not inspiring each other with conduct,
discarding righteousness without considering it burdensome,
ruining conduct without fearing the consequences.
These claims are false.
The scholars of ancient times
and scholars of today
both contain natures of humaneness and righteousness,
so when encountering events,
equally possess the integrity to exert themselves.
Ancient times had unrighteous people,
today has established integrity scholars,
good and evil intermingled -
what age lacks them?
Those recording events prefer exalting antiquity over the present,
valuing what they hear over what they see.
Disputants discuss the long-ago,
writers record the distant.
Recent marvels go unmentioned in debates,
present wonders go unrecorded in writing.
Take Lángyé's Ér Zǐmíng:
during famine years,
when his elder brother was about to be eaten by starving people,
he bound himself and kowtowed,
offering to replace his brother as food.
The starving people admired his righteousness,
and spared both without eating them.
After his brother died,
he raised the orphan,
loving it no differently than his own child.
When famine exhausted the grain,
unable to save both,
he starved his own child to death,
saving his brother's child.
Línhuái's Xǔ Jūnshū also raised his brother's orphan:
during urgent famine,
he starved his own child,
saving his brother's child,
sharing Zǐmíng's righteousness.
Kuàijī's Mèng Zhāng's father Mèng Yīng
served as commandery legal clerk.
When the commandery governor wrongly beat an innocent to death,
the case came for reinvestigation.
Yīng claimed the crime himself,
ultimately dying in the governor's place.
Zhāng later became commandery merit officer:
during campaign against bandits,
as troops were being defeated,
he was shot by bandits
while shielding the general,
dying without retreating.
How do these differ from Hóng Yǎn's integrity
or Chén Bùzhàn's righteousness?
Would current writers
cite these as examples?
For exemplary proofs,
above they seek Yú
and Xià, below they search Yīn
and Zhōu, Qín
and Hàn periods -
deeds marvelously unusual,
yet still considered recent;
how much more the present, a hundred generations later,
should eyewitnesses record events?
Painters enjoy depicting people of ancient times,
but refuse to paint the meritorious and extraordinary deeds
of Qin and Han dynasty figures.
Their refusal to portray contemporary individuals stems from
the tendency to revere antiquity and belittle the present.
This is like valuing swans while despising chickens—
swans are distant while chickens are near.
Even if contemporary scholars' doctrines surpassed those of Confucius
and Mòzǐ, their fame wouldn't equal them;
even if their conduct exceeded that of Zēng Shēn
and Yán Huí, their reputation wouldn't match theirs.
Why?
Because human nature
disparages what is seen
and values what is heard.
If someone today
established righteous principles and upheld integrity,
with verified moral character
unmatched in antiquity,
would record-keepers
be willing to document them in texts,
holding them up as exemplary models?
If one produced remarkable theories
and created new writings
not inferior to predecessors,
would enthusiasts abandon ancient books
to attentively read them?
When Yáng Zǐyún wrote "Tàixuán"
and "Fǎyán",
Zhāng Bósōng refused to even glance at them.
Being contemporaries,
he thus dismissed his works.
Had Zǐyún preceded Bósōng,
the latter would have treated them as sacred texts.
It's said that in ancient times,
sages possessed superior virtue,
achieving miraculous governance—
hence Confucius declared:
"How magnificent
was Yáo as ruler!
Only Heaven is great,
and only Yáo modeled it.
Vast and boundless, people could find no name for his virtue!
Towering were his achievements!
Resplendent were his cultural accomplishments!"
Shùn succeeded Yáo,
maintaining the grand enterprise;
Yǔ followed Shùn,
preserving the great achievements.
Later, Tāng
raised arms to fight Jié,
and King Wǔ wielded battle-axes to punish Zhòu—
their records lack the 'towering and vast' descriptions,
instead containing accounts of military campaigns.
This shows their inferior virtue requiring force,
with military action indicating shallow transformation.
This shallow transformation
clearly demonstrates their inability to match earlier sages.
By the Qin
and Han periods,
warfare clouded the land as factions vied for power,
and Qin gained the empire through might.
Having obtained the empire,
it showed no auspicious signs
like
"harmonizing all states"
or "phoenixes dancing ceremoniously"—
are these not evidence
that their virtue was inferior
and achievements paler?
Such claims are absurd.
When heaven and earth harmonize,
sages are born;
when sages govern,
great achievements follow.
If harmony isn't exclusive to antiquity,
why should ancient sages alone be superior?
Human nature
prefers praising antiquity while denigrating the present,
valuing rare hearsay over common sight.
Seeing classical texts exaggerate sage virtues—
Confucius particularly magnifying Yáo
and Shùn's achievements—
hearing how Yáo
and Shùn abdicated peacefully
while Tāng and Wǔ seized power militarily,
people assume ancient sages surpassed modern ones,
with greater accomplishments.
Yet classical texts contain exaggerations,
and empty praises fill the age—
as all text-readers witness.
Confucius said:
"Zhòu's wickedness
wasn't as extreme as portrayed.
Thus gentlemen dread occupying low ground
where all evils converge."
People constantly contrast Jié
and Zhòu with Yáo
and Shùn—
praising Yáo
and Shùn while condemning Zhòu
and Jié. Confucius said:
"Zhòu's wickedness
wasn't as extreme as portrayed."
Thus we know Yáo
and Shùn's virtue
wasn't as magnificent either.
The abdications of Yáo
and Shùn,
the executions by Tāng and Wǔ—
all followed Heaven's mandate,
not determined by superiority/inferiority
or human effort.
Had Tāng
and Wǔ lived in Yáo-Shùn's era, they'd have abdicated, not attacked;
had Yáo and Shùn lived in Shang-Zhou times,
they'd have executed, not yielded.
For there exists destiny's reality,
yet people idly speak of superiority.
Classics mention
"harmonizing all states"—
yet Dān River battles occurred then;
"phoenixes dancing ceremoniously"—
yet the Miáo tribes rebelled then.
Since wars occurred in both eras,
how can we claim virtue differed in scale?
People allege Jié
and Zhòu's evils
exceeded fallen Qin's,
but truth-seers say Qin's wickedness surpassed Jié
and Zhòu's.
Qin and Han represent opposite moral poles,
just as Yáo,
Shùn, Jié,
and Zhòu stood opposed.
Since fallen Qin and Han
are both recent history,
and Qin's evil exceeded Jié
and Zhòu's,
we know Great Han's virtue isn't inferior to Táng
and Yú's.
The Táng era's
"myriad states"
was clearly exaggerated fiction;
the Yú era's
"phoenixes"—
Emperor Xuān already hosted five times.
Emperor Míng received numerous auspicious signs.
Superior virtue brings omens;
equal omens indicate equal achievements.
If Xuān
and Míng were inferior,
unable to match Yáo
and Shùn,
how could they summon Yáo-Shùn's omens?
Emperor Guāngwǔ rose like dragon and phoenix,
gaining the empire like picking up lost items—
why should he rank below Shāng's Tāng
or Zhōu's Wǔ?
People praise Zhōu's Chéng
and Kāng periods for maintaining King Wén's glory,
just as Shùn maintained Yáo's magnificence.
Our current sacred dynasty,
continuing Guāngwǔ's legacy
and following Xiàomíng's path,
possesses ever-growing virtuous influence
without slightest flaw—
why should it fall short of Shùn
and Yǔ above,
or Chéng and Kāng below?
Seeing the Five Emperors' and Three Kings' deeds recorded in classics,
while Hàn's records remain mere documents,
people claim ancient sages superior with greater achievements,
modern ones inferior with weaker influence.
Confucian scholars claim that the Five Emperors and
the Three Sovereigns brought about great peace in the world,
yet since the rise of the Hàn dynasty,
there has been no such peace.
They say that the Five Emperors and
the Three Sovereigns achieved great peace,
while the Hàn has not,
because they see the Five Emperors and
the Three Sovereigns as sage rulers,
and the virtue of sages
can bring about great peace;
to say the Hàn lacks peace
is to claim the Hàn has no sage emperors,
and that the influence of worthy rulers
cannot achieve peace.
They also cite Confucius’s words:
"The phoenix does not come,
the river gives forth no chart—
it is all over with me!"
