Since now there are no phoenixes or
river charts,
and auspicious signs are not fully present,
they say there is no great peace.
This is absurd.
Great peace is evidenced by orderly governance,
and the people’s sign is peace and happiness.
Confucius said:
"Cultivate oneself to bring peace to the people—
even Yáo and Shùn found this difficult!"
The people’s peace
is proof of great peace.
Governance focuses on the people;
when the people are at peace,
yīn and yáng harmonize;
when yīn and yáng harmonize,
all things flourish;
when all things flourish,
auspicious signs appear.
Look at the world today—
is it peaceful?
Or in peril?
If peaceful, then there is order;
even if signs are incomplete,
it does not hinder peace.
Thus, the Kingly Way establishes affairs based on evidence,
and sets reality as the standard;
if evidence is not clear,
truth is not seen.
Sometimes reality is so,
yet proof is lacking;
therefore, the Kingly Way acts on reality,
not necessarily requiring full evidence.
Sage rulers govern the world,
aiming for peace and safety,
with no need for auspicious signs.
Moreover, signs of great peace
are like the appearances of sage kings.
Sage kings’ bone structures need not be alike,
so why should signs of peace be uniform?
They hear that in the times of Yáo and
Shùn,
phoenixes and
bright stars all appeared,
river charts and
Luò River writings emerged,
and think later kings ruling the world
must have such things again
to achieve peace.
Thinking this way
is like saying Yáo must have overlapping teeth again,
or Shùn must have double eyebrows.
If sage kings’ appearances differ across ages,
then auspicious signs need not match anciently and now.
To say the current king lacks phoenixes or
river charts,
thus has no peace,
is false.
When Confucius spoke of phoenixes and
river charts,
he used past signs as metaphors,
not necessarily meaning they must reappear.
Signs of imperial virtue
are numerous and varied:
some have phoenixes or
qílín,
some river charts or
Luò River writings,
some sweet dew or
sweet springs,
some harmony of yīn and yáng,
or peace among the people.
Modern signs need not match ancient ones,
ancient responses need not fit the present;
what is encountered
need not be inherited.
How to clarify this?
By the differing mandates
in emperors’ rise.
For Zhōu, it was birds and
fish; for Hàn, a great serpent slain.
Inferring from Táng
and Yú,
it’s like Zhōu and Hàn.
At their initial rise,
events and omens
were not inherited;
so why should signs of peace
be uniform?
Using past signs
to test future responses
is like guarding a stump for rabbits
or hiding in a broken net.
Under great peace,
signs vary,
just as a wealthy family’s
assets differ:
some hoard grain,
some store cloth,
some raise livestock,
some expand lands.
To prefer grain over cloth,
or rejoice in livestock over lands,
is to say grain surpasses cloth,
livestock beats land.
Now the people are at peace,
signs have arrived,
yet they insist ancient signs like river charts or
phoenixes are absent,
claiming no peace—
this is like a rice-eater
entering a millet region,
not seeing rice,
and denying millet is grain.
In truth,
the world is already at peace.
Without sage rulers,
how was this achieved?
Without seeing phoenixes,
how to verify reality?
I ask worldly Confucians, if they don’t know sages,
how do they know there are none now?
When people see phoenixes,
how do they recognize them?
If they cannot know,
how do they know there are no phoenixes now?
Since they can’t discern sages’ presence or absence,
nor distinguish phoenixes from non-phoenixes,
they certainly can’t determine if there is peace now.
Confucius said:
"If a true king arises,
it takes a generation to achieve benevolence."
Thirty years bring peace to the world.
From Hàn’s rise to Emperor Wén’s time,
over twenty years passed.
Jiǎ Yì proposed
that with the world in harmony,
the calendar should be reformed,
colors and
regulations updated,
titles standardized,
and rites and music revived.
Emperor Wén, newly enthroned,
was modest and delayed action.
Had Jiǎ’s proposal been followed,
peace was already achieved in Wén’s time.
With over twenty years since Hàn’s rise,
it matched Confucius’s words
"a generation to achieve benevolence";
Hàn’s first generation span fulfilled,
peace was established,
as Jiǎ Yì recognized.
Now, after nearly three hundred years,
to say there’s no peace
is wrong.
Moreover, Confucius’s "generation"
means thirty years.
The Hàn has lasted three hundred years,
with ten emperors displaying virtue—
how can it not be peaceful?
In Emperor Wén’s time,
peace was firm,
maintained through reigns.
By Emperor Píng’s era,
the Former Hàn ended,
but Emperor Guāngwǔ restored it,
again achieving peace.
The transmitted texts sometimes mention King Wǔ's campaign against Zhòu,
with Tàigōng's "Secret Plans"
stating they fed cinnabar to infants,
making their bodies entirely red.
When they grew up,
they were taught to say the Yīn dynasty had fallen.
When the Yīn people saw the children's red bodies,
they thought they were celestial gods.
Upon hearing the Yīn dynasty had perished,
they all believed Shāng was destroyed.
When the troops reached Mùyě,
they raised grease torches at dawn.
Such deceitful schemes deluded the people,
exploiting unpreparedness through stratagem—
these are acts the Zhōu dynasty preferred to conceal,
and later generations consider them fabrications.
When the Hàn dynasty seized the realm,
it employed no such false tales.
The chapter "Wǔ Chéng"
describes Zhōu's attack on Zhòu,
with blood flowing enough to float pestles.
Based on "Wǔ Chéng,"
feeding cinnabar to children
and raising torches at dawn
might indeed have occurred.
When Hàn fought the fallen Xīn dynasty,
Emperor Guāngwǔ led five thousand men,
while Wáng Mǎng dispatched two ministers with thirty thousand,
battling at Kūnyáng.
Thunderstorms darkened the sky,
obscuring visibility front and back.
The Hàn forces emerged from Kūnyáng city,
attacked the two ministers' armies,
one soldier matching ten,
and their troops scattered.
Did the heavens aiding Hàn with thunderstorms to intimidate the enemy
compare to using torch-raising and human deceit to seize Yīn?
Some say:
"When King Wǔ attacked Zhòu,
Zhòu threw himself into the fire and died,
yet King Wǔ approached and beheaded him with a battle-axe,
hanging his head on the great white banner."
King Xuān of Qí pitied the ox for the bell-sacrifice,
moved by its trembling appearance.
King Zhuāng of Chǔ pardoned the Duke of Zhèng's crime,
seeing him bared upper body and exposed form.
The nobleman hates evil,
but not the person's physical self.
Zhòu's corpse cast into the flames—
the sight was grievous and chilling,
far beyond mere trembling or
bared exposure.
To behead him with an axe
and hang his guilty head—
how cruel was that?
When Gāozǔ entered Xiányáng,
Yán Lè had killed the Second Emperor,
and Xiàng Yǔ slew Zǐyīng,
yet Gāozǔ entered Qín with dignity,
desecrating neither corpse.
When Guāngwǔ entered Cháng'ān,
Liú Shènggōng had already executed Wáng Mǎng,
and though troops were present,
they did not harm Wáng Mǎng's dead body.
Compare beheading a burned head
to sparing those slain by the blade—
which virtue or cruelty is greater?
Was it due to the grievance of Yǒulǐ?
For a ruler to detain a minister—
how does its treachery compare to Qín seizing Zhōu's state
or Wáng Mǎng poisoning Emperor Píng?
Zōu Bóqí argued that Jié and
Zhòu's evils paled against the fallen Qín,
and fallen Qín was lesser than Wáng Mǎng.
Thus, Zhòu's minor faults met severe punishment by Zhōu,
while Qín and Wáng Mǎng's grave crimes received lenient Hàn retribution—
whose justice was broader or narrower?
When Gāozǔ's mother was pregnant with him,
a dragon hovered above,
and she dreamed of union with a deity.
He loved wine and drank on credit,
incurring debts at taverns.
When drunk and lying asleep,
mystical signs often appeared above him.
He beheaded a serpent while traveling at night,
and an old woman mourned its death.
When he and Empress Lǚ hid in a field hut,
though he concealed himself,
his radiant aura shone through,
and Empress Lǚ always knew.
Qín Shǐhuáng saw an imperial aura in the southeast.
At his rise,
five planets converged at Jīng.
The Chǔ forces gazed at the Hàn army,
witnessing five-colored clouds.
When Guāngwǔ was about to be born,
phoenixes gathered over the city,
and auspicious grain sprouted on the roof.
His mother,
in the midnight darkness without a lamp,
saw the palace illuminated.
Earlier,
Sū Bó'ā observed the aura over Chōnglíng,
describing it as lush and vibrant.
When Guāngwǔ rose to power,
passing his old home,
he saw the aura soaring to the heavens.
The births and rises of the Five Emperors and Three Kings
heard no such wonders.
Yáo's mother was touched by a red dragon,
yet at his rise,
no extraordinary blessings were noted.
Yǔ's mother swallowed coix seeds,
and before his reign,
he obtained a dark jade tablet.
Xiè's mother swallowed a swallow's egg,
and at Tāng's rise,
a white wolf brought a hook.
Hòujì's mother trod in a giant's footprint,
and at King Wén's rise,
a red sparrow appeared,
while King Wǔ received fish and
crows. All paled before the omens of Hàn's peace.
For Huángdì,
Yáo, and Shùn,
a phoenix came once.
Among all auspicious signs,
repeated occurrences were rare.
Emperor Wén of Hàn had
yellow dragons and
jade staffs.
Emperor Wǔ had
yellow dragons,
qílín,
and joined trees.
Emperor Xuān saw
phoenixes five times,
qílín,
divine sparrows,
sweet dew,
sweet springs,
yellow dragons,
and divine light.
Emperor Píng had
white pheasants and
black pheasants.
Emperor Míng had
qílín,
divine sparrows,
sweet dew,
sweet springs,
white pheasants,
black pheasants,
mushroom grass,
joined trees,
and auspicious grain,
matching Emperor Xuān,
with added wonders like a divine tripod
and golden anomalies.
The omens of one era,
continuously abundant,
signified Hàn's virtuous prosperity,
hence the multitude of blessings.
When Emperor Míng passed away,
the current emperor succeeded,
and in the Yuán'èr period,
benevolent virtues spread widely.
In the third year,
Línglíng produced five stalks of mushroom grass.
In the fourth year,
sweet dew fell in five counties.
In the fifth year,
six more mushroom stalks grew,
yellow dragons appeared,
eight in total.
Previously, dragons never appeared in pairs,
nor mushrooms more than singly,
and sweet dew fell but once—
yet now eight dragons emerged together,
eleven mushroom stalks grew successively,
sweet dew flowed over five counties,
virtue and bounty blazed brightly,
hence the profusion of omens.
Among all ancient emperors and kings,
who could achieve such feats?
When grain is abundant and the year peaceful,
even mediocre rulers can rely on this
to establish virtuous governance;
but in times of颠沛流离 and peril,
only sages and wise men of exceptional ability
can achieve meritorious deeds and transformative rule.
Therefore, for minor illnesses,
ordinary physicians are all skillful;
for severe and critical conditions,
only a Biǎn Què becomes truly excellent.
In the first year of the Jiànchū era,
unexpected calamities arrived,
a year of pestilence and disease.
Compared to the drought and lack of rain,
where oxen died and people fled,
it could be called extreme.
The emperor promoted virtue,
with talented men in office.
The Minister of Works Dì Wǔ,
a pillar of the state,
transferred grain to relieve and support the people,
so that none suffered starvation.
The world admired this virtue,
and though in peril, it did not fall into chaos.
The people hungered for grain
but were satiated with morality and virtue.
Though their bodies wandered the roads,
their hearts turned back to their homeland.
Thus, the roads bore no traces of bandits or thieves,
and in the deep, remote wilderness, there was no villainy of robbery or plunder.
Turning danger into safety,
and hardship into smooth passage—
which of the Five Emperors or Three Sovereigns
could have surpassed this?
In the eleventh year of the Yǒngpíng era,
in the Marquisate of Wǎn in Lújiāng Commandery,
by the border there was a lake.
Two young boys of Wǎn, named Chén Jué
and Chén Tǐng,
both over ten years old,
went together to fish by the lakeshore.
Tǐng fished first,
Jué came later.
Jué asked Tǐng:
"Have you caught anything fishing?"
Tǐng said:
"Yes!"
Jué then went home to fetch his fishing rod and line.
About forty paces from Tǐng,
he saw a wine vessel on the lake shore,
of a pure yellow color,
submerged in the water.
Jué thought it was bronze,
waded into the water to retrieve it,
but it was slippery and heavy, impossible to lift.
Tǐng saw from a distance,
and shouted:
"What are you taking?"
Jué said:
"There's bronze here,
but I can't lift it."
Tǐng went to assist him.
Before they could grasp it while wading,
the vessel suddenly transformed into a covenant plate,
moved and entered the deep abyss,
disappearing from sight again.
Tǐng and Jué stayed looking,
and saw things like coins,
pure yellow,
hundreds and thousands of them.
They immediately gathered them together,
each filling their hands,
then ran home to show their families.
Jué's father, Guó,
formerly a dismissed clerk,
courtesy name Jūnxián,
exclaimed in surprise:
"Where did you get these?"
Jué described the circumstances.
Jūnxián said:
"This is gold!"
He immediately rushed to go with Jué.
Arriving at the place with the gold,
there was still much in the water.
Xián waded in himself to gather it.
Neighbors of Jué and Tǐng also heard
and all competed to collect it,
obtaining over ten catties in total.
Xián reported this to the Chancellor himself,
the Chancellor informed the Grand Administrator.
The Grand Administrator sent clerks to collect it.
He dispatched his subordinate clerk Chéng Gōng to present it,
fully describing the circumstances of obtaining the gold.
The imperial edict stated:
"If it is as in the report, then it is acceptable.
If not as in the report,
there will be proper punishment."
Gōng received the edict
and returned to show the Grand Administrator.
From the Grand Administrator down,
they pondered the edict,
considering it contained doubts and hidden meanings,
that their account might be untrue,
and merely embellished favorably.
So they again reported the true circumstances of obtaining the gold as in the previous report.
The matter was then dropped.
In the twelfth year,
Xián and others submitted a petition stating:
"We obtained gold from the lake water,
the commandery presented it,
but to this day we have not received its value."
The edict was sent down to Lújiāng,
inquiring why Xián and others had not been paid the gold's value.
The commandery reported:
"The gold collected by Xián and others
was from an official lake,
not from private waters of Xián and others,
therefore the value was not given."
In the twelfth year,
an edict declared:
"Assess the current gold price,
and pay Xián and others the gold's value."
Han's auspicious signs were not few;
the gold emerged strangely,
hence it is specially recorded.
Gold and jade are divine treasures,
therefore they manifest in strange ways.
The gold object,
first a wine vessel,
then a covenant plate,
moving into the abyss—
is this not strange?
When the Xià dynasty was flourishing,
distant regions depicted objects
and the Nine Provinces offered metal.
Yǔ considered it auspicious,
and cast it into a ding.
The Nine Tripods of Zhōu
were also metal from distant lands.
Whether men brought it as tribute
or it emerged spontaneously from the deep,
its essence is the same—
both arise from abundant virtue,
as auspicious signs for sage kings.
In an age of gold and jade,
there are naturally responses of gold and jade.
In Emperor Wén's time,
a jade club appeared.
Gold and jade
are the highest of auspicious signs.
The sound of gold and the color of jade
are extraordinary in man.
In Yǒngchāng Commandery there is also gold,
fine and small as millet grains,
in the sand at the water's edge.
When people gather it,
each day they obtain five zhū in weight of gold,
all of a pure yellow hue.
Earth generates metal;
earth's color is yellow.
Hàn embodies the virtue of Earth,
therefore transformed gold emerges.
Gold has three grades;
the yellow kind now seen—
yellow is auspicious.
The old man on the Yí Bridge gave Zhāng Liáng a book,
which transformed into a yellow stone.
The essence of the yellow stone
emerged as a tally.
Now stone
is of the same category as metal;
though their substance differs, their color is alike—
both are auspicious signs of Earth.
In the third year of the Jiànchū era,
at the residence of Fù Níng, a woman from Quánlíng in Línglíng,
five stalks of auspicious fungus suddenly grew from the earth.
The tallest measured one chi four or five cun,
the shortest seven or eight cun,
with purple stems and leaves—
indeed, they were purple zhi mushrooms.
Grand Administrator Shěn Fēng dispatched his subordinate Yǎn Shèng to present them as tribute.
The emperor was delighted,
and bestowed money, clothing, and food.
He issued an edict summoning the high ministers,
with officials and commoners from commanderies and states all present,
to announce the zhi fungus to the world.
All under heaven heard of it,
and officials and people rejoiced,
knowing fully that the abundant virtue of Hàn
had brought forth this auspicious response.
In the fourth year,
sweet dew fell upon five counties: Quánlíng,
Línglíng,
Táoyáng,
Shǐ'ān,
and Lěngdào.
On elms, cypresses, plums, and prunes,
the leaves were thoroughly moistened,
dripping and flowing copiously.
The people sipped it,
finding it sweet as candy and honey.
In the fifth year,
zhi fungus grew again at the home of Zhōu Fú, a man of Quánlíng—
six stalks,
in color and form like those of the third year,
making eleven stalks in total including the previous ones.
The Xiāng River flows seven lǐ from Quánlíng city,
where rocks in the water form Yānshì Hill.
By the water stands Xiá Mountain,
with cliffs below,
and the water depth immeasurable.
Two yellow dragons appeared,
the longer over sixteen zhàng in length,
their bodies larger than horses.
They raised their heads and gazed about,
resembling the dragons painted in pictures.
The people of Yānshì Hill all witnessed them.
Several tens of paces from the dragons,
creatures like colts appeared—
six in total, small and large,
emerging from the water to play on the hill—
likely the offspring of the two dragons.
With the two dragons, they made eight.
They remained for a while before submerging.
During Emperor Xuān’s reign,
a phoenix descended upon Péngchéng,
and Péngchéng reported it.
Emperor Xuān summoned the court attendant Sòng Wēngyī.
Wēngyī said:
"The phoenix ought to descend upon the capital,
gathering in the suburbs of the Son of Heaven.
For it to descend far away in Péngchéng
is unacceptable,
no different from not descending at all."
Emperor Xuān replied:
"Now the world is united as one family.
Descending upon Péngchéng is the same as the capital.
How can it be deemed no different from not descending?"
He ordered those versed in the classics among his attendants
to challenge Wēngyī’s view.
Wēngyī, cornered,
removed his cap, kowtowed, and apologized.
In Emperor Xuān’s time,
it was no different from now.
The gathering of the phoenix
and the appearance of the yellow dragon
are equally significant.
Péngchéng
and Línglíng,
whether near or far, are the same.
The emperor’s domain is vast and enduring,
bounded by the four extremities.
Línglíng lies within,
still considered close.
Gōngsūn Chén of Lǔ,
during Emperor Wén’s reign, declared that Hàn corresponded to the virtue of Earth,
its omen being the appearance of a yellow dragon.
Later,
a yellow dragon appeared in Chéngjì.
Chéngjì’s remoteness
was like that of Línglíng.
During the reigns of Emperor Wǔ
and Emperor Xuān,
yellow dragons emerged.
With dragons appearing repeatedly,
this makes the fourth instance,
confirming Hàn’s Earth virtue.
Jiǎ Yì first proposed in Emperor Wén’s court:
"Hàn’s color should honor yellow,
and its numbers should be based on five."
Jiǎ Yì,
a minister of great wisdom,
spoke of yellow as the color and five as the number—
clearly affirming Earth virtue.
Zhi fungus grows from earth;
when the earth’s energy is harmonious,
zhi emerges.
Earth fosters crops,
and crops produce sweetness,
hence sweet dew gathers.
In past eras, dragons appeared singly,
never in pairs,
except in the prosperous age of Xià,
when two dragons resided in the court.
Now two dragons emerge together,
matching the number of Xià,
a sign of harmonious governance.
In the past, when dragons appeared,
their offspring rarely emerged.
Now six young dragons
come out together to play,
symbolizing the six children of Qián and Kūn,
foretelling abundant heirs.
In the times of Táng and Yú,
all beasts danced in accord,
and now eight dragons play for a long while.
Zhi fungus prolongs life,
consumed by immortals.
In the past, one or two grew at most,
but now,
with all instances, eleven stalks in total,
a sign of many attaining longevity,
nourishment for nurturing
long-lived beings like Sōng and Qiáo.
In the past, sweet dew fell in one place,
but now it flows over five counties,
corresponding to the number of Earth,
a manifestation of virtue spreading widely.
Imperial auspices appear repeatedly,
their emergence not in vain—
they must have meaning,
responding in accord with virtue.
Confucius said:
"The wise find joy,
the benevolent enjoy longevity."
The emperor, sage and benevolent,
thus has the longevity omen of zhi fungus growing.
Yellow is the color of Earth,
positioned at the center.
Thus, Xuānyuán, superior in virtue,
took yellow as his emblem.
The emperor, generous and kind,
his virtue matching Huángdì’s,
so the dragons are yellow,
showing his virtue is no different.
The east symbolizes benevolence;
the dragon, a creature of the east.
The emperor, sage and benevolent,
thus has this benevolent omen appear.
Sweetness represents the flavor of nurturing;
the emperor, benevolent and loving his people,
thus sweet dew descends.
The dragon, a creature of hidden depths,
emerges outwardly—
the emperor, sagely and brilliant,
draws it from rocky caverns.
Auspicious signs arise from worthy individuals;
blessings come through fortunate people.
Heaven’s way is natural,
its responses coinciding.
When a sage ruler gains auspices,
it also brings forth many worthies.
With an enlightened ruler and capable ministers,
all affairs thrive in peace.
King Wén and King Wǔ received the mandate,
aided by the strength of
Zhōu and Shào.
The virtue of the Hàn dynasty is deemed inferior to that of the Six Dynasties,
because commentators fail to recognize its merits.
Just as land has hills and marshes,
there are high and level grounds;
some use spades and shovels to flatten and level them,
turning them into plains.
People see the Five Emperors and
Three Sovereigns recorded in classical texts,
while Hàn affairs are not documented,
so they claim the Five and
Three surpass the Hàn.
Some use arguments as spades and shovels,
diminishing the Three and
Five, slightly enriching the Hàn's foundation below,
how could they merely be leveled as equals?
The Hàn would become a hill,
while the Five and Three turn into marshes.
Lakes and ponds vary,
though their breadth may be similar;
erect a pole to measure them,
their depth can be gauged.
The Hàn and all past dynasties,
all ruled as masters,
examine them based on facts,
their strengths and weaknesses become visible.
Thus, without a long pole erected,
one cannot know the measure of depth;
without the arguments of "Lùn Héng",
one cannot grasp the reality of优劣.
The Hàn stands at the end of a hundred dynasties,
comparing its virtue with those above it,
is like comparing lakes and ponds;
without the discourse of great writers,
it cannot escape a mediocre reputation.
Commentators often praise the ancient and disparage the present,
fearing the Hàn might rank below all past eras,
how could it merely be equal?
Posthumous titles are
traces of one's conduct.
The admirable ones include
Chéng and Xuān,
the detestable ones are
Líng and Lì.
Chéng Tāng faced drought,
Zhōu Xuān Wáng did too,
yet Chéng Tāng received the title
"Chéng",
and Xuān Wáng was called
"Xuān".
Unexpected disasters
did not mar their governance,
so ministers and sons conferred posthumous titles,
without losing truthfulness.
From this, we discuss Yáo,
Yáo also has a laudable title.
In his time, there were floods,
and the people were unsettled,
yet he is still called
"Yáo",
because it reflects a truthful assessment.
A single-character posthumous title
still clarifies a ruler's stature,
how much more so a thousand-word discourse,
or a ten-thousand-word eulogy?
Boats and carriages carry people,
how do they compare to those who travel on foot?
Plain carts and simple boats,
how do they compare to those painted with lacquer and colors?
Thus, great writers are
the nation's boats and carriages,
adorned with paintings.
If farmers lack strong men,
grains will not thrive;
if a state lacks powerful writings,
its virtue remains obscure and unmanifested.
The Hàn's virtue does not cease,
yet amidst a hundred dynasties, it falls into chaos,
because strong writers fail to document it.
Since Gāozǔ's time,
authors have not thoroughly discussed the Hàn.
Sīmǎ Zhǎngqīng wrote "Fēng Shàn Shū",
but its text is brief and incomplete.
Sīmǎ Zǐcháng recorded from Huángdì to Xiàowǔ,
Yáng Zǐyún documented from Xuān Dì to Āi and
Píng; Chén Píngzhōng recorded Guāngwǔ,
Bān Mèngjiān eulogized Xiàomíng.
The Hàn dynasty's merits and virtues,
can be somewhat seen.
The current emperor has ascended the throne,
yet there is no praise recorded,
so the author of "Lùn Héng"
exhausts his efforts for this purpose,
hence works like "Qí Shì",
"Xuān Hàn",
"Huī Guó",
"Yàn Fú".
A dragon without clouds and rain
cannot reach the heavens;
great writers are
the state's clouds and rain.
They carry the nation's virtue onto historical records,
proclaiming its fame for ten thousand generations to come,
its height not merely reaching the heavens.
The earth of city walls
is soil from level ground,
but with human effort of building and trampling,
it stands tall overlooking the ponds.
A state's merits and virtues
are loftier than city walls,
and the文人's pen
is mightier than building and trampling.
When a sage ruler's virtue is abundant and achievements solid,
if not praised and recorded,
how can they spread and flow boundlessly?
People with noble conduct
may be praised truthfully,
some wish to commend but cannot speak,
others say it's not good,
unwilling to state a word.
Judging these three types,
which is the most virtuous?
In the eras of the Five and Three,
this was at its peak.
During Xiàomíng's reign,
numerous auspicious signs appeared together,
officials and ministers
were not few,
yet only Bān Gù and his like
praised the state's virtue,
they can be said to have praised truthfully.
Their eulogies, artful and extraordinary,
manifested the Hàn's virtue across a hundred dynasties,
making the emperor's name like the sun and moon;
how does this compare to being unable to speak or
speaking without beauty and goodness?
Qín Shǐhuáng traveled southeast,
ascended Kuàijī Mountain,
where Lǐ Sī inscribed on stone,
recording and eulogizing the emperor's virtue.
At Lángyá, it was the same.
Qín, an unprincipled state,
had stone inscriptions that lasted generations,
and those who read them
saw the beauty of Yáo and
Shùn.
From this, it is clear that
eulogies are necessary.
Today, it's not that there's no talent like Lǐ Sī,
but there's no opportunity to ascend Kuàijī or
pass through Lángyá's steps.
Exquisite and rare melodies played on strings,
if listeners do not call them good,
the musicians will slacken and not refine their art.
Why?
Because mastery and rarity are hard to achieve,
and observers may not recognize their excellence.
When a sage state promotes exquisite and rare governance,
if ministers do not eulogize it,
how can they support and extend its beauty,
and where can it be applied?
Now, books on arts and techniques exist on bamboo and silk,
without attribution of their origin,
readers dismiss them casually,
not adopting or trusting them.
But if titled
"So-and-so's formula",
or stated as
"tested and tried",
people compete to engrave and copy,
treasuring them as secrets.
Submitting memorials to the state,
presenting reports to the commandery,
praising and recommending scholars and officials,
commending their methods and abilities,
once the documents are issued and records made,
the scholars and officials are seen as virtuous and skilled.
Why?
Because the memorials manifest their conduct,
and the records clarify their talents.
The state's virtue overflows and blazes,
yet none proclaim or praise it,
causing the great Hàn, a sage state, to bear a mediocre name;
the fault lies with conventional scholars not arguing based on facts.
Confucius praised the Zhou dynasty, saying:
"In the era of Tang
and Yu,
it reached its peak.
The virtue of Zhou
can indeed be called the highest virtue!"
Confucius,
being a literatus of Zhou,
had he been born in the Han era,
would also have acclaimed Han's supreme virtue.
When Zhào Tuó ruled Nányuè,
he betrayed his sovereign and eliminated envoys,
refusing to follow Han institutions,
sitting arrogantly with his hair in a mallet-shaped bun,
immersed in barbarian customs.
Lù Jiǎ persuaded him with Han's virtue
and intimidated him with imperial authority,
causing him to awaken in realization,
suddenly rising from his seat.
The foolishness of worldly Confucians,
akin to Zhào Tuó's confusion,
when confronted by profound writers
presenting arguments like Lù Jiǎ's,
those who witness it
will experience the same sudden awakening as Zhào Tuó.
The Han dynasty's magnificence
lacks extraordinary acclaim.
The excellence of literati
is the nation's emblem.
Seeing grand houses reveals renowned families,
observing tall trees indicates ancient capitals.
The presence of great writings in a state
proves it is a sage-like era.
Mencius judged people by their pupils:
a clear mind makes bright eyes.
Brightness
means eyes with cultured clarity.
Assessing states and judging people
follows the same principle.
When rulers are sage, literati gather;
when people's hearts are wise, eyes gleam with color.
Trampling embroidered silk in the mud,
those who see it
all feel heartache.
They know the silk's value
but fail to honor literati—
this shows lack of analogical thinking.
Do literati's writings merely play with ink and brush for beauty's sake?
They record conduct,
transmit reputations.
Good people wish to be recorded,
striving to do good;
evil ones dread it,
restraining themselves.
Thus, the literati's pen
encourages good and punishes evil.
Posthumous titles highlight virtue
and expose wickedness.
Even a single-character title
motivates people;
those who learn of it
all strive to improve.
How much more so with writings' full power,
determining good and evil's truth,
completely recording words and deeds,
in texts numbering thousands,
passed down through ages,
becoming enduring records,
hence worthy of honor.
When Yáng Zǐyún wrote "Model Sayings,"
a wealthy Shǔ merchant offered a hundred thousand coins
to be included.
Zǐyún refused,
saying:
"Wealth without benevolent deeds
is like a deer in a pen
or an ox in a stall—
how could I falsely record it?"
Bān Shūpí, continuing "Records of the Grand Historian,"
included local villains as warnings.
Those who distort the Way,
condemned by moral standards,
cannot evade exposure.
Thus, Zǐyún wasn't swayed by wealth,
nor Shūpí by favoritism.
The literati's pen
stands uniquely impartial!
Sages fix intent with the brush,
composing collected texts;
writings complete, feelings revealed,
later readers
discern right and wrong—
how could records be reckless?
Feet tread the ground,
leaving fair or foul prints;
writings gather on slips, revealing good or evil intent.
So, examining footprints shows the foot,
reading texts reveals the heart.
"The three hundred 'Book of Songs' poems,
in one phrase summarized,
say:
'Thoughts without depravity.'"
The "Discourses Weighed" chapters, numbering tens,
also in one phrase,
say:
"Condemning falsehoods."
People claim the dead become ghosts,
conscious,
able to harm.
Testing by analogy:
the dead don't become ghosts,
lack consciousness,
cannot harm.
How to verify?
Verify through things.
Humans
are beings;
things are beings too.
Things don't become ghosts when dead,
why should humans alone?
If the world acknowledges things don't turn ghosts,
then whether humans do remains unclear.
If indistinguishable,
there's no basis to claim they can.
What gives life
is vital energy,
extinguished at death.
What produces this energy
is blood vessels.
Death exhausts the vessels,
ending the energy,
leading to decay,
turning to dust—
how could that make ghosts?
Without ears and eyes,
one knows nothing;
thus, the deaf and blind
resemble plants.
When vital energy departs,
isn't it worse than lacking senses?
Decay brings dissolution,
vanishing into obscurity,
hence called 'ghosts and spirits.'
What people see as ghostly forms
aren't spirits of the dead.
Why?
'Ghosts and spirits'
denote elusive, unseen entities.
At death, the spirit ascends,
bones return to earth,
thus termed 'ghosts and spirits.'
'Ghost'
means 'to return,'
'spirit'
means formless and fleeting.
Some say:
'Ghosts and spirits'
refer to yīn and yáng.
Yīn energy reverts things to origin,
hence 'ghost';
yáng energy guides life,
hence 'spirit.'
'Spirit'
means 'to extend,'
ceaselessly recurring,
ending and beginning anew.
Humans live by spiritual energy,
returning to it at death.
Yīn-yáng are called ghosts/spirits,
so are the dead.
Energy creating humans
is like water forming ice.
Water solidifies into ice,
energy condenses into humans;
ice melts into water,
death restores spirit.
Calling it 'spirit'
is like melted ice renamed water.
People see different names
and think ghosts are conscious,
taking form to harm—
this lacks evidential basis.
People see ghosts taking the forms of living persons.
Since they appear in the forms of living persons,
we know they cannot be the essences of dead people.
How can this be verified?
Consider bags filled with millet and rice.
When rice is in the bag,
or millet in the sack,
fully packed and firm,
standing upright and visible,
people looking at them
recognize them as bags of millet and rice.
Why is this?
Because the shapes of the bags,
their contents can be discerned.
If the bag tears and rice spills out,
the sack ruptures and millet is lost,
then the bags collapse and deflate,
and people looking at them
no longer see their contents.
Human spirit and vitality,
concealed within the physical body,
are like millet and rice inside bags.
When one dies, the body decays
and vital energy disperses,
just as bags tear and rupture,
with millet and rice spilling out.
When millet and rice are lost,
the bags no longer maintain their form;
when vital energy disperses and perishes,
how could there remain a body
for people to see?
When birds and beasts die,
their flesh completely withers away,
but their hides and fur remain.
These are made into fur garments,
and people seeing them
recognize the forms of those animals.
Hence, there are those who wear dog-skin coats pretending to be dogs,
and people don't realize it
because they borrow the dog's hide and fur,
so people don't suspect.
Now when humans die,
their skin and hair decay,
even if some vital energy remains,
how could the spirit borrow this form to appear and move about?
The dead cannot borrow the forms of the living to appear,
just as the living cannot borrow the souls of the dead to perish.
When domestic animals transform to resemble human forms,
their bodies are still alive,
and their vital energy remains present.
If they were dead,
their bodies decayed,
even tigers and rhinoceroses, fierce and brave,
could not transform again.
When Gōngniú Āi in Lǔ fell ill and transformed into a tiger,
it was because he hadn't yet died.
There are cases where living forms transform into other living kinds,
but none where dead bodies transform into living appearances.
Since heaven and earth opened
and the age of human sovereigns began,
those who died of old age,
or those dying young in middle age,
number in the hundreds of millions.
Counting the living today,
they are fewer than the dead.
If everyone who died became a ghost,
then on the roads,
there would be a ghost at every step.
When people are about to die and see ghosts,
they should see hundreds of thousands of them,
filling halls and courtyards,
crowding lanes and roads,
not just one or two.
When people die by violence,
it's said their blood becomes will-o'-the-wisp.
Blood
is the vital energy of life.
When people travel at night and see will-o'-the-wisp,
it doesn't resemble human form,
but appears as a chaotic accumulation,
like the shape of flames.
Will-o'-the-wisp is the blood of dead people,
its form unlike that of living humans.
Since its form doesn't resemble living humans,
and vital energy has left the person,
why would it take human form?
When people see ghosts,
if they all resembled dead people's forms,
then we might suspect ghosts are the dead,
but sometimes they resemble living people instead.
When sick people see ghosts,
they say "so-and-so is coming,"
yet that person isn't dead at the time,
only the energy resembles their form.
If the dead become ghosts,
why would the sick see the forms of living people?
The nature of heaven and earth
can regenerate fire,
but cannot make extinguished flames reignite;
can regenerate humans,
but cannot make the dead reappear.
If it cannot make dead ashes become burning fire again,
then I strongly doubt the dead can regain form.
Considering how extinguished fire cannot reignite,
it becomes clear
that the dead cannot become ghosts.
Those who become ghosts
are said to be the spirits of dead people.
If ghosts truly are
the spirits of dead people,
then when people see them,
they should only see naked forms,
not see them wearing clothes and belts.
Why?
Clothing has no spirit.
When people die,
it decays along with the body,
so how could it be worn?
Spirit fundamentally relies on blood and energy,
which always attach to the physical form.
Though the body decays,
if the spirit still remains,
it might become a ghost.
But clothing—
silk, cloth, and linen—
during life had no blood-energy attachment,
and inherently lacks blood-energy itself.
It decays and perishes,
equal to the body,
so how could it maintain the form of clothing?
From this perspective,
if the ghost's clothing resembles real clothing,
then the body must resemble a real body too.
Since it resembles,
we know it cannot be the spirit of a dead person.
Since the dead cannot become ghosts,
they also cannot have consciousness.
How can this be tested?
By the lack of consciousness before birth.
Before humans are born,
they exist in primordial energy;
after death,
they return to primordial energy.
Primordial energy is vague and indistinct,
with human energy within it.
Before birth, humans have no consciousness;
after death they return to this unconscious origin,
so how could they have consciousness?
The reason humans have intelligence and wisdom
is because they contain the energy of the five constants;
the reason the five constants' energy exists in humans
is because the five organs are within the body.
When the five organs are unharmed,
humans are wise;
when the five organs are diseased,
humans become confused,
and confusion leads to foolishness.
When humans die,
the five organs decay,
so the five constants have nothing to attach to,
the vessels that stored wisdom are ruined,
and what constituted wisdom has departed.
Form requires energy to exist,
energy requires form to know.
Just as there's no independently burning fire in the world,
how could there be a disembodied, independently knowing spirit?
Human death
is like dreaming.
Dreaming
is next to a trance,
and trance
is comparable to death.
When one falls into trance without waking, one dies.
If one could wake from trance,
or return from death,
it would resemble dreaming.
Thus dreaming,
trance, and death
are essentially the same.
In dreams, one cannot perceive what happens while awake,
just as in death one cannot recognize what one did while alive.
If people talk and act beside someone sleeping,
the sleeper cannot know it,
just as if good or evil deeds are done before a dead person's coffin,
the dead cannot know it either.
In sleep,
though vital energy remains
and the body is intact,
one still knows nothing—
how much more so when the dead person's spirit has vanished
and the body has decayed?
When a person is driven and injured by another,
they go to the officials to report their grievance and tell others about it,
because they possess consciousness.
If someone is killed by another,
would they not know who killed them?
Or if their family does not know where their corpse lies?
If the dead had consciousness,
they would surely resent the one who killed them,
and should be able to speak beside the officials,
informing them of the culprit's name;
if they could return to tell their family,
they would report where their body is located.
Yet now they cannot do so,
which is proof of their lack of consciousness.
In the world, when the dead are said to cause the living to perish,
and their words are heeded,
or when shamans pluck the mystic strings,
calling down the souls of the deceased,
and speak through the shaman's mouth,
these are all exaggerated and unfounded claims.
If not exaggerated,
then it is the essence of things manifesting as apparitions.
Some say:
They cannot speak.
If they cannot speak,
then they cannot know either.
Knowing relies on vital energy,
and speaking also uses vital energy.
When a person is not ill,
their wisdom and spirit are settled;
when ill, they become confused and disordered,
for their spirit is disturbed.
Death is
the extreme form of illness.
In minor illness or near death,
one is still confused,
how much more in its extreme!
When the spirit is disturbed,
one naturally lacks awareness,
let alone when it dissipates!
A person's death
is like the extinguishing of a fire.
When a fire goes out, its light does not shine,
and when a person dies, their knowledge lacks wisdom;
the two should be of the same nature.
Yet some argue that the dead have consciousness,
which is delusion.
How does a person's illness and impending death
differ from a fire about to go out?
When a fire extinguishes, its light vanishes, but the candle remains;
when a person dies, their essence perishes, but the body remains.
To say the dead have consciousness
is to claim that a fire can still have light after it is extinguished.
In the depths of winter,
when cold air prevails,
water freezes into ice.
When spring warmth returns,
the ice melts back into water.
Humans living between heaven and earth
are much like ice.
The energies of yin and yang
condense to form a person;
when the years end and life span is exhausted,
death returns them to energy.
Just as spring water cannot become ice again,
how can a dead soul regain its form?
Jealous husbands and resentful wives,
sharing the same room,
may engage in licentious and improper conduct,
filled with anger and disputes.
If the husband dies,
the wife remarries;
if the wife dies,
the husband takes another wife.
If the dead had consciousness,
they should be greatly angered.
Yet now, when a spouse dies,
there is silence and no sound;
those who remarry
encounter no calamity—
this is proof of the lack of consciousness.
Confucius buried his mother at Fáng,
and soon after, heavy rain came,
causing the tomb at Fáng to collapse.
Confucius heard of this,
shed tears and said:
"In ancient times, they did not repair tombs."
So he did not repair it.
If the dead had consciousness,
they would surely resent people for not repairing it.
Confucius, knowing this,
should have promptly repaired the tomb
to please the spirit,
yet he did not repair it,
showing the sage's clear understanding
that he knew the dead lack consciousness.
When dried bones in the wilderness
occasionally make sounds, as if calling out,
or if one hears crying at night,
some call it the voice of the dead,
but this is not so.
How to verify this?
The reason the living can speak or call out
is that air is contained in the mouth and throat,
moving the tongue,
and opening and closing the mouth,
thus enabling speech.
It is like blowing a flute or shēng;
if the flute or shēng is broken,
the air escapes uncontained,
and with no fingers to play it,
it produces no sound.
The pipes of the flute or shēng
are like a person's mouth and throat;
the fingers playing the holes
are like the movement of the tongue.
When a person dies, the mouth and throat decay,
and the tongue no longer moves—
how could they form words?
Thus, when dried bones occasionally moan,
it is because human bones can naturally produce such sounds.
Some consider it supernatural,
no different from ghosts crying at night.
Supernatural energy causes the variation of moaning,
having its own reasons,
lingering beside the dead bones,
leading people to think the bones still have consciousness,
moaning in the wild.
Countless exposed bodies lie in marshes and fields,
so the sounds of moaning
should be continuous everywhere.
While it is possible to make the mute speak,
there is no case where the dead, who have spoken, can be made to speak again,
nor can those who have spoken make them do so.
It is like living things having green as their vitality,
which is bestowed upon them;
when things die, the green departs,
as if taken away.
When green is given to a thing,
and then taken away,
after it is gone, it cannot be bestowed again,
nor can the thing become green again on its own.
Sound and color are both interconnected,
bestowed by nature.
The color green,
like the sound of calling,
cannot return to dead things;
so how could the dead alone regain the ability to speak?
This is delusion.
The reason people can speak
is because they have physical strength;
the abundance of this strength
comes from being able to eat and drink.
If eating and drinking decrease,
strength declines,
and the voice becomes hoarse.
When too weak to eat,
the mouth can no longer speak.
Death is
the ultimate weakness,
so how could it allow speech again?
Some say:
"The dead inhale the energy of food,
thus they can speak."
But the essence of the dead
is the same as that of the living.
If the living do not eat or drink,
but only inhale the energy of food
through the mouth,
in less than three days,
they would starve to death.
Others say:
"The essence of the dead
is more divine than that of the living,
so they can produce sound by inhaling energy."
Now, the essence of the living resides within the body,
while that of the dead lies outside it.
How does death differ from life?
What distinguishes inside from outside the body?
Take water contained in a large jar;
if the jar breaks, the water flows on the ground.
Is the water on the ground any different from that in the jar?
If the water on the ground is no different from that in the jar,
why should the essence outside the body differ from that within?
When a person dies, they do not become ghosts,
have no consciousness,
cannot speak,
and thus cannot harm people.
How can this be verified?
When a person is angry, they use their vital energy,
and when they harm others, they use physical force;
using force requires tendons and bones to be strong,
and only when strong can they harm others.
An angry person
breathing heavily beside someone,
with breath panting and shooting at the person's face,
even if as brave as Bēn or
Yù, their breath alone cannot harm others.
But if they stretch out a hand to strike,
or lift a foot to kick,
then whatever they strike or kick will surely break.
When dead,
bones decay and tendon strength ceases,
hands and feet cannot lift,
even if the vital essence still exists,
it is like the time of heavy breathing without any support.
How could they harm others?
The reason why people or creatures can harm others
is because of arms wielding blades,
or claws and teeth being sharp and strong.
Now, when a person dies,
their arms decay and deteriorate,
unable to hold blades again;
claws and teeth fall off,
unable to bite or chew again;
how could they harm others?
When a child is first born,
though hands and feet are fully formed,
the hands cannot strike,
and the feet cannot kick,
because the vital energy has just congealed,
not yet strong and firm.
From this perspective,
it is clear that the vital essence cannot be strong,
indeed.
Vital energy forms the body,
and if the body is weak,
it still cannot harm others;
how much more so after death,
when the energy departs and the spirit ceases,
being weak and unable to harm others?
Can cold bones be said to harm others?
Does the energy of the dead not depart?
How could it harm others?
When a chicken egg has not yet hatched,
it is murky within the shell,
and if broken open to look,
it appears like water in form.
Only when the good hen broods over it,
does the body gradually take form;
after it is formed,
it can peck and kick.
A person's death
is like the murky stage,
how could the murky energy harm others?
The reason why people can be fierce and harm others
is due to eating and drinking;
being full from eating and drinking makes them strong and fierce,
and being strong and fierce enables them to harm others.
When a person is ill and cannot eat or drink,
the body becomes weak and frail,
and extreme frailty and exhaustion
lead to death.
When critically ill,
even with enemies nearby,
they cannot shout at them;
if someone steals their belongings,
they cannot stop or seize them,
all due to weakness and exhaustion.
Death is
the ultimate state of weakness and exhaustion,
how could it harm others?
If one's poultry or livestock
are stolen by others,
even a timid and powerless person
will feel anger,
and in extreme anger,
may even fight to the death.
In times of chaos and collapse,
when people eat each other,
if their spirits were conscious,
they ought to be able to harm others.
Yet one's body is more valuable than poultry,
one's own death weightier than being stolen from,
but anger is directed at the poultry,
with no resentment towards those who eat one's flesh,
proving the inability to harm others.
Before a cicada sheds its skin,
it is a nymph;
after shedding,
it leaves the nymph's body behind,
and takes on the cicada's form.
If the spirit of a dead person leaves the body,
like the cicada leaving the nymph,
then the cicada
cannot harm the nymph.
Since the cicada cannot harm the nymph,
how could the spirit of a dead person
harm the body of a living one?
The meaning of dreams is doubtful.
Some say:
"In dreams,
the spirit remains within one's body,
presenting images of good or bad omens."
Others say:
"The spirit travels,
interacting with other people or things."
If it truly remains within the body,
then the spirit after death
would also be the same.
If it truly travels,
and one dreams of injuring or killing someone,
or being injured or killed in a dream,
as if retaliated against by others,
yet the next day, looking at that person's body,
or examining one's own,
there is no evidence of weapon wounds.
Dreams use the spirit,
and the spirit
is the same as the spirit after death.
If the spirit in dreams cannot harm others,
how could the spirit after death cause harm?
When fire blazes, the pot boils,
and when boiling stops, the steam ceases,
because the fire is the main cause.
Only when the spirit is angry
can it harm others;
if not angry,
it cannot harm others.
When fire rages in the stove,
the pot bubbles and steam rises;
when essence is angry in the chest,
strength peaks and the body heats up.
But when a person is about to die,
the body becomes cool,
increasingly cold,
until death occurs.
At the moment of death,
the spirit is not angry;
after the body perishes,
it is like soup leaving the pot,
how could it harm others?
Creatures can interact with people,
causing people to have foolish or mad illnesses.
If one understands the cause and addresses it,
the illness can be cured.
When a creature is not dead,
its spirit relies on its body,
thus it can transform
and interact with people;
once dead,
the body decays and rots,
the spirit scatters and perishes,
with nothing to rely on,
and cannot transform.
The human spirit
is like the spirit of creatures.
When creatures are alive,
their spirits can cause illness;
when they die,
their spirits vanish.
Humans are the same as creatures;
after death, the spirit also perishes,
how could it cause harm or misfortune?
Suppose it is argued that humans are noble,
and their spirits are different,
yet in reality,
creatures can transform,
while humans cannot,
this would mean human spirits are inferior to creatures',
and creature spirits are more remarkable than humans'.
Fire and water burn and drown,
all that can harm people
are things of the five elements.
Metal injures people,
wood strikes people,
earth buries people,
water drowns people,
fire burns people.
When causing death,
is the spirit then a thing of the five elements?
If it harms people,
if not,
it cannot harm people.
If not a thing,
then it must be a vapor.
Among vapors that harm people,
the vapor of the great yang is poisonous.
When causing death,
is that vapor poisonous?
If it harms people,
if not,
it cannot harm people.
Now, to argue that the dead do not become ghosts,
have no consciousness,
and cannot harm people,
then what is seen as ghosts
are not the essences of the dead,
and those that harm people
are not caused by their essences,
is clear.
The tradition says:
"King Xuān of Zhōu unjustly killed his minister Dù Bó.
When King Xuān was about to hunt in the garden,
Dù Bó appeared on the left side of the road,
grasped a vermilion bow and shot King Xuān,
who fell onto his quiver and died.
Duke Jiǎn of Yān unjustly killed his minister Zhuāngzǐ Yì.
As Duke Jiǎn was about to enter the main gate,
Zhuāngzǐ Yì appeared on the left side of the road,
grasped a vermilion staff and struck him,
killing him beneath his carriage."
These two cases
are evidence of the dead becoming ghosts,
proof that ghosts have consciousness
and can harm people.
If not,
how to explain this?
I say:
Humans live among all things,
and when things die, they cannot become ghosts;
why should humans alone become ghosts after death?
If it is because humans are noble and can become ghosts,
then all who die should become ghosts;
why are Dù Bó
and Zhuāngzǐ Yì alone ghosts?
If it is because those wrongfully killed can become ghosts,
there are many ministers and sons in the world who have been wronged;
figures like Bǐgān
and Wǔ Zǐxū did not become ghosts.
Now, Dù Bó
and Zhuāngzǐ Yì acted without principle,
resentfully killing their rulers in revenge;
no crime is greater than regicide.
Then the noble ghosts of the dead
should punish them again,
which is not something Dù Bó
or Zhuāngzǐ Yì would dare to do.
When people harm each other,
they hate their lives
and loathe seeing their persons,
so they kill and eliminate them.
The families of the murdered
go to officials to accuse their enemies,
and the enemies also loathe seeing them.
Life and death follow different paths,
humans and ghosts dwell apart.
If Dù Bó
and Zhuāngzǐ Yì resented King Xuān
and Duke Jiǎn,
they should not have killed them;
they should have become ghosts
and met with them.
The majesty of rulers
naturally overawes subjects,
and their guards and soldiers are many;
yet two ministers killed two rulers.
The deaths of the two rulers
should have been avenged,
not the result of deep calculation with consciousness
or acts of hatred.
If the two ministers were divine,
they should have known the two rulers would avenge their deaths;
if they did not know,
then they were not divine.
If not divine, how could they harm people?
The world has much that seems right but is wrong,
falsehoods resembling truth;
thus tales of Dù Bó
and Zhuāngzǐ Yì
often survive.
Duke Huì of Jìn reburied Crown Prince Shēnshēng.
In autumn, his servant Hú Tū went to a lower capital,
where he met the crown prince.
The prince hurriedly mounted the servant's carriage and told him,
saying:
"Yíwú has been disrespectful;
I have obtained permission from the Emperor,
and will give Jìn to Qín,
so Qín will sacrifice to me."
Hú Tū replied:
"I have heard
that spirits do not enjoy offerings from unrelated clans,
and people do not sacrifice to those not of their lineage.
Would your sacrifices not then be cut off?
Moreover, what crime have the people committed?
To lose punishment and lack sacrifices—
please consider this!"
The prince said:
"Very well,
I will request again.
In seven days,
in the western part of Xīnchéng,
there will be a shaman
through whom you may see me."
He agreed,
and then vanished.
When the time came,
Hú Tū went to the shaman's house in western Xīnchéng,
and again met with Shēnshēng.
Shēnshēng told him:
"The Emperor has permitted punishing the guilty!
He will die in Hán."
Four years later,
Duke Huì fought Duke Mù of Qín at Hán,
was captured by Duke Mù,
exactly as foretold.
If not divine, what is it?
I say:
This is also like the cases of Dù Bó
and Zhuāngzǐ Yì.
How to clarify this?
Reburial
is a private grievance,
while the Emperor
is a public deity.
To dispute with a public deity over a private grievance—
why would He listen?
The Emperor agreed to give Jìn to Qín,
but Hú Tū thought it improper;
Shēnshēng followed Hú Tū's words,
meaning the Emperor's agreement with Shēnshēng was wrong.
If the deity is the Emperor,
yet inferior to Hú Tū,
He cannot be the Emperor,
clearly.
Moreover, subjects dare not seek private favors from rulers
because rulers are exalted and subjects lowly,
and they dare not interfere improperly.
Shēnshēng compared to the Emperor—
is it merely like subject and ruler?
Resenting Duke Huì's reburial,
he interfered with the Emperor's noble decree,
which was not his place.
Lí Jī slandered him to death,
yet Duke Huì reburied his corpse.
The wrong of reburial is lesser than killing;
Duke Huì's crime is lighter than Lí Jī's.
He requested punishment for Duke Huì,
but not for Lí Jī's killing,
showing Shēnshēng hated the reburial
more than his own murder.
Qín Shǐhuáng adopted Lǐ Sī's proposal,
burned the Book of Songs
and Book of Documents,
and later buried scholars alive.
The resentment of the erudites
was no less than Shēnshēng's;
the evil of burying scholars
was more painful than reburial.
Yet the dead scholars of Qín
did not petition the Emperor,
appear as ghosts,
or gather to accuse Shǐhuáng of tyranny
and Lǐ Sī of wrongdoing.
King Wǔ of Zhōu fell ill and was unwell,
so the Duke of Zhōu prayed for his life,
setting up three altars on a single cleared ground,
propping up jades and holding a guǐ tablet,
then addressed Tàiwáng,
Wáng Jì,
and King Wén.
The scribe then wrote the prayer on bamboo slips,
the words saying:
"I am benevolent and compliant,
versatile and skilled in many arts,
capable of serving the ghosts and spirits.
But your eldest grandson so-and-so,
is not as versatile and skilled as Dàn,
and cannot serve the ghosts and spirits."
The ghosts and spirits referred to
are the three kings.
If the dead have no consciousness,
they cannot become ghosts and spirits,
yet the Duke of Zhōu,
a sage,
if his words are accurate,
then he grasped the reality of the netherworld;
grasping the reality of the netherworld,
then the three kings being ghosts and spirits
is clear.
It is said:
Can a sage truly be spiritual?
Or cannot be spiritual?
If spiritual,
he should know the hearts of the three kings,
not merely ascertain their being ghosts.
The Duke of Zhōu prayed for life,
the scribe wrote the prayer,
once the prayer ended and words ceased,
he did not know whether the three kings would grant it or not,
so he divined with three turtle shells,
all three shells showed auspicious signs,
only then was he pleased.
If he could know the three kings were conscious as ghosts,
he should not need to divine to know if they approved;
having to use three turtle shells
shows he knew the reality.
To confirm they were ghosts,
he had to inquire,
then he knew.
Whether the dead are conscious or not,
and whether they grant requests or not,
are one reality.
If he could know the three kings would surely grant his wish,
then his calling them ghosts
would be credible;
if he could not know,
calling them ghosts
is like ordinary people;
having the same knowledge as ordinary people,
then the reality of the dead
cannot be determined.
Moreover, how did the Duke of Zhōu's prayer
succeed?
Did utmost sincerity achieve it?
Or was it the correctness of his words?
If by utmost sincerity,
then his prayer's argument,
using sincerity to move ghosts,
would not care about the words' right or wrong.
Dǒng Zhòngshū's method for praying for rain
involved setting up earthen dragons to influence the energy.
Now earthen dragons are not real,
they cannot bring rain,
but Zhòngshū used them to express utmost sincerity,
disregarding the object's falseness or truth.
Thus, the Duke of Zhōu's prayer for life
is like Zhòngshū's prayer for rain;
the three kings not being ghosts
is like piled earth not being dragons.
In Jìn, Xún Yǎn attacked Qí,
but did not complete the campaign and returned.
He developed a carbuncle,
an ulcer on his head,
and when they reached the place of Zhùyōng,
he fell ill, his eyes bulging out,
and died with them open,
unable to receive the mouth-piece.
Fàn Xuānzǐ washed and stroked him,
saying:
"I will serve Wú no less than I served you, my lord."
But the eyes remained open.
Xuānzǐ saw they would not close,
thinking he resented his son Wú.
In human nature, what one resents
most is often about one's son,
so he mentioned Wú to comfort him.
"Eyes still open"
means the resentment was not addressed.
Luán Huáizǐ said:
"Is it because the campaign against Qí was unfinished?"
Then he stroked him again,
saying:
"If you die, my lord,
may I not continue the fight against Qí,
as the river is my witness!"
Then the eyes closed, and the mouth-piece was placed.
Not completing the attack on Qí
was what Xún Yǎn resented;
Huáizǐ understood it,
so the eyes closed and accepted the mouth-piece;
Xuānzǐ missed it,
so the eyes stayed open and the mouth shut.
It is said:
When Xún Yǎn fell ill and died,
he suffered from bulging eyes;
bulging eyes meant a clenched jaw,
a clenched jaw meant no mouth-piece could be inserted.
Freshly dead, the vital energy was strong,
the illness itself caused bulging eyes;
Xuānzǐ comforted him too early,
so the eyes did not close,
and the mouth did not open.
After a while, the energy faded,
and Huáizǐ comforted him then,
so the eyes closed and the mouth accepted the piece.
This was due to Xún Yǎn's illness,
not a dead spirit showing resentment through eyes and mouth.
Whenever people die,
they all have some regret.
The determined regret unfulfilled righteous deeds,
scholars regret unanswered questions,
farmers regret unharvested crops,
merchants regret unmultiplied wealth,
officials regret unattained high posts,
the brave regret underdeveloped talents.
All under heaven have their desires,
and thus their regrets;
if open eyes must mean resentment,
then all under heaven who die would die with eyes open.
Moreover, the deceased's essence and soul dissipate,
and they can no longer hear people's words.
Not hearing people's words
is what defines death;
if they separate from the body to become ghosts,
standing by people's sides,
even if they hear words,
having left their form,
how can they re-enter the body
to close eyes and open mouths?
If they could enter the body to show resentment through the corpse,
they could avoid departing,
staying with the form.
Considering how people discuss death,
saying the spirit remains as before,
able to use the essence to reappear in form,
making the corpse like a living person,
is mistaken.
King Chéng of Chǔ deposed the crown prince Shāngchén,
wishing to install Prince Zhí.
Shāngchén heard of this,
and surrounded the king with palace guards.
The king asked to eat bear's paw before dying,
but was refused.
The king hanged himself and died.
When given the posthumous title
"Líng",
he did not close his eyes;
when called
"Chéng",
then he closed them.
Being titled
"Líng"
and not closing eyes,
then titled
"Chéng"
and closing them,
is evidence that King Chéng was conscious.
When titled
"Líng",
he resented it in heart,
so his eyes did not close;
when retitled
"Chéng",
he was pleased in heart and closed them.
His spirit heard people's discussions,
saw them change his title,
so pleased, his eyes closed.
Originally, his eyes were not ill,
no one comforted him,
yet his eyes opened and closed on their own,
if not spiritual, then what?
It is said:
This is again similar to Xún Yǎn's case.
Although his eyes were not afflicted,
they were not open for no reason either.
When King Chéng died by hanging at that time,
his vital energy was still vigorous,
and the breath had just ceased,
so his eyes remained open,
thus he was posthumously titled
"Líng".
After a short while when his energy declined,
his eyes happened to be about to close,
and they successively changed his title to
"Chéng".
The closing of his eyes
and his posthumous title being
"Líng"
was a mere coincidence.
When people saw that his eyes closed in response to the title
"Chéng",
they assumed King Chéng's spirit was aware,
then he should have never closed his eyes at all.
Why so?
The crown prince killing him
was a grave evil;
adding the posthumous title
"Líng"
was a minor fault.
If he did not harbor resentment for the grave evil,
but instead held a grudge over the minor fault,
that would not be evidence of having a spirit,
nor proof of showing and informing people.
Now, bad posthumous titles are either
"Líng"
or
"Lì".
Recorded in bamboo and silk texts,
those titled
"Líng"
or
"Lì"
are numerous,
yet when their corpses were before being enshrouded,
not all failed to close their eyes.
Could it be that all the deceased rulers in the world had no grievances,
and only King Chéng hated his title?
Why are there so many titled
"Líng",
yet so few who did not close their eyes?
Bó Yǒu of Zhèng was greedy, stubborn, and full of desires,
Zǐ Xī enjoyed being above others,
and the two men could not get along.
Zǐ Xī attacked Bó Yǒu,
and Bó Yǒu fled into exile.
Sì Dài led the people of the state to attack him,
and Bó Yǒu died.
Nine years later,
the people of Zhèng frightened each other with tales of Bó Yǒu,
saying:
"Bó Yǒu has arrived!"
Then they all ran away,
not knowing where to go.
The following year,
someone dreamed of Bó Yǒu marching in armor,
saying:
"On the Rénzǐ day,
I will kill Dài.
Next year on the Rényín day,
I will also kill Duàn."
When the Rénzǐ day arrived,
Sì Dài died,
and the people grew more fearful.
Later, on the Rényín day,
Gōngsūn Duàn also died,
and the people became even more terrified.
Zǐ Chǎn established his descendant to appease him,
and only then did it stop.
Bó Yǒu appeared in a dream, saying:
"On Rénzǐ,
I will kill Dài;
on Rényín,
I will kill Duàn again."
When the Rénzǐ day came,
Sì Dài died,
and by Rényín,
Gōngsūn Duàn died.
Later, when Zǐ Chǎn went to Jìn,
Zhào Jǐngzǐ asked:
"Can Bó Yǒu still become a ghost?"
Zǐ Chǎn said:
"He can.
When a person is born and begins to transform, it is called the pò;
once the pò is born,
the yáng is called the hún.
If the essence of things used is abundant,
then the hún and pò are strong,
thus there is a refined vitality reaching divine intelligence.
When a common man or woman dies a violent death,
their hún and pò can still possess people to become malevolent specters,
let alone Bó Yǒu,
a descendant of our former lord Mùgōng,
grandson of Zǐ Liáng,
son of Zǐ Ěr,
a minister of our humble state,
who has been in government for three generations.
Although Zhèng is not rich,
or as the saying goes,
'a tiny state',
yet for three generations, they have held the reins of government.
The resources they used were vast,
and the essence they obtained was plentiful.
His clan is also large,
so what he relies on is substantial.
And having died a violent death,
is it not fitting that he can become a ghost?"
Bó Yǒu killed Sì Dài and
Gōngsūn Duàn without missing the dates,
which is proof of his divine accuracy.
Zǐ Chǎn established his descendant and the hauntings ceased,
showing his understanding of the ways of ghosts and spirits.
Knowing their ways,
he knew their reality.
Since there is reality and not emptiness,
he answered without doubt.
Zǐ Chǎn
was a wise man,
who understood things clearly.
If the dead have no consciousness,
how could he kill Dài and Duàn?
If he could not become a ghost,
why did Zǐ Chǎn not doubt it?
It is said:
The one who held a grudge against Bó Yǒu
was Zǐ Xī.
Zǐ Xī attacked him,
Bó Yǒu fled,
then Sì Dài led the men of the state to attack Bó Yǒu.
Gōngsūn Duàn followed Sì Dài,
not delving into the root of the dispute,
so his wrongdoing was minor.
Killing Sì Dài but not avenging Zǐ Xī,
Gōngsūn Duàn's evil was slight,
yet he died along with Dài.
This shows that Bó Yǒu's spirit was ignorant,
as a ghost seeking revenge,
he misjudged the severity of the offenses.
Moreover, Zǐ Chǎn stated:
"Those who die a violent death can become ghosts."
What does 'violent death' mean?
Does it mean Bó Yǒu's fate was not due for death but someone killed him?
Or that Bó Yǒu was innocent and people wronged him?
If it means his fate was not due but he was killed,
there are many who die before their time;
if it means he was innocent and wronged,
those who are wronged are not few either.
If Bó Yǒu, dying violently, could become a ghost,
then Bǐ Gān,
and Wǔ Zǐxū did not become ghosts.
During the Spring and Autumn period,
thirty-six rulers were assassinated.
These rulers, being assassinated,
could be said to have died violently.
Governing a state,
their use of resources was abundant.
Inheriting the throne and holding land,
not just for three generations.
Noble as rulers,
their status was not the same as ministers.
The founding ancestors,
must have been like Mù Gōng,
or Zǐ Liáng.
With the utmost honor as state rulers,
suffering assassination by rebellious ministers,
if their souls became ghosts,
they would certainly be more potent than Bó Yǒu;
avenging and killing enemies,
their vengeance would be fiercer than against Dài
and Duàn. Yet the thirty-six rulers did not become ghosts,
and the thirty-six ministers were not avenged upon.
If because Bó Yǒu was unprincipled,
his spirit was conscious,
then in the world, none were more unprincipled than Jié
and Zhòu. Jié
and Zhòu were executed,
yet their spirits did not become ghosts.
Thus, Zǐ Chǎn's theory
is based on past events;
seeing Bó Yǒu die violently,
he claimed that those who die violently can become ghosts.
If there were those who did not die violently yet became ghosts,
he would say that those who do not die violently can become ghosts.
Zǐ Xī in Zhèng,
how was he different from Bó Yǒu?
How did his death differ from Bó Yǒu's?
Both were killed by the state for being unprincipled,
yet Bó Yǒu could become a ghost,
while Zǐ Xī could not.
The theory of violent death
applies to Bó Yǒu,
but not to Zǐ Xī.
Therefore, the story of Bó Yǒu
and the tale of Dù Bó are similar;
if Dù Bó's case is not valid,
then Bó Yǒu's cannot be affirmed either.
Duke Huán of Qín attacked Jìn,
and encamped at Fǔshì.
The Marquis of Jìn conducted military exercises at Jì to encroach on Dí territory,
established the Lord of Lí and returned.
Reaching Luò,
Wèi Kē defeated the Qín army at Fǔshì,
capturing Dù Huí.
Dù Huí
was a man of great strength from Qín.
Earlier, Wèi Wǔzǐ had a favored concubine who bore no son.
When Wǔzǐ fell ill,
he instructed Kē, saying:
"You must marry off this concubine."
When his condition worsened,
he changed his order, saying:
"You must have her buried with me."
After Wǔzǐ died,
Kē did not bury the concubine alive.
Some questioned him,
but Kē said:
"In severe illness, one becomes confused;
I follow his rational order."
During the battle at Fǔshì,
Wèi Kē saw an old man weaving grass to trip Dù Huí.
Dù Huí stumbled and fell,
thus he was captured.
That night, he dreamed of an old man who said:
"I am the father of the concubine you married off.
You followed your father's rational order,
hence I repay you."
Now, the father of the favored concubine, knowing Wèi Kē's virtue,
manifested in form as a ghost,
weaving grass to aid in battle,
is evidence of a conscious spirit with awareness.
It is said:
If the concubine's father could know of Wèi Kē's virtue,
appear as a ghost to aid his battle,
he must be able to repay those who were good to him in life,
and kill those he hated in life.
In all social interactions,
there must be closeness and distance,
and such relations should be repaid,
just as the woman ought to be thanked.
If he cannot repay those close to him in life,
how can he only repay those he favors after death?
This is not proof of consciousness,
nor evidence of being able to become a ghost.
Zhāng Liáng walking by the Sì River,
an old man gave him a book;
Emperor Guāngwǔ in distress at Héběi,
an old man instructed him—
these are responses to noble fate and auspicious times,
encounters with fortune and joy.
Wèi Kē was fated to capture Dù Huí,
destined to achieve merit in battle,
so the old man's phantom image wove grass by the roadside.
Wáng Jì was buried at the foot of Huáshān,
where Luán River washed against his tomb,
exposing the front of his coffin.
King Wén said:
"Alas!
Our former lord must wish to see his ministers and people once more!
Thus he made the Luán River reveal it."
Thereupon, he had the coffin brought out and displayed in court,
and all the people saw it.
After three days, it was reburied.
King Wén,
being a sage,
understood the truth of events.
Seeing Wáng Jì's coffin exposed,
he knew his spirit wished to see the people,
so he brought it out for them to see.
It is said:
Throughout history, countless emperors and kings have died,
buried underground,
numbering in the thousands and tens of thousands,
yet none desired to reappear to see the people.
Why would Wáng Jì alone be an exception?
Along the banks of the Yellow River and Sì River,
there are numerous burial mounds,
where rushing waters cause collapses,
exposing coffins and outer containers,
too many to count.
Did all of them wish to see the people again?
The Luán River washing against Huáshān's foot
is like the Yellow River
and Sì River's currents eroding the banks.
King Wén saw the coffin exposed,
felt sorrow and regret—
did he truly believe the former lord wished to reappear?
A heart full of familial love and filial piety,
with hopeful intentions,
a sage's compassion,
left no time for reasoned thought;
extrapolating from the living to the dead,
he thus reburied the coffin.
If common belief trusts the sage's words,
then it is said Wáng Jì wished to see the people.
Duke Jǐng of Qí was about to attack Sòng,
and as his army passed by Tài Shān,
he dreamed of two tall men standing with intense anger.
The duke told Yànzǐ about it,
and Yànzǐ said:
"These are the ancestors of Sòng,
Tāng and Yī Yǐn."
The duke suspected they were mountain gods of Tài Shān.
Yànzǐ said:
"If you doubt it,
then I, Yīng, will describe the appearances of Tāng
and Yī Yǐn.
Tāng was fair-skinned and tall,
with a bearded chin,
a sharp upper face and full lower face,
standing erect with a resonant voice."
The duke said:
"Yes!
That's them!"
"Yī Yǐn was dark and short,
with disheveled hair and a beard,
a full upper face and sharp lower face,
stooped with a low voice."
The duke said:
"Yes!
That's them!
What should we do now?"
Yànzǐ said:
"Now, Tāng,
Tài Jiǎ,
Wǔ Dīng,
and Zǔ Yǐ
were illustrious rulers of the world,
and it is unfitting for them to have no descendants.
Now only Sòng remains,
and you attack it,
so Tāng
and Yī Yǐn are angry.
I urge you to disband the army and make peace with Sòng."
The duke did not heed this,
proceeded to attack Sòng,
and his army was indeed defeated.
Now, if Tāng
and Yī Yǐn had awareness,
they would detest Duke Jǐng's attack on Sòng,
hence appearing in a dream in great anger to stop it.
Duke Jǐng did not desist,
and the army indeed met with misfortune.
It is said:
Duke Jǐng also once dreamed of a comet,
though no comet appeared at that time. (
It is said that)
yet he dreamed of it,
but the comet was not real.
Dreaming of Tāng
and Yī Yǐn,
likewise, was not real.
Perhaps it was an omen of Duke Jǐng's military defeat and misfortune.
Yànzǐ believed in the dream,
clearly describing the forms of Tāng
and Yī Yǐn,
and Duke Jǐng followed Yànzǐ's words,
agreeing with them.
When Qín unified the world,
it ended the lineage of Yī Yǐn,
and to this day, Tāng
and Yī Yǐn receive no sacrifices;
why would they not be angry?
Zǐchǎn of Zhèng was on a diplomatic mission to Jìn.
The Marquis of Jìn was ill,
and Hán Xuānzǐ greeted the guest
and spoke privately,
saying:
"Our lord has been bedridden ill
for three months now,
and we have prayed to all the revered mountains and rivers,
but his condition worsens without recovery.
Now he dreams of a yellow bear entering his bedroom door;
what fierce ghost could it be?"
Zǐchǎn replied:
"With your lord's wisdom
and you in high office,
how could there be a fierce ghost?
In the past, Yáo executed Gǔn at Yǔ Shān,
and his spirit became a yellow bear,
entering the abyss of Yǔ,
and he was indeed honored in the Xià sacrifices,
worshipped by the three dynasties.
Jìn being the leader of the alliance,
perhaps it has not been offering sacrifices to him?"
Hánzǐ then offered sacrifices to the Xià ancestors,
and the Marquis of Jìn recovered.
The yellow bear,
being Gǔn's spirit,
entered the bedroom door because the Marquis of Jìn had not sacrificed to him.
When Jìn realized this and sacrificed,
the illness subsided.
Is this not proof that the dead have awareness?
It is said:
That Gǔn was executed at Yǔ Shān
is known to people;
but that his spirit became a yellow bear
and entered the abyss of Yǔ
—how could people know that?
If it were like Gōng Niú'āi of Lǔ transforming into a tiger due to illness,
and being present, it could be verified.
But Gǔn was executed far away at Yǔ Shān,
and people were not with him there,
so how could they know?
Moreover, the text says:
"His spirit became a yellow bear."
This means he was dead.
After death, his soul becoming a yellow bear
is not something people can know.
When people die, they are called ghosts in the world,
and ghosts resemble the forms of living people,
appearing no different from humans;
yet they are not the spirits of the dead,
let alone a bear,
which does not have a human form
and does not resemble humans!
If indeed Gǔn died
and his spirit became a yellow bear,
then when a bear dies,
its spirit might sometimes become human,
and if someone dreams of it,
how can we know it is not the spirit of a dead animal?
To believe the yellow bear is Gǔn's spirit
and also believe that the ghosts seen are the essences of the dead
—this shows that the essences of people and things are uncertain,
and that the yellow bear is Gǔn's spirit is not verifiable.
Moreover, dreams
are images;
when good or ill fortune approaches,
spirits may show images,
and the interpretation of bears and similar creatures
has its own reasons.
Even if Gǔn died
and his spirit truly became a yellow bear,
dreaming of a yellow bear
must it be Gǔn's spirit?
Feudal lords sacrifice to mountains and rivers;
if the Marquis of Jìn dreamed of mountains and rivers,
why not sacrifice to them instead,
or have the mountains and rivers appear themselves?
When people are ill,
many may dream of deceased ancestors standing by their side;
can we then say the deceased ancestors come in form because they seek food?
What people see in dreams
should be interpreted otherwise;
it is not necessarily real.
How to verify this?
If one dreams of a living person,
and the next day asks that person,
they have not met.
Since the person dreamed of has not met one,
then we know Gǔn's yellow bear did not enter the bedroom door.
Not entering,
then Gǔn was not seeking food.
Not seeking food,
then the Marquis of Jìn's illness was not due to neglecting the Xià sacrifices.
Not due to that,
then his recovery
was not due to offering the Xià sacrifices.
Without the reality of such a blessing,
