there is no proof of awareness.
It is like Liú Ān, the King of Huáinán, who died for plotting rebellion,
yet the world spread that he became an immortal and ascended to heaven.
The falsity of this account
even Zǐchǎn, upon hearing it,
could not verify.
Coincidentally, the Marquis of Jìn's illness happened to subside on its own,
and Zǐchǎn encountered the interpretation of the yellow bear,
so he believed it was Gǔn's spirit.
Emperor Gāozǔ thought King Rúyì of Zhào resembled him and wished to establish him as heir,
which angered Empress Lǚ,
who later poisoned King Rúyì to death.
Afterward,
Empress Lǚ went out
and saw a gray dog
that bit her left armpit.
She found it strange and divined,
learning it was King Rúyì's vengeful spirit,
then fell ill from the armpit wound,
which did not heal, and she died.
It seems Rúyì's spirit became a gray dog,
manifesting to avenge his grievance.
It is said:
When warriors in anger
cross blades and fight,
the defeated bear wounds,
fall to the ground and die.
Though they saw the other strike them,
after death their spirits still cannot seek revenge.
When Empress Lǚ Zhì poisoned Rú Yì,
she did not go herself,
but had someone give him the drink.
He did not know it was poison,
and in his resentment, did not know who killed him.
How could he haunt and take revenge on Empress Lǚ?
If the dead have consciousness,
none would hate more than Emperor Gāozǔ.
Emperor Gāozǔ loved Rú Yì,
yet Empress Lǚ killed him.
Emperor Gāozǔ's spirit should be enraged,
like thunder and lightning;
Empress Lǚ's death
should not have lasted a day.
Could it be that Emperor Gāozǔ's essence was inferior to Rú Yì's spirit?
Or that after death he hated Rú Yì
and approved of Empress Lǚ's killing?
When Chancellor Wǔ'ān Hóu Tián Fén and the former Grand General Guàn Fū had a grudge over a cup of wine,
the matter reached the emperor.
Guàn Fū was imprisoned,
and Dòu Yīng tried to save him,
but the situation was unavoidable.
Guàn Fū was convicted,
and Dòu Yīng also died.
Afterward,
Tián Fén fell gravely ill,
shouting:
"Yes, yes!"
When people looked in on him,
they saw Guàn Fū
and Dòu Yīng both sitting by his side.
Tián Fén's illness did not abate,
and he eventually died.
It is said:
Killing is not done by one person alone;
the killer later falls ill,
but does not see his victim.
Yet Tián Fén saw those he killed.
Tián Fén alone was like this
because his heart bore resentment,
and his illness caused delusions.
Perhaps he saw other ghosts,
and those who interpret ghosts,
hearing of his past conflicts with Guàn Fū
and Dòu Yīng,
wishing to establish their names as spirit judges,
saw his madness
and his "Yes, yes!"
then claimed that Guàn Fū
and Dòu Yīng sat by his side.
The Huáiyáng Commandant Yǐn Qí was a cruel and harsh official.
When he died,
his enemies wanted to burn his corpse,
but the corpse disappeared and was taken away for burial.
If he had consciousness,
he knew they were about to burn him;
as a spirit, he could thus disappear.
It is said:
Yǐn Qí's disappearance
was spiritual,
a kind of response.
When three mountains disappeared in the Qín era,
and the nine tripods were lost at the end of the Zhōu dynasty,
if disappearance is taken as spiritual,
then the three mountains
and nine tripods had consciousness.
Perhaps the officials knew the enemies' plot,
secretly took the corpse and fled,
fearing the enemies would blame them,
and claimed it left on its own.
When alive, one can disappear,
as feet can walk.
But now dead,
with blood and veins severed,
feet can no longer move.
How could it disappear?
Wú boiled Wǔ Zǐxū,
Hàn minced Péng Yuè.
Burning and mincing
are both forms of execution;
Zǐxū
and Péng Yuè
were both brave.
Wǔ Zǐxū
and Péng Yuè could not avoid being boiled or minced to disappear,
yet it is said that Yǐn Qí could return for burial.
This is an untrue statement,
an unverified tale.
When the fallen Xīn dynasty reburied Emperor Yuán's consort Fù,
they opened her coffin,
took the jade burial suit and seal,
sent them to Dìngtáo,
and buried her with commoner rites.
When the coffin was opened,
a stench rose to the heavens;
the Luòyáng assistant magistrate approached the coffin,
smelled the stench, and died.
When they also reburied Dìngtáo's King Gōng's consort Dīng,
fire emerged from the burial chamber,
burning to death hundreds of officers and soldiers.
Now, the reburial rites were humble,
and they seized precious items,
causing two resentments,
hence the stench
and the emerging fire,
to harm people.
It is said:
The stench reaching the heavens
was due to many stored foods
rotting and being exposed;
people could not endure the poisonous anger,
but it was not supernatural.
The fire from the burial chamber
was strange,
but not Consort Dīng's spirit.
How to verify this?
How does the resentment from reburial
compare to tomb robbery for wealth?
In years of famine,
those who dig up graves for clothes number in the tens of millions.
If the dead must have consciousness,
people take their clothes,
expose their skeletons,
yet at the time they cannot stop it,
and later cannot seek revenge.
This is still minor,
not worth mentioning.
Qín Shǐhuáng was buried at Líshān;
at the end of the Second Emperor's reign,
bandits under heaven dug up his tomb,
yet no stench emerged,
no fire started,
to kill a single person.
Noble as the Son of Heaven,
he could not become a spirit;
how could Consorts Dīng and Fù, mere women,
cause supernatural events?
Supernatural changes are not uniform,
arising from different places.
To see fire and smell stench
and attribute it to Consorts Dīng
and Fù's spirits
is mistaken.
Duke Líng of Wèi was about to go to Jìn,
and when he reached the banks of the Pú River,
he heard someone playing a new melody at night.
He was delighted by it,
and sent someone to inquire about it.
All his attendants reported hearing nothing.
So he summoned Master Juān and told him,
saying:
"There is someone playing a new melody.
I sent someone to ask my attendants,
and they all reported hearing nothing.
It seems as if it were ghosts or spirits.
Please listen for me and transcribe it."
Master Juān said:
"Yes."
Thereupon, he sat quietly, played the qín, and transcribed it.
The next day, he reported:
"I have obtained it!
However, I am not yet practiced in it.
I request to stay another night to practice it."
Duke Líng said:
"Yes."
So they stayed another night.
The next day, having practiced it,
they then departed for Jìn.
Duke Píng of Jìn hosted them at the Shīyí Terrace.
When the wine was at its height,
Duke Líng rose and said:
"There is a new melody;
I wish to have it performed for you, my lord."
Duke Píng said:
"Excellent."
So he summoned Master Juān,
had him sit beside Master Kuàng,
and he took up the qín and played it.
Before it was finished,
Master Kuàng pressed down and stopped him,
saying:
"This is the music of a doomed state;
it should not be completed."
Duke Píng said:
"From what source does this come?"
Master Kuàng said:
"This is the decadent music composed by Master Yán,
made for Zhòu as licentious tunes.
When King Wǔ punished Zhòu,
he hung him on a white banner,
and Master Yán fled east,
reaching the Pú River where he threw himself in.
Therefore, those who hear this music
must be by the banks of the Pú River.
The one who first hears this music,
his state will be diminished;
it should not be completed."
Duke Píng said:
"What I love is music;
please let him finish it."
Master Juān played it to the end.
Duke Píng said:
"What is this music called?"
Master Kuàng said:
"This is what is called the Qīng Shāng."
The Duke said:
"Is the Qīng Shāng indeed the most sorrowful?"
Master Kuàng said:
"It is not as sorrowful as the Qīng Zhǐ."
The Duke said:
"May I hear the Qīng Zhǐ?"
Master Kuàng said:
"No.
In ancient times, those who could hear the Qīng Zhǐ
were all rulers of virtue and righteousness.
Now, my lord's virtue is shallow,
and not sufficient to hear it."
Duke Píng said:
"What I love is music;
I wish to try and hear it."
Master Kuàng had no choice,
and took up the qín to play it.
At the first playing,
sixteen black cranes came from the south,
perching on the high points of the corridor gates;
at the second playing, they formed rows;
at the third playing,
they stretched their necks and sang,
spread their wings and danced.
The music matched the tones of gōng and shāng,
and the sound reached up to the heavens.
Duke Píng was greatly pleased,
and all who were seated rejoiced.
Duke Píng raised his cup and stood,
toasting Master Kuàng's health,
then returned to his seat and asked:
"Is no music more sorrowful than the Qīng Zhǐ?"
Master Kuàng said:
"It is not as sorrowful as the Qīng Jué."
Duke Píng said:
"May I hear the Qīng Jué?"
Master Kuàng said:
"No.
In the past, the Yellow Emperor assembled ghosts and spirits on top of the Western Great Mountain,
riding an ivory carriage,
with six jiao dragons,
Bìfáng at the reins,
Chīyóu leading the way,
the Wind Earl sweeping ahead,
the Rain Master sprinkling the path,
tigers and wolves in front,
ghosts and spirits behind,
insects and snakes prostrate on the ground,
white clouds covering above,
grandly assembling ghosts and spirits,
and then composed the Qīng Jué.
Now, my lord's virtue is shallow,
and not sufficient to hear it.
If you hear it,
I fear there will be disaster."
Duke Píng said:
"I am old;
what I love is music.
I wish to hear it through."
Master Kuàng had no choice but to play it.
At the first playing,
clouds arose from the northwest;
at the second playing,
a great wind came,
followed by heavy rain,
tearing the curtains,
breaking the sacrificial vessels,
and shattering the corridor tiles.
Those seated scattered and fled.
Duke Píng was terrified,
and crouched in the corridor room.
Jìn state suffered a great drought,
leaving the land barren for three years.
Duke Píng himself then fell ill with a debilitating disease.
What does this mean?
It is said:
This is an omen that either Duke Líng of Wèi's state would be diminished,
or Duke Píng of Jìn would fall ill,
as if his state were about to suffer drought.
Master Kuàng had said:
"The one who first hears this music will have his state diminished."
Both states heard it first.
How do we know the new melody was not played by Master Yán?
It is said: Master Yán threw himself into the Pú River,
his body decayed in the water,
his vital energy dissipated in the mud,
how could he still play the qín?
Qū Yuán drowned himself in the river;
Qū Yuán was skilled in writing,
just as Master Yán was skilled in playing the qín.
If Master Yán could play the qín,
then Qū Yuán should be able to write again.
Yáng Zǐyún lamented Qū Yuán,
why did Qū Yuán not respond?
When Qū Yuán was alive,
there was no writing he did not produce;
the reason he could not respond to Zǐyún
is that in death, he became mud,
his hands decayed,
and useless for writing.
If Qū Yuán's decayed hands were useless for writing,
then Master Yán's decayed fingers were useless for playing the qín.
Confucius was buried facing the Sì River,
and the Sì River flowed backward;
the world said Confucius had divine power to make the Sì River flow backward.
Confucius loved teaching,
just as Master Yán loved playing the qín.
If Master Yán could play the qín in the Pú River,
why could Confucius not teach by the side of the Sì River?
Zhào Jiǎnzǐ fell ill,
and for five days remained unconscious.
The high officials were all alarmed,
so they summoned Biǎn Què.
Biǎn Què entered,
examined the illness,
and came out. Dǒng Ānyú asked Biǎn Què.
Biǎn Què said:
"His pulse is normal,
yet it is strange.
In the past, Duke Mù of Qín once experienced this,
and after seven days he awoke.
On the day he awoke,
he told Gōngsūn Zhī and Zǐyú:
'I was very happy in the emperor's abode.
The reason I stayed so long
was precisely because I was learning something.
The emperor told me:
"The state of Jìn will face great turmoil,
and for five generations it will not be at peace.
After that, it will become hegemonic,
but the hegemon will die before growing old.
The son of the hegemon will cause the men and women of your state to have no distinctions."'
Gōngsūn Zhī wrote this down and stored it,
and the Qín strategies thus emerged.
The chaos under Duke Xiàn of Jìn,
the hegemony of Duke Wén,
and Duke Xiāng's defeat of the Qín army at Xiáo and subsequent indulgence in debauchery
are what this refers to.
Now your lord's illness is the same,
within three days he will surely recover from the illness,
and upon recovery he will certainly speak."
After two and a half days,
Jiǎnzǐ awoke,
and told the high officials:
"I was very happy in the emperor's abode,
traveling with numerous spirits in the heavens of equal height,
where grand music was played nine times and myriad dances performed,
unlike the music of the three dynasties,
its sound stirring the human heart.
A bear tried to seize me,
but the emperor ordered me to shoot it,
I hit the bear,
and the bear died.
A brown bear came,
I shot it again,
hit the brown bear,
and the brown bear died.
The emperor was very pleased,
and bestowed upon me two bamboo cases,
both with duplicates.
I saw a child at the emperor's side.
The emperor entrusted me with a Dí dog,
saying:
'When your son grows up, give it to him.'
The emperor told me:
'The state of Jìn will decline,
and in seven generations it will perish.
The Yíng clan will greatly defeat the Zhōu people west of Fànkuí,
but they too will not be able to possess it.
Now I recall the merits of Yú Shùn,
so I will bestow his descendant daughter Mèng Yáo to your seventh-generation descendant.'"
Dǒng Ānyú received these words,
wrote them down, and stored them.
He reported Biǎn Què's words to Jiǎnzǐ.
Jiǎnzǐ rewarded Biǎn Què with forty thousand mǔ of land.
Another day,
when Jiǎnzǐ went out,
someone blocked the road,
and would not move aside when ordered.
The attendants were about to arrest him.
The person blocking the road said:
"I wish to have an audience with the lord."
The attendants reported this.
Jiǎnzǐ summoned him,
and said:
"Ah,
I seemed to have seen you clearly before."
The person blocking the road said:
"Dismiss your attendants,
I wish to have an audience."
Jiǎnzǐ dismissed the people.
The person blocking the road said:
"On the day of your lordship's illness,
I was at the emperor's side."
Jiǎnzǐ said:
"Yes,
that happened.
What did you see me doing?"
The person blocking the road said:
"The emperor ordered your lordship to shoot a bear and a brown bear,
and both died."
Jiǎnzǐ said:
"That is so,
but what does it mean?"
The person blocking the road said:
"The state of Jìn will face great calamity,
and your lordship will lead it.
The emperor orders your lordship to destroy two ministers,
for the bear and brown bear
are their ancestors."
Jiǎnzǐ said:
"The emperor bestowed upon me two bamboo cases, both with duplicates,
what does that mean?"
The person blocking the road said:
"Your lordship's son will conquer two states among the Dí,
both of your own clan."
Jiǎnzǐ said:
"I saw a child at the emperor's side,
the emperor entrusted me with a Dí dog,
saying
'when your son grows up, give it to him'.
Why would a child be given a Dí dog?"
The person blocking the road said:
"The child
is your lordship's son,
the Dí dog
represents the ancestors of Dài.
Your lordship's son will certainly possess Dài.
And among your lordship's descendants,
there will be one who reforms the government and adopts Hú clothing,
annexing two states among the Dí."
Jiǎnzǐ asked his name and offered him an official position.
The person blocking the road said:
"I
am a rustic man,
merely conveying the emperor's command."
Then he disappeared.
What does this mean?
The explanation is:
These are all portents.
The interpretations all match what the person blocking the road said about the events before the emperor.
The person blocking the road seen
was a spectral figure.
Later, the two Jìn ministers, the Fàn clan
and the Zhōngháng clan, rebelled,
Jiǎnzǐ attacked them,
Zhōngháng Zhāozǐ
and Fàn Wénzǐ were defeated,
and fled to Qí.
Initially,
Jiǎnzǐ had Gūbù Zǐqīng physiognomize his sons,
but none were deemed auspicious.
When it came to the son of the Dí woman, Wúxù,
he was considered noble.
Jiǎnzǐ spoke with him
and found him worthy.
Jiǎnzǐ summoned his sons and said:
"I have hidden a treasure tally on Chángshān mountain,
the first to find it will be rewarded."
All the sons went up the mountain,
but found nothing.
Wúxù returned,
and said:
"I have found the tally!"
Jiǎnzǐ asked him about it.
Wúxù said:
"From Chángshān, one can look down upon Dài,
and Dài can be taken."
Jiǎnzǐ considered him worthy,
so he deposed the crown prince and established him instead.
After Jiǎnzǐ died,
Wúxù succeeded him,
becoming known as Xiāngzǐ.
Once Xiāngzǐ was established,
he tricked and killed the king of Dài and annexed his territory.
He also annexed the lands of the Zhì clan.
Later, he took the territory of the Kōngtóng Róng.
After Jiǎnzǐ,
seven generations later to King Wǔlíng,
Wú Guǎng presented his daughter Wá Yíng (
zǐ) Mèng Yáo.
Afterwards,
King Wǔlíng then took Zhōngshān,
and annexed Hú territories.
In the nineteenth year of King Wǔlíng's reign,
he changed to Hú clothing,
and the people of the state adopted it.
All happened as foretold,
without exception.
Thus, omens and portents appear in signs,
clearly,
though they are not actual events.
The progression of fortune and misfortune
is as if heaven announces it.
How do we know Heaven did not truly inform him?
Because the man blocking the path was at the Emperor's side.
Now, those at the Celestial Emperor's side
are all noble spirits;
conveying the Emperor's commands,
they are envoys of Heaven.
The envoys of a human ruler
have chariots and cavalry fully equipped,
but the envoys of the Celestial Emperor
stand alone blocking the path—
this is not their proper form.
The celestial officials number one hundred twenty,
no different from the kings on Earth.
The kings on Earth
have complete staffs of officials,
modeling themselves after the celestial officials,
adopting their systems and regulations.
Since the officials of Heaven and Earth are alike,
their envoys should also be equal.
If the officials are alike but the people differ,
it cannot be so.
How do we know the Emperor Jiǎnzǐ saw was not the true Emperor?
We know by interpreting dreams.
Towers, terraces, mountains, and hills
are symbols of official positions;
when people dream of ascending towers and terraces,
climbing mountains and hills,
they often gain official positions.
If real towers, terraces, mountains, and hills are not official positions themselves,
then we know the Emperor Jiǎnzǐ dreamed of was not the Celestial Emperor.
When a minister dreams of his ruler,
the ruler certainly does not appear,
and certainly does not bestow gifts.
Interpreting by the dreams of ministers,
we know the Emperor bestowing two bamboo boxes
and a Zhái dog
was not the Celestial Emperor.
If it was not the Celestial Emperor,
then his words about roaming the uniform heavens with hundreds of ghosts
were not about Heaven.
When Lǔ's Shūsūn Mùzǐ dreamed of Heaven pressing down on him,
if it were truly so,
it would mean Heaven reached the Earth.
If it did not reach the Earth,
then there would be the resistance of towers and terraces,
preventing it from reaching him.
If it reached him,
then the towers and terraces should have been destroyed.
Since the towers and terraces were not destroyed,
it means Heaven did not reach the Earth.
Not reaching the Earth,
it could not press down on him.
Since it could not press down on him,
then what pressed down on him
was not Heaven,
but an image of Heaven.
The Heaven that pressed down on Shūsūn Mùzǐ in his dream was not real Heaven,
so we know the Heaven that Zhào Jiǎnzǐ roamed was not real Heaven either.
Some say:
"People also have direct dreams.
If one dreams of Jiǎ,
the next day one sees Jiǎ;
if one dreams of the ruler,
the next day one sees the ruler."
I say: True.
People have direct dreams,
but direct dreams are all images,
and these images are direct.
How to clarify this?
In a direct dream,
one dreams of Jiǎ,
dreams of the ruler,
and the next day sees Jiǎ and the ruler—
this is direct.
But if one questions Jiǎ and the ruler,
Jiǎ and the ruler do not appear.
Since Jiǎ and the ruler do not appear,
the Jiǎ and ruler seen in the dream
are images resembling them.
If it is merely images resembling Jiǎ and the ruler,
then we know the Emperor Jiǎnzǐ saw
was an image resembling the Emperor.
Moreover, in people's dreams,
interpreters say it is the soul traveling.
Dreaming of the Emperor
means the soul ascends to Heaven.
Ascending to Heaven is like climbing a mountain.
When dreaming of climbing a mountain,
feet tread the slopes,
hands pull on trees,
and only then can one ascend.
But ascending to Heaven has nothing to cling to;
how can one reach it?
Heaven's distance from people
is counted in tens of thousands of lǐ.
A person traveling
covers one hundred lǐ a day;
even with the soul and body together,
they still cannot go fast,
let alone the soul traveling alone—
how could it be swift?
If the soul's travel were equal to the body's,
then Jiǎnzǐ's ascent and descent to Heaven
should have taken several years to realize.
Yet he awoke in just seven days—
how could it be so fast?
Now, the soul
is essential energy,
and the movement of essential energy is like clouds and smoke;
indeed, clouds and smoke cannot move fast.
Suppose the soul travels like flying birds?
It still cannot move fast.
When people dream of flying,
they use the soul to fly,
but their flight cannot be faster than birds.
Among the energies of Heaven and Earth,
the swiftest
is the whirlwind.
When a whirlwind arises,
it cannot last a full day.
Suppose the soul travels like a whirlwind?
Then its speed would not exceed a day's journey,
and it still could not reach Heaven.
When people dream of ascending to Heaven,
it is in a single sleep's moment;
upon awakening,
some may still be in Heaven,
not yet fully descended.
If one dreams of traveling to Luòyáng,
upon awakening, one realizes it from Luòyáng.
How swift the soul's flight is!
Such speed must not be its true state;
if not its true state, then the ascent to Heaven is not a real event,
and if not a real event, it is an omen.
The man blocking the path,
when Jiǎnzǐ was ill,
appeared at the Emperor's side;
later, he saw a figure resembling a man blocking the path and speaking,
no different from when he saw him at the Emperor's side.
From this we can say,
dreams in sleep are yin manifestations,
while waking interpretations are yang divinations—
this is clear.
After Zhào Xiāngzǐ was established,
Zhì Bó grew even more arrogant,
demanding land from Hán
and Wèi, and Hán
and Wèi gave it;
when he demanded land from Zhào,
Zhào refused.
Zhì Bó grew even angrier,
then led Hán
and Wèi to attack Zhào Xiāngzǐ.
Xiāngzǐ, afraid,
fled to defend Jìnyáng.
Yuán Guò followed,
lagging behind, and reached Wángzé,
where he saw three people,
visible from the waist up,
but not from the waist down.
They gave Yuán Guò two sections of bamboo,
with no openings.
They said:
"For us, take these and give them to Zhào Wúxù."
After arriving,
he reported this to Xiāngzǐ.
Xiāngzǐ fasted for three days,
then personally split the bamboo,
finding a red writing that said:
"Zhào Wúxù,
I am the celestial envoy of Huòdàshān Shānyáng Hóu.
On the third month, Bǐngxū day,
I will have you turn and destroy the Zhì clan,
and you shall also sacrifice to me in a hundred towns,
and I will grant you the land of Línhú."
Xiāngzǐ bowed twice,
accepting the command of the three spirits.
What does this mean?
It was said:
This was an omen foretelling Xiāngzǐ's imminent victory.
When the three states attacked Jìnyáng for over a year,
they channeled the Fén River to flood the city,
leaving only three planks' height unsubmerged.
Xiāngzǐ, in fear,
sent his minister Zhāng Mèngtán to secretly negotiate with Hán and
Wèi, whereupon Hán and
Wèi joined in the conspiracy.
Ultimately, on the day Bǐngxū in the third month,
they turned around and annihilated the Zhì clan,
dividing its territory among themselves.
It seems that ominous signs take human form,
claiming to be the deity of Huòshān Mountain,
just as the portent in the Xià court resembled a dragon,
claiming to be the two lords of Bāo;
the auspicious sign for Zhào Jiǎnzǐ appeared human,
claiming to be an envoy of the Emperor.
How do we know it was not the deity of Huòshān Mountain?
It is said:
A great mountain is the body of the earth,
much like humans have bones and joints—
how could bones and joints possess divinity?
If a great mountain had a deity,
it should resemble the mountain's form.
Why so?
What people call ghosts are
the essences of the deceased,
and their appearance is like that of living humans.
Now, a great mountain's vastness and length differ from humans,
yet its spiritual essence is no different from that of humans.
Being no different from humans,
then ghosts are akin to humans.
Ghosts being akin to humans
means they are manifestations of ominous energy.
In the thirty-sixth year of Qín Shǐhuáng,
Mars remained in the Heart constellation,
and a star fell,
reaching the ground as a stone.
Some among the people inscribed on the stone,
saying:
"Upon the First Emperor's death, the land will be divided."
The First Emperor heard of this,
ordered his censors to investigate and interrogate,
but none confessed.
He then had all the families near the stone executed
and burned the stone.
In autumn, an envoy passing Huàyīn Píngshū at night from Guāndōng
was met by someone holding a jade disc who stopped him, saying:
"Deliver this for me to the Lord of Hàochí."
And then added:
"This year, the Ancestral Dragon will die."
When the envoy questioned him,
he suddenly vanished,
leaving the jade disc behind.
The envoy presented the disc and reported everything.
The First Emperor remained silent for a long while,
then said:
"Mountain spirits only know events of the coming year."
He then stated:
"The 'Ancestral Dragon'
refers to the ancestor of humans."
He had the imperial treasury examine the disc,
and it turned out to be the one sunk in the river during his tour in the twenty-eighth year.
In the clear thirty-seventh year,
he dreamed of battling the sea god,
who had a human form.
What does this signify?
It is said:
These were all omens of the First Emperor's impending death.
The First Emperor dreamed of fighting the sea god,
and in anger, he went to sea,
awaiting the god to shoot a giant fish.
From Lángyá to Láo and
Chéngshān, he saw nothing.
Upon reaching Zhīfú Mountain,
he finally saw a huge fish,
shot and killed one,
then traveled along the coast west to Píngyuán Jīn, where he fell ill,
and died at Shāqiū.
When the star fell,
Mars caused the anomaly,
so the families near the stone inscribed it,
as if someone made them do it,
with the text reading
"The First Emperor will die,"
perhaps guided by others.
This is like worldly children's rhymes,
not created by the children themselves,
but led by an energy.
In general, when anomalies occur,
they may appear as ghosts in human form,
or humans may act as if guided by ghosts,
but in essence, they are the same.
When Prince Chóng'ěr of Jìn lost his state,
he ran out of food on the road
and begged a farmer for a meal.
The farmer offered him a clod of earth,
and the prince grew angry.
Jiù Fán said:
"This is auspicious,
a gift of land from heaven."
Later, the prince regained his state and territory,
just as Jiù Fán had said.
When Tián Dān of Qí defended the city of Jímò,
he wanted to deceive the Yān army,
saying:
"A heavenly god has descended to aid us."
A man came forward and said:
"Can I act as the god?"
Tián Dān stepped back, bowed twice, and served him,
eventually spreading word of the god's descent to the Yān army.
The Yān army believed a god was present,
and when they saw an ox with five-colored patterns,
they grew fearful,
leading to their defeat and retreat.
Tián Dān ultimately triumphed,
recovering the invaded land.
This is an example of a human imitating a ghostly omen.
When the envoy passed Huàyīn,
a person holding a jade disc blocked the way,
left the disc, and departed—
a ghostly omen in human form.
Now, sinking the jade disc in the river
was to seek blessings.
Its return
signified rejection of the offering,
meaning blessings could not be obtained.
The disc resembled the one previously sunk,
but it was not the real one.
How can we prove this?
Because the ghost appeared in human form,
it was not an actual person.
If someone sees a ghost that looks like a living person,
they would surely inquire about that person,
but if they do not meet them,
it is the ominous energy mimicking a human.
If the ominous energy takes human form,
then what it carries
cannot be genuine.
"The Ancestral Dragon will die"
referred to the First Emperor.
Ancestor symbolizes the origin of humans,
and dragon represents the symbol of a ruler.
Humans and objects have their categories,
so the prediction of disaster follows accordingly.
In the year of Qín Shǐhuáng's death, Hàn Gāohuángdì,
as a station chief in Sìshàng,
was escorting convicts to Líshān.
Many convicts escaped along the way,
so he released all those he was leading
and did not return.
Under the influence of alcohol,
he passed through a marsh at night
and ordered one man to go ahead.
The man returned and reported:
"There is a large snake blocking the path ahead;
we should turn back."
Gāozǔ, drunk,
said:
"A brave man travels—
what is there to fear!"
He then went forward,
drew his sword, struck, and cut the snake,
which split into two,
clearing the path.
After walking several miles,
drunk, he lay down to sleep.
Later, when Gāozǔ's followers reached the snake's location,
they found an old woman weeping over it at night.
They asked:
"Old woman, why are you crying?"
The woman said:
"Someone killed my son."
They asked:
"Why was your son killed?"
She replied:
"My son
was the son of the White Emperor,
transformed into a snake,
blocking the path.
Now,
the son of the Red Emperor slew him,
hence I weep."
The people thought her words were ominous,
and intended to whip her.
But she suddenly vanished.
What does this signify?
It is said:
This was the auspicious omen of Gāozǔ's initial rise to power.
How can this be proven?
By the old woman suddenly disappearing.
Her disappearance,
indicates she was not human,
and not being human means she was a ghost or apparition.
Since the old woman was not human,
then we know the snake that was beheaded was not a real snake.
It is said to be the son of the White Emperor,
but why would the son of the White Emperor appear as a snake blocking the path at night?
Calling the snake
the son of the White Emperor,
and Gāozǔ
the son of the Red Emperor,
with the White Emperor's son as a snake,
and the Red Emperor's son as a human—
the Five Emperors are all heavenly deities,
yet their sons either become snakes
or humans.
Humans and snakes are different beings,
yet they share the divine status of emperors—
this is not the way of Heaven.
Moreover, if the snake is the son of the White Emperor,
then is the old woman the consort of the White Emperor?
As the consort of an emperor,
she should have a full entourage;
as the son of an emperor,
his officials should be numerous.
Yet here, a single snake dies on the path,
an old woman weeps by the road,
claiming to be the son of the White Emperor—
this is not real,
it is clear.
What is not real is a semblance,
a semblance is an apparition,
and an apparition means what is seen is not the actual thing,
but rather an emanation of energy.
The snake that Gāozǔ killed was not a real snake,
just as when Duke Lì of Zhèng was about to enter Zhèng,
the battle between the snake inside the city and the one outside was not between real snakes;
as Duke Lì was entering Zhèng,
an apparition took the form of snakes fighting.
The battling snakes in Zhèng were not real snakes,
then we know the two dragons in the Xià court were dragon semblances;
being dragon semblances,
we understand that during Zǐchǎn's time in Zhèng, the fighting dragons were not real dragons.
The way of Heaven is hard to know;
if it is not real,
it is an apparition;
if it is real,
it is also an apparition.
Liú Hóu Zhāng Liáng attempted to assassinate Qín Shǐhuáng with an iron hammer,
but mistakenly hit the attendant's carriage.
The emperor was furious,
and ordered a search for Zhāng Liáng.
Zhāng Liáng changed his name
and fled into hiding in Xiàpī.
Once, while leisurely strolling on the bridge in Xiàpī,
an old man
dressed in coarse cloth
approached Liáng,
deliberately dropped his shoe under the bridge,
and turning to Zhāng Liáng, said:
"Young man, fetch my shoe!"
Liáng was taken aback,
and wanted to hit him,
but considering his age,
he forced himself to endure,
went down to get the shoe,
and knelt to present it.
The old man extended his foot to receive the shoe,
then left laughing.
Liáng was greatly astonished.
After the old man had gone about a li,
he returned,
saying:
"You are worth teaching, young man.
In five days at dawn,
meet me here."
Liáng found it strange,
but knelt and said:
"Yes."
Five days later at dawn,
Liáng went.
The old man was already there,
and angrily said:
"Meeting an elder,
and arriving late—why?"
Then he left,
saying, "Meet earlier in five days."
After five days,
Liáng went at cockcrow.
The old man was again already there,
and angrily said:
"Late again,
why?"
He left,
saying, "Come earlier again in five days."
After five days,
Liáng went before midnight.
After a short while,
the old man came,
and happily said:
"This is how it should be!"
He produced a book,
saying:
"Study this, and you will be the teacher of an emperor.
In ten years, you will rise.
Thirteen years from now,
young man, you will see me—
the yellow stone at the foot of Gǔchéng Mountain in Jǐběi is me."
Then he left,
with no further words,
and was never seen again.
The next day, Liáng looked at the book—
it was "The Art of War by Tàigōng."
Liáng thus regarded it as extraordinary,
and often studied and read it.
What does this signify?
It is said:
This was the auspicious omen of Gāozǔ's rise
and Zhāng Liáng's assistance.
Liáng lived in Xiàpī,
championing justice.
Ten years later, when Chén Shè and others rebelled,
Peì Gōng captured territory including Xiàpī,
Liáng joined him,
eventually becoming a strategist and general,
and was enfeoffed as Liú Hóu.
Thirteen years later, while passing through Jǐběi with Gāozǔ,
he indeed found the yellow stone at the foot of Gǔchéng Mountain,
took it, and cherished it as a sacred object.
When Liú Hóu died,
the yellow stone was buried with him.
Truly, the signs of fortune and misfortune
are divine;
the transformations of heaven and earth
are subtle.
For the old man to resemble the yellow stone,
and the yellow stone to resemble the old man—
how mystical indeed!
It is asked:
"Was the yellow stone truly the old man,
or was the old man truly the yellow stone?"
The answer: The yellow stone could not become the old man,
nor could the old man become the yellow stone.
The energy of omens and apparitions
manifests and thus verifies.
How can this be proven?
During the time of Duke Píng of Jìn,
a stone spoke in Wèiyú.
"Why did the stone speak?"
He replied:
"The stone itself cannot speak;
something must have borrowed it.
Otherwise,
it was the people hearing erroneously."
If a stone cannot speak like a human,
then it cannot take human form either.
The stone's speech
is no different from the stone that fell in Dōngjùn during Qín Shǐhuáng's time,
which the people inscribed—
there is no difference.
Inscribing creates writing,
speaking produces words;
words and writing
are of the same essence.
People inscribe writing,
energy emits speech;
people and energy
share the same nature.
Since a stone cannot inscribe itself,
it also cannot speak;
if it cannot speak,
then it cannot become human either.
The "Art of War by Tàigōng",
is a manifestation of energy.
How do we know it is not genuine?
Because the old man was not human,
we know the book is not Tàigōng's book either.
Energy can take the form of a human,
then it can also imitate Tàigōng's book.
Someone asks:
"Energy has no knife or brush,
how can it produce writing?"
The answer is: Zhòngzǐ, the wife of Duke Huì of Lǔ,
was born with writing on her palm,
saying
"Be the Lady of Lǔ".
Táng Shū Yú of Jìn had writing on his hand,
saying
"Yú".
Chéng Jì Yǒu of Lǔ had writing on his hand,
saying
"Yǒu".
These three instances of writing,
were natural to their nature;
the old man's book,
was spontaneously formed by energy.
Natural to nature,
spontaneously formed by energy,
is no different from
children's rhymes spoken by themselves.
When children chant rhymes,
they don't know where they receive them,
their mouths speak them spontaneously.
The mouth speaks by itself,
writing forms by itself,
perhaps something causes it.
Reasoning from this, we can understand that when Tàigōng fished and caught a huge fish,
cut it open and found a book,
saying
"Lǚ Shàng will be enfeoffed in Qí",
and when King Wǔ obtained a white fish,
with writing below its throat saying
"To give to Fā",
these are probably not false.
Therefore, restoring the original meaning of the "Hétú"
and "Luòshū", which speak of rise and fall, survival and demise,
and the encounters of emperors and kings,
it is clear that such writings truly exist.
They are all omens of energy,
portents of good and bad fortune.
Generally, the ghosts in the world,
are not formed by the spirits of the dead,
but are all caused by people's thoughts and imaginings.
How does this come about?
It arises from illness.
When people are sick, they worry and fear,
and when they worry and fear, ghosts appear.
Generally, if people are not sick, they do not fear.
So when they fall ill and lie in bed,
they fear that ghosts will come.
Fear leads to imagination,
and imagination causes their eyes to see illusions.
How can this be proven?
The "Zhuàn" says:
"Bólè learned to judge horses,
and everything he observed and studied,
was nothing but horses.
The cook of Sòng learned to butcher oxen,
and for three years, he saw no live oxen,
all he saw were dead oxen."
Both of them focused their essence to the utmost,
through thought and imagination,
they naturally saw different things.
When sick people see ghosts,
it is like Bólè seeing horses,
or the cook seeing oxen.
What Bólè
and the cook saw were not real horses or oxen,
then we also know that what the sick see are not real ghosts.
When the sick are severely afflicted and in pain,
they say ghosts are holding whips and sticks beating them,
or they see ghosts holding hammers, chains, and ropes standing guard beside them,
due to illness, pain, and fear,
they delusionally see these things.
At the onset of illness, fear and shock
make them see ghosts coming;
when critically ill and fearing death,
they see ghosts angry;
suffering from physical pain,
they see ghosts attacking them;
all are products of imagination and illusion,
not necessarily real.
Intense thoughts and imaginings
may manifest through the eyes,
or through the mouth,
or through the ears.
Manifested through the eyes,
the eyes see their forms;
manifested through the ears,
the ears hear their sounds;
manifested through the mouth,
the mouth speaks of these matters.
During the day, ghosts appear;
at night while lying down, one hears them in dreams.
Lying alone in an empty room,
if one feels fearful,
then dreams of someone pressing on their body.
Seeing while awake and hearing while asleep,
both use the spirit;
fear
and imagination,
are of the same reality.
One theory says:
When people see ghosts,
it is because their vision is confused as in sleep.
During the day, people
are weary and their essence exhausted,
at night they wish to sleep,
and when sleeping, vision turns inward,
and in that state, the spirit sees images of people and things.
When sick, people are also weary and essence exhausted,
even if their eyes are not closed in sleep,
their vision is already as confused as in sleep,
so they also see images of people and things.
What the sick see,
whether as if asleep or not,
is similar to dreams.
When they see these things,
they themselves cannot tell if awake or dreaming,
so when they see things, they cannot distinguish ghost from human,
this is the effect of exhausted essence and weariness.
How can this be verified?
By the mad who see ghosts.
The insane and foolish talk to themselves,
not interacting with normal people,
because illness afflicts them and their essence is disordered.
When people are critically ill and near death,
they are similar to the insane.
Sleeping, sick, and insane,
all three have declined essence and are weary,
with vision turned inward,
so they all uniquely see images of people and things.
Another theory says:
Ghosts are
the pathogenic energy that people
see when ill.
When unbalanced energy affects people,
that which affects people becomes ghosts,
this energy takes human form and appears.
So those severely ill have abundant energy,
abundant energy then brings human-like forms,
and when they come, the sick see their images.
For instance, if one falls ill in the mountains and forests,
the ghosts seen are the spirits of the mountains and forests.
If someone falls ill in Yuè territory,
they see Yuè people sitting beside them in their illness.
From this perspective,
figures like Guàn Fū
and Dòu Yīng,
might sometimes be images formed by such energy.
Generally, in the world,
all energy is governed by heaven,
heavenly phenomena manifest above,
and their energy descends to create things.
Harmonious energy nurtures life,
while discordant energy harms.
Since it originally has images in heaven,
when it descends,
it takes form on earth.
Therefore, the appearance of ghosts
is caused by energy taking form.
The forms of the constellations,
are humans, birds, and beasts,
so when they afflict people, they see the forms of humans, birds, and beasts.
One theory states:
Ghosts are
the essence of aged things.
When things grow old,
their essence takes human form;
there are also those not yet old,
whose inherent nature enables transformation,
assuming human likeness.
When humans receive vital energy,
if they share essence with certain things,
then those things interact with them.
When illness strikes,
as vital energy declines and weakens,
these entities come to invade and assault.
How can this be verified?
Documented cases:
Common people who interact with such entities
witness ghosts approaching.
The ghosts seen by the sick
are no different from those ailing entities.
When people fall ill and see ghosts coming,
resembling deceased from their tombs coming to summon them,
these are actually domestic animals from their households.
As for seeing other ghosts,
unfamiliar ones,
they are manifestations from others' homes or wilderness creatures.
Another theory:
Ghosts
originally originate from humans.
When failing to mature into proper humans,
they transform and depart.
Heaven and earth's nature
inherently contains such transformations,
beyond the debates of Daoist practitioners.
Those who encounter humans cause illness;
when the sick are destined to die,
the deceased remain connected to the living.
How to demonstrate this?
The Book of Rites states:
"Zhuānxū had three sons,
who fled after birth to become plague ghosts:
one dwells in the Jiāng River,
known as the cruel ghost;
one resides in the Ruò River,
called the wǎngliǎng ghost;
one inhabits human houses, corners, and damp storerooms,
fond of frightening young children."
Before Zhuānxū's era,
children born must have been numerous,
thus Zhuānxū's ghosts and spirits would number in hundreds.
Various ghosts and spirits possess form and method,
able to stand among trees and appear to people—
all originate from good people,
acquiring good people's energy,
thus able to resemble good people's forms,
and capable of harming good people.
Those floating yin-yang categories,
like cloud and mist energies,
cannot accomplish this.
Another theory:
Ghosts are
the spirits of Jiǎyǐ.
Jiǎyǐ represents
heaven's distinct energy,
its form resembling humans.
When people fall ill and approach death,
the Jiǎyǐ spirits arrive.
If illness occurs on a Jiǎyǐ day,
death will witness Gēngxīn spirits.
Why?
Jiǎyǐ ghosts
are countered by Gēngxīn against Jiǎyǐ,
so when patients near death,
the killing ghosts that arrive
are Gēngxīn spirits.
How to verify this?
Those falling ill on Jiǎyǐ days
have their life-or-death moment
often on Gēngxīn days.
This isn't what theorists consider factual.
The way of heaven is hard to know,
ghosts and spirits are obscure,
thus all are recorded here
for the world to examine.
Another theory:
Ghosts are
entities,
no different from humans.
Between heaven and earth,
there exist ghostly entities
constantly dwelling beyond the four borders,
sometimes coming to the Central States,
mixing among humans,
belonging to malignant categories,
thus only seen when people fall ill and approach death.
Heaven and earth produce creatures:
some human-like, some bird-like or beast-like;
when generating malignant entities,
some resemble humans, some imitate birds and beasts.
Thus in households facing misfortune,
some see flying corpses,
some see running horrors,
some see human forms—
all three are ghosts.
Some call them ghosts,
some call them horrors,
some call them mèi,
some call them chī,
all living real existences,
not illusory imitations.
How to demonstrate this?
Documented cases:
Common households facing misfortune
see flowing lights gathering in their rooms,
or see forms resembling birds,
sometimes flowing into halls—
observation shows they're not merely bird-like or beast-like.
Entities with form can eat,
able to eat thus excrete.
Excretion provides evidence,
thus physical forms have substance.
The Zuǒ's Spring and Autumn Annals states:
"Cast them to the four wildernesses
to ward off chīmèi."
The Classic of Mountains and Seas says:
"There is a ghost country in the north."
Those describing chī call them dragon-like entities,
and mèi connect with dragons,
thus mèi belong to dragon categories.
It also says
"country"
indicates communities of people and creatures.
The Classic of Mountains and Seas further states:
"Within the vast ocean,
stands Dùshuò Mountain,
where grows a giant peach tree,
its coiled span three thousand lǐ,
its northeastern branches called Ghost Gate,
where myriad ghosts come and go.
Above reside two divine beings,
one named Shēnshū,
one named Yùlǜ,
tasked with inspecting and leading myriad ghosts.
Malicious harmful ghosts
they bind with reed ropes
and feed to tigers.
Thereupon the Yellow Emperor established rituals to periodically drive them away,
erecting large peachwood figures,
painting Shēnshū
and Yùlǜ with tigers on gates,
hanging reed ropes for protection."
Malignant mèi possess form,
thus can be captured and fed to tigers.
Consider: edible things
cannot be insubstantial.
These entities
differ in nature from humans,
appearing and disappearing intermittently,
no different from dragons' rare appearances.
First, it is said:
When a person is about to encounter good or ill fortune,
omens appear beforehand.
When a person is about to die,
they see various strange phenomena,
and ghosts are among these phenomena.
Thus, when strange phenomena manifest,
they take the form of a human,
or mimic human voices as a response,
so the manifestations of strange phenomena never depart from human form.
Between heaven and earth,
strange phenomena are not uniform;
there are strange phenomena in speech,
in sounds,
and in writing.
Sometimes strange energies take the form of a human,
other times, humans harbor energies that become strange phenomena.
Those that take human form
are all the ghosts people see;
those where humans harbor energies to become strange phenomena
are the likes of shamans.
Therefore, the words of shamans
have no basis or evidence;
their pronouncements of good or ill fortune come solely from their mouths,
like children's rhymes.
Children's rhymes are spoken spontaneously,
and shamanic words emerge from their own thoughts.
Spoken from the mouth,
emerging from the mind,
then their human nature,
along with the spontaneous arising of sounds and energies,
and the spontaneous emission of voices,
are of the same essence.
It is said that during the time of Zhòu,
ghosts cried in the night suburbs,
and when Cāngjié created writing,
ghosts cried at night.
If energy can mimic human voices to cry,
then it can also mimic human form to appear,
and thus people regard them as ghosts.
The appearance of ghosts
is a strange phenomenon in humans.
Between heaven and earth,
the arrival of calamity or blessing
all has signs and manifestations;
they develop gradually, not suddenly,
and have forms, not appearing abruptly.
According to the way of heaven and earth,
when a person is about to perish,
ill omens also emerge;
when a state is about to fall,
strange phenomena also appear.
Just as when a person is about to be fortunate,
auspicious signs arrive;
when a state is about to prosper,
prosperous omens come.
Thus, auspicious responses and strange omens
are essentially the same.
Yet the world alone claims that ghosts are not among the strange omens,
saying ghosts are like spirits capable of harming people,
not understanding the principle of strange omens,
and not seeing the changes in the energy of things.
When a state is about to fall,
strange phenomena appear,
but its fall is not due to the strange phenomena.
When a person is about to die,
ghosts come,
but their death is not due to the ghosts.
What destroys a state
is warfare;
what kills a person
is illness.
How can this be clarified?
When Duke Xiāng of Qí was about to be killed by assassins,
he traveled to Gūfén,
then hunted at Bèiqiū,
where he saw a large boar.
His attendant said:
"It is Prince Péngshēng."
The duke angrily said:
"How dare Péngshēng appear!"
He drew his bow and shot at it,
and the boar stood like a man and cried.
The duke was terrified,
fell from his chariot,
injured his foot,
lost his shoe,
and was then killed by the assassins.
Now, what killed Duke Xiāng
were the assassins.
The prior sighting of the large boar on the road
was the omen of Duke Xiāng's impending death.
People called it Péngshēng
because it resembled Péngshēng's form.
The world knows that what killed Duke Xiāng was not the boar,
yet alone claims that ghosts can kill people—
this is one confusion.
The energy between heaven and earth that becomes strange phenomena
is the energy of the great sun.
Strange phenomena are akin to poison;
energy that harms people is called poison,
while energy that transforms is called strange phenomena.
The world says children's rhymes
are caused by Yínghuò,
meaning they have witnessed something.
Yínghuò is the fire star,
and fire has a poisonous glow,
so when Yínghuò guards a constellation,
the state suffers disaster and ruin.
The energy of fire is elusive,
hence strange phenomena reflect survival or demise.
The dragon is a yang creature,
so it changes with the times.
Ghosts are yang energy,
appearing and hiding at times.
Yang energy is red,
so when people see ghosts,
their color is pure vermilion.
Flying omens
are yang,
and yang is fire,
thus flying omens manifest as flames.
Fire burns and scorches things,
so when they alight on trees,
the branches and leaves wither and die.
The Hóng Fàn's five elements second is fire,
and the five affairs second is speech.
Speech and fire share the same energy,
hence children's rhymes
and poems are considered strange speech.
Speech emerges and writing forms,
so there are strange phenomena in documents.
The world considers children yang,
thus strange speech comes from young children.
Children and shamans contain yang,
so in the great rain-seeking sacrifice,
children dance and shamans are exposed.
The ritual of the rain sacrifice
doubles yin to harmonize yang,
just as in a solar eclipse yin overcomes,
and the community attacks the yin.
In a solar eclipse, yin overcomes,
so they attack what is yin-like.
In a drought, yang overcomes,
so they distress the yang faction.
Shamans are the yang faction,
so when Lǔ Xī encountered a drought,
it was proposed to burn the shamans.
Shamans contain yang energy,
thus people in yang lands often become shamans.
Shamans align with ghosts,
so shamans are ghost-shamans.
Ghost-shamans are comparable to children's rhymes,
thus shamans who are discerning
can determine good and ill fortune.
Being able to determine good and ill fortune,
they are among those of good and ill fortune,
hence Shēnshēng's strange manifestation appeared through a shaman.
Shamans contain yang,
enabling them to manifest as strange phenomena.
If Shēnshēng was a strange phenomenon,
then it is known that Dù Bó,
Zhuāngzǐ Yì,
and fierce ghosts of their kind are all strange phenomena.
If Dù Bó and his kind are strange phenomena,
then their bows and arrows,
staffs, and oars are all strange poisons.
Strange phenomena mimic human form,
and their poison mimics human weapons.
Ghosts and poison share the same color,
hence Dù Bó's bows and arrows are all vermilion.
Poison mimics human weapons,
so when it strikes a person,
the person dies immediately.
If the strike is mild, it causes swelling,
and the illness does not lead to immediate death.
Why is that?
Swelling
is caused by the influence of poisonous energy.
Some demons may inflict their poison,
without revealing their form;
some may show their shape,
but not release their poison;
some may emit sounds,
without forming words;
some may articulate words clearly,
yet their tone remains unrecognizable.
As for Shēn Shēng,
he revealed his form and
articulated words clearly;
those like Dù Bó
showed their forms and
released their poison;
phenomena such as poetic omens,
children's rhymes,
and speaking stones
clearly articulated words;
the lute sounds of Pú River,
the ghostly wails at Zhòu's outskirts,
were instances of emitting sounds.
The manifestation of demons
may either foretell impending misfortune,
or appear because misfortune has arrived.
When arising from the cause,
the demon and its poison act together;
when foretelling,
the demon appears but cannot inflict poison.
Shēn Shēng's apparition
was a demon foretelling;
the appearances of Dù Bó,
Zhuāngzǐ Yì,
and fierce ghosts
were demons arising from the cause.
King Xuān of Zhōu,
Duke Jiǎn of Yān,
and Sòng Yègū were fated to die at that time,
so demons appeared and poison struck accordingly.
Duke Huì of Jìn was destined to be captured,
but his time to die had not come,
so the demon merely appeared without poisoning him.
Thus, the apparitions of Dù Bó,
Zhuāngzǐ Yì,
and the fierce ghosts
were omens of the impending deaths of King Xuān of Zhōu,
Duke Jiǎn of Yān,
and Yègū.
Shēn Shēng's manifestation
was an omen that Duke Huì of Jìn would be captured.
Bó Yǒu's dream
was an omen of the imminent deaths of Sì Dài
and Gōngsūn Duàn.
The old man twisting grass
was an auspicious sign for Wèi Kē's impending victory,
or perhaps a demonic omen of Dù Huí's capture.
The gray dog biting Empress Lǚ
foretold her imminent death,
with the demon taking the form of a dog.
When Wèi Qí and
Guàn Fū guarded against Wǔ'ān,
and Wǔ'ān was about to die,
the demon resembled the faces of Wèi Qí
and Guàn Fū.
Therefore, all that are called omens and demons,
or so-called ghosts and spirits in the world,
are produced by the energy of the Great Yang.
The energy of the Great Yang
is the energy of Heaven.
Heaven can create the human body,
so it can also mimic human appearance.
What gives life to humans
are the energies of Yin and Yang.
Yin energy governs bones and flesh,
while Yang energy governs the essence and spirit.
When humans are born,
both Yin and Yang energies are present,
so bones and flesh are firm,
and essence-energy is abundant.
Essence-energy constitutes consciousness,
bones and flesh constitute strength,
thus enabling speech and thought through spirit,
and solid maintenance through physical form.
Bones, flesh, and spirit
interact and support each other,
allowing continuous existence without perishing.
The energy of the Great Yang,
being solitary and lacking Yin,
can only create images,
not solid forms.
Without bones and flesh,
but possessing essence-energy,
it appears fleeting and vague,
vanishing quickly after manifestation.
Someone may ask:
"Between heaven and earth,
among the natures of all things,
venomous creatures
like vipers,
snakes, wasps,
and scorpions all carry poisonous stings;
if they strike the human body,
causing swelling and pain,
and not treated promptly,
the effect spreads throughout the body.
Among plants,
there are things like croton seeds
and wild aconite,
eating which causes congestion and distress,
often killing people.
I wonder, what energy do these things receive from Heaven?
All living things
receive the primordial energy,
but does the primordial energy
contain such poison?"
The reply is:
Poison
is the hot energy of the Great Yang,
which harms people when it enters them.
When people eat something and feel congested,
it is because they cannot endure it.
What cannot be endured
is called poison.
The fiery energy of the Great Yang
often acts as poison,
due to its heat.
In regions dominated by the Great Yang,
people are hasty and impatient,
and such impatient people
can poison with their words.
Thus, people from Chǔ
and Yuè, being hasty and quick,
when speaking to others,
their saliva can hit people,
causing swelling,
which develops into sores.
In the extremely hot lands of Nánjùn,
if someone curses a tree, it withers;
if they spit at a bird, it falls.
Shamans like Wū Xián could prolong illnesses
or cure misfortunes
because they were born south of the river,
imbued with intense energy.
Poison,
being Yang energy,
when it strikes a person,
burns like fire.
If bitten by a viper,
cutting the flesh and placing it on the ground causes it to sizzle and scorch,
which is evidence of the fiery energy.
All four directions have their edges,
but only the southeast corner possesses warm, intense energy.
This warm, intense energy emerges
often in spring and summer.
For Yang rises in spring and summer.
The southeast corner
is the position of Yang.
When energies from other things enter the nose or eyes,
they do not cause quick pain.
But when smoke enters the nose, it irritates;
when it enters the eyes, they hurt,
because fiery energy is intense.
Many things can be ground into powder,
but fire is the most intense,
as it dries through its energy.
Eating sweet and delicious food
does not harm people.
But consuming honey in excess
can make one suffer from its poison.
Honey is the liquid of bees,
and bees are Yang creatures.
When a person, without any contact or offense,
feels unexplained pain in the body,
with the painful spot resembling marks from a whip or club,
it is called 'féi' in people,
and 'féi' is said to be caused by ghostly beating.
Ghosts are
demonic manifestations of the Great Yang;
minor cases
of illness are called 'biān',
treated with honey and cinnabar.
Honey and cinnabar are Yang substances,
used to treat it by similarity.
Just as wind is treated with wind,
heat with heat,
so 'biān' is treated with honey
and cinnabar, indicating that 'biān'
is caused by Yang energy,
inflicted by flowing poison.
Between heaven and earth,
poisonous energies flow;
when people encounter their force,
their faces swell and ache,
what the world calls being stabbed by flowing fire.
Those who have seen ghosts
describe their color as red;
the malignant energy of the sun
naturally resembles this hue.
Ghosts embody virulent poison,
striking people who immediately perish,
hence Dù Bó shooting King Xuān of Zhōu caused his instant collapse.
Objects carried by ghosts
belong to the category of yang fire,
such as Dù Bó's bow and arrows,
all appearing red in color.
Southern regions call poison "short fox."
The manifestation of Dù Bó
holds a bow to shoot.
When yang energy is trapped and agitated,
it erupts in shooting,
thus striking people in the form of arrows.
Fire constrained generates intense heat,
and when blood toxicity peaks,
eating horse liver can kill a person,
as trapped energy turns fervid.
Walking recklessly in midsummer
leads to heatstroke death,
for extreme heat becomes venomous.
People sweating from rapid movement,
sweating before a furnace,
sweating facing the sun,
or sweating with febrile diseases—
these four differ yet all cause sweating,
due to similar confinement and equal heat,
manifestations of fire and sun.
All things under heaven,
born containing solar energy,
possess some venomous sting.
Those heavily saturated with poison:
among insects include the viper,
snake, wasp,
and scorpion; among plants, croton
and poisonous vines;
among fish, the pufferfish and certain toxic species like
shū, hence eating pufferfish liver causes death,
as these fish
sting with venom.
Fish and birds share similarities,
thus birds fly and fish leap,
birds lay eggs and fish spawn,
vipers, snakes,
wasps, and scorpions all lay eggs,
sharing akin natures.
In humans, this manifests as petty individuals,
whose mouths
bring calamity to the world.
Petty people harbor toxic energy,
especially those in yang regions,
where their venom is most severe,
hence the people of Nányuè
find curses swiftly effective.
As the proverb says:
"Many mouths can melt metal."
The mouth
is like fire.
In the Five Phases, the second is fire;
in the Five Affairs, the second is speech.
Speech aligns with fire,
hence 'melting metal.'
To describe the mouth's melting power,
one doesn't say
"uprooting trees or flaming fire,"
but must state
"melting metal,"
for metal is subdued by fire,
and fire with speech are of the same kind.
Medicinal herbs don't grow in one place alone,
as Tàibó declined to rule in Wú;
casting isn't done by one artisan only,
hence the world praises Chǔ's Tángxī.
Warm energy exists everywhere under heaven,
yet roads fear leading into the Nán Hǎi.
The zhèn bird thrives in the south,
and drinking its poison kills.
Chén corresponds to the dragon,
sì to the snake,
their positions lying in the southeast.
Dragons possess venom,
snakes have stings,
so vipers bear sharp fangs,
and dragons have reverse scales.
Wood generates fire,
fire becomes poison,
thus the Azure Dragon creature contains Mars.
Poisonous vines
and croton are both toxic,
hence冶 (refining) is in the southeast,
and巴 (Ba) in the southwest.
Land varies in aridity and humidity,
so poisonous creatures differ in number;
their origins depend on location,
thus venom varies in potency.
Vipers and snakes associate with fish,
so they inhabit marshes.
Wasps and scorpions align with birds,
thus they nest in houses
and trees.
North of the river, land is arid,
hence many wasps
and scorpions;
south of the river, land is damp,
hence many vipers
and snakes.
Living in high, dry areas relates to yang,
yang creatures hang suspended,
so wasps
and scorpions sting with their tails.
Living in low, damp areas relates to yin,
yin creatures are pliable and extending,
so vipers
and snakes bite with their mouths.
Poison may hide in head or tail,
thus stings and bites are venomous;
or it may reside in skin and flesh,
so consuming them causes distress;
or cling to lips,
hence wagging tongues bring disaster.
The emergence of venomous stings
stems from the same energy,
though their activation differs,
internally they form one category.
Thus dreaming of fire
portends disputes;
dreaming of vipers
or snakes also means disputes.
Fire symbolizes disputes,
seen in vipers
and snakes, sharing kind and root,
endowed with the same energy.
Therefore, fire represents speech,
speech represents petty people,
and petty people create havoc through gossip.
The sign of gossip
stems from humans resonating with heaven.
Hence, among the Five Affairs, the second is speech,
and the portent of speech error
is "extravagance leads to constant yang."
"Extravagance"
means lavish beauty,
thus vipers
and snakes are often patterned.
Patterns arise from yang,
so they induce ornamentation.
"Yang response"
An aura of evil gives rise to beauty,
thus beautiful people are often wicked.
Shū Hǔ's mother was beautiful,
and Shū Xiàng's mother envied her,
not allowing her to attend to the bedchamber.
Shū Xiàng admonished his own mother.
His mother said:
"In deep mountains and vast marshes,
truly are born dragons
and snakes. That beauty of hers,
I fear she will give birth to dragons
and snakes to bring calamity upon you.
You belong to a declining clan,
the state has many powerful favorites,
if unkind people intervene,
will it not be difficult?
Why should I spare her?"
She then allowed her to attend the bedchamber,
and she bore Shū Hǔ,
who was handsome and courageous,
favored by Luán Huáizi.
When Fàn Xuānzī expelled Huáizi,
he killed Shū Hǔ,
and the disaster extended to Shū Xiàng.
Now deep mountains and vast marshes
are where dragons and snakes are born;
comparing them to Shū Hǔ's mother,
a beautiful woman harbors venomous stings.
She gave birth to Shū Hǔ,
handsome and courageous.
Courage and strength are born
from beauty;
calamities arise
from courage and strength.
Fire has radiance,
wood has appearance.
Dragons and snakes
belong to the east,
which is wood, containing fire's essence,
hence beauty is splendid in appearance.
The gallbladder attaches to the liver,
thus producing courage and strength.
Fire's energy is fierce,
so it brings much courage;
wood is firm,
so it brings much strength.
Those who produce strange phenomena
often come from fondness for beauty;
those who cause calamities
often arise from courage and strength;
those who inflict poison and harm
all lie in fondness for beauty.
Fine wine is poisonous,
wine is hard to drink much;
bee fluid makes honey,
honey is hard to benefit from eating;
courageous men strengthen the state,
courageous men are hard to be near;
beautiful women please the heart,
beautiful women are hard to keep;
eloquent scholars delight the mind,
eloquent scholars are hard to trust.
Thus rich flavors rot the belly,
beauty deludes the heart,
courageous men invite disaster,
glib tongues bring calamity.
These four things
are the poisons of the world.
The poison of a glib tongue
is especially cruel in its harm.
How to illustrate this?
When Confucius saw Yáng Hǔ,
he stepped back,
sweat pouring down.
Yáng Hǔ was eloquent,
possessing a sharp tongue.
The poison of a sharp tongue
afflicts people like a disease.
When a person is struck by various poisons,
he alone dies;
when struck by a sharp tongue,
an entire state collapses into chaos.
The Book of Songs says:
"Slanderous words know no bounds,
they throw the four states into confusion."
If four states can be thrown into chaos,
how much more one person!
Thus the noble person does not fear tigers,
but solely fears the slanderer's mouth.
The slanderer's mouth
is greatly poisonous!
The endeavors of sages and worthies
all take frugal burials and reduced expenses as their aim.
Yet the world favors lavish burials,
with the fault of extravagance,
because the Confucian arguments are not clear,
and the Mohist discussions are mistaken.
The Mohist arguments honor ghosts,
believing that when people die, they become spirits or ghosts and have consciousness,
able to take form and harm people,
thus citing examples like Dù Bó as proof.
The Confucians do not follow this,
believing that the dead have no consciousness,
cannot become ghosts,
yet they prepare full offerings for funeral sacrifices,
to show they do not neglect the dead and to set an example for the living.
Lù Jiǎ followed Confucianism in his discourse,
so in his established arguments,
he refused to take a clear stance.
Liú Zǐzhèng presented a memorial on frugal burial,
aiming to reduce expenses,
but could not argue thoroughly.
Thus, within society, people hold doubtful opinions,
and externally hear of cases like Dù Bó,
and also see the dying and deceased
appearing to them from the grave,
so they come to believe it,
thinking the dead are like the living.
Pitying the dead buried alone,
with lonely souls and no companion,
tombs sealed and hidden,
food and goods scarce,
they make figurines to attend the coffin,
and store abundant food to please the spirits.
This practice accumulates and spreads,
some ruining families and exhausting resources
to fill the coffins of the dead;
killing people for burial,
to satisfy the wishes of the living.
It is not that they do not know it is of no benefit within,
but that their extravagant minds admire it outwardly.
They believe the dead have consciousness,
no different from the living,
Confucius opposed this,
but also had no way to establish the truth.
And Lù Jiǎ's arguments
take no clear position on either side.
Liú Zǐzhèng's memorial
also could not clarify the Confucian proof of no consciousness
or the Mohist evidence of consciousness.
Nothing clarifies a matter like having proof,
no argument is settled without evidence.
Empty words and vain talk,
even if they grasp the heart of the way,
people still will not believe.
Thus the foolish in society who believe in fortune and misfortune,
fear death but not righteousness,
value death over life,
exhaust their wealth to serve spirits,
empty their homes to send off the dead.
If eloquent scholars and writers had proof,
like the Mohists' use of Dù Bó as evidence,
then the fact that the dead have no consciousness could be clarified,
and the teaching of frugal burial and saving wealth could be established.
Now the Mohists criticize the Confucians,
the Confucians criticize the Mohists,
each holding their own views,
thus they conflict and do not agree,
their endeavors are hard to unify,
so the two schools contend.
The world has no instances of people revived by sacrifices,
thus the truth about death and life remains undetermined.
In reality, the dead are obscure,
different from the living,
their state vague and elusive,
hard to know deeply.
Whether they have consciousness or not cannot be determined,
the reality of being a ghost cannot be affirmed.
Even learned men and knowledgeable scholars, though they study past and present,
examine all schools of thought,
and penetrate details and connections,
cannot ascertain it.
Only the sage's mind and worthy's insight,
comparing and categorizing things,
can truly determine it.
If discussions do not retain essence and clarify intentions,
but merely establish right and wrong based on external effects,
trusting only what is heard and seen externally,
without verifying and examining internally,
this is judging with the ears and eyes,
not deliberating with the mind and heart.
To judge with the ears and eyes
is to speak of illusory appearances.
When illusory appearances are validated,
then actual facts are deemed wrong.
Therefore, determining right and wrong does not rely solely on the ears and eyes;
one must open the mind and heart.
The Mohist debates do not use the heart to trace the nature of things;
if one merely trusts what is heard and seen,
even if the evidence is clearly demonstrated,
it may still be unrealistic.
Unrealistic arguments are difficult to use for teaching;
though they may satisfy the desires of the ignorant masses,
they do not align with the minds of the wise.
Losing the substance and seeking utility,
they bring no benefit to the world.
This is likely why Mohist techniques have not been passed down.
The people of Lǔ intended to use yúfán jade for burial,
and Confucius, hearing of this,
crossed the courtyard and stepped over the thresholds to admonish them.
Crossing the courtyard and stepping over thresholds
is contrary to ritual,
but Confucius did so to prevent a disaster.
The origin of disasters
often lies in greed.
Yúfán jade
is a treasure,
and if the people of Lǔ use it for burial,
unscrupulous people, upon hearing of it,
will develop desires.
When unscrupulous people develop desires,
they do not fear laws and punishments.
Not fearing laws and punishments,
they will dig up the graves.
Confucius perceived the subtle signs and foresaw the obvious outcome,
so he crossed the courtyard and stepped over thresholds
to admonish directly and prevent the disaster.
If the principle that the dead have no awareness is not clarified,
yet the admonition that graves will surely be dug is emphasized,
even if one were as persistent as Bìgān,
people would certainly not listen.
Why is that?
The feudal lords, wealthy and not worried about poverty,
powerful and strong, do not fear digging.
The debate about the dead
remains uncertain and doubtful;
the filial son's consideration
follows what is most important.
If it were clear that the dead have no awareness,
and lavish burials are of no benefit,
once the argument is settled and established,
clearly evident and known,
then the practice of using yúfán jade would not occur,
and the admonition by crossing the courtyard would not be needed.
Now, without clarifying the argument yet forcing the admonition,
this is likely why Confucius could not establish his teaching.
It is not that Confucius was unaware of the reality of death and life;
his intention in not making a distinction
is also the point of Lù Jiǎ's words.
To say that the dead have no awareness
might lead ministers and sons to betray their rulers and fathers.
Hence it is said:
"If funeral and sacrificial rites are abandoned,
then the kindness of ministers and sons becomes shallow;
if the kindness of ministers and sons becomes shallow,
they betray the dead and neglect ancestors;
if they betray the dead and neglect ancestors,
then cases of filial impiety increase."
The sage feared opening the source of filial impiety,
so he did not clarify the reality that the dead have no awareness.
Different ways are not connected;
if one treats the living generously,
transformation naturally occurs.
Even if one treats the dead sparingly,
what harm is there to transformation?
If the dead have awareness,
betraying them is wrong;
if they have no awareness,
what harm is there in betraying them?
Clarifying their lack of awareness
may not necessarily lead to the harm of betraying the dead;
not clarifying their lack of awareness
already results in the expense of fostering thieves.
When a filial son cares for his ill parent,
before death,
he seeks divination and calls for doctors,
hoping to avert disaster
and that medicine will be beneficial.
After death,
even if as discerning as Wūxián
or as skilled as Biǎnquè,
they can no longer be of use.
Why?
Knowing that death means the breath has ceased,
there is ultimately no benefit.
If managing death is of no benefit,
how is a lavish burial any different?
Fearing that betraying the dead might harm transformation,
yet stopping divination and refusing doctors—
does that not alone harm righteousness?
When the parent is alive,
they sit in the high hall;
when they die,
they are buried in the Yellow Springs below.
The Yellow Springs below
are not a place for the living to dwell,
yet they are buried without doubt,
because death separates them to a different place,
and they cannot be together with the living.
If it should be as when they were alive,
fearing that people might betray them,
they should be buried in the home,
together with the living.
Not clarifying the lack of awareness,
worried that people might betray their parents,
yet clearly burying them in the Yellow Springs—
is that not separating them from their ancestors?
If a parent is in prison,
with charges uncertain and undecided,
the filial son rushes about
to rescue them from hardship.
If the charges are set and the law applied,
with no way out ultimately,
even Zēngzǐ
or Zǐqiān
can only sit and weep.
Why?
Because any action is futile,
merely causing trouble in vain.
Now, the spirit of the deceased parent
certainly has no awareness;
how is this different from a parent imprisoned with charges irrevocable and beyond rescue?
Not clarifying the lack of awareness,
fearing that people might betray their ancestors,
yet clearly stating that charges are set—
is that not neglecting the parent?
The sage establishes principles
that benefit transformation;
even if small, they are not discarded.
What does not contribute to governance,
even if grand, is not endorsed.
Now, being generous to the dead—
what benefit is there to kindness?
Betraying them by not serving them—
what harm is there to righteousness?
Confucius also said that mingqì (spirit utensils) are not fully functional,
indicating that there is awareness implied.
Figurines are effigies,
resembling living people,
so when Lǔ used figurines in burial,
Confucius sighed.
He saw the omen of using live humans for sacrifice,
hence he sighed in grief.
If it were that the dead should be equipped as if alive,
yet not indicating they are as if alive,
the intention is to fully convey his teaching.
Using figurines for burial,
he feared later use of live sacrifices;
using mingqì,
is he not also concerned about later use of fine utensils for burial?
To stop the source of using humans,
yet not prevent the path of wasting objects,
valuing people but not caring about their use,
grieving for people but not worrying about the state—
this is the error in transmitted debates.
To rescue a leaking dam,
one must block all its holes,
then the water leakage ceases.
If the holes are not all blocked,
water will find leaks,
and leaks cause water disasters.
Similarly, if the concept of death is not fully understood,
extravagant rituals will not cease,
and not ceasing leads to wasteful consumption of resources.
With resources depleted and goods lost,
the people become impoverished and drained to the extreme,
which is the path to peril and ruin.
Sū Qín, serving Yān,
had the people of Qí build lofty tombs and mounds,
hoarding abundant wealth and goods,
yet Sū Qín himself did not practice what he urged.
When wealth was exhausted and the people impoverished,
the state was emptied and its military weakened,
the Yān army suddenly arrived,
with no means for self-defense,
the state was crushed, the city lost,
the ruler fled, and the people scattered.
Now, failing to clarify that the dead lack consciousness,
and making people exhaust themselves for lavish burials of their kin,
is the same disastrous ploy as Sū Qín's deceitful scheme.
The Mohist doctrines,
contradict their own methods,
advocating frugal burials yet endorsing ghosts.
Endorsing ghosts and citing evidence,
they use Dù Bó as proof.
Dù Bó is a dead person;
if they claim Dù Bó became a ghost,
then the dead indeed have consciousness.
If they have consciousness yet are given frugal burials,
this would anger the dead.
Human nature desires generosity and despises stinginess;
to incur the dead's reproach by being stingy,
even if endorsing ghosts,
what good does it do?
If ghosts are not the dead,
then their belief in Dù Bó is wrong;
if ghosts are the dead,
then their frugal burials are wrong.
Their methods are inconsistent and erroneous,
contradicting from start to end,
hence they are deemed incorrect.
Whether wrong or right remains unclear,
neither should be practiced.
Thus,
people of the world,
should carefully examine this.
Upon such examination,
they may adopt frugal burials.
There are four major taboos in custom:
First, taboo against expanding a residence westward.
Expanding westward is considered inauspicious,
and inauspiciousness surely brings death.
Fearing this,
no one dares to expand westward.
This prohibition has distant origins.
The records say:
"Duke Āi of Lǔ wished to expand his residence westward,
but the historian opposed it,
deeming it inauspicious.
Duke Āi changed countenance in anger,
and despite repeated remonstrations from his attendants, he did not listen,
so he asked his tutor Zǎi Zhìsuī:
'I wish to expand westward,
but the historian says it's inauspicious;
what do you think?'
Zǎi Zhìsuī replied:
'There are three inauspicious things in the world,
and expanding westward is not among them.'
Duke Āi was greatly pleased.
After a while,
he asked again:
'What are the three inauspicious things?'
The reply was:
'Not practicing ritual righteousness,
first inauspiciousness;
insatiable desires,
second inauspiciousness;
not heeding admonitions,
third inauspiciousness.'
Duke Āi fell into deep thought,
sighed with self-reflection,
and thus did not expand westward.
If the historian and Zǎi Zhìsuī stopped the expansion,
it was merely troublesome interference;
