then whether westward expansion is auspicious or not,
remains unknown.
If the historian and Zǎi Zhìsuī firmly believed westward expansion inauspicious,
then they are no different from common people today.'"
Now, all four sides of a residence are land;
why are three sides not considered ominous,
but expanding westward alone deemed inauspicious?
Why?
What harm does westward expansion do
to the earth's substance?
What injury to the residence's spirit?
If westward expansion is inauspicious,
would reducing it make it good?
If westward expansion is inauspicious,
would expanding eastward bring luck?
Where there is inauspiciousness, there must be auspiciousness,
just as where there is misfortune, there must be fortune.
A residence has form,
spirits have luck and harm;
virtuous actions bring blessings,
offending punishments incurs disasters.
Now, claiming westward expansion is inauspicious—
what expansion would be auspicious?
Moreover, who dislikes westward expansion?
If the earth dislikes it,
expanding the east house's west side,
reducing the west house's east side,
what harm to the earth?
If the residence's spirit dislikes westward expansion,
spirits are like humans;
humans dwelling in residences
desire spaciousness—
why would they dislike it?
And if the residence's spirit dislikes disturbance,
then expanding on all four sides
should all be inauspicious.
Various craftsmen and diviners
explain omens of luck and harm,
all with specific cases.
Residence experts speak of offending baleful spirits when building,
moving experts caution against certain years and months,
sacrifice experts warn of blood taboos,
burial experts mention violating hard and soft principles,
all with prohibitions on fierce ghosts and spirits.
If people do not avoid these,
they risk illness and death.
But what harm does westward expansion cause to be called inauspicious?
What kind of disaster
does this inauspiciousness bring?
To explain its true meaning,
"inauspicious"
refers to a prohibition of righteousness and principle,
not a taboo of luck and harm.
For the west
is the land of elders,
the position of honor.
The honored elders are in the west,
the humble young in the east.
The honored elders
are the masters;
the humble young,
the assistants.
Masters are few, assistants many;
honor has no second above,
humility has countless below.
Expanding westward
increases the master's side without adding assistants,
creating a second above without countless below,
which is improper in principle,
hence called inauspicious.
Inauspiciousness
means inappropriate.
Improper in principle,
it does not necessarily bring harm.
How to clarify this?
Tombs,
where the dead are stored,
fields, where people's food comes from,
residences, where people live—
these three for humans
should have equal considerations of luck and harm.
Expanding a residence westward is inauspicious,
but expanding a tomb or field westward
is not called inauspicious.
Tombs,
dwellings of the dead,
are often neglected and not cautious.
Fields, not human dwellings,
lack distinctions of honor and humility.
Residences,
shared by old and young,
require added caution and attention—
how can they not have taboos?
Thus, principles are detailed for residences,
but brief for tombs and fields.
The second taboo states that those punished and made convicts should not ascend burial mounds.
People only know it should not be done,
but do not understand the reason behind its prohibition.
When asked why it is forbidden,
they cannot explain the taboo;
those who follow the prohibition
are equally unaware of the reason for avoidance.
They merely imitate one another,
to the extent that some, having been punished,
when their parents die,
do not attend the funeral;
if they go to the graveside,
they dare not approach the burial;
this error leads to not offering condolences,
upon seeing others' coffins.
Now convicts
are originally good people,
but being punished makes them convicts.
Burial mounds
hold one's parents,
whose death makes them ancestors.
What difference is there between the home and the grave?
What distinction exists between parents and ancestors?
If it is because convicts, being punished,
would be reproached by their ancestors,
then they should not enter the home to see their parents either;
if it is because convicts cannot meet the dead,
then when a parent dies in the hall,
they should not weep by the coffin;
if it is because convicts cannot ascend burial mounds,
then they should not climb hills or tombs.
Why does custom forbid this?
On what basis is it upheld?
To explain the true meaning,
convicts not ascending burial mounds has two reasons,
based on principles of righteousness,
not fears of misfortune.
Convicts consider that ancestors gave them life whole,
and descendants should return whole.
Thus, when Zēngzǐ fell ill,
he summoned his disciples and said:
"Look at my feet!
Look at my hands!
From now on,
I know I am spared.
My children!"
Zēngzǐ, being cautious,
at life's end demonstrated wholeness,
rejoicing to avoid the harm of mutilation.
Confucius said:
"Our bodies, hair, and skin
are received from our parents;
we dare not injure them."
Filial children fear punishment,
which carves and marks the body,
damaging hair and skin,
resulting from lack of virtue and careless conduct,
and failure to be cautious.
Ashamed of bearing punishment's disgrace,
they deeply reproach themselves,
hence do not ascend graves to sacrifice to ancestors.
Ancient rites involved temple sacrifices,
but now customs favor grave offerings,
so not ascending the grave
expresses shame before ancestors.
This is the first reason.
The grave
is where spirits dwell,
the place for sacrifices.
The rites of sacrifice
require fasting and purity,
the utmost reverence.
Now, being punished,
as maimed persons,
they are unfit to serve ancestors in sacrifice,
showing humility and caution,
a mindset of self-abasement and deference.
Considering the ancestors' perspective,
seeing their descendants punished,
they would grieve and sorrow,
fearing that if they approached the sacrifice,
they could not bear to enjoy the offerings,
hence they do not ascend the grave.
This is the second reason.
In the past, Tàibó saw that Wángjì had a sage son, King Wén,
and knew King Tài intended to establish him,
so he went to Wú to gather herbs,
cut his hair and tattooed his body,
to follow Wú customs.
When King Tài died,
Tàibó returned,
and Wángjì declined the rulership.
Tàibó yielded twice,
but Wángjì did not accept.
Yielding a third time,
he said:
"I have been to Wú
and Yuè, where the custom
is to cut hair and tattoo the body.
I am a punished man,
unfit to be lord of the ancestral temple and state."
Wángjì, knowing it was futile,
reluctantly accepted.
Thus, convicts not ascending burial mounds
follows Tàibó's principle of not assuming leadership.
This means they should not participate in sacrifices,
not that they should not escort the coffin
when it is buried
or avoid the funeral.
Burying the dead
causes ancestors pain;
seeing the punished
causes ancestors sorrow.
But a sorrowful person
escorting a pained corpse—
if ancestors were aware,
they would mourn the corpse and pity the living—
what shame would there be?
If they are unaware,
the grave
is but a field,
what shame then?
The shame
lies in
having a punished, maimed body,
different from others.
In ancient times, corporal punishment
disfigured and incomplete,
made it truly unacceptable.
Nowadays, symbolic punishment
—the severest being
the shaving and clamping penalty—
or sentences like city guarding and below,
where the punished wear colored clothes,
their caps and belts differing from ordinary people's—
why should it be unacceptable?
Custom believes and deems it all unlucky,
leading to not mourning village corpses,
not ascending others' graves,
which is deluded.
The third taboo concerns women giving birth,
considered unlucky.
Those undertaking auspicious events,
entering mountains and forests,
traveling far,
or crossing rivers and marshes
all avoid contact with them.
The households of birthing women
also detest it,
avoiding graves, huts, and roadsides,
and only entering after a month,
such is the extent of their aversion.
If briefly encountering it seems unlucky,
examining its origin thoroughly,
what justifies this detestation?
When a woman gives birth to a child,
the child emerges containing the primordial energy.
Primordial energy
is the essence of heaven and earth—
why consider it inauspicious and detest it?
Humans are living beings,
and children are also living beings.
How is the birth of a child different from the birth of all things?
If labeling human birth as detestable,
then should the birth of all things also be detested?
The child is born together with the amniotic sac;
if the sac is considered unlucky,
humans having an amniotic sac
is like fruits having their husks.
It wraps the child's body
and thus comes out together;
like the shell of a bird's egg,
why should it be called detestable?
If detesting it as unlucky,
then all living things with husks or shells
should be detested alike.
The myriad things are vast and numerous,
making it hard to verify matters.
How is human birth different from that of the six domestic animals?
All contain blood and vital energy and bear young;
their births are no different from humans'.
To detest only humans but not animals—
is it because the human body is larger
and has abundant blood and energy?
But then oxen and horses have bodies larger than humans'.
Generally, detestable things
have no absolute standard;
if only one thing
lacks comparison,
then it may be questionable.
Now the six domestic animals are no different from humans;
their birthing processes are identical.
Since the six domestic animals and humans are no different,
why taboo humans but not the six animals?
I do not understand the reason.
If the world can distinguish human childbirth from animal birthing,
I will accept the taboo;
if not,
then I say the世俗 taboo is absurd.
Moreover, what people detest most
is putrid odor.
The stench of decay
harms and offends the human mind;
thus, the nose smelling rot,
the mouth eating spoiled food,
the heart is harmed, the mouth disgusted,
causing chaos, vomiting.
The restroom
can be called foul;
the meat of salted fish
can be called putrid.
Yet some willingly enter restrooms,
not avoiding them;
some eat spoiled fish meat,
not tabooing it.
Since the mind does not regard it as detestable,
they do not consider whether it should be or not.
Generally, what is detestable,
like splashed ink or lacquer,
adheres to the human body.
Now, what is seen by the eye or smelled by the nose,
once passed, is gone;
suddenly vanishes and departs—
why detest it?
Seeing someone carrying a pig on the road,
or rotting debris in a ditch,
is not considered inauspicious,
because the filth and shame belong to that person,
not attaching to oneself.
Now when a woman gives birth,
it is within her own body;
why should those observing purification
avoid her?
North of the river, when a woman gives birth,
she does not leave the room,
knowing there is nothing detestable.
As for a dog giving birth,
it is placed outside the house—
this is again confusing.
North of the river, they taboo dogs but not humans;
south of the river, they taboo humans but not dogs.
Customs for preventing evil
vary from place to place.
How are humans and dogs different?
The inner room
and outside the house—
what distinguishes them?
Some are detested, some not;
some are tabooed, some not.
世俗 precautions and prohibitions
ultimately have no consistent principle.
At the moon's dark phase (huì),
the sun and moon lodge together,
marking one month.
Around the eighth day,
the moon is half-full, called xián;
on the fifteenth day,
the sun and moon face each other, called wàng;
on the thirtieth day,
the sun and moon lodge together, called huì.
Huì, xián, and wàng are all the same in essence;
it's not that the light and energy of the sun and moon during huì differ from the new moon (suì),
so why consider passing the month as auspicious?
If it is truly inauspicious,
passing the month cannot be called auspicious;
if it is truly auspicious,
even before the month passes,
it should still be acceptable.
To speak truthfully,
the taboos against childbirth
and dogs giving birth
aim to make people maintain cleanliness,
not wanting them to be defiled.
Self-purification refines the mind,
a refined mind leads to pure conduct,
and pure conduct establishes integrity and virtue.
Fourth, there is the taboo against raising children born in the first or fifth month.
It is believed that children born in the first or fifth month
will kill their father and mother,
so they must not be raised.
If raised,
and the parents happen to die,
people believe it and consider it true.
Why would children born in the first or fifth month
kill their father and mother?
Humans contain vital energy
within their intestines and belly;
their birth
occurs after ten months of pregnancy,
all sharing the same primordial energy.
How is the first month different from the second?
How is the fifth month different from the sixth?
Yet they are called inauspicious?
This saying has been passed down for a long time;
those bound by superstition
dare not violate it;
but those with broad knowledge and great talent,
who examine facts and principles,
deeply perceive the distinction between auspicious and inauspicious,
then see through it.
In the past, Tián Yīng, the chancellor of Qí, had a son by a low-ranking concubine,
named Wén.
Wén was born in the fifth month.
Yīng told his mother:
"Do not raise him."
His mother secretly raised him.
When he grew up,
his mother, through his brothers, presented her son Wén to Yīng.
Yīng angrily said:
"I ordered you to abandon this child,
yet you dared to raise him.
Why?"
Wén kowtowed
and then said:
"The reason you did not want to raise a child born in the fifth month—
what is it?"
Yīng said:
"A child born in the fifth month,
when grown, will reach the height of the door
and harm his parents."
Wén said:
"Is human life bestowed by heaven,
or by the door?"
Yīng was silent.
Wén said:
"If it is bestowed by heaven,
what do you have to worry about?
If by the door,
then raise the height of the door—
who could reach it then?"
Yīng appreciated his words,
saying:
"Enough, my son!"
Afterwards, he had Wén manage the household and entertain guests;
guests increased daily,
and his reputation spread among the feudal lords.
Wén grew taller than the door, yet Yīng did not die.
From Tián Wén's argument
and Tián Yīng's survival as proof,
the世俗 taboo
is a false and baseless claim.
Now, Tián Yīng was a conventional father,
and Tián Wén an enlightened son.
Yīng believed in taboos, not in true principle;
Wén believed in fate, not avoiding taboos.
Enlightened and conventional differ in talent;
their actions and conduct vary,
hence Yīng's name remained obscure,
while Wén's fame spread far and wide, never fading.
To speak plainly,
the world has its taboos,
and there are reasons for them.
The first month marks the beginning of the year,
and the fifth month is the peak of yang energy;
if a child is born in these months,
their essence is fiery and intense,
overpowering their parents,
who cannot endure it,
and thus suffer harm.
People imitate and follow this belief,
none considering it untrue.
There are empty words of taboo,
but no real evidence of misfortune;
the world is deluded by them,
deeply mistaken in its criticism.
Taboos are not uniform;
they must be attributed to spirits and anomalies,
as if set with the threat of death,
only then do people of later times believe, fear, and avoid them.
The words of taboos
vary across regions;
I will briefly cite common sayings
for the world to observe.
As for minor, trivial taboos,
numerous and varied,
they all encourage people to do good,
making them cautious,
avoiding harm from ghosts and spirits,
or disasters of ill omen.
It is tabooed to make bean paste when thunder is heard,
so that if one person refrains,
it urges others to hurry in making it,
lest it accumulate past spring.
It is tabooed to sharpen a knife over a well,
for fear the knife might fall into the well;
some say it is because
the character for "punishment"
consists of
"well" and "knife,"
so sharpening a knife over a well
brings well and knife together,
fearing punishment.
Do not sit under the eaves,
for fear tiles may fall and hit one's head.
Do not hang a hat upside down,
as it resembles the clothing of the dead;
some say it is disliked for being inverted and catching dust.
Do not lie flat on your back,
as it resembles a corpse.
Do not pass chopsticks directly to another,
for it is insecure.
Do not sweep for each other,
as it imitates tomb caretakers
hoping others will replace them.
All sayings
"do not"
teach people caution,
urging them to do good.
The "Book of Rites" says:
"Do not grasp rice in lumps,
do not drink noisily."
These prohibitions of ritual propriety
are not necessarily words of fortune or misfortune.
Moreover,
when the world breaks ground for construction,
the year or month may inflict harm,
and where harm occurs,
there must be deaths.
Suppose the Grand Year (Tàisuì) is in the zǐ position,
the year harms the yǒu position,
the first month aligns with yín,
the month harms the sì position;
if construction occurs in zǐ or yín locations,
then households in yǒu
or sì suffer harm.
The afflicted households
perform counter-charms,
using elements of the five phases,
hanging metal, wood, water, or fire.
Suppose the year
and month harm the western household,
the western household hangs metal;
if they harm the eastern household,
the eastern household hangs charcoal.
They perform sacrifices to avert the misfortune,
or move away empty-handed to avoid calamity.
People imitate one another,
all claiming it is true.
But if examined,
it is false and delusional.
How to clarify this?
The spirits of heaven and earth
have impartial intentions.
If people act improperly,
they are punished for their crimes,
not with divided minds or conflicting wills,
inconsistent in their actions.
If moving without avoiding the year
or month, the year
and month dislike such disregard for their opposing positions,
and become angered.
Now, those who break ground for construction
also disturb the earth's body,
committing improper faults
similar to moving.
Why then should the constructing household,
destined to be harmed by the year
and month,
instead cause the sì
and yǒu locations to bear the blame?
Would the spirits of the year
and month punish movers but not constructors?
In their intentions and actions,
how could they be so unfair?
Ghosts and spirits punishing people
is like officials reprimanding the people.
People commit various crimes,
minor faults may be pardoned,
major evils face punishment,
but none are punished without fault.
To be punished without fault
is called injustice in the world.
Now, households in sì
and yǒu,
without offending the month
or year,
suffer harm when zǐ or yín sites are built upon,
vainly being afflicted—
this means the year
and month unjustly harm the innocent.
Moreover, when the Grand Year is in zǐ,
the zǐ residence aligns with it,
the wǔ residence opposes it,
yet without any construction or activity,
merely dwelling idly,
they still suffer harm.
If the harm by the year
and month
depends on actions in zǐ
or yín,
then sì and yǒu become ominous.
(The Grand Year)
The spirits of the year and month,
using punishment to cause harm,
would act inconsistently,
which is not the way heaven follows the will of the year
and month spirits.
Examining the spirits of the year
and month,
the year refers to the Grand Year.
It resides at the celestial border,
positioned in zǐ.
Those building houses are within a single province of the central kingdom;
suppose Yángzhōu is in the southeast,
and as Zōu Yǎn said,
if the world were one province,
also in the southeast,
and the year harms yǒu,
afflicting the western Qiāng lands,
how could the southeast suffer ill fortune?
If the year were among the people,
with western residences in yǒu,
then constructing households
would also have yǒu areas in their homes;
why not harm the yǒu area in their own residence
but instead harm others?
And who, precisely, is doing the harming?
If it is indeed the year
and month,
then as heaven's subordinate spirits,
their consumption should match heaven's.
Heaven does not consume humans,
hence suburban sacrifices do not use them as offerings.
If they are not heavenly spirits,
they do not consume humans either.
Among heaven and earth,
what the hundred spirits consume
sages say should be like that of humans.
Inferring from the living to serve the dead,
from human affairs to ghostly ones,
thus sacrifices to the hundred spirits
all use various objects,
not humans.
Beings that consume humans
are tigers and wolves.
Are the spirits of the year
and month then essences of tigers and wolves?
In times of crisis,
when grain is scarce,
people starve
and resort to cannibalism.
Could it be that those who consume the dead
have essences that become the year
and month spirits?
The year and
month have their spirits,
and so does the day.
The year and
month consume,
so why does the day not consume?
Accumulated days form a month,
accumulated months form a season,
accumulated seasons form a year.
One thousand five hundred and thirty-nine years make one tǒng,
four thousand six hundred and seventeen years make one yuán.
These are merely names for the increasing accumulations and doubled numbers,
the designations for the remainders and ultimate endings.
How could there be the strangeness of ghosts and spirits,
or the evidence of calamities and blessings?
If the endings of years and months should have spirits,
then the four seasons have spirits,
and the tǒng and yuán have spirits.
On the third day of the month, the moon is a crescent,
on the eighth day, it is a half-moon,
on the fifteenth day, it is full—
how is this different from the endings of the year
and month?
If the year and month have spirits,
do the crescent, half-moon,
and full moon also have spirits?
Within a single day,
it is divided into twelve hours:
at dawn, it is Yín,
at sunrise, it is Mǎo.
The twelfth month establishes Yín and
Mǎo, which are the Yín and
Mǎo added to the twelve
hours.
The day added to the twelve celestial stems does not consume,
yet the month established in the twelve stems alone consumes.
Could it be that the day addition has no spirit,
while the month establishment alone has one?
Why does only the month establishment consume,
while the day addition does not?
If the day addition has no spirit,
then using the hour to decide matters
is incorrect;
if the addition of the hour has a spirit,
yet it alone does not consume,
that is also incorrect.
The mouths and stomachs of spirits
are like those of humans.
When humans are hungry, they eat;
when full, they stop—
they do not eat only when a project is started.
If the spirits of the year and month
eat only when a project begins,
then within a year,
since those who start projects are few,
are the spirits of the year and month hungry?
In times of haste and disorder,
when people perish
and houses are abandoned,
and those who start projects cease,
are the spirits of the year and month starving?
Moreover, both fields and houses are managed by people;
starting projects requires effort,
and the toil is equal.
Building a house involves digging earth and erecting wood,
while farming requires digging ditches and building dikes.
Both dikes and wood are erected,
both digging and excavating are done.
When building a house,
the year and month consume,
but when managing fields,
they alone do not consume.
Could it be that when building a house, the year
and month are hungry,
but when farming, they are full?
Why is the work equal and the same,
yet the consumption differs?
Those who claim that the year
and month consume
must assess the size of the project
and set the range of steps.
Suppose a project of three chǐ in height
consumes within one step;
a labor of ten zhàng
consumes beyond one lǐ.
Projects have their sizes,
calamities have their proximity.
Méng Tián built the Great Wall for Qín,
spanning half the world,
so the calamity should have been countless.
Yet, examining the construction of the Great Wall,
the Qín people did not die in great numbers.
When the Duke of Zhōu built Luò,
the project was immense,
so at that time, the year
and month should have consumed greatly.
If the sages knew the specifics of consumption,
they should have moved the consumed land
to an auspicious position.
If they did not avoid it,
the people would have faced many misfortunes,
and in the classics and texts,
the sages should have criticized it.
But now, we hear that the people building Luò
gathered harmoniously from all directions,
the work was completed,
and no great deaths were heard of.
Thus, those who claim the year
and month consume
are likely false and not true.
Moreover, if the year
and month truly consume,
it is like a person's stomach being hungry and needing to eat.
Yet, if for the locations of Jǐ and Yǒu there are taboos for overcoming,
fearing a single metal blade,
or dreading a piece of dead charcoal,
would they shut their mouths and not dare to eat?
If they truly feared,
they should act accordingly.
The five phases overcome each other,
and the energies of things are balanced.
If Mount Tài were on fire,
could dousing it with a cup of water
extinguish it?
If the river burst for a thousand lǐ,
could blocking it with a handful of soil
hold it back?
It is not that the way of the five phases is lost,
but that the small and large, the few and many, cannot match.
The nature of heaven and earth,
the strength of people and things,
means the few cannot overcome the many,
the small cannot subdue the large.
If an army holds wooden sticks,
and a single man holds a blade,
and they exert their strength and clash,
the single man will surely die.
Metal's nature overcomes wood,
yet wood wins and metal loses
because wood is many and metal is few.
Pile metal as high as a mountain,
and light a single charcoal fire to melt it—
the metal will not vanish.
It is not that the way of the five phases is lost,
but that metal is much and fire is little,
and the few and many, small and large, are unbalanced.
A five-chǐ child competing with Mèng Bēn
will not win—
not because the child is timid,
but because his strength is small.
Many wolves eat people,
many people eat wolves.
In contests of strength and energy,
it is rare for the small to overcome the large;
in struggles for power and measuring merit,
it is seldom for the few to defeat the many.
The way of heaven and the nature of things mean the small cannot overcome the large,
the few cannot subdue the many.
How can a single metal blade
or a piece of charcoal fire
suppress and remove misfortunes,
or ward off the year's calamities?
How is it possible?
Common people believe in the influences of the year and season,
and also in those of the day.
If in undertaking affairs, they encounter sickness,
death, disaster,
or suffering, they attribute major issues to offending the year
and month, and minor ones to not avoiding daily taboos.
The traditions of the year and month are followed,
and books on daily taboos are also circulated.
Ordinary people
wholeheartedly believe in them;
even debaters
cannot settle the matter.
Thus, when people undertake affairs,
they do not examine their hearts but conform to the day,
not consider righteousness but adhere to the hour.
Books on timing and days
are numerous and varied;
briefly citing the more prominent ones,
to clarify their right and wrong,
so that those who believe in celestial timing
may doubt and turn away from them.
For calamities and blessings come with rise and decline,
alternating naturally.
If an undertaking is called unlucky,
people fear the unluckiness will take effect;
if called lucky,
people hope the luck will be proven.
When calamities or blessings occur on their own,
they recall past predictions of luck or unluckiness
to warn and fear each other.
This is why daily taboos remain unquestioned for generations,
and the confused remain unenlightened for years.
The Burial Almanac states:
"Burial should avoid the Nine Voids,
earthly pits,
and the hard and soft days of the sun,
the odd and even months of the moon."
Auspicious days bring no harm,
when hard and soft match,
odd and even correspond,
then it becomes fortunate and benign.
If it does not align with this almanac,
it turns into ominous evil.
Now burial
is interring the coffin,
while encoffining is storing the corpse.
Initially, the corpse is stored in the coffin upon death,
and shortly after, the coffin is buried in the tomb.
What difference is there between the tomb and the coffin?
What distinction between encoffining and burial?
If encoffining does not avoid inauspiciousness,
why seek only auspiciousness for burial in the tomb?
If the tomb is considered more important,
then the tomb
is earth,
the coffin is wood;
by the nature of the five elements,
wood and earth are equal.
Preparing wood to encase the corpse,
digging earth to bury the coffin,
preparing and digging are similar acts,
the corpse and coffin are one in essence.
If digging earth harms the body of the land,
then digging ditches or plowing gardens
should also require choosing days.
If people can differentiate these matters,
I would heed their prohibitions;
if they cannot differentiate,
I will not follow their taboos.
Not only must the day be harmless,
but also the hardness or softness of the day is sought,
and once hardness and softness match,
the oddness or evenness of the month is demanded.
Now the hardness and softness of the day
and the oddness and evenness of the month,
though they align with the Burial Almanac,
when tested against antiquity,
do not always correspond.
How can this be demonstrated?
During the Spring and Autumn period,
the Son of Heaven,
feudal lords,
ministers, and senior officials died by the hundreds and thousands,
yet examining their burial days,
they未必 aligned with the almanac.
It is also said:
"Rain prevented the burial,
so it was conducted at noon on Gēngyín day."
Suppose the consort of Lǔ died on a hard day,
and the burial day was Jǐchǒu,
then hard and soft were equal.
Hard and soft matching
makes an auspicious day.
The failure to bury
was due to avoiding rain.
If it was an auspicious day,
it should not have been abandoned because of rain
and not used.
Why so?
Rain merely inconveniences the affair;
not using the hard-soft principle
implies greater inauspiciousness and misfortune.
To seek convenience and risk inauspiciousness
was not the intention of the people of Lǔ,
nor the principle of caution by subjects and sons.
Now abandoning the hard-soft rule,
waiting until noon on Gēngyín day,
treats clear weather as auspicious.
The Rites state:
"The Son of Heaven is buried after seven months,
feudal lords after five months,
ministers, senior officials,
and scholars after three months."
Suppose the Son of Heaven passed away in the first month,
buried in the seventh;
if in the second month,
buried in the eighth.
Feudal lords,
ministers, senior officials,
and scholars all follow this.
If verified against the Burial Almanac,
then the burial months of the Son of Heaven
and feudal lords would always be odd or always even.
Decadent ages favor believing in taboos,
and unworthy rulers seek blessings.
The Spring and Autumn period
can be called decadent!
Between the times of Yǐn and Āi,
it was most unworthy!
Yet the days of burial
show no avoided taboos,
due to the absence of such superstitions.
In the era of King Wén of Zhōu,
laws and institutions were complete,
Kǒngzǐ's intentions were meticulous,
the principles in the Spring and Autumn Annals were fine,
yet if abandoning auspiciousness led to misfortune,
or rash actions incurred disaster,
there should be subtle texts and minor principles,
with critical and satirical words.
Now no such principles are seen,
indicating no Burial Almanac method existed.
The almanac for sacrifices
also has auspicious and inauspicious days.
Suppose on days like Xuèjì
or Yuèshā, inherently inauspicious,
if slaughtering animals for sacrifice,
disaster must follow.
Now sacrifice
is offering food to ghosts;
ghosts
are the spirits of dead people.
If not the spirits of the dead,
one has never seen ghosts eat or drink.
Extending the service to the living to the dead,
human affairs to ghosts,
seeing the living need food and drink,
the dead as ghosts should also be able to eat and drink;
moved by objects, thinking of kin,
hence sacrifices are made.
As for sacrifices to other spirits and various ghosts,
though not dead people,
the ritual of serving them
is the same as for the dead.
Since their forms are unseen,
they are approximated with the rites for the living.
The living eat and drink without fixed days,
why should ghosts and spirits have specific days?
If ghosts and spirits truly have consciousness,
no different from people,
then sacrifices should not require choosing days.
If they lack consciousness,
unable to eat or drink,
even if days are chosen and taboos avoided,
what benefit would it bring?
In reality,
no ghosts exist in the hundred sacrifices,
and the dead have no consciousness.
The hundred sacrifices repay merits,
showing no forgetfulness of virtue;
serving the dead as if alive,
showing no betrayal of the departed.
Sacrificing brings no blessings,
not sacrificing brings no harm.
Whether sacrificing or not,
there is neither harm nor blessing,
so how can the auspiciousness or inauspiciousness of days
cause any gain or loss?
If killing animals and seeing blood
requires avoiding Xuèjì
and Yuèshā,
then the living eating the six domestic animals
should also avoid such days.
Butcher shops across the land
slaughter thousands of the six animals daily,
without choosing auspicious or inauspicious times,
yet those dying early
are not necessarily the butchers.
Under heaven, those condemned to death,
with executions in winter months,
also number in the thousands,
and their punishment in the market
does not select auspicious days,
yet those suffering misfortune
are not necessarily the prison officers.
Meat requires slaughtering animals,
prisons necessitate executing prisoners.
Prisoners executed, animals slaughtered,
the reality of wounds and blood
—how does it differ from sacrificial animals?
Why establish an almanac only for sacrifices,
and not set days for butchers
and prison officers?
The intentions of common customs are not consistently logical.
Sacrificing to improper ghosts,
and believing in improper taboos,
holding two errors to seek one blessing,
cannot succeed.
The Washing Book says:
"Washing on a Zǐ day
makes people love you;
washing on a Mǎo day
makes one's hair turn white."
People's love and hate
lie in the beauty or ugliness of one's appearance;
the black or white color of hair
depends on the youth or old age of one's years.
If one were as ugly as Mómǔ,
and washed her hair on a zǐ day,
could she gain affection?
If a fifteen-year-old girl
washed her hair on a mǎo day,
could it turn her hair white?
Moreover, washing hair
removes dirt from the head.
Washing feet removes foot grime,
rinsing hands removes hand dirt,
bathing cleanses bodily filth—
all cleanse impurities from the same body,
their essence is equal.
Feet-washing, hand-rinsing,
and bathing don't require choosing days,
yet hair-washing alone has specific days.
If considering the head most honored,
then bathing also cleanses the face—
the face is part of the head.
If considering hair most honored,
then combing should also require day selection.
Combs are made of wood,
hair-washing uses water—
both water and wood belong to the Five Phases.
Using wood avoids no taboos,
yet using water alone requires day selection.
If water is more honored than wood,
then all water usage should require chosen days.
Yet water isn't as honored as fire—
if honor hierarchy must apply,
then all fire usage should require chosen days.
Moreover, who exactly
gains love from zǐ-day hair washing,
or turns white-haired from mǎo-day washing?
Now zǐ's nature
is water,
mǎo's is wood.
Water isn't lovable,
wood's color isn't white.
Zǐ's animal is the rat,
mǎo's creature is the rabbit.
Rats aren't lovable,
rabbit fur isn't white.
Washing hair on zǐ days—
who makes it lovable?
Washing on mǎo days—
who congeals whiteness?
Thus being so,
hair-washing days hold no fortune or misfortune—
those establishing calendars for hair-washing
cannot be followed.
There are manuals for tailoring clothes,
recording auspicious and inauspicious days.
Making clothes on unlucky days brings disaster,
on lucky days brings blessing.
Now clothing and food both support the human body:
food nourishes internally,
clothing protects externally.
Eating and drinking don't require day selection,
yet clothes-making avoids taboo days—
how can clothing be weightier for the body?
In human affairs, nothing
compares to food's urgency—
hence among the Eight Governmental Affairs, first comes food,
second comes goods.
Clothing
belongs to goods.
If adorning the body signifies honor,
among bodily items
none surpasses the crown.
Crown-making has no prohibitions,
clothes-cutting has taboos—
this neglects the honored,
while scrutinizing the humble.
Furthermore, hair-washing removes head dirt,
crowns adorn the head;
bathing eliminates body grime,
clothing guards against cold.
Hair-washing has taboos,
crowns have none;
bathing lacks fortune/misfortune,
clothing carries advantage/harm.
All belong to one substance,
share the same body—
some deemed good, some evil,
taboos applied unevenly:
commoners' shallow knowledge
cannot grasp reality.
Moreover, clothing ranks below chariots and horses.
In the Nine Bestowals ceremony,
first come chariots and horses,
second comes clothing.
Chariot-making seeks no auspicious hours,
yet clothes-cutting alone demands lucky days—
commoners' priorities
distort true weight and lightness.
Craftsman manuals
require day selection for building houses.
Houses shelter human forms,
dwellings host human bodies—
what harm do they pose to years
and months to require selection?
If gods dislike what shields human bodies,
then fitting chariots,
building boats,
attaching canopies,
and wearing hats should also require day selection.
If gods hate disturbing earth and digging soil,
then digging ditches and plowing gardens
should also need day selection.
Now disturbing earth annoys earth gods—
if earth gods can understand human lack of malice,
merely wanting bodily shelter,
then divine sage-hearts wouldn't rage.
Without rage,
even without day selection,
no disaster follows.
If earth gods cannot comprehend human intent,
but hate being disturbed,
then even with day selection,
what benefit emerges?
Royal law prohibits killing and injuring people—
offenders bear punishment,
even if choosing days to break laws,
they ultimately avoid no guilt.
If not prohibited,
even reckless killing
never enters legal jurisdiction.
Government laws
resemble spirit decrees;
the fault of digging
equals the crime of killing.
Human killing/injuring
doesn't consider day selection—
why should house repair
have taboos?
Also, learning calligraphy avoids bǐng days,
said because Cāngjié died on a bǐng day.
Ritual prohibits music on zǐ
and mǎo days—
because Yīn and Xià fell
on zǐ and mǎo days.
If writing on bǐng days
or making music on zǐ/mǎo days
might not cause disaster,
but honoring deceased kings' death dates
evokes sorrowful remembrance,
making action unbearable.
Taboo-day regulations
resemble bǐng, zǐ,
and mǎo categories—
perhaps having taboos,
but not necessarily misfortune.
Kānyú calendars
list numerous gods—
sages never mentioned them,
philosophers never transmitted them,
likely lacking substance.
Heaven's way is hard to know;
supposing it exists,
on days when gods hold power,
what blessing comes from avoidance?
What misfortune from non-avoidance?
When kings initiate affairs on jiǎzǐ days,
commoners also use them—
if kings hear this,
they don't punish by law.
If kings don't anger at people's non-avoidance,
why should heaven gods alone blame them?
Royal law conducts affairs
based on human feasibility,
not daily fortune/misfortune.
Confucius said:
"Divine for burial grounds and repose there."
The Spring and Autumn Annals record sacrifices
without mentioning day divination.
The Rites state:
"Internal affairs use soft days,
external affairs use hard days."
Hard/soft days caution internal/external,
not using fortune/misfortune to determine blessings/disasters.
It is a common belief to trust in divination,
saying that those who practice turtle shell divination inquire of Heaven,
and those who use milfoil stalks inquire of Earth,
believing the milfoil to be divine and the turtle to be numinous,
with the omens and numbers providing responses.
Thus, they abandon human counsel and turn to divination,
disregarding what is feasible or not to trust in auspicious or inauspicious signs.
Their idea is that Heaven and Earth carefully give answers,
and that the milfoil and turtle are truly spiritual.
But to discuss it based on reality,
divination does not involve questioning Heaven and Earth,
and the milfoil and turtle are not necessarily spiritual.
That they have spirituality
and are used to question Heaven and Earth
is what conventional scholars claim.
How can this be clarified?
Zǐlù once asked Confucius:
"Pig shoulders and sheep legs
can yield omens;
reeds and straws
can produce numbers—
why must we use milfoil and turtle shells?"
Confucius replied:
"Not so.
It is about adopting their names.
The word 'shī' (milfoil)
means 'qí' (elder),
and 'guī' (turtle)
means 'jiù' (aged),
implying that for matters of doubt,
one should consult the elders and the aged."
From this, it follows that
the milfoil is not divine,
the turtle is not numinous;
it is their names that are adopted,
not necessarily their substance.
Without that substance,
we know they lack spirituality;
without spirituality,
we know they do not question Heaven and Earth.
Moreover, where are the mouths and ears of Heaven and Earth that we could question them?
Heaven and humans share the same principles;
to understand Heaven,
one looks to human affairs.
When questioning someone,
if you do not face the person directly
and personally ask their intent,
that intent cannot be known.
If you wish to question Heaven,
Heaven is high,
and its ears are far from humans.
If Heaven has no ears,
it lacks physical form.
Without physical form,
it is but vapor.
Vapor, like clouds and mist,
how could it answer people?
Using milfoil to question Earth,
Earth has a physical form,
no different from humans.
When questioning a person,
if you are not close to their ear,
they will not hear;
if they do not hear,
their mouth will not answer.
To say one questions Heaven
means Heaven is vapor,
incapable of producing omens;
to question Earth
means Earth's ears are too distant
to hear human words.
To believe that Heaven and Earth answer people—
what evidence is there for this?
Humans exist between Heaven and Earth
like lice clinging to a person's body.
If a louse wished to know a person's thoughts
and chirped by their ear,
the person still would not hear.
Why?
Because of the disparity in size
and the barrier in language.
Now, for such tiny beings as humans
to question the vast Heaven and Earth,
how could their voices reach them?
How could Heaven and Earth grasp their intentions?
Some say:
"Humans embody the vapor of Heaven and Earth.
This vapor of Heaven and Earth
resides within the body,
and that is the divine intelligence.
When one is about to divine,
informing the milfoil and turtle,
the divine intelligence hears with ears and speaks with mouth.
As if one's own thoughts,
the divine intelligence from within the chest and abdomen hears and understands the intent.
Thus, by drilling the turtle and sorting the milfoil,
omens appear and numbers manifest."
But when a person uses their divine mind to ponder,
and pondering leads to no resolution,
they then consult the milfoil and turtle.
If the omens and numbers
match their intentions,
then it seems the divine has clearly informed them.
Sometimes one's intention deems something feasible,
yet the omens and numbers are inauspicious;
or the omens and numbers are auspicious,
while one's intention considers it unlucky.
Now, the faculty of thought
is one's own spirit,
and that which produces the omens and numbers
is also one's own spirit.
The spirit within one body,
residing in the chest as thought,
and outside the chest as omens and numbers,
is like a person entering a door to sit
or going out to walk.
Walking and sitting do not change the intent,
exiting and entering do not alter the sentiment.
If the divine intelligence produces the omens and numbers,
it should not differ from one's thoughts.
Heaven and Earth have form,
hence they can move.
That which moves
is of the category of the living.
Being alive, they are similar to humans.
To question the living,
one must use the living
to obtain a response.
If the dead were to question the living,
they certainly could not get an answer.
Now, Heaven and Earth are alive, while the milfoil and turtle are dead;
using the dead to question the living,
how could a response be obtained?
The bones of a dried turtle,
the stems of dead milfoil,
questioning the living Heaven and Earth—
for people to call this the response of Heaven and Earth
is mistaken.
If the milfoil and turtle are like wooden tablets,
and the omens and numbers like written words,
do they resemble a ruler issuing commands?
Then where are the mouth and ears of Heaven and Earth to issue such commands?
Confucius said:
"Does Heaven speak?
The four seasons proceed,
and all things are born."
Heaven does not speak,
so it also does not listen to human words.
The way of Heaven is called spontaneous and non-interfering;
now, for humans to question Heaven and Earth,
and for Heaven and Earth to respond,
would be nature acting purposefully to answer humans.
Examining the text of the Yì Jīng,
observing the method of sorting milfoil,
dividing into two to symbolize Heaven and Earth,
sorting four times to symbolize the four seasons,
and placing the remainder to symbolize the intercalary month—
this uses symbolic resemblance
to establish the hexagram numbers.
How can it be said that Heaven and Earth are answering humans?
In human interactions,
one responds when questioned,
and does not respond if not asked.
Without a request,
knocking on someone's door in vain;
without a question,
arguing pointlessly before someone—
the host will laugh without responding,
or become angry and not answer.
Suppose a diviner
drills a turtle shell without purpose,
sorts milfoil stalks emptily,
mocking Heaven and Earth—
would he still obtain omens and numbers?
Would Heaven and Earth falsely respond?
Or try having someone curse Heaven while divining,
insult Earth while casting stalks,
being extremely immoral—
would he still get omens and numbers?
If the omens and numbers
were from the spirits of Heaven and Earth,
why wouldn't they extinguish the fire,
burn his hand,
make his fingers tremble and numbers chaotic,
causing him physical pain,
and his blood and energy to surge?
Yet they still show him omens and produce numbers—
why would Heaven and Earth not mind the trouble,
and not detest such intentions?
From this, it is clear that
divination does not involve questioning Heaven and Earth,
and the omens and numbers are not responses from Heaven and Earth—
this is evident.
Then divination must also inherently possess auspicious and inauspicious signs.
Some theorists claim these correspond to people's good or evil conduct,
just as auspicious omens respond to goodness,
and disasters follow wickedness.
Whether governance is good or bad,
it is caused by good or evil deeds,
doubting that Heaven and Earth intentionally respond to them.
When virtuous persons drill tortoise shells,
they consistently obtain favorable omens;
when wicked persons manipulate yarrow stalks,
they always get adverse outcomes.
How can this be demonstrated?
King Zhòu, the most wicked ruler,
experienced numerous calamities in his time,
with seventy divinations all yielding inauspicious results,
so Zǔ Yī said:
"Even the great turtle cannot discern any good fortune."
Worthy men were not promoted,
the sacred turtle showed no auspicious signs,
catastrophes frequently occurred,
until King Wǔ of Zhōu received the Mandate.
When Emperor Gāozǔ rose like a dragon,
both Heaven and humanity supported him,
marvelous occurrences were plentiful,
and divinations for the men of Fēng and Pèi
all proved auspicious.
Thus, the substance of virtuous people
attracts nothing but favorable outcomes;
the emergence of wicked people
summons nothing but disgrace.
When Wèi's Shí Tái died,
having no legitimate heir
but six sons by concubines,
they divined to determine his successor.
The oracle stated:
"There will be a sign if one bathes and wears jade."
Five sons all bathed and wore jade.
Shí Qízi said:
"How can one observe parental mourning while bathing and wearing jade?"
He did not bathe or wear jade,
and the omen favored Shí Qízi.
The people of Wèi believed
the turtle possessed knowledge.
But the turtle had no such knowledge—
Shí Qízi knew himself.
Qízi practiced benevolent governance
and spoke wise words;
his speech was wise and his governance good,
hence the clear auspicious sign.
Had they not divined at that time
but consulted the public,
he would still have been praised as virtuous.
Why?
Because human hearts and divine intent align in judging fortune.
This argument seems plausible,
but it does not represent the reality of divination.
Drilling shells and counting stalks naturally produce signs;
the appearance of these signs
inherently contains good or ill fortune,
and people of corresponding fortune
happen to encounter them.
The virtuous coincide with auspicious signs,
the wicked meet with ominous counts,
just as virtuous people walking might encounter fortunate events
or glance upon auspicious objects—
not because these are celestial responses to their virtue.
When the wicked meet with misfortunes on their path,
it is similarly coincidental.
Witnessing good or evil
is not Heaven's deliberate response,
but mere chance encounters.
That divination yields auspicious or ominous signs
belongs to this category of coincidental meetings.
How can this be proven?
When King Wǔ of Zhōu fell ill,
the Duke of Zhōu divined with three turtles.
The Duke said:
"Thus we encountered this good omen."
When Lǔ minister Zhuāng Shū's son Mù Shū was born,
they consulted the Yì Jīng,
obtaining the hexagram Míng Yí changing to Qiān.
The shell divination said
"encountered,"
the stalk divination said
"met,"
indicating obtained through chance meeting,
not caused by good or evil.
Goodness leads to encountering fortune,
wickedness to meeting calamity—
this is the natural way of Heaven,
not contrived for humans.
Extending this argument,
the good or ill omens responding to rulers' governance
are also like this.
When a ruler's virtue encounters worthy times
and peace appropriately prevails,
auspicious marvels coincidentally appear.
With unworthy rulers,
the opposite occurs.
Most people discussing divination
lack genuine understanding.
Some theorists claim tortoise and yarrow can assist governance
but shouldn't be exclusively relied upon.
When drilling shells and counting stalks,
signs immediately appear.
These signs lack fixed interpretations—
diviners generate meanings.
Calling auspicious signs inauspicious,
or ominous counts fortunate,
makes divination ineffective,
leading to claims it's unreliable.
When King Wǔ of Zhōu attacked Zhòu,
divinations indicated
adversity, interpreted as:
"Greatly inauspicious."
But Grand Duke Jiāng pushed aside the stalks and trod on the turtle, saying:
"What can dead bones and dried grass know of misfortune?"
The divination signs themselves
weren't mistaken about fortune;
rather, the interpretation misjudged it,
confusing auspicious and inauspicious.
This confusion
led the Grand Duke to reject them.
Yarrow and turtle divination
resemble sage kings governing;
divinatory signs
parallel royal auspicious responses.
Auspicious responses are unpredictable,
divination signs mysterious.
Mystery confuses diviners,
unpredictability makes critics doubtful.
Doubt leads to calling peace disorder,
confusion to deeming fortune ill.
How to prove this?
Auspicious signs
can be encountered by good people;
encountering portents during orderly rule
testifies to sagely virtue.
When the Zhōu king attacked Zhòu,
he encountered the raven and fish omens—
why then did his divination meet inauspicious signs?
If King Wǔ shouldn't have risen,
he shouldn't have encountered omens;
if destined to prosper,
his divination shouldn't have yielded ill fortune.
Thus,
King Wǔ's divination
didn't truly obtain inauspicious readings—
calling it ominous
distorted reality.
When Lǔ prepared to attack Yuè,
divination yielded
"the cauldron's leg breaks."
Zǐgòng interpreted this as ominous,
reasoning:
"A cauldron with broken legs
cannot stand while moving,
hence inauspicious."
But Confucius interpreted it as auspicious,
saying:
"The Yuè people dwell on water,
traveling by boat,
not using legs,
hence auspicious."
Lǔ attacked Yuè
and indeed conquered it.
Zǐgòng's interpretation of the broken leg as ominous
resembles the Zhōu diviners calling signs adverse.
Within adversity lies fortune,
just as the broken cauldron interpretation
suited attacking Yuè.
The world has many like Zǐgòng with straightforward interpretations,
but few with Confucius' ingenious reasoning talent,
so when unusual signs appear,
they cannot properly discern them.
Because King Wǔ's divination
showed ill omens without cause,
people claim divination cannot be fully trusted,
but should partially assist governance,
demonstrating spiritual presence
and preventing arbitrary rule.
Authors who compile records
gather accounts of events,
such as Han Fei's chapter "Exposing Deceptions",
which demonstrates proven evidence,
denouncing turtle shell divination and milfoil stalk prognostication,
criticizing their worldly credence.
Divination is not unusable;
rather, it is the diviner's misinterpretation.
The "Great Plan" examines doubts,
and when divination yields variable results,
it necessarily consults the Son of Heaven and his ministers.
Sometimes the interpretation is accurate.
When one fails to interpret correctly,
and the omens prove unreliable,
then it is claimed that divination cannot be trusted.
When Duke Wén of Jìn battled the Viscount of Chǔ,
he dreamed of wrestling with King Chéng,
who was on top sucking his brains.
The diviner declared:
"Inauspicious."
But Jiù Fǎn said:
"Auspicious!
You have gained heaven's favor,
while Chǔ submits to its guilt.
Sucking your brains
signifies submission."
They indeed won the battle,
as Jiù Fǎn had interpreted.
Interpreting dreams is like interpreting turtle shells.
The Jìn dream-interpreter failed to see the omen's meaning,
just as the Zhōu shell-diviner missed the crack's significance.
Omens are never incorrect,
and cracks never unclear;
it is human understanding that is obscure,
and interpretations that miss the truth.
Some traditions say:
"When King Wǔ attacked Zhòu,
he consulted the turtle shell, which cracked unfavorably."
The diviner said:
"Inauspicious."
But Tài Gōng declared:
"The unfavorable crack
means inauspicious for sacrifice,
but victorious for battle."
King Wǔ followed him,
and ultimately conquered Zhòu.
If this account is true,
it again resembles Confucius discussing hexagrams
and Jiù Fǎn interpreting dreams.
For omens are never incorrect,
yet auspiciousness and inauspiciousness are misjudged
due to unskillful interpretation.
Common people believe in baleful influences,
thinking that human illness, death,
suffering misfortune, incurring guilt,
humiliation, and ridicule
all stem from some offense.
Initiating projects,
moving residences,
sacrifices,
funerals,
travel,
assuming office,
and marriages—if not done on auspicious days,
avoiding prohibitive years and months,
they fear encountering ghosts and gods,
violating taboos to their harm.
Hence, illnesses arise, misfortunes occur,
legal violations bring punishment,
leading to death,
family ruin, and extermination,
all blamed on carelessness
and violating taboos.
But in truth,
this is nonsense.
All people in this world
must act;
after acting,
outcomes inevitably follow.
Seeing good fortune, they attribute it to previously choosing dates;
seeing misfortune, they blame it on past taboo violations.
Yet often, choosing dates brings disaster,
while violating taboos yields good fortune.
Practitioners of these arts, to promote their methods,
see misfortunes and taboos but remain silent,
hear of blessings but conceal them,
accumulating fears to intimidate the careless,
listing blessings to encourage timeliness.
Thus, all people—foolish or wise,
worthy or unworthy,
rulers or commoners—
fear and believe in them,
daring not to transgress.
Over time,
none can discern the truth,
considering it the way of heaven and earth,
the method of sages.
Rulers cherish their positions,
people love their lives,
so they follow and believe,
without doubt.
Thus, when rulers undertake affairs,
diviners fill the court;
when people act,
they consult times to avoid harm.
Deceptive texts and false writings
proliferate therefrom.
Cunning schemes arise,
contrived wisdom seeks profit,
bewildering the foolish and ignorant,
exploiting the rich and cheating the poor,
further deviating from ancient laws and the sage's true intent.
When sages initiate affairs,
they first establish righteousness;
righteousness determined,
they then decide by divination,
showing they do not act arbitrarily,
but align with the spirits' shared intent,
ensuring the people trust without doubt.
Thus, the "Documents" list seven divinations,
the "Changes" record eight trigrams,
yet following them does not guarantee fortune,
nor violating them necessarily bring disaster.
For fortune and misfortune arrive
by timing;
life and death come
by fate.
Human life hangs on heaven,
auspiciousness and inauspiciousness reside in timing.
If fate is short, even good conduct cannot prolong it;
heaven cannot extend it.
If fate is long, even evil deeds cannot shorten it;
heaven cannot take it away.
Heaven is master of all spirits.
Morality, benevolence, and righteousness
are heaven's way;
trembling and fear
are heaven's heart.
Abandoning the way and destroying virtue
defiles heaven's path;
narrow-mindedness and willfulness
defy heaven's intent.
In history, none lacked morality more
than Jié
and Zhòu; none acted more recklessly
than Yōu
and Lì, yet Jié
and Zhòu did not die early,
Yōu and Lì did not perish young.
Thus, it is clear
that encountering fortune and joy
does not depend on choosing days or avoiding times;
suffering disaster and misfortune
does not stem from violating years or months.
This is evident.
Confucius said:
"Life and death are governed by fate,
wealth and honor depend on Heaven."
If there were indeed auspicious times,
and truly calamitous influences,
why would the sage refrain from speaking of them?
Why would he fear to discuss them?
Examining ancient records and documents,
the safety and danger of officials,
thousands of rulers and myriad ministers,
their successes and failures, fortunes and misfortunes,
the heights and lows of official positions,
the rise and fall of ranks and emoluments,
each had its different grade.
Households managing their livelihoods,
poverty and wealth, gains and losses,
long and short lifespans,
each had its varying degrees.
It is not that the high and great, noble and honored, conduct affairs on auspicious days,
while the low and small, humble and mean, do so at inauspicious times.
Reasoning from this,
we also know that misfortune, fortune, life, and death,
do not lie in encountering auspicious signs,
or violating inauspicious taboos.
Thus, when a person is born,
it is through the nurturing of vital energy;
when a person dies,
it is because fate has reached its end.
When a person is born,
it is not necessarily by obtaining good fortune or encountering joy;
when they die,
why uniquely call it violating inauspiciousness or transgressing taboos?
Using Confucius as evidence,
and discussing it in terms of life and death,
we then also know that the hundred misfortunes and thousand calamities,
are not caused by one's actions.
Confucius was a sage,
one who understood government,
life and death
are great matters,
and great matters
are manifestations of the Way.
Confucius said:
"Life and death are governed by fate,
wealth and honor depend on Heaven."
Numerous texts and subtle words cannot overturn this,
vulgar people and ignorant men cannot change it,
this is clear.
For humans in the world,
misfortune and fortune are governed by fate;
human conduct and actions,
also bring about their own consequences.
If one dwells in peace without action,
misfortune and fortune come of themselves,
that is fate;
if one undertakes tasks and initiates works,
good and bad fortune befall the person,
that is due to human effort.
Human illnesses
rarely occur without being due to wind, dampness, or diet.
Sleeping in drafts and dampness,
then grasping coins to inquire of malign influences;
overeating and indulging in food,
then fasting and refining to resolve misfortune,
yet the illness is not cured,
they say the malign influence was not obtained;
fate naturally ends,
they say the divination was inaccurate,
such is the knowledge of vulgar people.
Now, there are three hundred sixty kinds of naked creatures,
and humans are their chief.
Humans are beings,
the ones with wisdom among the myriad things.
They receive their mandate from Heaven,
inherit their energy from the origin,
no different from other beings.
Birds have nests to roost in,
beasts have dens and caves,
insects, fish, shelled and scaly creatures,
each have their own domains,
just as humans have houses, mansions, and towers.
Among creatures that can move,
death, injury, sickness, and distress,
the small and large harm each other.
Some are caught by humans,
to fill their stomachs,
not because they built nests or dug burrows and thereby transgressed something,
or moved east or west and thereby violated something.
Humans have life and death,
beings also have beginnings and ends;
humans have daily activities,
beings also have movements and actions.
Blood vessels,
head and feet,
ears and eyes,
nose and mouth are no different from humans',
only their likes and dislikes differ from humans',
so humans cannot understand their sounds,
and do not see their intentions!
But when they move among their own kinds,
interact with their own species,
their knowledge of advancing and withdrawing,
is no different from humans.
Sharing the same heaven and earth,
together looking up to the sun and moon,
yet the calamities from ghosts and spirits,
uniquely fall upon humans,
not upon other beings,
the reason for this is not understood.
Among the natures of heaven and earth,
humans are the most noble,
could it be that Heaven's calamities are made for the noble,
and not set for the lowly?
Why, when their natures and kinds are the same, are their misfortunes and disasters different?
"Punishments do not extend up to senior officials,"
showing the sage kings' breadth towards the noble.
If sage kings punish the lowly but not the noble,
and ghosts and spirits bring calamity to the noble but not disaster to the lowly,
this is not what the "Yì" means by
"the great man aligns his good and bad fortune with ghosts and spirits."
Sometimes if one offends,
confronts the county authorities,
and becomes entangled in criminal law,
it is not said to be due to fault,
but that the family has incurred a debt.
If one is not cautious in dwelling,
or excessive in eating and drinking,
it is not said to be lack of proper regulation,
but that moving violated the timing.
If deaths occur in succession,
with coffins for burial reaching ten,
it is not said to be due to contaminated energies,
but that the burial day was inauspicious.
If something happens, it is attributed to a violation;
if nothing is done, it is attributed to the dwelling place.
Residing in a declining house causes loss,
flying calamities and floating corpses,
gather in people's living quarters,
then they pray to ancestors,
to suppress misfortune and dispel disaster.
When ill, they do not call a doctor,
when troubled, they do not cultivate conduct,
but attribute everything to misfortune,
calling it violation and transgression.
Using knowledge that is shallow and sketchy,
and tracing events unrealistically,
such is the capability of vulgar people.
Those who are bound in penal servitude under the Minister of Works,
it is not necessarily because the day they faced the officials was inauspicious,
but because the time of their confinement and labor was unlucky.
If a murderer were to choose an auspicious day to appear before the officials,
confess the crime,
and select a favorable time to enter prison and be bound,
could that possibly resolve the matter,
or bring about a pardon?
One does not encounter misfortune without provoking it,
and without incurring guilt, one does not enter prison.
Once the pardon order arrives,
shackles are removed and one walks straight out—
it is not necessarily due to any ritual that removed the inauspiciousness.
Under heaven, there are a thousand prisons,
and in them, ten thousand prisoners;
their actions are not necessarily in violation of taboos.
Those holding office and drawing salaries,
governing cities and towns,
number in the tens of millions,
yet their transfers do not necessarily coincide with auspicious times.
The capital of Lìyáng
sank overnight to become a lake,
but its people were not necessarily all offenders against the year or
month.
When Gāozǔ first rose,
Fēng and Pèi were both exempted from taxes,
yet their people were not necessarily all cautious about dates.
When Xiàng Yǔ attacked Xiāng'ān,
not a soul was left alive in Xiāng'ān,
yet it was not necessarily due to lack of sacrificial prayers.
When the Zhào army was buried alive by Qín at Chángpíng,
four hundred thousand perished simultaneously,
but when they left home,
they might not have failed to choose an auspicious time.
On chén days, one does not weep,
lest it lead to repeated bereavements.
For those who die on wù or jǐ days,
the corpse may be followed by others.
Yet when an entire family is wiped out,
the day the first one died
may not necessarily be chén, wù, or
jǐ.
On blood taboo days, no livestock is slaughtered,
yet butcher shops do not suffer more disasters;
on the first day of the month, no assemblies are held,
yet taverns do not incur misfortunes.
Corpses exposed on the roads
are not necessarily there because they set out on a 'departure to death' day;
coffins in homes
are not necessarily returned on a 'return taboo' day.
From this perspective,
all those who divine misfortunes and calamities
are unreliable;
those who trust them
should not be considered correct.
Suppose ten people
live in one house,
without moving a spade,
without changing residence,
conducting sacrifices and weddings
only on chosen auspicious days,
from spring to winter,
never violating taboos—
can it be that these ten people, even after a hundred years,
will not die?
Diviners will surely say again:
"Houses have their prosperous and declining phases,
like 'year breach' or
'direct talisman',
which they failed to avoid."
If that is so,
then repeatedly consult the experts in techniques,
stay when the house is prosperous,
and avoid it when it declines,
and for 'year breach'
or 'direct talisman',
move the whole family each time—
after a hundred years,
can they avoid death?
Diviners will surely say again:
"Moving may clash with the timing,
coming and going is inauspicious."
If that is so,
again, repeatedly consult the experts in techniques,
move when it is permissible to go,
return when it is permissible to come back—
after a hundred years,
can they avoid death?
Diviners will surely say again:
"Their allotted lifespan has ended."
If that is so,
then human life and death
ultimately have their own destiny,
not caused by clashing with the year or
month,
nor resulting from violating taboos and inauspicious signs.
Common people have apprehensive hearts,
prone to believe in taboos,
while even the wise are doubtful,
unable to ascertain the truth.
Thus, the refined scholars yield,
and the technicians prevail.
Books on auspicious and inauspicious signs
usurp the meaning of classics;
the theories of technicians
override the discussions of the refined scholars.
Now, to briefly argue based on facts,
for the world to observe,
to examine right and wrong comprehensively,
to make the world awaken at once.
The "Method of Moving" states:
"Moving toward Tàisuì,
is inauspicious; moving away from Tàisuì,
is also inauspicious."
Moving toward Tàisuì is called 'beneath the year',
moving away from Tàisuì is called 'breach of the year',
hence both are inauspicious.
Suppose Tàisuì is in the zǐ position,
then no one under heaven should move north or south,
and building houses or marrying should also avoid it.
Moving east or west,
or to the four corners,
as if moving accordingly,
is all auspicious.
Why?
Because it does not clash with Tàisuì,
nor confront Tàisuì directly.
Let me ask plainly:
What is the reason for avoiding Tàisuì?
Does Tàisuì dislike people moving?
Then all who move should meet with disaster;
if Tàisuì does not prohibit movement,
does it dislike people confronting it?
Then all travelers on the road,
going north or south, should suffer calamity.
The intention of Tàisuì
is like the mind of a senior official.
If a senior official is on the road,
and someone walks into his carriage and horses,
disturbing his retinue,
the official may get angry—
but would he blame only those
carrying utensils or moving households,
while not reproaching others?
In the past, when Emperor Wén went out
and crossed the Bàlíng bridge,
a man encountered the imperial procession
and hid under the bridge.
Thinking the Emperor's carriage had passed,
he rushed out quickly
and startled the imperial horses.
Emperor Wén was angry
and handed him over to his court minister Zhāng Shìzhī.
Shìzhī pronounced judgment.
If the spirit of Tàisuì were to emerge like Emperor Wén,
then those who offend it
would surely be like the man who ran out from under the bridge.
Now, when people traveling on roads
die suddenly from drowning or falling,
how can we know it is not from encountering Tàisuì's emergence?
As for those who move,
they cannot determine
whether they have offended or not.
If it cannot be determined,
then whether Tàisuì is active or not
cannot be verified.
Moreover, does the Grand Year Deity actually move about?
Then it should follow a winding path,
not simply proceed straight north-south.
When senior officials leave their residences,
their movements involve turns.
Would a celestial deity really travel straight without any bends?
Then those moving from east to west,
or along the four diagonals,
would still offend it.
If senior officials travel north-south,
and people pass from east to west,
or move along the four diagonals similarly,
it would still constitute a collision.
If it's not aligned exactly north-south,
how could north-south movement offend it?
If the Grand Year doesn't move at all,
then it should have palaces and fortresses,
not interacting with people -
how could anyone possibly collide with it?
If the Grand Year has no physical form,
differing from senior officials,
like mist, clouds, or rainbows,
stretching straight across heaven and earth,
aligned precisely along the north-south axis,
then east-west movement,
or movement along the four diagonals,
would still offend it.
Just like people nowadays walking into dense fog or miasma -
regardless of direction, all get afflicted.
If it truly resembles such vapors,
people should be able to see it,
and even without moving,
all would still be afflicted.
Furthermore, the Grand Year
is a separate celestial deity,
no different from the Azure Dragon.
The dragon's body measures only several thousand zhang;
if deities should be enormous,
let's generously say tens of thousands of zhang,
enough to cover the northern region -
then we should say the Grand Year is in the north,
not say
"in zǐ".
To its east lies chǒu,
to its west lies hài,
clearly showing it doesn't exclusively cover the north;
its span reaching east and west's breadth
is evident.
Now specifically saying it's at the zǐ position,
only those precisely aligned north-south at zǐ-wǔ cannot move north-south;
those due east at chǒu
and sì locations,
and those due west at hài
and wèi areas,
why can't they move north-south?
Residents of chǒu and hài territories,
if the Grand Year extends left and right,
cannot move north-south or east-west.
Why?
Chǒu lies east of zǐ,
hài lies west of zǐ;
east-west movement by chǒu and hài residents
would collide with the Year's position;
east-west movement by sì and wèi residents
would violate the Year's destructive force.
Confucian scholars describe the world's nine provinces,
considering east, west, north, south,
covering the land's full breadth and length,
five thousand li within the nine provinces,
centered around the Three Rivers region.
When the Duke of Zhōu divined for the capital,
the Classic says:
"The king came to succeed God,
submitting himself at the earth's center."
Luòyì is thus the earth's center.
Zōu Yǎn argued
that within the nine provinces' five thousand li,
they combine into one province,
located in the southeast position,
named Chìxiàn Shénzhōu.
Beyond this exist nine such nine-province systems,
nine times nine making eighty-one,
totaling eighty-one provinces.
This statement is probably false.
Landforms are hard to verify,
but even if they exist,
it presents another difficulty.
If the world's nine provinces
follow the Confucians' view,
directly south of Luòyì,
north of the Three Rivers region,
only Yùzhōu,
Jīngzhōu,
and Jìzhōu territories would have the Grand Year.
Between Yōng and Liáng,
in Qīng, Yǎn,
Xú, and Yáng lands,
how could the Grand Year exist?
If following Zōu Yǎn's theory,
then the world's nine provinces lie southeast,
not aligned with zǐ
or wǔ - how could the Grand Year exist?
If the Grand Year isn't at heaven and earth's extremes,
but scattered among the populace,
then every household
would have a Grand Year,
and even without north-south movement,
people would still collide with it.
Suppose moving from east village to west village -
the west village has a Grand Year;
moving from east residence to west residence -
the west residence has a Grand Year.
Whether east or west of people,
or north or south of people,
it's like traveling on roads
where all directions bring collisions.
With Grand Year positions numbering millions and billions,
all moving people under heaven would meet misfortune -
how could relocators possibly verify this?
If it truly stands between heaven and earth,
like the king's position at the earth's center,
when easterners
draw bows shooting west,
no one calls it shooting at the king,
since arrows cannot reach the king's capital,
only reaching their local target.
Now can relocation reach the Grand Year's position?
Stopping within a hundred paces,
how can this be called harming the Grand Year?
Moreover, relocating families avoid north-south movement
because the Year occupies zǐ position,
zǐ destroys wǔ;
north-south movers
collide with its opposing force,
hence deemed unlucky.
Now destruction
requires something to smash with.
If there actually exists such means,
then even non-movers
would all suffer destruction;
if no such means exists,
how can it destroy?
Thunder,
a celestial force,
splits things in midsummer,
shattering trees and mountains,
sometimes suddenly killing people.
If the Grand Year's destruction
resembles violent thunder,
then the sound should be swift,
and deaths sudden;
if unlike thunder,
it cannot destroy.
If collision itself constitutes destruction,
how can mere collision cause destruction?
East and west oppose each other,
while north and south conflict with each other.
If opposition necessarily means misfortune,
then east-west would always be unlucky,
and north-south always bad.
If because the Grand Year is divine,
only its opposition is unlucky,
nothing surpasses heaven and earth in divinity,
yet heaven and earth oppose each other -
then no living person could exist between them.
The twelve deities on the cosmograph,
Dēngmíng,
Cóngkuí and their kind,
technicians call them all celestial deities,
constantly positioned at zǐ,
chǒu locations,
all possessing opposing forces;
though less divine than the Grand Year,
they should cause minor harm.
Relocators avoiding the Grand Year's misfortune
would still encounter the twelve deities' harm -
why don't those
timing
relocations
prohibit this?
The winter's qi is cold,
being water,
and the position of water is in the north.
The summer's qi is hot,
being fire,
and the position of fire is in the south.
Considering that autumn and winter are cold,
while spring and summer are hot,
this is universal under heaven,
not solely due to the opposition of water and fire in the northern and southern directions.
Now, the position of Tàisuì is merely at zǐ,
yet all under heaven is subject to Tàisuì,
not only the opposition between zǐ and wǔ.
If we carefully take the established position as primary,
then wǔ can represent great summer,
and zǐ can represent great winter.
Would those moving north or south in winter or summer
necessarily encounter misfortune?
At the beginning of spring,
Gèn is in its kingly phase,
Zhèn is in its ministerial phase,
Xùn is in its embryonic phase,
Lí is in its submerged phase,
Kūn is in its dead phase,
Duì is in its imprisoned phase,
Qián is in its abandoned phase,
Kǎn is in its resting phase.
The opposition to the kingly phase is death,
the opposition to the ministerial phase is imprisonment;
in positions opposing the kingly and ministerial phases,
there are qi of death
and imprisonment.
The six children of Qián and Kūn
are the proper way of heaven and earth,
with Fúxī
and Wénwáng using their symbols to govern the world.
Their writings are recorded in the classics,
and their ways are trusted by sages,
clearly examined in relation to Tàisuì.
Some people move northeast at the beginning of spring,
reaching below Gèn,
without suffering harm or misfortune.
If Tàisuì is positioned at zǐ,
and they move northeast,
the Kūn trigram is near wǔ,
similar to Gèn with Kūn;
moving and touching the zǐ position,
why should it alone be considered inauspicious?
The first month is established at yín,
and broken at shēn;
moving from yín
or shēn,
those who act accordingly
encounter no harm or misfortune.
Tàisuì does not point to wǔ,
yet it is baselessly called the year's breach;
wǔ actually holds no misfortune or disaster,
yet prohibitions on north-south movement are groundlessly imposed—
is this not absurd?
Twelve months make a year,
with the four seasons completing their cycles,
and the yin and yang qi reaching their ends,
then starting again as a new year;
it is merely a name for the accumulation of days and months,
so why should there be a deity said to stand at the zǐ position?
Accumulated moments form a day,
accumulated days form a month,
connected months form a season,
and concluded seasons form a year.
A year is thus of the same category as days,
months,
and seasons.
If a year has a deity,
then should days, months,
and seasons also have deities?
One thousand five hundred and thirty-nine years form a tǒng,
and four thousand six hundred and seventeen years form a yuán.
A year is like tǒng
and yuán.
If a year has a deity,
should tǒng and yuán also have deities?
Upon discussion, I believe there are none.
Even if they existed,
why would they harm people?
No deity surpasses heaven and earth,
yet heaven and earth do not harm people.
People speak of hundreds of deities,
but these hundreds of deities do not harm people.
The qi of Tàisuì
is the qi of heaven and earth;
why would it bear hatred towards people,
causing harm upon contact?
Moreover, the text says:
