"On jiǎzǐ days, do not move."
This means jiǎ and zǐ are distinct positions;
when Tàisuì stands at zǐ, it does not reside at jiǎ.
For those moving residences,
if they are redirected and again reside at jiǎ,
or after acting, again reside at jiǎ,
then for movers,
prohibitions on east-west movement should also apply.
Jiǎ and zǐ are equivalent,
so their inauspiciousness should be the same.
Not prohibiting jiǎ
but solely fearing zǐ
makes the rules for movers
utterly baseless and unusable.
People in their dwellings cannot avoid moving,
moving cannot avoid touching the year,
and touching the year cannot avoid dying in due time.
Craftsmen and diviners, seeing people die today,
attribute the misfortune to past moves.
With common minds fearful and insecure,
and deaths never ceasing,
the tales of Tàisuì are passed down through generations without fading.
The art of dwelling divination states:
"There are eight techniques for dwellings,
using the names of the six jiǎ,
to number and rank them;
once the ranking is fixed and names established,
gōng and shāng are distinctly separated.
Dwellings have the five notes,
and surnames have the five sounds.
If a dwelling does not suit the surname,
and the surname conflicts with the dwelling,
then illness, death,
crime, and encountering misfortune will follow."
I question this:
Humans in the realm between heaven and earth
are the most noble among all things.
That they have dwellings
is like birds having nests
and beasts having dens.
If dwellings are said to have jiǎ and yǐ,
do nests and dens also have jiǎ and yǐ?
The deities of jiǎ and yǐ
are solely in people's homes;
why are they not in the nests and dens of birds and beasts?
That people have dwellings
is like having fields;
with fields, they eat and drink,
with dwellings, they reside and dwell.
Among what people value,
nothing is more urgent than food,
so fields come before dwellings,
and fields are more important than dwellings.
The paths between fields
could be governed by the eight techniques,
and the soil compared to form fields
could be numbered with jiǎ and yǐ.
Why is the technique of jiǎ and yǐ
applied only to dwellings
and not extended to fields?
Within government offices,
official residences adjoin each other;
in form and structure, official residences
are no different from dwellings.
The living quarters of officials
are no different from those of common people.
Why are official residences not ranked by jiǎ and yǐ,
while only dwellings are numbered with jiǎ and yǐ?
Common people's dwellings
are adjacent to those in villages
and towns, connected house to house,
with boundaries joining each other.
Why are villages
and towns not included in the numbering,
but only common people's homes ranked?
Why do the deities of jiǎ and yǐ
reside solely in common people's homes?
The technique of numbering dwellings is not applied to market towns,
nor are streets and alleys numbered with jiǎ and yǐ.
Upon entering the market gate, with its twists and turns,
there are also streets and alleys.
People stay at home day and night,
and spend their mornings and evenings in the market;
in essence, they are the same.
Why are the shops in the market not ranked with jiǎ and yǐ?
Prefectures, commanderies, counties,
and towns are interspersed,
no different from the homes in streets and alleys.
Why are prefectures, commanderies, counties, and towns
not numbered with jiǎ and yǐ?
Did heaven and earth have jiǎ and yǐ at creation,
or did later kings establish jiǎ and yǐ?
If heaven and earth had jiǎ and yǐ from the beginning,
then in ancient times,
when people lived in nests and dens,
with no dwellings or houses,
nor the system of streets and alleys,
where were the deities of jiǎ and yǐ then?
Since dwellings are already assigned to the Jiǎ-Yǐ (甲乙) system,
the Five Elements practitioners should likewise assign days to Jiǎ-Yǐ.
Jiǎ-Yǐ have their heavenly stems and earthly branches,
and these stems and branches have their designated hours.
When stems and branches are matched with hours,
those that are in harmony bring good fortune,
while those that conflict bring misfortune.
Yet when a case is not prosecuted,
it does not necessarily mean added worry or disgrace to the branches.
Matters have their right and wrong,
crimes have their light and heavy penalties,
and when officials judge impartially,
examining the details of the case,
there is no evidence of the stems and branches' influence on fortune or misfortune,
but rather the effect lies in the right or wrong of the matter itself.
For those who rely on stems and branches,
how can they explain this?
King Wǔ achieved victory on a Jiǎzǐ (甲子) day,
while Zhòu suffered defeat on a Jiǎzǐ day.
Both sides had set the same date,
their armies were equally matched,
their flags visible to each other,
both using the same day,
yet one survived and the other perished.
Moreover, Jiǎ and Zǐ are in harmony.
At dawn, the hour was Yín,
and Yín does not conflict with Jiǎzǐ,
yet King Wǔ ultimately defeated Zhòu—
why is that?
The sun
is fire;
in heaven, it is the sun,
on earth, it is fire.
How can this be verified?
When a burning mirror faces the sun,
fire descends from the sky.
From this, it can be said
that fire is the essence of the sun.
The sun has Jiǎ-Yǐ,
but why does fire not have Jiǎ-Yǐ?
There are ten heavenly stems and twelve earthly branches,
and when stems and branches are paired,
thus Jiǎ connects with Zǐ.
What is meant by the ten stems?
What are they exactly?
Are there ten distinct suns?
Or does one sun have ten names?
If there are ten distinct suns,
and Jiǎ-Yǐ are their names,
why not simply refer to them as Jiǎ-Yǐ,
but must mention Zǐ-Chǒu?
In the celestial diagram, Jiǎ-Yǐ have their positions,
Zǐ-Chǒu also have their places,
each with its arrangement,
distributed across the five directions,
like the guards of a king,
constantly stationed without moving.
But the actual sun moves in its course,
rising in the east at dawn,
setting in the west at dusk,
ceaseless in its motion,
differing from the celestial diagram—
how can Jiǎ-Yǐ be considered names for the sun?
Practitioners further explain
that Jiǎ-Yǐ for the sun
are spirits of heaven and earth themselves;
the sun alternates in its influence,
using Jiǎ-Yǐ to determine fortune or misfortune based on victory or defeat,
not as names for the actual sun.
If that is the case,
then for the symbols of the Five Elements,
one should only use Jiǎ-Yǐ to decide fortune or misfortune;
why mention the addition of hours?
Consider the addition of hours—
it refers to the actual sun's timing.
How can the actual sun have victories or defeats?
The Five Tones practitioners
use the mouth's movements to harmonize surnames and personal names,
using the surname to determine the personal name,
and the personal name to rectify the style name.
The mouth opens and closes,
sounds have outer and inner qualities,
thereby determining the substance of the five tones: Gōng and Shāng.
Now, humans having surnames
is due to receiving them from heaven.
Do people receive the qi of the Five Elements to form their surnames?
Or are surnames determined by the mouth's opening and closing,
and the outer and inner qualities of sounds?
If surnames are based on what is received from heaven,
like the five grains and all things receiving qi,
why use the mouth's opening and closing,
and the inner and outer qualities of sounds to determine and rectify them?
In ancient times, surnames were bestowed based on birth,
granted according to the circumstances of one's birth.
For instance, Xià's ancestor swallowed a Job's tear and gave birth,
so the surname was Yìshì (苡氏);
Shāng's ancestor swallowed a swallow's egg and gave birth,
so the surname was Zǐshì (子氏);
Zhōu's ancestor trod in a giant's footprint,
so the surname was Jīshì (姬氏).
As for establishing personal names,
they were based on trust,
righteousness,
resemblance,
borrowing,
or likeness.
Naming based on birth circumstances is trust,
as when the Lǔ prince Yǒu was born,
the character
"Yǒu"
appeared on his hand.
Naming based on virtue is righteousness,
as with King Wén named Chāng,
and King Wǔ named Fā.
Naming based on category is resemblance,
as with Confucius named Qiū.
Borrowing from objects is borrowing,
as with the Sòng duke named Chǔjiù.
Taking from the father is likeness,
indicating similarity to the father.
As for establishing style names,
they expand on the personal name with synonymous meaning,
such as personal name Cì, style name Zǐgòng;
personal name Yǔ, style name Zǐwǒ.
Thus, surnames are based on the origin of birth,
personal names on trust,
righteousness, resemblance,
borrowing, or likeness,
and style names expand on the personal name with synonymous meaning—
not using the mouth's opening and closing,
or the outer and inner qualities of sounds.
The principle of harmonizing Gōng and Shāng for the Five Tones method—
on what basis is it observed and used?
In ancient times, there were original surnames,
and there were clan surnames.
Táoshì (陶氏),
Tiánshì (田氏)—
these are clan surnames based on occupation;
Shàngguānshì (上官氏),
Sīmǎshì (司马氏)—
these are clan surnames based on official posts;
Mèngshì (孟氏),
Zhòngshì (仲氏)—
these are clan surnames based on the grandfather's style name.
Clan surnames have three types:
occupation!,
official post!,
grandfather's style name!
Original surnames use the birth origin,
while clan surnames use occupation,
official post, or grandfather's style name—
what place is there for using mouth movements to harmonize surnames?
The custom of the Xiōngnú (匈奴)
is to have personal names but no surnames
or style names, with nothing to harmonize;
yet they live out their natural lifespans—
where is the influence of fortune or misfortune?
The "Lǐ" (《礼》) says:
"If one buys a concubine and does not know her surname, then divine it."
Not knowing means
not knowing her original surname.
A concubine must have a parental family surname,
yet it is necessary to divine it
because parental surnames can change and lose authenticity.
The "Lǐ" emphasizes avoiding marriage with the same surname,
hence it must be divined.
If surnames were merely harmonized by mouth movements,
then why would the "Lǐ" require divination when buying a concubine?
The Dwellings Chart method states:
"For those with the Shāng tone, the door should not face south;
for those with the Zhǐ tone, the door should not face north."
This is because Shāng corresponds to metal,
and the south corresponds to fire;
Zhǐ corresponds to fire,
and the north corresponds to water.
Water overcomes fire,
fire harms metal—
the qi of the Five Elements are incompatible,
so for dwellings of the five surnames,
doors have appropriate directions.
If the direction is appropriate,
there is wealth, nobility, and prosperity;
if the direction is inappropriate,
there is poverty, low status, and decline.
How does a gate differ from a hall?
The gates of the five surnames,
each have halls corresponding to the five surnames,
so why is there no proper orientation?
The gate covers less ground
than the hall and its corridors,
and the place where one stays day and night
is the hall, not the gate.
Those who chart fortunes and misfortunes
should all base it on the hall.
If it is because people come and go through the gate,
then the door should be considered likewise.
Confucius said:
"Who can go out without passing through a door?"
He spoke of the door, not the gate.
In the sacrifices to the five household gods,
the gate and the door are treated equally.
If one should use the gate to determine the orientation,
then why shouldn't the door correspond to the gate?
Moreover, within government offices today,
the officials' quarters are connected,
with gates facing north or south;
senior officials reside in lodgings,
and their dwellings may face east or west.
The surnames of senior officials
must include Gōng,
or Shāng; the quarters of various officials,
must include Zhǐ,
or Yǔ. Those who secure their posts or get transferred,
are not necessarily Jué surnames with south-facing gates;
those who lose their positions or are demoted,
are not necessarily Shāng surnames with north-facing exits.
Why is it that some secure their posts or get transferred,
while others lose their positions or are demoted?
Surnames have the five notes,
and human nature also has the five phases.
According to the experts of the five notes,
a Shāng surname should not have a south-facing gate,
but for people endowed with the nature of metal,
should they also avoid sitting facing south
or walking southward?
One theory says:
For gates of the five notes,
there are people of the five phases.
Suppose a Shāng surname household has five members,
each with one of the five colors:
the wood person is green,
the fire person is red,
the water person is black,
the metal person is white,
the earth person is yellow.
If these five-colored people
all exit through a south-facing gate,
some may meet misfortune, others good fortune,
some may have short lives, others long.
Those with misfortune and short lives
are not necessarily white in color;
those with good fortune and long lives
are not necessarily yellow.
How do the experts of the five phases
decide this?
If a south-facing gate
harms a Shāng surname family,
how does it actually happen?
The south is
fire,
so if the harm of fire's energy
spreads like flames,
does it come directly from the south?
Then even with a north-facing gate,
it would still be inauspicious.
If the harm of fire's energy
is like the heat of summer,
does it permeate all directions?
Then throughout heaven and earth,
all receive its energy,
so why would only households with south-facing gates
suffer misfortune?
As for fire being associated with the south,
it means fire's position is in the south.
One theory says:
its energy spreads to the four directions,
not that only the south has fire,
and the other directions have none,
just as water's position is in the north,
yet all directions still have water.
Fire fills the world,
water is distributed in all directions,
fire may be to a person's south,
or to a person's north.
To say fire is always in the south
would mean the east could lack metal,
and the west could lack wood?
The world believes in sacrifices,
thinking they must bring blessings;
they also practice exorcisms,
believing they must remove misfortunes.
At the beginning of the exorcism ritual,
sacrifices are first set up.
This is like
living people hosting guests.
First, a meal is prepared for the guests,
after they have eaten,
they are driven away with blades and sticks.
If the ghosts and spirits have awareness,
they would surely be angered and resist,
unwilling to leave directly;
if they hold a grudge,
they may return to cause harm.
If they have no awareness,
they cannot cause misfortune,
so exorcising them is futile,
and not exorcising them does no harm.
Moreover, what do people think ghosts and spirits look like?
If ghosts are said to have form,
resembling living people,
then living people who hold grudges
would surely harm others.
If they have no form,
but are like smoke and clouds,
then driving away smoke and clouds
cannot remove them either.
Since their form cannot be known,
their intentions cannot be guessed.
When ghosts and spirits gather in a person's house,
what do they seek?
If their intent is to kill people,
during the exorcism,
they would hide and avoid people;
once the exorcism stops,
they would return to their original place.
If they do not intend to kill people,
but merely dwell in a house,
even without exorcism,
they would cause no harm.
When a noble person goes out,
countless people gather to watch,
filling the streets and alleys,
pushing forward to get ahead.
If soldiers drive them away,
they retreat and flee;
when the soldiers leave,
they return to their spots;
if soldiers stand guard,
not leaving all day,
they can barely keep them away.
Why is that?
Because their desire is to watch,
not to leave just because they are driven away once.
If ghosts and spirits are like living people,
and have desires in the house,
just as the people have desires to watch,
then unless soldiers drive them away
and stand guard for a long time,
the onlookers will not retreat.
Thus, to drive away ghosts,
unless done for nearly a year,
the ghosts will not leave.
Now, when people perform exorcisms,
it lasts only the time of a meal,
then they stop;
once they stop,
the ghosts return.
How can this restrain them?
If grain is spread in the courtyard,
chickens and sparrows will peck at it;
if the owner drives them away, they flee,
but if left alone, they return.
Unless he stands guard all day,
he cannot keep the chickens and sparrows away.
If ghosts are spiritual,
they will not leave just because they are driven away.
If ghosts are not spiritual,
they are like chickens and sparrows;
unless constantly driven away,
they cannot be restrained.
When tigers and wolves enter the capital,
patrols with bows and crossbows are deployed;
though the tigers and wolves may be killed,
the underlying cause of their arrival remains unresolved.
When bandits attack the city,
government troops strike them;
though the bandits may be repelled,
the calamity that brought them about is not eradicated.
The coming of tigers and wolves
responds to failures in governance;
the arrival of bandits
arises from societal chaos;
similarly, the gathering of ghosts and spirits
is due to the exhaustion of fate.
Killing tigers and wolves,
repelling bandits,
cannot restore good governance or social order;
likewise, performing elaborate exorcisms,
driving away ghosts and spirits,
cannot avert misfortune or prolong life.
When a patient is critically ill,
they may see ghosts approaching;
those of fierce and resolute nature
grasp swords and staffs
to battle the ghosts.
After one or two fights,
they retreat, submit, or surrender,
realizing that without submission,
the struggle cannot end.
The ghosts driven off by exorcisms
are no different from those seen by the sick;
the act of driving them away
is no different from battling them.
If the sick person fights
and the ghosts still do not leave,
how can a homeowner's exorcism
ensure the departure of ghosts and spirits?
From this perspective,
what benefit does exorcising a house
truly offer?
Believing it dispels misfortune
is unfounded.
Moreover, what is being expelled
are guest ghosts within the house.
The host spirits in a dwelling number twelve,
with Qīnglóng
and Báihǔ among them.
These dragon and tiger spirits, fierce and divine,
are the proper ghosts of heaven;
how dare wandering evils and flying corpses recklessly gather?
Just as a brave host
deters treacherous guests from peeping,
with these twelve spirits residing there,
if the homeowner drives them out,
it amounts to expelling the guests of the twelve spirits,
incurring their resentment;
how can this bring good fortune?
If there were no twelve spirits,
there would be no flying corpses or wandering evils either.
With no spirits or evils,
what good is exorcism?
What is being driven away?
The methods of exorcism and expulsion
stem from ancient rites of expelling pestilence.
In the past, Zhuānxū had three sons,
all of whom died young;
one dwelled in the Jiāng River as a cruel ghost,
one in the Ruò River as a phantom,
and one in the Ōu region,
presiding over illnesses and plagues.
Thus, at year's end when tasks were done,
they drove out the plague ghosts,
thereby sending off the old
and welcoming the new,
ushering in auspiciousness.
Generations imitated this,
hence the practice of exorcism arose.
Yet the method of expelling pestilence
is also a deviation from proper rites.
If one practices the virtues of Yáo
and Shùn,
the world is at peace,
all disasters vanish,
and even without expelling pestilence,
plague ghosts do not come;
if one acts like Jié
and Zhòu,
the land falls into turmoil,
countless calamities arise,
and even with daily expulsions,
plague ghosts still arrive.
Decadent ages favor belief in ghosts,
foolish people seek blessings.
In the late Zhōu dynasty,
they trusted ghosts and held sacrifices,
hoping for divine aid and fortune.
Foolish rulers, deluded in heart,
neglected their own conduct,
yet achievements did not follow,
order did not stabilize.
Thus, it lies in people, not ghosts,
in virtue, not sacrifices.
A state's duration has its limits,
human life its length.
If sacrifices could bring fortune,
exorcisms could remove misfortune,
then rulers could exhaust the world's wealth
to perform rites prolonging their reign;
wealthy elders
could seek blessings through exorcisms
to gain life beyond their years.
Yet observe the people of the world:
early death, longevity, nobility, baseness—
all are governed by destiny;
conduct, good or ill—
all follow cycles of rise and fall.
Sacrifices do not bring fortune,
fortune does not come from sacrifices;
the world believes in ghosts and spirits,
hence they favor sacrifices.
Since sacrifices involve no real ghosts or spirits,
the wise do not pursue them.
Sacrifices,
though earnest in serving ghosts and spirits,
show no proof of bringing good fortune;
how much less can employing force and authority,
driving away ghosts and spirits,
offer any benefit?
The rites of sacrifice,
the methods of exorcism,
are numerous and varied,
but let one example reveal their fallacy.
A small sacrifice can represent a great one,
one ghost can signify all spirits.
In society, when building or repairing houses,
digging the ground and excavating earth,
upon completion of the work,
they perform rites to appease the earth spirit,
called
"jiětǔ" (resolving the earth).
They make clay figurines
to represent ghosts and spirits,
have shamans recite prayers,
to appease the earth spirit.
After the sacrifice,
they feel relieved and pleased,
believing the ghosts and spirits are appeased,
and calamities are removed.
But upon examination,
this is mere delusion.
How can this be verified?
The earth is like the human body;
all under heaven
is one entity,
with head and feet separated
by tens of thousands of miles.
People living on the earth
are like fleas and lice on the human body.
Fleas and lice bite people,
harming their skin and flesh,
just as humans dig the earth,
injuring its body.
If the fleas and lice inwardly knew
and wished to appease the person,
gathering together
to offer apologies beside the flesh they've bitten,
could the person be aware of it?
Just as people cannot understand the sounds of fleas and lice,
so the earth cannot comprehend human speech.
People from Hú and Yuè,
with similar ears and mouths,
and akin thoughts,
speaking face-to-face and ear-to-ear,
still may not understand each other;
how much less can humans, who do not resemble the earth,
and whose ears and mouths are vastly different from the earth's, communicate?
Now, is it the earth that is being appeased?
Then the earth's ears are too distant
to hear.
If it's the earth of one house being appeased,
then that patch of earth
is like a small portion of human flesh;
how can it understand?
If it's the house spirit being appeased,
then this should be called
"jiězhái" (resolving the house),
not
"jiětǔ" (resolving the earth).
In rites,
when entering the ancestral temple,
with no definite idea in mind,
they cut a piece of wood one foot two inches long,
call it a "spirit tablet,"
concentrate their minds and serve it,
without making it in human likeness.
Now, in the sacrifice to release the earth,
they make an earthen image,
resembling the form of a ghost.
How can this bring release?
Spirits are vague and without form,
coming and going without a door,
hence they are called spirits.
Now, creating forms and images
contradicts the rites,
losing the true nature of spirits,
so we know it is wrong.
They should resemble cloth offerings,
not set up ghostly forms.
The ritual of releasing the earth
erects an earthen figure;
if one can make a stone form for sacrificing to the mountains,
can one make a wooden figure for sacrificing to the door?
When Zhōng Xíng Yǐn of Jìn was about to perish,
he summoned his Grand Invocator,
intending to punish him,
saying:
"You performed invocations for me;
were the sacrificial animals not plump and glossy?
Or was the fasting not reverent?
That you caused our state to perish—
why is this?"
The invocator Jiǎn replied:
"In the past,
our former lord Zhōng Xíng Mìzǐ had ten chariots,
yet he did not worry about their meagerness,
but worried about insufficient virtue and righteousness.
Now, my lord has a hundred armored chariots,
yet you do not worry about scant virtue and righteousness,
only fretting that the chariots are too few.
When boats and chariots are adorned, taxes become heavy;
when taxes are heavy, the people curse and execrate.
If you think invocations benefit the state,
then curses would also lead to its ruin!
With one person invoking blessings,
and a whole state cursing,
one invocation cannot overcome ten thousand curses—
the state's demise,
is it not fitting?
What crime has the invocator?"
Zhōng Xíngzǐ then felt ashamed.
Those in the present age who believe in sacrifices
are of the same kind as Zhōng Xíngzǐ.
They do not cultivate their conduct but enrich their invocations,
do not revere their superiors but fear their ghosts;
when death and disaster come,
they attribute it to hauntings,
saying the haunting was not addressed;
upon addressing the hauntings with sacrifices,
if disasters continue unceasingly,
they blame the sacrifices,
saying they were not reverent enough.
Now, discussing exorcism,
exorcism brings no benefit;
discussing sacrifices,
sacrifices offer no remedy;
discussing shamans and invocators,
shamans and invocators have no power.
It lies in humans, not ghosts,
in virtue, not sacrifices—
how clear this is!
The world believes in sacrifices,
thinking those who sacrifice will surely have blessings,
and those who do not sacrifice will surely have misfortune.
Thus, when illness strikes, they divine for hauntings;
upon finding the hauntings, they perform sacrifices;
after sacrificing, their anxiety eases;
with eased anxiety, the illness ceases—
they insist that sacrifices helped,
and diligently continue them without end.
They claim the dead have consciousness,
that ghosts and spirits eat and drink,
like hosting guests;
if the guests are pleased,
they repay the host's kindness.
That they perform sacrifices
is correct;
but believing the spirits enjoy them
is wrong.
In reality,
the intention of sacrifices
is for the host to express their earnest devotion,
but ghosts and spirits may not necessarily enjoy them.
How to clarify this?
Now, sacrifices are made to repay merits,
based on the sense of gratitude among the living;
how can there be enjoyment?
Now, they sacrifice to the dead,
but the dead have no consciousness,
unable to eat or drink.
How can we be sure they cannot enjoy the food and drink?
Heaven is a substance,
a body,
the same as Earth.
Heaven has its constellations,
Earth has its dwellings;
dwellings adhere to Earth's body,
constellations attach to Heaven's form.
With a body formed,
then having a mouth, it can eat.
If Heaven and Earth had mouths to eat sacrifices,
they should eat them all.
If they have no mouths,
then they have no bodies;
without bodies, they are but ether,
like clouds and mist,
and also cannot eat.
If Heaven and Earth have spirits,
like humans having spirits,
with human spirits,
how should they eat and drink?
An average human body is seven or eight feet tall,
four or five arm-spans in girth,
eating a peck of food,
drinking a peck of soup,
to be full and satisfied;
some may consume three or four pecks.
Heaven and Earth's vastness measures in tens of thousands of miles;
on the circular mound,
a calf thin as a cocoon,
millet sweets and grand soup,
amount to no more than a few hu;
with this to feed Heaven and Earth,
how could Heaven and Earth be full?
Heaven and Earth's intent
is like human intent;
if humans eat without being full,
they resent the host,
and do not repay with virtue.
If one insists that Heaven and Earth can truly eat their fill,
then the ancients who performed suburban sacrifices cheated Heaven and Earth.
Mountains are like the skeletal joints of a person,
and waters are like the blood vessels of a person.
Thus, when a person eats and their intestines are full,
their skeletal joints and blood vessels thereby flourish.
Now, when sacrificing to Heaven and Earth,
the mountains and rivers are sated along with them.
Yet now, to separately sacrifice to mountains and rivers,
considering them as different deities,
is like a person eating their fill
and then additionally eating their skeletal joints and blood vessels.
Shèjì (the gods of soil and grain)
repay the merit of producing grains
and other things.
All things are born from Heaven and Earth,
just as fine hairs grow from the body.
When sacrificing to Heaven and Earth,
Shèjì is included within that;
but rulers value it,
so they again sacrifice to it separately.
If one must consider it to have spirits,
then a person's skin and flesh should likewise be eaten again.
The five sacrificial rites (to door, gate, well, stove, and middle room) originally stem from the earth:
doors and gates use wood and soil,
wood and soil are born from the earth;
wells, stoves,
and the middle room's eaves all belong to the earth.
When sacrificing to the earth,
the five sacrificial rites are included within that;
but rulers value them,
so they again sacrifice to them separately.
If one must consider them to have spirits,
then after eating, one should again eat their physical form.
The Earl of Wind,
the Master of Rain,
and the Duke of Thunder
are among the multitude of spirits.
Wind is like a person having exhalation,
rain is like a person having essence and fluids,
and thunder is like a person having stomach rumblings.
These three adhere to Heaven and Earth;
when sacrificing to Heaven and Earth,
these three are present;
but rulers value them,
so they again sacrifice to them separately.
If one must consider them to have spirits,
then a person's exhalation,
essence and fluids,
and stomach rumblings should likewise be eaten again.
The sun and moon are like a person having eyes,
and the stars are like a person having hair.
The three lights (sun, moon, stars) adhere to Heaven;
when sacrificing to Heaven,
the three lights are present;
but rulers value them,
so they again sacrifice to them separately.
If one must consider them to have spirits,
then after a person eats,
they should again eat their eyes and hair.
Ancestral temples
concern one's own ancestors.
While they were alive,
they were carefully and reverently provided for;
after death, one dares not be unfaithful,
so one performs sacrifices,
following the principle of serving the dead as they were served in life,
to show one does not forget their forebears.
The Five Emperors and Three Sovereigns made suburban and ancestral sacrifices to Huángdì,
Dì Kù, and others,
repaying their merits and honoring their efforts,
not daring to forget their virtue—
this does not necessarily mean there are ghosts and spirits that truly can enjoy the offerings.
If they cannot enjoy the offerings,
then they cannot be divine;
if they cannot be divine,
then they cannot bring blessings,
nor can they bring calamities.
The arising of calamities and blessings
stems from joy and anger;
the expression of joy and anger
stems from the stomach and intestines.
Those who have stomach and intestines can eat and drink;
if they cannot eat and drink, they have no stomach or intestines;
without stomach and intestines, they have no means for joy and anger;
without means for joy and anger, they have no means to cause calamities or blessings.
Some say:
"They enjoy the qi,
they do not eat."
But enjoying and eating and drinking
are one and the same in substance.
One uses the mouth to eat,
and uses the mouth to enjoy.
Without stomach and intestines, there is no mouth;
without a mouth,
there is no means to eat,
and thus also no means to enjoy.
How can it be tested that they cannot enjoy?
By the fact that when people err in sacrifices,
they are not immediately punished.
If enjoyment does not use the mouth, then it uses the nose.
If the mouth and nose can enjoy,
then the eyes can see;
if the eyes can see,
then the hands can strike.
But now the hands cannot strike,
so we know the mouth and nose cannot enjoy.
Some object, saying:
"Duke Bào of Sòng himself had an illness.
The invoker, named Yègū,
was in charge of serving the malevolent spirit.
The malevolent spirit, leaning on a staff, spoke to him, saying:
'Why are the grain offerings not rich?
Why are the animal sacrifices not plump?
Why are the jade discs and bi not of proper measure?
Is it your fault?
Or is it Bào's fault?'
Yègū, with a compliant expression, replied:
'Bào himself is still young,
in swaddling clothes,
and unaware of these matters.
I am truly the one in charge.'
The malevolent spirit raised his staff and struck him,
and he died at the altar's base.
Is this not evidence of speaking and using hands?'"
I say: Yègū's death
was not necessarily due to the malevolent spirit striking him;
his time and fate destined him to die.
An apparition resembling a malevolent spirit,
taking the form of a ghost, then spoke like a ghost;
speaking like a ghost, it then struck like a ghost.
How can this be clarified?
Ghosts are spirits;
spirits then have foreknowledge;
having foreknowledge, they should naturally see that the grain offerings are not rich,
the jade discs and bi are off measure,
and the sacrificial animals are meager and small;
then they should thereby reprimand Yègū
and strike him with the staff—
there is no need to ask first.
Asking first
is evidence of not knowing;
not knowing
is proof of not being divine;
not knowing and not divine,
then they cannot manifest a body and speak out,
striking people with a staff.
Yègū was a righteous minister;
he took the blame upon himself,
so the ghost struck him.
If he had been unrighteous and shifted it to Duke Bào,
then the malevolent spirit would have again used the staff to strike Bào himself.
Moreover, if sacrifices are incomplete,
and spirits show anger by manifesting a body
to kill the one in charge of sacrifices,
then if the rites are complete and spirits are pleased,
would they manifest a body to bestow food upon the chief sacrificer?
People have joys and angers;
ghosts also have joys and angers.
People do not have their bodies preserved due to anger,
nor do they perish due to joy;
yet the malevolent spirit's anger
manifests a body to punish.
If Sòng's sacrifices
were always timely and according to ritual,
then why did the spirit not manifest a body to reward them?
If their joys and angers are not the same as humans',
then their rewards and punishments are not equal to humans';
if their rewards and punishments are not equal to humans',
then their striking of Yègū
is not credible.
Now, the act of smelling the sacrifice
is an inward breath,
while speaking
is an outward breath.
Being able to smell means one can speak,
just as being able to inhale means one can exhale.
If ghosts and spirits could smell,
they should be able to speak during sacrifices.
Since they cannot speak,
we know they cannot smell—
this is the first point.
All who can smell
have unobstructed mouths and noses.
If the nose is blocked and cannot breathe,
or the mouth is clamped shut,
then one cannot smell.
When a person dies,
their mouth and nose decay;
how could they smell again?—
this is the second point.
The Rites state:
"When a person dies,
they become repulsive."
Being of a different category from the living,
they are thus disliked.
As a corpse, they do not move;
rotting and perishing,
their bodies are not the same as the living,
so we know their consciousness does not communicate with the living.
Their bodies are different,
their consciousness does not communicate,
so their eating and drinking cannot be the same as humans.
The Hú and Yuè are different peoples,
with distinct tastes in food.
The dead and the living
are not merely like the Hú and Yuè.
From this perspective,
the dead do not smell sacrifices—
this is the third point.
When a person is asleep,
if food is placed beside them,
they are unaware of it.
Only upon waking do they know,
and only then can they eat.
Death is
a long slumber without waking;
how could they know to eat?
They cannot smell sacrifices—
this is the fourth point.
Some may object:
" 'When sacrificing, the ghosts enjoy it'—
what does this mean?"
The reply: It means that when the preparations are meticulous and pure,
with clean grains and fat, fragrant animals,
and people personally present to see it,
they imagine the act of eating and drinking.
Projecting their own thoughts onto the ghosts and spirits,
if the ghosts and spirits were conscious,
they would surely enjoy this sacrifice,
hence it is said
"the ghosts enjoy it."
Another objection:
"The Yì Jīng says:
'The eastern neighbor's slaughter of an ox
is not as good as the western neighbor's yuè sacrifice.'
Saying the eastern neighbor is inferior to the western neighbor
means the eastern neighbor's large sacrifice brings little blessing,
while the western neighbor's small sacrifice brings much blessing.
Now if you say ghosts do not enjoy sacrifices,
how can one know the blessings are more or less?"
The reply: This also refers to whether the preparations are meticulous and pure or not.
King Zhòu slaughtered oxen for sacrifice,
but did not uphold the rites;
King Wén performed the yuè sacrifice,
exhausting all reverence.
When rites are not upheld,
people criticize it;
when reverence is complete,
people approve of it.
Approval
leads to more support in undertakings;
criticism
leads to opposition in words and actions.
Opposition
is like the misfortune of sacrifices not being enjoyed;
more support
is like the blessing of sacrifices being smelled—
it is not that ghosts feel joy or anger because of the sacrifices.
How to clarify this?
If they are truly ghosts and spirits,
they should not need humans to eat;
needing humans to eat
means they cannot be divine.
To believe that ghosts smell sacrifices
and that sacrifices bring fortune or misfortune—
what would the dwelling of ghosts be like?
Do they have their own stores?
Or do they depend on human food for hunger and satiety?
If they have their own stores,
these stores must differ from humans',
so they should not eat human food;
if they have no stores,
then humans would need to sacrifice morning and evening to suffice.
Sacrificing once and not another time
would mean the spirits are hungry once and full once;
hungry once and full once,
then the spirits would be angry once and happy once.
Moreover, when the sick see ghosts,
or when dreaming they meet the dead,
they appear in human form,
so sacrifices to them
resemble human meals.
Since there is eating and drinking,
there should also be clothing,
hence again silk is used to make garments,
imitating the appearance of the living.
If sacrifices are like the food of the living,
and people wish to eat,
they hope the ghosts will enjoy it.
When making clothes for them,
the width and length do not exceed one foot or five to six inches.
For the tall and large spirits seen,
to wear clothes of one foot—
would they be pleased and bestow blessings?
Are the ghosts seen truly the dead?
Then the clothes made should be like those of the living.
If the clothes made are truly worn by ghosts,
then the ghosts seen should resemble doll-like figures.
If so,
the ghosts seen in the world
are not the spirits of the dead;
or the spirits clothed
are not the ghosts seen.
With ghosts and spirits uncertain,
to serve them with lavish rites—
how can one obtain blessings and firmly believe in them?
The Rites:
The king sacrifices to Heaven and Earth,
feudal lords sacrifice to mountains and rivers,
ministers and great officers sacrifice to the five household gods,
scholars and commoners sacrifice to their ancestors.
Ancestral temples
and altars of soil and grain
are sacrificed to from the Son of Heaven down to commoners.
The Shàng Shū states:
"Thereupon he sacrificed specially to Shàngdì,
offered to the six honored ones,
presented to the mountains and rivers,
and extended to all the spirits."
The Rites say:
"The Yǒuyú clan honored Huángdì as the distant ancestor and offered to Kù in the suburb,
took Zhuānxū as progenitor and Yáo as ancestor;
the Xiàhòu clan also honored Huángdì as the distant ancestor and offered to Gǔn in the suburb,
took Zhuānxū as progenitor and Yǔ as ancestor;
the Yīn people honored Kù as the distant ancestor and offered to Míng in the suburb,
took Qì as progenitor and Tāng as ancestor;
the Zhōu people honored Kù as the distant ancestor and offered to Jì in the suburb,
took Wénwáng as progenitor and Wǔwáng as ancestor.
Burning firewood on the great altar
is sacrificing to Heaven;
burying in the great trench
is sacrificing to Earth,
using a red calf.
Burying a shàoláo in the great brightness
is sacrificing to the seasons;
sacrificing at the pit and altar
is for cold and heat;
the royal temple
is for the sun;
the night bright
is for the moon;
the dark shrine
is for the stars;
the rain shrine
is for flood and drought;
the four pits and altars
are for the four directions.
Mountains and forests,
rivers and valleys,
hills and mounds
that can produce clouds,
create wind and rain,
or reveal strange creatures
are all called spirits.
Those who possess the world sacrifice to the hundred spirits.
Feudal lords
sacrifice to those in their territory,
but not to those whose lands they have lost."
These are all sacrifices according to regulations,
the constant rules of the rites.
The king serves Heaven as his father,
and Earth as his mother.
Extending the human practice of serving one's parents,
thus there are also sacrifices to Heaven and Earth.
For mountains and rivers and below,
it is the principle of rewarding merit.
Since living people are rewarded for their merits,
spirits and deities with merits are also sacrificed to.
Mountains produce clouds and rain to nourish all things.
The Six Zōng reside between the six directions,
assisting Heaven and Earth in transformation.
The king honors and sacrifices to them,
hence they are called the Six Zōng.
Shèjì,
rewards the merit of generating all things,
Shè rewards all things,
Jì rewards the five grains.
The Five Sacrifices,
reward the merits of the gate,
door, well,
hearth, and central roof opening,
the gate and door,
are where people pass through,
the well and hearth,
are for people's drinking and eating,
the central roof opening,
is where people dwell,
these five have equal merit,
thus all are sacrificed to.
The "Zhuàn" says:
"Shǎohào had four uncles,
named Zhòng,
named Gāi,
named Xiū,
named Xī,
who truly mastered metal, wood, and water.
He made Zhòng the Jùmáng,
Gāi the Rùshōu,
Xiū and Xī the Xuánmíng,
they never failed in their duties,
thus they aided in Qióngsāng,
these are the three sacrifices.
Zhuānxū had a son named Lí,
who became Zhùróng;
Gònggōng had a son named Gōulóng,
who became Hòutǔ,
these are the two sacrifices.
Hòutǔ is Shè.
Jì is the field official.
The son of Lièshānshì, named Zhù, became Jì,
and was sacrificed to from the Xià dynasty upwards.
Zhōu Qì also became Jì,
and has been sacrificed to since the Shāng dynasty."
The "Lǐ" says:
"When Lièshānshì ruled the world,
his son named Zhù,
could cultivate all grains.
When the Xià declined,
Zhōu Qì succeeded him,
thus he is sacrificed to as Jì.
When Gònggōngshì dominated the Jiǔzhōu,
his son named Hòutǔ,
could level the nine lands,
thus he is sacrificed to as Shè."
The "Zhuàn" says:
"Yándì created fire,
and upon death became the hearth.
Yǔ labored to control the world's waters,
and upon death became Shè."
The "Lǐ" says:
"The king establishes seven sacrifices for the multitude,
called Sīmìng,
called Zhōngliù,
called Guómén,
called Guóxíng,
called Tàilì,
called Hù,
called Zào.
Feudal lords establish five sacrifices for the state,
called Sīmìng,
called Zhōngliù,
called Guómén,
called Guóxíng,
called Gōnglì.
Great officers establish three sacrifices,
called Zúlì,
called Mén,
called Xíng.
Appointed scholars establish two sacrifices,
called Mén,
called Xíng.
Commoners establish one sacrifice,
either Hù,
or Zào."
Shèjì,
and the Five Sacrifices,
though not fixed in form,
all are to remember their virtue,
and not forget their merits.
Loving them in the heart,
thus offering food and drink.
Loving the spirits and deities, thus sacrificing to them.
Since Yǔ revived the Shè sacrifice,
and Jì sacrificed to Hòujì,
they later fell into disuse.
In the fourth year of Emperor Gāo,
he decreed the sacrifice to Língxīng throughout the land;
in the seventh year,
he ordered the sacrifice to Shèjì throughout the land.
The sacrifice to Língxīng,
is to pray against flood and drought,
in rites formerly called Yú.
The rite of Yú,
is to pray for grain rain for the people,
and for grain to bear fruit.
Praying for rain in spring,
and for fruition in autumn,
twice a year,
showing the importance of grain.
In spring in the second month,
in autumn in the eighth month.
Thus the "Lúnyǔ" says:
"In late spring,
with spring clothes already made,
five or six adults,
six or seven youths,
bathe in the Yí River,
enjoy the breeze at the Wǔyú altar,
and return singing."
Late spring,
is the fourth month.
The fourth month in Zhōu,
is the second month of the correct calendar.
In the second month,
the Dragon Star first appears,
thus the "Zhuàn" says:
"When the dragon appears, perform Yú."
When the Dragon Star appears,
the year's hibernating insects have already awakened,
thus it is also said:
"Perform Yú when the insects awaken."
The spring Yú rite was abolished,
while the autumn Yú rite remains,
thus the world often performs the sacrifice to Língxīng,
which continues to this day.
Its name changed from the old,
so people do not recognize it;
the rite was abolished and incomplete,
so Confucians do not know it.
Contemporary Confucians examine the rites,
but do not know what sacrifice Língxīng is,
finding it hard to understand and unable to explain,
the officials call it
"Míngxīng",
based on the name Míngxīng,
they explain it as
"Suìxīng".
Suìxīng,
is in the east,
the east governs spring,
spring governs the generation of things,
thus sacrificing to Suìxīng,
seeks the blessings of spring.
All four seasons contribute to things,
yet only spring is sought,
emphasizing the root and honoring the beginning.
If indeed as the Confucians say,
seeking spring's blessings,
but sacrificing in autumn instead,
is not seeking spring.
The "Yuèlìng" sacrifices to the door in spring,
and to the gate in autumn,
each in its appropriate time.
If one sacrifices to the gate in autumn,
but calls it sacrificing to the door,
would commentators agree?
If not,
then Míngxīng is not Suìxīng,
but rather the Dragon Star.
The Dragon Star appears in the second month,
then spring Yú prays for grain rain;
the Dragon Star is about to set in the eighth month,
then autumn Yú prays for grain fruition.
Some Confucians grasp its meaning,
their words are not baseless.
Spring Yú was abolished,
autumn Yú arose,
thus the name of autumn Yú,
naturally became Míngxīng,
actually called
"Língxīng".
Língxīng,
is a spirit,
the spirit,
refers to the Dragon Star.
The host of spirits refers to the likes of the Wind Lord,
the Rain Master,
and the Thunder Duke.
The wind sways things,
the rain moistens them,
the thunder stirs them,
the four seasons bring about growth,
and cold and heat alternate.
The sun, moon, stars, and constellations
are what people gaze up to.
Floods and droughts
are what people dread and despise,
the four directions
are where the vital energy emanates from.
The mountains, forests, rivers, and valleys
are where the people obtain their materials.
These are the achievements of the spirits and ghosts.
Generally, the meaning of sacrificial rites has two aspects:
one is to repay merits,
the other is to honor the ancestors.
Repaying merits encourages exertion,
honoring ancestors venerates kindness;
with exertion encouraged and kindness venerated,
merits are established and transformation is achieved—
this is the duty of the sage kings.
Therefore, when the sage kings instituted sacrifices,
they sacrificed to those who had established models for the people;
to those who had died in diligent service;
to those who had toiled to stabilize the state;
to those who could ward off great disasters;
to those who could defend against great calamities.
Dì Kù could order the stars and constellations to illuminate the masses;
Yáo could reward evenly and enforce penalties justly, ending with righteousness;
Shùn toiled for the people's affairs and died in the wilderness;
Gǔn labored against the flood and was executed;
Yǔ could continue Gǔn's work;
Huángdì gave correct names to all things to enlighten the people and share resources;
Zhuānxū could build upon this;
Qì served as Minister of Education and the people became accomplished;
Míng was diligent in his office and died in the waters;
Tāng governed the people with leniency and removed their oppressor;
Wénwáng ruled with civility;
Wǔwáng used military achievements to rid the people of disasters.
All these great deeds
were bestowed upon the people,
and the people relied on their efforts,
hence they sacrificed to repay them.
The ancestral temples and forebears
are one's own kin;
in life, there is the way of caring for parents,
in death, it is right not to betray them,
hence they perform sacrifices,
showing as if they were still alive.
Extending human affairs to serve the spirits,
based on life to serve the dead,
humans have the way of rewarding merits and providing support,
hence there is the meaning of repaying kindness and sacrificing to ancestors.
When Confucius's pet dog died,
he had Zǐ Gòng bury it,
saying:
"I have heard that
one does not discard a worn-out curtain,
using it to bury a horse;
one does not discard a worn-out cover,
using it to bury a dog.
I, Qiū, am poor,
and have no cover,
but in its burial,
I still give it a mat,
so that its head does not sink into the earth!"
When Yánlíng Jìzǐ passed through Xú,
the Lord of Xú admired his sword,
but Jìzǐ, because he had to go on a mission to the superior states,
did not promise it to him then.
When Jìzǐ returned from his mission,
the Lord of Xú had already died,
so Jìzǐ untied his sword and hung it on the tree at his tomb.
His charioteer said:
"The Lord of Xú is already dead,
who are you doing this for?"
Jìzǐ replied:
"I had already promised him in my heart;
how can I betray my own heart because the Lord of Xú has died?"
So he hung the sword on the tomb tree and left.
Sacrificing to repay merits
is akin in intent to Confucius burying his pet dog;
sacrificing to not betray ancestors
is akin in kindness to Jìzǐ hanging the sword on the tomb tree.
The sages knew it was like this,
yet they still sacrificed with fasting and reverence,
as if spirits and ghosts existed;
they maintained and performed them without cease,
as if there were blessings and calamities.
They emphasized kindness and honored merits,
being earnest and deeply kind,
though there may not necessarily be ghosts to enjoy the offerings.
How can this be demonstrated?
By the practice of offering food and drink to the earth.
When people are about to eat or drink,
they modestly decline,
showing that something should come first.
Confucius said:
"Even with coarse rice and vegetable soup,
one must offer a portion solemnly."
The "Lǐ" says:
"When serving a ruler at a meal,
the ruler orders one to make an offering,
and only then does one eat."
Offering is like the various sacrifices in ritual.
One could also forgo offering when eating and drinking,
just as one could forgo sacrificing
to the various spirits in ritual.
The substance of offering and sacrificing
is the same;
the expense of the items used
is identical.
To know that offering to the earth has no spirit,
yet claim that the various sacrifices have ghosts,
is to fail to understand the analogy.
In the classics and commentaries recorded,
and in the accounts of the worthy,
there are still no ghosts or spirits,
let alone in texts not preserved in writings!
The excessive sacrifices in the world that are not offerings to true ghosts,
are believed to have spirits that bring fortune or misfortune.
Those who love the Way and study immortality,
abstain from grains and do not eat,
eating differently from others,
wishing to be pure and clean.
If spirits and ghosts are purer and cleaner than immortals,
how could they eat the same as humans?
I argue that when humans die, they have no consciousness,
and their essence cannot become ghosts.
Even if they did exist,
they would eat differently from humans.
Eating differently means they would not eat human food;
not eating human food means they have no demands on humans;
having no demands on humans means they cannot bring fortune or misfortune to people.
Generally, when humans have joy or anger,
it is due to obtaining or not obtaining what they seek.
Obtaining brings joy,
not obtaining brings anger.
Joy leads to bestowing kindness and bringing fortune;
anger leads to venting rage and bringing calamity.
If spirits and ghosts have no joy or anger,
then even if sacrifices are constantly made without cease,
or long abandoned and not maintained,
how could they bring fortune or calamity to people?
Confucian scholars discuss the sage,
believing that they know a thousand years ahead,
and ten thousand generations behind,
possessing unique clarity of vision,
unique acuity of hearing,
naming things as they come,
knowing without learning,
understanding without asking,
hence called sage,
and sage means divine.
Like the yarrow stalks
and tortoise shells knowing good and bad fortune,
the yarrow stalks are called divine,
the tortoise shells are called numinous.
The worthy, with lesser talent, cannot reach this,
with inferior wisdom, cannot foresee,
hence they are called worthy.
Now, different names mean different realities;
the same substance means the same designation;
judging by the name of sage,
we know the sage is outstanding,
and different from the worthy.
When Confucius was about to die,
he left a book of prophecies,
saying:
"I do not know what man,
calling himself Qín Shǐhuáng,
will ascend my hall,
sit on my bed,
topsy-turvy my robes,
and die at Shāqiū."
Later,
the King of Qín annexed all under heaven,
took the title Shǐhuáng,
toured to Lǔ,
visited Confucius' house,
then reached Shāqiū,
where he fell ill on the road and died.
It also said:
"Dǒng Zhòngshū
will disrupt my writings."
Later,
Dǒng Zhòngshū, Chancellor of Jiāngdū,
discoursed on the Spring and Autumn Annals,
and composed commentaries.
It further wrote:
"The one who will destroy Qín
is Hú."
Later, the Second Emperor Húhài
ultimately lost the empire.
Using these three cases to discuss,
it shows the sage's knowledge of effects ten thousand generations later.
Confucius was born not knowing his father,
as his mother concealed it;
by blowing pitch-pipes he knew himself to be a descendant of the noble Zǐ lineage of Yīn and Sòng.
Without consulting the Charts
or Books,
without hearing others' words,
by blowing pitch-pipes and deep thought,
he knew his own lineage—
this is evidence of the sage's foreknowledge of a thousand years earlier.
I say:
These are all fabrications.
Examining supernatural claims,
all are in prophetic records,
and what they express all imitates the Charts
and Books.
"The destroyer of Qín is Hú"—
this is text from the River Chart.
Confucius elaborated and expanded it
to manifest the supernatural;
or later people fraudulently recorded it
to demonstrate proof.
When Emperor Gāo enfeoffed the King of Wú,
seeing him off,
he patted his back, saying:
"Fifty years after Hàn,
there will be a rebel in the southeast—
could it be you?"
By Emperor Jǐng's time,
Liú Bì conspired with the Seven States to rebel against Hàn.
The one who made this statement
might have observed omens and signs,
recognizing rebellion would occur there,
but not knowing the principal's name;
Emperor Gāo, seeing Bì's valor,
then said it was him.
Reasoning from this,
Confucius foreseeing Shǐhuáng
and Dǒng Zhòngshū
might have merely said
"someone will visit my house"
and "disrupt my writings."
Later people, seeing Shǐhuáng enter his house
and Dǒng Zhòngshū read his books,
then amplified his words,
specifying their names.
If Confucius supernaturally foresaw Shǐhuáng
and Dǒng Zhòngshū,
then regarding his own lineage as a descendant of the Zǐ line of Yīn,
he should have silently known it,
without needing to blow pitch-pipes to confirm it.
If Confucius did not blow pitch-pipes,
he could not establish his surname;
yet when he saw Shǐhuáng
and observed Dǒng Zhòngshū,
it again resembled blowing pitch-pipes.
Examining Shǐhuáng's actual events,
Shǐhuáng never went to Lǔ—
how could he have ascended Confucius' hall,
sat on Confucius' bed,
or topsy-turvied Confucius' robes?
In the tenth month, guǐchǒu day, of Shǐhuáng's 37th year, he traveled,
reached Yúnmèng,
and worshipped Yú Shùn from afar at Jiǔyí.
He floated down the river,
viewed Jièkē,
crossed Méizhǔ,
passed Dānyáng,
reached Qiántáng,
faced the Zhèjiāng River,
where waves were fierce,
so he went west 120 lǐ to cross from Xiázhōng.
He ascended Kuàijī,
sacrificed to Dà Yǔ,
erected a stone with inscribed praise,
gazing toward the South Sea.
Returning, he passed Wú,
crossed from Jiāngshèng.
Along the coast,
he went north to Lángyá.
From Lángyá north to Róngchéng Mountain,
then to Zhīfú,
and proceeded west along the sea.
He fell ill at Píngyuán Crossing.
He died at the Shāqiū Platform.
Since he never went to Lǔ,
how could the prophecy claim Shǐhuáng reached Lǔ?
Whether he reached Lǔ is uncertain,
and the saying attributed to Confucius
"I do not know what man"
cannot be relied upon.
If "I do not know what man"
is unreliable,
then the statement
"Dǒng Zhòngshū
will disrupt my writings"
is also untrustworthy.
Historical accounts
and records often contain anomalies—
they are merely human words,
not texts of heaven and earth,
so they all follow precedents and antiquity,
having some basis in form;
if there were no hearing or seeing,
there would be nothing to form.
When sages foresee fortune and disaster,
they also measure beginnings and infer categories,
trace origins to see ends,
from alleyways discuss the court,
from the clear perceive the obscure.
Prophecies and secret texts,
foreseeing the distant unrealized,
empty and obscure,
predicting what has not occurred,
hearing remotely and glimpsing briefly,
extraordinarily strange and supernatural—
these are not what ordinary mouths can tell.
By imitating and categorizing events, one can foresee calamities;
by tracing past experiences, one can handle future affairs.
Even the worthy are capable of this,
not only the sages.
When the Duke of Zhōu governed Lǔ,
the Grand Duke knew that his descendants would face the peril of decline;
when the Grand Duke governed Qí,
the Duke of Zhōu foresaw that his descendants would suffer the disaster of usurpation and regicide.
They perceived the ultimate principles of statecraft,
and saw the precursors of turmoil and chaos.
When King Zhòu used ivory chopsticks, Jīzǐ criticized him;
when Lǔ buried figurines with the dead, Confucius sighed,
for from the ivory chopsticks, he saw the omen of extravagance leading to disaster,
and from the figurines, he foresaw the evil of human sacrifice in burial.
The Grand Duke
and the Duke of Zhōu
both saw what had not yet occurred;
Jīzǐ
and Confucius
also perceived what was not yet manifest.
The means by which they foresaw the future
are the same for both the worthy and the sages.
When the ruler of Lǔ was old
and the crown prince weak,
a woman from the side chamber
leaned against a pillar and sang mournfully,
recognizing from the signs of age and weakness
the portents of collapse and disorder.
Even the knowledge of a woman
could infer from analogy to foresee the future;
how much more so for sages, gentlemen,
and those of high talent and clear intelligence?
In the seventh year of Qín Shǐ Huáng's reign,
Xià Tàihòu, mother of King Yánxiāng, passed away.
King Xiàowén's queen, known as Huáyáng Hòu,
was buried with King Wén at Shòulíng,
while King Yánxiāng, son of Xià Tàihòu, was buried at Fànlíng.
Thus, Xià Tàihòu was separately interred at Dùlíng,
saying:
"Looking east, I see my son;
looking west, I see my husband.
After a hundred years,
there will be a city of ten thousand households beside me."
Later events all matched her words.
If foreseeing the future through analogy defines a sage,
then the woman from the side chamber
and Xià Tàihòu were sages.
In the seventh year of King Zhāo of Qín's reign,
Chūlǐzǐ died
and was buried east of Zhāngtái, south of the Wèi River,
saying:
"After a hundred years,
there will be an imperial palace flanking my tomb."
By the time of the Hàn dynasty's rise,
the Chánglè Palace stood to its east,
the Wèiyāng Palace to its west,
and the armory directly faced his tomb,
exactly as predicted.
This demonstrates foresight,
the evidence of perceiving the future.
If this qualifies one as a sage,
then Chūlǐzǐ
was a sage;
if not,
then foresight
and perceiving the future
are not sufficient to prove sageliness.
Thus, Chūlǐzǐ foreseeing the imperial palaces flanking his tomb
is similar to Xīn Yǒu knowing that Yīchuān would become territory of the Róng people.
In the past, Xīn Yǒu passed through Yīchuān
and saw people sacrificing with disheveled hair,
saying:
"In less than a hundred years,
this place will be occupied by the Róng!"
A hundred years later,
Jìn relocated the Lùhún Róng to Yīchuān,
just as he said.
Xīn Yǒu's knowledge that it would become Róng territory
came from observing the omen of disheveled hair;
Chūlǐzǐ's foresight of the imperial palaces flanking his tomb
also stemmed from observing the elevated terrain of his burial site.
When Hán Xìn buried his mother,
he also chose a high, open location,
so that ten thousand households could settle beside it.
Eventually, ten thousand households did reside near her tomb.
Thus, Chūlǐzǐ's insight that the king of Bópíng would have palaces and towers
is akin to Hán Xìn envisioning a high, open area for ten thousand households.
The foresight of future events
does not require supernatural vision or hearing,
but rather examining omens and traces,
and inferring from analogies.
During the Spring and Autumn period,
when ministers and officials met,
they observed changes in behavior
and listened to unusual speech.
If favorable, they anticipated auspicious blessings;
if unfavorable, they prepared for ominous disasters.
Understanding blessings and handling calamities,
planning for what had not yet occurred,
required no supernatural knowledge,
but all came from interpreting signs and categories.
In modern terms,
what can be known
is within the reach of thought and consideration;
what cannot be known
cannot be understood without learning and inquiry.
To know without learning,
to comprehend without asking,
has never occurred
in all of history.
For knowable matters,
with concentrated thought,
even the great ones are not difficult;
for unknowable matters,
even with diligent study,
the small ones are not easy.
Therefore, those with intelligence and ability
cannot achieve without learning,
nor know without asking.
The objection says:
"Xiàng Tuō at age seven taught Confucius.
Consider that a seven-year-old had not yet entered elementary school,
yet taught Confucius—
this shows innate knowledge.
Confucius said:
'Those born with knowledge are the highest;
those who learn and thereby know are next.'
When speaking of being born with knowledge,
without mentioning learning or inquiry,
he meant people like Xiàng Tuō.
During Wáng Mǎng's time,
Yǐn Fāng of Bóhǎi, aged twenty-one,
having no teacher or friends,
was naturally intelligent and quick-witted,
mastering the Six Arts.
Governor Chúnyú Cāng of Wèi capital reported:
'Fāng, without studying,
could read and recite texts when he obtained them;
discussing meanings he quoted from the Five Classics;
his literary explanations and deliberations
satisfied people's minds.'
The emperor summoned Fāng,
had him identify flying insects,
and his answers left nothing unknown—
the world called him a sage.
Having no teacher or friends,
yet mastering the Six Arts;
never having studied writing,
yet able to read texts when obtained—
this is a sage.
Able without learning,
understanding without teachers—
if not divine, then what?"
The response:
Though without teacher or friends,
he still must have received some instruction;
though not studying writing,
he had already handled brush and ink.
When a child is first born,
with ears and eyes just opening,
even with sage nature,
how could it have knowledge?
Xiàng Tuō at seven—
at three or four years old
was already receiving human speech.
Yǐn Fāng at twenty-one—
at fourteen or fifteen
had already heard and seen much.
Though keen-natured and talented,
solitary thought without basis,
not observing omens and signs,
nor seeing categorical proofs—
could one envision a hundred generations hence
horses bearing oxen,
oxen bearing donkeys,
peaches bearing plums,
plums bearing apricots?
Could a sage know this?
Ministers assassinating rulers,
sons murdering fathers—
though benevolent as Yán Yuān,
filial as Zēng Shēn,
courageous as Bēn or Yù,
eloquent as Cì or Yǔ—
could a sage foresee this?
Confucius said:
"One may know the next hundred generations
if continuing after Zhōu."
He also said:
"The young are to be respected—
how can we know the future won't surpass the present?"
Discussing additions and omissions,
he said "may know";
referring to the young,
he said "how can know".
The young are hard to assess,
while additions and omissions are easily discerned.
These are still distant matters,
beyond direct observation.
Place someone east of a wall,
have them make a sound—
could a sage listening west of the wall
know their complexion,
height,
hometown,
name,
or origin?
In ditches flow broken ice,
in marshes lie dried bones—
hair and skull decayed,
flesh rotted away—
could a sage examining them
know whether they were farmers or merchants,
old or young,
or what crime they sat condemned for?
Not that the sage lacks knowledge,
but his knowledge cannot know this.
When knowledge cannot know,
inquiry is essential for knowing.
Unable to know—
this is the common failing of sages and worthies alike.
The objection states:
"Zhān Hé was sitting,
with his disciples attending him,
when an ox lowed outside the gate.
A disciple said:
'That is a black ox
with white hooves.'
Zhān Hé said:
'Yes,
it is a black ox,
but its hooves are made white.'
Someone was sent to look,
and indeed it was a black ox with cloth wrapped around its hooves.
Zhān Hé
is a worthy man;
he could discern its color by listening to its sound.
With the wisdom of a sage,
would one instead be unable to know such things?"
The response: He could know the black ox had whitened hooves,
but could he know whose ox this was?
Or for what reason its hooves were whitened?
Arts and calculations merely reveal one aspect,
and cannot exhaust the full reality.
Even if one examines a single matter,
and cross-examines it with detailed questions,
one still cannot know everything.
Why is that?
Without seeing with one's own eyes or inquiring with one's own mouth,
one cannot know completely.
In the 29th year of Duke Xī of Lǔ,
Jiè Gélú came to court,
and lodged above Chāngyǎn,
where he heard an ox lowing.
He said:
"This ox has produced three sacrificial animals,
all of which have already been used."
Someone asked:
"How do you know this?"
He replied:
"Its sound says so."
People asked the ox's owner,
and it was exactly as he had said.
This again employed arts and calculations;
it was not something knowledge alone could perceive.
Yáng Wēngzhòng of Guǎnghàn could understand the sounds of birds and beasts.
Riding a lame horse in the wild,
there was a released one-eyed horse in the fields,
several lǐ away,
their calls audible to each other.
Wēngzhòng said to his driver:
"That released horse knows this horse is lame and one-eyed."
His driver said:
"How do you know?"
He replied:
"It scolds the horse in our shafts for being lame,
and this horse scolds it back for being one-eyed."
His driver did not believe him,
but sent someone to look,
and the horse's eye was indeed blind.
Wēngzhòng's understanding of horse sounds,
like Zhān Hé's
and Jiè Gélú's comprehension of ox lowing,
relied on arts and depended on calculations,
matching their meanings accordingly,
not through penetrating sight,
acute hearing,
distant vision,
or sweeping glances to observe them.
If listening to sounds involves arts,
then observing colors involves calculations.
Applying arts and calculations,
as if having heard or seen beforehand,
when ordinary people do not understand,
they call it divine and sage-like.
Like Confucius seeing an animal
and naming it a 'xīngxīng';
or Sīmǎ Qiān seeing Zhāng Liáng
as resembling a woman's form.
In fact, Confucius had never seen a xīngxīng,
yet upon encountering it, he could name it;
Sīmǎ Qiān and Zhāng Liáng lived in different eras,
yet he saw his form with his own eyes.
If ordinary people heard of this,
they would say it was divine foreknowledge.
However, Confucius named the xīngxīng
from hearing the songs of the Zhāo people;
Sīmǎ Qiān's vision of Zhāng Liáng
came from viewing portraits in the Xuānshì.
It was unseen observation and silent remembrance,
employing deep and secret thought.
Ordinary people are粗略,
with little awareness,
so when they see sages naming things,
they call it divine.
Extending this argument,
Zhān Hé seeing the black ox with white hooves
is similar to these cases.
If he did not use arts and calculations,
then he must have heard or seen it outside beforehand.
Nowadays, skilled prognosticators
rely on proper arts and calculations;
when arts and calculations fail,
they supplement with human affairs.
Those who use human affairs alongside arts and calculations
are no different from the divine.
Followers of Zhān Hé
are like today's prognosticators.
If people like Zhān Hé
were inherently able to know,
without using arts and calculations,
then nest-dwellers would know the wind beforehand,
and cave-dwellers would know the rain in advance.
Wisdom that matures early,
like in Xiàng Tuō
and Yǐn Fāng, are examples.
The objection states:
"Huángdì was born divine and intelligent,
and could speak in infancy.
Emperor Kù could speak his own name at birth.
Without having heard or seen anything outside,
they could speak at birth,
stating their names.
Is this not proof of divinity
and evidence of innate knowledge?"
The response: Huángdì could speak at birth,
but his mother carried him for twenty months before birth;
calculating the months,
he was already two years in his mother's womb.
Emperor Kù could speak his own name,
but could not speak others' names;
though having one ability,
he was not universally proficient.
What is called divine and innate knowledge—
does it mean being able to speak one's name at birth?
It should mean knowing without receiving
or being able to see without having obtained.
Huángdì
and Emperor Kù, though showing signs of divinity,
were both early-maturing talents.
Talents may mature early,
but there are also late bloomers.
Even if they did not study under teachers,
they learned at home from family.
People see their early maturity and quick achievements,
and praise them excessively.
It is said Xiàng Tuō was seven,
but he must have been ten;
it is said he taught Confucius,
but it must have been Confucius asking him;
it is said Huángdì
and Emperor Kù could speak at birth,
but it was likely after several months;
it is said Yǐn Fāng was twenty-one,
but he was nearly thirty;
it is said he had no teachers or friends,
and did not study books,
but he must have traveled to learn or studied at home.
Worldly praise exaggerates reality,
and criticism exceeds the faults.
It is popularly said that Yán Yuān, at eighteen, ascended Tài Shān
and saw a white horse tied outside the Wú Chāng gate.
Verifying the facts, Yán Yuān died at thirty without ascending Tài Shān,
nor seeing the Wú Chāng gate.
The claims about Xiàng Tuō,
the praises of Yǐn Fāng,
are of the same kind as those about Yán Yuān.
People's talents vary in superiority and inferiority,
and understanding things comes from learning.
One knows through learning,
and without inquiry, one remains ignorant.
Zǐgòng said:
"How is there anything our Master does not learn?
But why would he have a constant teacher?"
Confucius said:
"At fifteen, I set my heart upon learning."
The Five Emperors and
Three Sovereigns
all had their teachers.
It is said:
"This is meant to set an example for others."
It is said: profound thinking can also serve as an example for others,
so why must one rely on learning?
Matters cannot be known through emptiness,
for the talents of sages and worthies are established thereby.
What is called
"divine"
is knowing without learning;
what is called
"sagehood"
requires learning to achieve sageliness.
Through the learning of sages,
we know they are not inherently divine.
Between heaven and earth,
among blood-endowed creatures,
none possess innate knowledge.
The xingxing knows the past,
the gānquè knows the future,
endowed with heavenly nature,
they are natural beings.
If we consider sages as like the xingxing,
then the xingxing's kind
are birds and beasts.
Children's rhymes are known without learning,
could this be called divine foreknowledge?
If we consider sages as like children's rhymes,
then those children's rhymes
are supernatural phenomena.
Are the sages and divine beings in the world
considered to be like shamans?
Ghosts and spirits use the shaman's mouth to speak to people.
If we consider sages as like shamans,
then those who are shamans
are also supernatural.
Sharing the same energy as supernatural beings,
they then differ in category from sages.
If shamans differ from sages,
then sages cannot be divine.
If they cannot be divine,
then they belong to the group of worthies.
Belonging to the same group,
their knowledge is not different.
Where they differ
lies in their approach to the Way:
sages are swift,
worthies are slow;
worthies have more talent,
sages have more wisdom.
Their knowledge shares the same foundation,
differing only in quantity;
the path they follow is the same,
yet their strides differ in passing.
Some matters are difficult to know while others are easy to understand,
both worthies and sages ponder over them together.
As for the alternation of refinement and substance,
the repetition of the three teachings,
the succession of calendar systems,
and the mutual influence of decrease and increase,
these are known to both worthies and sages.
The water and fire of ancient times
and today's water and fire are the same,
today's sounds and colors
will be the same as those of later generations.
Birds, beasts, plants, and trees,
people's likes and dislikes
—through the present we see the past,
through this we know the future.
A thousand years before,
ten thousand generations after,
there is no difference.
Looking back at high antiquity,
exploring the coming ages,
categories of refinement and substance,
kinds like water and fire
are shared by worthies and sages;
seeing omens and hearing signs,
depicting fortune and misfortune
are shared by worthies and sages;
encountering strange phenomena and naming things,
without any doubts or confusion
are shared by worthies and sages.
What can be known
is known by both worthies and sages;
what cannot be known
cannot be known even by sages.
How can this be demonstrated?
If a sage could sit empty-minded and foreknow rain,
if his nature enabled him to know one distant matter,
but his senses were not universal,
this would be insufficient to discuss.
What is discussed as prophetic nature and comprehension
means knowing all natures of things,
and seeing completely the essentials of all ways.
If knowing one thing but not understanding another,
comprehending left but not seeing right,
partial and inconsistent, impure,
lopsided and incomplete,
this cannot be called sagehood.
If one must call this sagehood,
then clearly there is nothing extraordinary about sages.
If followers of Zhān Hé are sages,
and Confucius' group is also called sages,
then sages are no different from worthies,
and worthies lack nothing compared to sages.
If both worthies and sages are capable,
why praise sages as extraordinary compared to worthies?
If both employ methods and calculations,
why are worthies inferior to sages?
In reality,
sages and worthies cannot know by nature,
they must rely on ears and eyes to determine true circumstances.
In relying on ears and eyes,
matters that can be known
are decided upon through thought;
matters that cannot be known
require inquiry to resolve.
Among the world's affairs,
and things in the world,
those that can be known through thought
even foolish men can comprehend thoroughly;
those that cannot be known through thought
not even the highest sage can understand.
Confucius said:
"I once spent the whole day without eating,
the whole night without sleeping,
engaged in thought,
but it was useless,
not as good as learning."
Some matters in the world cannot be known,
just as some knots cannot be untied.
Ér Yuè was skilled at untying knots,
and there were no knots he could not untie.
But if there truly are knots that cannot be untied,
then Ér Yuè could not untie them either.
It's not that Ér Yuè couldn't untie them,
but that some knots cannot be untied;
when it comes to untying them,
he would be unable to use his skill.
Sages know matters,
and there are no matters they cannot know.
But if there are matters that cannot be known,
then sages cannot know them either.
It's not that sages cannot know them,
but that some matters cannot be known;
when it comes to knowing them,
they would be unable to use their knowledge.
Therefore, difficult-to-know matters
can be reached through learning and inquiry;
but unknowable matters
—even through inquiry and learning
—cannot be understood.
Generally, in discussing matters,
if one violates reality without citing evidence,
then even with sweet reasoning and elaborate explanations,
the crowd will not believe.
To argue that sages cannot be divine with foreknowledge,
that in matters of foreknowledge
they cannot have unique insight,
is not merely empty talk or vain words,
but directly uses intelligence and wisdom to measure accurately,
with matters having proof and verification
to demonstrate the actual reality.
How can this be demonstrated?
Confucius asked Gōngmíng Jiǎ about Gōngshū Wénzǐ, saying:
"Is it true,
that the Master does not speak,
does not laugh,
and does not take?
Is this so?"
He replied:
"The one who told you this was mistaken.
The Master speaks only when it is timely,
so people do not tire of his words;
he laughs only when he is joyful,
so people do not tire of his laughter;
he takes only when it is righteous,
so people do not tire of his taking."
Confucius said:
"Is that really so?
Is that really so?"
If there were anyone in the world as incorruptible as Bóyí,
taking not even a blade of grass from others,
there has never been one who did not speak
or laugh.
Since Confucius could not speculate according to his heart
to determine its truth or falsehood,
and found it strange and unbelievable in his heart,
nor could he see from afar with penetrating vision
to verify the reality,
he asked Gōngmíng Jiǎ to know the truth.
That Confucius could not foreknow
is the first point.
Chén Zǐqín asked Zǐgòng:
"Whenever the Master arrives in a state,
he always learns about its governance.
Does he seek it,
or is it given to him?"
Zǐgòng said:
"The Master obtains it through being gentle,
good, respectful,
temperate,
and deferential."
Gentleness, goodness,
respect, temperance,
and deference are noble conducts.
Having noble conducts among people,
they become close and attached to him.
When people are close and attached,
then they inform him.
Thus, Confucius learned about governance through people's words,
not through supernatural self-knowledge.
Duke Jǐng of Qí asked Zǐgòng:
"Is the Master worthy?"
Zǐgòng replied:
"The Master is a sage,
how could he merely be worthy!"
Duke Jǐng did not know Confucius was a sage,
so Zǐgòng corrected his designation;
