Zǐqín also did not know how Confucius learned about governance,
so Zǐgòng established the fact.
To Duke Jǐng he said:
"The Master is a sage,
how could he merely be worthy!"
Then to Zǐqín,
he should have said:
"He knows it supernaturally by himself,
not hearing from others."
From Zǐgòng's reply to Zǐqín,
the sage could not foreknow,
is the second point.
Yán Yuān was cooking rice,
and dust fell into the pot.
To leave it would make the rice unclean,
to throw it away would waste the rice,
so he picked it out and ate it.
Confucius saw from a distance,
thinking he was stealing food.
That the sage could not foreknow
is the third point.
On the road, there was a madman
waiting with a blade drawn;
in the marsh, a fierce tiger
grinding its teeth and watching.
Those who know and see them
dare not advance.
If one does not know or see,
then they meet the madman's blade,
or encounter the fierce tiger's teeth.
When the people of Kuāng surrounded Confucius,
if Confucius had truly foreknown,
he should have changed his route early to avoid the harm.
Not knowing, he encountered them,
thus meeting with the disaster.
From Confucius being besieged,
the sage could not foreknow,
is the fourth point.
When the Master was in danger in Kuāng,
Yán Yuān was late.
Confucius said:
"I thought you were dead."
If Confucius had foreknowledge,
he should have known Yán Yuān would not encounter harm,
and the people of Kuāng would not act violently.
Seeing Yán Yuān come,
he then knew he was not dead;
before he came,
he believed him to be dead.
That the sage could not foreknow
is the fifth point.
"Yánghuò wanted to see Confucius,
but Confucius would not see him,
so he sent Confucius a pig.
Confucius waited for when he was out,
and went to pay his respects,
meeting him on the road."
Confucius did not wish to see him,
yet having gone,
waiting for when he was out,
this meant he certainly did not want to see him.
Instead, he met him on the road.
From Confucius encountering Yánghǔ,
the sage could not foreknow,
is the sixth point.
"Chángjū
and Jiénì were plowing together.
Confucius passed by,
and sent Zǐlù to ask them the ford."
If Confucius knew the ford,
he should not have asked again.
Some argue:
"He wanted to observe the recluses' conduct."
Then if Confucius had foreknowledge,
he should have known it himself,
with no need to observe.
If he did not know and asked,
this shows he could not foreknow,
is the seventh point.
When Confucius's mother died,
"he did not know his father's tomb,
so he encoffined her at the crossroad of Wǔfǔ.
Those who saw it
thought it was a burial."
Probably because there was no place for joint burial,
and the encoffining was careful,
so people thought it was a burial.
His neighbor Zōu Mànfǔ's mother told him,
then he could bury them together at Fáng.
There was a cemetery at Fáng all along,
yet he encoffined her at the crossroad;
that the sage could not foreknow
is the eighth point.
"After the joint burial was done,"
"Confucius returned.
His disciples came later;
it was raining heavily when they arrived.
Confucius asked:
'Why are you so late?'
They said:
'The tomb at Fáng collapsed.'
Confucius did not respond.
After they repeated it three times, Confucius shed tears and said:
'I have heard that
in ancient times, they did not repair tombs.'"
If Confucius had foreknowledge,
he should have known beforehand about the tomb's collapse at Fáng;
when his disciples arrived,
he should have been waiting in tears.
He knew only when others came;
that the sage could not foreknow
is the ninth point.
When the Master entered the Grand Temple,
he asked about everything.
He inquired precisely because he did not know,
setting an example for others.
Confucius had never entered this temple before,
and the ritual vessels inside
were numerous and varied.
Though Confucius was a sage,
how could he have known them all?
Some argue:
"Having seen them before,
he actually already knew,
yet asked again,
to set an example?"
Confucius said:
"When in doubt, one should ask."
Should one only ask when in doubt?
If he truly knew,
why ask again
to set an example?
Confucius knew the Five Classics,
and disciples learned from him.
If he should repeatedly ask to set an example,
why did he solely orally instruct his disciples?
Why not use his knowledge of the Five Classics to ask repeatedly as an example,
but only did so with the Grand Temple?
The sage's intentions
– why were they not consistent?
From Confucius entering the Grand Temple,
it shows a sage cannot foreknow –
point ten.
When a host invites a guest to dine,
or calls them to stay at their home,
if the guest hears the host has frivolous sons or grandsons,
they would advise the host to clear the feast and withdraw the meal,
refraining from eating and drinking;
close the lodging and shut the doors,
avoiding staying over.
The guest's decision
would surely be not to go.
Why?
Knowing the invitation holds no joy,
it would be a futile, laborious, and humiliating trip.
If going brings no joy,
and one returns weary and disgraced,
it's because they didn't know the household,
unaware of the reality.
People are truly hard to know,
fortune and misfortune difficult to predict.
If Confucius had foreknowledge,
he should have known that feudal lords, deluded by slanderous ministers,
would certainly not employ him,
leading to vain labor and self-humiliation.
Upon receiving invitations and summons,
he should have rested and not gone.
A nobleman does not engage in futile endeavors,
nor tread paths that bring personal disgrace.
There was no need to travel around accepting appointments,
only to suffer the humiliation of being erased from traces,
or to speak vainly to unreceptive rulers,
encountering the plight of running out of provisions.
From this, it's said
he could not foresee even nearby events.
Some argue:
"Confucius knew he wouldn't be employed,
but his sage heart grieved over the Dao not being practiced,
with the people in dire distress.
He hoped to assist the feudal lords,
practice the Dao, and save the people,
hence he accepted invitations and traveled widely,
not avoiding hardship and shame.
He acted for the Dao, not for himself,
thus facing troubles without resentment;
for the people, not for fame,
hence enduring slander without evasion."
I say: This is not the truth.
Confucius said:
"Only after I returned from Wèi to Lǔ
did I correct the music,
placing the 'Yǎ' and
'Sòng' in their proper order."
This indicates Confucius knew his time.
How did he know?
Lǔ and Wèi
were the most virtuous states under heaven.
If Lǔ and Wèi could not use him,
then no one in the world could.
Thus, he retired to compose the Spring and Autumn Annals,
editing and finalizing the Book of Songs
and Book of Documents.
From his return from Wèi to Lǔ,
it's clear that when he was accepting appointments,
he did not yet know his fate.
Why?
Without omens and verifications,
even a sage cannot determine things.
Not being used by Lǔ and Wèi
made him aware of his extremity;
the capture of the unicorn in Lǔ
made him realize his end was near.
With the Dao exhausted and fate severed,
omens became clear,
his hopes dashed,
he retreated into deep reflection.
To keep traveling incessantly
is like being ill but not dead,
praying and divining for recovery.
If signs of death aren't seen,
there's hope to live on.
Similarly, without clear evidence of rejection while seeking employment,
he hoped to be employed.
When death signs appear, one stops divining and medical help ends,
then he takes up the brush to finalize his writings.
From his accepting appointments and traveling,
it shows a sage cannot foreknow –
point eleven.
Confucius said:
"Fish can be caught with a line,
birds with a tethered arrow.
But as for the dragon,
I do not know how it rides the clouds and wind to ascend!
Having met Lǎozi today,
is he not like a dragon!"
A sage knows objects and events.
Lǎozi and the dragon
are beings and things;
their ascents and descents
are events –
why did he not know?
If Lǎozi was divine,
and the dragon divine too,
and the sage also divine,
divine beings share the same Dao,
their essences interconnected,
why then did he not know?
From Confucius not knowing about the dragon and Lǎozi,
it shows a sage cannot foreknow –
point twelve.
Confucius said:
"How filial is Mǐn Zǐqiān!
No one finds fault with the words of his parents
and brothers."
Yú Shùn,
a great sage,
concealed the faults of his kin,
surely surpassing Zǐqiān.
Gǔsǒu and Xiàng
made Shùn repair the granary
and dredge the well,
intending to kill him.
If he foresaw their intent to kill him,
he should have remonstrated early to prevent it;
if that was impossible,
he should have avoided going,
feigning illness to abstain.
Why let his father and brother succeed in their murderous plot,
causing people to hear of his father and brother's wrongdoing,
enduring for millennia?
From Yú Shùn not foreseeing this,
it shows a sage cannot foreknow –
point thirteen.
King Wǔ fell ill,
and the Duke of Zhōu prayed for his life.
After the altar was set up
and the prayers concluded,
he did not know if Heaven would grant his request.
So he divined with three turtle shells.
All three shells showed auspicious signs.
If a sage has foreknowledge,
the Duke of Zhōu should have known Heaven had already consented,
needing not to divinely use three shells to confirm.
Sages do not establish laws based solely on personal insight,
so he further prayed,
keeping it secret and unseen.
Heaven's will is hard to know,
hence divination to match the omens,
and once the omens decided his mind,
he proceeded accordingly.
A sage cannot foreknow –
point fourteen.
Yànzǐ was on a mission to Lǔ.
He did not hasten in the hall when others did not,
but Yànzǐ hastened;
when others did not kneel to present jade,
Yànzǐ knelt.
A disciple found it strange and asked Confucius.
Confucius did not know,
so he asked Yànzǐ.
Yànzǐ explained it,
and only then did Confucius understand.
A sage cannot foreknow –
point fifteen.
Chén Jiǎ asked Mèngzǐ, saying:
"What kind of person was Duke Zhōu?"
He replied:
"A sage."
"He sent Guǎn Shū to oversee Yīn,
yet Guǎn Shū rebelled.
Are both these things true?"
He said:
"Yes."
"Did Duke Zhōu know he would rebel when he sent him?
Or did he send him without knowing?"
He said:
"He did not know."
"Then can even a sage make mistakes?"
He said:
"Duke Zhōu
was the younger brother,
Guǎn Shū
was the elder brother.
Wasn't Duke Zhōu's mistake
quite natural?"
Mèngzǐ
was a man who dealt with facts,
speaking of Duke Zhōu's sageliness,
he placed himself below,
unable to foresee Guǎn Shū's rebellion.
That a sage cannot foreknow
is the sixteenth point.
Confucius said:
"Cì does not accept fate,
yet engages in trade,
and his speculations are often correct."
He criticized Zǐgòng for being skilled at hoarding,
anticipating price fluctuations,
often timing it right,
thus his wealth multiplied,
making him as rich as Táo Zhū.
If sages had foreknowledge,
Zǐgòng's successful speculations would be similar.
Sages base their judgments on signs and omens,
infer from categories of things,
and deduce accordingly;
they observe changing phenomena and names,
learning broadly and remembering.
Skillful in calculation and good at deduction,
with wide knowledge and strong memory,
they discern patterns from subtle clues,
as if measuring the present to see a thousand years ahead,
this is what's called wisdom deep as oceans.
Confucius could perceive subtleties and see minutiae,
his thoughts penetrating,
his talent and wisdom doubly superior,
vigorous and tireless,
surpassing ordinary people!
His eyes had no supernatural vision,
nor did he know things beyond human knowledge.
If a sage had far-reaching vision,
could hear hidden sounds,
converse with heaven and earth,
speak with spirits and ghosts,
know matters of heaven above and earth below,
then he could be called divine with foreknowledge,
truly exceptional among humans.
But what they see and hear with their own eyes and ears
is no different from others';
facing events and observing things,
they are no different from others,
merely a degree wiser than the worthy,
how can they be called divine and outstanding?
Now, sagehood is akin to worthiness,
those exceptionally different among people are called sages,
thus sage and worthy differ only in degree of designation,
not as absolutely distinct names.
How to clarify this?
Duke Huán of Qí and Guǎn Zhòng plotted to attack Jǔ,
before the plan was executed, it was known throughout the state.
Duke Huán found it strange,
and asked Guǎn Zhòng:
"I plotted with Zhòngfǔ to attack Jǔ,
before execution,
it's known in the state,
what is the reason?"
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"There must be a sage in the state."
Shortly after,
when Dōngguō Yá arrived,
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"This must be him."
Then he had the usher invite him up,
standing by rank.
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"Was it you who spoke of attacking Jǔ?"
He replied:
"Yes."
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"I did not speak of attacking Jǔ,
why did you mention attacking Jǔ?"
He replied:
"I hear the nobleman is good at planning,
the commoner at deducing,
I privately deduced it."
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"I did not speak of attacking Jǔ,
how did you deduce it?"
He replied:
"I hear the nobleman has three expressions:
joyful and happy,
is the look of bells and drums;
sorrowful and serene,
is the look of mourning garments;
flushed and intense,
with gesturing hands and feet,
is the look of arms and armor.
Your lord's mouth hung slightly open,
the word was 'Jǔ';
your lord raised an arm and pointed,
the direction was again Jǔ.
I privately considered which small state among the vassals might be disobedient,
surely only Jǔ!
Thus I spoke of it."
Now Guǎn Zhòng
was a man of superior wisdom,
he discerned things and examined affairs clearly.
Saying
"there must be a sage in the state"
meant he sincerely believed the state must have one.
When Dōngguō Yá arrived,
he said:
"This must be him."
Meaning Dōngguō Yá was a sage.
If worthies and sages were absolutely different,
Guǎn Zhòng, knowing there were no twelve sages around,
should have said
"there must be a worthy in the state",
not unnecessarily said
"sage"
.The plan not executed yet known in the state,
Guǎn Zhòng said
"there must be a sage in the state",
this means sages have foreknowledge.
When he saw Dōngguō Yá,
saying
"this must be him",
he called a worthy a sage.
Dōngguō Yá's knowledge was precise,
this is the same as a sage's.
A guest introduced Chúnyú Kūn to King Huì of Liáng,
after two audiences,
he remained silent throughout.
King Huì found it strange,
and reproached the guest, saying:
"You praised Mr. Chúnyú,
saying Guǎn
and Yàn couldn't compare.
But when he met me,
I gained nothing.
Am I not worth speaking to?"
The guest told Kūn.
Kūn said:
"Exactly!
The first time I saw the king, his mind was on distant things,
the second time, his mind was on music,
thus I remained silent."
The guest fully reported this.
The king was greatly astonished,
saying:
"Alas!
Is Mr. Chúnyú truly a sage?
The first time he came,
someone had presented a dragon-horse,
I hadn't yet looked at it,
when he arrived.
The second time,
someone had presented a singer,
I hadn't yet tested him,
and he arrived again.
Though I dismissed my attendants,
my private thoughts were on those things."
Now Kūn perceiving King Huì's mind was on distant things and music,
even the discernment of Tāng
and Yǔ
could not surpass.
Intentions hidden in the breast,
concealed and unseen,
yet Kūn could know them.
If considering Kūn's equal as sages,
then Kūn
is a sage;
if considering Kūn's equal not sages,
then how can a sage's knowledge
surpass Kūn's knowledge of King Huì?
Observing demeanor to glimpse the heart,
all have basis and standard to judge by.
King Líng of Chǔ convened a meeting of the feudal lords.
Zǐchǎn of Zhèng said:
"Lǔ,
Zhū, Sòng,
and Wèi will not come."
When the feudal lords assembled,
these four states indeed did not arrive.
Zhào Yáo served as the Seal-bearing Censor.
Fāngyǔ Gōng of Zhào said to the Grand Censor Zhōu Chāng:
"Your subordinate Zhào Yáo will soon replace your position."
Later, Yáo indeed became the Grand Censor.
Thus, the absence of the four states
was deduced by Zǐchǎn through reasoning;
Zhào Yáo's becoming Grand Censor
was foreseen by Fāngyǔ Gōng through observation.
By reasoning and observation,
they determined future events,
having the means to scrutinize them.
Gōngsūn Chén of Lǔ,
during the reign of Emperor Wén of Hàn,
submitted a memorial stating that the Hàn dynasty corresponded to the virtue of Earth,
and its omen would be the appearance of a yellow dragon.
Later, a yellow dragon appeared in Chéngjì.
Thus, Gōngsūn Chén knew the yellow dragon would emerge,
based on his examination of pitch-pipes and calendars to determine it.
The wisdom of sages and worthies in foreseeing events is thus verified.
The talent of sages and worthies
enables them to foreknow.
This foreknowledge
employs methods and calculations,
sometimes through skillful estimation and clever insight,
not empty knowledge without basis.
Divine marvels and sage worthiness
follow different paths and principles.
The knowledge of sages and worthies does not transcend limits,
so they use thought to interrelate matters;
encountering events without divine marvels,
hence their designations are interchangeable.
Therefore, the term "sage" or "worthy"
denotes one with moral integrity, virtue, wisdom, and ability;
while "divine"
refers to the reality of the vague, elusive, and formless.
Their realities differ,
so their natures cannot be the same;
if their realities were equal,
their effects would not differ.
Since the designations of sage and divine are not equivalent,
it is said that the sage is not divine,
and the divine is not sage.
Dōngguō Yá, with good insight,
knew the state's affairs;
Zǐgòng, with good insight,
gained wealth and profit.
The foreknowledge of sages
is like that of Zǐgòng
and Dōngguō Yá's kind.
If one is similar to Zǐgòng
and Dōngguō,
then Zǐgòng
and Dōngguō's kind are also sages.
If so,
the reality of sages and worthies is the same though their names differ,
not necessarily that their talents are vastly unequal
or their wisdom multiples apart.
The Grand Steward asked Zǐgòng:
"Is your master a sage?
Why is he so multi-talented?"
Zǐgòng replied:
"Heaven intended him to become a sage,
and also granted him many talents."
"To become"
means "not yet."
Not claiming he was already a sage,
but saying
"to become a sage"
indicates that Confucius had not yet fully achieved sagehood.
If sagehood is akin to worthiness,
cultivating conduct and refining character,
and if character is not yet established,
one would say
"to become worthy."
Now saying
"to become a sage"
implies that sagehood can be attained.
Confucius said:
"At fifteen, I set my heart on learning;
at thirty, I stood firm;
at forty, I was free from doubts;
at fifty, I understood the decrees of Heaven;
at sixty, my ear was attuned."
From understanding Heaven's decrees to having an attuned ear,
learning culminated in clear knowledge,
which is the evidence of becoming a sage.
Before fifty
and sixty,
he had not yet understood Heaven's decrees
or attained an attuned ear,
so it was said
"to become"
a sage. When Zǐgòng answered the Grand Steward,
it was probably around thirty
to forty years of age.
King Zhāo of Wèi asked Tián Qū:
"When I was in the Eastern Palace,
I heard your discourse stating:
'Becoming a sage is easy.'
Did you say this?"
Tián Qū replied:
"That is what I have learned."
King Zhāo said:
"Then are you a sage, sir?"
Tián Qū said:
"To recognize someone as a sage before they have achieved merit
was Yáo's recognition of Shùn.
To recognize someone as a sage only after they have achieved merit
is the common people's recognition of Shùn.
Now Qū has not achieved merit,
yet Your Majesty asks Qū:
'Are you a sage?'
May I ask if Your Majesty is also like Yáo?"
That sageliness can be learned
is why Tián Qū called it easy.
If it were like being exceptionally different from others,
endowed by heavenly nature and spontaneous,
how could it be learned?
And how could striving for it succeed?
Tián Qū's statement
"it is easy to become a sage"
does not necessarily mean he could achieve it;
Tián Qū's claim that it is easy
is not necessarily correct.
His statement
"that is what I have learned"
probably reflects the truth.
Worthiness can be learned,
though the effort varies,
hence the titles of worthy and sage
are shared by the benevolent and wise.
Zǐgòng asked Confucius:
"Is the Master a sage?"
Confucius said:
"As for sageliness, I cannot claim it.
I learn without satiety
and teach without weariness."
Zǐgòng said:
"'Learning without satiety'
is wisdom,
'teaching without weariness'
is benevolence.
Being both benevolent and wise,
the Master is already a sage."
From this perspective,
a benevolent and wise person
may be called a sage.
Mèngzǐ said:
"Zǐxià,
Zǐyóu,
and Zǐzhāng each grasped one aspect of the sage;
Rǎn Niú,
Mǐnzǐ Qiān,
and Yán Yuān had all aspects in miniature."
These six in their time
all had the talent of sages,
some possessing it partially but not fully,
others having it completely but not distinctly,
yet all were called sages,
showing that sageliness can be achieved through effort.
Mèngzǐ also said:
"Not to serve a sovereign who is not his own,
not to command a people who are not his own,
to advance when order prevails,
and to withdraw when chaos reigns—
such was Bóyí.
To serve any sovereign,
to command any people,
to advance whether order or chaos prevails—
such was Yī Yǐn.
To take office when possible,
to resign when necessary,
to stay long or briefly as appropriate—
such was Confucius.
All were sages of antiquity."
He further said:
"Sages are teachers for a hundred generations,
as Bóyí
and Liǔxià Huì were.
Thus, those who hear of Bóyí's character
become honest though greedy,
and resolute though timid;
those who hear of Liǔxià Huì's character
become sincere though shallow,
and broad-minded though narrow.
Rising high above a hundred generations ago,
those hearing of them a hundred generations later
are all inspired to action.
If not sages, how could they have such an effect?
And how much more those who personally received their influence?"
Now Yī Yǐn,
Bóyí,
and Liǔxià Huì were not equal to Confucius,
yet Mèngzǐ called them all
"sages"
because worthies and sages are of the same category,
and can share the same title.
Zǎi Yǔ said:
"In my view of the Master,
he is far superior to Yáo
and Shùn."
Since Confucius was a sage,
he should have been said to be
"more sage than Yáo
and Shùn,"
yet Zǎi Yǔ said
"superior"
because sages and worthies overlap,
hence their designations are interchangeable.
Sages are hard to recognize;
worthies are easier to recognize compared to sages.
If people cannot even recognize worthies,
how can they recognize sages?
Though people claim to recognize worthies,
such claims are false.
What is the use of recognizing worthies?
How can they be recognized?
Is holding high office and enjoying wealth and honor a sign of worthiness?
But wealth and honor
are matters of fate.
Being fated for wealth does not make one worthy,
nor does being fated for poverty make one unworthy.
If wealth is used to judge worthiness or unworthiness,
then office should be based on talent, not fate.
Is serving one's sovereign harmoniously and with few errors a sign of worthiness?
But sycophantic ministers
and flattering favorites do just that.
Pleasing the sovereign in speech,
acting according to the times,
avoiding opposition at court,
they escape the risk of dismissal.
Some with elegant figures
and charming, flattering faces
are not disliked by the superior and gain favor,
receiving excessive grace and bounty,
yet they cannot be called worthy.
If we consider those recommended by the court as all being virtuous and worthy?
Then those who are prominent and known by people are mostly recommended,
while those who are obscure and unrecognized are seldom recommended,
as exemplified by Yú Shùn.
When Yáo sought [counsel],
he consulted Gǔn
and Gòng Gōng,
yet Yuè could not obtain [their approval].
From this perspective,
the number of recommendations
cannot reveal the truth.
Some may have high virtue but few recommendations,
while others may have low talent but many recommendations.
An enlightened ruler seeks the good and detects the wicked by examining the numbers,
and thus sometimes grasps the reality of good and evil.
Moreover, those who associate widely and have many followers,
seeking to please the masses,
are loved and praised by people;
those who are pure and upright but not tolerated by their local community,
with aspirations too lofty to associate with the unworthy,
losing the hearts of the masses,
are hated and slandered by people.
Hence, fame often arises from knowing how to express gratitude,
while slander often stems from losing popular favor.
King Wēi of Qí, based on slander, enfeoffed the governor of Jímò,
and based on praise, boiled the governor of Ā.
The governor of Jímò had achievements but no praise,
while the governor of Ā had no results but a reputation.
Zǐgòng asked:
"If everyone in the village likes him,
what do you think?"
Confucius said:
"That is not enough."
"If everyone in the village hates him,
what do you think?"
He said:
"That is not enough either.
It is better that the good people in the village like him,
and the bad people hate him."
If so,
one who receives much praise and is called good by all, great and small,
is not necessarily worthy.
When good people praise him,
and wicked people slander him,
and praise and slander are half and half,
then he may be considered worthy.
Can we know worthiness
by the praise of good people
and the slander of wicked people?
If so,
Confucius' words can help us know the worthy,
but how do we know if those who praise this person
are worthy?
Or those who slander this person
are wicked?
What if the praisers are wicked and the slanderers are good?
People are confused and cannot distinguish.
If we consider those to whom the masses adhere
and guests gather like clouds as worthy?
Then those to whom the masses adhere
may also be people who associate widely and have many followers;
if the masses love and praise them,
they will swarm like ants and adhere to them.
Some may be noble and act for profit,
others may cherish scholars and lower themselves to guests,
humbling themselves to await the worthy.
Lord Xìnlíng,
Lord Mèngcháng,
Lord Píngyuán,
and Lord Chūnshēn
had several thousand retainers
and were called worthy lords.
Great Generals Wèi Qīng and Huò Qùbìng,
had not a single guest at their gates,
yet were called famous generals.
Hence, the gathering of guests
depends on lords who enjoy lowering themselves
and worthy men who consider profit and loss.
If one does not cherish scholars,
and cannot influence [their status],
then the masses will not adhere nor will scholars attach themselves.
If we consider those in office who govern people
and win the people's hearts, earning their songs and praises, as worthy?
Then winning the people's hearts
is no different from winning the scholars' favor.
They may feign kindness to comfort their people,
and when the people get what they desire,
they become joyful.
How to verify this?
Tián Chéngzǐ of Qí
and King Gōujiàn of Yuè are examples.
Chéngzǐ wanted to monopolize the government of Qí,
so he lent with large measures and collected with small ones, pleasing the people;
Gōujiàn wanted to avenge the shame of Kuàijī,
so he comforted his people,
mourning the dead and inquiring after the sick, and the people were pleased.
Both had their own desires for other purposes,
yet deceptively won over their people;
without sincere intent,
the people were still pleased.
When Lord Mèngcháng left the Qín pass at night,
the roosters had not crowed and the gate was not open;
a lowly guest among his retinue
flapped his arms and imitated the rooster's crow,
and all the roosters responded;
the gate opened,
and Lord Mèngcháng escaped.
If roosters can be moved by deceptive sounds,
then people can also be stirred by feigned kindness;
if people can be stirred by feigned kindness,
then Heaven can also respond to cunning deceit.
To move and attract the qi of Heaven,
one should use essence and spirit,
yet people use burning mirrors to obtain fire from Heaven,
smelt the five minerals,
and in the height of summer in the fifth month,
cast them into vessels to obtain fire.
Now, if one simply takes a knife,
sword, or ordinary bronze hook,
and polishes it facing the sun,
one can also obtain fire.
If burning mirrors,
knives, swords,
and hooks can obtain fire from the sun,
then even non-sages can move the qi of Heaven.
If Dǒng Zhòngshū believed that clay dragons could bring clouds and rain,
perhaps there was a reason.
If so,
responding to Heaven's governance
cannot yet be called worthy,
so how can merely winning people's hearts be called worthy?
If we consider holding office and achieving success with visible results as worthy?
What constitutes achievement in office?
If it is the adherence of the people,
then the people can be pleased with feigned kindness.
When yin and yang harmonize
and the common people are at peace,
it is due to the times.
In harmonious times,
the unworthy encounter peace;
in disharmonious times,
even sages face danger.
If we judge the worthy and unworthy by the harmony of yin and yang,
then Yáo should have been dismissed for the great flood,
and Tāng should have been demoted for the great drought.
If achievement means concrete deeds,
those who personally perform them
have visible and prominent merits;
those who strategize with the Way
have results that are submerged and unapparent.
A drum is not equivalent to the five notes,
but without the drum, the five notes do not harmonize;
a teacher is not equivalent to the five degrees of mourning,
but without the teacher, the five degrees do not foster closeness;
water is not equivalent to the five colors,
but without water, the five colors do not appear vivid.
The Way is the root of achievement,
achievement is the manifestation of the Way;
to judge worthiness based on achievement
is to consider those who follow the Way as unworthy.
When Gāozǔ won the empire,
he rewarded his ministers for their achievements,
and Xiāo Hé received the highest reward.
Why?
Gāozǔ assessed achievements
by comparing them to hunters unleashing dogs;
the dogs catch the prey,
but the credit goes to the man.
The ministers fought with their hands,
like the dogs;
Xiāo Hé maintained heavy responsibilities,
like the man.
If we must judge worthiness based on success,
then Xiāo Hé had no achievement.
That achievement and reward cannot prove worthiness
is one point.
The sages and worthies have methods for governing the world;
with the right methods, they achieve success;
without them, affairs fall into ruin.
It is like a physician treating an illness:
with a proper prescription,
even severe cases can be cured;
without one,
even minor ailments won't heal.
The prescription is like the method,
the illness like disorder,
the physician like an official,
and the medicine like instruction.
When the prescription is applied and medicine administered,
when methods are established and instructions followed,
disorder ceases with compliance,
and illness is cured with treatment.
A physician who cures diseases
may not be more benevolent than non-physicians.
Similarly, officials who govern the state
may not be wiser than those who cannot govern,
but happen to have found the right method
and encountered understanding of its techniques.
Governing a state requires methods to achieve merit,
yet there are times when it is destined to be chaotic;
even with methods applied,
success may not be attained.
There are also times of inherent stability,
where even without specific methods,
success is still achieved.
Thus, those who govern
may succeed by seizing the right timing,
or fail by missing it.
Skilled individuals can achieve merit by aligning with the times,
but cannot reverse the times to force stability.
A good physician can treat those not fated to die,
but if destiny is exhausted and life span ended,
even the best prescriptions prove ineffective.
So when the era is destined for chaos,
even Yáo and Shùn employing their methods
cannot achieve merit;
when death is fated,
even Biǎn Què applying his prescriptions
cannot cure the illness.
Archery, charioteering, and various crafts,
all skilled artisans
rely on techniques and methods
to accomplish their tasks and achieve success,
making their efficacy visible.
Observing state governance
is similar to these crafts;
establishing merit
is like completing a task.
To claim that those with achievements are worthy
is to say all artisans are worthy people.
The Zhào person Wú Qiū Shòuwáng,
an attendant during Emperor Wǔ's reign,
was sent by the emperor to study the Spring and Autumn Annals with Dǒng Zhòngshū,
gifted with high talent,
thoroughly understanding affairs,
later became the commandant of Dōngjùn.
Considering Shòuwáng's worthiness,
the emperor did not appoint a grand administrator.
At that time, with military campaigns launched,
the people were in turmoil,
the harvest was poor,
and banditry did not cease.
The emperor wrote to Shòuwáng:
"When you were before me,
ideas converged like spokes to a hub,
I thought you peerless under heaven,
rarely matched within the seas.
Yet now, with authority over more than ten cities,
bearing the responsibility of four thousand shi,
bandits raid armories by boat,
greatly inconsistent with your former self.
Why is this?"
Shòuwáng apologized, saying it was hard to suppress.
He was recalled as a grand master of the palace,
often staying by the emperor's side,
discussing matters and proposing ideas,
never being wrong,
with high talent and deep wisdom,
thoroughly understanding and widely knowledgeable.
Yet as commandant of Dōngjùn,
with poor harvests,
banditry unceasing,
and people in turmoil,
he could not control it.
Was it that Shòuwáng lacked the method to govern Dōngjùn?
Or was it that Dōngjùn was destined to be chaotic again,
and his governance coincidentally met that time?
With Shòuwáng's worthiness,
he could not achieve merit in governing Dōngjùn;
if judging worthiness solely by merit,
then Shòuwáng would be discarded and not selected.
I fear there must be many like Shòuwáng in the world,
yet critics, seeing no merit, overlook their worthiness.
In Yān, there was a valley
with a cold climate,
where the five grains would not grow.
Zōu Yǎn blew his pitch-pipes to summon energy,
turning the cold into warmth,
allowing Yān to plant millet,
which grew abundantly and ripened,
and to this day it is called Millet Valley.
Harmonizing yīn and yáng
should be done through virtue and sincerity.
Yet Zōu Yǎn, by blowing his pitch-pipes,
warmed the cold valley,
and millet grew and thrived.
Extending this analogy to all successful endeavors,
they are like Zōu Yǎn's method of blowing the pipes.
Thus, with the right method,
even the unworthy can achieve anything;
without the proper technique,
even sages and worthies may fail to govern.
This shows that merit cannot fully validate worthiness—
the second point.
When people undertake tasks,
sometimes intentions are sincere but success is not achieved,
or endeavors fail yet their influence shakes mountains.
Jīng Kē
and the physician Xià Wúqiě exemplify this.
Jīng Kē's plan to enter Qín
was originally to capture the Qín king alive and bring him to Yān,
but by unfortunate chance,
he was captured by Qín.
When Jīng Kē pursued the Qín king,
and the king ran around a pillar,
physician Xià Wúqiě threw his medicine bag at Jīng Kē.
Later, the world honored Kē as a heroic martyr,
and the Qín king rewarded Wúqiě with two hundred yi of gold.
Though captured by Qín,
the merit of capturing the king alive was not achieved.
Throwing a medicine bag at an assassin
did little to save the ruler,
yet they were still praised and rewarded,
because their intentions were sincere and their spirit strong.
The world's scholars do not deny Jīng Kē's righteousness for his lack of success,
nor did the Qín king withhold reward from Wúqiě for his ineffectiveness.
Good intentions may not result in success;
supreme righteousness may not accomplish the task.
Righteousness abundant,
efficacy insufficient;
ambition grand,
achievement minor—
the wise reward this,
the foolish punish it.
If we only consider success without examining intent,
evaluating overt results while ignoring hidden plans,
then Yù Ràng drawing his sword to cut Lord Xiāng's robe
would not be worth recognizing;
Wǔ Zǐxū whipping King Píng's corpse
would not be worth recording;
Zhāng Liáng's hammer throw at the First Emperor,
missing and hitting a secondary carriage,
would not be worth noting.
These three faced unfavorable circumstances,
their plans unfulfilled,
possessing the momentum but not the achievement,
holding the strategy but unable to execute it.
This demonstrates that merit cannot fully validate worthiness—
the third point.
Is being filial to one's father and
deferential to one's elder brother considered virtuous?
Then those who are filial and deferential
have fathers and elder brothers.
If the fathers and elder brothers are not kind,
the filial piety and deference become manifest.
Shùn had Gǔsǒu,
Shēn had Zēngxī,
thus their filial piety was established and their reputations achieved,
praised by the masses.
If one had no father or elder brother,
or if the father and elder brother were kind and good,
there would be no conspicuous demonstration,
and the names of filial piety and deference
would not be seen.
Loyalty to one's ruler
is also the same as this.
Lóng Péng and
Bǐgān's loyalty was prominent in the Xià and
Yīn dynasties because
Jié and Zhòu were wicked;
Jì, Qì, and
Gāoyáo's loyalty was obscure in the Táng and
Yú eras because
Yáo and Shùn were virtuous.
Thus the brightness of a firefly
is overshadowed by the light of the sun and moon;
the reputation of a loyal minister
is obscured by the name of a virtuous ruler.
Dying for the ruler's calamity,
offering one's life and sacrificing oneself,
is the same as this.
If a minister encounters such a time
and dies in that calamity,
he thus establishes his righteousness and gains his fame.
When a great worthy engages with the world,
he hovers before alighting,
raises when the signs appear,
so that the troubles of a chaotic ruler do not burden his person,
and the disasters of a perilous state do not reach his family.
How could he encounter such disasters and die in those troubles?
The Marquis of Qí asked Yànzǐ,
"How does a loyal minister serve his ruler?"
He replied,
"He does not die when there is calamity,
nor does he escort when the ruler flees."
The Marquis of Qí said,
"I grant him land,
bestow titles to honor him.
If the ruler has calamity and he does not die,
or flees and he does not escort,
can this be called loyalty?"
He replied,
"If his words are heeded,
the ruler will have no calamity for life—
how would the minister die then?
If his advice is followed,
the ruler will never flee—
how would the minister escort then?
If his words are not heeded
and he dies in calamity,
that is a vain death;
if his advice is not followed
and he escorts the fleeing ruler,
that is hypocrisy.
Therefore, a loyal minister
can exhaust goodness for his ruler,
but cannot join him in falling into calamity."
Considering Yànzǐ's response,
to seek worthies in the world,
those who die for the ruler's calamity
and establish loyal integrity do not meet the standard.
Thus, great worthies have few nameable virtues,
while minor worthies have many commendable deeds.
What can be counted is small,
and what can be measured is few.
When evil is extreme,
calculation cannot encompass it;
when numbers are vast,
measures cannot contain them.
Deeds that are minor and easily named,
and occur in times of decline and chaos that are easily seen,
thus make integrity conspicuous and reputations heard.
Those floating on the sea
lose their bearings east and west—
because it is vast;
those walking in a ditch
all recognize the traces of boats and oars—
because it is small.
Small things are easily seen,
and decline and chaos are also easily observed.
Thus, if the world is not perilous and chaotic,
extraordinary conduct does not appear;
if the ruler is not perverse and deluded,
loyal integrity is not established.
Lofty righteousness
emerges in tumultuous courts;
pure and noble conduct
becomes evident in times of decline and chaos.
Is preserving oneself from harm,
avoiding punishment and execution,
like Nánróng who feared the "White Scepter," considered virtuous?
Then those who avoid harm are fortunate,
and it is due to auspicious fate and fortune,
not something that intelligence can prevent
or conduct can avert.
A divine snake can be severed and rejoin,
but it cannot prevent others from cutting it;
a sage can be trapped and then escape,
but cannot prevent others from harming him.
Nánróng could avoid punishment himself,
while Gōngyě was imprisoned though innocent;
Bóyù could maintain his integrity in a lawless state,
yet King Wén was confined in Yǒulǐ,
and Confucius was distressed in Chén and
Cài—these difficulties were not caused by their conduct,
but befell them unexpectedly,
so they had the misfortune of being unable to avoid it themselves,
burdened and hindered.
Those who cannot avoid calamity themselves
are like those who cannot prolong their lives in the world.
When fate is exhausted,
even a worthy cannot extend it;
when times are adverse,
even a sage cannot escape.
Is abandoning the state and leaving one's position,
forsaking wealth and honor for poverty and lowliness, considered virtuous?
Then those who abandon the state
are compelled by something.
Like the followers of Bóyí,
who yielded the state among brothers,
ashamed of having a name for dispute,
and like Tàiwáng Dǎnfǔ who valued his old people over war—
all who abandoned the state and left their positions
did so because their way was not practiced and their aspirations unfulfilled.
If their way was practiced and aspirations met,
they would not leave their positions.
Thus, abandoning the state and leaving positions
all have reasons;
to call them virtuous—
what about those without such reasons?
Can they be called unworthy?
Moreover, those with state positions
can indeed abandon and leave them,
but those without state positions—what can they abandon?
Dividing wealth and yielding portions to subordinates
is of the same nature.
Without wealth, what is there to divide?
With hungry mouths, what is there to yield?
When granaries are full,
the people know ritual and integrity;
when food and clothing are sufficient,
the people know honor and shame.
Yielding arises from surplus,
strife from insufficiency.
Some people divide wealth to aid others—
like General Yuán repeatedly dividing family property with his brother's son,
many consider this kind and righteous.
At the foot of Kūnlún Mountain,
jade is treated as stone;
on the shores of Pénglí Lake,
fish are fed to dogs and pigs.
If those who are yielding
had wealth like the jade of Kūnlún
or the fish of Pénglí,
dividing family property repeatedly
would be insignificant.
Hán Xìn depended on meals from the chief of Náncháng village—
what wealth did he have to divide?
Yán Yuān with his single bamboo bowl of food and gourd of drink—
what wealth did he have to yield?
Guǎn Zhòng took more when dividing wealth,
lacking the integrity of honesty and yielding,
because poverty and insufficiency
led to the abandonment of moral principles.
Is withdrawing from the world and separating from customs,
purifying oneself and maintaining clean conduct, considered virtuous?
This is the same category as abandoning the state and leaving positions.
Wealth and honor
are what human nature covets;
high offices and great positions
are what people desire and enjoy.
To leave them and live in seclusion
is due to lack of opportunity in life,
and unfulfilled aspirations.
Chángjū and
Jíenì withdrew from the world to live in seclusion;
Bóyí and
Yúlíng abandoned honor for lowliness—
not because it was their true aspiration.
If one regards being tranquil and free from desires,
with no intention to serve in office,
and merely seeking to preserve one's body and nurture one's nature as worthy—is that so?
Then such a person belongs to the school of Lǎodān.
The reason why the Dàoist differs from the worthy lies in
the latter's concern for the world and aiding the people in times of hardship.
Thus, Confucius was restless,
and Mòzǐ was hurried.
Not advancing to align with the endeavors of Confucius and
Mòzǐ,
but instead reverting to the conduct of Huángdì and
Lǎozǐ—this is not worthy.
If one regards traveling a thousand lǐ to uphold righteousness,
and never neglecting rituals toward teachers, commanders, and friends as worthy—is that so?
Then those with abundant family wealth and resources,
and strong physical strength can bear it.
If one lacks the means to perform rituals,
or is too weak to travel far,
they cannot undertake it.
Therefore, in families with a hundred gold,
no friendships are severed beyond the borders;
in states with a thousand chariots,
no gifts are omitted among allies—
all due to ample wealth.
If grains were as plentiful as water and fire,
even the greedy and stingy
would cross borders to give alms.
Thus, with little wealth, one cannot uphold even one proper ritual;
with surplus, reckless giving can reach a thousand.
For families so poor they lack even a peck or basket of reserves,
it is hard to demand mutual generosity.
Those who carry loads for a thousand lǐ,
or scholars who traverse borders with their strategies,
with calloused hands and feet,
and faces darkened by the sun,
free from ailments that hinder their duties—
their sinews, strength, and skin must differ from others.
Extending this analogy to officials who bear crucial evidence for their lord,
those who endure physical pain without uttering a word—
it is also due to their robust muscles and bones.
Robustness enables them to conceal affairs and establish righteousness;
weakness leads to deceiving the times and destroying integrity.
Yǜ Ràng mutilated himself,
and his wife could not recognize him;
Guàn Gāo was flogged,
leaving no part of his body unharmed—
their physical endurance differed from others,
and thus their integrity and conduct were not equal to others.
If one regards being well-versed in classics and gathering disciples as worthy—is that so?
Then those who are classically learned,
the Rúists, fit this.
Rúists are
what learning produces.
Rúists learn;
learning makes one a Rúist.
Transmitting the legacy of earlier masters,
practicing oral teachings to instruct,
without original creation in mind,
nor critical thought to affirm or deny arguments—
they are like couriers delivering letters,
or gatekeepers transmitting orders.
If the seal is intact and nothing is lost,
and the teaching is precise without error,
that is considered good.
Rúists transmit learning,
not altering a single word;
the ancient words of prior masters
remain complete to this day.
Even if they lead over a hundred disciples,
holding positions like academicians or
literary officials,
they are akin to couriers and
gatekeepers.
If one regards comprehending ancient and modern times,
and memorizing all secret and obscure records as worthy—is that so?
Then this is secondary to the Rúist.
Those with high talent and enthusiasm,
diligent in study without cease,
like descendants of specialized achievers,
inheriting ancestral writings,
able to complete their textual work,
reading and reciting them—
such as archival officials handling documents,
or figures like Sīmǎ Qiān and Liú Xiàng,
who held positions overseeing records,
then they gain a reputation for broad learning and thorough understanding.
If one regards being shrewd in stratagems and deceit,
and capable of leading troops and commanding masses as worthy—is that so?
Then such are followers of Hán Xìn.
In the Warring States period, they achieved merit,
and were called famous generals;
in peaceful times, with no arena for their skills,
they instead meet with disaster.
When the high-flying birds are dead,
the good bows are stored away;
when the cunning hares are caught,
the good hounds are cooked.
Ministers of deceit and stratagem are
the bows for high birds and
the hounds for cunning hares.
In times of peace, they have no proper place,
so bows are stored and hounds cooked.
The rulers of peaceful times
do not abandon ministers or despise scholars;
rather, the aids used in the world
are not suited to the era.
Had Hán Xìn applied his talent for adaptability
to tasks like Shūsūn Tōng's,
how could he have met the disaster of being executed for rebellion?
Possessing the power to achieve strong merits,
but lacking the wisdom to maintain peace,
understanding strategies for leading troops,
but failing to see the righteousness of an settled order—
living in peaceful times,
yet plotting rebellion—
this is why his achievements were erased and his state ended,
and he cannot be called worthy.
If one regards eloquence in speech,
with sweet words and clever phrases as worthy—is that so?
Then such are followers of Zǐgòng.
Zǐgòng's debate skills surpassed Yán Yuān's,
yet Confucius ranked him lower.
If one's true ability is not high,
but their speech is sharp and clever,
people may still praise them.
Since Emperor Wén admired the Tiger Enclosure Keeper,
more than the Shanglin Park Captain,
and Zhāng Shìzhī praised Zhōu Bó and
Zhāng Xiàngrú,
Emperor Wén then realized his error.
Those eloquent in speech,
like the Tiger Enclosure Keeper,
are hard to regard as worthy.
If one regards quickness with the brush,
with writings pouring down like rain as worthy—is that so?
The brush and the mouth
are essentially the same.
The mouth speaks to form words,
the brush writes to form texts.
Eloquence in speech
does not necessarily mean high talent;
likewise, quickness with the brush
does not necessarily mean great knowledge.
Moreover, what is quickness with the brush for?
Is it for efficiency in official duties?
Among duties, none is more difficult
than legal cases;
in doubtful cases, there are requests for deliberation.
The most expert in the world
was none other than Zhāng Tāng;
Zhāng Tāng's writings were severe,
and in the Hàn court,
he was not considered worthy.
Sīmǎ Qiān in his accounts
deemed Zhāng Tāng cruel,
and cruelty is not the conduct of the worthy.
The weeping woman in the Lǔ woods—
a tiger killed her husband,
and then her son,
yet she did not leave—
because the governance was not harsh,
and the officials were not violent.
Cruelty belongs to the faction of
harshness and violence,
and is hard to consider worthy.
If one regards skill in composing rhapsodies and eulogies,
creating grand and elegant writings as worthy—is that so?
Then such are Sīmǎ Xiàngrú and
Yáng Xióng.
Their writings are beautiful and ambitious,
their words subtle and profound,
yet they cannot determine right and wrong,
or debate the reality of truth and falsehood.
Even if their texts are like brocade,
deep as the Yellow River and
the Hàn River, people do not perceive the distinction of right and wrong,
and it contributes nothing to promoting a culture of honoring substance.
Is it virtuous to maintain one's purity and integrity,
refusing to lower one's aspirations or disgrace oneself?
This refers to those who withdraw from society and detach from the mundane world,
like Cháng Jū
and Jié Nì.
Although not entirely detached from worldly affairs,
their integrity equals that of recluses,
purifying themselves without assisting their rulers,
guarding their principles without burdening the people.
The truly virtuous in the world
act when the time is right,
and stop when necessary,
weighing what is appropriate
to regulate their conduct between purity and compromise.
Zǐgòng's refusal of reward discouraged goodness,
while Zǐlù's acceptance encouraged virtue.
Refusal signifies integrity;
acceptance implies greed.
Yet greed can be beneficial,
while integrity may cause harm.
In practicing moral principles,
one cannot always maintain absolute purity.
Bóyí's inflexibility
was criticized by Confucius.
Conduct contrary to the sage's teachings
can hardly be considered virtuous.
Someone asked Confucius:
"What kind of person is Yán Yuān?"
He replied:
"A man of benevolence,
whom I cannot equal."
"What kind of person is Zǐgòng?"
He said:
"An eloquent man,
whom I cannot equal."
"What kind of person is Zǐlù?"
He answered:
"A courageous man,
whom I cannot equal."
The visitor said:
"All three excel you,
yet they serve you.
Why?"
Confucius said:
"I can be benevolent yet resolute,
eloquent yet reticent,
courageous yet cautious.
To exchange my way
for their abilities
is something I would not do."
Confucius knew how to apply his qualities appropriately.
One may have outstanding talent and pure conduct,
but without wisdom to apply them properly,
they are no different from the foolish and unprincipled.
Thus,
all have their faults.
Can one without any fault
be considered virtuous?
This would describe the village hypocrite.
Mèngzǐ said:
"Nothing to criticize in his conduct,
nothing to censure in his behavior.
Conforming to vulgar customs,
blending with the corrupt world,
appearing loyal and trustworthy in residence,
seeming pure and honest in conduct,
pleasing everyone,
self-righteous,
yet incapable of embracing the way of Yáo
and Shùn.
Therefore Confucius said:
'The village hypocrite
is the thief of virtue.'"
What resembles virtue but is not
was despised by Confucius.
Thus,
how can we recognize true virtue?
What is the use of knowing the virtuous?
Ordinary people's standard
is simply to see outstanding talent and ability,
with achievements and results,
then call them virtuous.
If it were this easy,
what difficulty would there be in knowing the virtuous?
The Book of Documents says:
"To know men is wisdom,
which even the Emperor found difficult."
To regard the highly talented and exceptional
as virtuous
poses no difficulty.
Yet it is considered difficult
for specific reasons.
Even Yú Shùn found it hard to know people,
yet ordinary people claim they can recognize virtue -
this is mistaken.
Then are the virtuous ultimately unknowable?
I say: They are easy to know.
Those who claim difficulty
fail to see the method of knowing them.
Without this method,
even sages would find it difficult;
with the method,
people of average ability can discern them.
Like craftsmen making vessels:
understanding makes it easy,
lack of understanding makes it hard.
Knowing the virtuous is easier than making vessels.
The world lacks discrimination,
so true virtue remains among ordinary scholars.
Common scholars, with their debating skills
and high official positions,
enjoy prominent favor
and monopolize the reputation of virtue.
The truly virtuous remain in alleys and lanes,
poor and lowly till old age,
slandered without evidence.
Under such circumstances,
when can they be recognized?
However, if we must know them,
observe their good hearts.
The virtuous
may not have high ability but possess enlightened hearts,
may not have great intelligence but act correctly.
How to observe the heart?
Necessarily through words.
With a good heart,
come good words.
Through words we examine conduct:
good words lead to good deeds.
When words and deeds are faultless,
managing family shows proper relationships,
governing the state maintains proper order between noble and humble.
Those without good hearts
cannot distinguish black from white,
treat good and evil as equal,
create political chaos,
and lose balance in laws and measures.
Therefore, with a good heart,
nothing is not good;
with an evil heart,
nothing can be good.
A good heart can distinguish right from wrong.
When the meaning of right and wrong is established,
the effect of a good heart becomes clear.
Even in poverty and distress,
without achievements or established results,
one can still be virtuous.
Thus, in governance we don't seek achievement,
but require correct methods;
in conduct we don't demand results,
but expect proper actions.
With correctness and truth clearly established,
words need not be numerous,
deeds need not be many.
Therefore it is said:
"Words don't need to be many,
but must clarify what is said;
deeds don't need to be far-reaching,
but must examine their origins."
When words capture the heart of truth,
though the mouth may be inarticulate,
eloquence resides within the breast.
Thus we desire eloquence of heart,
not eloquence of tongue.
Eloquence of heart means plain words that don't violate truth,
while eloquence of tongue means fine rhetoric without substance.
Confucius described Shǎozhèng Mǎo's evil thus:
"His words are wrong yet voluminous,
he follows error yet makes it attractive."
When internal error is decorated with external talent,
the masses cannot perceive it,
and consider him virtuous.
When internal error is externally adorned as truth,
the world considers it virtue,
then those with internal truth but no external display
will also be considered unworthy by the masses.
When right and wrong are in chaos and order is lost,
only the sage understands this.
People's words and actions are often like those of Shǎozhèng Máo,
and only the worthy recognize this.
In the world, there are erroneous and confused statements about right and wrong,
as well as intricate and disordered affairs.
To resolve erroneous statements
and settle disordered affairs,
only the worthy and sage individuals are capable of undertaking such tasks.
The sage's mind is clear and not obscured,
the worthy's mind is orderly and not chaotic.
Using clarity to examine what is wrong,
nothing erroneous escapes notice;
using reason to weigh doubts,
no doubt remains unresolved.
When one's views differ from the world's,
even if the words are correct,
the multitude fails to comprehend.
Why is this?
Because they have long been immersed in conventional discourse,
unable to free themselves and follow the truth.
Therefore, correct words
are condemned by the multitude,
and customs-defying rituals
are ridiculed by the world.
Guǎnzǐ said:
"When a gentleman speaks in the hall, the hall is full;
when he speaks in the chamber, the chamber is full."
One may wonder about this saying—
how can it be considered 'full'?
If correct words are spoken,
and everyone in the hall possesses the understanding of correctness,
then it can be called full.
If the words are not correct,
and people's views conflict and differ,
how can it be considered full?
Exquisite songs
have few who can harmonize;
words that capture truth
are rarely affirmed.
Harmonizing with songs and heeding words
share the same essence.
If a song is exquisite,
not all can harmonize;
if words are true,
not all will believe.
When Duke Wén of Lǔ reversed the sacrificial order,
three officials departed;
when Duke Dìng followed the proper order,
five officials rebelled.
Those accustomed to conventions
will deem the rites wrong.
Few understand the rites,
so those who know what is right are rare.
When a gentleman speaks,
how can the hall or chamber be full?
If people do not call it full,
the world cannot witness the truth in spoken words.
Only the traces of ink
laid out on bamboo slips
can make it known.
Thus, though Confucius did not become king,
he composed the *Spring and Autumn Annals* to express his intent.
Examining the literary work of the *Spring and Autumn Annals*,
one can understand Confucius's capability for kingship.
Confucius
was a sage.
Those who undertake Confucius's work,
even without his talent,
still demonstrate the substance of worthiness.
The worthy and the sage follow the same path but bear different names;
if worthiness can be determined,
then sageliness can be discussed.
Question:
"If the Way of Zhōu had not declined,
Confucius would not have composed the *Spring and Autumn Annals*.
The composition of the *Spring and Autumn Annals*
arose from the decline of the Zhōu Way.
If the Zhōu Way had not declined,
and Confucius had not composed it,
it would not mean he lacked the talent of Confucius,
but that there was no impetus.
If so,
then Confucius's composition of the *Spring and Autumn Annals*
cannot be used to observe his sageliness;
and those who undertake Confucius's work
cannot be known as worthy."
Reply: When the Zhōu Way declined,
Confucius arose and composed it,
using literary meaning to praise and condemn, affirming right and wrong,
capturing the substance of the Way and principle,
without errors or deviations,
thereby revealing Confucius's worthiness,
which is real.
If there are no words,
examine through writing;
if there is no writing,
examine through speech.
Suppose Confucius had not composed it,
there would still be his遗留 words,
and words must have an origin,
just as writing must have a purpose.
To judge the right and wrong of writing,
without regard to its origin,
there are many writers in the world,
yet right and wrong are not distinguished,
affirmation and denial are uncertain.
When桓君山 discusses this,
it can be said he grasps the truth.
To evaluate writing and examine reality,
then桓君山
is a worthy of the Hàn dynasty.
Before Chén Píng entered office,
he distributed meat in the village,
dividing it equally and fairly,
which was evidence of his capability to become chancellor.
Distributing meat and composing writings
share the same essence.
If桓君山 had held power like Chén Píng in Hàn,
his efforts and arguments would not have differed in intent.
Though Confucius did not become king,
his work as an uncrowned king
lies in the *Spring and Autumn Annals*.
Similarly, though桓君山 did not serve as chancellor,
the traces of an uncrowned chancellor remain in his *New Discourses*.
Confucian scholars explaining the Five Classics
often miss their true substance.
Earlier scholars did not see the whole context,
idly producing empty theories;
later scholars trust the words of former masters,
following old narratives and traditions,
skillfully using phrases,
hastily claiming the learning of a single master,
rushing to teach as masters,
seeking early official posts,
eagerly competing for advancement,
with no time to focus their minds
and examine the roots and core of reality.
Thus, empty theories are transmitted without end,
while factual matters are buried and unseen,
and the Five Classics all lose their true substance.
The *Book of Documents*
and *Spring and Autumn Annals* have events that are relatively easy to compare,
allowing a rough correction of the main points
to illuminate the subtle texts within the chapters.
Those who explain the *Book of Documents*
sometimes say it originally had one hundred and two chapters,
but later, after the Qín burning of the *Book of Songs*
and *Book of Documents*,
only twenty-nine chapters remained.
The twelve dukes recorded in the Chūnqiū,
are like the hundred chapters of the Shàngshū;
since the hundred chapters had no model to follow,
how could the twelve dukes have one?
Those who explain the Chūnqiū say:
"Over the course of 242 years,
human principles were fully expressed,
the way of kings was complete,
good was promoted and evil condemned,
chaotic times were set in order,
and all was returned to correctness.
Nothing comes closer to this than the Chūnqiū."
According to this view,
human principles
and the way of kings were perfectly fulfilled.
An army of three divisions with six brigades totaling twelve thousand men
is sufficient to overwhelm enemies and suppress rebels,
dominating the world,
with orders obeyed and prohibitions heeded,
yet it need not follow any specific model.
When Confucius composed the Chūnqiū,
recording the twelve dukes of Lǔ,
it was like the three divisions having six brigades;
the twelve thousand troops
correspond to the 242 years.
Six brigades with twelve thousand men
are enough to form an army;
twelve dukes over 242 years
are sufficient to establish righteousness.
Those who interpret events tend to mystify principles and exaggerate meanings,
failing to acknowledge coincidental misfortunes,
hence they claim the numbers of chapters in classics and commentaries
all follow certain models.
But examining the facts and origins,
and analyzing their literary meaning,
shows they are no different
from other worthy writings
(and poems).
Thus when sages create classics
and worthies write books,
once the meaning is exhausted and reasoning complete,
with literary expression fully adequate,
then a chapter is formed.
In organizing chapters,
similar categories are grouped together,
with sections and clauses attached accordingly.
When kinds and categories differ,
and discussions vary,
separate chapters are created.
Different intentions lead to distinct writings,
changed events result in altered chapters—
based on events and intentions in composition,
how could there be any principle of modeling after patterns?
Some explain that the 242 years of the Chūnqiū
correspond to a long lifespan of ninety years,
middle lifespan of eighty,
and short lifespan of seventy,
with Confucius composing based on three middle lifespans;
three times eighty makes 240,
hence the 240 years.
Others say it matches the middle number of the red system.
Still others claim that over 242 years,
human principles were fully expressed,
and the way of kings was complete.
Now if we accept the three-lifespan theory,
then the completeness theory is wrong;
if the completeness theory is correct,
then the three-lifespan argument is mistaken.
These two contradict each other,
yet both establish their meanings—
how can the sage's intention be determined?
Generally, recording events with years, months, and days
indicates thoroughness and importance.
The Hóng Fàn mentions five calendrical measures:
year, month,
day, and stars.
These are records of events,
not statements about modeling patterns.
Recording the twelve dukes' reigns
totaling 242 years
is used to support the three-lifespan theory.
But did Confucius record the twelve dukes
because their events
were恰好 sufficient to manifest kingly righteousness?
According to the three-lifespan theory,
does the three-lifespan count
恰好 require twelve dukes to be complete?
If based on twelve dukes,
then 242 years don't serve to manifest three lifespans;
if based on three lifespans,
taking three times eighty,
240 years would suffice—
why necessarily take
"two" more?
Explanators also say:
"To align with Duke Yīn's first year.
Without taking the second year,
Duke Yīn's first year wouldn't be recorded in the classic."
But if the Chūnqiū was composed based on the three-lifespan number,
why use Duke Yīn's first year events as the beginning?
If Duke Yīn's first year events must be the start,
this ultimately makes completeness the principle,
and the three-lifespan theory becomes unusable.
Suppose Duke Yīn reigned for fifty years—
would all years from his accession be recorded?
Or interrupted to fit three times eighty?
If all years from his accession are recorded,
the three-times-eighty count would be broken;
if interrupted to fit three lifespans,
then Duke Yīn's first year wouldn't align.
What then?
Moreover, years versus months and days
differ only in scale;
what they record
is of the same nature.
If 242 years are called based on three lifespans,
then the months and days within those years must have their counts too.
If years are based on three lifespans,
what are months and days based on?
The years in the Chūnqiū
are like the chapters in the Shàngshū:
chapters begin meanings,
years record events.
To say the Chūnqiū's years have a basis
is to say the Shàngshū's chapters also have one.
Those explaining the Yì all say Fúxī created the eight trigrams,
and King Wén expanded them to sixty-four.
When sage kings arise,
the River produces the Diagram,
the Luò produces the Writing.
When Fúxī ruled,
the River Diagram emerged from the river—
this is the Yì's hexagrams.
In Yǔ's time,
the Luò Writing was obtained—
the Writing emerged from the Luò River,
which is the nine chapters of the Hóng Fàn.
Thus Fúxī used trigrams to govern the world,
and Yǔ followed the Hóng Fàn to control floods.
In ancient times, when King Lièshānshì obtained the River Diagram,
the Xià followed it as the Liánshān;
when King Guīcángshì obtained the River Diagram,
the Yīn followed it as the Guīcáng;
when King Fúxīshì obtained the River Diagram,
the Zhōu followed it as the Zhōuyì.
Their basic trigrams were all eight,
their derivatives all sixty-four.
King Wén
and Duke Zhōu based on the eighteen tuàn explanations investigated the six lines.
Common traditions about the Yì
say Fúxī created the eight trigrams;
not knowing their true origin,
they claim Fúxī actually created them.
Fúxī obtained the eight trigrams,
he did not
"create"
them; King Wén achieved the sixty-four,
he did not
"expand"
them.
Such terms of expansion and creation
arise from popular tales.
If we blindly believe one text,
the true reality may be nearly lost.
Since they don't know the Yì originally was the River Diagram,
nor which school's Yì survives in common practice—
whether sometimes the Liánshān,
the Guīcáng,
or sometimes the Zhōuyì.
Examining the Lǐ,
the systems of Xià, Yīn,
and Zhōu with their modifications
show clear differences.
If because the Zhōu came later,
we say the current Yì is the Zhōuyì,
then the Lǐ should also be called the Zhōulǐ.
But the six codes don't match the current Lǐ,
so the current Lǐ may not be Zhōu's—
thus we may doubt whether the current Yì is necessarily Zhōu's either.
Examining Zuǒ Qiūmíng's commentary,
which quotes the Zhōu's use of hexagrams
matching the current Yì,
it is probably the Zhōuyì.
Those who discuss the Rites
all claim to know the Rites.
But which school's Rites are they referring to?
Confucius said:
"The Yin dynasty followed the Xia rites,
and what was abolished or added can be known.
The Zhou dynasty followed the Yin rites,
and what was abolished or added can be known."
From this perspective,
the Xia, Yin,
and Zhou each had their own rites.
Are we now following the Zhou rites?
Or those of Xia and Yin?
When we speak of Zhou rites,
the "Zhōu Lǐ" comprises six codes,
yet examining the current "Lǐ Jīng," these six codes are not found.
Perhaps the Yin rites were not entirely lost,
but the six codes of the Rites were not transmitted,
so people consequently call these the Zhou rites?
Examining the laws of the Zhōu guān,
they do not correspond to the current "Lǐ,"
yet the "Zhōu Lǐ" with its six codes is the true one.
Its failure to be transmitted
is like the ancient script "Shàng Shū"
and "Chūn Qiū Zuǒ Shì" not flourishing.
Those who discuss the "Analects"
only know how to explain the text and phrases,
unaware of how many chapters the original "Lún Yǔ" had;
they only know that the Zhou used eight inches as a foot,
but do not understand why the "Lún Yǔ" specifically used a one-foot measure.
The "Lún Yǔ"
was a collective record of Confucius's words and actions by his disciples,
with many records at the time,
numbering in the tens to hundreds of chapters.
Using eight inches as a foot
made the records concise and economical,
convenient for carrying.
Because what was left was not canonical scripture,
and the transmitted texts were recorded to prevent forgetting,
they used only an eight-inch foot,
not the two-foot-four-inch standard.
It was lost during the Hàn dynasty's rise.
By Emperor Wǔ's time, the ancient texts were retrieved from Confucius's wall,
yielding twenty-one chapters,
with two from Qí and Lǔ,
and nine from Héjiān,
making thirty chapters in total.
By Emperor Zhāo's time, his daughter read twenty-one chapters.
Emperor Xuān assigned it to the Tàicháng academicians,
who then found the text difficult to understand,
calling it a commentary;
later, it was transcribed in clerical script for transmission and recitation.
Initially, Confucius's descendant Kǒng Ān Guó taught it to Fú Qīng of Lǔ,
who rose to be Governor of Jīngzhōu,
and it first came to be called "Lún Yǔ."
Today, the "Lún Yǔ" is referred to as having twenty chapters,
having lost the Qí,
Lǔ, and Héjiān nine chapters.
Originally thirty chapters,
they were dispersed and lost;
sometimes only twenty-one remain.
The number of chapters varies,
and the text may be correct or erroneous.
Those who discuss the "Lún Yǔ"
only know to dissect it with questions,
focusing on minute difficulties,
unaware of preserving the root in terms of chapter numbers and sections.
Reviewing the old to understand the new
qualifies one to be a teacher;
if one does not know the past,
how can they be called a teacher?
Mèng Zǐ said:
"When the traces of the kings vanished, the 'Shī' perished,
and after the 'Shī' perished, the 'Chūn Qiū' was created.
The 'Shèng' of Jìn,
the 'Táowù' of Chǔ,
and the 'Chūn Qiū' of Lǔ
are all the same."
According to Mèng Zǐ's words,
the "Chūn Qiū"
is the name for Lǔ's historical records,
similar to the "Shèng"
and "Táowù."
Confucius used the old name
to title the classic "Chūn Qiū,"
not necessarily with extraordinary theories or profound meanings,
nor with deeply elegant evidence.
Common scholars today claim:
"'Spring' is the start of the year,
'autumn' is its end.
The classic 'Chūn Qiū'
can serve to honor the beginning and nurture the end,
hence it is called 'Chūn Qiū'."
How does the classic "Chūn Qiū"
differ from the "Shàng Shū"?
Those who discuss the "Shàng Shū"
regard it as the book of ancient emperors,
or as what was done by superiors and recorded by subordinates,
naming it based on factual events,
not crafting meanings to appear novel.
Those who discuss the "Shàng Shū" grasp the reality of the classic,
while those who discuss the "Chūn Qiū" lose the sage's intent.
The "Chūn Qiū Zuǒ Shì Zhuàn" states:
"In the winter, tenth month, first day of Duke Huán's seventeenth year,
there was a solar eclipse,
but the day was not recorded,
due to an error by the officials."
This statement about official error
likely reflects the truth.
Historians recording events,
like today's county officials' documents,
may find it hard to miss the year and month,
but the day, being minor, is easily forgotten.
Records focus on good and evil as the substance,
not on the specific dates.
As for the "Gōngyáng"
and "Gǔliáng" commentaries,
if the date is incomplete,
they impose their own interpretations.
Ordinary events
are given strange explanations;
straightforward texts
are twisted into convoluted meanings,
which is not Confucius's intent.
The "Chūn Qiū" does mention winter and summer,
but when it omits them,
it is similar to not recording the day and month,
based on the same principle.
Táng,
Yú, Xià,
Yīn, and Zhōu
are names of lands.
Yáo succeeded from being Marquis of Táng,
Shùn rose from the land of Yú,
Yǔ emerged from Xià,
Tāng flourished from Yīn,
and King Wǔ attacked from the base of Zhōu,
all naming after their places of origin,
emphasizing the root and not forgetting the beginning,
hence adopting these as titles,
much like people having surnames.
Those who discuss the "Shàng Shū" claim that Táng,
Yú, Xià,
Yīn, and Zhōu as dynastic names
signify merit and virtue,
with connotations of prosperity and grandeur.
Thus, Táng is interpreted as
"vast and expansive,"
Yú as
"joy,"
Xià as
"great,"
Yīn as
"central,"
and Zhōu as
"utmost."
Yáo was so vast that people could not name him;
Shùn brought joy to all under heaven;
Yǔ inherited the legacy of the two emperors,
promoting a way that was vast and expansive,
so people could not name him;
Yīn achieved the central Way,
and King Wǔ of Zhōu had merit and virtue that reached the utmost.
Their established meanings are beautiful,
and they praise the five houses greatly,
yet they deviate from the true facts,
losing the original intent.
Táng, Yú,
Xià, Yīn,
and Zhōu are like Qín being Qín,
Hàn being Hàn.
Qín originated from Qín,
Hàn rose from Hànzhōng,
hence they are called Qín and
Hàn. Similarly, Wáng Mǎng started as Marquis of Xīndū,
so his fallen
dynasty was called "Xīn."
If Qín
and Hàn were mentioned in the Classics and commentaries,
commentators would again create moral theories for Qín
and Hàn.
When Yáo grew old and sought to abdicate,
the Four Peaks recommended Shùn.
Yáo said:
"Let me test him!"
An interpretation of the Shàngshū states:
"'Test'
means to employ;
it means I will employ him as the Son of Heaven."
This text means to make him the Son of Heaven.
The text further says:
"He married them to observe his conduct through the two daughters."
"Observe" here means
to display Yú Shùn to the world,
not that Yáo personally observed him.
According to this view,
they elevate Yáo and
Shùn,
believing that when sages meet, their recognition is already thorough,
requiring no observation or testing,
as their radiant spirits illuminate each other,
leading to profound mutual trust.
It also says:
"The four gates were reverent; he entered the great wilderness,
and amid violent winds and thunderstorms, he did not lose his way."
It explains
"great wilderness"
as the position of the Three Dukes.
Holding the office of one duke,
he greatly oversaw the affairs of the two other dukes,
with numerous matters all auspicious,
even as if facing swift winds and heavy rain.
Now, even if a sage's talent is lofty,
it does not mean they necessarily know each other.
To accomplish sagely deeds,
Shùn found it difficult to recognize flatterers,
so he had Gāo Yáo present methods for knowing people.
Flatterers are hard to discern,
and sages are also hard to distinguish.
Yáo's talent
was like Shùn's wisdom;
Shùn knew flatterers,
while Yáo knew sages.
When Yáo heard of Shùn's worthiness,
recommended by the Four Peaks,
he knew in his heart that he was extraordinary,
but not necessarily that he was capable,
hence he said:
"Let me test him!"
He tested him in office,
gave him his two daughters in marriage,
to observe the principles of husband and wife,
finding his governance well-ordered and uninterrupted,
and his conduct as a husband upright and unperverted.
He further sent him into the great wilderness to observe his sageliness,
where, encountering violent winds and torrential rain,
he never became confused.
Only then did Yáo know his sageliness
and entrusted him with the world.
Now, the text mentions observation and
testing—observing and testing his ability.
Some interpreters take it as metaphorical embellishment,
causing the facts to lose their correctness,
vanishing without trace;
twisting the meaning,
allowing false theories to be transmitted without end.
The transmission of fabricated theories
has been erroneous for a long time.
Later scholars of refinement,
wishing to elucidate the classics,
do not seek the truth,
and those who do seek it
also collate ancient texts and follow old ways,
emphasizing these writings,
using them as evidence for their theories.
The transmitted commentaries on the classics cannot be followed,
as the Five Classics all contain many inaccurate accounts.
The Shàngshū and
Chūnqiū record events and form texts,
clearly visible for comparison,
hence I particularly discuss them.
Some say:
Why must a scholar's lofty arguments rely on writing?
The reply is:
A person must have both substance and refinement to be complete.
There are things that are flowery but not substantial,
and others that are substantial but not flowery.
The Yì says:
"The feelings of the sage are seen in his words."
Speech uttered from the mouth is words,
collected on slips it becomes writing;
when literary expressions are arranged,
true feelings are fully displayed.
Now, cultural virtue
is the attire of the age.
Empty writing constitutes refinement,
actual conduct constitutes virtue,
and displaying it on clothing constitutes attire.
Hence it is said:
The more abundant the virtue, the more ornate the refinement;
the more manifest the virtue, the more brilliant the refinement.
The great man's virtue expands, and his refinement shines;
the petty man's virtue blazes, and his refinement is variegated.
High office brings complex refinement,
lofty virtue accumulates refinement.
That which is ornate and gleaming—
the mat of a senior official—
when Zēng Zǐ lay ill,
he ordered Yuán Qǐ to change it.
From this it follows that
clothing is used to rank the worthy,
and worthiness is graded by refinement;
the foolish and outstanding cannot be distinguished
without refinement to decide.
This is not only true for people,
