but for all things.
The dragon's scales have patterns,
making it divine among serpents;
the phoenix's feathers are five-colored,
making it sovereign among birds;
the tiger is fierce,
with striped fur;
the tortoise is wise,
with patterns on its back.
These four, whose forms are not plain,
are the sages and worthies among creatures.
Moreover, if a mountain has no forests,
it is but a mound of earth;
if land has no vegetation,
it is barren soil;
if a person has no refinement,
they are a commoner.
A barren hill has no deer,
barren soil yields no grains,
and a person without cultural virtue
cannot be a sage or worthy.
Heaven above is richly patterned, and Earth below is richly ordered;
the two energies harmonize,
sages and worthies receive them,
modeling themselves on their origins,
hence they are richly adorned.
Auspicious signs and mandated tokens,
all are forms of refinement.
Jìn's Shū Yú of Táng,
Lǔ's Jì Yǒu of Chéng,
and the wife of Duke Huì, named Zhòngzǐ,
were born strangely,
with writing on their hands.
Zhāng Liáng was destined for nobility;
going out, he met a spirit,
an old man gave him a book,
and he was enfeoffed as Marquis of Liú.
The River Deity,
thus produced the diagram;
the Luo Spirit,
thus produced the writing.
The strange things recorded on bamboo and silk
do not emerge from muddy ponds.
Things use refinement as their exterior,
people use refinement as their foundation.
Jí Zǐchéng wished to eliminate refinement,
and Zǐgòng criticized him.
Those who say refinement is not worthy of admiration
are followers of Zǐchéng.
Those who write works are literary scholars,
those who expound the classics are worldly scholars.
These two types of scholars exist in the world;
which is superior is unknown?
Some say:
Literary scholars are not as good as worldly scholars.
Worldly scholars explain the classics of the sages,
interpret the commentaries of the worthies,
their principles are broad and vast,
all based on solid understanding,
hence they hold constant official positions;
the highest among them are erudites,
their disciples gather in crowds,
attracting followers from a thousand miles away;
though they themselves die,
their learning is transmitted to later generations.
Literary scholars produce extravagant and flowery theories,
of no benefit to the world,
hence they hold no constant office,
with not a single disciple or follower visible,
and after their death,
none carry on their transmission.
This is why they are inferior to worldly scholars.
The reply states:
Not so.
The worldly Confucians expound on the sentiments of the sages,
arising together and being verified collectively,
all pursuing the path of the sages.
Their tasks differ but their endeavors align,
their words vary but their meanings converge.
How can one claim that the theories of literary Confucians offer no benefit to the world?
The profession of worldly Confucians is easy to practice,
hence many people study it;
their affairs are not complex enough to rank,
so courts establish positions for them.
The profession of literary Confucians,
is extraordinary and unconventional;
few people read their books,
their teachings may not be widely discussed,
their schools may lack followers,
yet their writings are profound and grand,
and still passed down by the world.
Their empty theories,
these substantial texts—
when comparing the two,
which can be considered superior?
Consider the ancient sages who composed texts and discourses,
they relied on their own work,
and made themselves known to the world.
Though worldly Confucians were revered in their time,
without encountering the works of literary Confucians,
their traces would not have been transmitted.
The Duke of Zhōu established rituals and music,
his name endures without fading;
Confucius composed the "Spring and Autumn Annals",
his reputation spreads unceasingly.
The Duke of Zhōu,
and Confucius—
it is difficult to discuss them with mere words.
Literary figures of the Hàn dynasty,
such as Lù Jiǎ,
Sīmǎ Qiān,
Liú Zǐzhèng,
Yáng Zǐyún,
their talents were exceptional,
their acclaim did not depend on others.
The world transmits the "Shī" school of Lǔ Shēngōng,
the "Shū" school of Ōuyáng from Qiānshèng,
and Gōngsūn,
yet without encountering Grand Historian Sīmǎ Qiān,
the world would not have known of them.
To become renowned through one's own work—
how does that compare to needing others to achieve fame?
To record the deeds of a hundred people,
how does that compare to barely making one's own name known?
Some say:
Those who write
do so in moments of leisure and contemplation,
not necessarily because their wisdom surpasses others.
If one does not dwell in seclusion,
thoughts do not reach profundity.
If writers
are burdened with managing all affairs,
overseeing duties within the state's borders,
rushed and busy,
how would they have time to write?
If an ordinary person were to accumulate thoughts in leisure,
they too could produce some eighty chapters.
King Wén had no time to eat until sunset,
the Duke of Zhōu paused his bath three times to attend to guests—
how could they find leisure to craft elegant writings with their brushes?
Confucius composed the "Spring and Autumn Annals",
because he was not employed in the Zhōu court;
Sīmǎ Xiàngrú did not participate in the affairs of high ministers,
thus he could write the "Rhapsody of Zǐxū";
Yáng Zǐyún held the position of a palace attendant,
so he could complete the "Classic of Tàixuán",
and finalize the "Exemplary Sayings".
Had Confucius become a king,
the "Spring and Autumn Annals" would not have been written;
had Xiàngrú
or Zǐyún become chancellors,
the "Rhapsodies"
and "Tàixuán" would not have been meticulously crafted.
The reply states:
King Wén had no time to eat until sunset—
this refers to his elaboration on the "Yì" and adding hexagrams.
The Duke of Zhōu paused his bath three times to attend to guests—
this was for reforming laws and establishing institutions for Zhōu.
If the way of Zhōu had not decayed,
Confucius would not have written,
not for lack of leisure or contemplation,
but because Zhōu's laws had become lax and flawed,
and could not be followed.
To embody the patterns of heaven and earth,
and express them from one's heart—
how could it be due to leisure or lack of time?
Inspiration arises from confronting falsehoods and delusions,
stemming from the flow of vital energy.
Guǎn Zhòng served as minister to Duke Huán,
achieving multiple alliances;
Shāng Yāng served as minister to Duke Xiào,
opening the path to imperial rule for Qín,
yet both men authored books,
comprising dozens of chapters.
Xiàngrú
and Zǐyún
belong to the same category.
Both were inspired,
hence their talents flourished together;
with similar talents,
their achievements aligned.
All were scholars who authored works,
not because they had leisure for contemplation.
The more one engages in affairs, the broader one's perspective;
the busier one's official duties, the more profound one's insights.
If one does not dwell in seclusion, thoughts do not reach depth;
if thoughts do not reach depth, the brush cannot flow effectively.
Even a stubborn person may have secluded thoughts,
but without worries or inspiration,
they cannot write a single word.
Human talent has its capabilities,
but none are without some leisure.
Some lack talent and cannot think deeply,
none have wisdom but cannot write;
some with great talent wish to write but lack inspiration,
while those with modest wisdom, given leisure, can record their thoughts.
For exceptional insights, there is no fixed cause;
none with ability fail to express themselves;
with dual perspectives, nothing remains unseen;
none lack the leisure to create.
Some say:
All writers exhaust their refined thoughts,
and thus cannot fulfill official duties while in position.
For when human thought fixates on one focus,
its essence becomes entirely consumed.
Those who write
produce extraordinary and profound texts,
their talent already pushed to the limit,
their wisdom already spent.
Consider ancient authors:
many held scattered or humble positions;
to support a collapsing or stabilize a precarious state
is not something writers can accomplish.
When under pressure,
or constrained,
then there is a source,
for hundreds of chapters.
Lǚ Bùwéi composed the "Spring and Autumn Annals",
and his entire family was exiled to Shǔ;
the King of Huáinán wrote texts on the Way,
and disaster led to his clan's extermination;
Hán Fēi wrote on governance techniques,
and ended up in a Qín prison.
If one cannot even preserve oneself,
how can one assist the state?
To excel in that,
must one not be deficient in this?
Profound in writing,
must one not be shallow in governance?
The reply says:
Where a person has strengths,
there are inevitably weaknesses;
where one is skilled,
there are inevitably clumsinesses.
It is not due to inferiority,
but because the will is not directed there;
it is not due to clumsiness,
but because sincere effort is not applied.
When the mind is fixed on something,
one may overlook Mount Tài;
when thoughts are focused on a goal,
one may have no leisure to attend to oneself.
Take the sharpness of the sword Gānjiàng:
it can stab but not strike,
or strike but not stab;
it is not that the blade is not sharp,
but that it cannot do both at once.
Shoot at a sparrow and you miss the quail;
aim at a magpie and you lose the wild goose;
square and circle cannot be drawn together,
left and right cannot be seen simultaneously;
if a person tries to accomplish two things,
they cannot perfect one.
If Gānjiàng were to stab less and strike more,
or the shooter abandon the magpie for the wild goose,
then their aim would not fail.
If a person devotes their writings
solely to governance,
then the achievements of Zǐchǎn
and Zǐjiàn would not be unmatched.
Ancient authors
often achieved merits without holding office.
Guǎn Zhòng
and Yàn Yīng
both wrote works and accomplished deeds;
Shāng Yāng
and Yú Qīng
authored texts and administered states.
After Gāozǔ won the empire,
his military strategies remained unspoiled,
yet Lù Jiǎ composed the "New Discourses,"
and Gāozǔ roughly adopted them.
When the Lǚ clan transgressed,
and the Liú house was near collapse,
were it not for Lù Jiǎ's strategies,
the imperial house would not have been pacified.
Thus, talent and wisdom can achieve anything,
depending on circumstances;
encountering chaos, they establish merits;
arising in times of peace, they use their abilities to write books.
Spoken words become speech,
written words become texts.
In ancient times, many gained merit through speech,
few met failure through writing.
Lǚ Bùwéi
and the King of Huáinán erred in their actions,
not in their books;
they had guests write their texts,
not composing personally,
yet even if they had not written,
they would still have suffered such evident calamities.
People across ages,
are not all ultimate in literary talent and wisdom.
Zōu Yáng presented a memorial,
and was pardoned in Liáng;
Xú Yuè submitted a petition,
and was appointed as a court gentleman.
If one's writings can benefit others,
why suspect they cannot protect oneself?
Had Hán earlier trusted Lord Hán Fēi,
the state would not have faced peril.
But when Fēi died,
due to Lǐ Sī's jealousy of his genius,
Fēi, despite his ultimate literary talent,
could achieve no more.
Spring's growth may be harmed,
some dying from it;
if unharmed,
autumn brings great maturity.
Had Fēi not died,
Qín's fate might have been different.
Thus, the talented can make their conduct respectable,
but cannot force others to emulate them;
they can make their words practicable,
but cannot compel others to adopt them.
Some say:
Throughout history, authors are many,
each distorting the truth of the classics and commentaries,
deviating from the sages' essence,
hence called fragments and debris,
compared to jade dust.
Thus it is said:
"A cartload of fragments
does not form a Way;
a chest full of jade dust
does not constitute a treasure."
Earlier writers, close to sages,
are still deemed fragments,
how much more those distant from sages, following later?
Their works must be false,
their words unclear,
how can they be adopted and implemented?
The reply says:
Sages created the classics,
worthies composed the commentaries,
expounding the authors' intent,
capturing the sages' aspirations,
thus the classics need commentaries.
Both are works of worthies,
why deem only classics and commentaries right,
and other writings wrong?
They see the texts
of commentaries and classics,
which the classics rely on for explanation,
so they call them correct.
Other writings differ from these,
creating new beginnings,
so they call them wrong.
Such a view
favors only the Five Classics.
If a statement is not from the Five Classics,
even if right, it goes unheeded.
Had the Five Classics emerged from Confucius's school,
remaining intact to this day,
they could be called pure and unified,
and trusted rightly.
But the Five Classics suffered Qín's extravagance,
encountered Lǐ Sī's arbitrary policies,
were burned and banned,
so scholars like Fúshēng
hid the classics deeply.
When Hàn arose,
it collected the Five Classics,
but they were fragmented and unclear,
their chapters scattered and incomplete.
Men like Cháo Cuò
split the texts according to personal views,
teachers and disciples passing them down,
uncertain what was correct.
The lawless Qín dynasty
ruined and disordered them.
Though Qín was lawless,
it did not burn the various philosophers' works;
their texts,
with chapters intact,
can be read to correct doctrines,
and selected to show later generations.
Later writers' works
are like those of earlier ones.
Both are profound and wise,
praised in commentaries and records,
their meaning aligning with the classics;
why say they lose the classics' truth?
Thus,
the classics are incomplete,
while other texts are not lost;
the classics have missing chapters,
so weighing the two,
which are the fragments?
"The Yì" bases on events and images,
"The Shī" gathers folk songs into verses,
"The Yuè" requires people's joy,
"The Lǐ" awaits people's peace.
These four classics have foundations,
then their chapters form.
"The Shàngshū"
and "The Chūnqiū"
draw from historical records.
When histories flourished,
there were no different books,
unifying people
and events in one intent.
The six classics all have bases.
Thus,
other texts can be the root,
the classics the branches;
if branches lose facts,
and root gains essence,
weighing the two,
which is the jade dust?
Those under the eaves know the roof leaks;
those in the wilds know governance's failures;
the various philosophers know the classics' errors.
Their texts
are clear and truthful.
Commentators on chapters and sentences
never seek deep understanding or clarity,
passing them down teacher to teacher,
for the first commentators
were not broadly learned.
The "New Discourses",
composed by Lù Jiǎ,
it seems Dǒng Zhòngshū also adopted their influence,
both discuss the merits and faults of sovereign-subject relations and governance,
their words can be adopted and implemented,
their affairs are commendable and worthy of observation.
The vast knowledge they speak of,
references and compares with the "Classics" and "Commentaries",
even the words of ancient sages
could not surpass or augment them.
Lù Jiǎ's words
show no omissions or deficiencies;
yet Dǒng Zhòngshū's claim that the Yú sacrifice can respond to Heaven,
and earthen dragons can bring rain,
is rather difficult to comprehend.
Using the Yú sacrifice to relieve drought,
but neglecting the summer suburban sacrifice—
was this the fault of the Marquis of Jìn?
It was due to governance losing the Way,
causing yīn and yáng to fall out of harmony.
When Jìn abolished the summer suburban sacrifice,
the Marquis of Jìn fell ill;
following the advice of Zhǎng Zǐchǎn of Zhèng,
he performed the summer suburban sacrifice and recovered from his illness.
If indeed the Yú is not performed,
and dragons are not managed,
sharing the same misfortune as Jìn,
then repeating it would be appropriate.
If drought is caused by governance,
it should be remedied through governance.
If governance is deficient,
and instead one performs the Yú and manages dragons,
what benefit would that bring?
The Gōngyáng school's interpretation of the "Spring and Autumn Annals" states:
"The extreme yang phase
is sufficient to restore governance."
Yīn and yáng intermingle,
drought and flood reciprocate—
such is the Way of Heaven;
why then perform the Yú and set up dragons?
Do the Yú sacrifices please the gods?
Sometimes rain comes,
yet extreme yang remains unchanged,
the drought disaster unrelieved—
in such cases, where can the principle of transformation and restoration
be applied?
Moreover, cold and warmth are akin to drought and flood,
both caused by governance,
the fault lies with humans.
To seek blessings only for extreme drought,
and not for cold or warmth,
I fail to understand the reason.
If reciprocity for cold and warmth should be sought,
then the practices of Yú
and dragons would be appropriate.
With great talent and vast knowledge,
I hold both views in doubt.
Dǒng Zhòngshū, in writing his books,
did not use the title "zǐ",
likely considering himself superior to the various masters.
There were many writers in the Hàn dynasty;
Sīmǎ Zǐcháng
and Yáng Zǐyún
are like the Hé and Hàn rivers,
while the rest
are like the Jīng and Wèi streams.
Yet Zǐcháng had few
subjective assertions,
and Zǐyún lacked commonplace opinions.
Dǒng Zhòngshū's discourse on the Way and techniques is remarkable;
the three northern schools esteemed him.
Apocryphal texts say:
"Dǒng Zhòngshū,
disordered my books."
This is likely a saying of Confucius.
Readers sometimes interpret
"disordered my books"
as meaning he confused and disordered Confucius's books;
others take "disordered"
to mean "ordered",
i.e., he organized Confucius's books.
With the same single
"disordered"
character, ordering and disordering
are vastly different.
Yet readers' intentions differ,
they do not examine the original truth,
hence errors in interpretation arise.
To say he disordered Confucius's books
is a statement of high talent;
to say he ordered Confucius's books
is also a remarkable claim.
Having passed through the gate of the sage,
to disorder or order Confucius's books—
Zǐcháng
and Zǐyún never said such things.
Common people lack sincerity in intention,
examine matters but miss the truth,
wavering between two statements,
tossing and turning in uncertainty.
Examining Dǒng Zhòngshū's writings,
they do not violate the Ruist school,
nor oppose Confucius.
The claim that he disordered Confucius's books
is incorrect;
Confucius's books were not disordered,
and the claim that he ordered them
is also incorrect.
Confucius said:
"From the beginning of Master Zhì's performance,
to the finale of the 'Guān Jū',
how overflowing it was, filling the ears!"
Here, "finale"
concludes Confucius's speech.
Confucius lived in Zhōu,
initiating its foundation;
Dǒng Zhòngshū was in Hàn,
completing its end.
Bān Shūpí's continuation of the "Records of the Grand Historian"
follows this principle.
In the sections of fǔ and eulogies, there is
"Finale says"
chapter, which belongs to the same category.
Confucius's final discourse
was settled through Dǒng Zhòngshū's words;
his practices of Yú sacrifices and managing dragons
must have had their rationale,
and should not be deemed strange.
Yán Yuān said:
"What kind of person was Shùn?
What kind of person am I?"
Among the Five Emperors and Three Sovereigns,
Yán Yuān uniquely admired Shùn,
knowing his own steps and strides shared similarities.
Knowing the virtue one admires,
silently recognizing what one pursues,
are of the same essence.
Dǒng Zhòngshū's discourse on morality and governance
is praiseworthy and admirable;
in substantiating worldly affairs,
and discussing contemporary doubts,
none surpass Huán Jūnshān.
Thus, Dǒng Zhòngshū's writings can be matched,
but Huán Jūnshān's arguments are hard to equal.
A steed leaves ordinary horses far behind—
can one tread in its footsteps?
Suppose there is a horse here:
its feet travel a thousand lǐ,
yet it is never called a steed—
because its coat color differs from a steed's.
Suppose there is a person here:
his writings parallel Dǒng Zhòngshū's,
his arguments rank with Huán Jūnshān's,
yet he is never considered equal to these two—
because his name is different.
Thus, a horse that achieves a thousand lǐ
need not be a steed or a courser;
a person expected to be wise and virtuous
need not be a Confucius
or a Mòzǐ. How to verify this?
Huán Jūnshān's arguments are hard to equal.
When two blades cross,
sharpness and dullness are known;
when two arguments contend,
right and wrong become apparent.
Hence, Hán Fēi's "Four Difficulties",
Huán Kuān's "Discourses on Salt and Iron",
and Huán Jūnshān's "New Discourses" are of the same kind.
Some people doubt them,
saying they are false,
but the authors substantiate them,
making them hard to rival.
A minister resolving doubtful cases,
settling lawsuits and suspected crimes—
if right and wrong remain undecided,
straight and crooked unestablished,
people will surely say the minister or judge is incompetent.
As for argumentation,
if it does not aim to resolve all doubts,
recording both "Commentaries" side by side,
without clear distinction—
how can it compare to splitting chaos open,
untangling knotted threads,
making words all understandable,
and texts all comprehensible?
Consider Confucius composing the "Spring and Autumn Annals":
he praised goodness as fine as a hair,
condemned evil as slight as a speck.
Where praise was due,
he used righteousness to highlight good conduct;
where condemnation was due,
he clarified the evil to criticize the behavior.
The principles of the "New Discourses"
align with those of the "Spring and Autumn Annals".
Therefore, the creation of the "Lùn Héng" arose
from the fact that numerous texts had lost their authenticity,
and empty, baseless words prevailed over truth and beauty.
Thus, if such falsehoods are not eliminated,
then ornate writings will not cease;
if ornate writings are allowed to spread unchecked,
then practical matters will not be applied.
Hence, the "Lùn Héng" is
a means to weigh the significance of words,
establishing a standard for truth and falsehood,
not merely to embellish language or rhetoric
for the sake of spectacular display.
Its foundation stems from the faults in human society,
so it exhausts thought and mind
to critique worldly customs.
The nature of worldly customs
favors strange and bizarre talk,
delighting in baseless writings.
Why is that?
Because practical matters do not satisfy desires,
while flashy emptiness startles the ears and stirs the heart.
Thus, talented individuals
who enjoy discussion
exaggerate facts,
creating grandiose language;
those who wield the brush
fabricate empty texts,
producing baseless "records."
Listeners take them as true,
speaking of them without cease;
readers regard them as factual,
passing them on without end.
If not ended,
they are recorded on bamboo and silk;
if not ceased,
they mislead the ears of the wise.
Some even face south as teachers,
expounding deceitful theories;
officials in high positions
read baseless books.
Clearly discerning right from wrong,
it pains the heart to see this—
how can one not discuss it?
Mèngzǐ lamented that the debates of Yáng and Mò
greatly usurped the Confucian discourse,
so he presented straightforward arguments,
praising the right and suppressing the wrong,
yet the world thought him fond of disputation.
Mèngzǐ said:
"How could I be fond of disputation?
I have no choice!"
Now, I too have no choice.
Falsehoods overshadow truth,
sincerity is confused with deceit;
the world does not realize it,
right and wrong are unsettled,
purple and red intermingled,
tiles and jade piled together.
Speaking from emotion,
how can my heart endure it!
Like the carriage attendant who overstepped his duty to call out,
moved by compassion,
fearing the ruler's peril,
so the discussant grieves for the world and worries over customs,
sharing the same heart as that attendant.
It troubles the spirit and darkens the soul,
stirring the calm within the chest,
harming years and shortening life,
with no benefit to nature,
a misfortune heavier than Yán Huí's,
contravening the teachings of Huáng and Lǎo,
not something one covets,
but having no alternative,
thus the "Lùn Héng" was written.
Its language is plain and its intent straightforward,
its words critical but its feelings sincere.
Its "Zhèng Wù" speaks on the way to govern the people.
The essays of the "Lùn Héng"
are what ordinary people in the world can see,
no different from those of other writers.
As for the nine "Xū,"
three "Zēng,"
"Lùn Sǐ,"
"Dìng Guǐ,"
they address long-standing delusions of the world,
what people fail to perceive.
When a ruler faces corruption,
he reforms governance from above;
when a minister encounters confusion,
he composes discourses below.
If the lower level grasps the truth,
then the upper governance follows.
Hoping to awaken the confused hearts,
to make known the distinction between false and true.
Once the distinction is fixed,
then ornate and deceitful writings will perish;
when such writings perish,
then pure sincerity's influence will daily flourish.
Some say:
Sages create,
worthies transmit;
for a worthy to create is wrong.
"Lùn Héng"
and "Zhèng Wù"
could be called creations.
I say they are not creations,
nor are they transmissions,
but discussions.
Discussion
is secondary to transmission.
The rise of the Five Classics
can be called creation.
"The Grand Historian's Records,"
Liú Zǐzhèng's prefaces,
Bān Shūpí's biographies,
can be called transmissions.
Huán Jūnshān's "Xīn Lùn,"
Zōu Bóqí's "Jiǎn Lùn,"
can be called discussions.
Now, looking at "Lùn Héng"
and "Zhèng Wù,"
they are like the two discussions of Huán and Zōu,
not what is called creation.
To initiate something anew,
unprecedented before,
like Cāng Jié creating writing
or Xī Zhòng making the cart, that is creation.
"The Yì" says Fúxī created the Eight Trigrams;
before that, there were no trigrams,
Fúxī made them,
so it is called creation.
King Wén doubled them,
expanding to sixty-four,
so it is called derivation.
To say "Lùn Héng" is like the sixty-four hexagrams
is also incorrect.
The sixty-four hexagrams were derived and augmented,
their trigrams overflowing,
their numbers multiplied.
Now, "Lùn Héng" takes the world's books,
corrects their truth and falsehood,
distinguishes their reality and emptiness—
it does not initiate anew,
nor is it without precedent.
Confucian scholars question and challenge
their predecessors' theories;
clerks review and examine
legal officials' cases.
If "Lùn Héng" is called creation,
would Confucian scholars
and clerks call it creation?
Submitting memorials and reports,
presenting expedient proposals,
all aim to assist governance.
Now, writing books
is like submitting memorials and reports:
ideas spring from the heart,
texts form in the hand—
their essence is the same.
Submitting memorials is called "zòu,"
and reports are renamed "shū."
In the first year of Jiànchū,
Zhōngzhōu suffered famine,
and people from Yǐngchuān
and Rǔnán scattered in exile.
The sage ruler, concerned,
issued repeated edicts.
The author of "Lùn Héng"
submitted reports to the commandery governor,
advising to curb extravagance
to prepare for hardship.
The words were not heeded,
so he titled the draft "Bèi Fá."
Alcohol wastes grains,
breeds thieves and bandits;
indulgence in drink
leads to unending theft.
He reported to the governor
to ban alcohol among the people,
and titled the draft "Jìn Jiǔ."
From this, it is clear
that writing books
is like submitting memorials and reports.
If records are called creation,
are memorials and reports creation?
The "Chéng" of Jìn,
the "Táowù" of Chǔ,
and the "Chūnqiū" of Lǔ,
each recorded human affairs differently.
The Qián and Kūn of the "Yì",
the Yuán of the "Chūnqiū",
and Yáng Zǐ's "Xuán",
all signify the unevenness of vital forces.
From this perspective,
the memorials of Táng Lín,
the petitions of Gǔ Yǒng,
the "Lùnhéng",
and the "Zhèngwù",
share the same purpose.
The Hàn dynasty reached the forest of writing,
the creation of books and discourses,
was especially abundant in the Hàn dynasty.
Yángchéng Zǐcháng composed the "Yuè",
Yáng Zǐyún created the "Xuán",
both classics were issued from beneath the court,
read within the palace gates,
extraordinary and astonishing to the ear,
written without mere narration,
their talent rivaled the sages,
yet the Hàn court did not criticize them.
Moreover, the "Lùnhéng" offers detailed explanations and subtle discourses,
resolving doubts of common customs,
debating and illuminating the principles of right and wrong,
enabling later generations to understand the distinction between affirmation and denial,
fearing these would be lost,
they were recorded on bamboo slips,
following the explanations of classical texts and chapters,
and the unique theories of earlier masters.
Its words stretch the measuring line,
cutting down popular traditions.
Popular traditions are misleading and confusing,
false writings spread widely,
wise and enlightened people
incessantly detest them.
Confucius said:
"The poet detests it and cannot remain silent,
I, Qiū, detest it and cannot conceal it."
Hence, discourse is necessary.
If jade is mixed with stone,
people cannot distinguish it;
like the jade official of Chǔ who mistook jade for stone,
finally causing Biàn Hé to suffer the punishment of foot amputation.
When wrong is turned into right,
and falsehood transformed into truth,
how can one remain silent?
Popular traditions are already erroneous,
common writings are also false.
As for Zōu Yǎn claiming the present world is one continent,
beyond the four seas there are nine more like it.
The "Huáinán Shū" says Gònggōng contended with Zhuānxū to become the Son of Heaven,
was defeated,
angrily struck the Bùzhōu Mountain,
causing the pillar of heaven to break,
and the cords of the earth to snap.
In Yáo's time, ten suns appeared together,
Yáo shot down nine of them.
Lǔ Yáng fought as dusk fell,
raised his spear and commanded the sun,
and the sun retreated back.
Worldly books and traditions,
many are like these examples,
frivolous, absurd, and false,
obscuring and usurping the correct truth.
The heart surges,
the hand and pen stir,
how can one not discourse?
Discourse then examines with the mind,
verifies with facts,
for floating and empty matters,
immediately establishes proof.
Like the writings of Grand Historian Sīmǎ Qiān,
recording Xǔ Yóu without concealment,
and that Yān Prince Dān did not make the sun stand at noon again,
readers who see this,
all praise it as excellent.
"Zhèngwù" advises commandery governors and state chancellors,
county magistrates and district chiefs on governmental affairs to prioritize,
aiming to preserve the people and establish transformation,
upholding and matching the state's grace.
The "Lùnhéng" with its nine "Xū"
and three "Zēng" essays,
serves to make customs practical and sincere;
"Lùn Sǐ"
and "Dìng Guǐ",
aim to make customs frugal in funerals.
Confucius crossed courtyards and ascended steps directly,
yet those encoffined did not reflect;
Liú Zǐzhèng advocated simple burials,
yet those conducting funerals did not restrain;
Emperor Guāngwǔ used straw carts and thatch horses,
yet those making burial objects were not deceitful.
Why do worldly books and customs not record this?
Belief in death's tales muddies them.
Now writing "Lùn Sǐ" and "Sǐ Wěi" chapters,
clarifies that death brings no consciousness,
cannot create ghosts,
hoping readers will understand and adopt simple burials,
and practice greater thrift.
This is the beneficial proof of the "Lùnhéng".
If words are beneficial,
what harm is there in writing?
Cāngjié's writing,
the world uses to record events;
Xīzhòng's cart,
the world uses for transport;
Bóyú's clothing,
to ward off cold and heat;
Jié's tiled house,
to shelter from wind and rain.
If one does not discuss their benefits and harms,
but only criticizes their creation,
then Cāngjié and his kind would be at fault,
and the fifteen schools of the "Shì Běn" would all be blamed.
Therefore, if it is beneficial,
even if created, it is harmless.
Even if harmless,
what does it supplement?
In ancient times, envoys were appointed to collect songs,
to observe customs,
and understand the people's condition.
Poems were made among the people;
could a sage king say:
"You are common people,
how dare you create?"
Imprison them as criminals,
and destroy their poems?
Now it is not so,
hence the "Shī" tradition continues to this day.
The "Lùnhéng"
and "Zhèngwù",
are like the poems,
hoping to be selected,
yet said to have faults.
This is why the "Lùnhéng" was written.
Moreover, the fault in creation
lies in the intention to speak falsely and slander.
The "Lùnhéng" deals with facts and hates falsehoods,
its chapters "Qí Shì",
"Xuān Hàn",
"Huī Guó",
"Yàn Fú",
"Shèng Bāo",
and "Xū Sòng" contain
no slanderous words;
created thus,
it can avoid guilt.
Wáng Chōng
was from Shàngyú, Kuàijī,
courtesy name Zhòngrèn.
His ancestors were originally from Yuánchéng, Wèi Commandery.
A forefather several generations back served in the army with merit,
and was enfeoffed at Yángtíng in Kuàijī.
Within a year, due to sudden changes, the fief was lost,
so the family settled there,
engaging in farming and sericulture.
His ancestors were brave and willful,
ultimately not getting along with others.
In years of famine,
they harmed and killed across the roads,
accumulating many enemies.
During turbulent times,
fearing capture by enemies,
his grandfather Fàn moved the whole family carrying their belongings,
seeking safety in Kuàijī,
settling in Qiántáng County,
engaging in trade.
He had two sons,
the elder named Méng,
the younger named Sòng,
Sòng being Chōng's father.
The ancestral generations were willful,
by Méng's
and Sòng's time, it intensified,
so Méng
and Sòng in Qiántáng
used their bravery to bully others.
Later, they again made enemies with the powerful family of Dīng Bó,
so the whole family moved to Shàngyú.
In the third year of the Jiànwǔ era,
Chōng was born.
As a child,
when playing with his peers,
he disliked frivolous teasing.
His peers enjoyed catching sparrows,
capturing cicadas,
gambling with coins,
and frolicking in the woods,
but Chōng alone refused.
Sòng Qí found this remarkable.
At six, he was taught writing;
respectful, earnest, benevolent, and obedient,
he fully observed rites and courtesy,
dignified and serene,
with the ambition of a great man.
His father never caned him,
his mother never reproached him,
and the neighborhood never criticized him.
At eight, he entered a schoolhouse,
where over a hundred young pupils
were all punished for their faults by baring and reprimand,
or whipped for poor handwriting.
Chōng's calligraphy improved daily,
and he had no faults.
Once his handwriting was proficient,
he bid farewell to his teacher to study the *Analects*
and the *Book of Documents*,
reciting a thousand characters a day.
Mastering the classics and cultivating virtue,
he thanked his teacher to specialize independently,
wielding his brush to the amazement of all.
The texts he read
grew broader and more numerous daily.
Though highly talented, he did not indulge in careless writing;
eloquent, yet he disliked casual debates,
and unless with the right person,
he would not speak all day.
His arguments might at first seem contrary to the crowd's,
but upon hearing him through,
all would agree.
The same held for his literary compositions;
likewise,
in conduct and service to superiors,
it was so.
In the county, he rose to Assistant Merit Officer;
in the Commandant's office, also Assistant Merit Officer;
in the Grand Administrator's office, he served as Acting Assistant in the Five Officials' Merit Section;
in the provincial administration, he became an Attendant Officer.
He did not seek fame in the world,
nor did he flatter superiors for gain or avoidance of harm.
He often spoke of others' strengths,
rarely of their shortcomings.
He focused on recommending the unrecognized,
and rectifying the faults of those already advanced.
As for those he disapproved of,
he did not praise them;
if they had faults he couldn't resolve,
he did not further entrap them.
He could forgive major errors in others,
yet lamented their minor faults.
He preferred self-concealment,
unwilling to showcase himself,
striving to base his life on conduct and integrity,
ashamed to gain fame through talent.
In gatherings,
he spoke only if asked;
when granted an audience with a lord or general,
he replied only to what was addressed.
In his village,
he admired the integrity of Qú Bóyù;
at court,
he valued the conduct of Shǐ Zǐyú.
If slandered or wronged,
he refused to justify himself;
if not promoted,
he bore no resentment.
Poor without even an acre for shelter,
his spirit rivaled that of nobles;
humble without a peck of official salary,
his mind felt as if feasting on ten thousand dàn.
He did not rejoice at gaining office,
nor regret losing it.
Amid ease and pleasure, his desires were unrestrained;
in poverty and hardship, his will never wearied.
He immersed himself in ancient texts,
delighting in unconventional views.
Contemporary writings and common theories
often dissatisfied him,
so he secluded himself alone,
examining and debating their truth and falsehood.
Chōng was pure and dignified in character,
choosing friends carefully in his travels,
disdaining casual acquaintances.
Those he befriended, though low in status
or young in age,
if their conduct transcended the vulgar,
he would surely befriend them.
He favored outstanding and refined companions,
not indiscriminately bonding with common talents.
Common talents, seizing on minor faults,
fabricated accusations against him,
yet he never justified himself,
nor blamed or resented them.
Some asked:
"With fine talent and extraordinary writing,
wronged without crime,
why not defend yourself?
Followers like Yáng Shèng
whet their tongues with honey;
Zōu Yáng justified himself
and was released from prison.
If one has flawless conduct,
they shouldn't be slandered;
since you can strive to assert yourself,
you shouldn't be subdued by others."
He replied:
"Without purity, one isn't dusted;
without height, one isn't perilous;
without breadth, one isn't trimmed;
without fullness, one isn't depleted.
A scholar with many critics,
being slandered by others,
is perhaps fitting.
Those eager for advancement justify themselves;
those fearing demotion plead their case.
I have no such eagerness or fear,
so I remain silent.
Yáng Shèng slandered others—
something compelled him;
Zōu Yáng was spared—
something rescued him.
Confucius spoke of fate,
Mencius of heaven;
fortune, misfortune, safety, danger
do not depend on man.
The ancients understood this,
thus attributing it to fate,
entrusting it to the times,
serene and detached,
without complaint or blame.
When fortune came, they didn't claim it as their gain;
when disaster struck, they didn't attribute it to their actions.
So, when advancing, their satisfaction wasn't greater;
when retreating, their resolve wasn't diminished.
They didn't resent lack to seek abundance,
nor avoid danger to chase safety;
they didn't sell wisdom for salary,
nor refuse rank to court fame;
they didn't crave advancement to justify themselves,
nor hate withdrawal to resent others.
They equated safety and danger, life and death,
balanced fortune and misfortune, failure and success;
even encountering ten Yáng Shèngs,
they deemed it harmless.
Actions归于 heaven,
hence I do not justify myself.
Chōng's nature was tranquil and indifferent,
he did not covet wealth or nobility.
When recognized by his superiors,
promoted beyond the usual order,
he did not admire high office.
When not recognized by his superiors,
demoted and suppressed,
he did not resent low positions.
Serving as a county official,
he made no choices or avoidances.
Some said:
"Your mind is hard to please but your actions are easy;
befriending like-minded companions,
serving without choosing the place,
muddying your integrity and harming your conduct—
what in this world is worth emulating?"
He replied:
The one most worthy of emulation
is none other than Confucius.
In Confucius's service,
he avoided nothing.
As a keeper of fields
or a storehouse clerk,
he had no feelings of discontent;
as a minister of works or prime minister,
he showed no look of pleasure.
Shùn plowed at Lìshān,
as if he would never escape it;
and when he received Yáo's abdication,
as if it were his natural due.
He worried about the inadequacy of his virtue,
not about the lowliness of his rank;
he felt shame if his reputation was not untarnished,
not annoyance if his position did not advance.
A precious pearl and a tile in the same casket,
a bright moon and gravel in the same bag—
if they possess the substance of two treasures,
it does not harm them to be treated the same by the world.
If the world can recognize goodness,
even the lowly become illustrious;
if it cannot distinguish clearly,
even the honored suffer disgrace.
To maintain the same conduct in humility as in honor,
to match virtue in low position with that in high—
this is acceptable.
Common nature greedily advances and heedlessly retreats,
gathering success and discarding failure.
When Chōng was promoted and in office,
crowds clung to him like ants;
when dismissed and living in poverty,
old acquaintances betrayed and left.
Resenting the common people's lack of gratitude,
he therefore composed in leisure "Criticizing Customs and Upholding Righteousness" in twelve chapters.
Hoping that common people would read the book and awaken themselves,
he thus made his writing plain,
compiling it in common language.
Some criticized it as shallow.
He replied:
To show sacred texts to the uncultured,
to speak elegantly to country folk,
when they cannot understand,
none will not oppose it.
Thus Sū Qín's refined persuasions in Zhào,
yet Lì Duì was not pleased;
Shāng Yāng's kingly discourse in Qín,
yet Xiào Gōng did not employ it.
When one does not get what the heart desires,
even if hearing all the words of Yáo
and Shùn,
it is like giving wine to an ox,
or feeding dried meat to a horse.
Therefore, grand and profound words
are suited to the great but not understood by the small.
If forced to listen unwillingly,
little enters the heart.
When Confucius lost his horse in the wilds,
the rustic closed it off and would not return it;
Zǐgòng's exquisite reasoning angered him,
but the horse keeper's jesting words pleased him.
Common folk understand plain and exposed speech;
to urge them with deep and grand writing
is like using immortal's medicine to treat a sneeze,
or making a marten-fur coat for gathering firewood.
Moreover, ritual has its unprepared moments,
affairs have their unnecessary aspects.
To judge a known crime,
one need not be Gāo Yáo;
to mix mustard greens and leeks,
one need not wait for Dí Yá;
the music of the lanes,
does not use the "Sháo"
or "Wǔ";
the village mother's sacrifice,
does not require the grand sacrifice.
Since there is what is unnecessary,
there is also what is unsuitable.
Using a butcher's knife to cut a chicken,
a long halberd to pick greens,
a battle-ax to trim chopsticks,
a basin to fill a cup—
when large and small are mismatched,
few will approve.
How to be persuasive?
Explain the deep with the shallow.
How to be wise?
Explain the difficult with the easy.
The sages assessed what was appropriate to the material,
hence their writings could vary in depth and shallowness.
Since Chōng detested common sentiments,
he wrote the book "Criticizing Customs";
and pitying the governance of rulers,
who merely wished to rule people
without attaining appropriateness,
unaware of the essentials,
worrying with exhausted spirit and bitter thoughts,
not seeing the direction to take,
he therefore wrote the book "On Government."
Also grieving that false books and vulgar writings were mostly untruthful,
he composed the book "Discourses Weighed in the Balance."
For when the sages perished, the great meaning split,
stumbling in different directions,
each opening their own school.
Learned men observed,
but could not adjudicate.
Hearing transmissions from afar,
written by brush and heard by ear,
from a century before.
As days passed long,
they considered ancient events,
and what was said seemed nearly right,
believed to the marrow,
unable to free themselves,
hence he wrote a truthful discourse.
Its language is abundant,
its arguments contentious,
and flowery, false statements
are all verified and corrected.
Eliminating ornate and empty writings,
preserving the simplicity of honesty;
redirecting the lost trends,
returning to the customs of Fú Xì.
Chōng's writings are easily understood due to their clear form.
Some say:
"Those skilled in debate speak profoundly,
while agile writers compose深沉 texts.
Consider the writings of classical canons
and the words of sages and worthies—
majestic, weighty, elegant, and refined,
difficult to fully comprehend.
When readers of this age study them,
they rely on ancient commentaries to grasp them.
It is because the talents of sages and worthies are vast,
thus their language does not align with the common tongue.
Jade lies hidden within stone,
pearls are concealed in fish bellies;
unless one is a jade artisan or pearl expert,
none can retrieve them.
Since precious things remain hidden and unseen,
truthful words should also be deep and unfathomable.
The book *Jī Sú*
aims to enlighten ordinary people,
so its intent is made clear,
written in explicit language;
why then is the *Lùn Héng*
also like this?
Is it due to shallow talent,
incapable of creating depth and subtlety?
Why are its writings so plain,
diverging from the path of those classical canons?"
The reply:
Jade hidden in stone,
pearls concealed in fish bellies
are indeed deeply obscured.
But once jade's hue is revealed from the stone's core,
or a pearl's gleam emerges from the fish's belly,
do they remain hidden?
Before my words are gathered on bamboo slips,
stored within my breast and mind,
they are like concealed jade and pearls.
When they emerge and are exposed,
is it not like jade being cut open or pearls appearing?
Brilliant as the shining celestial patterns,
clear as the comprehended terrestrial order,
doubts and subtleties
can all be identified and addressed.
Moreover, with names made clear,
matters settle themselves.
The *Lùn Héng*
signifies balance in discourse.
Speech should strive for clarity,
writing for transparency.
The writings of noble scholars,
with no word incomprehensible,
no point unobservable.
Those who read them
understand as if the blind opened their eyes,
hear as if the deaf cleared their ears.
A child blind for three years,
suddenly seeing parents,
if not recognizing them clearly,
how could they feel joy?
A giant tree by the path,
a long ditch by the trench,
their presence obvious,
none fail to know them.
If the tree were small and hidden,
the ditch short and concealed,
showing these to people,
even Yáo and Shùn would be perplexed.
Human faces have over seventy regions,
cheeks bright and pure,
five colors distinct,
hidden worries or joys
can all be discerned;
those who physiognomize
rarely err.
If a face were dark and ugly,
layers of grime covering its features,
physiognomists
would often mistake.
Writing follows speech;
some clear and explicit,
some deep and迂曲 elegant—
which is more discerning?
Thus, speech clarifies intent,
fearing it may be lost,
it is recorded in writing.
Writing and speech share the same aim;
why should meaning be obscured?
In court, doubtful cases,
officials resolving uncertainties—
if murky and hard to grasp,
compared to those clear and knowable,
which makes a better official?
Debate values clarity for fairness,
writing prizes exposure for understanding,
official documents excel in transparency.
Deep, obscure elegance,
with hard-to-see meanings,
belongs only to rhapsodies and odes.
The texts of classics and commentaries,
the words of sages and worthies,
differ in ancient and modern speech,
vary across regions.
When they addressed events,
they did not aim to be hard to understand,
nor to hide their meanings.
Later generations not comprehending
is due to temporal distance;
this is called linguistic difference,
not talent's vastness.
Shallow writings hard to read
are deemed unskillful,
not wise and clear.
Qín Shǐ Huáng reading Hán Fēi's books,
sighed:
"If only I could have met this man in my time."
The text was comprehensible,
so its ideas could be pondered.
Had it been deeply elegant,
requiring a teacher to learn,
it might have been cast aside—
what sigh would there be?
Writers
should make their work easy to grasp yet hard to craft,
not value difficulty to understand with ease in creation.
Debate aims to resolve and be audible,
not to be profoundly迂曲 and obscure.
Mèngzǐ judged worthies
by the brightness of their pupils;
examining writings,
by the comprehensibility of their meaning.
Chōng's writings defy conventions.
Some challenge:
"Writings should align with public opinion,
not contradict people's views,
so none of a hundred readers blame it,
nor a thousand listeners find it strange.
Thus, Guǎnzǐ said:
'Speaking in a room, fill the room;
speaking in a hall, fill the hall.'
Now, your theories differ from the world,
so your writings offend customs,
not fitting the majority."
The reply:
Discourse values truth over flourish,
affairs uphold correctness over conformity.
Arguing right and wrong,
how can it not startle common hearts
and go against vulgar ears?
When the crowd is wrong, do not follow;
thus, discard the false,
and preserve the true.
If one should always conform
and顺从人心,
it's merely following tradition,
reciting and practicing—
what debate is there?
Confucius sat with Lǔ Āi Gōng,
who offered peaches and millet.
Confucius ate the millet first, then the peach,
rightly ordering the meal,
yet attendants covered their mouths to laugh,
so long had customs been ingrained.
Now, I am like Confucius ordering food;
commoners oppose it,
like those attendants covering their mouths.
Elegant songs,
in Zhèng are deemed not moving;
ritual dances,
in Zhào are considered unappealing.
The classics of Yáo and Shùn,
street toughs won't read;
the texts of Confucius and Mòzǐ,
Jì and Mèng won't peruse.
Plans to avert danger
are rejected in alleys;
words to rectify the age
are scorned by common taste.
A delicious flavor here,
commoners won't savor,
yet Dí Yá would relish it.
A precious jade here,
commoners would discard,
but Biàn Hé would treasure it.
Which is right, which wrong?
Who can be trusted?
Ritual and custom often clash;
what age is free of this?
In Lǔ, Wén Gōng reversed sacrifices,
three ministers left;
Dìng Gōng followed order,
five defected.
Thus, words that stand alone for truth,
noble scholars embrace,
common folk dislike;
books that mislead the crowd,
the worthy praise,
the foolish shun.
The writings of Chōng are not entirely perfect.
Some say:
"Speech should be without careless words,
writing should be without careless prose.
Prose must be beautiful and fine,
speech must be eloquent and clever.
When speech is clear to the ear,
then matters are savored in the heart;
when prose is perceptible to the eye,
then the essay is retained in hand.
Thus, eloquent speech is always heeded,
beautiful prose is always transcribed.
Now this new book is engaged in argument and analogy,
explaining customs in a perverse manner,
and is not beautiful or fine,
offering no pleasure to the reader.
Just as Shī Kuàng tuned music,
with no melody that was not moving;
Dí Yá harmonized flavors in meals,
with no dish that was bland.
Therefore, when a master creates a book,
the prose should be without flaw or impurity.
The "Lǚshì"
and "Huáinán"
were hung at the city gate,
and among those who viewed and read them,
not a word of criticism was uttered.
Now, lacking the beauty of these two books,
even if the prose is abundant and vigorous,
it still faces much censure and condemnation."
The reply is:
Those who cultivate substance do not nurture flowers,
those who regulate conduct do not adorn words.
Lush grass has many blossoms,
dense forests have many withered branches.
In writing, one wishes to make one's actions clear,
how can one ensure the prose is without censure?
Rescuing from fire or saving from drowning,
the righteousness does not allow for elegance;
debating right and wrong,
the words cannot be clever.
Entering the marsh to follow the turtle,
there is no time to adjust one's steps;
diving into the abyss to catch the jiāo dragon,
there is no time to steady one's hand.
Words that are straightforward and concise,
point to profound and distant meanings;
language that is sweet and prose that is sharp,
strive for shallow and petty intentions.
With a thousand zhōng of rice grains,
chaff and husks make up more than half;
examining coins filling hundreds of millions,
pierced and broken ones amount to tens of thousands.
The grand soup must have bland flavors,
the most precious treasure must have flaws and impurities,
the greatest simplicity must have great merits,
the finest craftsman must have unskillful moments.
Thus, eloquent speech must have its shortcomings,
masterful writing may still have its rejections.
Words of gold arise from noble households,
prose like dung comes from humble rooms.
That the "Huáinán"
and "Lǚshì" are free from fault and harm,
the reason for this
is that their authors were of wealthy families and high officials.
Being noble,
thus they could be hung at the market;
being rich, thus they had a fortune to back them.
Those who view and read them,
are fearful and apprehensive,
even if they see inconsistencies and disagreements,
how dare they criticize a single word?
Once Chōng's book was completed,
some compared it with the ancients,
finding it unlike previous writers.
Some said:
"Call it adorned prose and paired phrases,
sometimes direct, sometimes circuitous,
sometimes bent, sometimes relaxed.
Call it discussing the Way,
yet it deals with trivial practical matters,
the prose offers sweet and sour flavors,
harmonizing with the classics but not verified by them,
gathering from the traditions but not conforming to them,
examining it against Zǐcháng, it does not fit,
placing it within Zǐyún, it does not belong.
The prose does not resemble the past,
how can it be named excellent and fine,
called skillful and clever?"
The reply is:
Adorning appearances to force similarity loses the true form,
adjusting words to strive for likeness loses the genuine sentiment.
A hundred men's sons,
from different parents,
born of diverse kinds,
need not be similar;
each, according to their innate nature,
is in itself excellent and fine.
If prose must match the past to be called good,
then it is like saying a substitute carpenter won't cut his hand,
and only then be called skillful.
The tasks of literary scholars,
each follow their own path,
some adjust words to craft elegant prose,
some debate falsehoods to verify facts.
If one must always have matching plans and thoughts,
and prose must be inherited from the past,
then the Five Emperors would not have different deeds,
and the Three Kings would not have distinct achievements.
Beautiful faces do not share the same features,
yet all are pleasing to the eye;
moving music does not share the same sound,
yet all are delightful to the ear.
Wines and spirits have different aromas,
yet drinking them all intoxicates;
the various grains have distinct tastes,
yet eating them all satiates.
To say that prose must match the past,
is to say that Shùn's eyebrows should again have eight colors,
and Yǔ's eyes should again have double pupils.
My writings are voluminous.
Some say:
"Good writing values conciseness with clear intent,
speech should be brief yet directed towards clarity.
Debaters' words are essential and penetrating,
literati's expressions are sparse yet illustrious.
Now the new book you've composed,
exceeds ten thousand words,
too profuse and not succinct,
so readers cannot finish it;
its chapters are not few,
so transmitters cannot grasp it all.
You'll bear the name of a restless man,
criticized for excess as a flaw.
Simple language is easy to convey,
heavy texts are hard to obtain.
If jade is scarce and stones abound,
the plentiful aren't treasured;
if dragons are rare and fish numerous,
the scarce are inherently divine."
I reply:
There is truth in these words.
But few words may lack substance;
while florid writing isn't necessarily scant.
If useful to the world,
even a hundred chapters do no harm;
if not useful,
a single piece offers no benefit.
If all are useful,
then more is superior,
less is inferior.
Accumulating a thousand pieces of gold
compared to a hundred,
which makes one richer?
Indeed, abundant writing surpasses sparse,
as wealth exceeds poverty.
If the world has not a single volume,
and I have a hundred chapters;
if others have not a word,
and I have ten thousand sayings,
who then is the worthy one?
Now, they don't say what I say is wrong,
but claim it's too much;
not that the world dislikes goodness,
but that they cannot comprehend it.
This is precisely why my book cannot be abbreviated.
If houses are many,
the land cannot be small;
if households are numerous,
the registers cannot be few.
Now, false facts abound,
empty rhetoric is rampant,
to point out reality and establish what's right,
in arguments and debates,
how can one be brief and direct?
Hán Fēi's writings,
each argument distinct,
chapters numbered in tens,
words counted in myriads.
If the body is large,
the clothes cannot be tight;
if affairs are many,
the writing cannot be scant.
Many affairs require ample text,
as great waters host many fish.
The capital has abundant grain,
the king's market bustles with crowds.
Though my book is voluminous,
it discusses a hundred topics.
Consider ancient Tài Gōng Wàng,
or recent Dǒng Zhòngshū,
their transmitted works exceed a hundred chapters,
my book has barely passed a hundred,
yet they say it's too much,
probably because my status is lowly,
and readers cannot but criticize.
The river's waters surge mightily,
compared to many streams,
which is the greater?
The silkworm cocoon is thick and heavy,
weighed for the silk it produces,
which yields more?
I, Chōng, have repeatedly failed in official posts,
and merely write books to record my thoughts.
Some mockingly say:
"What is valued in great talent
is fitting into officialdom,
being accepted and one's counsel heeded,
achieving deeds and meritorious service,
hence considered lofty.
Now, you, sir, wander through life in distress,
repeatedly dismissed from office,
your talent unrefined in practical affairs,
your strength not fully applied in duties,
so you merely dwell in secluded thoughts, composing texts,
writing down elegant words,
what benefit does it bring you?
With so many desires, what aim do you pursue?"
I reply:
No talent greater than Confucius's.
Yet Confucius's abilities were not tolerated,
he was driven away,
trees were cut down where he taught,
he had to rinse rice hastily to flee,
was besieged,
his traces erased,
stranded and hungry in Chén and Cài,
his disciples pale with hunger.
Now, my talent does not reach Confucius's,
the adversity of not fitting in,
is not equal to his,
yet how can it be lightly dismissed?
Moreover, the successful are not necessarily wise,
the impoverished not necessarily foolish.
Those who meet opportunity gain,
those who don't, lose.
Thus, with a fate of generous salary and good fortune,
even mediocrities rise to honor;
with a fate of meager pay and misfortune,
the extraordinary and brilliant fall into distress.
If one must judge talent and virtue by success,
then those ruling cities and enjoying fiefs,
would be deemed more talented and virtuous than Confucius
or Mòzǐ. If one is noble in status but base in name,
living purely but acting corruptly,
enjoying a salary of a thousand zhōng,
without a single virtue to boast,
that is truly mockable.
But if one has high virtue and a spotless name,
low office and modest pay,
it is no fault of ability,
nor should it be a burden.
A scholar would wish to share a hut with Yuán Xiàn,
not envy being in the same carriage with Duanmu Cì;
delight in traveling with Bó Yí,
not crave to walk alongside Zhí.
What the noble scholar values,
differs from the vulgar,
hence his reputation does not align with the world's.
Though his body decays with grass and trees,
his fame shines alongside the sun and moon;
his hardships compared to Confucius's,
his writings paired with Yáng Xióng's,
this I glory in.
To be successful in life yet lacking in wisdom,
high in rank but low in virtue,
for them it's glory,
for me, a burden.
Coincidental success and flattery,
high position and ease,
a hundred years later,
perish with all things,
not a trace of name passed on,
not a scrap of writing left behind,
though granaries of salary were amassed,
if literary virtue is not rich,
it is not what I praise.
Virtue deep and profound,
wisdom overflowing and abundant,
brush pouring like gathering rain,
words gushing like a spring,
rich in talent and ample in knowledge,
noble in conduct and lofty in ambition,
standing out in one's generation,
name transmitted for a thousand years,
this is what I call extraordinary.
Chōng came from a humble clan and solitary household.
Some mocked him, saying:
"Your ancestors laid no virtuous foundation,
left no legacy of literary works or texts.
Though you compose grand and magnificent discourses,
you have no heritage to stand upon,
and in the end, it will not be esteemed.
For when qi arrives abruptly without gradual accumulation, it is called an anomaly;
when things appear without belonging to any category, it is called an aberration;
what is uncommon and suddenly manifests is called a portent;
what defies the norm and stands out starkly is called a monstrosity.
What ancestors do you have?
Your forebears are unrecorded.
Moreover, you have never trodden the path of ink
nor emerged from the gate of Confucianism,
yet you spout theories numbering tens of millions of words.
This should be considered a portentous anomaly;
how can such writings be treasured and praised by many?"
He replied:
"Birds do not inherit phoenixhood through generations,
beasts do not pass down unicorn nature by lineage,
humans have no ancestral claim to sagehood or worthiness,
and objects lack perpetual excellence or rarity.
Great talent often meets with suppression,
a fate dictated by the times.
Just as rare gems emerge in isolation,
and unique objects are produced alone.
If literary talent always required models from worthies,
then sweet springs would have ancient sources,
and fine grain would sprout from old roots.
Extraordinary individuals appear,
and unparalleled writings are born,
their measures incompatible with vulgar customs,
beyond the assessment of mediocre rulers.
Thus, rarely seen traces
are recorded in archives;
scarcely emerging objects
are inscribed on bronze vessels.
The Five Emperors did not arise in a single era,
Yī Yǐn and Lǚ Wàng came from different families.
A thousand li apart, their paths diverged;
a hundred years separated, their emergences varied.
Scholars value refined talent and cautious advancement,
not relying on high status for renown.
A black cow may bear a red calf—
it does not harm its sacrificial worth;
muddy ancestry may yield pure descendants—
it does not hinder extraordinary individuals.
Gǔn was wicked, yet Yǔ was sage;
the old man was stubborn, yet Shùn was divine.
Bó Niú lay ill,
yet Zhòng Gōng was pure and whole.
Yán Lù was ordinary and dull,
yet Huí was outstanding and peerless.
The ancestors of Confucius and Mòzǐ were foolish,
yet Qiū and Dí became sages and worthies.
The Yáng family was unaccomplished,
yet exceptionally produced Zǐyún;
the Huán clan was ordinary,
yet gave rise to Jūnshān.
Receiving endowment from the primordial source,
thus I am able to compose writings.
In the third year of Yuánhé, Chōng moved his household to escape calamity,
traveling to Dānyáng,
Jiǔjiāng,
and Lújiāng in the Yángzhōu region.
Later, he served as a junior official,
with small talent bearing great responsibility,
his duty involving criticism and judgment,
so his literary reflections
languished over the years.
In the second year of Zhānghé,
he left office and resided at home.
Approaching seventy years of age,
it was time to hang up the carriage.
The path of officialdom blocked,
his aspirations thwarted and helpless.
Affairs have their successes and failures,
the body its gains and losses.
Hair white, teeth fallen,
sun and moon swiftly passing,
companions increasingly scarce,
with little left to rely on.
Poor, without means of support,
his heart finds no joy.
The years slowly advance,
reaching the border of Gēngxīn,
though fearing the end approaches,
my foolish heart still surges,
thus I composed the book 'Nurturing Nature' in sixteen chapters.
Cultivating qì through self-restraint,
moderating food and drink,
closing eyes and blocking ears,
cherishing essence to preserve health,
supplemented by medicine and guidance exercises,
hoping life might be prolonged,
and aging briefly delayed.
Since twilight permits no return,
I leave this book for posterity.
Human life and fate
have their allotted span;
humans too are creatures like insects,
born and dying in a single moment.
When the calendar of years concludes,
who can make it remain?
We descend to the Yellow Springs,
dissolving into earth and ashes.
From high antiquity—Huángdì
and Táng Yáo—down to Qín
and Hàn times,
I've judged all by the sage's way,
analyzed principles with comprehensive talent,
balanced as a scale,
clear as a mirror's reflection.
Youth and age, life and death, past and present—
none have escaped my detailed embrace.
But life cannot be extended;
alas, a sigh of sorrow!"
